b_acropolis_barricade.lead: When Xerxes' army reached Athens in 480 BCE, most Athenians had left for Salamis, Aegina and Troezen. A few who stayed, some too poor to leave, blocked the way up to the Acropolis with doors and timbers, believing this was the wooden wall of the oracle. Herodotus tells how the Persians burned it with fire arrows and then took and burned the citadel.
b_acropolis_barricade.play: The Wooden Barricade stands on a level's map as a historic structure that the player does not build. The game's note follows Herodotus's account of the doors, timbers and burning arrows.
b_acropolis_barricade.s0: Herodotus says that before the invasion the Pythia at Delphi told the Athenians that only a wooden wall would stay unsacked. Some older Athenians thought this meant the Acropolis, which he says had once been fenced with a thorn hedge. Themistocles argued that it meant the fleet, and the Athenians decided to meet the invader with their ships.
b_acropolis_barricade.s1: According to Herodotus, the Persians found the city empty except for a few people in the sanctuary: the temple treasurers and some poor men. They fenced the Acropolis with doors and planks, partly because they could not afford to go to Salamis and partly because they believed they had found the true meaning of the oracle. He dates the capture to the archonship of Calliades.
b_acropolis_barricade.s2: Herodotus says the Persians held the Areopagus hill opposite and shot arrows wrapped in burning tow at the barricade until it caught fire. The defenders still held out, rolling stones on the attackers and refusing terms offered through the exiled Pisistratids. Some Persians finally climbed an unguarded steep face near the shrine of Aglaurus, killed the defenders, and plundered and burned the sanctuary.
b_acropolis_barricade.s3: An inscription found at Troezen and published in 1960 presents itself as Themistocles' decree for evacuating Athens. It says the treasurers and priestesses were to stay on the Acropolis to guard the gods' property. The stone was cut in the early third century, long after 480 BCE, and its timing of the evacuation does not match Herodotus. Historians still argue whether it preserves a genuine decree or a later reconstruction.
b_acropolis_barricade.s4: Nothing of the timber barricade survives. Excavations on the Acropolis in the 1880s uncovered deep fills of burned and broken sculpture, pottery and building stone. These are traditionally linked to the Persian sack and the later clearing of the site, though archaeologists debate how much of the fill dates from 480 BCE. Damaged statues from these deposits are now displayed in the Acropolis Museum.
b_acropolis_shrines.lead: Before 480 BCE the Athenian Acropolis was crowded with altars, small shrines and hundreds of offerings: marble maidens, horsemen, bronzes and inscribed bases set up by families and officials. When Xerxes' army took the rock, it looted and burned the sanctuary. The broken statues later buried by the Athenians are now among the best surviving works of Archaic Greek sculpture.
b_acropolis_shrines.play: The Altars and Statues stand on a level's map as a historic structure that the player does not build. The game's description follows Herodotus 8.53 on the Persian plunder and burning of the rock.
b_acropolis_shrines.s0: Excavation shows that in the 6th and early 5th centuries Athenians filled the open ground between the temples with dedications to Athena. Many were marble korai and riders, and others were bronze figures and vessels. Hundreds of inscribed bases survive, naming potters, officials and wealthy families who gave the goddess a tenth of their profits or a first-fruits offering.
b_acropolis_shrines.s1: Herodotus says that Persian soldiers climbed the unguarded steep face near the shrine of Aglaurus. Some defenders leapt from the wall to their deaths, and the Persians killed those who had taken refuge in the temple, then plundered the sanctuary and set fire to the whole Acropolis. Xerxes next ordered Athenian exiles in his train to sacrifice there in their own way.
b_acropolis_shrines.s2: After the war the Athenians cleared the wreckage and buried broken statues and burnt architecture in the fill of new terraces. Excavators uncovered these deposits between 1885 and 1890 and found korai with their paint still visible. Burnt column drums and pieces of entablature were also built into the north wall of the Acropolis, where they can still be seen.
b_acropolis_shrines.s3: Archaeologists call the deposits the Persian debris, but not all of it was buried at once, and some fill may date to building works decades later. Athens was also occupied a second time, in 479 BCE, when Herodotus says Mardonius burned whatever still stood. Historians still argue over whether certain statues, such as the Kritios Boy, were made before or after 480 BCE.
b_acropolis_shrines.s4: In the 4th century Athenians claimed that the Greeks had sworn, before Plataea, to leave the burned sanctuaries in ruins as a memorial. The orator Lycurgus quotes the oath and the historian Diodorus repeats it. Theopompus, however, called the oath an Athenian fabrication, and a 4th-century inscribed copy found at Acharnae lacks the clause on temples. Scholars remain divided, though the long gap before new temples rose on the Acropolis fits the story.
b_apis_vault.lead: The Apis was a living bull kept at Memphis and honoured as the herald of the god Ptah. When one died it was embalmed and laid in a stone sarcophagus in galleries cut into the desert edge at Saqqara, known since Ptolemaic times as the Serapeum. An Apis was buried under Cambyses in 524 BCE, and the Egyptian record of that burial casts doubt on the Greek story that the Persian king killed the god.
b_apis_vault.play: The vault is raised in stages from limestone, Elephantine granite and timber for sledges and rollers. In reality each sarcophagus was one granite box with a separate lid, not a set of parts.
b_apis_vault.s0: Herodotus says the Apis was a calf born to a cow that could bear no other. He says priests knew it by its markings: a black hide, a white mark on the forehead, an eagle-like shape on the back, doubled tail hairs and a beetle-shaped mark under the tongue. Its appearance set off public feasting in Egypt, and he notes that the Greeks called it Epaphus.
b_apis_vault.s1: Auguste Mariette uncovered the vaults in 1850 and 1851. The older Lesser Vaults go back to the reign of Ramesses II, while the Greater Vaults were begun under Psamtik I in the 7th century. Long corridors open onto side chambers, many holding sarcophagi of granite and other hard stone weighing many tonnes. Hundreds of stelae left by priests and visitors record burials and dates.
b_apis_vault.s2: A stela from the vaults records the burial of an Apis in year 6 of Cambyses, that is 524 BCE, and shows the king kneeling before the bull as a pharaoh. A granite sarcophagus carries an inscription naming Cambyses as the one who made it for the god. These texts present the Persian ruler as a pious Egyptian king carrying out the proper rites.
b_apis_vault.s3: Herodotus tells that Cambyses, returning from a failed campaign against the Ethiopians, found Memphis celebrating a new Apis and took it as mockery of his defeat. He says the king had the priests flogged and stabbed the bull in the thigh, and that it wasted away and was buried by the priests in secret. The Egyptians, he reports, said this crime drove Cambyses mad.
b_apis_vault.s4: Most historians think the stela and sarcophagus tell against the killing, since the bull of 524 BCE was buried with royal honours. Some have proposed that the wounded bull was its successor, but that Apis, born under Cambyses, lived until year 4 of Darius, in 518 BCE. Many see the tale as hostile priestly memory, perhaps sharpened by Cambyses' cuts to temple incomes recorded in a later Demotic text.
b_archery_range.lead: The bow was the chief weapon of the Persian foot soldier. Greek writers say Persian boys learned to shoot from childhood, and Darius called himself a good bowman in his tomb inscription. No purpose-built Achaemenid range has been excavated, so practice probably took place on open ground near towns, estates and camps.
b_archery_range.play: The Archery Range trains archers who outrange raiders but must stay behind spearmen. This simplifies history: many Persian infantrymen carried both bow and spear, and the game splits them into separate troop types.
b_archery_range.s0: In his tomb inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam, Darius lists his own skills and says he was a good bowman both on foot and on horseback. On the Behistun relief he holds a bow as he faces the captive rebel kings. The royal gold and silver coins first struck under Darius show the king holding or drawing a bow, which suggests the bow stood for royal strength as well as for war.
b_archery_range.s1: Herodotus says Persian boys were taught three things from the age of five to twenty: to ride, to shoot with the bow, and to speak the truth. Strabo gives a later and fuller picture of Persian youths trained in groups to shoot, throw the javelin and endure hardship. Xenophon's Cyropaedia describes a similar schooling, but it is an idealised work and cannot be taken as a plain description.
b_archery_range.s2: Excavators of the Treasury at Persepolis found large numbers of arrowheads among the weapons stored there. At Thermopylae, Spyridon Marinatos's dig on the Kolonos hill in 1939 recovered many arrowheads, including three-bladed bronze types common in the Persian world. The finds fit Herodotus's account of the last defenders being overwhelmed by missiles on that hill.
b_archery_range.s3: Herodotus says Xerxes' Persians carried wicker shields, short spears, large bows with reed arrows and daggers, and at Plataea they fought behind a wall of planted wicker shields. The glazed-brick guards from Susa hold both spear and bow. Historians still argue whether front ranks held shields and spears while rear ranks shot, or whether most men used both weapons in turn.
b_archery_range.s4: Herodotus tells that before Thermopylae a man from Trachis warned that the Persian archers would hide the sun with their arrows. The Spartan Dieneces replied that this was good news, since they would then fight in the shade. The story is a Greek saying about courage and shows how Greeks remembered Persian archery, not a measure of it.
b_armoury.lead: The Persian army fought mainly with the bow, the short spear and the wicker shield, and these had to be made and stored in great numbers. Excavated weapon stores, temple archives and Greek descriptions show that arms came from royal stores, from temple and craft workshops, and from soldiers who equipped themselves.
b_armoury.play: The Armoury turns timber into spears, shields and bows, and carts take them to the barracks. This simplifies history: real arms also needed bronze, iron, horn and sinew, and many soldiers brought their own.
b_armoury.s0: Excavators at Persepolis in the 1930s found large numbers of weapons in the Treasury building, among them bronze and iron arrowheads, spearheads and other fittings. The finds show that the King kept stocks of arms at his residences alongside precious goods. They reflect the building as it stood when it was burned in 330, during Alexander's occupation, so they date mostly from well after Darius and Xerxes.
b_armoury.s1: Cuneiform texts from the Eanna temple at Uruk, from the sixth century and including the reigns of Cyrus and Cambyses, show the temple organising craftsmen to make bows and arrows and sending them for royal service. Arms production was therefore spread across the empire's existing institutions, not confined to one royal workshop. The temple carried this work as part of its obligations to the King.
b_armoury.s2: Herodotus, listing Xerxes' army in 480 BCE, says the Persians wore soft felt caps, sleeved tunics with iron scale armour, and trousers. He says they carried wicker shields, short spears, large bows with cane arrows, and daggers hung at the right thigh. On this description, most of the gear was wood, cane and wicker, with metal for points, blades and armour scales.
b_armoury.s3: Herodotus says that at Plataea in 479 BCE the Persians were as brave and strong as the Greeks but lacked heavy armour and skill, and so lost in close fighting. He also says the cavalry commander Masistius wore a golden scale corselet under his purple tunic, which turned Greek blows until he was struck in the eye. Greek writers may have stressed the contrast to praise their own hoplites.
b_armoury.s4: Babylonian documents, especially the Murashu archive of the later fifth century, show plots called bow land, horse land and chariot land whose holders owed armed service or its cost. Historians debate how far this system already worked in Darius's time and how much the army relied on it rather than on royal arsenals. Most agree both existed side by side.
b_athena_temple.lead: The Old Temple was the main temple of Athena Polias, guardian of Athens. It stood on the Acropolis between the sites of the later Parthenon and Erechtheion and probably housed the ancient olive-wood image of the goddess. When Xerxes' army took the Acropolis in 480 BCE the sanctuary was plundered and burned, and its ruin became one of the lasting Greek memories of the Persian invasion.
b_athena_temple.play: The Old Temple stands on a level's map as a historic building that the player cannot build. The game's note that the Persians burned it in 480 BCE follows Herodotus 8.53.
b_athena_temple.s0: Wilhelm Dörpfeld identified its limestone foundations in 1885, just south of the Erechtheion. They belong to a Doric temple with columns on all four sides. It was probably built about 525-500 BCE, perhaps under the sons of Pisistratus or soon after the reforms of 508 BCE. Parts of its marble pediment survive, showing Athena fighting the giants, and are now in the Acropolis Museum.
b_athena_temple.s1: Historians disagree about what stood here earlier. Some place a temple of about 570-560 BCE on these foundations, decorated with limestone sculpture such as the three-bodied monster nicknamed Bluebeard. Others put that early building under the later Parthenon. Herodotus says a priestess stopped the Spartan king Cleomenes at the doors of the goddess's shrine in 508 BCE, so a temple of Athena stood on the rock by then, though he does not say which building it was.
b_athena_temple.s2: Herodotus says most Athenians left the city, but temple treasurers and poor citizens held the Acropolis behind a wooden barricade. The Persians climbed the steep side near the shrine of Aglaurus, killed the defenders and suppliants, plundered the sanctuary and burned the whole Acropolis. He adds that Xerxes sent a rider to Susa with the news. No Persian text that survives mentions the event.
b_athena_temple.s3: Excavations on the Acropolis in 1885-1890 found burned sculpture, offerings and building pieces buried in fill laid down when the Athenians levelled the rock after the war. This deposit is called the Persian debris, though some of it may have been buried later. Blocks from the Old Temple and column drums from the unfinished Older Parthenon were built into the north wall of the Acropolis, where they can still be seen.
b_athena_temple.s4: Historians still argue over whether the burned temple was patched up. Some think its western rooms were repaired as a treasury, and that the old temple of Athena which Xenophon says caught fire in 406 BCE was this building. Others think it was cleared soon after 480 BCE. Lycurgus and Diodorus report an oath sworn before Plataea not to rebuild temples burned by the barbarians, but its authenticity was doubted in antiquity and still is.
b_athens_house.lead: In 480 BCE, as Xerxes' army marched south after Thermopylae, the Athenians abandoned their city and carried their families across the water to Troezen, Aegina and Salamis. The houses of the lower town stood empty when the Persians arrived, and most were wrecked when Mardonius burned Athens again in 479 BCE. The evacuation kept the Athenian people and fleet intact for the battle of Salamis.
b_athens_house.play: The Empty House stands on a level's map as a historic structure that the player does not build. Its note recalls the families sent to Salamis, Troezen and Aegina, following Herodotus 8.41.
b_athens_house.s0: Herodotus says the Athenian fleet put in at Salamis after Artemisium. A proclamation then told each household to save its children and servants as best it could. Most families went to Troezen, some to Aegina and some to Salamis. He adds that the priestess reported that the sacred snake of the Acropolis had left its honey cake untouched, and the Athenians took this as a sign that Athena too had left the city.
b_athens_house.s1: Herodotus says Xerxes' army entered a deserted Athens. Only a few temple treasurers and poor citizens remained, holding the Acropolis behind a wooden barricade. The Persians climbed the steep face near the shrine of Aglaurus, killed the defenders and burned the sanctuary. The empty houses below were probably plundered and partly burned at the same time.
b_athens_house.s2: An inscription found at Troezen in 1959 claims to record the Athenian vote, moved by Themistocles, to send women and children to Troezen and the old men and movable property to Salamis. The stone was cut in the third century, about two hundred years later. Historians still argue whether it preserves a genuine decree or a later patriotic version. It also sets the decision before the fleet sailed for Artemisium, while Herodotus puts the evacuation after that battle.
b_athens_house.s3: In 479 BCE Mardonius reoccupied Athens, which Herodotus says he again found empty. Before he withdrew to Boeotia, he burned the city and pulled down whatever wall, house or temple still stood. Thucydides says that when the Athenians came home, only short stretches of the circuit wall remained. Most houses had fallen, except a few in which Persian nobles had lodged.
b_athens_house.s4: Excavations in the Athenian Agora have found wells and pits filled with broken pottery, roof tiles and rubble, which T. L. Shear Jr. linked to clearing up after the Persian sacks. Houses of this time were probably mostly mud brick on stone footings, so they collapsed easily once their roofs burned. The deposits are widely used to date pottery, though some scholars question whether all of them belong to 480-479 BCE.
b_athos_canal.lead: Xerxes' Canal was a channel cut across the narrow neck of the Athos peninsula so that the royal fleet could avoid the dangerous cape where a Persian fleet had been wrecked in 492 BCE. Herodotus describes the work in detail, and modern surveys have confirmed that the canal really existed. It shows how far the King could reach in moving labour, food and skill from across the empire.
b_athos_canal.play: The canal is laid across the neck of land with each end on water, using barley for the diggers, limestone for the moles and timber for ladders and baskets. Herodotus's moles were heaped earth, so the limestone is the game's departure.
b_athos_canal.s0: Herodotus says that in 492 BCE a fleet under Mardonius was caught by a storm while rounding Mount Athos and driven onto the rocks. He puts the losses at about 300 ships and more than 20,000 men, figures historians treat with caution. He links the canal directly to this disaster and says preparations for the Athos work took about three years.
b_athos_canal.s1: Herodotus says men from every part of the army were sent to dig in relays, driven by the whip, under the direction of Bubares and Artachaees. The line was marked out by the town of Sane and divided among the peoples. Diggers at the bottom passed soil up to men on steps above. Only the Phoenicians, he says, made the trench wider at the top so its sides did not collapse, and a market nearby sold grain and flour shipped from Asia.
b_athos_canal.s2: Herodotus says the canal was wide enough for two triremes to be rowed side by side and that moles were heaped up at its mouths against the surf. The fleet sailed through in 480 BCE on its way west. Thucydides later mentions the King's canal as a landmark of the region. Herodotus also records that Artachaees died at nearby Acanthus and was buried with honour by the army.
b_athos_canal.s3: A British and Greek team surveyed the isthmus between 1991 and 2001 using geophysics, boreholes and sediment cores. They traced a filled-in channel running across the neck of land, roughly two kilometres long, along the line Herodotus describes. Its silted course is no longer open water, but the work settled the old question of whether the canal had existed at all.
b_athos_canal.s4: Herodotus judged the canal an act of pride, since ships could have been hauled across the isthmus on land. Many modern historians see practical reasons: a safe passage for a large fleet, and a way to keep fleet and army moving together. Others stress its message to the Greek cities about royal power. Some Roman writers, such as Juvenal, mocked the story as a Greek lie, a doubt the surveys have answered.
b_athos_canal.s5: Plutarch, writing some six centuries later, tells that Xerxes wrote a letter to Mount Athos threatening to cut it down and throw it into the sea if it hindered his work. The story belongs with Greek tales of the King's arrogance, such as the whipping of the Hellespont. It is a moral lesson about anger rather than a record of events.
b_athos_depot.lead: Before Xerxes invaded Greece in 480 BCE, his officials laid up food for the army at chosen points on the Thracian coast and in Macedonia. Herodotus names the sites. The depots let a very large force march through poor country without starving, and they show how far ahead the Persian administration could plan.
b_athos_depot.play: The game's depot is filled by carts bringing barley from the granaries, four to a load, and its stores feed only the army. Herodotus (7.25) says the food came by ship from across Asia, so the cart supply is a simplification.
b_athos_depot.s0: Herodotus says that while the Athos canal was being dug, Xerxes had provisions gathered so that neither the army nor its pack animals would go hungry on the march. The sites were chosen after inquiry, and the food was shipped from all parts of Asia in merchant ships and transports. The largest store was at Leuke Akte in Thrace, and others were at Tyrodiza near Perinthus, at Doriscus, at Eion on the Strymon and in Macedonia.
b_athos_depot.s1: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, written between about 509 and 493 BCE, record barley, flour, wine and beer issued day by day to workers, officials and travellers who carried sealed authorisations. They show storehouses, suppliers and accountants working on a large scale. The tablets say nothing about the Greek campaign, but they show the kind of administration that could stock depots in Thrace.
b_athos_depot.s2: Herodotus says the towns on the route also had to feed the army and lay on a dinner for the King, gathering grain and livestock for months beforehand. He reports that Antipater of Thasos spent 400 talents of silver feeding the host on behalf of the Thasian towns on the mainland. He adds a joke by Megacreon of Abdera, who told his people to thank the gods that Xerxes ate only once a day.
b_athos_depot.s3: Herodotus puts the whole force, with servants and crews, at over five million people, and reckons that at one choenix of wheat a head it ate more than 110,000 medimni a day. Historians reject these figures as greatly exaggerated. The limits of supply by depot and ship are a main argument for a much smaller force. Many modern estimates put the land army at perhaps 100,000 to 200,000, with the fleet's crews besides, but there is no agreement.
b_audience_hall.lead: The so-called Audience Hall, or Palace S, was one of the stone halls that Cyrus raised at Pasargadae, his new royal seat in Persis. A lofty central room of columns, opened by porticoes on every side, it set the pattern for the great columned halls later built by Darius and Xerxes at Susa and Persepolis.
b_audience_hall.play: In the Pasargadae level the hall rises stone by stone from limestone blocks and timber. That is broadly fair, but the real hall mixed white and dark stone, and 'audience hall' is a modern label, not an ancient one.
b_audience_hall.s0: Excavation by Ali Sami and later by David Stronach showed a rectangular main hall with two rows of four tall columns, once carrying a timber roof. Porticoes with lower columns ran along all four sides. The column shafts were of white limestone on bases of dark stone, and fragments suggest animal-headed capitals. The hall stood near the gatehouse known as Gate R and the residential Palace P, among gardens and water channels.
b_audience_hall.s1: The doorways carried carved reliefs, of which only the lower parts survive. They include a bull-man and a figure wrapped in a fish-skin cloak, both protective beings borrowed from the palace art of Assyria. They show that Cyrus's builders drew on older Mesopotamian royal imagery while working out a new Persian style.
b_audience_hall.s2: Tool marks on the stone, notably those of the toothed chisel, and the use of dovetail clamps to bind blocks point to craftsmen trained in Lydia and Ionia. Carl Nylander argued that western masons came east after Cyrus took Sardis in the 540s BCE. Most historians accept a strong Lydian and Ionian hand, though how many such workers came, and on what terms, is still debated.
b_audience_hall.s3: Short texts in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian on the palaces say, in substance, that the speaker is Cyrus the King, an Achaemenid (CMa). Darius later claimed to have created a written form of Persian (DB §70), so many scholars think these labels were added under Darius to link himself with Cyrus. Others hold that they were cut in Cyrus's own reign.
b_audience_hall.s4: No ancient text says how Palace S was used. Its open plan suggests a place for receiving subjects and envoys, which is why it is called an audience hall, but this is an inference. Stronach placed the start of building after the conquest of Lydia, in the 540s BCE. Palace P at least was left unfinished when Cyrus died in 530 BCE, and parts may have been completed under Darius.
b_barracks.lead: The Achaemenid kings kept soldiers in fortresses and garrison towns across the empire, fed from royal and provincial stores. Most men who fought for the King, however, did not live in barracks: they held land in return for service or were called up when a campaign was ordered. A building like the game's Barracks was therefore only a small part of how the Persian army was housed, fed and trained.
b_barracks.play: The game's Barracks has drill-masters train spearmen from households, supplied by carts of arms and barley. This simplifies history: no Persian building of this exact kind is attested, and most soldiers held service land and trained in youth.
b_barracks.s0: Herodotus says that Persians and their auxiliaries were stationed in the White Fort at Memphis and received 120,000 measures of grain from Egypt, on top of its silver tribute. He also tells how Artaphernes held the citadel of Sardis with a strong force when the Ionians burned the lower city in 498 BCE. Troops like these lived in fortified places and were fed by the province, the nearest Achaemenid parallel to a barracks.
b_barracks.s1: Babylonian documents show land granted in units called bow-land, horse-land and chariot-land, whose holders owed a soldier with his equipment when called. The system was in use by the early reign of Darius. The later Murashu archive shows such holdings grouped into units called hatru, which sometimes paid silver instead of serving. The soldier came from the household and the land, not from a barracks.
b_barracks.s2: Aramaic papyri from Elephantine, on Egypt's southern frontier, record a garrison of Judaean and Aramaean soldiers organised in detachments under commanders. They lived with their families in the town, owned houses, and drew rations from royal stores. Most of the papyri date from later in the 5th century, after the game's period, but they show how a frontier garrison worked in daily life.
b_barracks.s3: Herodotus says Persian boys were taught three things from the age of five to twenty: to ride, to shoot the bow and to tell the truth. Strabo, writing centuries later, describes groups of youths trained in hardship, running and archery under older men. Both describe training as part of growing up, not as drill in a barracks.
b_barracks.s4: Herodotus describes the Immortals, 10,000 picked Persian infantry kept always at full strength, and many historians accept a core of permanent royal troops. How large and professional that core was, and how much of any campaign army was a levy called up for the occasion, is still argued. Herodotus's totals for the whole army of Xerxes are widely held to be greatly exaggerated.
b_bazaar.lead: The word bazaar comes from Persian bāzār, Middle Persian wāzār, but the covered market halls it now suggests belong to much later centuries. Under the early Achaemenid kings, goods moved in two ways: through busy markets in old trading cities such as Babylon and Sardis, and through rations issued from royal stores in the Persian heartland. How the two fitted together shows how the empire fed its people.
b_bazaar.play: Buyers fetch goods from storage and a trader carries them door to door, serving about 15 houses. This is a simplification: no such rounds are known, and in Persis many workers drew rations from royal stores.
b_bazaar.s0: Herodotus tells that when a Spartan herald warned Cyrus not to harm the Greek cities, Cyrus scorned people who kept a place in the middle of their city where they met to cheat one another under oath. Herodotus explains that the Persians did not use markets and had no marketplace of their own. The story is a Greek view of Persian custom, set against the Greek agora.
b_bazaar.s1: Herodotus says the Lydians were the first people known to strike coins of gold and silver and the first retail traders, though the earliest Lydian coins were in fact electrum. He describes the marketplace of Sardis with the gold-bearing Pactolus flowing through it. There the trapped Lydians and Persians gathered to defend themselves when Ionians, Athenians and Eretrians burned the city in 498 BCE. Under Persian rule Sardis was the seat of the satrap of Lydia.
b_bazaar.s2: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, written in Elamite in the reign of Darius, record barley, wine, beer, flour, fruit and livestock issued from royal stores to workers, travellers and officials. Workers received monthly rations graded by rank, sex and age rather than buying food in a market. The later Treasury tablets show some wages paid partly in silver, reckoned against set amounts of sheep or wine.
b_bazaar.s3: Babylonian business archives tell a different story. The Egibi family of Babylon bought and sold dates, barley and houses, lent silver and rented out property. The later Murashu firm of Nippur managed land and leased it for rent in produce and silver. Weighed silver served as money and prices moved with supply, so markets were part of everyday life in the province.
b_bazaar.s4: Historians still debate how much of the empire's economy ran through markets and how much through royal and temple redistribution. Some stress the Persepolis ration system and the King's control of stores. Others point to the Babylonian evidence for price-setting markets and the growing use of silver. Most now accept that both systems worked side by side, in proportions that differed from region to region.
b_bazaar.s5: Xenophon, writing about a century and a half after Cyrus, describes an ideal Persia in which a free square near the palace was kept clear of goods and traders so that their noise would not disturb the training of the young. The Cyropaedia is a moral and political romance, and this picture of Persian life is shaped to teach virtue rather than to record practice.
b_behistun.lead: The King's Relief is the monument Darius I had carved on the cliff of Bagastana, modern Bisotun in western Iran, above the road from Babylon to Ecbatana. A sculpted panel shows the King standing over the rebels he defeated in 522-521 BCE, and beside it runs his account in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. It is the longest royal inscription of the empire and Darius's own version of how he won the throne.
b_behistun.play: In the Bagastana level the relief is raised part by part against the rock above the road, with limestone for each part and timber for scaffolds every third part. The game dates it 521 BCE; the carving probably began about 520 BCE and was extended later.
b_behistun.s0: The relief sits some 60 metres up the cliff, and Darius, larger than the other figures, rests his foot on the fallen magus Gaumata. He raises a hand towards a winged figure in a disc, while two attendants with bow and spear stand behind him. Before him eight rebel kings wait, bound at the hands and roped together by the neck. A ninth figure, Skunkha the Saka in his pointed cap, was squeezed in at the end of the line after a later campaign.
b_behistun.s1: Darius says that Cambyses secretly killed his brother Bardiya, and that in 522 BCE the magus Gaumata claimed to be Bardiya and took the kingship. Darius and six helpers killed him in Media (DB §§10-13, §68). Revolts then broke out in Elam, Babylon, Media, Persis, Margiana and elsewhere, and Darius claims nineteen battles and nine captured kings within one year (DB §52). A fifth column, added later, tells of campaigns against Elam and the Saka.
b_behistun.s2: The text was probably carved first in Elamite, then in Babylonian, with the Old Persian added last; when Skunkha was inserted, part of the first Elamite text was cut away and a second Elamite copy was made. In DB §70 Darius says he made the inscription in a new way, in Aryan, and sent it to every land, which many scholars read as the creation of the Old Persian script. A Babylonian copy survives in fragments from Babylon, and an Aramaic version on papyrus from Elephantine.
b_behistun.s3: Herodotus tells a similar story, calling the false king Smerdis and listing seven conspirators, though one of his names, Aspathines, differs from the Ardumanish named by Darius. Both versions may go back to the same court tradition, so nothing independent confirms the impostor tale. Some historians think Darius killed the real Bardiya and invented the magus to justify taking the throne, while others accept the King's account. The question remains open.
b_behistun.s4: Some Greek writers credited the relief to someone other than Darius. Ctesias, as used by Diodorus, said the Assyrian queen Semiramis laid out a park at Bagistanon and had her own image carved on the cliff with an inscription in Syrian letters. The story belongs to the tales told about Semiramis and has nothing to do with the real monument, which names Darius throughout.
b_boatyard.lead: For his campaign against the Scythians, Darius ordered the Greek cities of Ionia and the Hellespont to sail their fleet up the Ister (the Danube) and bridge it. Their shipwrights and crews built the crossing and guarded it, and Herodotus makes the King's safe return depend on their loyalty. The episode shows how the Persian kings drew on the skills of subject peoples for great works.
b_boatyard.play: The game shows shipwrights framing new boats on a riverside slipway from woodcutters' timber. Herodotus says the Ionians sailed their own fleet upriver, and historians think those ships probably formed the bridge, so this is a simplification.
b_boatyard.s0: Herodotus says Darius ordered the Ionians, Aeolians and Hellespontine Greeks to sail through the Black Sea to the Ister. They went two days upstream from the sea and bridged the river where its mouths divide. He reports a fleet of 600 ships for the campaign, a figure many historians think too high.
b_boatyard.s1: Herodotus never describes how the Ister bridge was built. He says Darius later told the Ionians to break it and follow him by land with their crews. For that reason most historians think the bridge was a line of the fleet's own ships lashed together, as Xerxes' Hellespont bridges later were. Whether new boats were also built on the spot is unknown.
b_boatyard.s2: Excavated wrecks from the Mediterranean show that hulls of this period were built shell first. Shipwrights joined the planks edge to edge, with mortise-and-tenon joints or, in some older Greek hulls, by sewing, and added the frames afterwards. The work needed seasoned timber, skilled carpenters and time, which makes it likely that an existing fleet was used.
b_boatyard.s3: Herodotus says Darius gave the Ionians a thong tied with sixty knots and told them to untie one each day and sail home if he had not returned when all were undone. When the Scythians urged them to break the bridge, he reports that Miltiades of Athens agreed but Histiaeus of Miletus persuaded the tyrants to keep it, and only the Scythian end was dismantled.
b_boatyard.s4: A later Aramaic letter from Elephantine, dated 412 BCE, records the satrap Arsames ordering the repair of a boat and lists the planks, nails and other materials by number. It comes long after Darius, but it shows how closely Persian officials tracked the materials used on vessels.
b_boatyard_phoenician_shipyard.lead: The Phoenician cities of the Levant coast, above all Sidon, Tyre and Arwad, supplied the core of the Persian navy from Cambyses to Xerxes. Their shipwrights and crews built and sailed the triremes that carried armies to Egypt, fought the Ionians at Lade and crossed to Greece. Their merchant ships also traded under the King's rule, and in Egypt they paid duties to his customs officers.
b_boatyard_phoenician_shipyard.play: In the game the yard builds triremes beside water and sends marines to the host. Historically the King's warships came from the Phoenician cities, Cyprus, Cilicia and Egypt, not from yards at Sardis or in Greece.
b_boatyard_phoenician_shipyard.s0: Herodotus says that the whole of Cambyses' fleet depended on the Phoenicians, who refused to sail against Carthage, their own colony. For Xerxes' fleet of 480 BCE he counts 300 ships from the Phoenicians and the Syrians of Palestine, the largest contingent, under kings of Sidon, Tyre and Arwad. He ranks the Phoenician ships as the best sailers and the Sidonian as the best of those. He says Xerxes reviewed the fleet at Doriscus from a Sidonian ship.
b_boatyard_phoenician_shipyard.s1: A customs account of about 475 BCE, written in Aramaic, survives from Elephantine. It was later erased so the scroll could be reused for the story of Ahiqar. It lists Ionian and Phoenician ships entering Egypt over most of one year, and the duties the King's officials took from their cargoes. It shows Phoenician merchant shipping working within the royal tax system under Xerxes.
b_boatyard_phoenician_shipyard.s2: Herodotus says that at the Athos canal only the Phoenicians dug their stretch wider at the top than at the bottom, so its sides did not fall in. For the Hellespont bridges the Phoenicians made cables of white flax and the Egyptians cables of papyrus. After Salamis, he says, Xerxes had some Phoenician captains beheaded when they blamed the Ionians for their losses.
b_boatyard_phoenician_shipyard.s3: Thucydides credits the Corinthians with the first Greek triremes. Herodotus says the pharaoh Necho built triremes for both the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. Some historians think the type began in Phoenicia. Others argue it spread widely only in the later sixth century, partly because Persian kings paid for large fleets. Herodotus gives 1,207 triremes in 480 BCE, and Aeschylus gives a similar figure, but many historians think the number too high.
b_boatyard_phoenician_shipyard.s4: Herodotus reports a story that Xerxes sailed home from Eion on a Phoenician ship and met a storm. When the helmsman said the ship was too heavy, Persian courtiers leapt into the sea to save the King. Xerxes then rewarded the helmsman with a gold crown and beheaded him for the Persian lives lost. Herodotus says he does not believe it and that Xerxes went home by land.
b_brewery.lead: Beer was the everyday drink of Egypt, brewed from barley and emmer wheat in households, temples and estates for thousands of years before the Persians arrived. It was food as much as drink. Rations for workers and officials were counted in loaves and jugs of beer, and the Persian conquerors found a brewing system already old when they took Memphis in 525 BCE.
b_brewery.play: Breweries take barley from granaries and supply beer to Noble Residences, only in the Memphis level. The game's bread-and-jar method is the older textbook picture; residue studies suggest malted grain was also used, and emmer as well as barley.
b_brewery.s0: Egyptian tombs show brewing from the Old Kingdom onward. Painted and carved scenes, and wooden models placed in burials, show workers grinding grain, shaping and baking loaves, mashing them in vats and pouring the liquid into jars. A well-known model of a combined bakery and brewery comes from the Middle Kingdom tomb of the official Meketre at Thebes and survives today.
b_brewery.s1: Scholars long held that Egyptian beer was made by crumbling half-baked bread into water and letting it ferment. Microscope study of residues in brewing vessels from Amarna and Deir el-Medina found instead a mix of malted grain and cooked grain, with no clear sign of bread. Many now think methods varied, and that the bread scenes may show only part of the process.
b_brewery.s2: Herodotus, who says he visited Egypt, probably in the mid-fifth century, about two generations after the Persian conquest, reports that the Egyptians drank a wine made from barley because the country had no vines. The drink he means is beer. His reason is wrong, since Egypt grew grapes and made wine for the elite, but his note shows how ordinary beer drinking looked to a Greek visitor.
b_brewery.s3: Across Egyptian history, labour was paid largely in bread and beer, and ration records from workers' villages such as Deir el-Medina list both. The Persian administration ran a similar system in its own heartland. The Persepolis Fortification tablets, written in Elamite in the reign of Darius, record issues of grain, wine and beer to workers, travellers and officials.
b_brewery.s4: An Egyptian myth, written in New Kingdom royal tombs, tells how the sun god Ra sent his fierce Eye, the goddess Hathor in the form of the lioness Sekhmet, to destroy rebellious humans. To stop the slaughter he had beer dyed red with ochre and poured over the fields. Thinking it was blood, the goddess drank it, grew drunk and calm, and spared mankind.
b_brick_kiln.lead: The walls of Darius's palace at Susa were faced with moulded bricks glazed in bright colours, showing guards, lions, bulls and winged creatures. Darius's own building charter says Babylonians moulded the baked brick. The craft had deep roots in Mesopotamia, where glazed relief brick had decorated Babylon's gates about two generations earlier. At Susa it became one of the clearest signs of an empire drawing on the skills of many peoples.
b_brick_kiln.play: The kiln turns clay-pit clay into glazed palace bricks made by Babylonians, as DSf says of the brick-moulders. In fact many Susa bricks had a sandy siliceous body rather than plain clay, and used more colours than blue, yellow and white.
b_brick_kiln.s0: In his foundation charter from Susa, Darius lists the materials of his palace and the peoples who worked them. He states that the men who moulded the baked brick were Babylonians, while the stone-cutters were Ionians and Sardians and the goldsmiths Medes and Egyptians. The text survives in Old Persian, Elamite and Akkadian versions, and a further Elamite charter, DSz, gives a similar account.
b_brick_kiln.s1: Glazed and moulded relief brick had a long history in Mesopotamia. Its best-known example is the Ishtar Gate and Processional Way of Babylon, built under Nebuchadnezzar II in the first half of the 500s BCE, with lions, bulls and dragons in coloured glaze. German excavators led by Robert Koldewey uncovered these remains between 1899 and 1917. Susa itself also had an older Elamite tradition of glazed brick, which Darius's builders could draw on alongside the Babylonian one.
b_brick_kiln.s2: French excavations, beginning with Marcel and Jane Dieulafoy in the 1880s, recovered thousands of glazed brick fragments from the palace. They show rows of guards carrying spears and bows, striding lions, winged bulls, griffins and sphinxes, many now reassembled in the Louvre. Analysis shows that many bricks had a sandy, quartz-rich body and that raised lines kept the colours apart in firing. No kiln for them has been securely identified in the published excavations.
b_brick_kiln.s3: The best-known panels show long lines of robed men holding spears, with bows and quivers on their backs. Some historians identify them with the royal guard that Herodotus calls the Immortals. Others see them as Persian nobles or as a symbol of the Persian people as the King's army. The modern reconstructions also combine bricks found in different places, so the original arrangement of the friezes is partly uncertain.
b_builders_yard.lead: Most buildings of the Achaemenid world were not cut stone but sun-dried mud brick laid on stone footings, with timber beams carrying flat roofs of packed earth. Crews of brickmakers, carpenters and labourers raised them, fed and paid from royal and local stores.
b_builders_yard.play: The game gathers builders in a yard that sends crews to every new site on its roads, while carts bring timber, stone and clay. This is a simplification: real crews were hired, rationed or levied by the job, not kept in one standing yard.
b_builders_yard.s0: Excavated houses, storerooms and palace wings at Pasargadae, Persepolis and Susa stood on footings of rubble or cut stone, with walls of sun-dried mud brick above. Brick kept the rooms cool in summer and warm in winter, but rain and rising damp wore it away, so a good stone base and a sound roof mattered most.
b_builders_yard.s1: Roofs were carried on wooden beams, and the long timbers of the great halls were brought from far away: Darius's Susa charter names cedar from Lebanon and yaka wood from Gandhara and Carmania. Ordinary buildings used poplar and other local wood, which also served for doors, ladders and the scaffolds the builders worked from.
b_builders_yard.s2: The Persepolis Fortification and Treasury tablets list work groups (kurtaš) by trade and by the rations or silver they drew, among them carpenters, brickmakers and plasterers. They show building as organised, paid work done by crews brought together for a job, men and women alike.
b_builders_yard.s3: Historians still argue over how many of these workers were hired craftsmen, how many were levied from their villages for a season, and how many were deportees settled near the royal works. The tablets record their pay and food, not their status, so the answer may have differed from crew to crew.
b_burial_ground.lead: Most people in the Persian empire buried their dead in the earth, in pits, jars or coffins, often with a few personal goods. Herodotus says the Persians coated the body in wax before burial, while the magi first left their dead to be torn by birds or dogs. Burial customs show both how Persians thought about death and how varied the King's many peoples remained.
b_burial_ground.play: Bearers carry the city's dead to the Burial Ground, and unburied dead sicken nearby houses. The wax and the magi follow Herodotus, though he names dogs as well as birds. The sickness rule is a game simplification.
b_burial_ground.s0: Herodotus says the Persians covered a corpse in wax and then buried it. He adds that it was said, as a half-secret matter, that a Persian body was not buried until a bird or dog had torn it, and he was certain that the magi did this. Elsewhere he says the Persians did not burn their dead, because they held fire to be a god, and it was not right to give a god a corpse.
b_burial_ground.s1: Excavations in Elam, Mesopotamia and Persis have found ordinary burials of the Achaemenid period in the ground, some in simple pits and others in pottery jars or coffins. At Susa in 1901, J. de Morgan's mission found a late Achaemenid burial in a bronze tub-shaped coffin with gold jewellery and coins. Such finds show that burial in the earth was common, though rich and plain graves differed greatly.
b_burial_ground.s2: Elamite tablets from the Persepolis Fortification archive record sheep issued for offerings at the šumar of members of the royal house, among them Cambyses and Darius's father Hystaspes. The word probably meant a tomb or memorial building. The tablets show that the King's administration paid for regular rites for the royal dead.
b_burial_ground.s3: Historians still argue how widely the exposure Herodotus describes was practised in Achaemenid times. The kings were laid in closed tombs: Cyrus in a stone house at Pasargadae, Darius and three successors in rock tombs at Naqsh-e Rostam. That suggests royal bodies were not left in the open. The towers for exposing the dead known from later Zoroastrian practice belong to much later centuries and should not be read back into this period.
b_burial_ground.s4: Arrian, drawing on Aristobulus, who was with Alexander, says the tomb of Cyrus bore an epitaph asking the passer-by not to grudge the founder of the empire his monument. Plutarch's version, written centuries later, has Cyrus ask not to be grudged the little earth that covered his body. No such text survives on the monument, and the versions were told as moral tales about the passing of power.
b_burial_ground_burial_mound.lead: Across Thrace and the northern Aegean, important men were buried under round mounds of heaped earth, often after feasting and funeral games. Herodotus describes the custom. He also tells how at Acanthus, near Athos, in 480 BCE Xerxes had the whole army raise a mound for Artachaees, the Persian who had overseen the canal.
b_burial_ground_burial_mound.play: In Athos the Burial Ground takes this form; bearers carry the dead to it, and unburied dead sicken nearby houses. The Thracian label fits Herodotus 5.8, but the sickness rule is a game mechanic, not a historical claim.
b_burial_ground_burial_mound.s0: Herodotus says that wealthy Thracians laid out the body for three days, sacrificed animals of every kind and feasted after mourning. The dead man was then burned or buried in the earth, a mound was heaped over him, and games of all sorts were held, with the largest prize given for single combat.
b_burial_ground_burial_mound.s1: Herodotus reports that Artachaees, an Achaemenid who supervised the digging of the Athos canal, died at Acanthus while Xerxes was there. The King gave him a splendid funeral and the whole army heaped up a mound over his grave. On an oracle's instruction, Herodotus adds, the Acanthians sacrificed to him as a hero.
b_burial_ground_burial_mound.s2: Thousands of tumuli survive across ancient Thrace, in what is now Bulgaria, northern Greece and European Turkey. Excavated mounds of the late sixth and fifth centuries, such as those at Duvanli near Plovdiv, held burials with weapons, gold ornaments and silver vessels, some in shapes copied from Achaemenid tableware. They show an elite that shared the habits Herodotus describes.
b_burial_ground_burial_mound.s3: Herodotus treats the Thracians as one people, yet lists tribes with different rites, such as those living north of the Crestonaeans, whose widows competed to die at the grave. Thucydides says the Athos towns were mixed and bilingual: Pelasgians, Bisaltians, Crestonaeans and Edonians beside a few Greeks. Herodotus does not call Artachaees' mound Thracian, so how far one custom held here is uncertain.
b_burial_ground_cemetery_by_the_road.lea: Greek cities usually buried their dead outside the settled area, along the roads leading out of town, so that anyone entering or leaving passed the graves of its families. At Athens the largest of these cemeteries lay in the Kerameikos. The wars with Persia in 490 and 480-479 BCE added another kind of grave: mounds raised for the fallen on the battlefields themselves.
b_burial_ground_cemetery_by_the_road.pla: The game shows roadside graves with stelae and mounds, served by bearers. Its rule that unburied dead sicken houses simplifies history: Greeks feared ritual pollution and dishonour more than disease, and many battle dead were buried on the field.
b_burial_ground_cemetery_by_the_road.s0: Excavations in the Kerameikos at Athens have uncovered graves lining the roads northwest of the city, in use from the early Iron Age onward. After 479 BCE these roads ran through the Dipylon and the Sacred Gate of the new city wall. Burial inside the settled area, including ground later used for the Agora, had probably largely ceased by about 700 BCE. Roadside cemeteries of the same pattern are known outside many other Greek towns.
b_burial_ground_cemetery_by_the_road.s1: Wealthy Attic families of the 6th century marked graves with tall carved stelae, painted reliefs of the dead, or marble kouroi. Surviving examples include the kouros of Kroisos from Anavyssos, about 530 BCE, and the stele of Aristion signed by Aristokles, about 510 BCE. Simpler graves had earth mounds, plain slabs or a pot set on top. Many markers carried a short verse naming the dead.
b_burial_ground_cemetery_by_the_road.s2: Plutarch says Solon limited the cost and noise of funerals at Athens. Cicero reports a later law that restricted the size of tombs and banned elaborate monuments. Historians argue over when that later law was passed. Some link it to the decline of lavish Attic grave markers around 500-480 BCE, while others think the change in taste had other causes.
b_burial_ground_cemetery_by_the_road.s3: Thucydides says the Athenians normally brought their war dead home to a public tomb in the city's finest suburb, usually identified as the Kerameikos. He adds that they buried the men of Marathon on the field to honour their courage. Herodotus describes the markers and epitaphs raised at Thermopylae and the separate graves dug at Plataea for Spartans, Tegeans, Athenians and others. Pausanias later saw the Marathon grave with stones listing the dead by tribe.
b_burial_ground_cemetery_by_the_road.s4: The Soros is a mound about 9 metres high on the plain of Marathon. Valerios Stais excavated it in 1890-1891 and found a layer of ash and burnt bone with Attic black-figure lekythoi of about 490 BCE. These finds support its identification as the tomb of the Athenian dead. Herodotus gives 192 Athenians killed against 6,400 on the Persian side, and historians still debate how reliable the Persian figure is.
b_burial_ground_cemetery_by_the_road.s5: Herodotus says it was reported that a Persian's body was not buried until birds or dogs had torn it, a practice he was certain the magi followed. He adds that other Persians coated the dead in wax before burial. Pausanias says the Athenians claimed to have buried the Persian dead at Marathon in a trench, though he could find no mound for them.
b_burial_ground_cemetery_by_the_road.s6: The Persian monuments themselves show that burial was practised at the highest level. Cyrus lies in a stone tomb at Pasargadae. Darius and his successors were placed in rock-cut tombs at Naqsh-e Rostam. These remains fit Herodotus's report of burial after the body had been treated, though they say nothing about the customs of ordinary Persians.
b_burial_ground_necropolis.lead: West of Memphis, on the dry plateau above the Nile flood, lay one of the largest burial grounds in Egypt, now known by names such as Saqqara and Abusir. For more than two thousand years before the Persian conquest, Memphites buried their dead there. Kings, priests, officials and the sacred Apis bulls were laid to rest on the same desert edge.
b_burial_ground_necropolis.play: In the Memphis level the Burial Ground appears as the Necropolis, where bearers carry the dead. Sickness from unburied dead is a game simplification, and the seventy days in natron follows Herodotus, though the drying probably took less.
b_burial_ground_necropolis.s0: Excavation shows that the Memphite cemeteries ran for many kilometres along the desert edge west of the city, from Giza through Abusir and Saqqara to Dahshur. The sand lay above the reach of the yearly flood and was too dry to farm, which is partly why burials were made there. At Saqqara, the Step Pyramid of Djoser stood among tombs from every later age, including many shaft tombs of the Saite period just before the Persians came.
b_burial_ground_necropolis.s1: Herodotus says that embalmers offered three grades of treatment at three prices. For the costliest, they drew out the brain with an iron hook, opened the flank with a sharp Ethiopian stone, and removed the organs. They then laid the body in natron and wrapped it in linen bands smeared with gum. He says cheaper methods used injections of cedar oil or a simple purge before the natron.
b_burial_ground_necropolis.s2: Herodotus says the body lay in natron for seventy days and no longer. Most Egyptologists read the seventy days as the length of the whole rite, from death to burial. They think the drying in natron itself probably took about forty days. The biblical account of Jacob's burial also separates forty days of embalming from seventy days of mourning by the Egyptians.
b_burial_ground_necropolis.s3: In 2018 excavators at Saqqara found an embalming workshop of the Saite and Persian periods, with vessels for oils and resins, beside burial shafts. Nearby at Abusir, Czech archaeologists cleared the great shaft tomb built for Udjahorresnet, the Egyptian official who served Cambyses and Darius. Carian and Aramaic funerary stones from Saqqara show that foreigners living in Memphis were buried there too.
b_burial_ground_necropolis.s4: The Apis bulls of Memphis were buried in great underground galleries at Saqqara, the Serapeum. An Apis died and was buried in Cambyses' sixth regnal year, about 524 BCE, and a stela from the burial shows Cambyses kneeling before the bull. Herodotus later told how Cambyses killed an Apis, a story this evidence does not support, though some scholars link his tale to the next bull.
b_burial_ground_royal_tumulus.lead: The kings of Lydia were buried under great earth mounds raised on stone foundations at Bin Tepe, a cemetery about 10 km north of Sardis. The largest, which Herodotus calls the tomb of Alyattes, father of Croesus, ranks among the biggest mounds in Anatolia. Lydian and Persian nobles kept building such tumuli after Cyrus took Sardis in about 546 BCE, so the mounds also show a local elite carrying on under Persian rule.
b_burial_ground_royal_tumulus.play: In Sardis the Burial Ground becomes a town-funded Royal Tumulus where bearers carry the dead. Herodotus credits traders, craftsmen and prostitutes, and the real royal mounds stood apart at Bin Tepe, not among the town's graves.
b_burial_ground_royal_tumulus.s0: Herodotus counted the tomb of Alyattes as the one great work in Lydia to rival those of Egypt and Babylon. He says it had a base of large stones with a mound of earth above, and that the market traders, craftsmen and prostitutes of Sardis raised it. Inscribed markers on top, he says, recorded each group's share, and the prostitutes' share was the largest. Strabo later describes the same mound near the Gygaean lake.
b_burial_ground_royal_tumulus.s1: Bin Tepe, Turkish for 'thousand mounds', lies across the Hermus plain from Sardis, beside the lake Herodotus calls Gygaean. The mound usually identified as Alyattes' tomb, Kocamutaf Tepe, is about 355 metres across. Tunnelling in 1854 reached a burial chamber of finely cut marble blocks, long since robbed. Excavators later found a stone retaining wall, or crepis, inside Karnıyarık Tepe.
b_burial_ground_royal_tumulus.s2: Survey and excavation suggest that many of the Bin Tepe and other Lydian tumuli were probably built after the Persian conquest, through the fifth and fourth centuries. Their chambers, couches and grave goods mix Lydian and Persian styles. Archaeologists read this as a sign that Lydian families and Persians settled in the satrapy both used the old royal form of burial to display rank.
b_burial_ground_royal_tumulus.s3: The names given to the big mounds rest on Herodotus and on scholars' inference, not on inscriptions naming the dead. Karnıyarık Tepe has been linked to Gyges because marks on its wall were read as his name, but the reading and the date are debated. Many historians also doubt the tale of prostitutes paying for the tomb, which fits Greek stories about Lydian luxury. Herodotus himself adds that common Lydian girls earned their dowries this way.
b_camp.lead: The palaces, terraces and tombs of the Achaemenid kings were cut and laid by large workforces of masons and labourers. They came from many lands and were fed from royal stores. Darius's own building texts and the clay tablets of Persepolis show these workers far more clearly than any Greek writer does.
b_camp.play: The game gathers masons in one camp that serves every site, with up to 36 masons per site. This is a simplification: real royal works drew on large rationed workforces of many peoples, organised by the royal administration.
b_camp.s0: In his foundation charter for the palace at Susa, Darius listed where his materials and workers came from. He said the stonecutters were Ionians and Sardians. Medes and Egyptians worked the gold, Sardians and Egyptians the wood, and Babylonians the baked brick. The text presents the building as the work of the whole empire, so it carries a political message as well as a record of labour.
b_camp.s1: The Persepolis Fortification tablets record monthly rations of grain, wine and beer issued to workers called kurtaš in Elamite. Many work groups were large, and the tablets name stoneworkers and other craftsmen, sometimes by origin. The Treasury tablets from Persepolis record payments in silver, made in place of part of the rations, to craftsmen working on the terrace under Darius and Xerxes.
b_camp.s2: The stonework of Cyrus's Pasargadae shows techniques known from Lydia and Ionia. Masons used the toothed claw chisel and smoothed joints only at the edges, a method called anathyrosis. Blocks were tied with dovetail iron clamps set in lead. Scholars take this as evidence that western craftsmen probably came east after Cyrus took Sardis, and unfinished surfaces show the stages of their work.
b_camp.s3: Greek writers tended to picture Persian subjects as the King's slaves, and some modern accounts followed them. The tablets give a more varied picture. Men, women and children received graded rations, and some workers drew silver pay, or extra rations for women after childbirth. Historians still argue over how many kurtaš were deportees, conscripts or hired craftsmen, and over how free any of them were.
b_caravan_yard.lead: Goods crossed the Persian empire on donkeys, mules and camels along roads that the King's administration kept and supervised. Long-distance trade was mostly run by private merchants and temple households, while the state profited by taxing it and by moving its own stores of grain, wine and silver.
b_caravan_yard.play: The Caravan Yard lets the player set each good to off, import or export, and royal caravans then buy and sell there. This is a simplification: the sources point to trade run by private merchants and taxed by the King, not royal caravans trading with towns.
b_caravan_yard.s0: The Persepolis Fortification tablets record parties travelling under sealed authorisations and drawing rations at stations along the roads of Persis and Elam. Donkeys, horses and camels appear in these texts as working animals with their own fodder allowances. On the Apadana reliefs at Persepolis, delegations such as the Bactrians lead two-humped camels as gifts for the King.
b_caravan_yard.s1: The Egibi archive of Babylon shows a family firm that lent silver, rented land and traded in dates, barley and other goods under Cyrus, Cambyses and Darius. Babylonian contracts often describe business partnerships with the word harranu, which also means road or journey. Such firms moved much of their goods by boat along the rivers and canals as well as overland.
b_caravan_yard.s2: An Aramaic customs account from Egypt, probably dated to Xerxes' eleventh year, about 475 BCE, lists Ionian and Phoenician ships arriving at a port and the duties taken from their cargoes for the royal house. It is a sea-trade record, but it shows how the administration taxed commerce rather than running it itself.
b_caravan_yard.s3: Herodotus says Cyrus mocked the Greeks for their marketplaces, and he claims the Persians did not use markets at all. He also reports that Persians called Darius a shopkeeper because he fixed regular tribute. He tells of camels brought to the field at Sardis, and of the Arabs paying their yearly gift to the King in frankincense, which he describes as a product of Arabia.
b_caravan_yard.s4: Herodotus describes royal stations with good lodgings along the road from Sardis to Susa. The walled caravanserai built for traders is a much later form, and historians debate whether private merchants could use the King's stations. The tablets mostly record official travellers.
b_cavalry_stable.lead: Horsemen were among the most valued troops of the Achaemenid kings, and horses needed steady feeding, grooming and handling. The Persepolis tablets show officials issuing grain to horses, and Babylonian archives show land granted in return for cavalry service. No stable compound of this period has been securely excavated, so how horses were housed is less clear than how they were fed.
b_cavalry_stable.play: In the game, grooms and riding-masters train Persian horsemen and carts bring arms and barley, as fodder issues in the tablets suggest. One training stable is a simplification: many riders learned as boys or served from granted land.
b_cavalry_stable.s0: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, written in Elamite in about 509-493 BCE, record grain issued as fodder for horses. Some went to royal horses and some to the mounts of travellers and messengers on the roads. Officials counted the animals and set a ration for each, just as they did for workers. This careful accounting shows that keeping horses was part of the regular business of the royal economy in Persis.
b_cavalry_stable.s1: Business archives from Nippur, above all the Murashu texts of the later 5th century, mention estates called horse land. Holders of such land owed the crown a mounted soldier with his equipment, and they could sometimes pay silver instead. These texts date from after the game's period, but they show one way the empire raised horsemen without keeping them all in royal stables.
b_cavalry_stable.s2: Herodotus says that Persian boys were taught three things between the ages of five and twenty: to ride, to shoot the bow and to tell the truth. He also writes that a governor of Babylon in his own day kept a huge stud of stallions and mares. He describes the great Nisaean horses that marched with Xerxes in 480 BCE. On his account, horsemanship was a skill of the Persian nobility as much as a trade for grooms.
b_cavalry_stable.s3: In the Cyropaedia, written more than a century and a half after Cyrus, Xenophon has Cyrus persuade the Persians, then mostly foot soldiers, to become horsemen. The work is an idealised portrait of a model ruler, not a history. It may reflect a real memory that Persian cavalry grew under Cyrus, but its scenes and speeches cannot be taken as fact.
b_cavalry_stable.s4: Archaeologists have not securely identified an Achaemenid stable building at Persepolis, Susa or Pasargadae. Greek writers stress great herds grazing on the pastures of Media, which suggests that many horses lived on open land and estates rather than in stalls. Historians still debate how large a standing royal cavalry was, compared with horsemen raised from land grants and from subject peoples.
b_clay_pit.lead: Earth dug from the ground was the most common building material of the Persian empire. Stone platforms and columns survive at Pasargadae and Persepolis, but most walls were of mud brick. Clay also made pots, baked bricks and the tablets on which the King's scribes kept their accounts.
b_clay_pit.play: In the game the Clay Pit is an industry that digs river clay and must stand within four cells of water. Real builders often dug local earth near the site. Water was needed to mix it, so the river rule simplifies a real need.
b_clay_pit.s0: Excavations at Pasargadae and Persepolis show that the stone platforms, column bases and doorframes were joined by thick walls of sun-dried mud brick. Such brick needed only earth, water and usually a temper such as chopped straw, pressed into moulds and dried in the sun. Because mud brick crumbles once roofs fall, the stone parts are what visitors see today.
b_clay_pit.s1: In his foundation charter for the palace at Susa, Darius says that the earth was dug down until rock was reached. Rubble was then packed in to raise the base. He adds that the baked brick was moulded by Babylonians, a people with a long tradition of brickmaking. The charter presents earthwork and brick as royal work alongside timber, gold and stone.
b_clay_pit.s2: Thousands of unbaked clay tablets were found in the fortification wall at Persepolis. They date from about 509 to 493 BCE and are written mostly in Elamite. They record rations of grain, wine and beer issued to workers and officials in Persis, including the labour groups who built for the King. The administration of the heartland depended on a steady supply of good clay.
b_clay_pit.s3: Herodotus says that the Babylonians dug a moat around their city and made the dug earth into bricks. They fired the bricks in kilns and laid them in hot bitumen. At every thirtieth course they added a layer of woven reeds. His description fits the Mesopotamian practice that Persian kings drew on.
b_clay_pit.s4: Historians debate how literally to read the list of peoples and materials in Darius's Susa charter. Some take it as a record of who worked where, while others see it mainly as royal ideology showing the whole empire serving the King. Studies of the Susa glazed bricks add a complication, since many were made from a siliceous paste of crushed sand rather than ordinary clay. Brick at Susa was therefore not one simple product of the clay pit.
b_column_porch.lead: A column porch was a deep portico of tall, slender columns carrying a flat timber roof, set in front of a palace or hall. Under Cyrus, Darius and Xerxes it became the signature of Persian royal building. Its capitals were carved as the foreparts of paired animals, most often bulls, holding the roof beams between their necks.
b_column_porch.play: The game shows a shady porch of tall columns with double-bull capitals and lists it as housing. Historically such porches fronted royal palaces and audience halls, not ordinary homes, so this placement is a simplification.
b_column_porch.s0: Excavations in western Iran show that halls with rows of wooden columns were built long before Cyrus. Examples have been found at Hasanlu, south of Lake Urmia, and at Godin Tepe and Nush-i Jan in Media, dating from roughly the 9th to the 7th centuries. The Persian porch probably grew out of this older highland tradition, now worked largely in stone.
b_column_porch.s1: At Pasargadae, Palace S had a central hall of eight columns with porches on all four sides. Palace P had a hall of thirty columns with two long porches. Their column bases contrast dark and pale stone, and the shafts are of white limestone. Fragments of capitals carved with paired animal foreparts, including bulls and lions, are probably among the earliest known examples of the form.
b_column_porch.s2: At Persepolis the Apadana begun by Darius had porches on three sides, with stone columns around 20 metres tall. Their capitals show back-to-back bulls, and elsewhere on the terrace lions and horned griffins, with timber beams resting in the saddle between the heads. At Susa, Darius's charter says the cedar came from Lebanon and the stone columns from a village in Elam.
b_column_porch.s3: Darius's Susa charter names Ionians and Sardians as the stoneworkers. Nylander found Lydian and Ionian tool marks and masonry techniques at Pasargadae. Historians disagree on how much the design itself owed to Ionian, Egyptian or Iranian models. Most now see a deliberate royal blend, made to suit Persian taste and to display the skills of many subject peoples.
b_column_porch.s4: Arrian, Diodorus and Plutarch tell how Alexander burned the palaces of Persepolis in 330. Arrian presents it as deliberate revenge for the Persian burning of Athens. Diodorus and Plutarch describe a drunken revel urged on by the Athenian Thais. Excavators found the timber roofs had burned, while some stone columns of the Apadana still stand on the terrace today.
b_cypress_row.lead: Tall, narrow evergreen trees, usually identified as cypresses, appear in rows on the carved stairways of Persepolis, where they divide the processions of the subject peoples. The Persians also laid out gardens in straight lines along water channels. The rows on the reliefs are probably the clearest surviving image of how ordered planting looked to the court.
b_cypress_row.play: The game places the Cypress Row among its housing buildings, as a line of tall dark trees modelled on those between the figures on the Apadana stair reliefs. That the carved trees are cypresses is a probable reading, not a certainty.
b_cypress_row.s0: The staircases of the Apadana at Persepolis, carved probably under Darius and Xerxes, show delegations from the lands of the empire bringing gifts towards the King. Tall, slender conifers stand between the groups and separate one delegation from the next. Similar trees recur elsewhere on the stair façades. The Oriental Institute of Chicago uncovered the reliefs in the 1930s, first under Ernst Herzfeld and then under Erich Schmidt, who published them.
b_cypress_row.s1: At Pasargadae, David Stronach excavated the stone water channels of Cyrus's garden. Small basins stand at intervals along them, and they frame rectangular plots beside the palace buildings. The plants themselves do not survive, so which trees grew along the channels is unknown. Elamite tablets from the Persepolis Fortification archive use partetaš for royal estates, a loan from the Old Persian word that also gave Greek paradeisos.
b_cypress_row.s2: Xenophon tells how the Spartan Lysander visited the younger Cyrus at Sardis near the end of the 5th century. Lysander admired the park because its trees stood in straight rows at regular angles, and Cyrus said he had measured it out and planted some trees himself. The story is later than the game's period and does not name the trees, but it shows that orderly rows were a mark of a Persian royal garden.
b_cypress_row.s3: The carved trees are stylised. They are usually taken for the Mediterranean cypress, which grows in the region, but some prefer a generic conifer or a pine. No Achaemenid text explains them. Some modern writers read them as symbols of evergreen life or of the royal garden, while others see them mainly as a device that divides the long processions into units.
b_cypress_row.s4: Much later Persian tradition made the cypress a sacred tree. Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, completed around 1010 CE, says Zoroaster planted a cypress at Kashmar, and later writers claimed that a caliph had it felled. These stories were written down well over a thousand years after Darius and say nothing reliable about Achaemenid planting.
b_darius_statue.lead: A greywacke statue of Darius, carved in Egypt in the Egyptian manner but dressed in the Persian court robe, was found at Susa in 1972. It is headless and stands about 2.5 metres high on its base. Its texts, in Egyptian hieroglyphs and in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, say why it was made, and its base shows the peoples of the empire holding up the King.
b_darius_statue.play: The game offers the Statue of Darius as a decoration at Susa only, drawn whole with the head it has lost. It is the one statue among the game's Persian decorations, because it is a real one.
b_darius_statue.s0: The cuneiform text on the robe says, in substance, that Darius ordered this stone statue made in Egypt so that whoever saw it in time to come would know that the Persian man holds Egypt. The stone is greywacke from the Wadi Hammamat in Egypt's eastern desert, and the pose, striding with the left foot forward against a back pillar, is Egyptian.
b_darius_statue.s1: On each long side of the base twelve figures, each in his own people's dress, raise their hands under the King. Below each is an oval ring of the kind Egyptians drew for the names of foreign lands, holding that people's name in hieroglyphs, from Persia, Media and Elam to Egypt, Libya and Kush. On the ends two Nile gods tie together the plants of Upper and Lower Egypt, the old sign of the Two Lands united.
b_darius_statue.s2: French excavators at Susa found the statue in 1972 lying beside the passage of the great gatehouse east of Darius's palace, broken and without its head. Xerxes' inscriptions found at the gate name it as his father Darius's work. The statue is now in the National Museum of Iran in Tehran.
b_darius_statue.s3: In the hieroglyphic texts Darius bears the titles of a pharaoh and is called the beloved of Egyptian gods, while his robe, belt and dagger are Persian. The statue shows how Darius presented himself in Egypt: as a lawful king in the country's own forms, ruling it as a Persian.
b_darius_statue.s4: The hieroglyphs name Atum, the god of Heliopolis, so many scholars think the statue first stood in a temple there and was brought to Susa later, perhaps under Xerxes. Others think it was made for Susa from the start. No text says when or why it made the journey.
b_farm.lead: Barley was the main grain of the Achaemenid heartland and much of the empire. It fed workers, soldiers, animals and the royal table, and it served as a measure of payment. The clay archives of Persepolis show barley moving through the King's storehouses on a vast scale, which makes it one of the best documented parts of Persian life.
b_farm.play: The game's farm grows barley on canal-watered land near the Pulvar and carts it to a granary. The game simplifies a system that the tablets show was run through royal storehouses and scribal accounts.
b_farm.s0: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, written mostly in Elamite in the years around 509-493 BCE, record grain more often than any other commodity. Barley was issued as monthly rations to workers, including men, women and children, as seed for sowing and as fodder for horses and other animals. Officials logged deliveries, stores and payments place by place across Persis and towards Elam.
b_farm.s1: The same archive shows barley given for offerings to several gods, Elamite and Iranian alike. Travellers on the roads who carried sealed documents drew rations, mostly flour made from grain, along with beer and wine. Barley was also brewed into beer, which appears among the commodities the administration handled. Grain was therefore a tool of government as well as food.
b_farm.s2: Persis has cold winters and dry summers, so reliable harvests depended on rivers and channels.
