At Pasargadae, beside the Pulvar, excavators found stone water channels running through the royal gardens, evidence of careful water management under Cyrus. Later surveys of the plains around Persepolis have recorded ancient canals and dams, though dating each work precisely is often difficult.
b_farm.s3: In Babylonia the Murashu archive from Nippur dates to about 455-403 BCE, later than the game's period. It shows land granted to soldiers and dependants in return for military service and taxes, known as bow land, horse land and chariot land. The Murashu firm leased such holdings, supplied water, seed and animals, and collected barley and dates as rent. The texts show how imperial landholding and irrigation were tied together.
b_farm.s4: Herodotus says Babylonian fields returned two hundred and sometimes three hundred times the seed, a figure historians regard as greatly exaggerated. Polybius, writing centuries later, says the Persians granted the use of land for five generations to anyone who brought water to unwatered ground in the dry country south of the Caspian. Scholars debate whether this refers to underground channels and whether such channels were already widespread under the Achaemenids.
b_feasting_hall.lead: Feasting was one of the main ways Persian households and the royal court showed rank and rewarded loyalty. Herodotus describes birthday banquets with animals roasted whole and heavy drinking. The Persepolis tablets show the king's table drawing on great stores of grain, wine, beer and livestock, which historians think was shared out to those he favoured.
b_feasting_hall.play: The Feasting Hall is a service building whose hosts invite the houses they pass, and its birthday note follows Herodotus 1.133. No such building type is known: Persians feasted in palace halls, courtyards, tents and homes.
b_feasting_hall.s0: Herodotus says the Persians honoured their own birthday above every other day. A rich household roasted an ox, a horse, a camel or a donkey whole in an oven, while poorer families served smaller animals such as sheep. Main dishes were few, but many extra courses followed one after another. The Persians, he adds, said that Greeks left the table still hungry because nothing worth eating came after the main meal.
b_feasting_hall.s1: Herodotus also reports that Persians were very fond of wine and that they debated their most serious affairs while drinking. The next day the master of the house where they had met put the decision to them again when they were sober, and they kept it only if it still pleased them. A choice first made sober was tested again over wine. Some historians suspect a Greek stereotype here, but Herodotus presents it as settled custom.
b_feasting_hall.s2: The Persepolis Fortification tablets record grain, flour, wine, beer and animals issued for the king and the royal household, including when the court travelled. Other tablets record food issued for offerings to the gods, which Wouter Henkelman argues was afterwards eaten by those taking part. He has also argued that the royal table worked as a system of redistribution, with food passed on from the court to nobles and guards as a sign of the king's favour.
b_feasting_hall.s3: Athenaeus, writing around 200 CE, cites Ctesias and Dinon for the claim that the king dined with 15,000 people at a cost of 400 talents. Heracleides of Cyme, also quoted by him, says about a thousand animals were slaughtered daily and much of the food went to guards and troops. Polyaenus tells of a bronze pillar at Persepolis listing the dinner's provisions. Some treat these figures as Greek exaggeration, while Briant reads them as counting all fed from royal stores.
b_feasting_hall.s4: Herodotus says that once a year, on the king's birthday, the Persians held a royal feast called tykta, which he renders as perfect. On that day the king anointed his head and granted the requests of his guests. In his story, Queen Amestris used the custom to claim the wife of Masistes, and cruelty followed. The tale is shaped as a moral drama of court passion. The custom of birthday gifts may be real, but the story cannot be checked.
b_festival_quay.lead: Egyptian religious festivals drew large crowds, and many pilgrims came by river. Herodotus describes boats packed with men and women sailing to the festival of Bastet at Bubastis with music, singing and clapping. A landing place for such boats served both worship and the river traffic that linked Egyptian towns.
b_festival_quay.play: The game's note follows Herodotus 2.59-60, but he describes boats bound for Bubastis in the Delta. Offering the quay at Memphis and requiring it within four cells of water is the game's own setting, not a site named in the sources.
b_festival_quay.s0: Herodotus says that men and women sailed together to Bubastis, many in each boat. Some women shook rattles, some men played pipes the whole way, and the rest sang and clapped. When a boat passed a town it drew close to the bank, where some women jeered at the townswomen, some danced and some lifted their skirts. At Bubastis, he says, more wine was drunk than in all the rest of the year.
b_festival_quay.s1: Herodotus lists six great Egyptian festivals and ranks the one at Bubastis first. He gives the gods Greek names: Artemis for Bastet at Bubastis and Athena for Neith at Sais, with others at Busiris, Heliopolis, Buto and Papremis. He reports a local claim that 700,000 men and women, not counting children, gathered at Bubastis. Historians generally take this figure as greatly exaggerated.
b_festival_quay.s2: Egyptian evidence for river festivals long predates Herodotus. Reliefs of the Opet festival at Luxor temple show the gods' barques towed along the Nile, escorted by musicians, dancers and crowds on the bank. Excavations at Bubastis uncovered the great temple of Bastet, confirming the importance of the site he describes.
b_festival_quay.s3: Herodotus says that when a new Apis bull appeared at Memphis, the Egyptians feasted in festive clothes. Cambyses, thinking they were mocking his failures, then wounded the bull. Yet an Apis stela records a bull buried in Cambyses' sixth year, with a sarcophagus dedicated in his name. Historians debate whether the story is hostile tradition or refers to the next Apis, which died under Darius.
b_fire_altar.lead: A fire altar was a stone stand, stepped at top and foot, on which a fire burned in the open air. The best evidence for it is the relief carved on the tomb of Darius at Naqsh-e Rostam, where the King raises a hand before such an altar. With the Persepolis tablets, it shows that fire had an important place in Persian worship, even though Greek writers described that worship very differently.
b_fire_altar.play: The game shows a stepped stone altar with its fire in the open air, modelled on the Naqsh-e Rostam relief. Placing it on Pasargadae's sacred precinct simplifies matters: the stone blocks found there may not be altars at all.
b_fire_altar.s0: In the upper register of Darius's rock-cut tomb, beside the inscription DNa, the King stands on a three-stepped platform holding a bow and raises his right hand towards a stepped altar topped by flames. A winged figure, usually taken to be Auramazda, hovers above. The throne platform rests on the raised arms of figures representing the subject peoples. The same scene recurs on the later royal tombs at Naqsh-e Rostam and Persepolis.
b_fire_altar.s1: North-west of the palaces at Pasargadae lies an open area with two limestone plinths, one of them reached by a flight of steps. David Stronach suggested that the King stood on the stepped plinth while a fire burned on the other, which would match the tomb reliefs. The plinths themselves give no direct proof of fire, and other scholars are less certain of their purpose. The date of the terraces beside them is also debated.
b_fire_altar.s2: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, from about 509 to 493 BCE, record grain, wine and animals issued from royal stores for offerings to Iranian and Elamite gods alike. Some recipients carry the title haturmakša, which probably meant an official who tended the fire. Seals impressed on these tablets also show figures standing before altars. The texts describe a regular, state-funded cult rather than a single uniform religion.
b_fire_altar.s3: Herodotus says the Persians set up no statues, temples or altars. He adds that they sacrificed on the highest mountain peaks to the sky, sun, moon, earth, fire, water and winds, with no altar or lit fire, while a magus chanted. The reliefs plainly show a royal altar with fire, so his picture cannot be complete. Some historians think he meant the victim was not burned, since elsewhere he says Persians held fire to be a god.
b_fire_altar.s4: Strabo, writing about five centuries later, says the Persians made offerings especially to fire and water and took care not to pollute the fire. He describes magi tending fires that burned constantly in enclosed sanctuaries, which he saw in Cappadocia. This was the practice of his own time, and it should not be read back into the reign of Darius without caution.
b_fishers_landing.lead: Fish fed many of the empire's people, from the Babylonian marshes to the Nile and the Aegean coast. Greek writers describe whole communities who lived on it, and the Persian treasury drew money from Egypt's fisheries. Few sources say how ordinary fishers worked, so much of their daily life is known from older tomb paintings and from the salted fish shipped across the sea.
b_fishers_landing.play: The landing stands with its back at the water's edge and sends small boats out to net fish, which carts take to a granary. Households eat fish or meat for up to half their ration. This is a simplification: many fishers worked from the bank with nets and traps, and no source describes fishing on the rivers of Persis itself, so a landing there is our inference.
b_fishers_landing.s0: Herodotus says the water of Lake Moeris in the Fayum ran in for six months and out for six. While it ran out, he says, the catch brought a talent of silver a day to the royal treasury, and twenty minae a day while it ran in. He adds that Egypt's tribute to Darius of 700 talents came on top of the money from the lake's fish. His figures may be inflated, but they show a fishery treated as a source of state income.
b_fishers_landing.s1: Herodotus says three Babylonian tribes ate nothing but fish, dried in the sun, pounded and sifted through linen. He says Egyptians ate fish dried or salted, though priests refused it. Around 325 BCE Alexander's admiral Nearchus reported Fish-eaters on the Gedrosian coast of the Arabian Sea, who used nets of palm bark and ground dried fish into meal. These are outsiders' reports and tend to make such peoples sound strange.
b_fishers_landing.s2: Egyptian tomb reliefs show fishers in light papyrus skiffs hauling drag nets between two boats, or working with hand nets, baskets and lines. The Old Kingdom tomb of Ti at Saqqara has a well known example. These scenes are far older than the Persian conquest and were made for the tombs of the rich, but papyrus skiffs and nets remained in use on the river, and Herodotus describes the marsh people's nets in his own day.
b_fishers_landing.s3: Salting let fish travel. A building at Corinth held jars from the western Mediterranean in the 5th century BCE, and fish bones in them point to a trade in preserved fish. Herodotus has a guard at Sestos in 479 BCE frying salted fish when, he says, it leapt in the pan. The evidence is thin for how much of this trade reached the towns of the Persian empire, and most people probably ate what was caught close to home.
b_flax_field.lead: Flax was the main fibre plant of the ancient Mediterranean and Near East, grown for linen cloth, sailcloth and cord. Herodotus says that while Xerxes prepared to cross into Europe, cables of 'white flax' and papyrus were made for the bridges over the Hellespont. Those ropes are why flax belongs in the story of the Athos years.
b_flax_field.play: The game builds Flax Fields at Athos to feed its ropewalk and files them as food. Flax is a fibre crop, and Herodotus says Phoenicians made the white-flax cables; no flax fields at Athos are recorded.
b_flax_field.s0: Linen textiles survive in large numbers from Egypt, and New Kingdom tomb paintings, centuries older than Xerxes, show flax being pulled up by the roots and bound in sheaves. The stalks were then retted, soaked in water or left on damp ground until rot loosened the fibres from the woody core. Breaking, scutching and combing followed before spinning. Flax seed could be pressed for oil, but the plant was grown above all for its fibre.
b_flax_field.s1: Herodotus says that while the Athos canal was being dug, Xerxes had cables of papyrus and white flax prepared for bridging the Hellespont. He gave this work to Phoenicians and Egyptians, and also had food stockpiled at depots along the Thracian coast. When the first bridges were built, the Phoenicians used white-flax cables and the Egyptians papyrus. In his telling, the craft lay with these peoples, not with farmers near Athos.
b_flax_field.s2: After a storm broke the first bridges, Herodotus says the new ones were rigged with two cables of white flax and four of papyrus each. He says the cables were alike in thickness and appearance, but the flax ones were heavier in proportion. He reports that a cubit of flax cable weighed a talent.
b_flax_field.s3: Herodotus's word leukolinon is usually translated 'white flax', but the plant is not certain. Many take it as a form of ordinary linen flax. Some commentators have suggested a coarser fibre, such as esparto grass, that would suit heavy cables better. Modern studies of the bridges also debate how such ropes were made, anchored and tensioned across the strait.
b_gaming_court.lead: Games of chance and skill were played across the Persian empire, in courtyards, streets and palaces. Herodotus records a Lydian claim to have invented dice, knucklebones and ball games during a long famine. The claim cannot be true as history, but it shows the Lydians wanting credit for pastimes they shared with the Greeks.
b_gaming_court.play: In the Sardis level the Gaming Court is a services building. Its note follows Herodotus fairly, but no dedicated gaming buildings are known; games were played in open courts and streets, so the building is the game's invention.
b_gaming_court.s0: Herodotus says the Lydians claimed to have invented the games shared by them and the Greeks, including dice, knucklebones and ball games, though not draughts. He tells how, in a famine under King Atys, they played all day on one day so as not to think of food, and ate on the next. After eighteen years, he says, half the people left by lot and sailed west under Tyrrhenus.
b_gaming_court.s1: Historians do not accept the Lydian claim of invention. Dice and knucklebones were already old in Egypt, Mesopotamia and the Indus valley long before the Lydian kings. The tale of the emigration under Tyrrhenus, once used to explain the origin of the Etruscans, is also much argued over and generally doubted.
b_gaming_court.s2: French excavators at Susa in 1901 found a bronze knucklebone weighing over 90 kilograms, inscribed in Greek as a tithe offered to Apollo. It probably came from the sanctuary of Apollo at Didyma near Miletus and was carried off as booty after the Persians took Miletus in 494 BCE. It is now in the Louvre and shows that knucklebones could be sacred offerings as well as playthings.
b_gaming_court.s3: Plutarch describes Queen Parysatis playing dice with her son Artaxerxes II and winning from him the eunuch Masabates, whom she blamed for mutilating the body of her younger son Cyrus and then had put to death. The story is set soon after the battle of Cunaxa in 401 BCE, well after this game's period, and is told as court drama, but it suggests dice were a familiar pastime among the Persian elite.
b_gaming_court.s4: Herodotus tells that the young Cyrus, raised as a herdsman's son, was chosen king by the village boys in their game and had a nobleman's son beaten for disobeying him. The episode is a moral tale about a born ruler revealed through play, not a record of real events.
b_garden.lead: The Persians probably called a walled, irrigated garden paridaida, a word reconstructed from its Elamite and Babylonian forms. The Greeks borrowed it as paradeisos, the origin of the word paradise. Kings, satraps and nobles laid out such gardens with rows of trees and stone-lined channels, and a well-watered garden showed that its owner could command land, water and labour.
b_garden.play: In the game the Formal Garden is a service building of shade trees and stone channels that Noble Residences need within ten cells. Real Persian gardens were walled royal or noble estates, so this rule is a simplification.
b_garden.s0: Excavations at Pasargadae in the 1960s uncovered limestone water channels in the royal garden laid out under Cyrus, between Palace P and two small pavilions. The channels ran in straight lines and opened at intervals into small square basins. Planting beds lay between them, and the throne portico of Palace P looked out over the whole layout.
b_garden.s1: The Elamite administrative tablets from Persepolis, written about 509 to 493 BCE, use the word partetaš, borrowed from the Persian term. They record such estates at several places in Persis, with workers assigned to them and produce and young trees passing through them. They show gardens as working parts of the royal economy, not only places of pleasure.
b_garden.s2: Xenophon tells how Cyrus the Younger, a Persian prince, showed the Spartan Lysander his paradeisos at Sardis late in the fifth century, with trees in straight rows, and said he had planted some himself. Herodotus says Xerxes, marching towards Sardis in 481 BCE, found a fine plane tree in Lydia, adorned it with gold and left a guard over it. Both writers present tree care as something Persian rulers valued.
b_garden.s3: Stronach, the excavator, later argued that the Pasargadae channels framed four quarters, making this the earliest known fourfold garden and an ancestor of the later Persian chahar bagh. Others note that only parts of the layout survive, and geophysical surveys of the site since about 2000 point to a less tidy arrangement. Whether the fourfold plan began here remains debated.
b_garden.s4: A Greek inscription records a letter in which Darius praises his official Gadatas for planting trees from beyond the Euphrates in western Asia Minor. The stone itself was cut centuries later, in the Roman period. Historians disagree over whether it copies a genuine royal letter or is a later composition.
b_garden_pavilion.lead: Persian kings and nobles laid out walled gardens, later called paradises by the Greeks, with trees in rows, stone water channels and small columned buildings for shade. At Pasargadae, Cyrus's garden had two such pavilions. They show how the court used gardens to display order, plenty and royal care for the land.
b_garden_pavilion.play: A service building in Pasargadae, Parsa and Susa: a columned shade-house cooled by running water, whose hosts invite the houses they pass. Its feast echoes Herodotus's tale of Cyrus feasting the Persians in a meadow, not a pavilion.
b_garden_pavilion.s0: David Stronach's excavations in the early 1960s uncovered a garden in front of the residential building known as Palace P. Two small columned structures, called Pavilion A and Pavilion B, stood at its corners. Limestone channels with square basins at intervals carried water through the garden, and parts of them survive today.
b_garden_pavilion.s1: The Greek paradeisos came from an Old Persian word, reconstructed as paridaida, meaning an enclosed park or walled garden. Elamite administrative tablets from Persepolis use a related term, partetaš, for managed estates that held trees, fruit and stores. These texts show that such gardens were working properties run by officials, not only places for leisure.
b_garden_pavilion.s2: Xenophon tells how the Spartan Lysander visited the younger Cyrus in his paradise at Sardis and admired the straight rows of trees. Cyrus said he had planned the garden and planted some trees himself. The scene is set around 407 BCE, long after the game's period, but it shows how Greeks saw gardening as a royal skill.
b_garden_pavilion.s3: Stronach argued that the channels divided the Pasargadae garden into four parts, an early form of the later Persian fourfold garden. Later geophysical survey around the site found more channels and buildings, and some scholars now doubt the neat fourfold plan. Whether running water cooled the pavilions, as the game suggests, is a reasonable guess rather than a proven fact.
b_garden_pavilion.s4: Herodotus says Cyrus made the Persians clear thorny ground for a day, then feasted them in a meadow the next. He asked which day they preferred and told them that freedom from the Medes would bring the second kind of life. The story is a moral tale and does not describe a garden pavilion.
b_gate.lead: A gatehouse stood where a wall met a road. It was one of the few ways into a walled city or palace and often the first place an attacker struck. In the Persian empire gateways served both defence and display: town walls had strong gates, while the King's residences had monumental gatehouses that controlled who came near him.
b_gate.play: The Gatehouse is a historic structure already on a level's map, not built by the player. Its cedar doors open in peace and shut against raiders; rams and fire harm it and masons repair it. Real town gates more likely used local timber.
b_gate.s0: At Pasargadae the gatehouse known as Gate R kept a carved four-winged figure on one of its doorjambs. At Persepolis, Xerxes says in his inscription on the Gate of All Nations that he built that gateway. At Susa, excavators found a large gatehouse east of the palace of Darius, and a statue of Darius made in Egypt was found there in 1972.
b_gate.s1: The gate doors themselves have not survived. Stone sockets for door pivots show that heavy double doors turned in the great gateways. Darius's foundation charter from Susa says cedar was brought from the Lebanon mountains for his palace. Fine imported timber of this kind went to royal buildings, and there is no record of it being used for ordinary town gates.
b_gate.s2: Herodotus says the walls of Babylon had a hundred gates all of bronze. He probably meant wooden doors sheathed in bronze. He also tells how the Persians took Soli in Cyprus, about 497 BCE, in the fifth month of the siege by digging mines under its wall. In 480 BCE, he says, Persians on the Areopagus shot arrows wrapped in burning tow at the wooden barricade on the Acropolis of Athens.
b_gate.s3: At Palaepaphos in Cyprus, excavators found a great siege mound of earth, stone and rubble heaped against the wall beside the northeast gate. It is dated to the Persian reconquest of Cyprus after the revolt of 498-497 BCE. Its fill included broken statues and votive offerings, and the defenders dug tunnels beneath it to make it collapse. No ancient writer describes this siege.
b_gate.s4: Historians still debate how far the royal gatehouses were built for defence. Persepolis had a fortification wall with towers on the hillside behind it. The Gate of All Nations and Gate R at Pasargadae look more like formal entrances for receiving visitors. Many scholars think these gates were mainly meant to regulate approach to the King and to impress those who came.
b_gate_bulls.lead: Pairs of colossal stone bulls stood at the doorways of Persian royal gatehouses, first at Cyrus's gate at Pasargadae and later at Xerxes' Gate of All Lands at Persepolis. The Persians took the idea from the human-headed winged bulls of Assyrian palaces. The bulls probably served to mark the threshold between the outside world and the King's own ground.
b_gate_bulls.play: The game lists Gate Bulls with its housing buildings, as a piece of gateway sculpture. Historically, such colossi stood only at royal gatehouses and palaces, never at ordinary homes or streets.
b_gate_bulls.s0: Assyrian kings of the 9th to 7th centuries set human-headed winged bulls at the gates and throne-room doors of their palaces at Nimrud, Khorsabad and Nineveh. Most were carved from a single huge block. The Assyrian versions were usually given five legs, so that they looked complete from both the front and the side. Excavators recovered many of them in the 19th century.
b_gate_bulls.s1: The gatehouse at Pasargadae, known to excavators as Gate R, was a columned hall built under Cyrus. Excavation showed that colossal bulls flanked its main doorways, but only their lower parts survive. A side doorway kept a relief of a four-winged figure wearing an Egyptian-style crown. The figure mixed Assyrian, Elamite and Egyptian elements in a way typical of Cyrus's builders.
b_gate_bulls.s2: At the top of the great stairway onto the Persepolis terrace, Xerxes built a four-columned gatehouse. Bulls without wings or human heads guard its western doorway, facing the stairs; human-headed winged bulls with horned crowns guard the eastern one. A trilingual inscription above them (XPa) says that Xerxes built this Gate of All Lands by the favour of Auramazda. Bull colossi also flanked the porch of the Hall of a Hundred Columns, finished under Artaxerxes I.
b_gate_bulls.s3: In Assyria such figures were protective spirits that kept evil away from the doorway. Historians still argue over whether the Persians shared that belief or used the bulls mainly as a sign of royal power borrowed from an older empire. The Persepolis bulls have four legs, not the Assyrian five. Because the heads at Pasargadae are lost, it is also uncertain whether all of Cyrus's bulls were human-headed.
b_glazed_panel.lead: Glazed-brick panels were walls faced with moulded bricks, each carrying part of a figure in relief and coated in coloured glaze. Darius and his successors used them to line the courts and gateways of the palace at Susa with lions, griffins, winged bulls and rows of archers. The craft came from Babylon, and its use at Susa shows how the King drew the skills of many subject peoples into his own house.
b_glazed_panel.play: In the game the Glazed-brick Panel is a housing building showing striding lions like the Susa friezes. Its credit to Babylonian craft follows DSf, though the charter names Medes and Egyptians as the men who adorned the wall.
b_glazed_panel.s0: Moulded glazed brick was a Mesopotamian art before the Persians took it up. Under Nebuchadnezzar II, in the early 6th century, Babylon's Ishtar Gate and Processional Way were faced with blue-glazed brick showing bulls, dragons and striding lions. German excavators uncovered these walls between 1899 and 1917, and reconstructed parts now stand in Berlin.
b_glazed_panel.s1: Darius's foundation charter for his Susa palace lists the peoples who supplied its materials and labour. It says the baked brick was moulded by Babylonians, and that the men who adorned the wall were Medes and Egyptians. Other craftsmen in the list came from Ionia, Sardis and elsewhere, so the charter presents the palace as the work of the whole empire.
b_glazed_panel.s2: French excavators led by Marcel and Jane Dieulafoy found the friezes in fallen fragments at Susa in 1884 to 1886, and later French missions recovered more. Many Susa panels were made not of fired clay but of a siliceous, quartz-rich body, a change from Babylonian practice. The pieces were reassembled in the Louvre, where the lion frieze and the frieze of archers are on display today.
b_glazed_panel.s3: The frieze of spear-carrying archers in rich robes is often called the Immortals, after the 10,000 picked Persians whom Herodotus describes. No inscription names them, and some scholars see them as royal guards in general. Because the bricks were found fallen and scattered, their original places in the palace are uncertain, and some may belong to the rebuilding under Artaxerxes II rather than to Darius.
b_gold_refinery.lead: The Pactolus stream ran down from Mount Tmolus through Sardis carrying flakes of natural gold mixed with silver. Beside its bank, excavators found a Lydian refinery where this metal was purified into nearly pure gold. The workshop helps explain the wealth of Croesus and the early gold coinage that Sardis passed to its Persian rulers.
b_gold_refinery.play: The game's washers and refiners follow the excavated method in outline. The dug workshop probably went out of use by the mid-sixth century, so a working refinery in the 490s BCE is the game's assumption.
b_gold_refinery.s0: Herodotus says that Lydia had few marvels worth recording except the gold dust washed down from Tmolus. Describing the burning of Sardis by the Ionians and Athenians in 498 BCE, he says the Pactolus flowed through the market place carrying gold dust. Strabo, writing much later, says the river had once carried gold but that the supply had given out by his own day.
b_gold_refinery.s1: In the 1960s and 1970s the Harvard-Cornell expedition to Sardis excavated an industrial area on the east bank of the Pactolus, known as Pactolus North. It held many small hearths and furnaces, fragments of coarse refining pots, lead-soaked hearth linings and tiny specks of gold. A small altar, probably for the goddess Kybebe or Cybele, stood among the workings.
b_gold_refinery.s2: River gold at Sardis was electrum, a natural alloy of gold with a good deal of silver. The finds show that refiners first melted it with lead to remove base metals. They then packed the gold with salt in pots and heated it for a long time, so that the silver turned to a chloride and soaked into the pot walls. Analysis of the debris suggests the silver was probably recovered as well.
b_gold_refinery.s3: Herodotus says the Lydians were the first to strike coins of gold and silver. The excavators date the refinery to the Lydian kings and link it to separate gold and silver coins, but its exact dates are argued. Scholars also debate whether these coins were struck by Croesus or by the first Persian governors after the conquest in the 540s BCE, and how long refining went on at Sardis under Persian rule.
b_gold_refinery.s4: Greek writers told how King Midas of Phrygia was granted the power to turn whatever he touched into gold. In the version best known from Roman writers, he was told to wash it off in the Pactolus, and the river's sands turned golden. The fullest telling is by the poet Ovid, about five centuries after the events of this game. It is a moral tale about greed, not a record of how the gold got there.
b_governors_house.lead: The Persian empire was held from governors' seats. The Old Persian word for a provincial governor, xšaçapāvan, which the Greeks turned into satrap, means protector of the realm. From his house a governor took in the province's dues, kept its stores and records, and answered to the King.
b_governors_house.play: The game gives each city one Governor's House, its heart. His retinue raises and works it, and his wagons and families are the town's first stores and first settlers. Newcomers report at its door, its scribes walk the first streets, and without it half the dues go astray. This is a simplification: towns held by lesser officers had no such building, and no source sets out these rules.
b_governors_house.s0: At Behistun Darius names his men by this title: Dadarshi, xšaçapāvan in Bactria, and Vivana, xšaçapāvan in Arachosia, both of whom fought rebels for him. Herodotus says Darius divided his empire into twenty governments, which the Persians call satrapies, and fixed what each should pay. Governors were held to the King by his messengers on the royal road and by the tribute they had to send.
b_governors_house.s1: Letters on leather in Aramaic show such men at work. Arshama, satrap of Egypt in the 5th century BCE, wrote to his officers about his estates and workers, and sent a steward with an order for his rations at each stop on the road. In Bactria, Akhvamazda wrote to a local governor, Bagavant, about a town's wall and the men who should build it, in letters of about 353-324 BCE.
b_governors_house.s2: At Daskyleion near the Sea of Marmara, seat of the satraps of Hellespontine Phrygia, excavators found hundreds of clay sealings from an archive whose documents have perished. Many carry Persian court scenes in the seal designs. They show how much of a governor's rule passed through sealed orders and receipts, like the tablets of the Persepolis storehouses.
b_governors_house.s3: No governor's house has a plan everyone accepts, so the game's is interpretive: a walled court with porticoes, towers and a gatehouse. Its nearest model is Dahan-e Gholaman in Sistan, a Persian town founded in the 6th or early 5th century BCE, whose large buildings stood round central courts. One is read as administrative, but archaeologists still debate what its greatest court building was for.
b_granary.lead: Barley was the staple of Persis. The King's administration collected it as tax and produce from royal estates, held it in stores across the countryside and paid it out as rations to workers, officials, travellers and animals. Clay tablets from Persepolis show this system at work, and Greek writers describe the great stockpiles that fed the King's armies.
b_granary.play: The game's granary stores barley and up to 160 fruit, and bazaar buyers collect food from it. In Persis most stored grain went out as fixed rations rather than through a market, so the bazaar link is a simplification.
b_granary.s0: The Persepolis Fortification archive, written mostly in Elamite between about 509 and 493 BCE, records grain arriving from farmers and estates and being held by named suppliers at many places around Persepolis. From these stores barley went out as monthly rations to work groups, as travel rations, as fodder, as seed, and as offerings for the gods.
b_granary.s1: Each store had an official who answered for what came in and went out. Scribes wrote receipts and accounts that were later checked, and the whole system answered to a senior director, Parnaka, during much of the archive's span. The aim was to know where every measure of grain had gone.
b_granary.s2: The tablets also track fruit, wine, beer, flour and livestock, usually in their own separate accounts and handled by their own officials. Grain was by far the largest item, but a worker's ration could include other foods, and special rations went to mothers, skilled craftsmen and high officials.
b_granary.s3: Herodotus says Babylonia supplied food for the King and his army for four months of every year. Before Xerxes marched on Greece, he says, grain and other provisions were gathered in depots along the Thracian coast, at places such as Doriscus and Eion on the Strymon, brought by ship from across Asia.
b_granary.s4: Herodotus tells how Cyrus mocked the Greeks for their marketplaces, and he adds that the Persians did not use markets at all. The Persepolis tablets do show an economy run largely on rations, but Babylonian business archives record barley bought, sold and lent for silver. Historians still debate how much grain moved through official stores and how much through trade.
b_guard_post.lead: The Persian kings kept soldiers at bridges, river crossings, mountain gates and frontier forts. These posts held the routes that tied the empire together and controlled who passed. Greek writers describe the guarded gates, and Persian administrative records show how royal travellers were authorised and fed along the way.
b_guard_post.play: The game places guards at a post, as on the Royal Road. Their rounds through town, keeping houses peaceful, are a dramatization: the evidence shows guards at crossings and forts, not street patrols in towns.
b_guard_post.s0: Herodotus describes the road from Sardis to Susa with its royal stations and lodgings. He says that at the Halys river travellers had to pass through gates held by a strong guard-post, and that on entering Cilicia there were two gates and two guard-posts. Where he got this description is debated: it may draw on a Persian itinerary or on the reports of Greek travellers.
b_guard_post.s1: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, from about 509 to 493 BCE, record travellers drawing rations at supply points along the roads on the strength of a sealed document, called halmi in Elamite, issued by the King or a high official. The tablets often note where a party came from and where it was going. An Aramaic letter of the satrap Arshama, from the later 5th century, authorised rations for his steward from officials at named places along his journey.
b_guard_post.s2: The Elephantine papyri, most of them from the 5th century, show a garrison on Egypt's southern border, with Judean soldiers on the island of Elephantine and Aramaeans at Syene across the river. The soldiers were organised in units under commanders and received rations and silver. Their letters and contracts show a settled military community serving the Persian administration of Egypt.
b_guard_post.s3: Herodotus says that in his day the Persians kept guards at Elephantine and at Daphnae, in the same places where the Saite king Psammetichus had posted them. He also mentions Persians and their hired troops quartered in the White Fort at Memphis, fed with grain from the Egyptian tribute.
b_guard_post.s4: Xenophon says that Cyrus kept the commanders of garrisons separate from the satraps and answerable to the King alone, so that no governor held all the armed force of a province. The Cyropaedia is an idealised portrait, and historians debate how far this division held in practice. Modern studies, Briant's among them, point to cases where satraps clearly commanded troops and forts in their provinces.
b_gymnasium.lead: A gymnasium was a place where Greek men exercised, ran and wrestled, usually naked, to prepare for war and for contests such as the games at Olympia. In the years of the Persian wars it was probably still an open, watered ground with shade trees, often beside a shrine. Greek writers made athletic nakedness a mark of difference between Greeks and the peoples of the King's empire.
b_gymnasium.play: The game offers the Gymnasium as a service building in Greek towns, with a note on the olive wreath drawn from Herodotus 8.26. As a single building it simplifies history, since most training grounds of the time were probably open spaces.
b_gymnasium.s0: The word comes from gymnos, naked. Excavated gymnasium buildings with colonnades and walled wrestling courts, as at Olympia and Delphi, date from the 4th century and later. For the late 6th and early 5th centuries historians rely mainly on later texts, and they debate how much was built. Most think early gymnasia were tracks and open land with water and trees, often outside a city's walls.
b_gymnasium.s1: By the classical period Athens had three such grounds outside its walls, each linked to a sanctuary. Later writers credit Hipparchus, son of Pisistratus, with building a costly wall at the Academy. Plutarch says that Cimon, after the Persian wars, brought water to the Academy and planted it with trees, turning a dry place into a shaded grove with paths for running.
b_gymnasium.s2: Thucydides says the Spartans were the first to strip and rub themselves with oil for exercise, and that loincloths at the games had been given up not many years before his time. Herodotus notes that among the Lydians, and nearly all non-Greek peoples, it was shameful even for a man to be seen naked. Herodotus also tells how Alexander of Macedon had to prove Greek descent before he was allowed to run at Olympia.
b_gymnasium.s3: Herodotus says the Olympic festival fell in the same weeks as Thermopylae in 480 BCE and slowed the Greek muster. After the battle, he says, deserters from Arcadia told the Persians that the Greeks were at the games and that the prize was an olive wreath. Tritantaechmes, son of Artabanus, then said to Mardonius that these men contended for excellence, not money. Herodotus adds that the King judged him a coward for it.
b_gymnasium.s4: Pindar's victory odes tell that Heracles founded the Olympic games. The familiar starting date of 776 BCE rests on a list of victors drawn up by Hippias of Elis around 400 BCE, long after the events it records. Plutarch already warned that this list had no firm basis. The early history of the games is therefore largely tradition.
b_healer.lead: The Persian empire had no single medical profession. Egyptian, Babylonian and Greek healers each worked in their own traditions, and the King drew the best of them to his court. Most of what survives tells of court physicians and temple schools. It says little about how ordinary households were cared for.
b_healer.play: In the game a healer walks from the Healer's House to homes along the road, and Courtyard Houses need one. This is a simplification: no source describes a public street healer service in Persian towns.
b_healer.s0: Herodotus says Cyrus asked the pharaoh Amasis for Egypt's best eye doctor, who resented being sent away and later urged Cambyses to seek Amasis's daughter, a demand that helped bring war. He also tells how Darius twisted his ankle while hunting and his Egyptian doctors made it worse. Democedes of Croton, a Greek captive from the household of the satrap Oroetes, cured him and was richly rewarded. Both stories show the King relying on foreign healers.
b_healer.s1: A statue of Udjahorresnet, now in the Vatican Museums, carries his own account in hieroglyphs. He served the last Saite kings, then Cambyses and Darius, and calls himself chief of physicians. He says Darius, while in Elam, sent him back to Egypt to restore the House of Life, the temple institution where texts, medical ones among them, were copied and taught. It is one of the few documents from the time that shows royal interest in medicine.
b_healer.s2: Herodotus writes that Egyptian medicine was divided up, with each doctor treating one illness only. In his account some treated the eyes, others the head, the teeth or the belly. Egyptian medical papyri confirm that specialist titles existed, though historians think he made the division sound stricter than it was.
b_healer.s3: Herodotus writes that the Babylonians had no physicians and instead laid their sick in the square so that passers-by could give advice. Cuneiform tablets contradict him. Babylonia had two kinds of trained healer: the asû, who worked with drugs and bandages, and the āšipu, who diagnosed and treated through ritual. Their handbooks were still being copied in the Persian period.
b_healer.s4: The Videvdad is a Zoroastrian priestly text whose date of composition is debated, and it was written down only much later. It names three kinds of healer: those who heal with the knife, with plants and with the holy word, and it ranks the last highest. It also sets fees according to the patient's rank. How far any of this reflects practice under Darius is unknown, so it is best read as later tradition.
b_herm.lead: A herm was a square stone pillar topped with the bearded head of the god Hermes, protector of travellers and boundaries. In Athens and Attica such pillars were set along roads from the late sixth century, and by the fifth they stood at crossroads, gateways and house doors. They were at once road markers, guardians and objects of everyday worship, and they became one of the most familiar sights of an Athenian street.
b_herm.play: In Greek towns the game offers the Herm as a housing building. Its note credits the road herms to Plato's Hipparchus. That dialogue was handed down under Plato's name, but most scholars doubt he wrote it.
b_herm.s0: Surviving archaic and classical herms are plain rectangular shafts carrying a carved head of a bearded Hermes, often with stylised curls. Many also had male genitals carved on the front and short square stumps at the shoulders, which may have held wreaths or offerings. Fragments recovered in excavations of the Athenian Agora show that they were common in the city's public spaces.
b_herm.s1: The dialogue Hipparchus says that Hipparchus, son of the tyrant Pisistratus, set up herms along the roads of Attica. Each one stood halfway between the city and a country village, or deme. One side named the place, and the other carried a short verse of moral advice, such as a call to walk with just thoughts. Hipparchus was killed in 514 BCE, so the series probably belongs to the years before.
b_herm.s2: Herodotus says the Athenians were the first Greeks to make statues of Hermes with an erect phallus. He claims they learned the custom from the Pelasgians, an earlier people of Greece, and links it to the mysteries of Samothrace. His explanation reflects Greek ideas about the past more than any firm evidence for the origin of the type.
b_herm.s3: The Hipparchus was transmitted with Plato's works, but most modern scholars think it was written by someone else, so its story of the road herms may be a later tradition. Historians also argue over whether Hipparchus invented the pillar form or adapted older roadside markers, such as the stone heaps linked to Hermes. An inscribed herm fragment found in the Attic countryside is often connected with his series, but the link is not certain.
b_herm.s4: Thucydides shows how widespread herms had become by the late fifth century. He says that in 415 BCE, just before the expedition to Sicily, most of the stone herms in Athens had their faces mutilated in a single night. He describes them as a traditional feature standing at the doorways of both private houses and sanctuaries, and the attack caused great alarm in the city.
b_house.lead: Most people in the Persian empire lived in simple houses of mud brick, reed and timber, often built around a yard and roofed flat with beaten earth. Kings left stone palaces and inscriptions. The homes of farmers, craftsmen and labourers are known mainly from a handful of excavations, from business contracts, and from a few remarks by Greek writers.
b_house.play: Settlers build a hut, and it grows as water, food, faith and health reach it. This is a game simplification: real houses did not upgrade through services, and a family's home depended on land, income and its duties to the King.
b_house.s0: Excavations show that ordinary houses were built of sun-dried mud brick, often on a low stone footing, with wooden beams and reed matting under a flat earth roof. At Susa, Roman Ghirshman dug a quarter of modest houses that he dated to the Persian period, though later study has questioned how much of it is that early. In the Merkes quarter of Babylon, houses were built around an inner courtyard that gave light and air to the rooms.
b_house.s1: Clay tablets from Babylonian family archives, such as that of the Egibi family, record houses being sold, leased and pledged as security for loans under Cyrus, Cambyses and Darius. The contracts give rents, boundaries and the names of neighbours. They show that a house in a large city was property that could be bought, rented out or inherited.
b_house.s2: Herodotus says that Ionian raiders and their Athenian and Eretrian allies burned Sardis in 498 BCE. He explains that the fire spread quickly because most houses in the city were made of reeds, and even the brick ones had reed roofs. In his telling, a single house set alight was enough for the flames to run from roof to roof across the town.
b_house.s3: Pasargadae and Persepolis are known for palaces, but where their workers and residents lived is less clear. David Stronach saw Pasargadae as a spread of palaces and gardens with only scattered settlement. Later surveys have found traces of wider occupation around both sites, and historians still debate how large and how dense these towns were.
b_house.s4: The Persepolis Fortification tablets record grain, wine and beer issued to groups of workers, including men, women and children, across Persis and neighbouring Elam. They say almost nothing about where these workers slept. Their homes were probably simple and close to the farms, workshops and building sites where they worked.
b_hunters_lodge.lead: Persian kings were shown as hunters, and Greek writers describe hunting as the training ground of Persian youth. Lions, leopards, wolves and wild boar still ranged across the empire, and the herds and fields of ordinary people had to be kept from them. How much game ordinary households ate is not recorded.
b_hunters_lodge.play: The lodge's hunters walk out over the open land and bring meat home, and they carry back the carcass of any beast your soldiers kill. Beasts kill hunters and walkers who come near them. This is a simplification: the sources tell us far more about royal and noble hunting than about the work of common hunters.
b_hunters_lodge.s0: A cylinder seal inscribed with the name of Darius, now in the British Museum, shows the king in a chariot shooting arrows at a rearing lion beneath a winged symbol. Royal seals and reliefs across the Near East had long shown the king killing lions, a sign that he protected his land and people from the wild.
b_hunters_lodge.s1: Herodotus says Persian boys were taught three things from the age of five to twenty: to ride, to shoot the bow and to speak the truth. Xenophon, writing in the fourth century, says the king led the young men out to hunt because hunting was the truest practice for war. His picture is idealised, but both writers link the hunt and the army.
b_hunters_lodge.s2: Herodotus tells of a huge boar that came down from Mysian Olympus and wrecked the farmers' fields, while the men sent against it were hurt and could do nothing. They begged Croesus of Lydia for help, and his son Atys went on the hunt and was killed by a spear thrown at the boar. The story shows how a single wild beast could threaten a countryside.
b_hunters_lodge.s3: Herodotus says that on their birthdays wealthy Persians roasted a whole ox, horse, camel or donkey, while poorer families served smaller animals. Meat from flocks was also issued to officials in the Persepolis records. How often common households ate wild game, rather than the meat of their own flocks, is not known.
b_hunting_park.lead: The Persian kings and their satraps kept enclosed parks of trees, water and wild animals, which Greek writers called paradeisoi. Some were hunting grounds where the King and his nobles rode after deer, boar and lions. Hunting from horseback with the bow showed the qualities a Persian ruler claimed for himself, and the parks became one of the marks of Persian power across the empire.
b_hunting_park.play: The Hunting Park is a service at Pasargadae, Parsa and Susa whose huntsmen invite the houses they pass. Its note cites Herodotus 1.136, which is about boys' training, not parks; no game park is proven at these towns.
b_hunting_park.s0: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, written in Elamite under Darius, mention estates called partetaš, a loan from a Persian word usually reconstructed as paridaida, meaning an enclosed place. The tablets show such estates holding fruit trees, stores and workers. Greek took the word over as paradeisos, Hebrew as pardes, and through later Greek and Latin it gave English the word paradise.
b_hunting_park.s1: Xenophon, who marched with Cyrus the Younger in 401 BCE, says Cyrus had a large park full of wild animals at Celaenae in Phrygia, where he hunted on horseback. He also describes the satrap Pharnabazus at Dascylium, whose land held plentiful game, some in enclosed parks and some in open country. These are later than the game's period but are the clearest descriptions of Persian game parks.
b_hunting_park.s2: A cylinder seal inscribed in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian with the name of a King Darius, probably Darius I, shows the king in a chariot shooting arrows at a rearing lion, beneath a winged figure. Many seals impressed on the Persepolis Fortification tablets also show hunts and combats with animals. Hunting was part of how the Persian elite pictured royal strength and skill.
b_hunting_park.s3: Herodotus says Persian boys were taught three things between the ages of five and twenty: to ride, to shoot the bow and to speak the truth. He does not connect this with parks. On the Persian side, Darius's own tomb inscription calls him a good horseman, archer and spearman, so the Greek report and the royal claim agree on these skills.
b_hunting_park.s4: Excavations at Pasargadae revealed a garden laid out with stone water channels, but nothing proves it held game, and scholars debate how far it was a pleasure garden or a park. The partetaš of the Persepolis tablets look mostly like productive estates. Historians therefore argue over how many paradises were hunting grounds and how many were orchards, farms or display gardens.
b_inscribed_stone.lead: The Achaemenid kings had their words cut in stone, usually in three languages and three forms of cuneiform. These texts named the king, his ancestry, his god Auramazda and his deeds. They are the main surviving voice of the kings themselves, set beside the Greek accounts of Herodotus and others.
b_inscribed_stone.play: The game lists the Inscribed Stone among its housing buildings and presents it as the King's words in three languages. Its note that kings spoke through inscriptions rather than statues overstates the case: a statue of Darius survives from Susa.
b_inscribed_stone.s0: Darius's long inscription at Behistun was cut in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, each in its own form of cuneiform. His foundation charter for the palace at Susa survives in the same three languages. Elamite was also the working language of the Persepolis Fortification tablets, so the choice probably reflected the scribes the court employed. Xerxes kept the pattern, as in his inscription on the suppression of the daiva.
b_inscribed_stone.s1: The Behistun text says that the King sent copies of it out among the lands of the empire. A Babylonian version survives on a stone fragment from Babylon. An Aramaic version was copied on papyrus at Elephantine nearly a century later. The King's words travelled further as copies than on the rock itself, which stood high above the road.
b_inscribed_stone.s2: At Pasargadae, short texts in the three languages name Cyrus the king, an Achaemenid. Many scholars hold that Old Persian cuneiform was devised under Darius, and they read a passage at Behistun as his claim to a new form of writing. On that view the Cyrus texts were added later by Darius. Others argue that the script existed before him, and the question remains open.
b_inscribed_stone.s3: Persian kings did not rely on inscriptions alone. A statue of Darius, carved in Egypt and found at Susa in 1972, is now headless but was probably larger than life. It carries texts in Egyptian hieroglyphs and in the three cuneiform languages. Kings also appeared in relief on rock faces and tombs, with inscriptions beside the image, as at Behistun and Naqsh-e Rostam.
b_inscribed_stone.s4: Herodotus says that Darius, crossing into Europe about 513 BCE, set up two pillars of white stone at the Bosporus. They listed the peoples of his army, one in Assyrian letters and one in Greek. Herodotus also reports a pillar at the springs of the Tearus in Thrace praising the river and the King. Neither stone has been found, but Persian practice elsewhere makes the story plausible.
b_ister_bridge.lead: During his campaign against the Scythians north of the Black Sea, Darius had the Greek fleet from Ionia and the Hellespont lay a bridge of boats across the Ister, the lower Danube. Herodotus makes this bridge the turning point of the expedition: the Ionians guarding it could have stranded the King in Scythia, and they chose not to.
b_ister_bridge.play: The bridge is founded on the bank, with limestone for its stone anchors, boats moored and lashed in turn, and a timber deck. Herodotus gives no building details for this bridge, so the game borrows them from his Hellespont bridges (7.36).
b_ister_bridge.s0: Herodotus says Darius crossed the Bosporus on Mandrocles' bridge and marched through Thrace, while the Greek fleet sailed up the Ister. Ionians, Aeolians and Hellespontine Greeks bridged the river two days' sail from the sea, where its mouths divide; the exact site is unknown. He puts the army at 700,000 men and the fleet at 600 ships, figures historians think greatly exaggerated.
b_ister_bridge.s1: Herodotus says Darius first ordered the bridge broken up so the crews could march with him, but Coes of Mytilene advised keeping it as a way home. Darius then tied sixty knots in a cord and told the Ionian tyrants to untie one each day. If he had not returned when the knots ran out, they were to sail home. Coes was later rewarded with rule over Mytilene.
b_ister_bridge.s2: Herodotus says Scythians reached the bridge before the retreating Persians and urged the Greeks to destroy it. Miltiades of the Chersonese backed them, but Histiaeus of Miletus argued that the tyrants owed their power to Darius, and the rest agreed. Many historians think Miltiades' proposal was a story told later in Athens to honour him, since Darius left him in place afterwards.
b_ister_bridge.s3: According to Herodotus, the Ionians removed only the span on the Scythian side to look obedient. When the Persians arrived at night and found the bridge apparently gone, an Egyptian with a loud voice called for Histiaeus, who brought the boats back. Ctesias tells a different story, in which Darius broke his bridges too soon in his flight and abandoned part of his army to the Scythians.
b_ister_bridge.s4: No Persian inscription or tablet mentions the Ister bridge or describes the campaign. Darius's tomb inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam lists among his peoples the Saka beyond the sea. Many scholars connect them with the Scythians of Europe, which may mean the Persian court counted the expedition a success.
b_judgment_seat.lead: Royal judges heard disputes and crimes in the King's name and were expected to speak his law. Greek writers remembered them as a powerful body of chosen Persians. Persian inscriptions present the King as the guardian of justice, and documents from Babylonia and Egypt show judges at work under Persian rule.
b_judgment_seat.play: The Judgment Seat is a service building where a Royal Judge hears cases, and houses within eight cells are calmer, a simplification of how royal justice worked. Its note on Cambyses follows Herodotus 5.25.
b_judgment_seat.s0: Herodotus says the royal judges were chosen men among the Persians who held office for life unless found guilty of injustice. They interpreted the ancestral laws and settled cases brought to them. When Cambyses wished to marry his sister, he says, the judges found no law allowing it but pointed to one letting the King do as he pleased.
b_judgment_seat.s1: At Behistun Darius says the lands respected his law and that he rewarded the loyal and punished the wicked. His tomb inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam has him declare that he is a friend to right and does not want the weak wronged by the strong, nor the strong by the weak. Justice was part of how the King described his rule.
b_judgment_seat.s2: Babylonian legal texts of the Persian period use the loanword databari, from an Old Persian title reconstructed as dātabara, law-bearer, for some judges. Aramaic papyri from Elephantine mention judges of the king and judges of the province hearing disputes in the garrison community. These texts show local courts working alongside officials who answered to the King.
b_judgment_seat.s3: Historians disagree on whether Darius imposed one law across the empire or approved local laws instead. A Ptolemaic text on the back of the Demotic Chronicle papyrus says he ordered Egyptian laws collected, and Diodorus names him among Egypt's lawgivers. Some scholars see a policy of royal authorisation of local law, while others think the evidence is too thin to show a system.
b_judgment_seat.s4: Herodotus tells that Cambyses executed the royal judge Sisamnes for taking a bribe, had him flayed, and covered the judgment seat with strips of his skin. He then made the dead man's son Otanes judge and told him to remember what he sat on. Herodotus also says Darius crucified the judge Sandoces for corruption but had him taken down on recalling his services. Both stories read as moral tales.
b_kings_eye.lead: Greek writers say the Persian king had an officer called the King's Eye, who watched and reported for him. The figure shows how Greeks imagined royal power reaching across a vast empire. No Persian document of the period uses the title, so historians still debate whether it was a single post or a Greek way of describing the king's many informants.
b_kings_eye.play: In the game the House of the King's Eye halves thefts and riots while staffed. No such building is known, and the sources place the Eye's watch over officials and subjects for the King, not over street crime, so this is a dramatization.
b_kings_eye.s0: Herodotus tells how the young Cyrus, raised as a herdsman's son, was chosen king by the village boys in a game. He gave them roles: builders of houses, bodyguards, a bearer of messages, and one boy he named the King's Eye. Herodotus presents this as a sign of royal nature, so the tale tells us what he thought a Persian court contained rather than proving the office existed under Cyrus.
b_kings_eye.s1: Aeschylus, writing in 472 BCE, has the Persian chorus ask Xerxes about a trusted companion called his Eye, which suggests Athenians already knew the phrase. Herodotus says the Median king Deioces kept watchers and listeners across his land. Xenophon later explains the saying that the king had many eyes and ears: he rewarded anyone who brought useful reports, so subjects feared to speak against him anywhere.
b_kings_eye.s2: Aristophanes, in a comedy staged in 425 BCE, brought on a Persian envoy called Pseudartabas, the King's Eye, wearing a costume with one huge eye. The joke only works if the Athenian audience recognised the title. It shows the idea was familiar in Greece, though comedy is poor evidence for how the office actually worked.
b_kings_eye.s3: No royal inscription or Persepolis tablet uses the title King's Eye. An Aramaic petition from Elephantine names local officers called gaushaka, listeners, whom some link to the king's ears. Some historians accept a real inspector who reported on satraps. Others, such as Steven Hirsch, think the Greeks turned general royal watchfulness into one post. The Persian record does show officials, sealed travel documents and couriers that kept the court informed.
b_kore.lead: A kore (Greek for 'maiden', plural korai) was a marble statue of a young woman, usually life-size or smaller, standing and richly dressed and often holding out an offering. Greeks set them up as gifts to the gods in sanctuaries and sometimes as grave markers. The largest group, from the Athenian Acropolis, survives largely because the statues were broken in the Persian sack of 480 BCE and later buried.
b_kore.play: The game offers the Kore in its housing category in Greek towns and at Sardis, as a painted maiden in a pleated chiton. Its note names only sanctuary offerings, but some korai, such as Phrasikleia, also marked graves.
b_kore.s0: Inscribed bases show that korai were dedications. The giver named himself or herself and the deity, often calling the statue an agalma, a gift meant to delight. One of the earliest, from Delos about 650 BCE, was offered to Artemis by a woman, Nikandre of Naxos. On Samos, a man named Cheramyes dedicated a kore to Hera about 570-560 BCE. It is now in the Louvre.
b_kore.s1: Some korai wear the heavy woollen peplos. The Peplos Kore from the Acropolis, of about 530 BCE, is named for it, though painted reconstructions suggest she may be a goddess in a different garment. From the middle of the 6th century many korai wear the Ionian fashion of a thin pleated linen chiton under a cloak draped diagonally. Traces of red, blue and other pigment survive on hair, eyes and hem patterns, showing that the marble was painted.
b_kore.s2: Not every kore stood in a sanctuary. The statue of Phrasikleia, found in 1972 at Merenda in Attica and signed by Aristion of Paros, marked the grave of a girl about 550-540 BCE. Her inscribed base says, in substance, that she will be called maiden forever, having received that name from the gods in place of marriage.
b_kore.s3: Herodotus says that in 480 BCE Xerxes' troops climbed the Acropolis at a sheer, unguarded spot near the shrine of Aglaurus. Some defenders threw themselves from the wall and others fled into the temple. The Persians killed those who had taken refuge there, plundered the sanctuary and set the whole citadel on fire. Herodotus does not say what became of the statues.
b_kore.s4: Excavations on the Acropolis in 1885-1890 found many korai, some still bright with paint, in fills of broken sculpture usually linked to the clean-up after the sack. Some scholars argue the debris was not all buried at once soon after 480 BCE, which affects how statues are dated. Historians also argue whom korai show: a goddess, the dedicator, a priestess or an idealised girl. Most Acropolis dedicators were men, which weakens the idea of a portrait of the giver.
b_local_shrine.lead: The empire held many peoples and paid for many gods. A town's second people wants its own priests and its own feasts, and the King's officials knew it.
b_local_shrine.play: A level's own shrine serves its second people: Humban at Parsa, Marduk at Susa, Hera on the Ister, Apollo at Marathon, a shrine at Acanthus at Athos.
b_local_shrine.s0: Fortification tablets issue grain and wine for Humban and other Elamite gods, on the same terms as Ahuramazda.
b_local_shrine.s1: Darius's charter says Babylonians made Susa's bricks. Their god's shrine there is the game's reasonable guess, not an excavated building.
b_local_shrine.s2: Mandrocles dedicated to Hera after the Bosporus bridge, and Datis to Apollo on Delos. The Ionians came with their gods, though what they built on campaign is unknown, so these shrines are guesses too.
b_magi_altar.lead: Where the town's main temple is someone else's, the Persians still need a fire and a magus. Two plinths and a stepped altar in the open air, after Pasargadae and the tomb reliefs, is as much as the evidence allows.
b_magi_altar.play: Built where another people's temple is the main one (Memphis, Susa, Sardis, Plataea). Its magus walks to the Persian quarters, and the Persian rites can be held here.
b_magi_altar.s0: Two limestone plinths stand in the sacred precinct at Pasargadae, one with a stair. What stood on them is inferred from later reliefs: the king, a fire, or both.
b_magi_altar.s1: Above Darius's tomb the King stands on a stepped base before a burning altar, a winged figure above. It's the model for this altar's shape.
b_magi_altar.s2: No Achaemenid fire temple is secure. So the Altar has no roof and no door.
b_magi_lodge.lead: Inside the enclosure of Cyrus's tomb at Pasargadae stood a small house for the magi who guarded it. Arrian, drawing on Alexander's officer Aristobulus, says these men held the post from father to son from the reign of Cambyses onward, fed by the King with rations and animals for sacrifice to the dead founder. The lodge shows how the Persian court kept up the cult of its royal dead.
b_magi_lodge.play: The game follows Arrian's daily sheep, flour and wine and monthly horse, though in 530 BCE Cambyses' arrangement would be brand new and no son had yet inherited it. The magus blessing nearby houses is a game invention, not a recorded duty.
b_magi_lodge.s0: Arrian, drawing on Aristobulus, who served Alexander, describes the tomb standing in a royal park with trees, water and deep grass. Within the enclosure was a small house built for the magi who guarded the tomb. He says the charge had passed from father to son since the time of Cambyses. Strabo gives a similar description of the tomb, also citing Aristobulus.
b_magi_lodge.s1: According to Arrian, the King gave the guardians a sheep each day, a fixed amount of wheat flour and wine, and a horse each month to sacrifice to Cyrus. No Persian text names these amounts. Herodotus separately says magi sacrificed white horses at the Strymon in 480 BCE, so horse offerings led by magi appear in more than one Greek source.
b_magi_lodge.s2: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, from about 509 to 493 BCE, record grain, wine and animals issued for offerings at the tombs, in Elamite šumar, of royal figures such as Cambyses and Hystaspes. They also name magi, makuš, receiving supplies for sacrifices. They do not mention the guardians of Cyrus's tomb, and excavation at Pasargadae has not identified any building as the magi's house.
b_magi_lodge.s3: Herodotus calls the magi a tribe of the Medes, and Darius's Behistun inscription calls the usurper Gaumata a magus. The tablets show magi in Persis as paid ritual specialists who also made offerings to gods outside any strictly Zoroastrian scheme. Historians still argue over how far Achaemenid religion was Zoroastrian, so the beliefs of the tomb's guardians remain uncertain.
b_magi_lodge.s4: Arrian says Alexander found the tomb robbed on his return from India in 324. He had the magi arrested and tortured to make them name the thieves, but they revealed nothing and he released them. He then ordered Aristobulus to restore the burial.
b_mardonius_fort.lead: Before the battle of Plataea, the Persian commander Mardonius built a square wooden fort in Theban territory beside the Asopus as a refuge for his army. Herodotus says it measured about ten stades on each side. After Mardonius fell, his beaten troops fled inside, and its storming by the Greeks ended the last Persian land campaign in mainland Greece.
b_mardonius_fort.play: The game sets it within four cells of the Asopus and builds it from barley, timber and limestone. Herodotus mentions only a wooden wall, built in 479 BCE; the rampart, ditch, towers and limestone gates are the game's reconstruction.
b_mardonius_fort.s0: Herodotus says that in 479 BCE Mardonius withdrew from Attica into Boeotia and camped along the Asopus, from Erythrae past Hysiae into Plataean land. He had the trees of the district felled to build a wooden wall, even though the Thebans were his allies. The fort was meant as a refuge if the battle went badly. Herodotus gives its size as about ten stades a side, roughly 1.8 kilometres.
b_mardonius_fort.s1: No trace of the fort has been found and no Persian text mentions it, so its exact site north of the Asopus is still argued over. A square of ten stades could not have held the 300,000 men Herodotus gives Mardonius, a figure most historians think greatly exaggerated. Many scholars therefore see the fort as a guarded base for baggage, supplies and a garrison rather than a camp for the whole army.
b_mardonius_fort.s2: After Mardonius was killed, Herodotus says, the Persians ran back to the wooden wall and held it against the Spartans, who had little skill in attacking walls. When the Athenians came up they made a breach, the Tegeans entered first, and a slaughter followed. Herodotus claims that fewer than 3,000 survived apart from the 40,000 led away by Artabazus, numbers modern historians treat with caution.
b_mardonius_fort.s3: Herodotus describes gold and silver vessels, rich tents and furnishings taken from the Persian camp. The Tegeans carried off a bronze manger from Mardonius's horses and dedicated it to Athena Alea. Pausanias had the spoil gathered by helots, and a tenth was set aside for the gods at Delphi, Olympia and the Isthmus.
b_mardonius_fort.s4: Herodotus tells that Pausanias, finding the tent Xerxes had left to Mardonius, ordered the Persian cooks to prepare a royal banquet and his own servants a plain Spartan meal beside it. He then laughed at the folly of a man who lived so richly yet came to rob the Greeks of their poor fare. The story is shaped as a moral tale about wealth and simplicity.
b_muster_ground.lead: The Persian kings raised armies by calling men to gather at set places, where they were counted, inspected and put under commanders. The muster linked the King's power to the households that owed him service. It was how an empire of many peoples turned farmers, landholders and subject contingents into a fighting force.
b_muster_ground.play: The Muster Ground calls up to a quarter of the town's men to form up with spear, shield and bow. No ancient source gives a fixed share like this. Real levies drew on service-holdings and royal demands, and their size varied.
b_muster_ground.s0: In the Behistun inscription, Darius uses the Old Persian word kāra for the body of men he sent against the rebels. The same word can mean both the people and the army. This suggests that, for the Persians, the armed host was the Persian and Median people called out under the King's generals. The inscription names the commanders Darius sent with these forces in 522-521 BCE.
b_muster_ground.s1: Babylonian documents show plots of crown land granted as bow-land, horse-land and chariot-land. Holders owed the King a soldier equipped to match the type of land. Over time many paid silver instead of serving in person. The fullest evidence comes from the Murashu archive of Nippur, which dates from later in the fifth century.
b_muster_ground.s2: Herodotus says that Xerxes' army for Greece assembled at Critalla in Cappadocia. It was later counted on the plain of Doriscus in Thrace. There, he says, ten thousand men were packed into a space, a wall was built round it, and the enclosure was filled again and again until all had passed through. His total of 1,700,000 foot soldiers is far larger than modern historians accept.
b_muster_ground.s3: Xenophon, writing in the fourth century, says the Persian king reviewed the garrison troops he maintained each year. He did this himself near his residence and sent trusted men to review the garrisons further away. He rewarded officers whose men were full in number and well armed, and punished those who neglected them. Xenophon admired the Persians and may have idealised the practice.
b_muster_ground.s4: Historians still argue over how large royal levies were and who was called. Some stress Persian and Median core troops and the holders of service-land. Others weigh Herodotus's long lists of subject contingents. Most modern estimates for Xerxes' land army in 480 BCE fall somewhere between about 70,000 and 300,000, far below Herodotus's figure.
b_obelisk.lead: An obelisk was a tall, four-sided stone shaft that tapered to a small pyramid at the top. Egyptian kings usually set obelisks in pairs before temple gates as signs of the sun god. By the Persian conquest of 525 BCE many had stood for centuries, and the Saite kings had recently added more. No obelisk is securely known to have been raised for a Persian king.
b_obelisk.play: The game offers the Obelisk as a housing building in Memphis only. Its note cites Herodotus, but those passages describe obelisks at Heliopolis and Sais, not Memphis. Most obelisks were Aswan granite, though not all.
b_obelisk.s0: Most obelisks were cut from the red granite of Aswan, at the southern edge of Egypt, though a few were made of quartzite or other stone. An unfinished obelisk still lies in the Aswan quarry. It cracked before it could be freed and was abandoned. Workers shaped it by pounding the granite with balls of hard dolerite, and the trenches they made can still be seen around the shaft.
b_obelisk.s1: Obelisks were linked to the sun cult of Heliopolis, and their tips were sometimes sheathed in metal to catch the light. The obelisk of Senusret I, raised about 1950, still stands there, and inscriptions on Hatshepsut's obelisks at Karnak record their making. The Saite kings Psamtik II and Apries set up obelisks at Heliopolis and Sais in the decades before the Persian conquest. Both now stand in Rome, where emperors later carried them.
b_obelisk.s2: Herodotus says that a king he calls Pheros dedicated two obelisks at the temple of the Sun in Heliopolis. He says each was made of one stone and was a hundred cubits high, roughly 45 to 50 metres. The tallest standing obelisk, now in Rome, is about 32 metres, so his figure is probably exaggerated. He also describes great stone obelisks in the sacred precinct at Sais, beside a lake.
b_obelisk.s3: Herodotus tells how Pheros hurled a spear into the flooding Nile and was struck blind. An oracle said he would be cured by washing his eyes in the urine of a woman faithful to her husband. His own wife failed, and he burned the women who had failed, married the one who cured him and then gave gifts to the temples, the obelisks among them. The name Pheros is probably the royal title pharaoh mistaken for a name.
b_obelisk.s4: No Egyptian text explains how an obelisk weighing hundreds of tonnes was moved and stood upright. Scholars have proposed earth ramps, levering, and lowering the shaft into a pit of sand that was slowly emptied. Modern experiments have shown that some of these methods can work, but which methods the Egyptians used, and whether they varied, remains uncertain.
b_older_parthenon.lead: The Older Parthenon was a large temple to Athena, set on a limestone platform with columns of Pentelic marble. It was still under construction when the Persians took the Acropolis in 480 BCE. Its fire-damaged column drums were later built into the Acropolis wall, and its platform carried the Parthenon that Pericles began in 447 BCE.
b_older_parthenon.play: The Older Parthenon stands on a level's map as a historic structure; the player does not build it. The game dates its start to after Marathon, the most common modern view, though historians still debate that date.
b_older_parthenon.s0: Excavations in the 1880s and later studies show a massive podium of limestone blocks, deepened on the south side where the rock fell away. On this podium builders had begun a temple in white marble from Mount Pentelicus, one of the first large marble buildings in Athens. Only the lower parts were ever set in place. Many drums still keep the rough protective surface that masons would have removed at the end of the work.
b_older_parthenon.s1: W. B. Dinsmoor argued that the temple was started soon after Marathon in 490 BCE, probably as a thank-offering for the victory. Others think the limestone podium is older and belonged to an earlier plan, with the marble temple added on top in a second phase. The link to Marathon is likely, but it rests on building evidence and inference, not on any ancient text.
b_older_parthenon.s2: Herodotus says that in 480 BCE the Persians climbed the steep face of the Acropolis near the shrine of Aglaurus. They killed the Athenians who had stayed behind, plundered the sanctuary and set the whole citadel on fire. He does not name the unfinished temple, but it stood within the area he describes as burned.
b_older_parthenon.s3: After the war the Athenians rebuilt the north wall of the Acropolis. They set into it a row of the temple's marble drums beside blocks from the Old Temple of Athena. The drums are cracked and discoloured by fire, which suggests the wooden scaffolding around them burned. They are still visible from the Agora below. Many historians read this as a deliberate reminder of the sack, though it also reused heavy stone close at hand.
b_older_parthenon.s4: The orator Lycurgus, writing about 330, and later Diodorus say the Greeks swore an oath before Plataea in 479 BCE. In it they promised to leave the temples burned by the Persians unrebuilt, as memorials.
