Theopompus already called the oath an Athenian forgery, and a fourth-century copy inscribed at Acharnae lacks that clause. Scholars remain divided, but the site did lie unfinished for about thirty years until the Periclean Parthenon rose on the old podium.
b_orchard.lead: Across the empire, fruit trees grew on watered land: date palms in Babylonia, figs, vines and other fruit in Persis, and mixed groves on royal estates. Palace records show fruit as rations and as royal food. Greek writers, and a royal letter of disputed authenticity, link the planting of trees to good rule, so the orchard was both a working farm and a mark of the King's care for the land.
b_orchard.play: In the game the Orchard is a food building of fruit trees watered from canals, and Elder's Houses want its fruit. This is a simplification: real orchards also grew on upland estates in Persis, fed by channels from streams.
b_orchard.s0: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, written in Elamite between about 509 and 493 BCE, record fruit moving through the King's economy. Dates and figs appear as rations for workers and as supplies for royal and elite households. Some texts appear to concern fruit trees for planting on estates, including the walled parks the tablets call partetaš, the Elamite form of the Persian word that lies behind the Greek paradeisos.
b_orchard.s1: In Babylonia the date palm was the main orchard tree, planted along canals on the river plain. Business archives such as the Egibi texts, and the later Murashu archive from Nippur (after 479 BCE), record leases of date groves, the shares owed by gardeners and rents paid in dates. These documents show orchards as carefully managed property, tied to access to canal water.
b_orchard.s2: Herodotus says palm trees grew all over the Babylonian plain and that people made food, wine and honey from their fruit. He also describes growers tying the fruit of the palms the Greeks called male to the fruit-bearing trees. He explains this, mistakenly, by comparing it with the Greek treatment of fig trees. His account fits the importance of dates shown in Babylonian documents.
b_orchard.s3: A Greek inscription from Magnesia on the Maeander presents a letter of Darius praising his official Gadatas for planting fruit trees from beyond the Euphrates in the lower parts of Asia, while rebuking him for taxing the sacred gardeners of Apollo. The surviving stone was cut in Roman times. Some historians accept it as a copy of a real royal letter. Others, notably Pierre Briant, have argued that it is a later forgery.
b_orchard.s4: Xenophon, writing in the 4th century, says the Persian king saw to it that his parks were full of trees and that the land was well cultivated. He tells how Cyrus the Younger showed the Spartan Lysander his park at Sardis, with trees planted in straight rows, and claimed to have planted some himself. The scene is later than this game's period, but it shows how Greeks linked planting to royal virtue.
b_orchard_date_grove.lead: The date palm had grown in Egypt for many centuries and was among its most useful trees. Its fruit was eaten fresh or dried and used as a sweetener, and its trunks and fronds served as timber, roofing, matting and rope. When Cambyses conquered Egypt in 525 BCE, palm groves stood among the fields and villages around Memphis, as they had long before Persian rule.
b_orchard_date_grove.play: In the Memphis level the Orchard takes the form of a Date Grove of palms on the black land, and Elder's Houses want dates. Black land renders kemet, the Egyptians' name for their country, taken from the dark Nile soil.
b_orchard_date_grove.s0: Date stones and dried fruit have been found in Egyptian graves and settlements, and dates were laid among the food offerings in tombs. Such finds become much more common from the second millennium, when the cultivated palm spread widely. New Kingdom tomb paintings show date palms and the branching dom palm in gardens and beside pools. The ruins of Memphis at Mit Rahina still lie among palm groves today.
b_orchard_date_grove.s1: Texts and remains show dates eaten whole, dried for storage and used to sweeten bread, since honey was costly. Older studies held that dates also flavoured beer, but residue analysis has not confirmed this. Palm trunks made beams and roofing, the ribs of the fronds made baskets and crates, and the fibre made rope. A grove gave a household food and materials from the same trees.
b_orchard_date_grove.s2: Herodotus says Egyptian embalmers washed out the body cavity with palm wine and then with ground spices before filling it. Writing of Babylonia, he describes a plain full of palms that gave bread, wine and a kind of honey. He compares the fertilising of the palms with the treatment of figs, which shows that he misunderstood how palms are pollinated.
b_orchard_date_grove.s3: Date palms grew in the warm lowlands of Elam and southern Persis. The Elamite tablets of the Persepolis Fortification archive, written under Darius, record dates among the commodities issued from royal stores, alongside grain, wine and beer. The Persians who came to Egypt therefore already knew the tree and its fruit.
b_orchard_date_grove.s4: Herodotus lists Egypt's tribute in silver, fish revenue and grain for the Persian garrison at Memphis, but says nothing of dates. How palm groves were taxed under Cambyses and Darius is not known in detail. Historians debate how far Persian rule changed Egyptian landholding, and many, Briant among them, stress continuity. Strabo, writing under Augustus, judged the dates of Lower Egypt poorer than those of the south.
b_orchard_olive_grove.lead: Olive groves covered the dry hillsides of Greece and the Aegean coasts in the years of the Persian Wars, and their oil served as food, lamp fuel and the cleanser of bathers and athletes. Later Greek writers say Athenian law let oil alone of the farm's produce be sold abroad. For a Persian official the olive marked the Mediterranean edge of the empire, far from the sesame-oil lands of Babylonia.
b_orchard_olive_grove.play: In the Greek levels, from Marathon to Plataea, the Orchard becomes an Olive Grove on dry ground that needs no river soil. It is slow to bear, its oil is pressed on the estate, and Elder's Houses want it.
b_orchard_olive_grove.s0: Linear B tablets from Knossos and Pylos, written centuries before the Persian Wars, already list olive oil, much of it perfumed. Stone press weights, oil jars and olive stones are found on Archaic Greek sites. At Klazomenai in Ionia, a city under Persian rule from the 540s BCE, excavators uncovered a workshop of probably the 6th century. There, crushed olives were squeezed under a weighted wooden beam, and the oil was left to separate from the watery juice.
b_orchard_olive_grove.s1: Plutarch, writing some seven centuries later, says that Solon in the early 6th century allowed Athenians to export olive oil but no other produce of the soil. He adds that Solon set a minimum distance between a newly planted olive and a neighbour's land. The Constitution of the Athenians, written in Aristotle's school about 330, describes oil from Athena's sacred olives being given as prizes at the Panathenaic games.
b_orchard_olive_grove.s2: Herodotus says the land of Babylonia did not even try to bear the olive, and that the Babylonians used oil pressed from sesame instead. The olive belonged to the Mediterranean rim of the Persian empire: the Ionian and Carian coast, Cyprus, Phoenicia and the Levant. The armies that crossed into Greece in 490 and 480 BCE entered country where the olive was everywhere.
b_orchard_olive_grove.s3: A new olive grove took years to bear a good crop, so invaders were thought to strike hard by cutting and burning it. Herodotus says Mardonius burned Athens before he withdrew in 479 BCE, though he does not speak of the groves. Victor Davis Hanson argued that mature olives are hard to fell or burn and grow back from the stump, so the real loss was a few harvests. Other historians think repeated raids could do lasting harm to farms.
b_orchard_olive_grove.s4: Athenians believed Athena had given them the olive in her contest with Poseidon for the land. Herodotus says the Persians burned the sacred tree with the sanctuary in 480 BCE, yet the next day a shoot a cubit long had sprung from the stump. He also passes on a story that at one time olives grew nowhere but at Athens, a claim that does not fit the evidence.
b_palace.lead: Palace P is the modern name for a large columned building beside the royal garden at Pasargadae, the first royal centre built by Cyrus. Scholars call it the residential palace, though its exact use is unknown. Its excavator concluded that Cyrus began it and left it unfinished at his death in 530 BCE, and that work went on under Darius.
b_palace.play: In the Pasargadae level (530 BCE) the Residential Palace is a monument raised stone by stone from limestone blocks and timber. The game does not show the later work, probably under Darius, that finished its carved doorways.
b_palace.s0: David Stronach's excavations of 1961 to 1963 uncovered a central hall with thirty columns set in five rows of six, flanked by two porticoes, the longer one facing the garden. The column bases paired dark and pale stone, a two-coloured effect also seen in Palace S nearby. The roof and ceilings were of timber, which has not survived.
b_palace.s1: Parts of the building were left rough or incomplete, and the doorway reliefs differ in style from the rest of the work. Only the lower parts of the reliefs survive, showing the King's feet and the hem of his robe. A short trilingual inscription on the robe folds names Cyrus as Great King, an Achaemenid. Stronach concluded that Cyrus died before the palace was done and that Darius completed it.
b_palace.s2: The inscriptions are in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. At Behistun, Darius claims that a new form of writing was made under him, and many scholars take this to mean the Old Persian script was created in his reign. If so, the inscriptions naming Cyrus were added by Darius, who had reason to honour the founder. Others argue that the script may already have existed under Cyrus.
b_palace.s3: Tool marks and joints show techniques known from western Asia Minor, such as the claw chisel, iron clamps and finely dressed joint surfaces. From this evidence Carl Nylander argued that craftsmen from Lydia and Ionia worked at Pasargadae after Cyrus took Sardis. If he is right, the building drew on the skills of newly subject peoples.
b_palace.s4: Strabo, writing more than five centuries later, says that Cyrus honoured Pasargadae because he had defeated Astyages the Mede there in his last battle, and that he built a city and palace on the spot. No excavated evidence ties the site to that battle. The story may have grown from the place's fame as Cyrus's city.
b_palace_bath.lead: The palaces of the Persian kings had built drains and paved or plastered rooms where water could be poured and carried away. Excavation shows a careful system of channels beneath the terrace at Persepolis. Exactly which rooms served for washing is still argued, and no known text of the period names a bath.
b_palace_bath.play: The game's Palace Bath is a service that Elder's Houses and Noble Residences within nine cells use. That is a simplification: palace washrooms belonged to royal buildings, and nothing shows a shared bath serving several households.
b_palace_bath.s0: Excavators at Persepolis found a network of channels cut into the rock and built under the terrace. The system was probably laid out before the palaces were raised on top of it. It carried rainwater and wastewater from roofs, courts and some rooms down and away from the platform. At Pasargadae, stone water channels ran through the royal garden, which shows the same skill in handling water.
b_palace_bath.s1: Some small rooms in the palaces have paved or plastered floors with outlets that lead into the drains. Excavators have read some of these as washrooms or latrines. Other scholars think some were service or storage rooms that simply needed drainage. No known inscription or tablet of the period labels a room as a bath, so each identification rests on the floor and the plumbing alone.
b_palace_bath.s2: Herodotus says that Persians did not urinate or spit into a river and did not wash their hands in one. Strabo, writing much later, also describes Persian reverence for water. If the Greek writers are right, washing was probably done with water drawn into basins and then drained away, not in streams. They may have simplified a custom they knew only at second hand.
b_palace_bath.s3: Plutarch tells how Alexander, after the battle of Issus in 333, entered the captured tent of Darius III. There he found a bath fitted with gold vessels, basins and perfumes, and remarked that this, it seemed, was what being a king meant. The story was written down more than four centuries later. It is shaped as a moral tale about Persian luxury and says little about palace bathrooms in the time of Darius I.
b_pasture.lead: Sheep and goats were kept in every province of the Persian empire. They gave meat for royal tables and offerings, milk, skins, goat hair and wool for cloth. The Persepolis tablets count flocks held by the administration in Persis, and Babylonian temple archives show flocks entrusted to herdsmen who owed fixed returns of young animals and wool.
b_pasture.play: The pen keeps sheep and goats, sends wool to the weavers and culls the flock for meat. This is simplified: goats give hair rather than wool, and many real flocks probably moved between seasonal pastures rather than living in a fixed pen.
b_pasture.s0: The Elamite tablets of the Persepolis Fortification archive, written in about 509 to 493 BCE, record sheep and goats held by the administration around Persepolis. Animals were counted by kind, age and sex, and issued to officials and the royal household, and for offerings to the gods. On the Apadana reliefs at Persepolis, several subject delegations lead rams as gifts for the King.
b_pasture.s1: The Eanna temple at Uruk owned large flocks, which it handed to herdsmen under contract. Each herdsman owed a set number of young animals and a quantity of wool, and inspectors checked the flocks and chased up losses. These records run on without a break into the reigns of Cyrus and Cambyses, showing that Persian rule left the system in place. Temple wool went to weavers who made garments for the gods' statues.
b_pasture.s2: Herodotus lists the Persian tribes and says that four of them, the Dai, Mardi, Dropici and Sagartians, were nomads, while others, such as the Panthialaei, Derusiaei and Germanii, were farmers. His picture is a Greek outsider's, but it fits a Persis where settled farming and herding existed side by side.
b_pasture.s3: Historians usually assume that flocks in Persis moved between lowland winter grazing and highland summer pasture, as herds in the region did in later times. The tablets do not describe these routes directly, and scholars still argue over how far the early Persians were pastoral nomads and how far settled farmers. It is also unclear how often wool was shorn with blades or plucked by hand, as older Mesopotamian practice had been.
b_pasture.s4: Herodotus tells how Cyrus, planning revolt against the Medes, made the Persians clear a field of thorns one day and the next day feasted them on his father's goats, sheep and oxen. He then asked which day they preferred, offering freedom as the feast and Median rule as the toil. The story is a moral tale, not a record, but it assumes that a Persian noble's wealth lay in his herds.
b_perfumer.lead: Greek writers counted scented oil among the luxuries of Lydia, and some linked a Lydian unguent with the name bakkaris. Perfume was made by steeping flowers, spices and resins in oil. It was used on the body and hair and given as gifts between rulers. Under Persian rule Sardis was the seat of a satrap, and its trade in fine oils probably carried on.
b_perfumer.play: In the Sardis level perfumers steep pressed fruit and flowers in oil, drawing fruit from the granaries to supply unguent to Noble Residences. Real perfumers scented oil with flowers, spices and resins, not fruit alone.
b_perfumer.s0: The poet Xenophanes of Colophon, writing in the 500s BCE, complained that his fellow citizens had learned useless luxuries from the Lydians. He pictured them in purple cloaks, proud of their dressed hair and soaked in scented oil. Athenaeus, writing many centuries later, preserves these lines. He also discusses bakkaris, a word some Greeks linked with Lydian unguent, though others used it for a plant.
b_perfumer.s1: Theophrastus, writing about 300, describes how Greek perfumers worked. They first treated an oil so that it would take up scent. Then they steeped aromatics such as flowers, spices and resins in it, sometimes with gentle heat. His account comes two centuries after the Persian period, but the basic craft was old and was probably similar in Lydia.
b_perfumer.s2: Excavators at Sardis have found many lydia, small round jars with a flaring foot and lip, and the shape was traded and copied in Greek lands. Many scholars think these jars held unguent, perhaps bakkaris, because of their size and wide spread. Their contents have not been firmly established, so the link between the jar and the perfume trade remains a likely guess.
b_perfumer.s3: Doorway reliefs in the palace of Darius at Persepolis show the King followed by attendants carrying items for his person, among them a towel. A small vessel held by an attendant is often read as a flask of scented oil, though that reading is an interpretation. The reliefs say nothing about where such oils were made, and Sardis is only one of several possible sources.
b_perfumer.s4: Herodotus says that Cambyses sent Fish-eaters from Elephantine as spies to the king of the Ethiopians. Their gifts included a purple garment, gold ornaments, palm wine and an alabaster jar of myrrh ointment. The story is told to make a point about Ethiopian simplicity, but it shows that Greeks expected Persian kings to give scented oils as marks of favour.
b_physician.lead: Egyptian doctors had a high reputation across the ancient Near East, and the Persian kings sent for them. Herodotus tells of an eye doctor sent to Cyrus, and the Egyptian chief physician Udjahorresnet served Cambyses and Darius. Their presence at court shows how the empire drew skilled people from its provinces into the King's service.
b_physician.play: An Egyptian physician walks the streets and cures the sickness he passes, each healing one disease as Herodotus describes. Real royal physicians mostly treated the court, and the one-disease rule is overstated.
b_physician.s0: Herodotus says that Cyrus asked Amasis, king of Egypt, for the best eye doctor in the country. Amasis sent one, parting him from his wife and children, and the doctor bore a grudge. In Herodotus's telling he later urged Cambyses to ask for Amasis's daughter in marriage, knowing the request would cause offence. Herodotus presents this as one cause of the Persian invasion of Egypt in 525 BCE.
b_physician.s1: Herodotus writes that in Egypt each physician treated one disease only, so the country was full of doctors for the eyes, head, teeth, belly and hidden ailments. Egyptian titles do name specialists, such as physicians of the eyes and of the belly. But the surviving medical papyri, such as the Ebers and Edwin Smith papyri, cover many conditions, and many doctors held general titles, so historians think Herodotus overstated the rule.
b_physician.s2: The statue of Udjahorresnet, now in the Vatican, carries his own account of his career. He served as chief physician under Cambyses and Darius. He says Darius, while in Elam, sent him back to Egypt to restore the House of Life, a temple institution for learned texts including medicine, probably at Sais, and to furnish it with staff and equipment. The text shows a Persian king supporting Egyptian medical learning.
b_physician.s3: Herodotus tells that Darius twisted his ankle leaping from his horse while hunting. The Egyptian doctors at court wrenched the foot and made it worse, until a Greek captive, Democedes of Croton, eased it with gentler treatment. Darius meant to impale the Egyptians, but Democedes pleaded for them. The story flatters Greek medicine, and only Greek sources tell it.
b_physician_greek_surgery.lead: A Greek surgery, or iatreion, was the room where a physician saw patients, set bones and dressed wounds. Herodotus says some Greek cities of this period paid a doctor a yearly fee from public funds to keep him in town. Greek doctors also served the Persian kings, most famously Democedes of Croton at the court of Darius.
b_physician_greek_surgery.play: The game's yearly city fee follows Herodotus on Democedes. A doctor who cures whatever sickness he passes is a simplification: Greek physicians treated patients in the surgery or at home, and many illnesses they could not cure.
b_physician_greek_surgery.s0: Herodotus says Democedes left Croton and settled in Aegina, where in his first year he outdid the established physicians even though he had no instruments. In the second year the Aeginetans hired him for a talent of public money, in the third the Athenians paid him 100 minas, and in the fourth Polycrates of Samos paid two talents. Herodotus adds that the doctors of Croton were then thought the best among the Greeks.
b_physician_greek_surgery.s1: After the satrap Oroetes had Polycrates killed, about 522 BCE, Democedes was seized among his followers and later brought to Susa. Herodotus says Darius twisted his ankle leaping from his horse while hunting, his Egyptian doctors made it worse, and Democedes cured him with gentler Greek treatment. The King rewarded him richly. No Persian document mentions Democedes, so the story rests chiefly on Herodotus.
b_physician_greek_surgery.s2: A bronze tablet from Idalion in Cyprus, written in the Cypriot syllabic script and probably dating to the first half of the 5th century, records a contract with a doctor. When the Medes, meaning the Persians, and the Kitians besieged the city, the king Stasikypros and the city engaged the physician Onasilos and his brothers to treat the wounded without charging them. Instead of the promised silver, the city granted them land.
b_physician_greek_surgery.s3: Herodotus does not say what Aegina expected for its talent. L. Cohn-Haft argued that such fees paid a doctor to settle in a city and that he still charged his patients. Other historians think some citizens were treated free. Most evidence for public physicians comes from inscriptions of the 4th century and later, so how common the arrangement was around 500 BCE is uncertain.
b_physician_greek_surgery.s4: The Hippocratic treatise In the Surgery describes the physician's workroom: good light, ready instruments, and careful rules for bandaging and splinting. Other Hippocratic writings show doctors also visiting patients in their homes. These texts were probably written in the late 5th or 4th century, so they describe practice somewhat later than the game's levels.
b_plane_tree.lead: The oriental plane (Platanus orientalis) is a broad, long-lived tree native to the eastern Mediterranean and western Asia. It gives deep shade near water. Greek writers linked it with the Persian kings: Herodotus tells how Xerxes honoured a plane tree in Lydia, and the kings owned a famous plane tree made of gold.
b_plane_tree.play: The game offers the Plane Tree as a shade tree among housing, with a note on Xerxes taken from Herodotus 7.31. The game sets it in town, while the tree Xerxes honoured stood along his line of march in Lydia.
b_plane_tree.s0: Excavations at Pasargadae uncovered a royal garden laid out with stone water channels and planting beds around Cyrus's palaces. The remains show that trees and plants were set out in an ordered plan. They do not show which species were grown, so the plane tree cannot be securely placed there, although it suits such watered ground well.
b_plane_tree.s1: Herodotus says that in 481 BCE, while marching from Phrygia to Sardis, where the army wintered, Xerxes came upon a plane tree just beyond Callatebus in Lydia. He found it so beautiful that he gave it gold ornaments and left one of the Immortals to guard it. Herodotus tells the story briefly and without criticism.
b_plane_tree.s2: Herodotus reports that the Lydian Pythius had earlier given Darius a plane tree and a vine made of gold. Xenophon describes the Arcadian envoy Antiochus, back from the royal court in 367, scoffing that the famous golden plane tree was too small to shade a grasshopper. If this was the same object, as is probable, it stayed a known treasure of the royal household for well over a century.
b_plane_tree.s3: Historians disagree about what Xerxes' gesture meant. Some read it as private delight in a fine tree. Others, including Briant, connect it to royal ideas of the king as the one who makes the land fertile and keeps it green, an idea also seen in the kings' gardens and the golden plane. The Persian sources themselves say nothing about this tree.
b_plane_tree.s4: Aelian, a Greek writer of the Roman period around 200 CE, turned the Lydian plane into a moral story. He presented Xerxes' love for a tree as foolish excess, the kind of tale used to contrast Persian luxury with Greek restraint. His version adds details that Herodotus does not give and should not be taken as fact.
b_plataea_demeter.lead: A sanctuary of Eleusinian Demeter stood near the river Moloeis below Mount Cithaeron. In 479 BCE the Spartans and Tegeans fought Mardonius's Persian infantry beside it, and the battle that ended the invasion of Greece was decided there. Herodotus noted that no Persian was found dead inside the sacred ground.
b_plataea_demeter.play: The precinct stands on the Plataea map as a historic structure; the player does not build it. The game's note on the fighting and the missing Persian dead follows Herodotus.
b_plataea_demeter.s0: Herodotus says that when the Greeks shifted position by night, the Spartans were the last to move because one officer, Amompharetus, refused to retreat. They halted near the river Moloeis, at a place called Argiopion, where there was a sanctuary of Eleusinian Demeter. There they waited for his company to rejoin them.
b_plataea_demeter.s1: Mardonius led his Persians across the Asopus at a run to attack the Spartans and Tegeans, and the fighting took place by the precinct. Herodotus says the Persians matched the Greeks in courage and strength but lacked armour and skill, rushing forward singly or in small groups. Mardonius fell fighting with his picked guard of a thousand, and the Persians then fled.
b_plataea_demeter.s2: Herodotus records it as a wonder that, although the battle was fought by Demeter's grove, no Persian was seen to enter the precinct or die inside it; most fell around the shrine on unconsecrated ground. He suggests, with caution about judging divine matters, that the goddess refused them because they had burned her sanctuary at Eleusis. He adds that the battle at Mycale was also fought beside a precinct of Eleusinian Demeter.
b_plataea_demeter.s3: Plutarch, writing some six centuries later, tells of a Delphic oracle bidding the Athenians fight in the plain of Eleusinian Demeter and Kore. The Plataean general Arimnestus dreamed that Zeus the Saviour told him the places of the oracle lay near Plataea. The oldest Plataeans then showed him an ancient temple of Eleusinian Demeter and Kore near Hysiae under Cithaeron.
b_plataea_demeter.s4: The precinct has not been securely located, and the Moloeis and Argiopion cannot be fixed with certainty. Topographers have placed it at different points on the ridges between the Asopus and Cithaeron, some near Hysiae and others further west. Because the course of the battle depends on these positions, reconstructions of Plataea still differ.
b_plataea_heraion.lead: The Plataeans honoured Hera in a sanctuary that stood in front of their city. At the battle of Plataea in 479 BCE it became a fixed point in the story. Many allied contingents halted there after a confused night march, and the Spartan commander Pausanias turned towards it to pray before his men charged the Persian army of Mardonius.
b_plataea_heraion.play: The sanctuary stands on the Plataea map as a historic structure. The player cannot build it.
b_plataea_heraion.s0: Herodotus says the Greeks were short of water and harried by Persian cavalry, so they planned to move by night to a new position called the Island. The contingents of the centre did not go there. They hurried back towards Plataea and halted at the Heraion. He places it in front of the city, about twenty stades from the spring Gargaphia. The Spartans and Athenians were left on their own, some way off.
b_plataea_heraion.s1: Herodotus says that when the Persians attacked the Spartans and Tegeans the following morning, the sacrifices gave bad omens, and the hoplites stood under arrow fire without moving. Pausanias looked towards the Heraion of the Plataeans and called on the goddess not to let the Greeks be cheated of their hope. While he still prayed, the Tegeans moved forward. Soon afterwards the omens turned good and the Spartans advanced as well.
b_plataea_heraion.s2: Herodotus says the Greeks camped around the Heraion took no part in the main fighting. When they heard that Pausanias was winning, they set off in disorder. The Megarians and Phliasians crossed open plain and were caught by Theban cavalry, who killed about six hundred of them.
b_plataea_heraion.s3: Thucydides says that after Plataea fell to Sparta and Thebes in 427 BCE and was razed, a large hostel was built near the Heraion, along with a stone temple of Hera about a hundred feet long. Pausanias the travel writer later saw a temple of Hera at Plataea with statues of Hera and Rhea by Praxiteles. Modern scholars still disagree over where the sanctuary of 479 BCE stood, and this affects how the movements of the battle are reconstructed.
b_plataea_heraion.s4: Pausanias the travel writer tells a story from the region. Hera quarrelled with Zeus and withdrew to Cithaeron. Zeus won her back by pretending to marry a wooden figure dressed as a bride. The Plataeans said this was the origin of their festival of the Daedala, held in honour of Hera. The tale was written down more than six centuries after the battle.
b_potter.lead: Potters supplied the jars, bowls and jugs that every household, temple and royal storehouse depended on. In the Persian empire the potter's wheel and kiln were old, local crafts that carried on under the new rulers, and much of the empire's wine, beer and oil was stored and carried in clay jars.
b_potter.play: The Potter's Yard turns clay into pottery, which Courtyard Houses want. The game reduces a varied craft to one good; real potters also made the large jars used to store and carry wine, beer and oil.
b_potter.s0: Excavations at Pasargadae and Persepolis have produced plenty of plain, wheel-made pottery: storage jars, jugs, cooking pots and bowls. Most of it is practical rather than decorated, which suggests local workshops making the vessels that builders, guards and court staff needed day to day. Painted wares are uncommon at these sites compared with earlier periods in western Iran.
b_potter.s1: The Persepolis Fortification tablets record wine, beer and oil issued to workers, travellers and officials, counted in fixed capacity units such as the quart and the marriš. The tablets rarely name the containers, but liquids on this scale had to be stored and moved in vessels, and clay jars were the cheapest and most common kind. The tablets themselves were mostly unbaked clay, a sign of how basic the material was to the administration.
b_potter.s2: Herodotus says that the wine jars shipped into Egypt twice a year from Greece and Phoenicia were gathered at Memphis once empty, filled with water and sent to the waterless country on the road to Syria, an arrangement he credits to the Persians after their conquest. He also says Darius stored tribute by pouring molten gold and silver into earthenware jars, then breaking the clay away and cutting off metal as needed.
b_potter.s3: A thin, carinated drinking bowl modelled on metal vessels spread through many provinces in this period, from Anatolia to the Iranian plateau. Historians debate what it means: some see local elites copying court dining habits, others stress that regional pottery traditions mostly continued unchanged and that the shape spread through ordinary fashion and trade.
b_privy.lead: A privy was a fixed seat or small room where a household relieved itself, usually over a pot, a pit or a drain. Such fittings were centuries old by the time of Cyrus, known from Egyptian houses and Mesopotamian palaces, but they were a comfort of the better-off. Most people in the empire probably made do with open ground, pots and cesspits.
b_privy.play: The game shows a seat over a sand pot emptied onto fields, keeping houses within four cells clean; Elder's Houses need one. Sand-pot seats are known from Egypt, but there is no firm evidence of emptying them onto fields, and such seats were rare.
b_privy.s0: The clearest Egyptian evidence comes from Amarna, the city of Akhenaten, built about 800 years before Cyrus. Excavators found limestone seats with a keyhole-shaped opening, set on brick supports above a removable vessel that probably held sand. They stood in small washrooms in the larger houses, not in ordinary homes.
b_privy.s1: In Mesopotamia, palaces and some houses had latrines draining into pipes or soak pits from the third millennium onward. At Persepolis, the royal terrace was laid out with a network of drains cut into the rock beneath the buildings to carry off rain and waste water. Excavation has not shown in detail how latrines on the terrace worked.
b_privy.s2: Herodotus lists Egyptian customs that seemed the reverse of Greek ones. He says Egyptians relieved themselves indoors and ate outside in the streets, explaining that shameful necessities should be done in private. His remark fits the household latrines found in Egyptian houses, though he wrote as an outsider looking for contrasts.
b_privy.s3: Herodotus says Persians were not permitted to vomit or urinate in front of others. He adds that they would not urinate or spit into a river, nor wash their hands in one, because they held rivers in great reverence. These customs suggest care about where waste went, but he gives no description of Persian latrines.
b_privy.s4: Most archaeologists think built latrines were limited to wealthier houses and palaces, but how waste was cleared remains unclear. Pots may have been emptied outside the house, into pits or onto rubbish heaps; there is no firm evidence that it was spread on fields. Later Zoroastrian purity rules about bodily waste were written down long after the Achaemenids, and historians differ on how far they reflect Persian practice in this period.
b_quarry.lead: The great Persian building works at Pasargadae, Persepolis and Susa needed huge amounts of cut stone, much of it limestone taken from hills in the surrounding region. Quarrying drew on skilled masons from across the empire. Its traces, such as tool marks, unfinished blocks and abandoned quarry faces, still show how the King's builders worked.
b_quarry.play: The game's quarry cuts limestone blocks and must touch rocky hills, which fits real Achaemenid practice of cutting stone from hill outcrops. It simplifies history: real quarries could lie many kilometres from the building site.
b_quarry.s0: The buildings of Pasargadae, begun under Cyrus, were raised in finely dressed limestone. In some palaces pale stone was set beside dark stone for contrast. Investigators traced much of the pale limestone to quarries near Sivand, south-west of the site. The blocks still carry claw-chisel marks and sockets for metal clamps that once tied them together.
b_quarry.s1: The techniques used at Pasargadae match Ionian and Lydian masonry of western Anatolia, including the toothed chisel, carefully fitted joints and swallowtail clamps. Cyrus conquered those lands in the 540s BCE, and many historians conclude that masons from there worked at Pasargadae. How many came, whether they were compelled or paid, and how much local skill was involved are still argued.
b_quarry.s2: In his foundation charter for the palace at Susa, Darius listed where his materials came from. He says the stone columns were brought from a village called Abiradush in Elam, and that the stonecutters who worked the stone were Ionians and Sardians. The text shows stone moving within a province and craftsmen moving across the empire.
b_quarry.s3: The terrace at Persepolis was built against the foot of a mountain and faced with grey limestone cut from the surrounding hills, where quarry faces and half-finished blocks survive. The Persepolis Fortification tablets record rations paid to large groups of workers, including craftsmen. They show the scale of state-organised labour behind such projects.
b_quarry.s4: In the Wadi Hammamat, in Egypt's Eastern Desert, hieroglyphic inscriptions left by a Persian official named Atiyawahy are dated to the reigns of Cambyses, Darius and Xerxes. They attest his visits to the old quarries there. The stone was a dark greywacke rather than limestone. The texts show that the Persian administration kept Egyptian quarrying going under its own officers.
b_raider_camp.lead: The mountains around Persis and along the road from Susa were home to herding peoples who lived partly outside the King's direct rule. Greek writers call them robbers who took payment from travellers in the passes. The game's raider camp stands for these communities, although the sources suggest their relations with the Persian kings were more complicated than simple raiding.
b_raider_camp.play: The camp stands on the level's map and is not built by the player: tents hidden behind a stake fence, which must be burned to stop raids. This is a simplification, since the sources also record kings paying such peoples.
b_raider_camp.s0: Herodotus lists the tribes of the Persians and says that some were farmers while others, among them the Dai, Mardians and Sagartians, were nomads. This suggests that tents and moving herds were part of life in Persis itself, not only on its edges. He gives no description of their camps.
b_raider_camp.s1: Arrian says that the Uxian hill people held the pass between Susa and Persepolis and had received payment from the Persian kings whenever they went through. When Alexander came in late 331 they asked the same of him. He attacked their villages and forced them to pay a yearly tribute in horses, pack animals and sheep instead. Diodorus tells a similar story.
b_raider_camp.s2: Strabo, drawing on Nearchus, writes that the Cossaeans of the Zagros received gifts from the kings when the court moved between Ecbatana and Babylon. Nearchus, as reported by Arrian, groups the Uxians, Mardians and Cossaeans together as peoples living by plunder. Alexander campaigned against the Cossaeans in the winter of 324-323.
b_raider_camp.s3: The reports of payments come from Alexander's historians and later Greek writers, who saw the mountain peoples through his campaigns. Pierre Briant argued that the payments were not ransom to bandits but a regular exchange of gifts that bound the herding peoples to the King and kept the routes open. Others see more real tension and violence. No camp of such raiders from the Achaemenid period has been identified by excavation.
b_road.lead: Roads tied the Persian empire together. Most were levelled earth tracks, not paved highways, but the King's officials ran them as a system, with rest stations, guides and ration points. Couriers, officials, workers and armies moved between Sardis, Susa, Persepolis and the far satrapies along them, and the records of that traffic are among the best evidence for how the empire worked.
b_road.play: In the game, walkers, carts and immigrants can only travel on roads. This is a simplification: real travellers, herders and soldiers also crossed open country, and most Persian roads were cleared tracks rather than built paving.
b_road.s0: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, clay records from about 509 to 493 BCE, list rations of flour, beer and wine issued to travellers at stations along the roads. Many travellers carried a sealed authorisation from the King, a satrap or a senior official, which entitled them to draw supplies. The tablets name journeys between Persepolis and Susa and to places as far off as Sardis, Egypt, Arachosia and India.
b_road.s1: Herodotus describes a road from Sardis to Susa with royal stations and good lodgings all along it, passing through settled and safe country. He counts 111 stations over about 450 parasangs and reckons the journey at some ninety days at a steady pace. His figures are rounded and schematic, and their source is unknown, but they show how the road looked to a Greek writer in the 5th century.
b_road.s2: Herodotus says the Persians sent royal messages by relays of mounted riders, one man and horse posted for each day's stage, so that nothing stopped them. Xenophon later credits Cyrus with founding this system, but his Cyropaedia is an idealised portrait and cannot be taken as a firm record of who began it.
b_road.s3: Persian roads were mostly beaten earth, cleared and levelled, with fords, ferries and some rock-cut or embanked stretches where the ground required. Surveys in Fars and elsewhere have traced possible stretches of ancient road, but dating a track or causeway to the Achaemenid period is difficult. Historians also still argue over the exact line of Herodotus's Royal Road through Anatolia, whether it ran by a northern route or further south.
b_road.s4: Modern scholars stress that the Sardis road was only one branch of a wider network linking Persis, Susa, Babylon, Ecbatana, Egypt and the eastern satrapies. The Fortification tablets show travel documents issued far from Persepolis, but how far the network was run from the centre and how much was left to satraps and local officials is still debated.
b_road_station.lead: Road stations were posts set along the main routes of the Persian empire, where travellers on the King's business received food, fodder and fresh animals. They let messages, officials and work gangs cross the empire at speed, and they tied the provinces to the courts at Susa and Persepolis.
b_road_station.play: Built only in the Susa level, a staffed station speeds charter caravans and its riders spot raiders. Historically stations fed state travellers carrying sealed passes; serving merchant caravans is the game's simplification.
b_road_station.s0: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, written in Elamite between about 509 and 493 BCE, record flour, beer, wine and fodder issued to people on the road. Travellers carried a sealed document, called halmi, naming who had authorised the journey. Recipients include express messengers (pirradaziš), officials and groups of workers moving between Persis, Susa, Kandahar, India and Sardis.
b_road_station.s1: An Aramaic letter of Arshama, satrap of Egypt in the late fifth century, orders his officials at a list of places along the route to give his steward Nehtihor and his men set daily rations on their way to Egypt. It shows the same system still working long after Darius. A great man issued a sealed order, and stores along the route honoured it.
b_road_station.s2: Herodotus describes the road from Sardis to Susa with royal stations and fine inns along its length, counting 111 stations and about three months of travel on foot. Elsewhere he describes the relay of mounted messengers, with a fresh man and horse posted for each day's stage, so that a message passed from rider to rider without stopping.
b_road_station.s3: Few stations have been firmly identified. A pillared building at Qaleh Kali in Fars, of Achaemenid date, has been proposed as a waystation on the road between Susa and Persepolis, but its purpose is still argued. Historians also debate how far Darius created the network and how far he reorganised older Assyrian and Median roads.
b_road_station.s4: Xenophon credits Cyrus the Great with inventing the relay, after testing how far a horse could go in a day. He reports that some claimed the couriers outflew cranes, though he doubts it himself. His Cyropaedia is a moral portrait of an ideal king, and the earliest firm evidence for the system comes from the tablets of Darius's reign.
b_ropewalk.lead: To march his army from Asia into Europe, Xerxes had two bridges of ships built across the Hellespont near Abydos, held in place by huge cables. Herodotus says these cables were made of white flax and papyrus, and that Phoenician and Egyptian crews made and laid them. Rope on this scale was part of the long preparations that also cut the canal through Athos.
b_ropewalk.play: The game has ropemakers at Athos twist flax from the storeyards. The game uses flax alone. In Herodotus most cables were papyrus, made by Phoenicians and Egyptians at a place he does not name.
b_ropewalk.s0: Herodotus says that while the Athos canal was being dug, Xerxes also had cables of papyrus and white flax prepared for bridging the Hellespont. In his account the Phoenicians built one bridge with flax cables and the Egyptians the other with papyrus. The first bridges were finished, but a storm broke them apart, and Herodotus says Xerxes had the men in charge of the work beheaded.
b_ropewalk.s1: For the rebuilt bridges, Herodotus says, each line of ships was held by six cables, two of flax and four of papyrus, tightened with wooden windlasses on the shore. He says both kinds were equally thick, but the flax was heavier, a cubit of it weighing a talent. After Mycale the Athenians besieged Sestos, took it after a long siege, and carried the cables home to dedicate in their temples.
b_ropewalk.s2: Herodotus gives a weight for the flax cables but no measurement of their thickness, and historians and engineers have argued over what his figure implies. Modern reconstructions, such as that of Hammond and Roseman, try to work out the cable size, the number of ships and how the tension was held across the strait. Scholars also discuss what fibre Herodotus meant by white flax.
b_ropewalk.s3: Egyptian ropemaking was very old by Xerxes' time, though the surviving evidence is much earlier than his reign. A painting in the Theban tomb of the vizier Rekhmire, about a thousand years earlier, shows workers twisting fibre into rope. Coils of ship rope survive from the Middle Kingdom harbour at Mersa Gawasis on the Red Sea. No remains of the Hellespont cables themselves are known.
b_ropewalk.s4: Herodotus tells that when the storm broke the first bridges, Xerxes ordered the strait given three hundred lashes and a pair of fetters thrown into it, while the men lashing it spoke insulting words to the water. The story fits the Greek picture of a king punished for pride, and many historians treat it as a moral tale rather than a plain report.
b_royal_garden.lead: At Pasargadae, Cyrus the Great probably laid out a planted garden beside his palaces, watered by narrow channels cut from limestone. It is probably the oldest Persian royal garden whose plan survives on the ground. It joined palace, water and trees into one setting for kingship, and Greek writers later took the Persian word for such parks into their language as paradeisos.
b_royal_garden.play: The game treats the garden as a monument that gives a garden to every house within sixteen cells. This is a simplification: the real garden was a royal space beside the palaces, not a public amenity for townspeople.
b_royal_garden.s0: Excavations in the 1960s found stone water channels, about a quarter of a metre wide, running around a rectangular plot beside the residential palace. Small square basins were set into the channels at intervals. Two small pavilions stood at corners of the garden, and the long portico of the palace looked out over the planting.
b_royal_garden.s1: Stronach reconstructed the garden as a rectangle divided into four by channels and walks, and saw it as the ancestor of the later Persian fourfold garden. A geophysical survey of the site in the early 2000s traced a wider network of channels across the plain. Historians now debate whether the four-part layout is certain, and how much of the system belongs to Cyrus or to later work under Darius.
b_royal_garden.s2: Arrian draws on Aristobulus, who saw Pasargadae with Alexander about two centuries after Cyrus. He says the tomb of Cyrus stood within the royal park, in a grove of many kinds of trees with running water and deep grass. Strabo gives a similar picture from the same source. The tomb lies some distance from the palaces, so this park was probably a wider planted landscape, not the channelled garden itself.
b_royal_garden.s3: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, from the reign of Darius, name estates called partetaš in Elamite, from the Old Persian word behind Greek paradeisos. These were managed royal properties where trees, crops and stores were kept, not only pleasure gardens. The Pasargadae garden belongs to this wider pattern of the king as owner and improver of land.
b_royal_garden.s4: Xenophon tells how the younger Cyrus, a Persian prince, showed the Spartan Lysander his park at Sardis in about 407 BCE. Cyrus said he had planned it and planted some of it himself. Xenophon uses the scene as a moral lesson that a good ruler cares for farming. It concerns a later Cyrus and shapes an ideal, so it cannot describe the garden of Cyrus the Great directly.
b_royal_mint.lead: Between about 515 and 500 BCE, Darius began issuing royal coins: gold darics and silver sigloi showing the King as an archer. Sardis, the old Lydian capital where, Herodotus says, the first gold and silver coins were struck, was probably their main mint. The coins mostly served the western provinces, paying soldiers and settling dues, while most of the empire still counted wealth in weighed silver and goods.
b_royal_mint.play: The mint at Sardis turns storeyard gold, also needed by the citadel and fleet, into a fixed 12 silver per gold for the treasury. The rate is a game simplification; Herodotus reckoned gold at 13 times silver.
b_royal_mint.s0: Excavators at Sardis found a gold refinery beside the Pactolus stream, dated to the Lydian period in the sixth century. Workers there separated gold from the natural gold and silver alloy of the river sands by heating it with salt. This made it possible to strike coins of pure gold and pure silver instead of the mixed electrum of the earliest Lydian coins.
b_royal_mint.s1: Herodotus says the Lydians were the first people to strike gold and silver coins. Gold and silver pieces showing a lion and a bull, called Croeseids, are traditionally given to Croesus. Some numismatists argue that many of them, especially the lighter issues, were struck by the Persians at Sardis after its capture in about 546 BCE, before Darius created his own designs.
b_royal_mint.s2: The surviving coins show a crowned figure with a bow. The earliest show him half-length, and later issues show him kneeling to shoot or running with bow and spear. The reverse carries only a rough punch mark, with no inscription. A seal used on Persepolis Fortification tablets dated 500 BCE was made from an archer siglos, which shows the coins existed by then. Whether the name daric comes from Darius himself is still debated.
b_royal_mint.s3: Herodotus says Darius struck coins of gold refined to the highest purity. He adds that Aryandes, governor of Egypt, issued silver of equal purity to rival the King, and Darius had him killed on a charge of rebellion. Elsewhere Herodotus says the tribute was melted and poured into clay jars, which were then broken, and pieces were cut off as needed.
b_royal_mint.s4: Darics and sigloi are found mostly in western Asia Minor and seldom in Persia, Babylonia or Egypt. In the heartland, officials recorded wages in barley, wine and livestock, and the Persepolis Treasury tablets give silver by weight. Coins were therefore a tool for the western provinces, where Greek cities, soldiers and mercenaries were used to coined money.
b_royal_pavilion.lead: Herodotus says that Xerxes watched the fighting at Thermopylae in 480 BCE from a royal seat, and that he was said to have sprung up from it three times in fear for his troops. The Persian kings travelled with thrones, canopies and richly hung tents, and the seated King under his canopy was a central image of royal power. Nothing of the seat at Thermopylae survives, and its form is unknown.
b_royal_pavilion.play: Built only at Thermopylae, it takes limestone for platform and stair, timber for its painted posts and Sardis cloth for its hangings. No source describes such a building; a tent and portable throne are likelier.
b_royal_pavilion.s0: Herodotus says Xerxes waited four days at Thermopylae, expecting the Greeks to withdraw, before sending in the Medes and Cissians. During the fighting the King watched from a throne. Herodotus reports the story that he leapt up from it three times in fear for his army. He does not describe the seat or what stood around it, and he does not say exactly where it was.
b_royal_pavilion.s1: Herodotus places Xerxes on a seat at other moments of the campaign. At Abydos he sat on a throne of white stone set on a hill to view his army and fleet. At Salamis he watched from below Mount Aegaleos while scribes noted who fought well. Herodotus also describes the royal tent left to Mardonius and captured after Plataea, furnished with gold and silver and embroidered hangings.
b_royal_pavilion.s2: The Persian record says nothing about Thermopylae, but it shows how the King wished to be seen when seated. The audience reliefs found in the Persepolis Treasury show the King on a high-backed throne with his feet on a footstool, a figure usually taken as the crown prince behind him and incense burners before him. Doorway reliefs at Persepolis show the King enthroned beneath a fringed canopy, his throne held up by figures of the subject peoples.
b_royal_pavilion.s3: No remains of a royal seat or pavilion have been found at Thermopylae, and its site is unknown. An army halted for a few days would most likely have used a tent, a portable throne and a parasol rather than a built stone platform. Some historians see Herodotus's frightened, leaping King as a Greek literary motif. On that view the scene tells more about how Greeks imagined Xerxes than about Persian practice.
b_royal_pavilion.s4: Writers of the Roman period reported that Pericles' Odeion in Athens, a roofed hall of many columns, imitated the King's tent. Pausanias the travel writer and Plutarch both pass this on as something that was said. They wrote some six centuries after the war, and the story cannot be checked. M. C. Miller has argued that captured Persian tents may indeed have influenced Athenian building.
b_royal_relief.lead: The great reliefs of Persepolis lined the stairways of the Apadana, the audience hall begun by Darius and finished under Xerxes. They show twenty-three delegations from the King's lands bringing gifts, with ranks of Persian and Median nobles and guards. Together they presented the empire as an orderly gathering of peoples around the throne.
b_royal_relief.play: The game lists the Royal Relief as housing: panels of tribute-bearers from every nation and the King's guards. The real reliefs lined a royal hall's stairs and show twenty-three delegations, not every people.
b_royal_relief.s0: Excavations at Persepolis uncovered matching relief programmes on the north and east stairways of the Apadana; the east stair, long buried under debris, survives best. On one wing, files of nobles in Persian and Median dress stand in rows with armed guards. On the other, twenty-three delegations climb towards the centre, each led by an usher who takes the leader by the hand. Scenes of a lion attacking a bull fill the triangular corners.
b_royal_relief.s1: Each delegation wears its own dress and carries its own goods: garments, metal vessels, weapons, jewellery and animals such as horses, camels, humped cattle and rams. Some bring chariots, and one group carries small jars on a yoke that may hold gold dust. Scholars identify many groups by comparing their dress with the labelled throne-bearers on the royal tombs, and traces of pigment show the panels were once painted.
b_royal_relief.s2: Two large panels found in the Treasury show a seated king receiving an official who raises his hand to his mouth, with the crown prince behind the throne. Later study showed they first stood at the centre of the Apadana stairs and were moved, probably under Artaxerxes I, when new central panels replaced them. The official is often identified as the hazarapatish, and the king as Darius or Xerxes.
b_royal_relief.s3: Herodotus lists the yearly tribute of the provinces in silver and goods, and he says some peoples, such as the Arabs and the Ethiopians, sent gifts instead of fixed tribute. The reliefs never label what is carried. Many historians therefore call the figures gift-bearers rather than tribute-bearers, since the scene stresses willing service rather than a tax payment.
b_royal_relief.s4: Some scholars have read the procession as a record of a yearly ceremony, often linked to a New Year festival held at Persepolis. Others, notably M. C. Root, argue there is no evidence for such a festival and that the reliefs show a timeless picture of imperial harmony. The question remains open, as no text from the site describes the event.
b_sacred_olive.lead: Athena's Olive was the sacred olive tree on the Acropolis of Athens, which Athenians believed the goddess herself had made grow there. Herodotus says it burned when Xerxes' army sacked the Acropolis in 480 BCE, and that a day later a new shoot had sprung from the stump. Athenians probably told the story as a sign that their city would outlast the invasion.
b_sacred_olive.play: The olive stands on a level's map as a historic feature and is not built by the player. The game sets it by the old temple. Herodotus puts it inside the shrine of Erechtheus, so the game's placement is a simplification.
b_sacred_olive.s0: Athenians told that Athena and Poseidon once competed for their land: Poseidon struck the rock and brought up a spring of salt water, and Athena made an olive grow. The land was awarded to Athena. Herodotus mentions the olive and the salt spring only as the tokens of this contest. The fuller versions of the myth come from much later writers such as Apollodorus.
b_sacred_olive.s1: Herodotus places the olive inside the temple of Erechtheus, the earth-born king of early Athens, together with the salt-water spring. Later ancient writers and modern scholars put the tree in the Pandroseion, the open precinct of Pandrosos west of the later Erechtheion. Pausanias, describing the Acropolis in the 2nd century CE, still knew of the olive and repeated that it was the goddess's proof in the contest.
b_sacred_olive.s2: In 480 BCE the Persians climbed the Acropolis, killed its last defenders and burned the sanctuary. Herodotus says that the next day Xerxes ordered the Athenian exiles in his following to go up and sacrifice in their own manner, perhaps because of a dream or regret for the burning. The exiles found that a shoot about a cubit long, roughly half a metre, had grown from the burnt olive.
b_sacred_olive.s3: Excavations on the Acropolis in the 1880s uncovered debris from the Persian destruction. It included burnt building stone and broken marble statues, among them many korai, buried when the Athenians later cleared and levelled the hill. The sacred tree itself left no remains that can be identified. The olive growing on the spot today is a modern planting.
b_sacred_olive.s4: Pausanias, writing some six centuries later, reports a tradition that the olive grew again on the very day it burned and reached two cubits. Herodotus gives one cubit, a day later. Historians note that olives often resprout from burnt stumps, so the regrowth could be real. Many also see the tale as Athenian tradition shaped into an omen of the city's survival.
b_sanctuary.lead: As far as the evidence shows, Persian worship in this period centred on offerings made in the open air rather than in enclosed temples housing statues. Places of cult still mattered: the sacred precinct at Pasargadae, the local offerings supplied through the Persepolis tablets, the ayadana Darius says he restored, and the many temples of subject peoples that the kings protected or tolerated.
b_sanctuary.play: A Sanctuary sends a magus through the streets to bless households, and houses need its faith to become Terrace Houses. These rounds are the game's invention: the tablets show magi receiving rations to perform offerings, not visiting homes.
b_sanctuary.s0: Herodotus says the Persians set up no statues, temples or altars, and thought those who did were foolish. He reports that they sacrificed to Zeus on the highest mountains, giving that name to the whole circle of the sky; modern scholars often link this god with Auramazda. They also sacrificed to the sun, moon, earth, fire, water and winds, and no sacrifice was lawful without a magus to chant.
b_sanctuary.s1: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, written in Elamite between about 509 and 493 BCE, record grain, wine and animals issued for offerings. A magus often performed the commonest offering, called lan. Those who received offerings included Auramazda, Elamite gods such as Humban, and mountains and rivers. The tablets show worship spread across many local places and paid for by the royal economy rather than by a single great temple.
b_sanctuary.s2: North-west of the palaces at Pasargadae lies a sacred precinct with two limestone plinths standing in the open, one reached by a stair. David Stronach, who excavated the site, read them as a setting for royal worship before a fire or altar. A terraced mound stands nearby, though its date and purpose are debated. The rites performed there are unknown, but the layout suits open-air worship rather than a roofed temple.
b_sanctuary.s3: At Behistun, Darius says he rebuilt the ayadana that Gaumata the magus had destroyed. The Old Persian word is usually rendered as places of worship, but historians disagree about whether these were buildings, open precincts or the estates that supported cult. Xerxes later claimed to have destroyed a place where false gods, the daivas, were worshipped. Scholars still argue about where it was and whether the claim describes a real event.
b_sanctuary.s4: The kings did not impose Persian cult on their subjects. The Cyrus Cylinder, a royal text in Babylonian style, presents Cyrus returning gods to their shrines. The statue of Udjahorresnet records that Cambyses had foreigners cleared out of the temple of Neith at Sais and its revenues restored. A petition from Elephantine written in 407 BCE claims the Jewish temple of Yahu already stood when Cambyses came and was spared when Egyptian temples were overthrown.
b_sardis_citadel.lead: The citadel of Sardis stood on a steep spur of Mount Tmolus above the Lydian capital. It was fortified by the Lydian kings and taken by Cyrus, probably in the 540s BCE, and under Persian rule it was the seat of the satrap of Sparda and the strongest point at the western end of the Royal Road. In 498 BCE it held out while Ionian, Athenian and Eretrian raiders burned the city below.
b_sardis_citadel.play: The game has the citadel built new, with gold for its gatehouse and treasury. In history its walls and terraces were mostly Lydian work that the Persians took over, and the gold is a game simplification.
b_sardis_citadel.s0: American excavations since 1958 have traced Lydian terrace walls of finely cut stone on the acropolis, though erosion has carried much of the hilltop away. In the lower city, archaeologists found a fortification wall of mudbrick on a stone base, many metres thick, which was destroyed in the mid-6th century. Most scholars link that destruction to the Persian conquest.
b_sardis_citadel.s1: Herodotus says Cyrus defeated Croesus on the plain outside Sardis and then besieged him in the city. On the fourteenth day a Mardian soldier named Hyroeades saw a defender climb down the sheer side facing Tmolus to fetch a fallen helmet, then led others up the same way. The year is usually given as about 547 BCE, but the place name in the Nabonidus Chronicle once read as Lydia is damaged, so the date remains uncertain.
b_sardis_citadel.s2: Herodotus adds a story told about the walls. An earlier king, Meles, carried a lion born to his concubine around the circuit, as seers advised, so that the walls could never be taken. He skipped the steep side toward Tmolus because no one could climb it, and that was where the Persians got in. The tale explains a surprise defeat as a flaw in an old ritual.
b_sardis_citadel.s3: Darius's inscription at Behistun lists Sparda, the Old Persian name for Sardis and Lydia, among the lands that obeyed him. Persepolis Fortification tablets record travellers on the road between Sardis and the Persian heartland. Excavated seals, tombs and building remains show a Persian elite living at Sardis alongside Lydians and sharing a mixed style of art and burial.
b_sardis_citadel.s4: Herodotus says the Ionians, with Athenian and Eretrian allies, took the lower city unopposed, but Artaphernes held the acropolis with a strong force. A soldier set fire to one house, and the flames spread across the reed roofs and burned the town, including the temple of the goddess Cybebe. Arrian says the citadel was still very strong, with a triple wall, when its commander Mithrenes surrendered it to Alexander in 334.
b_scout_post.lead: Persian commanders sent riders ahead to see the ground, count the enemy and bring word back. Herodotus tells how Xerxes sent a single horseman to look at the Greeks holding Thermopylae, and how the King let Greek spies caught in his camp see everything. The game's Scout Post is a place where such riders are kept and sent out.
b_scout_post.play: In the game the Scout Post is the first military building: its scouts ride on their own to land no one has seen and lift the fog over it. No Achaemenid text names a scouts' building; the post is the game's simplification of riders kept by a garrison or a station of the King's road.
b_scout_post.s0: Herodotus says that while Xerxes waited at Thermopylae he sent a mounted scout to see how many the Greeks were and what they were doing. The rider could only see the men outside the wall. He found Spartans exercising and combing their hair, counted them, and rode back unhindered, for no one paid him any attention.
b_scout_post.s1: Herodotus also says the Greeks sent three spies to Sardis to see the King's army. They were caught and condemned, but Xerxes had them led round the whole host and sent home, reasoning that word of its size would make the Greeks give up their freedom without a fight.
b_scout_post.s2: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, written between about 509 and 493 BCE, record rations and fodder for express messengers and other travellers on the royal roads, who carried sealed passes. The same roads and stations that carried the King's letters could carry a report from the frontier at speed.
b_scout_post.s3: Greek writers say the Persian king had many 'eyes and ears' who reported to him, and Xenophon makes this a gift of Cyrus. Historians argue whether this was a body of officials, an honorary title, or a Greek picture of an all-seeing despot. The game's scouts look only at the land, not at the King's subjects.
b_scribal_school.lead: The Persian empire ran on written records, kept by trained scribes in Elamite on clay and in Aramaic on leather. How those scribes learned their trade is mostly unrecorded. No school of the period has been excavated in Persia, so the evidence is the records themselves and the better-known training of Babylonia and Egypt.
b_scribal_school.play: The Scribal School sends a teacher along the streets, and Elder's Houses and Noble Residences need his visits. Walking teachers and schooling as a household need are the game's simplifications: formal schooling reached few people, and as far as we know only boys. At Memphis it is the House of Life, on the Greek coast a Letter School.
b_scribal_school.s0: Two Elamite tablets from Persepolis, dated to Darius's twenty-third year (499 BCE), issue grain and wine to Persian boys copying texts (Hallock's nos. 871 and 1137). They are the nearest thing to a schoolroom in the archive. The Elamite word for boys, puhu, is also used of servants and subordinates, so these may be young dependants at work rather than pupils.
b_scribal_school.s1: The Fortification tablets, about 509-493 BCE, are mostly Elamite cuneiform on clay, with a smaller group in Aramaic. Aramaic was also written in ink on leather, as in the letters of the satrap Arshama. A scribe of the empire could need more than one language and more than one way of writing.
b_scribal_school.s2: Herodotus's three lessons for Persian boys include no reading or writing, and Dandamayev argues that writing played no part in a Persian noble's standard education: scribes were a separate trade, often Elamite, Babylonian or Aramaic. The boys of the tablets show that some Persians did learn it. How many is unknown.
b_scribal_school.s3: Babylonia had the older tradition. The tablet house, a school for scribes, is best known from the early second millennium BCE, a thousand years and more before Cyrus. In the first millennium pupils still copied set texts, often taught at home or by a master, and Babylonian scribes of the Persian period included sons of shepherds, fishermen and weavers.
b_scribal_school.s4: The Egyptian official Udjahorresnet says on his statue that Darius sent him home from Elam to restore the House of Life, the temple's place of learning and of medicine. He says he filled it with students, sons of men of standing and no poor man's son. Darius paid for this in Egypt: the statue is our one account of it.
b_scribal_school.s5: Herodotus gives the first Greek school on record only because it fell. On Chios, shortly before the Ionian fleet's defeat about 494 BCE, a roof collapsed on boys learning their letters, and of a hundred and twenty one lived. Herodotus takes it as a sign of the disaster coming to the island.
b_scribe.lead: Persian rule ran on written records. Scribes counted rations, livestock, workers, land and dues on clay tablets and leather in several languages, so that officials at Persepolis, Susa or Babylon could check what was owed and what was paid. Without them the King's estates, roads and tribute could not have been managed.
b_scribe.play: Scribes register households, and only registered houses pay silver. This simplifies history: Persian dues fell mostly on land, were often paid in grain, livestock or labour, and silver was usually weighed rather than counted as coin, even after Darius's coinage.
b_scribe.s0: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, dated about 509-493 BCE, are thousands of records of food issued to workers, travellers, animals and gods, mostly in Elamite with some in Aramaic. Scribes are named on them and drew rations themselves. Some tablets mention scribes who wrote on hides, probably in Aramaic, which shows that leather documents once existed alongside the clay ones that survive.
b_scribe.s1: Babylonian archives show how dues were tracked. Land was granted to soldiers and their families as bow-land, horse-land or chariot-land, and holders owed service, produce and silver. The Murashu texts from Nippur, written later in the fifth century, record firms that managed such plots and paid the dues for them, so the system was well established by then.
b_scribe.s2: Herodotus places royal scribes close to power. In his story of Oroetes, a royal scribe read out sealed letters from the King to the satrap's guard. At Salamis, he says, Xerxes watched the fighting while his scribes wrote down the names of captains who did well, along with their fathers and cities.
b_scribe.s3: At Behistun Darius says he made a new form of writing, which many scholars take to mean the Old Persian cuneiform script. Others argue it existed earlier, though the short inscriptions in Cyrus's name at Pasargadae are now usually thought to have been added later. Either way, daily administration was written in Elamite, Aramaic and Babylonian, and almost never in Old Persian.
b_scribe.s4: Herodotus says Darius divided the empire into provinces and fixed each one's yearly tribute in talents of silver, while the Persians of Persis paid none. His totals are schematic and historians treat them with caution. The tablets show that much of what the crown collected came in kind, as barley, wine, sheep and labour.
b_sestos_house.lead: Sestos was a walled town on the European shore of the Hellespont, facing Abydos across the strait. After the Greek victory at Mycale in 479 BCE, Persians from the surrounding country took refuge there, and an Athenian fleet besieged them until hunger forced them out. Herodotus ends his narrative of the war with this siege, which many historians read as the moment the Greeks turned from defending their homeland to attacking Persian positions.
b_sestos_house.play: A house of Sestos stands on a level's map as a historic structure that the player cannot build. Herodotus names no particular house, so it is a generic dwelling of the besieged town.
b_sestos_house.s0: Herodotus says that after Mycale the Spartan king Leotychides took the Peloponnesian ships home, while the Athenians under Xanthippus stayed to besiege Sestos. The Persians of the nearby towns had gathered there because it was the strongest fortress in the region. A Persian named Oeobazus came in from Cardia, bringing the cables from Xerxes' bridges across the Hellespont. The town's governor was Artayctes, a Persian appointed by Xerxes.
b_sestos_house.s1: The siege dragged on into the autumn. Herodotus says the Athenian soldiers grumbled at being kept from home, but their generals refused to leave until the town fell or Athens recalled them. Inside, food ran out, and the defenders boiled the leather straps of their beds and ate them. When even that was gone, Artayctes, Oeobazus and the Persians slipped out by night at the back of the wall, where the besiegers were thinnest, and the townspeople opened the gates.
b_sestos_house.s2: Oeobazus escaped into Thrace, where, Herodotus says, the Apsinthian Thracians caught him and sacrificed him to their god Pleistorus. Artayctes was captured near Aegospotami. Herodotus accuses him of plundering the shrine of the hero Protesilaus at Elaeus, and says the Athenians, on Xanthippus's orders, nailed him to a board while his son was stoned before his eyes. The Athenians then sailed home carrying the bridge cables as offerings for their sanctuaries.
b_sestos_house.s3: Herodotus tells that a guard was roasting salted fish when the fish began to leap and quiver as if freshly caught. Artayctes read this as a sign from Protesilaus that the hero, though dead, had power to punish the man who had robbed him. The story is shaped as a moral tale about sacrilege and retribution, a theme that runs through the closing chapters of the Histories.
b_sestos_house.s4: Herodotus places the fall of Sestos before the fleet went home for winter, while Thucydides says the Athenians and their Ionian and Hellespontine allies wintered there and took the town after a siege. Historians therefore argue whether it fell in late 479 BCE or early 478 BCE. They also debate how far Herodotus chose this episode as an ending because it hints at the Athenian empire that followed.
b_ship_camp.lead: In 490 BCE the fleet of Datis and Artaphernes crossed from Eretria and put in at Marathon, on the north-east coast of Attica. The ships, the horse transports and the shore camp beside them were the army's base and its only way home. When the Persian line broke, the fighting ended at the water's edge as the Athenians tried to seize and burn the ships.
b_ship_camp.play: The game builds the camp as a monument with limestone footings, hauling ways and a timber stockade. Herodotus records no such works at Marathon; the stockade resembles the beach rampart he describes at Mycale in 479 BCE.
b_ship_camp.s0: Herodotus says the exiled Athenian tyrant Hippias guided the Persians to Marathon because it was the best ground in Attica for horsemen and lay close to Eretria. He says Hippias brought the ships to anchor there and set the troops in order as they came ashore. He gives the fleet as 600 triremes with horse transports, a figure most historians think too high.
b_ship_camp.s1: Oared warships of the period were light enough to be hauled up onto a beach, where their hulls could dry and their crews could eat and sleep ashore. At Mycale in 479 BCE, Herodotus says, the Persians dragged their ships onto the land and threw up a rampart of stones and timber around them, cutting down orchard trees for it. He describes no such defence at Marathon, and some ships there may simply have lain at anchor.
b_ship_camp.s2: No ancient writer fixes the spot. Many historians place the fleet at the sheltered north-east end of the bay near Schinias, behind the Cynosura headland, with the Great Marsh between it and the plain. Others argue for a more central beach. A note in the Suda, a tenth-century Byzantine lexicon, claims the Persian horsemen were absent when the Athenians attacked, perhaps because they were being loaded back onto the ships, but this is still argued over.
b_ship_camp.s3: Herodotus says the Athenians chased the broken Persians to the sea, called for fire and laid hold of the ships. The polemarch Callimachus died there, and Cynegirus, son of Euphorion, had his hand cut off by an axe as he gripped a ship's stern; later writers make him the brother of the poet Aeschylus. The Athenians took seven ships; the rest pushed off, collected the Eretrian captives left on the island of Aegilia and sailed round Sunium.
b_ship_camp.s4: Writing more than six centuries later, Pausanias says that every night at Marathon people heard horses neighing and men fighting. He also reports stone mangers said to belong to the horses of Artaphernes and marks on a rock said to show where his tent had stood. These are local tales told to visitors, not evidence for the camp.
b_sphinx_pair.lead: Egyptian temples were often approached along a processional way flanked by pairs of stone sphinxes, lions with the head of a king or a ram. Herodotus says Amasis, the last long-reigning pharaoh before Cambyses conquered Egypt in 525 BCE, set up great man-headed sphinxes at Sais. Strabo later saw sphinxes half-buried in sand near Memphis, though that avenue was mostly built after the Persian conquest.
b_sphinx_pair.play: The game offers the Sphinx Pair among its housing buildings at Memphis. Real sphinx avenues led to temples, not homes, and the Serapeum avenue Strabo saw was mostly laid out in the 4th century, after the game's period.
b_sphinx_pair.s0: From the New Kingdom onward, Egyptian builders lined the approach to a temple, the dromos, with rows of sphinxes facing each other across the path. Surviving examples at Karnak use ram-headed sphinxes, while others have the face of a ruling king. On festival days the god's image was carried along these routes, so the sphinxes framed processions rather than everyday streets.
