b_sphinx_pair.s1: Herodotus says that Amasis, who ruled Egypt until shortly before the Persian conquest, built a gateway for the temple of Athena at Sais, meaning the goddess Neith. He adds that Amasis set up colossal statues and large man-headed sphinxes there and hauled in huge blocks of stone. Little of Sais survives above ground, so the description rests mainly on his account.
b_sphinx_pair.s2: The statue of Udjahorresnet, a priest and official from Sais, records that he served Cambyses after 525 BCE. He says he persuaded the King to clear foreigners out of the temple of Neith and to restore its revenues and rites. This suggests that the temple Amasis had adorned kept working under its new Persian master.
b_sphinx_pair.s3: Strabo, who visited Egypt about five centuries after Cambyses, describes the Serapeum near Memphis as standing in a very sandy place. Wind-driven dunes had buried some of its sphinxes up to the head and others halfway. He remarks that the sight showed how dangerous a sandstorm could be for anyone walking to the temple.
b_sphinx_pair.s4: In 1850 Auguste Mariette found the Serapeum by clearing the avenue Strabo had seen. Its sphinxes are mostly dated to the 30th Dynasty in the 4th century, long after 525 BCE. Older sphinxes survive at Memphis, such as the New Kingdom alabaster sphinx at Mit Rahina. The city was robbed for stone and is only partly excavated, so historians cannot say how many sphinx avenues stood when Cambyses arrived.
b_stone_drain.lead: Under the royal terrace at Persepolis ran a network of covered drains, some cut into the bedrock and some built of stone. They carried rain water off flat roofs and paved courts and away from the buildings. Without them, the mud-brick walls of the palaces would probably have been badly damaged by the winter rains of Persis.
b_stone_drain.play: The game's Stone Drain keeps houses within seven cells clean. The excavated drains at Persepolis served the palace terrace and mainly carried rain water. Little is known of drainage in the town below.
b_stone_drain.s0: Excavators found that the drainage network was laid out while the terrace was being levelled, before the halls and palaces were built over it. Channels were cut into the living rock or lined and roofed with stone slabs, then hidden under later floors. This shows the drains were planned as part of the terrace from the start, not added afterwards.
b_stone_drain.s1: The buildings had flat roofs of earth laid over timber beams, which collected rain. Excavators traced vertical shafts built into the thick mud-brick walls that led water down to the channels beneath. The drains then carried it to outlets at the edges of the terrace, away from the foundations.
b_stone_drain.s2: Scholars agree the network chiefly handled storm water, both from roofs and from runoff off the mountain behind the terrace. How much household waste it carried is less clear, since the terrace was a royal and ceremonial site with few known latrines. Some also link parts of the system to the cisterns on the terrace, and the exact working of the whole network is still argued.
b_stone_drain.s3: Drains of baked brick were long known in Elam and Mesopotamia, and Persian builders probably drew on these traditions. At Pasargadae, Cyrus's garden had channels of cut limestone with small basins at intervals. Those channels fed water into the garden rather than draining it away, but they show the same skill in cutting stone to carry water.
b_stone_drain.s4: The Persepolis Fortification tablets record rations of grain, wine and beer paid to large groups of workers at Parsa, many of them from distant peoples of the empire, among them skilled craftsmen. The digging of the drains was probably part of the general labour of building the terrace, carried out by workers like these.
b_stone_lion.lead: Carved lions guarded tombs, gates and sacred places across western Asia long before the Persians came, and in Lydia the lion came close to being a royal emblem. In Persia the animal appeared mostly in palace reliefs, glazed brick and seals, attacking a bull, striding in procession or fighting a royal hero. In both lands it stood for strength and royal power.
b_stone_lion.play: The game offers the Stone Lion, a crouching lion on a plinth, in Sardis, Pasargadae, Parsa and Susa. Freestanding lions fit Lydia, but Persian palaces showed lions mostly in relief and glazed brick, so this is a simplification there.
b_stone_lion.s0: Excavations at Sardis have recovered several archaic marble lions, most of them crouching or seated, from the 6th century. Many were probably set over tombs or at entrances as guardians. Early electrum coins from Lydia, among the first coins anywhere, carry a lion's head and were probably struck under the Lydian kings. Together these finds suggest how closely the lion was tied to Lydian kingship.
b_stone_lion.s1: Herodotus says that Croesus sent Apollo at Delphi a lion of refined gold weighing ten talents, set on a pile of gold half-bricks. When the temple burned, in a fire that later writers date to 548 BCE, the lion fell and lost three and a half talents of its weight. Herodotus adds that in his own day it was kept in the treasury of the Corinthians. Nothing of it survives.
b_stone_lion.s2: At Persepolis, lions attacking bulls are carved on the stairways of the Apadana and other buildings, and palace doorways show a royal hero stabbing a rearing lion or monster. At Susa, a frieze of striding lions in glazed brick, probably from Darius's palace, is now in the Louvre. Seal impressions on the Persepolis Fortification tablets also show heroes gripping lions. Few freestanding guardian lions are known from Persia, unlike Lydia.
b_stone_lion.s3: Gold and silver coins stamped with the foreparts of a lion and a bull facing each other are called croeseids and were long credited to Croesus. Some scholars argued that part of the series was struck at Sardis under Persian rule, before Darius introduced his own coinage. Coins from excavated contexts at Sardis, published in 2005, support a start under Croesus, but how long the series ran remains debated.
b_stone_lion.s4: Herodotus tells that an early king of Sardis, Meles, was given a lion born to his concubine. Seers said the city would never be taken if the lion were carried round its walls. Meles left out one steep stretch of the citadel, and that was where the Persians climbed in when Cyrus took Sardis. The tale explains the city's fall as fate rather than weakness.
b_storeyard.lead: The Persian kings ran an economy of stores. Grain, wine, timber, stone, cloth and weapons were received, counted, kept and issued by officials who wrote down each movement. These stores fed workers, supplied building sites and armed troops, and the surviving records from Persepolis show how closely the system was managed.
b_storeyard.play: The Storeyard keeps timber, clay, pottery, limestone, arms, wool, cloth and wine together, with caps on bulk goods so space stays for pottery, cloth and wine. Real Persian stores were spread across many offices and places.
b_storeyard.s0: The Persepolis Fortification tablets were written mostly in Elamite between about 509 and 493 BCE. They record goods received into store and issued from it across Persis. Named suppliers held grain, wine, beer, fruit and livestock at many local places and released them on sealed orders. Each transfer was noted, so that stock could be checked against what had gone out as rations or travel supplies.
b_storeyard.s1: The tablets use the Elamite word kapnuški, usually translated treasury, for institutions at Persepolis, Shiraz and other places. Some held valuables and materials, while others employed groups of workers who made goods. Historians still debate how far these were storehouses, workshops or both at once, and how they related to the stores of grain and wine.
b_storeyard.s2: Excavators of the Treasury on the Persepolis terrace found storerooms that had held stone vessels, objects probably brought as gifts or tribute, and large numbers of weapons, including thousands of arrowheads. Most of what survived reflects the building as Alexander left it in 330. A separate group of tablets found there, dating from 492 BCE to the 450s BCE, records silver paid to workers on royal building projects, partly in place of rations in kind.
b_storeyard.s3: Darius's foundation charter from Susa lists where his building materials came from. It names cedar from Lebanon, other timber from Gandara and Carmania, gold from Sardis and Bactria, and stone and brick worked by peoples from across the empire. Materials on this scale had to be gathered and kept at the building site until the craftsmen needed them.
b_storeyard.s4: Herodotus says that the King stored the tribute he received by melting the metal and pouring it into earthenware jars. Once it had set, the jars were broken away, and pieces were cut from the solid mass when money was needed. The story may be simplified, but it reflects a Greek view of Persian wealth kept in store rather than spent at once.
b_stud.lead: The Nisaean plain in Media bred the largest and most valued horses of the Persian empire. Greek writers describe them as mounts of kings and nobles and as sacred horses led before the chariot of the god. The plain is usually placed in the Zagros valleys of Media, perhaps near Bagastana, close to where Darius and a few companions killed the man he called Gaumata in 522 BCE.
b_stud.play: Grooms raise horses on fertile meadow at Bagastana, and every horseman the Cavalry Stable trains needs one. This simplifies history: Nisaean horses were prized royal mounts, and cavalry horses also came from other herds and tribute.
b_stud.s0: Herodotus says the Nisaean horses took their name from a wide plain in Media that bred very large horses. In Xerxes' march of 480 BCE he places ten sacred Nisaean horses ahead of the chariot of Zeus, with Xerxes following in a chariot drawn by Nisaean horses. He also ranks them above the horses of India, and says the Persian cavalry commander Masistius rode a Nisaean horse with a golden bridle at Plataea.
b_stud.s1: In the Behistun inscription Darius says that he and a few men killed Gaumata at the fortress of Sikayauvati, in the district called Nisaya in Media. Many historians link this district with the Nisaean plain of the Greek writers. If they are right, the royal horse country lay close to the scene of Darius's seizure of power.
b_stud.s2: The Persepolis Fortification tablets were written in Elamite between about 509 and 493 BCE. They record rations of grain and fodder issued to horses, including animals belonging to the king and horses used by travellers on the royal roads. They show that horses were a regular charge on the stores of the royal economy, issued and accounted for by named officials.
b_stud.s3: Later writers give huge herd sizes. Arrian says Alexander found little more than 50,000 mares on the Nisaean plain, where once there had been about 150,000. Diodorus, writing of pastures near Bagistane, gives 160,000 once and 60,000 in Alexander's day. Strabo notes that some traced the breed to Armenia. Historians still debate where the plain lay and treat these numbers with caution.
b_stud.s4: Herodotus tells how the seven conspirators agreed that the man whose horse neighed first at sunrise would be king. Darius's groom Oebares used a trick to make his master's stallion neigh, and Herodotus gives two versions of how he did it. The story is a Greek tale about cunning, not a record of how Darius became king, and the Behistun inscription says nothing of it.
b_susa_palace.lead: The Palace of Darius was the royal residence Darius I built at Susa, the ancient Elamite city that became a chief seat of the Persian kings. His foundation charter names the lands that sent its materials and the peoples who worked on it, so the building itself declared that the whole empire served the King. Its remains include a courtyard palace, a great columned hall and friezes of glazed brick.
b_susa_palace.play: The game raises the palace in stages from the charter's materials, with timber for every fourth part. The real work took many years. Its walls were mud brick faced with glazed brick, and the level's 519 to 515 BCE span simplifies an uncertain start.
b_susa_palace.s0: In his charter Darius says the earth was dug down until bedrock was reached, then packed with rubble, 40 cubits deep in one part and 20 in another, and the palace was raised on it. Cedar came from Lebanon, carried by Assyrians to Babylon and by Carians and Ionians to Susa. Gold came from Sardis and Bactria, lapis lazuli and carnelian from Sogdiana, and ivory from Kush, Sind and Arachosia.
b_susa_palace.s1: The charter also lists who did the work. Babylonians moulded and baked the brick, Ionians and Sardians cut the stone, Sardians and Egyptians worked the wood, Medes and Egyptians worked the gold, and Medes and Egyptians adorned the walls. A related text, DSz, known chiefly in Elamite, repeats much of this list. The charter presents the palace as a picture of the empire, each people bringing its share.
b_susa_palace.s2: French teams have dug at Susa since the 1880s, when Marcel Dieulafoy recovered glazed-brick friezes of archers now in the Louvre. Jean Perrot's work in the 1970s clarified a residential palace of mud brick built round courtyards in a Babylonian manner, and a hall of 36 columns. In 1972 a statue of Darius, carved in Egypt and inscribed in hieroglyphs and cuneiform, was found at the gate of the palace.
b_susa_palace.s3: The charter carries no date. Some historians place the start as early as about 520 BCE, soon after the rebellions of 522 to 521 BCE, and others somewhat later. Later kings altered the site: Artaxerxes II says the columned hall burned under Artaxerxes I and that he rebuilt it. Scholars also debate whether the glazed archers show a royal guard, such as the troops Herodotus calls Immortals, or Persians in general.
b_susa_palace.s4: Herodotus makes Susa the King's residence and the place of his treasuries. He has Aristagoras of Miletus describe the road from Sardis to Susa, a journey Herodotus reckons at about three months. For Greek writers Susa stood for the wealth and distance of the Persian court, though they say little about the palace itself.
b_symposium_house.lead: The symposium was the Greek drinking party, held on couches in the men's room of a private house, with mixed wine, songs and the aulos. In 479 BCE, as the armies gathered near Plataea, the Theban Attaginus held one for Mardonius and fifty Persians. Herodotus tells of it as an evening of friendship between Persians and their Greek allies, shadowed by the defeat that followed.
b_symposium_house.play: In the Plataea level, Greek towns can build the Symposium House as a service. Real symposia were held in private houses, not in a separate public building, so the game simplifies here.
b_symposium_house.s0: Athenian painted cups and mixing bowls of the late 6th and early 5th centuries show men reclining on couches, wine mixed with water in a large krater, and a piper, often a hired woman, playing the double pipe called the aulos. The custom of reclining to drink probably reached Greece from the Near East by about 600 BCE. Excavated classical houses, best known at Olynthus, have a men's room, the andron, with an off-centre door so that couches could line the walls.
b_symposium_house.s1: Herodotus says that Attaginus son of Phrynon, a leading Theban, prepared a great feast at Thebes and invited Mardonius with fifty of the most notable Persians, together with fifty Thebans. The guests did not lie apart by people: a Persian and a Theban shared each couch. The meal took place shortly before the battle of Plataea.
b_symposium_house.s2: Herodotus heard from Thersander of Orchomenus, who was at the feast, that his Persian couch-mate wept over the wine. The Persian foresaw that few of the guests would live long, and said the bitterest pain was to understand much yet have no power to change it. The scene is shaped as a warning before disaster, and whether the words were spoken as told cannot be checked.
b_symposium_house.s3: Herodotus counts Thebes among the Greeks who gave earth and water to Xerxes and has the Thebans advising Mardonius on strategy. Half a century later, Theban speakers in Thucydides claimed the city had been ruled in 480 BCE by a narrow clique of powerful men, not by its people, and so should not bear the blame. Historians still debate how far the city as a whole chose the Persian side.
b_symposium_house.s4: After the Greek victory the allies besieged Thebes and demanded the surrender of the leaders of the pro-Persian party, Attaginus among them. Herodotus says Attaginus escaped. His sons were handed over instead, but Pausanias released them, saying children had no share in their father's siding with the Medes.
b_temple_forecourt.lead: An Egyptian temple was built as a series of spaces that grew more private toward the god's shrine. The forecourt behind the great gateway was where most worshippers came closest to the god, and where festival crowds gathered and processions set out. At Memphis the chief temple belonged to Ptah, whose cult included the sacred Apis bull.
b_temple_forecourt.play: A service building offered at Memphis, described through Egypt's festivals. The game draws on Herodotus, but the boat and lamp festivals he describes centred on Bubastis and Sais, not on a Memphis forecourt.
b_temple_forecourt.s0: Egyptian temples opened through a pylon gateway into a court, often lined with columns. Beyond it, halls led to the dark sanctuary where the god's image stood. Ordinary people seem to have been admitted at most to the outer courts, while priests served the god inside. At Mit Rahina, the site of Memphis, excavators have found parts of the Ptah temple and the embalming house of the Apis, with its alabaster tables.
b_temple_forecourt.s1: Herodotus says the Egyptians held many festivals each year and that the Greeks learned processions from them. He describes crowds sailing to Bubastis. Women played clappers and men played pipes, while the rest sang and clapped. He also tells of a night at Sais when lamps burned outside houses across Egypt, and says that when a new Apis appeared, Egyptians put on their best clothes and feasted.
b_temple_forecourt.s2: Herodotus says the pharaoh Psammetichus I added a southern gateway to the temple of Ptah, whom he calls Hephaestus. Opposite it he built a colonnaded court where the Apis was kept and fed, with tall statues standing in place of pillars. This court has not been securely identified on the ground.
b_temple_forecourt.s3: Udjahorresnet was an Egyptian official who served Cambyses and Darius. The inscription on his statue records that he asked Cambyses to remove foreigners who had settled in the temple of Neith at Sais. The text says the king ordered the temple cleansed, its revenues restored and its festivals and processions held as before. It is one man's account of himself, but it shows a Persian king acting as a pharaoh was expected to act.
b_temple_forecourt.s4: Herodotus says Cambyses, angered by the Apis festival, stabbed the bull in the thigh and it died. Yet a stela from the Serapeum at Saqqara records an Apis buried with honour in Cambyses' sixth year, about 524 BCE, and a sarcophagus was dedicated in his name. Many historians therefore treat the story as hostile Egyptian tradition, though some argue the dates still leave room for a bull to have been wounded.
b_terrace.lead: The Royal Terrace is the great stone platform on which the palaces of Parsa stood, set against the Kuh-e Rahmat with its back to the rock. Darius began it, probably about 518 BCE, and his successors built on it for over a century. It raised the King's halls above the plain of the Pulvar and gave the empire a ceremonial and administrative centre in the Persian homeland.
b_terrace.play: The game builds the terrace in the Parsa level, dated 521 to 509 BCE; real work probably began about 518 BCE and went on under Xerxes and Artaxerxes I. The barley and wine costs simplify the ration system of the Fortification tablets.
b_terrace.s0: Excavation shows a platform of roughly 455 by 300 metres, partly levelled from bedrock and partly built up with large limestone blocks. The blocks were fitted without mortar and held by iron clamps set in lead. On the west its face rose more than 10 metres above the plain in places, and a mudbrick wall ran along the eastern side up the slope. Drains cut in the rock carried rainwater away beneath the buildings.
b_terrace.s1: Darius set inscriptions in Old Persian, Elamite and Akkadian into the south face of the terrace. In the Elamite text he says that no fortress had stood on this spot before, and that by the favour of Auramazda he built one, secure and fine. Another text asks the god to protect the land from hostile armies, famine and the Lie.
b_terrace.s2: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, written mostly in Elamite between 509 and 493 BCE, record rations of barley, wine and other goods to workers called kurtash. Men, women and children of many peoples, including Lydians, Ionians, Egyptians and Bactrians, appear in them. The later Treasury tablets show some workmen at Parsa paid partly in silver.
b_terrace.s3: No text gives the founding year, so the start is dated from the inscriptions, the archives and the building sequence, usually to about 518 BCE or a little later. Historians also argue over the purpose of the complex. Some see it mainly as a stage for royal ceremony, even a New Year festival, which no ancient source describes; others stress its role as a treasury, residence and centre of the royal economy.
b_terrace.s4: Greek writers of the Roman period describe the end of the terrace palaces. Diodorus describes the citadel and its walls before telling how Alexander burned the palaces. Arrian says Alexander did so as revenge for the Persian burning of Greek temples in 480 BCE. Diodorus and Plutarch add the story that the courtesan Thais urged the fire at a drinking party, a tale many historians doubt.
b_theatre.lead: The Theatre of Dionysus stood on the south slope of the Acropolis, where the Athenians watched tragedies at the City Dionysia, the spring festival of the god. In the years of the Persian wars it was probably still a simple dancing floor with wooden seating. Athenian tragedy of those decades turned the fall of Miletus and the defeat of Xerxes into shared public memory.
b_theatre.play: The game offers it in Greek towns as a service building of wooden benches, and Herodotus 6.21 does record Athens weeping at Phrynichus. Few Greek cities had a theatre this early; Athens is the clear case, so the game generalises.
b_theatre.s0: The theatre lay inside the sanctuary of Dionysus Eleuthereus, where excavators found the foundations of a small temple of the sixth century. Remains from before 480 BCE are scanty. They include some early walls and traces that may belong to a circular dancing floor, the orchestra. The stone seating that survives today belongs mostly to a rebuilding of about 330 under Lycurgus, with later Roman alterations.
b_theatre.s1: Later Greek lexicographers say that early audiences sat on wooden stands called ikria. The Suda reports that stands collapsed around 500 BCE during a contest in which Pratinas competed against Aeschylus, after which the Athenians built a theatre. Some historians think the earliest plays were staged in the Agora and moved to the slope only then. Others place them at the sanctuary from the start, and the dating of the earliest remains is still argued over.
b_theatre.s2: Herodotus says that Phrynichus staged a tragedy, The Capture of Miletus, after the Persians took the city in 494 BCE, and the whole audience burst into tears. The Athenians fined him a thousand drachmas for reminding them of their own misfortunes and banned the play from being performed again. Herodotus gives no date, and scholars usually place it about 493 BCE. Athens had sent twenty ships to help the Ionian revolt and then withdrawn them, which may explain why the play stung.
b_theatre.s3: Plutarch says Themistocles paid for a winning chorus of Phrynichus in 476 BCE. Modern scholars often identify the play as the Phoenician Women, a drama about Salamis. Aeschylus, who had fought at Marathon, staged The Persians in 472 BCE, set at the Persian court as news of Xerxes' defeat reaches the queen mother. It is a Greek imagining of Persia rather than a Persian source, and it is the oldest Greek tragedy that survives.
b_theatre.s4: Later Greeks told that tragedy began when Thespis stepped apart from the chorus and first spoke as a character. A chronicle carved in the third century, the Parian Marble, places his first production at Athens in the 530s BCE. Plutarch tells a moral tale in which the aged Solon watched Thespis perform and scolded him for telling lies in public. These stories were written down centuries afterwards and cannot be checked.
b_tomb.lead: The Tomb of Cyrus is a small gabled stone chamber on a high stepped plinth on the plain of Pasargadae, the city Cyrus founded in Persis. Writers who came with Alexander, preserved by Arrian and Strabo, say it held the king's body in a golden coffin and was guarded by magi. It still stands, one of the best preserved buildings of the early Persian empire.
b_tomb.play: In the game Cyrus commissions the tomb in 530 BCE, and masons set it stone by stone from limestone blocks. The commission is a dramatized scene. Whether Cyrus ordered it himself or it was finished after his death is not known.
b_tomb.s0: The tomb rises about 11 metres in pale limestone. A plinth of six steps carries a single chamber about 3 by 2 metres, entered by a low, narrow doorway and covered by a gabled stone roof. The blocks are very large and were held together by metal clamps, many of them later torn out by robbers. David Stronach's excavations in 1961-63 studied the tomb and its surroundings closely.
b_tomb.s1: The fine joints and clamp work match stone techniques of Lydia and Ionia, and many scholars think craftsmen from Sardis worked here after Cyrus took that city. The stepped plinth and gabled chamber have been compared with Lydian tombs, Mesopotamian and Elamite stepped platforms, and gabled houses of the Iranian highlands, with no agreement on one model. Most date it to the later years of Cyrus, but it may have been completed under Cambyses.
b_tomb.s2: Arrian, drawing on Aristobulus, says the chamber held a golden coffin, a couch, tables, cups and fine garments, and that an inscription named Cyrus. He says magi guarded it from the time of Cambyses, receiving a sheep a day and a horse each month to sacrifice to Cyrus. When Alexander returned from India, about 324, he found it plundered and had Aristobulus restore it. Strabo and Plutarch also tell of the robbery and the inscription.
b_tomb.s3: Cyrus died in 530 BCE, and the ancient writers disagree on how. Herodotus says he fell fighting the Massagetae, and admits his version was one of many. Ctesias says he died of wounds after a battle with the Derbices and that his body was sent home to Persia, while Xenophon has him die peacefully in his bed. No text survives on the tomb, but almost all scholars accept it as his.
b_tomb.s4: Herodotus records a tale that Queen Tomyris of the Massagetae dipped the dead king's head in a skin of blood, a story shaped as a moral lesson rather than a report. In medieval times local tradition called the building the tomb of the mother of Solomon, and a small mosque was built around it with columns taken from the ruined palaces. Travellers of the early 19th century later matched it with Arrian's description.
b_training_ground.lead: Greek writers describe Persian boys trained from childhood to ride, to shoot and to tell the truth, and Darius himself boasts of those skills. No Persian text describes the schooling and no training ground has been found, so the picture comes from outsiders, and some of it is idealized.
b_training_ground.play: The Youths' Training Ground sends an instructor along the streets, and Noble Residences need his visits. A Sanctuary with a Teaching Porch serves too, its magus teaching as he walks. The building, the rounds and the porch are the game's inventions: the sources give the lessons, not the place.
b_training_ground.s0: Herodotus says Persian boys were taught three things only, from five years old to twenty: to ride, to shoot the bow and to speak the truth. Before five a boy lived among the women and did not come into his father's sight, so that if he died young his father would not grieve.
b_training_ground.s1: The one Persian voice on these skills is the King's. In his tomb inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam Darius says he is a good horseman, a good bowman and a good spearman, on foot and on horseback, and at Behistun he sets himself against the Lie. It is royal self-praise and says nothing of how a boy was taught, but Herodotus's lessons match it closely.
b_training_ground.s2: Strabo, writing about five centuries after Darius, has the training run from five to twenty-four: the bow, the javelin, riding and truth, under chosen teachers who weave in tales of gods and noble men. The boys are roused before dawn, run in companies, cross torrents keeping their gear dry, and live off what they gather. He does not call the teachers magi.
b_training_ground.s3: Xenophon has boys go to school to learn justice as Greek boys learn letters, in a free square by the palace kept clear of traders, with elders judging their quarrels. The Cyropaedia is a moral romance about an ideal Persia, written for Greeks, and cannot be taken as a description of one.
b_training_ground.s4: Xenophon knew Persians at first hand, and in the Anabasis he says Persian nobles' sons were brought up at the King's door, where they saw who was honoured and who disgraced, and learned to rule and obey. He says Cyrus the Younger excelled among them at riding and the bow. This is a eulogy, but of a man the writer served.
b_training_ground.s5: A dialogue passed down under Plato's name, its authorship doubted, says a Persian prince at fourteen went to four royal tutors, the first of whom taught him the magian lore of Zoroaster, which is the worship of the gods, and what belongs to a king. That is a Greek's account of princes, not townsfolk. Nothing else ties the magi to teaching, and the Teaching Porch stands on this alone.
b_vineyard.lead: Vines were grown in the uplands of Persis, in Media, Armenia, Syria and Anatolia, and wine was one of the main goods counted by the royal storehouses. Administrative tablets from Persepolis show wine moving through the King's economy as pay, travel supplies and offerings. Greek writers saw heavy drinking as a mark of Persian luxury.
b_vineyard.play: The game's Vineyard trains vines on posts, presses the grapes and ferments the wine on the estate for Noble Residences. In the tablets wine also went to some workers, travellers and gods, not only to the elite.
b_vineyard.s0: The Elamite Fortification tablets, written at Persepolis between about 509 and 493 BCE, record wine collected into royal stores and paid out again. It went to officials, to travellers on the roads, to some groups of workers and to the households of royal women. Wine also appears among the goods issued for offerings to several gods. The tablets show it as a managed commodity, stored and accounted for alongside grain, beer and fruit.
b_vineyard.s1: On the stairways of Darius's palace at Persepolis, and on later palace stairways there, carved servants climb towards the royal rooms. They carry young animals, covered vessels and wineskins, bringing food and drink up for the King's table. The reliefs survive in place today and fit the tablets' picture of a court supplied with wine.
b_vineyard.s2: Herodotus says the Persians were very fond of wine. He claims that they debated serious matters while drunk and then reconsidered the decision when sober, or the other way round. Greek writers often used Persian feasting to suggest softness and excess, so the description says as much about Greek attitudes as about Persian custom.
b_vineyard.s3: Herodotus says Babylonia grew no vines and drank date-palm wine, and that grape wine came down the river from Armenia in boats loaded with palm-wood casks. He also says Egypt had no vines, though elsewhere he mentions grape wine given to priests. Egyptian tomb paintings and labelled wine jars show that vineyards had long existed in the Delta and the oases. Egypt also imported wine in jars from Greece and Phoenicia.
b_vineyard.s4: Herodotus tells two moral tales about wine. Before Croesus attacked Cyrus, a Lydian named Sandanis warned him that the Persians drank water, not wine, and had nothing worth taking. Later, Cyrus was said to have left a camp full of wine for the Massagetae, who drank it and were slaughtered. Both stories are built to make a point about luxury and ruin, not to record events.
b_wall.lead: Cities and royal sites of the Persian empire were ringed by walls of mudbrick raised on stone foundations, often with towers and fortified gates. Excavation and Greek writers show both how such walls were built and how Persian armies overcame them, by earth ramps, mining and storming.
b_wall.play: The wall is dragged out on stone footings, with a gatehouse where it crosses a road; soldiers stand on it and masons repair it. Hill raiders break, burn, climb or undermine it, though in the sources these were the methods of organised armies.
b_wall.s0: The usual wall of the period was a footing of rubble or cut stone that kept damp away, carrying a tall body of sun-dried mudbrick. At Sardis, excavators found a Lydian city wall some 20 metres thick at its base, built this way. At Persepolis a mudbrick wall with towers ran along the edges of the terrace and up the slope of the mountain behind it.
b_wall.s1: Herodotus says Harpagus took the Ionian cities, after Cyrus had conquered Lydia, by piling earth mounds against their walls. He tells how the Persians tried to mine under the walls of Barca in Libya, and how the defenders found the tunnels by tapping a bronze shield on the ground. In the Cypriot revolt, he says, Soli held out longest and fell in the fifth month when the Persians undermined its wall.
b_wall.s2: At Old Paphos on Cyprus, excavators uncovered a ramp of earth, stone and timber built against the city wall by the northeast gate, probably during the revolt of about 498 BCE. Into it were thrown broken statues and altars from a nearby shrine, and hundreds of arrowheads lay around it. The defenders dug tunnels under the ramp and burned out its supports.
b_wall.s3: Herodotus says Cyrus's men took the citadel of Sardis by climbing a steep, unguarded stretch where a Lydian had been seen fetching a fallen helmet. Excavation shows the lower city wall was stormed and burned in the mid-6th century, with arrowheads and dead soldiers in the destruction layer. The exact year is argued over, since the Nabonidus Chronicle line once read as naming Lydia is damaged.
b_wall.s4: Herodotus says Mardonius pulled down what was left of the walls of Athens before he withdrew to Boeotia in 479 BCE. Thucydides tells how the Athenians then rebuilt their wall in haste with any stone to hand, including grave markers, while Themistocles stalled Spartan objections at Sparta.
b_watch_post.lead: Towns of the Persian empire were built of mud brick, with roofs of timber beams, reeds and matting that burned easily. Garrisons and local officials kept guard, but no organised fire service is recorded in the period. When fire broke out, neighbours probably fought it with water jars, and the damage was repaired afterwards by hired or levied labour.
b_watch_post.play: Watchmen walk the streets, put out fires and repair damaged buildings as one service. This is a dramatization: no fire brigade is recorded before Rome, and in this period neighbours probably fought fires with water jars.
b_watch_post.s0: Excavation at Persepolis shows how Persian builders worked: walls of mud brick on stone footings, and flat roofs carried on wooden beams, some of cedar, covered with reeds and packed earth. The Treasury and the halls were found under thick layers of ash and charred timber from the fire of 330. Walls survived where the roofs and stored goods burned, which shows that timber was the weak point of mud-brick building.
b_watch_post.s1: Herodotus says that most houses in Sardis were made of reeds, and even the brick ones had reed roofs. When the Ionians and Athenians took the lower city in 498 BCE, a soldier set one house alight. The fire ran from roof to roof across the whole town and burned the temple of the goddess Cybebe. Herodotus adds that the Persians later named this burning as their reason for burning Greek temples.
b_watch_post.s2: Aramaic papyri from the garrison at Elephantine record that in 410 BCE the temple of the Jewish soldiers' god Yahu was wrecked and burned by local Egyptians, backed by the Persian commander Vidranga. In 407 BCE the community wrote to Bagavahya, governor of Judah, asking for leave to rebuild. The letters show that repair went through petitions to officials, not a standing repair service. The event falls after the game's period.
b_watch_post.s3: Greek writers describe night watches and guard posts kept against enemies and traitors. Aeneas Tacticus, writing in the 4th century, gives detailed advice on sentries and patrols in a threatened town. He also explains how to quench fires set by attackers, but describes no standing fire corps. The best-documented ancient fire brigade is the Roman vigiles, which Cassius Dio says Augustus set up in 6 CE.
b_watch_post.s4: Later writers disagree about the fire of Persepolis in 330. Arrian presents it as Alexander's deliberate revenge for the Persian burning of Athenian temples in 480 BCE. Plutarch and Diodorus tell a moral tale in which the courtesan Thais urged a drunken Alexander to set the palace alight after a feast. Many historians think the burning was a political decision and treat the Thais story as later colouring.
b_watchtower.lead: Forts, garrisons and lookout posts guarded the roads, river crossings and frontiers of the Persian empire. Their men watched for trouble, and Greek writers describe warnings passed by fire or by shouting from height to height. Few single towers of the period have been excavated, but documents and Greek writers show that guarded posts and signals were part of how the King held his lands.
b_watchtower.play: Two guards shoot raiders within eight cells and light a beacon when raiders gather; it needs a road, and masons repair it. Real lookouts probably sat in garrisoned forts, and kings sometimes paid hill peoples instead.
b_watchtower.s0: The Elamite tablets of the Persepolis Fortification archive, written between about 509 and 493 BCE, mention fortified places in Persis and Elam. The Elamite word halmarriš is usually translated as fortress or fortified settlement. The same archive records rations issued to travellers, guides and express messengers on the roads, which shows a route network supplied and overseen by the administration.
b_watchtower.s1: Aramaic papyri from Elephantine, at Egypt's southern border, describe a garrison of Judaean soldiers in the fortress of Yeb, with Aramaeans based mainly at nearby Syene. The soldiers were organised in units under commanders with Iranian, Babylonian and other names. The papyri date mostly from the later 5th century, after the period of the game, but they show the empire keeping soldiers permanently at frontier points.
b_watchtower.s2: Herodotus says that in 479 BCE Mardonius hoped to send word to Xerxes at Sardis that he had taken Athens a second time, using fire signals passed across the islands. He also says that in 480 BCE, when Persian ships captured Greek guard ships off Skiathos, the news reached the Greek fleet at Artemisium by fire signals from the island. Both stories show that beacon chains were a familiar way to send warning quickly.
b_watchtower.s3: Diodorus describes lookouts in Persis under the Macedonian governor Peucestas in 317, who shouted messages from height to height so that news crossed a month's journey in a day. The treatise On the World, wrongly attributed to Aristotle, claims beacons brought the King news from all his lands within a day. Many historians think these are late and exaggerated, and that signal chains were local or set up for campaigns rather than one standing network.
b_watchtower.s4: Arrian says that the Uxians, a hill people between Susa and Persis, demanded payment from Alexander in 331 for passage through their mountains, as they had received it from the Persian king. Alexander forced them to submit. His account suggests that keeping the roads of the homeland open could mean bargaining with hill peoples as well as watching them.
b_water_channel.lead: At Pasargadae, Cyrus's builders laid narrow channels of cut limestone, broken at intervals by small square basins, to carry water through the royal garden. They are among the earliest surviving stone-built formal garden channels known. They show how Persian kings used controlled water to make a dry upland plain green and to display royal power.
b_water_channel.play: The game lists the Water Channel among its housing buildings. The real stone channels at Pasargadae served a royal garden beside the palaces, not ordinary neighbourhoods, so the game simplifies their setting.
b_water_channel.s0: David Stronach's excavations at Pasargadae in the early 1960s uncovered limestone channels about 25 centimetres wide running along the edges of a rectangular garden in front of the residential palace and near its pavilions. Small square basins were set into the channels at intervals. The blocks were cut and fitted with care, matching the fine masonry of the palaces nearby.
b_water_channel.s1: Pasargadae lies on the plain of the Pulvar river, and the garden channels were probably fed by water drawn from it. Later surveys of the plain and the valleys around it have traced other ancient water works, including dams and canals. The garden channels were probably the most refined part of a wider system for managing water on the plain.
b_water_channel.s2: Stronach reconstructed the channels as framing a garden divided into four parts, and argued it was an early ancestor of the later Persian fourfold garden. Other scholars doubt that the plan was truly quadripartite. Geophysical survey by a Franco-Iranian team suggested the layout of water and planting may have been more complex. The exact design remains debated.
b_water_channel.s3: Polybius, writing in the second century, says that when the Persians ruled Asia they granted the use of land for five generations to anyone who brought water to ground that had not been watered before. He tells this in connection with the underground channels on the route toward Hyrcania. His account is late, but it fits the royal interest in irrigation seen at Pasargadae.
b_water_channel.s4: Xenophon, in a dialogue told by Socrates, says the Persian prince Cyrus the Younger showed the Spartan Lysander his garden at Sardis, with trees planted in straight rows. Lysander admired the order, and Cyrus said he had measured out and arranged it all himself and planted some of the trees. The visit took place about 407 BCE, long after Pasargadae, but it shows how Greeks saw the planned Persian garden.
b_water_house.lead: Greek writers noticed that Persians treated running water with unusual care and would not wash in a river or foul it. Washing therefore had to be done with water taken away from the stream. No building made for this purpose has been identified, but the stone watercourses at Pasargadae and the drains at Persepolis show how carefully Persian builders managed water.
b_water_house.play: In the game, houses within six cells wash at a Water House, and Noble Residences need one. No public washing house of this kind is known from Persia, so the game turns the rule against fouling rivers into a service building.
b_water_house.s0: Herodotus says that Persians did not urinate or spit into a river, did not wash their hands in one, and did not let others do so, because they honoured rivers greatly. Strabo, writing more than four centuries later, adds that they did not bathe in water or throw anything dead or unclean into it. Both are outsiders' reports, but they agree that washing was kept away from flowing water.
b_water_house.s1: The royal garden that Cyrus laid out at Pasargadae was watered by narrow channels cut in limestone blocks. Small square basins were set at intervals along them. The water probably came from the Pulvar river. These were garden works for irrigation and display, and nothing shows that they were used for washing.
b_water_house.s2: Excavators found a network of drains cut into the bedrock beneath the Persepolis terrace, planned before the buildings rose above them. The drains carried off rain and waste water, and there were cisterns as well. Such works show that the King's builders planned water supply and drainage from the start.
b_water_house.s3: Polybius reports that when the Persians ruled Asia, they gave people the use of land for five generations if they brought water to places that had none. Historians link this to qanats, underground channels that tap groundwater. Scholars still argue over whether the Persians spread this technique or whether it was older and local, and over how to date similar channels found in Egypt's western oases.
b_water_house.s4: Zoroastrian texts such as the Videvdad set out strict rules against polluting water. They were written down many centuries after the Achaemenid kings. Historians disagree about how far these rules reflect Persian practice in the time of Cyrus and Darius. The Greek reports are closer in date, but they describe the custom from outside.
b_water_house_fountain_house.lead: A fountain house was a roofed building where spring water, often brought by underground pipes, ran from spouts into basins for people to fill their jars. Several Greek tyrants of the later sixth century built them as public works, and Athens's Enneakrounos, the Nine Spouts, was the best known. They gave towns clean water and served as daily meeting places.
b_water_house_fountain_house.play: In the Sardis and Greek levels the Water House takes this form; homes within six cells wash here and Noble Residences need one. Thucydides 2.15 says Nine Spouts, not Nine Springs, and mentions rites, not washing.
b_water_house_fountain_house.s0: Excavated examples share a common plan: a roofed hall, often with a columned front, where water ran from spouts, sometimes shaped as lion heads, or gathered in draw-basins. In the Athenian Agora a line of terracotta pipes, laid in a rock-cut channel in the later sixth century, fed the Southeast Fountain House. Painted Athenian water jars of the late sixth century often show women filling their jars at such buildings.
b_water_house_fountain_house.s1: Thucydides describes a fountain in old Athens that the tyrants had fitted out, so that it was called Enneakrounos, the Nine Spouts. Before that, he says, the springs lay open and were called Kallirrhoe. He adds that Athenians still used its water before weddings and for other sacred rites, a custom he takes as proof of where the early city lay.
b_water_house_fountain_house.s2: Thucydides links the fountain with the old shrines south of the Acropolis, and its earlier name, Kallirrhoe, was later given to a spring in the bed of the Ilissos. Pausanias, writing in the second century CE, puts the Enneakrounos near the Agora. Agora excavators have often matched his account with the Southeast Fountain House of about 530 to 520 BCE, while others place the Pisistratid fountain by the Ilissos. The question is not settled.
b_water_house_fountain_house.s3: Water supply was a favoured public work of sixth-century tyrants. Herodotus praises the tunnel that Eupalinus of Megara cut through a hill on Samos to bring water to the city. He does not name the ruler, but the tunnel is usually dated to the time of Polycrates. Pausanias credits Theagenes, tyrant of Megara, with a fountain house there. Such works probably won rulers goodwill and displayed their resources.
b_water_house_fountain_house.s4: Herodotus reports an Athenian tale of the distant past. Athenian girls went to fetch water at the Enneakrounos, since, he explains, there were no household slaves in those days, and Pelasgian settlers living below Mount Hymettus assaulted them. For this the Pelasgians were driven from Attica. Herodotus also gives Hecataeus's version, in which the Athenians expelled them out of envy for their well-worked land.
b_water_house_river_steps.lead: Memphis, the old capital of Egypt that Cambyses took in 525 BCE, stood on the west bank of the Nile, and its people drew water, bathed and washed their clothes at the river and its canals. Linen was the common cloth of Egypt, and keeping it clean was a daily chore for most people and a religious duty for priests. The game's River Steps stand for these riverside washing places.
b_water_house_river_steps.play: The River Steps are Memphis's Water House: houses within six cells wash here and Noble Residences need one. The game gathers into one building what Memphites did all along the river and its canals.
b_water_house_river_steps.s0: Herodotus visited Egypt some decades after the Persian conquest. He says the Egyptians wore linen and took special care to keep it freshly washed. In the same passage he says priests shaved their bodies and bathed in cold water twice by day and twice by night. Elsewhere he describes a fringed linen tunic worn with a white woollen cloak over it, and notes that wool was not taken into temples or buried with the dead.
b_water_house_river_steps.s1: Egyptian evidence much older than the Persian period shows that laundering was a trade, and Middle Kingdom tomb paintings at Beni Hasan show men beating and wringing cloth. The Satire of the Trades, a school text that praises the scribe's life by mocking other trades, pictures the washerman at work on the riverbank with crocodiles nearby. The satire exaggerates, but it confirms that men did laundry at the water's edge.
b_water_house_river_steps.s2: Herodotus says Memphis was built on land won from the Nile when its first king, Min, dammed the river and turned its course. He adds that the Persians of his own day still strengthened this dyke every year. He also says that Amasis moved communities of Carians and Ionians to Memphis to serve as his guard, so the town by the river held foreign settlers as well as Egyptians.
b_water_house_river_steps.s3: No excavated washing steps from Persian-period Memphis are known. Over the centuries the Nile has moved eastward, and much of the ancient riverside now lies under silt and fields near Mit Rahina, so its quays and landings are reconstructed rather than seen. Stone stairs to the water are known from Egyptian temple quays and from the Nilometer at Elephantine that Strabo describes. How ordinary townspeople reached the river at Memphis remains uncertain.
b_weaver.lead: Cloth was among the most valuable goods of the ancient Near East, and spinning and weaving took up a large share of ordinary labour. In the Achaemenid empire weaving went on in households, in temple workshops and on the King's estates. Fine garments served as wages, dowries, offerings to the gods and gifts from the King to men he wished to honour.
b_weaver.play: The game's workshop spins and weaves wool into cloth for Elder's Houses. This simplifies: much cloth was linen, above all in Egypt, and most weaving was done in homes, temples and royal estates, not in shops.
b_weaver.s0: Babylonian temple archives of the sixth century, from the Ebabbar at Sippar and the Eanna at Uruk, record weavers who were paid in rations and issued wool, linen and dyed yarn. They made garments for the statues of the gods, which were dressed in new clothing at set festivals. Wool dyed red-purple and blue was costly and carefully counted. These records continued into the years of Persian rule after Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BCE.
b_weaver.s1: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, from about 509 to 494 BCE, record rations for large groups of workers, men and women, on royal estates in Persis. Some female groups are called pashap, a word that several scholars connect with making garments, though its exact meaning is still debated. Mothers in these groups received extra rations after childbirth, which shows that women were a settled part of the workforce.
b_weaver.s2: Aramaic papyri from the Jewish garrison at Elephantine in Egypt list garments among a bride's dowry, each valued in silver. The marriage contract of Mibtahiah and Eshor was written in the mid-fifth century, a little after the game's period. It names several garments, mostly of wool, beside bronze vessels and furniture. Clothing was treated as property worth recording, like any other valuable goods.
b_weaver.s3: Herodotus says the Persians took up Median dress, and that the family of Otanes received a Median robe from the King every year as a mark of honour. He also tells how Cambyses sent a purple cloak among his gifts to the Ethiopian king. He describes Babylonian men wearing a linen tunic to the feet, a woollen tunic over it and a white cloak, which shows both fibres in daily use.
b_well.lead: Wells were among the oldest ways of reaching water in the dry lands the Persian kings ruled. Alongside rivers, canals, springs and underground channels, they watered households, travellers and armies. Control of water shaped where people could farm and settle, and the sources show water being found, shared and fought over under Persian rule.
b_well.play: The game's Well supplies water to houses within five cells and needs no workers. In reality drawing and carrying water was daily labour, and many towns relied on rivers, canals and underground channels as much as on wells.
b_well.s0: Herodotus describes a well near Ardericca in Cissia, where Darius settled captive Eretrians after 490 BCE. Bitumen, salt and oil were drawn from it with a swing beam that carried half a skin in place of a bucket. Counterweighted lifting beams of this kind were already old in the Near East; a separate line of evidence, Assyrian palace reliefs, shows them in use.
b_well.s1: Polybius wrote in the 2nd century. He says that when the Persians ruled Asia, they granted the use of land for five generations to anyone who brought water to a place that had none. He links this to underground channels dug from the hills, of the kind later called qanats, which tapped groundwater through a line of shafts. His report is late, but it fits the interest in new farmland seen elsewhere in Persian administration.
b_well.s2: Historians still debate where underground channels began. Some favour the Iranian plateau and spread under Persian rule; some archaeologists argue that galleries in south-east Arabia are older. At Ayn Manawir in Egypt's Kharga Oasis, excavated galleries and Persian-period demotic ostraca recording transactions in water shares show such systems working under Achaemenid rule. Firm dates for the channels of Persis itself are harder to establish.
b_well.s3: Herodotus says that when Darius crossed into Scythia, about 513 BCE, the Scythians retreated and stopped up the wells and springs along their route to deny his army water. Earlier, he says, Cambyses could cross the desert to Egypt in 525 BCE only after an Arab king agreed to carry water to the army in skins on camels. In both stories, water points decided where large forces could march.
b_well.s4: Herodotus tells a story set at Sardis. Darius saw a Paeonian woman carry a jar on her head to fetch water, lead a horse and spin flax all at once. He was so struck by her people's industry that he ordered them moved to Asia. The tale is shaped to explain a deportation and is not a record, but it treats fetching water as ordinary daily work, often done by women.
b_woodcutter.lead: Timber roofed the halls of the Persian kings, fuelled their brick kilns, built the ships of their fleets and warmed ordinary households. Everyday wood was cut close to home, but the great beams for royal buildings were often hauled across the empire, and Darius boasted of this in his building inscriptions.
b_woodcutter.play: The Woodcutter fells trees near woodland and supplies timber. This is a simplification: local felling gave fuel and lesser timber, while royal palaces drew long cedar and other beams from distant provinces.
b_woodcutter.s0: In his foundation charter for the palace at Susa, Darius listed where the building materials came from. Cedar was cut on a mountain called Lebanon, carried to Babylon by the Assyrians and taken on to Susa by Carians and Ionians. Another timber, called yaka, came from Gandhara and Carmania. The king presented this long haul as proof of how far his rule reached.
b_woodcutter.s1: The columned halls at Persepolis spanned wide spaces with flat roofs laid on heavy wooden beams resting on the column capitals. When Alexander's army burned Persepolis in 330, much of this woodwork fell and charred. Excavators found burnt timber and thick ash in the destruction layers. These remains show how much wood the terrace buildings held.
b_woodcutter.s2: Herodotus says that Darius granted Histiaeus of Miletus the site of Myrcinus near the Strymon, and that the general Megabazus later warned the King against it. The place, Megabazus said, had plenty of timber for ships and oars, as well as silver mines. The story shows that forests suited to shipbuilding were treated as strategic resources worth controlling.
b_woodcutter.s3: Most felling served daily needs: fuel for hearths, ovens and kilns, poles for scaffolding and beams for houses. Historians still debate how wooded Persis and the Zagros were in this period and how quickly cutting thinned the oak, juniper and other trees. The written sources say little about ordinary woodcutters, so much of the picture rests on later evidence and environmental studies.
e_alexander_embassy.lead: After Salamis, Mardonius wintered in Thessaly and tried to win Athens over before the next campaign, sending Alexander I of Macedon, a Persian vassal with ties to Athens, to offer the King's friendship and generous terms. The Athenians refused, and Herodotus made their answer a statement of what bound the Greeks together. The refusal kept the Athenian fleet on the Greek side, and the war was decided by battle at Plataea.
e_alexander_embassy.play: The game shows this as a 479 BCE event in which Mardonius sends Alexander to Athens to offer the King's friendship and the Athenians refuse. It leaves out the Spartan envoys and the second offer brought by Murychides.
e_alexander_embassy.s0: Herodotus says Mardonius first consulted Greek oracles and then picked Alexander for two reasons. Alexander's sister Gygaea had married the Persian noble Bubares, so he was linked to the Persians by marriage. He was also a proxenos and benefactor of Athens, an official friend of the city. Mardonius hoped the Athenians, with their many ships, would join him and give Persia control of the sea.
e_alexander_embassy.s1: In Herodotus's version, Alexander relayed a message from Xerxes. The King would forgive all past wrongs, return the Athenians' land and let them take more land of their choosing, leave them to govern themselves, and rebuild the temples his army had burned, if they made an alliance. Alexander added his own advice that Persian power was too great to resist and that Attica lay in the path of any new invasion.
e_alexander_embassy.s2: Spartan envoys arrived, fearing Athens would accept, and offered to feed Athenian families through the war. Herodotus says the Athenians told Alexander they would never come to terms with Xerxes while the sun kept its course, and warned him not to return. To the Spartans they cited the burned shrines and a shared Greek blood, language, gods and customs, and asked for an army in Boeotia soon.
e_alexander_embassy.s3: Herodotus presents Alexander as a Greek at heart. He says Alexander had Persian envoys killed years earlier and later rode to the Greek camp before Plataea to warn them. Many historians, notably Badian, think these stories came from Macedonian claims made after Persia's defeat, to clean up the record of a king who served Xerxes loyally. No Persian source mentions the embassy, and the Athenian speeches are probably largely Herodotus's own composition.
e_alexander_embassy.s4: Herodotus says Mardonius then marched south and occupied Athens a second time, the people having again fled to Salamis. He sent a Hellespontine Greek named Murychides with the same offer. One councillor, Lycidas, proposed putting it to the people, and the Athenians stoned him to death. After some delay the Spartans sent their army north, and the campaign ended at Plataea.
e_ammon_ethiopia.lead: After taking Egypt, Cambyses tried to push Persian power west into the desert towards the oracle of Ammon at Siwa, and south up the Nile into Kush, which the Greeks called Ethiopia. Herodotus tells both as disasters caused by the king's rage. Persian records suggest the southern venture was not a complete failure, since Kush later appears among the King's subject lands.
e_ammon_ethiopia.play: The game follows Herodotus: the Ammon army is said to be buried by a sandstorm and hunger halts the march south. It leaves out his own note that some Ethiopians were subdued, and the 524 BCE date is a modern estimate.
e_ammon_ethiopia.s0: Herodotus says that once Egypt was his, Cambyses planned three campaigns: against Carthage, against the Ammonians of the western desert, and against the long-lived Ethiopians on the southern sea. The Phoenician fleet refused to sail against Carthage, its own colony, so that plan was dropped. The other two went ahead. Herodotus gives no year, and historians usually place them around 524 BCE.
e_ammon_ethiopia.s1: Herodotus tells how Cambyses sent Fish-eaters from Elephantine as spies bearing gifts. The Ethiopian king saw through them, mocked the gifts and sent back a huge bow, saying the Persians should come only when they could draw bows that size as easily as his people did. The story has the shape of a moral tale about a greedy conqueror and a wise, distant people, with marvels such as men living to 120 and the Table of the Sun.
e_ammon_ethiopia.s2: In Herodotus the king set out in fury without stores of food. Before a fifth of the way was covered the supplies ran out, the men ate the pack animals and then, he says, drew lots to eat one man in ten, so Cambyses turned back to Thebes and Memphis. Yet Herodotus also says elsewhere that Cambyses subdued the Ethiopians next to Egypt on this march, and that they afterwards sent gifts of gold, ebony and ivory every other year.
e_ammon_ethiopia.s3: Herodotus says about 50,000 men, probably an exaggerated figure, left Thebes to enslave the Ammonians and burn their oracle. They reached a town called Oasis and vanished; he admits the sandstorm story came from the Ammonians. Modern claims to have found their remains are unproven. O. Kaper has argued that a rebel Egyptian king, Petubastis IV, attested in the Dakhla Oasis, defeated the force and that the storm tale hid the loss.
e_ammon_ethiopia.s4: Darius's inscriptions name Kush among the lands under the King, and his Susa building charter says ivory for the palace came from Kush. Reliefs at Persepolis show Kushite gift-bearers. These show that by Darius's reign at least northern Kush was counted within the empire's reach, though whether Cambyses or Darius first secured it cannot be settled from the records.
e_armenian_war.lead: Armenia was one of the lands that rose against Darius in the first months of his reign. His inscription at Behistun records five battles fought for him by two generals, Dadarshish the Armenian and Vaumisa the Persian. It is one of the least-known theatres of the revolts of 522-521 BCE, and the inscription never says that the war ended in a clear victory.
e_armenian_war.play: The game shows a 521 BCE campaign fought battle after battle by Dadarshish and Vaumisa, as Behistun does. It simplifies the dates: Vaumisa's first battle, at Izala, probably fell at the very end of 522 BCE.
e_armenian_war.s0: Armenia (Old Persian Armina) is not in the list of rebel countries that Darius gives at the start of his account of the revolts. It appears later, where he tells of rebels in Armenia who would not call themselves his, beside the Median revolt of Fravartish. The Babylonian version renders the name as Urashtu, after Urartu, the kingdom that once ruled these highlands. Unlike most of the revolts, the Armenian rising is tied to no named pretender.
e_armenian_war.s1: Darius says he sent Dadarshish, an Armenian loyal to him, against the rebels. Dadarshish fought them at a village called Zuzahya, then at the fortress of Tigra ten days later, and then at the fortress of Uyama in the following month, probably in May and June 521 BCE. Each time the text says the rebels were beaten, yet afterwards Dadarshish waited in Armenia until Darius came to Media. He is not the Dadarshish who, as satrap of Bactria, fought the Margian rebels.
e_armenian_war.s2: A second general, Vaumisa the Persian, was also sent to Armenia. His first battle took place at Izala in Assyria, outside Armenia proper, and his second in an Armenian district called Autiyara at the end of the month Thuravahara. Like Dadarshish, he then waited in Armenia for the King. Behistun later calls Arakha, leader of the second Babylonian revolt, an Armenian, but does not connect him with this war.
e_armenian_war.s3: Historians note that five reported victories, with no captured leader and no stated end, suggest the generals could not settle Armenia on their own. Many think the rising was only held in check until Darius was free to act after defeating Fravartish in Media. The dates are also debated. On the usual reckoning Vaumisa's fight at Izala fell around the turn of 522-521 BCE, before Dadarshish's battles, and why it was fought in Assyria remains unclear.
e_armenian_war.s4: Greek writers say nothing of the Armenian war itself. Herodotus places the Armenians, with their neighbours as far as the Black Sea, in Darius's thirteenth tax district, paying 400 talents of silver a year. Xenophon, marching through the region in 401 BCE, found western Armenia under a Persian governor, Tiribazus, which shows that the land stayed in the empire.
e_athos_canal_digging.lead: In about 483 BCE Xerxes began a ship canal across the narrow isthmus behind Mount Athos in the northern Aegean, so that his fleet would not have to round the cape where Mardonius's ships had been wrecked in 492 BCE. Herodotus describes the digging in detail and judges it vanity. The buried channel has since been traced, and with the Hellespont bridges it was part of Xerxes' long preparation for the invasion of Greece.
e_athos_canal_digging.play: The Athos level is built around the canal, dug under Bubares and Artachaees with the Phoenicians' stretch the best, as Herodotus tells it. The game's notes also give his view that the work was vanity.
e_athos_canal_digging.s0: Herodotus says Mardonius's fleet was wrecked rounding the cape of Athos in 492 BCE. By his figures some 300 ships and more than 20,000 men were lost, numbers that may well be inflated. Xerxes, who succeeded Darius in 486 BCE, chose not to risk the cape again. Herodotus says the work at Athos went on for about three years, with triremes based at Elaeus in the Chersonese sending men across in relays.
e_athos_canal_digging.s1: Herodotus says the ground was marked out along a line from the town of Sane and shared among the peoples of the army. They dug under the lash, joined by the people living around Athos, with the Persians Bubares son of Megabazus and Artachaees son of Artaeus in charge. As the trench deepened, earth was passed up on ladders. The sides kept falling in, except in the Phoenicians' stretch, which they cut twice as wide at the top as at the bottom.
e_athos_canal_digging.s2: No Persian inscription or tablet mentions the canal, but the ground preserves it. From 1991 a British and Greek team used geophysical survey and boreholes to trace a buried channel about 2 km long across the isthmus, between the coast near Nea Roda and the bay at Trypiti. Its line fits Herodotus's account. It seems to have been kept open only briefly before it silted up.
e_athos_canal_digging.s3: Herodotus thought the canal was dug from pride, since the ships could have been hauled over the isthmus. He adds that it was wide enough for two triremes to row abreast. Many historians now see sound reasons too: hauling hundreds of warships was slow, and the cape was a known danger. The Roman poet Juvenal doubted it had ever existed, but Thucydides named it as the King's canal, and the survey confirms it.
e_athos_canal_digging.s4: Later Greek writers made the canal a lesson in royal arrogance. Plutarch tells that Xerxes wrote a letter to Athos, warning the mountain not to put great stones in his workmen's way or he would cut it down and throw it into the sea. The tale belongs with Greek stories of Xerxes punishing the Hellespont, and no early source supports it.
e_battle_of_artemisium.lead: Artemisium was a series of sea fights in late summer 480 BCE off the northern tip of Euboea, fought on the same days as the land battle at Thermopylae. The Greek fleet held the strait against the larger fleet of Xerxes for three days, suffered heavy damage, and withdrew south when news came that the pass had fallen. Neither side won outright, though Plutarch later judged that the Greeks learned there that the King's ships could be faced.
e_battle_of_artemisium.play: The game follows Herodotus's account of the three days and the withdrawal. It shows the wreck of the two hundred ships sent round Euboea as fact, though many historians doubt that story.
e_battle_of_artemisium.s0: Herodotus says the Greeks gathered 271 triremes at Artemisium under the Spartan Eurybiades, with Athens providing the largest share; 53 more Athenian ships came later. The King's fleet, already battered by a storm off Magnesia, anchored opposite at Aphetae. The Greek position guarded the sea route that ran alongside the road through Thermopylae, so the fleet and the army in the pass covered each other.
e_battle_of_artemisium.s1: Herodotus tells that the Greeks attacked late on the first day. The Persians, with more ships that sailed better, tried to surround them, and the Greeks drew into a circle with prows outward and took thirty ships. On the second evening they struck at Cilician ships. On the third day the King's fleet came on in a crescent, crowded and fouled itself, and both sides lost many ships; half the Athenian ships were damaged.
e_battle_of_artemisium.s2: Herodotus says 200 ships were sent round Euboea to cut off the Greek retreat, and that a night storm wrecked them all on the coast called the Hollows; he saw this as the god's work to make the fleets more nearly equal. Many historians doubt the story: the detachment is hard to fit into the timetable. His total of 1,207 triremes for the King's fleet is also widely thought too high.
e_battle_of_artemisium.s3: Herodotus notes that the sea fights and the assaults at Thermopylae fell on the same days. Modern scholars argue over whether the Greeks planned pass and strait as a single defence, and how long the fleet meant to stay. No Persian inscription or tablet mentions Artemisium, so the Persian side is known only through Greek writers; Herodotus names the Egyptian ships as the best in the King's fleet.
e_battle_of_artemisium.s4: Herodotus says the battered Greeks were already planning to withdraw when Abronichus brought word by boat that Leonidas had fallen; they then sailed south, and the fleet later gathered at Salamis. Themistocles cut messages on rocks at watering places urging the Ionians in the King's fleet to desert or fight badly. Plutarch, writing centuries later, cited Pindar's verse that at Artemisium the Athenians laid the foundation of their freedom.
e_battle_of_ephesus.lead: After burning Sardis, the Ionian rebels and their Athenian and Eretrian allies fell back to the coast. Herodotus says Persian troops caught them near Ephesus and beat them badly. Soon afterwards Athens withdrew from the Ionian Revolt, and the rebels fought on without Athenian help.
e_battle_of_ephesus.play: The game lists it as a battle of 498 BCE in which the retreating Greeks were beaten and the Athenians went home for good. This follows Herodotus; the game does not show Charon's version, in which no defeat took place.
e_battle_of_ephesus.s0: Herodotus says the Ionians sailed to Ephesus, left their ships at Coressus and marched inland with Ephesian guides along the Cayster and over Mount Tmolus. They took the lower city of Sardis, but Artaphernes held the citadel. A fire spread through the reed-roofed houses and burned the temple of the goddess Cybebe. Faced with the Lydians and Persians gathered by the Pactolus, the Greeks withdrew towards the coast.
e_battle_of_ephesus.s1: Herodotus says the Persians who held lands west of the Halys came to help Sardis, found the Greeks gone and followed their tracks. They overtook them at Ephesus, where the Ionians formed up and were heavily defeated. Many were killed, among them Eualcides, general of the Eretrians and a victor at the games, whom the poet Simonides had praised. The survivors scattered to their own cities.
e_battle_of_ephesus.s2: Herodotus says the Athenians then abandoned the Ionians completely and refused to help again, although Aristagoras sent messengers asking them to return. He had already called the twenty Athenian ships the beginning of troubles for Greeks and barbarians. He links Darius's anger against Athens to the burning of Sardis, not to the defeat.
e_battle_of_ephesus.s3: Plutarch accused Herodotus of inventing or exaggerating the defeat. He cited Charon of Lampsacus, who told of the Athenian ships, the capture of Sardis except the royal wall, and a return to Miletus, with no battle at Ephesus. Most modern historians still accept a real setback near Ephesus but treat its scale and details as uncertain.
e_battle_of_ephesus.s4: The raid on Sardis and the fight near Ephesus are usually dated to 498 BCE, though some historians prefer 499 BCE. No Persian inscription or tablet mentions either event, so the whole story rests on Greek writers. How the Persian commanders saw the action, and how many troops took part on each side, is not known.
e_battle_of_erythrae.lead: In the first major clash of the Plataea campaign, Mardonius sent his whole cavalry under Masistius against the Greeks camped on the slopes of Cithaeron near Erythrae. Masistius was thrown when an arrow struck his horse, and Athenian soldiers killed him. Herodotus says his death was mourned across the Persian camp and gave the Greeks the confidence to move down onto the plain of Plataea.
e_battle_of_erythrae.play: The game presents this as the cavalry battle at Erythrae, with Masistius unhorsed and killed, as Herodotus tells it. The horsemen were Mardonius's command; Xerxes had already gone back to Asia and was not at the fight.
e_battle_of_erythrae.s0: Herodotus says the allied Greek army under the Spartan Pausanias came over Cithaeron and took up position on its lower slopes near Erythrae, keeping off the open plain. Mardonius, camped by the Asopus river, sent all his cavalry against them. Their commander was Masistius, whom Herodotus describes as highly regarded among the Persians, riding a Nisaean horse with a golden bit and rich trappings.
e_battle_of_erythrae.s1: The horsemen attacked squadron by squadron, shooting and taunting the Greeks. The Megarians held the most exposed ground and sent word to Pausanias that they could not hold without relief. Herodotus says only the Athenians volunteered: 300 picked men under Olympiodorus son of Lampon, with archers among them.
e_battle_of_erythrae.s2: An arrow struck Masistius's horse in the flank; it reared and threw him. The Athenians closed on him, but he wore a corselet of golden scales beneath a purple tunic and their blows did no harm until one man stabbed him through the eye. The cavalry at first did not see him fall, then charged together for the body; the Athenians gave way until the rest of the Greek army came up, and the horsemen withdrew.
e_battle_of_erythrae.s3: Herodotus says the Persian camp mourned Masistius as the man most honoured after Mardonius himself: the soldiers shaved their heads and cut the manes of their horses and pack animals, and their wailing carried across Boeotia. The Greeks laid the body on a cart and drove it along their lines, and men left their ranks to see his size and looks. Encouraged, the army then moved west towards Plataea and the spring Gargaphia.
e_battle_of_erythrae.s4: No surviving Persian text describes this fight, and every detail comes from Greek writers whose informants were probably Athenian. Historians note that the story credits Athens with rescuing the Megarians, which suited Athenian pride, and that Herodotus gives no size for the cavalry or count of losses. Most accept a real skirmish and a commander's death, but its weight rests on Greek telling. The travel writer Pausanias later saw a corselet said to be his at Athens.
e_battle_of_lade.lead: In 494 BCE a royal fleet, drawn mainly from Phoenicia, Cyprus, Cilicia and Egypt, defeated the combined fleet of the rebel Ionian Greeks off the island of Lade near Miletus. The defeat ended the Ionian Revolt at sea and left Miletus open to siege and capture. No Persian record of the battle survives, so the story is almost entirely Herodotus's.
e_battle_of_lade.play: The game follows Herodotus: 600 royal ships against 353 Ionian triremes, an abandoned drill and a Samian flight. The 600 is his round figure, and the Chronicle's description of the diekplous is a modern reconstruction.
e_battle_of_lade.s0: Herodotus says the Ionians chose to defend Miletus at sea and gathered 353 triremes at Lade, then an island off the city and now a hill in the silted Maeander plain. The largest squadrons came from Chios (100), Miletus (80), Lesbos (70) and Samos (60). Against them he sets 600 royal ships, with the Phoenicians the keenest. Six hundred is a round figure he gives for other royal fleets, and many historians doubt it.
e_battle_of_lade.s1: Herodotus tells how Dionysius of Phocaea, who had brought only three ships, persuaded the Ionians to accept his command. For seven days he kept the rowers at the oars and the marines under arms, practising the manoeuvre called the diekplous. Then the crews, unused to such labour and suffering in the heat, refused to go on. They pitched tents on the island and stayed in the shade.
e_battle_of_lade.s2: Herodotus says the former tyrant of Samos, Aeaces son of Syloson, sent word to the Samian captains that their island would be spared if they deserted. When the fleets met, most of the Samians sailed off, followed by the Lesbians and then by many others. Eleven Samian ships stayed and fought, and Samos later honoured their captains on a pillar. Herodotus admits the Ionians blamed one another and he could not say exactly who fled.
e_battle_of_lade.s3: The Chians, Herodotus says, fought hardest, with 100 ships each carrying 40 picked citizens as marines, and they took enemy ships before losing most of their own. Survivors beached at Mycale and crossed into Ephesian land on foot, where Ephesians took them for raiders and killed them.
