Dionysius captured three ships and left to raid, first off Phoenicia and later from Sicily. Herodotus dates the capture of Miletus to the sixth year of the revolt.
e_battle_of_lade.s4: Herodotus names the diekplous but never describes it. Many historians read it as rowing through a gap in the enemy line and turning to ram exposed sides or sterns, but they argue over how it was formed, how it was countered, and whether a week of drill could teach it. Some also suspect that the tale of idle Ionians echoes the blame the cities traded after the defeat, as it later reached Herodotus.
e_battle_of_marathon.lead: In 490 BCE an Athenian and Plataean army defeated the Persian force of Datis and Artaphernes on the coastal plain of Marathon in north-eastern Attica. For the empire it was the setback of one expedition on its western edge, not a threat to its power. It ended Darius's attempt to punish Athens for the burning of Sardis and became the founding story of Athenian pride.
e_battle_of_marathon.play: The Marathon level is built around the battle, with the Greek line thin in the centre and strong on the wings. The game's summary passes over Herodotus's report that the Persian centre first broke the Greek centre.
e_battle_of_marathon.s0: Herodotus says the exiled tyrant Hippias guided the Persians to Marathon, and that the Plataeans joined the Athenians in full force. The Greeks stretched their line to match the Persian front, thin in the centre and strong on the wings, and charged at a run. The Persians and Saka broke the Greek centre, but both wings won and then closed on it. They drove the Persians to their ships and took seven of them.
e_battle_of_marathon.s1: Herodotus gives 6,400 Persian and 192 Athenian dead but no army sizes. Later writers fill the gap. Pausanias puts the Athenians at no more than 9,000, Nepos gives 10,000 Athenians and 1,000 Plataeans against 200,000 Persian foot, and Justin raises the Persians to 600,000. Modern historians generally think of about 10,000 Greeks against perhaps 20,000 to 30,000 Persians, though no figure for the Persian army can be checked.
e_battle_of_marathon.s2: No Persian document mentions Marathon, so how the court saw it is unknown. Herodotus says nothing of the Persian horse during the fight. A proverb explained in the Suda, a Byzantine lexicon of the tenth century CE, led some historians to think the cavalry was already embarking, but this is unproven. Before this check the campaign had taken Naxos and Eretria, and Herodotus says Darius afterwards resolved on a larger war.
e_battle_of_marathon.s3: The burial mound called the Soros still stands on the plain, about 9 metres high. Excavation in 1890-91 found a layer of ash and burnt bone with pottery of about this date. This fits Thucydides' statement that only the Marathon dead were buried where they fell. A second tomb near Vrana has been identified as that of the Plataeans, but the identification is less certain.
e_battle_of_marathon.s4: Herodotus reports that the runner Pheidippides, sent to Sparta before the battle, said he had met the god Pan on the way. The tale of a runner who ran from Marathon to Athens, announced the victory and died appears only centuries later, in Plutarch and Lucian, who give him different names. Plutarch also reports that many soldiers thought they saw Theseus in armour fighting for Athens.
e_battle_of_mycale.lead: In 479 BCE a Greek fleet under Leotychides of Sparta and Xanthippus of Athens attacked a Persian army camped behind a stockade around its beached ships at Mycale, the promontory facing Samos. The Ionians in Persian service changed sides, the camp fell and the ships were burned. The defeat began a second Ionian revolt and carried the war from Greece to the coasts of Asia.
e_battle_of_mycale.play: The epilogue shows Leotychides and Xanthippus landing, the Ionians turning and the beached ships burned. The game calls them the King's last ships, but Herodotus says the Phoenician ships had been sent away first.
e_battle_of_mycale.s0: Herodotus says the King's fleet wintered at Cyme and gathered at Samos in spring, about 300 ships with the Ionians among them. The Greek fleet of 110 ships under Leotychides waited at Aegina and then Delos, where envoys from Samos urged it to cross and free Ionia. When the Greeks reached Samos, the Persian commanders sent the Phoenician ships away and drew the rest back to the mainland at Mycale.
e_battle_of_mycale.s1: There, Herodotus says, the ships were hauled ashore and ringed with a wall of stones and timber near a precinct of Demeter of Eleusis. A land army under Tigranes guarded them; Herodotus gives it as 60,000 men, a figure historians treat as probably inflated. Distrusting the Samians, the Persians disarmed them and sent the Milesians to hold the paths up the mountain.
e_battle_of_mycale.s2: Leotychides first sailed close inshore and had a herald call on the Ionians to remember their freedom. The Athenians and the troops beside them advanced along the shore and broke the Persian wall of wicker shields, then the stockade, while the Spartans came round by a ravine and the hills. Tigranes and Mardontes were killed; Herodotus says the fleet commanders Artayntes and Ithamitres escaped.
e_battle_of_mycale.s3: Herodotus says the disarmed Samians helped the Greeks as best they could and the other Ionians followed them. The Milesians led fleeing Persians onto the wrong paths and killed them. He calls this the second revolt of Ionia from Persia. The Greeks burned the ships and the stockade, then debated moving the Ionians to Greece; the Athenians refused, and Samos, Chios and Lesbos joined the alliance instead.
e_battle_of_mycale.s4: Herodotus dates Mycale to the same day as Plataea, with Plataea in the morning and Mycale in the afternoon, and treats the rumour of victory that reached the Greeks before they attacked as a sign from the gods. Diodorus says Leotychides invented the report to hearten his men. Many historians doubt the exact coincidence. No Persian text mentions the battle, so the Greek story stands alone.
e_battle_of_pasargadae.lead: This battle ended the war between Cyrus, king of Anshan, and Astyages, king of the Medes. A Babylonian chronicle records that Astyages' own army rebelled and handed him over to Cyrus, who then plundered the Median capital at Ecbatana. Greek writers place the final fight near Pasargadae, where Cyrus later built his residence.
e_battle_of_pasargadae.play: The game stages the Median desertion and the women on the hill, with Astyages taken alive in 550 BCE. The women's story comes from Nicolaus and Plutarch, not Herodotus, and the kinship of Cyrus and Astyages rests on Herodotus alone.
e_battle_of_pasargadae.s0: The Nabonidus Chronicle, under the sixth year of Nabonidus (about 550 BCE), says that Astyages gathered his army and marched against Cyrus, king of Anshan. His army rebelled, seized him and handed him over to Cyrus. Cyrus then went to Ecbatana and carried silver, gold and other goods back to Anshan. The Chronicle makes Astyages the attacker and names no battlefield.
e_battle_of_pasargadae.s1: Herodotus says Astyages, his judgement clouded by the gods, gave his army to Harpagus, a noble he had once cruelly punished. When the armies met, a few Medes fought, some went over to the Persians, and most fled on purpose. Astyages then impaled the magi who had advised him, armed the men left in his city, and was beaten and taken alive. This fits the Chronicle's report of a mutiny.
e_battle_of_pasargadae.s2: Nicolaus of Damascus, probably following Ctesias, tells of fighting near Pasargadae in which the Persians were driven up a mountain, where their mothers and wives shamed them into turning back. Plutarch adds that Cyrus rewarded the women: whenever a king entered the city, each woman received a gold piece. Herodotus does not tell the story. The gold-piece custom looks like a later explanation, since Persian kings struck no gold coins of their own before Darius.
e_battle_of_pasargadae.s3: Nabonidus's Sippar cylinder says that in his third year, about 553 BCE, Cyrus scattered the large Median army and took Astyages captive. The Chronicle puts the capture in the sixth year, about 550 BCE. Some historians think the war ran from 553 to 550 BCE, and others think the Sippar text compresses events. Strabo says Cyrus honoured Pasargadae because he beat Astyages there in the last battle, but no Persian record confirms the site.
e_battle_of_pasargadae.s4: Herodotus makes Cyrus the son of Astyages' daughter Mandane, so the war becomes a grandson's revolt. Ctesias denied any blood tie between the two men. In his own Cylinder, Cyrus names only his descent from the kings of Anshan and claims no Median ancestry. The game's note treats the kinship as fact, but it rests on Herodotus alone.
e_battle_of_pelusium.lead: In 525 BCE Cambyses, son of Cyrus, defeated the new pharaoh Psamtik III near the Pelusian mouth of the Nile, the eastern gateway to the Delta. The victory opened the way to Memphis and brought Egypt into the Persian empire, where it stayed for more than a century. Almost everything known about the fighting comes from Herodotus.
e_battle_of_pelusium.play: The game shows Cambyses beating Psamtik III and his Greek and Carian mercenaries, and the Egyptians fleeing to Memphis. Following Herodotus, the Chronicle gives no army sizes and treats Ctesias's casualty figures as unreliable.
e_battle_of_pelusium.s0: Herodotus says the mercenary captain Phanes of Halicarnassus deserted Amasis and advised Cambyses to ask the Arabs for safe passage across the desert, and the Arab king sent camels loaded with water skins. Psamtik III, king for only a few months after his father's death, waited at the Pelusian mouth of the Nile. Herodotus reports a hard fight with heavy losses on both sides before the Egyptians broke and ran for Memphis.
e_battle_of_pelusium.s1: Herodotus tells that before the battle Psamtik's Greek and Carian mercenaries killed the sons of Phanes where their father could see, mixed their blood with wine and water in a bowl and drank it. He says he later saw the bones of the dead lying in separate heaps. The local people showed him that Egyptian skulls were hard and Persian ones thin. They put this down to Egyptians shaving their heads in the sun while Persians wore felt caps, and he accepted their explanation.
e_battle_of_pelusium.s2: No Egyptian text describes the battle. The inscribed statue of Udjahorresnet, now in the Vatican Museums, shows that he commanded the royal ships under Amasis and Psamtik III and then served Cambyses as chief physician, helping to compose his Egyptian royal titles. It speaks of Cambyses coming to Egypt with foreigners of every land, but says nothing of the fighting itself.
e_battle_of_pelusium.s3: Herodotus gives no army sizes. Ctesias, writing about 400 BCE, says 50,000 Egyptians and 7,000 Persians died and that a eunuch named Combaphis betrayed the Egyptian defences. Yet he also calls the pharaoh Amyrtaeus, and historians treat his figures as guesswork. Some ask whether Udjahorresnet's fleet stood aside, but his own text does not say. The battle is usually dated 525 BCE, though some scholars argue for 526 BCE.
e_battle_of_pelusium.s4: Polyaenus, a writer of the second century CE, says Cambyses set dogs, sheep, cats, ibises and other animals sacred to the Egyptians in front of his army at Pelusium, so that the defenders would not shoot for fear of harming them. The story first appears some seven centuries after the battle and is found in no earlier writer. Modern pictures of Persians carrying cats on their shields go further still.
e_battle_of_plataea.lead: The battle of Plataea, fought in Boeotia in the summer of 479 BCE, ended Xerxes' invasion of Greece. A Greek army under the Spartan regent Pausanias defeated the force that Mardonius had kept in Greece after Salamis, and Mardonius died in the fighting. Persia never again sent an army into mainland Greece.
e_battle_of_plataea.play: The Plataea level is built around this battle: days of skirmishing, the fouling of Gargaphia, Mardonius's attack, his death and the storming of his fort. The Chronicle follows Herodotus but omits his guess of 50,000 Greek allies of Persia.
e_battle_of_plataea.s0: Herodotus says Mardonius wintered in Thessaly, retook Athens in 479 BCE, then fell back to Boeotia, where the open ground suited his cavalry, and built a wooden fort by the Asopus. The Greeks camped on the slopes of Cithaeron. His horsemen harried them for days, and their commander Masistius was killed in one clash. They then cut off Greek supply convoys in the passes and finally fouled the spring of Gargaphia.
e_battle_of_plataea.s1: Short of water, the Greeks tried to move by night to new ground nearer Plataea, and Herodotus describes the move as confused. At dawn Mardonius attacked the Spartans and Tegeans. The Persians fought from behind a wall of wicker shields, and when the Spartan Arimnestus killed Mardonius his men broke. The Athenians beat the Boeotians, and the Greeks stormed the fort.
e_battle_of_plataea.s2: Herodotus gives 110,000 Greeks, 300,000 for the King's army and perhaps 50,000 Greek allies of Persia. Historians broadly accept his Greek figures but put Mardonius's force at perhaps 60,000 to 120,000. His claim that barely 3,000 survived, apart from 40,000 led off by Artabazus, is not credible, and his 159 Greek dead look too few. Historians also debate whether the night move was planned or a near-rout.
e_battle_of_plataea.s3: Herodotus says the Greeks set aside a tenth of the spoils for a gold tripod at Delphi, standing on a bronze column of three twisted snakes. The bronze shaft survives, inscribed on its coils with the names of 31 Greek states that fought the war, and stands today in the Hippodrome of Istanbul. No Persian inscription or tablet mentions the battle, so it is known almost only from the Greek side.
e_battle_of_plataea.s4: The Athenian orator Lycurgus in the fourth century, and Diodorus much later, quoted an oath the Greeks supposedly swore before the battle, promising to fight to the death and to leave the temples burned by the Persians in ruins as a memorial. A version without the temples clause is carved on a fourth-century stele from Acharnae. Theopompus already called it an Athenian fabrication, and historians still argue over whether any of it is genuine.
e_battle_of_salamis.lead: Salamis was the sea battle fought in the narrow strait between the island of Salamis and the coast of Attica in late summer or early autumn of 480 BCE. The Greek fleet, commanded by the Spartan Eurybiades and guided in practice by Themistocles of Athens, defeated the King's fleet soon after Xerxes had taken Athens. The defeat ended Persian hopes of a quick victory at sea and led Xerxes to return to Asia, leaving Mardonius with an army in Greece.
e_battle_of_salamis.play: The game's Chronicle follows Herodotus: Sicinnus's message, the closed strait, Xerxes watching, Artemisia, Ariabignes and Psyttaleia. The King's remark is Herodotus's report, and whether both channels were blocked is debated.
e_battle_of_salamis.s0: Herodotus says that Themistocles, afraid the allied fleet would break up and sail for the Isthmus, sent his household slave Sicinnus to tell the Persian commanders that the Greeks meant to flee. That night, he says, the King's ships moved to close the strait, and troops were landed on the islet of Psyttaleia to deal with men washed ashore. Aeschylus also has a Greek bring a false report to Xerxes, and the crews row on watch all night.
e_battle_of_salamis.s1: Herodotus says he cannot tell exactly how each man fought, but in the narrows the King's ships lost order, and many were wrecked when the front ships turned back into those pressing on behind. Ariabignes, son of Darius and admiral of the Ionian and Carian ships, was killed. Many Greeks whose ships sank swam to Salamis, while most of the King's men could not swim and drowned. Aristides then took hoplites onto Psyttaleia and killed the Persians there.
e_battle_of_salamis.s2: Herodotus says Xerxes sat at the foot of Mount Aegaleos with scribes who wrote down the names of captains who fought well. He tells how Artemisia of Halicarnassus, chased by an Athenian ship, rammed a ship of her own side, and how Xerxes, thinking she had sunk an enemy, remarked that his men had turned into women and his women into men. When Phoenician captains blamed the Ionians for their losses, he had them beheaded.
e_battle_of_salamis.s3: No Persian document mentions Salamis. Herodotus gives the Greeks about 380 ships and implies the King still had over a thousand; Aeschylus, who may have fought there, gives 310 against 1,207, and historians think the Persian figures much exaggerated. They also argue over where the lines stood, which islet was Psyttaleia, whether Egyptian ships really sealed the western channel as Diodorus says, and whether the Persians were tricked or meant to attack anyway.
e_battle_of_salamis.s4: Herodotus reports the Athenian claim that the Corinthian admiral Adeimantus fled at the start and turned back only when a mysterious boat told him the Greeks were winning; he adds that the Corinthians and the rest of Greece denied it. He also records a tale that a phantom woman appeared and called to the Greek fleet, asking how long they would keep backing water. Such stories reflect rivalries among the Greek cities after the war.
e_battle_of_thermopylae.lead: In late summer 480 BCE a Greek force under King Leonidas of Sparta tried to stop Xerxes' army in the narrow pass of Thermopylae, between the mountains and the Malian Gulf. After two days of failed Persian assaults, troops under Hydarnes came round by a mountain path. On the third day Leonidas and those who stayed with him were killed, and the road into central Greece lay open.
e_battle_of_thermopylae.play: The Thermopylae level is built around the battle. The game says the Spartans and Thespians died to a man. Herodotus mentions two Spartans, Aristodemus and Pantites, who were away from the fight and survived.
e_battle_of_thermopylae.s0: Herodotus says Xerxes waited four days at Trachis, expecting the Greeks to withdraw. Then he sent in the Medes and Cissians, and after them the Immortals under Hydarnes. In the narrow ground their numbers counted for little, and Herodotus says the Spartans drew them on with feigned retreats before turning on them. The second day of fighting went the same way.
e_battle_of_thermopylae.s1: Herodotus says a Malian named Ephialtes led Hydarnes' troops over the Anopaea path by night. A thousand Phocians guarded the heights but fell back to a summit, and the Persians marched past. Most allies then left, sent away by Leonidas or by their own choice, while the Spartans, Thespians and Thebans stayed. Herodotus says the Spartans and Thespians died on a hillock in the pass, and the Thebans surrendered and were branded.
e_battle_of_thermopylae.s2: Herodotus gives Xerxes 1,700,000 infantry and over five million people with fleet and followers, figures historians regard as wildly exaggerated; modern estimates are a small fraction of them. Ancient writers also disagree on the size of the Greek force. Historians argue over whether Leonidas stayed for honour and an oracle, as Herodotus says, or to cover the retreat. Plutarch rejected Herodotus's claim that the Thebans stayed only as unwilling hostages.
e_battle_of_thermopylae.s3: In 1939 Spyridon Marinatos excavated the low hill of Kolonos in the pass and found many bronze and iron arrowheads. Most scholars take the hill to be the place of the last stand. River silt has since pushed the coastline far back from the old pass. No Persian document mentions the battle, so the Persian side of it is known only through Greek writers.
e_battle_of_thermopylae.s4: Plutarch's collection of Spartan sayings has Leonidas answer a demand to hand over his arms with the words come and take them. Diodorus tells of a Greek night raid on the King's tent, which Herodotus does not mention. These stories were written down centuries later and shaped to praise Spartan courage. They are best read as tradition, not as reports of what was said or done.
e_bosporus_bridge.lead: At the start of his campaign against the Scythians, about 513 BCE, Darius had a bridge of boats laid across the Bosporus so that his army could march from Asia into Thrace. The engineer was a Greek, Mandrocles of Samos. Herodotus is the main source for the crossing. Xerxes would bridge the Hellespont with boats in a similar way a generation later.
e_bosporus_bridge.play: The game shows Mandrocles bridging the strait, Darius watching the army cross and the two inscribed pillars, following Herodotus 4.87-88. The firm date of 513 BCE is a simplification; the year is only approximate.
e_bosporus_bridge.s0: Herodotus says Darius marched from Susa to Chalcedon, sailed out to view the Black Sea, and then returned to the bridge Mandrocles had built. He gives the strait's width at its narrowest as four stades, well under a kilometre. By his own reckoning the bridge lay about midway between Byzantium and the temple at the strait's mouth. The Ionian fleet meanwhile sailed on to bridge the Ister.
e_bosporus_bridge.s1: According to Herodotus, Darius set up two pillars of white stone by the Bosporus. They were carved in Assyrian and Greek letters with the names of all the peoples in his army. He adds that the Byzantines later carried the stones into their city for an altar of Artemis, leaving one stone covered in Assyrian letters beside a temple of Dionysus. No fragment of either pillar has been found.
e_bosporus_bridge.s2: Herodotus says Darius rewarded Mandrocles generously. With part of the reward the engineer paid for a painting of the whole scene: the bridge, the army crossing and the King seated watching. He dedicated it in the temple of Hera at Samos with a verse inscription naming himself and Darius, which Herodotus quotes.
e_bosporus_bridge.s3: Herodotus gives Darius 700,000 men and 600 ships. Historians treat these figures as greatly exaggerated. The year is uncertain, usually put at about 513 or 512 BCE. No Persian inscription describes the bridge, though Darius's tomb inscription lists Saka beyond the sea and Skudra among his lands, which many scholars link to this campaign in Europe.
e_bosporus_bridge.s4: Most scholars take Herodotus's Assyrian letters to mean cuneiform. Others note that Greek writers also used the phrase for Aramaic script, as Thucydides does for a captured Persian letter. If it was cuneiform, the language might have been Akkadian, Elamite or Old Persian, as on Darius's other monuments. Since the pillars are lost, the wording cannot be checked against the royal inscriptions.
e_burial_of_cyrus.lead: Cyrus died in 530 BCE while campaigning in the far north-east, and Babylonian tablets show Cambyses reigning by the end of that year. A stone tomb at Pasargadae, still standing, was later known as Cyrus's resting place. No text from the time describes the funeral, so the story is pieced together from the tomb itself and from Greek writers.
e_burial_of_cyrus.play: The first level is built around making the tomb ready, and magi guard it afterwards; the body's homecoming follows Ctesias. Herodotus does not mention it, and no Persian text of the time records the funeral.
e_burial_of_cyrus.s0: The ancient writers disagree. Herodotus says Cyrus was killed fighting the Massagetae beyond the Araxes, while Xenophon has him die peacefully in his bed among his sons. Ctesias says he died of a wound taken against the Derbices and that Cambyses sent the body home to Persia. He is the only one of the three who clearly describes the body being brought back, and historians cannot say which version of the death is true.
e_burial_of_cyrus.s1: The tomb stands on the plain south-west of the palaces. It is a gabled stone chamber on a plinth of six steps, about 11 metres high, built of large limestone blocks joined with metal clamps. The chamber inside is small, a little over 3 metres long and about 2 wide, with a low doorway, and it bears no inscription today. In medieval times local tradition called it the tomb of the mother of Solomon.
e_burial_of_cyrus.s2: Arrian, following Aristobulus, says the tomb stood in a park of trees. Inside were a gold coffin, a couch, a table with cups, and fine garments. Magi kept guard, a duty passed from father to son since the time of Cambyses, and they received a sheep each day and a horse each month to sacrifice to Cyrus. By 324 the tomb had been robbed, and Alexander ordered it restored.
e_burial_of_cyrus.s3: Historians argue over whether Cyrus built the tomb in his lifetime or Cambyses finished it after his death. The fine masonry and clamps point to Lydian and Ionian stoneworkers, so it probably dates after the conquest of Sardis. Under Darius, Persepolis tablets record regular offerings for dead members of the royal house. They show such cults existed, but they do not describe the funeral of Cyrus.
e_burial_of_cyrus.s4: Herodotus tells that Tomyris, queen of the Massagetae, dipped the dead king's head in a skin of blood so that he might have his fill. The tale is shaped as a lesson about greed for conquest. Later writers record an epitaph in which Cyrus asks the passer-by not to begrudge him the little earth that covers him. No trace of that inscription survives, and it may be a literary invention.
e_burning_of_sardis.lead: In 498 BCE an army of rebel Ionians, with Athenian and Eretrian allies, marched inland and took the lower city of Sardis, seat of the satrap Artaphernes. Fire spread through the town and destroyed the temple of the goddess Cybebe. Herodotus treats the raid as the cause of the Persian wars against Athens and Eretria.
e_burning_of_sardis.play: The game shows the Ionians taking Sardis except the citadel, and fire spreading through the reed roofs and the temple of Cybebe. Darius's oath of vengeance comes from a story in Herodotus, not from any Persian record.
e_burning_of_sardis.s0: Herodotus says Aristagoras of Miletus won twenty Athenian ships for the revolt, and Eretria sent five more. The army sailed to Ephesus, left the ships at Coressus, and marched up the Cayster valley and over Mount Tmolus with Ephesian guides. They took Sardis without a fight, but the satrap Artaphernes held the citadel with a sizeable force.
e_burning_of_sardis.s1: Herodotus says most houses were of reed, or of brick under reed roofs, so when one soldier set a house alight the flames ran through the whole town. Trapped Lydians and Persians gathered in the market place by the Pactolus and fought back, and the Greeks withdrew to Tmolus. The temple of Cybebe, the local mother goddess, burned as well. Persian troops then caught the retreating army near Ephesus and defeated it.
e_burning_of_sardis.s2: Excavators at Sardis have found Lydian houses of mud brick and rubble near the Pactolus, and a sixth-century gold refinery beside an altar probably sacred to Cybebe. A heavy destruction layer marks Cyrus's capture of the city about 547 BCE. No layer has been securely tied to the fire of 498 BCE, and the temple of Cybebe itself has not been found.
e_burning_of_sardis.s3: No Persian text mentions the raid, and the story rests almost entirely on Herodotus. He says Athenian envoys had given earth and water to Artaphernes, about 507 BCE by modern dating. In Persian eyes Athens may therefore have been a subject city in revolt rather than a foreign power. Numbers are uncertain too: the crews of twenty-five ships and the Ionians together were perhaps a few thousand men, and no source counts the garrison.
e_burning_of_sardis.s4: Herodotus says the Persians later gave the burned temple of Cybebe as their reason for burning the temples of Greece. When Datis took Eretria in 490 BCE, his men burned its sanctuaries in return for those at Sardis. Herodotus builds the whole war as a chain of reprisals, a frame that may simplify the King's wider aims in the west.
e_burning_of_sardis.s5: Herodotus tells that Darius, told the Athenians had helped burn Sardis, asked who they were, shot an arrow into the sky and prayed to Zeus for vengeance. He then ordered a servant to tell him three times at every dinner to remember the Athenians. The tale is shaped for Greek listeners: a Persian king would have prayed to Auramazda, and the scene sets up the wars to come.
e_campaign_against_skunkha.lead: In about 519 BCE, Darius led an army against the Saka who wore the pointed cap, crossed a sea or great water to reach them and took their chief Skunkha prisoner. The campaign is known almost only from the fifth column of the Behistun inscription, and Skunkha was carved as the last captive in the row before the King. It carried Darius's power onto the steppe frontier where, Herodotus says, Cyrus had died.
e_campaign_against_skunkha.play: The game shows Darius marching out, crossing the water and capturing Skunkha, as Behistun tells it. Its date of about 519-518 BCE fits Darius's third regnal year; the inscription itself gives no exact day or month for the campaign.
e_campaign_against_skunkha.s0: The fifth column of the Behistun inscription was carved in Old Persian only and added after the main text. It groups the campaign with deeds of Darius's second and third years. Darius went with an army against the Saka who wear the pointed cap, reached the sea, crossed it with his army and defeated them. Their chief Skunkha was seized and led to him, and Darius made another man chief in his place.
e_campaign_against_skunkha.s1: The same column calls these Saka faithless and says they did not worship Auramazda, while Darius did. By the god's favour he therefore dealt with them as he wished. The text ends with a lesson that whoever worships Auramazda will be blessed in life and after death. The campaign was thus presented as a sign of divine support, like the earlier victories over the rebels of 522-521 BCE.
e_campaign_against_skunkha.s2: A figure of Skunkha, wearing a tall pointed cap, was cut at the end of the row of bound rebel kings facing Darius on the cliff. Making room for him destroyed part of the first Elamite version of the text, which was then carved again nearby. The later addition shows that the monument was updated as the reign went on, rather than finished in a single campaign of work.
e_campaign_against_skunkha.s3: The Old Persian word for the water Darius crossed, draya, normally means sea, though some read a great river here, and the text names no place. Most historians place the pointed-cap Saka east of the Caspian in Central Asia. They think of the Caspian itself, the Aral Sea, or a great river such as the Oxus or Jaxartes. The year is also argued; most settle on about 519 BCE, in Darius's third regnal year.
e_campaign_against_skunkha.s4: Herodotus does not mention this campaign; his Scythian war of Darius is the later crossing of the Ister in Europe. He describes Saka in Xerxes' army with tall stiff pointed caps, bows, daggers and axes, and calls them Amyrgian Scythians. Persian lists, however, keep the Amyrgian (haumavarga) Saka apart from the pointed-cap Saka. Royal lists such as DNa name the pointed-cap Saka among the King's subject peoples.
e_carthage_expedition.lead: After conquering Egypt, Cambyses planned to push the empire west by sending his fleet against Carthage in North Africa. Herodotus says the plan failed because the Phoenicians, who supplied the core of the fleet, refused to attack a city their own people had founded. The episode shows how much the King's sea power rested on the willing service of subject peoples.
e_carthage_expedition.play: The game shows this as a 524 BCE event in which Cambyses drops the plan after the Phoenicians refuse, as Herodotus tells it. Herodotus gives no exact year, so the date is the game's choice.
e_carthage_expedition.s0: Herodotus says that once Egypt was taken, Cambyses planned three further campaigns: against the Carthaginians, against the Ammonians of the western desert, and against the long-lived Ethiopians to the south. Carthage was to be attacked by sea, the other two by land. The Libyans and the Greek cities of Cyrene and Barca had already submitted to him, which opened the coast to the west.
e_carthage_expedition.s1: Herodotus says the Phoenicians would not sail, because they were bound by oaths and it would be an impious act to make war on their own children. Carthage was by tradition a foundation of Tyre. Since the Phoenicians had joined the Persians of their own will, Cambyses did not think it right to force them, and without them the rest of the fleet was too weak, so the plan was dropped.
e_carthage_expedition.s2: No Persian, Egyptian or Phoenician document mentions the expedition, so it rests on Herodotus alone. Some historians accept it as a natural next step after the submission of Libya and Cyrene. Others doubt that a long voyage against a distant city was ever planned in earnest, or suspect the story was shaped to contrast Cambyses' restraint here with the cruelty Herodotus gives him elsewhere. It fits the central place of the Phoenician fleet in Persian naval power.
e_carthage_expedition.s3: Writers of the Roman period told further stories of Persian dealings with Carthage. Justin says Darius sent envoys forbidding the Carthaginians human sacrifice and the eating of dogs, and asking for help against the Greeks. Diodorus says Xerxes made a pact with Carthage so that it would attack the Sicilian Greeks in 480 BCE. Both stories come long after the events, and many historians treat them as later inventions.
e_conquest_of_egypt.lead: In 525 BCE Cambyses, son of Cyrus, led a Persian army, supported by Phoenician, Cypriot and Greek ships, against Egypt, the last great independent kingdom of the Near East. After a victory at Pelusium and the surrender of Memphis, he made Egypt a satrapy and ruled it as pharaoh. Herodotus says Psamtik III was spared at first but was put to death when he was caught stirring up revolt.
e_conquest_of_egypt.play: The Memphis level sets the campaign in 525 BCE, with Phanes guiding the army, the Arabs supplying water and a Phoenician fleet, as Herodotus tells it. The real fleet also included Cypriot and Greek ships.
e_conquest_of_egypt.s0: Herodotus says Cambyses counted the Ionian and Aeolian Greeks among the subjects he inherited from Cyrus, and that he took them with him against Egypt. The expedition gained a guide when Phanes of Halicarnassus, a mercenary officer of Pharaoh Amasis, deserted to the Persians and advised asking the Arab king for safe passage. Amasis died before the invasion, and Herodotus gives his son Psamtik III a reign of only six months.
e_conquest_of_egypt.s1: According to Herodotus, the Arab king loaded skins of water onto camels and set them along the desert road. He also reports a story of a leather pipeline from a river, which he finds less believable. The armies met at Pelusium on the eastern edge of the Delta, where the Egyptians were routed and fled to Memphis. When the Egyptians there killed a Persian herald and his crew, Cambyses besieged the city until it surrendered.
e_conquest_of_egypt.s2: The inscribed statue of Udjahorresnet, a naval commander under Amasis and Psamtik III, says that he served Cambyses and composed his royal titles, including the throne name Mesutira. It also says he persuaded the King to clear foreigners from the temple of Neith at Sais and restore its rites. The Behistun inscription of Darius says only that Cambyses went to Egypt and that disloyalty spread at home while he was away.
e_conquest_of_egypt.s3: Herodotus, drawing on Egyptian informants, says Cambyses stabbed the Apis bull and that it died of the wound. A stela and an inscribed sarcophagus from the Apis galleries at Saqqara show an Apis buried with honours in 524 BCE, the sarcophagus given by Cambyses, and the next Apis lived into the reign of Darius. Many historians trace the madman story to priestly resentment over cuts Cambyses made to temple revenues, which a later Demotic text reports.
e_conquest_of_egypt.s4: Herodotus reports tales that Cambyses went to war because Amasis had sent him a false bride, Nitetis, daughter of the earlier pharaoh Apries, in place of his own daughter. He also reports an Egyptian claim that Cambyses was the son of Nitetis, which he rejects. Much later, Polyaenus told how Cambyses placed animals sacred to the Egyptians in front of his troops at Pelusium so that the defenders would not shoot. No source of the time supports these tales.
e_conquest_of_ionia.lead: After Cyrus took Sardis, the Greek cities of the Ionian coast, once subject to the Lydian king Croesus, offered to submit on their old terms, and Cyrus refused. Herodotus tells how Harpagus, the Mede who had helped Cyrus overthrow Astyages, then reduced them one by one with siege mounds in the mid-540s BCE. The conquest probably brought Ionian and Lydian craftsmen into the King's service, and their methods appear in the stonework of Pasargadae.
e_conquest_of_ionia.play: The game has Harpagus take the coastal cities with earth mounds, as in Herodotus, and links him to Ionian stone-cutters at Pasargadae. Its 546-545 BCE date is approximate, and the masons' origin is inferred from technique.
e_conquest_of_ionia.s0: Herodotus says the Ionians and Aeolians sent envoys to Cyrus at Sardis, offering to submit on the terms they had held under Croesus. Cyrus refused, since they had ignored his earlier call to desert Croesus, and granted such terms only to Miletus. Soon after, the Lydian Pactyes, left in charge of Croesus's gold, rose in revolt. The Mede Mazares crushed it, enslaved the people of Priene and plundered the Maeander plain, then fell ill and died.
e_conquest_of_ionia.s1: Harpagus succeeded Mazares and, Herodotus says, took the cities by penning the defenders inside their walls and heaping earth mounds against them. The Phocaeans abandoned their city and sailed west, though more than half soon turned back, and the people of Teos left to found Abdera in Thrace. The other mainland cities fought and fell one by one, and the Ionian islanders surrendered. Harpagus then moved against Caria and Lycia.
e_conquest_of_ionia.s2: Herodotus has Cyrus answer the Ionian envoys with a fable. A piper played to the fish to draw them ashore, and when they would not come he caught them in a net. As they leapt about, he told them it was too late to dance. The story works as a moral about submitting in good time, and it owes more to Greek storytelling than to any record of what Cyrus said.
e_conquest_of_ionia.s3: Excavations at Pasargadae show masonry methods new to Persis: finely dressed joints, the toothed chisel, and swallowtail iron clamps linking the blocks. Carl Nylander traced these methods to Lydian and Ionian workshops, which suggests that craftsmen came east after Sardis and the coast were taken. No text from Cyrus's reign names these workers. Darius's later Susa charter does record Ionians and Sardians cutting stone at Susa.
e_conquest_of_ionia.s4: Herodotus gives no year. The fall of Sardis is usually placed about 547 or 546 BCE, partly on an entry in the Nabonidus Chronicle for 547 BCE whose country name is damaged and may not be Lydia at all. Ionia therefore fell in the mid-540s BCE, but the exact years are uncertain. Scholars also debate whether building at Pasargadae began before or after Lydian and Ionian craftsmen arrived.
e_cypriot_revolt.lead: After the burning of Sardis in 498 BCE, almost all the city-kingdoms of Cyprus joined the Ionian Revolt, led by Onesilus of Salamis. A Persian army crossed from Cilicia with a Phoenician fleet, won a land battle near Salamis and then took the rebel cities one by one. Herodotus says the island was free for a single year, and its loss probably weakened the Ionian cause in the east.
e_cypriot_revolt.play: The Chronicle records Cyprus joining the revolt and a Persian army from Cilicia winning it back within a year, dated 497 BCE. This matches Herodotus, though the island rose in 498 BCE and some sieges ran on after the main battle.
e_cypriot_revolt.s0: Herodotus says Onesilus, younger brother of King Gorgus of Salamis, had long urged revolt against the Persians. When Gorgus refused, Onesilus shut him out of the city and Gorgus fled to the Persian side. Every Cypriot kingdom then joined except Amathus, which Onesilus put under siege.
e_cypriot_revolt.s1: Herodotus reports that the Persian Artybius brought an army across from Cilicia while Phoenician ships sailed round the island, and an Ionian fleet came to help the rebels. The Ionians won at sea, but on land near Salamis Stesenor of Curium went over to the Persians, followed by the Salaminian chariots. Onesilus fell, as did Aristocyprus, king of Soli. Artybius was also killed in the fighting.
e_cypriot_revolt.s2: Herodotus says the Salaminians handed their city back to Gorgus, while the other Cypriot cities were put under siege. Hearing that Onesilus was dead, the Ionian fleet sailed home. Soli held out longest and fell in the fifth month, when the Persians dug under its wall. Herodotus ends by saying the Cypriots had been free for one year before they were brought under the King again.
e_cypriot_revolt.s3: Excavations at Kouklia, the site of Old Paphos, uncovered a large siege ramp built against the city wall near its north-east gate. Its fill held broken sculpture and votive pieces, and hundreds of arrowheads and other weapons were found in and around it. The defenders dug tunnels beneath the ramp to bring it down. The excavators date the assault to the Persian reconquest of about 497 BCE, giving physical evidence for sieges that Herodotus mentions only in general terms.
e_cypriot_revolt.s4: Herodotus tells that the people of Amathus cut off the head of Onesilus and hung it over their gate. When bees filled the hollow skull with honeycomb, an oracle told them to bury the head and offer yearly sacrifice to Onesilus as a hero. The story explains the origin of a local cult and is shaped as a wonder tale rather than a record.
e_cyrus_revolt.lead: Between about 553 and 550 BCE, Cyrus, king of Anshan in Persis, fought and defeated Astyages, king of the Medes, and took the Median royal city of Ecbatana. The victory turned a regional Persian kingdom into the core of an empire. Babylonian texts written at the time confirm the outcome, which Greek writers later turned into a tale of kinship, betrayal and revenge.
e_cyrus_revolt.play: The Chronicle opens the game with the revolt and Cyrus's reply to the summons, taken from Herodotus 1.127. Calling Astyages his grandfather follows Herodotus; Ctesias denied it and Cyrus's own texts never mention it.
e_cyrus_revolt.s0: A Babylonian chronicle records that in the sixth year of King Nabonidus, 550/549 BCE, Ishtumegu (Astyages) mustered his army and marched against Cyrus, king of Anshan. His own troops rebelled, seized him and handed him over to Cyrus. Cyrus then marched to Ecbatana, the royal city, and carried silver, gold and other goods back to Anshan. In this text Astyages, not Cyrus, makes the first move.
e_cyrus_revolt.s1: A building cylinder of Nabonidus, found at Sippar, tells how Marduk told him in a dream to rebuild the temple of Sin at Harran and promised that the Medes would be removed. In the third year, probably meaning Nabonidus's third year, about 553 BCE, Marduk raised up Cyrus, king of Anshan, his young servant. Cyrus scattered the Medes with his small army and took Astyages captive to his own land. The text calls the Medes Umman-manda, an old term for barbarian northern foes.
e_cyrus_revolt.s2: Herodotus says Harpagus, a Mede whom Astyages had punished cruelly, urged Cyrus to revolt in a letter hidden inside a hare. Cyrus rallied the Persian tribes, and when Astyages summoned him he replied that he would come sooner than the king would like. Astyages gave command to Harpagus, many Medes deserted, and Astyages was captured after a second battle. Cyrus kept him at court until he died.
e_cyrus_revolt.s3: Herodotus and Xenophon make Cyrus the son of Astyages' daughter Mandane, but Ctesias denied the kinship, and the Cyrus Cylinder names only his Persian forebears, kings of Anshan. The dates also differ: the Sippar text may point to 553 BCE, the Chronicle to 550 BCE, so the war may have lasted several years. Some historians doubt that the Medes ruled a centralised empire at all, which affects whether this was a revolt or a war between neighbours.
e_cyrus_revolt.s4: Herodotus tells that Astyages, warned by dreams, ordered the infant Cyrus killed, and that a herdsman's wife raised him instead; he admits other versions existed. Later writers such as Justin and Plutarch add that Persian men fleeing the Medes were shamed by their mothers and wives into fighting on. Both stories follow familiar folk patterns and cannot be taken as history.
e_daric.lead: Under Darius the empire began to strike its own coins: the gold daric and the silver siglos, both showing a crowned archer. They followed the Lydian gold and silver coins attributed to Croesus in western Asia Minor and became the coins Greeks most linked with Persian wealth. Inside Persia most payments were still made in kind or in silver weighed out by the shekel.
e_daric.play: The game shows a dramatized decree by Darius creating the daric and siglos at Sardis, about 510-500 BCE. No text names Sardis as the mint, and the first archer coins were silver only.
e_daric.s0: The surviving coins fall into a short series of types. The earliest appear to be silver sigloi showing a half-length crowned archer. Later types show the archer in a kneeling or running pose, either drawing a bow or holding a spear and bow, and these were struck in both gold and silver. A daric weighed about 8.4 grams of very pure gold, and an early siglos about 5.4 grams of silver.
e_daric.s1: An official at Persepolis used a silver siglos of an archer type as his seal, catalogued as PFS 1393s. Its impressions appear on Fortification tablets dated to year 22 of Darius, about 500 BCE. This shows that archer coins were already in use by that date.
e_daric.s2: Herodotus says Darius refined gold to the greatest purity and struck coin from it. Aryandes, governor of Egypt, then struck silver of equal purity, and Darius had him killed, formally on a charge of rebellion. Herodotus also says the Lydian Pythius offered Xerxes nearly four million gold darics, a figure probably inflated. He adds that the King stored tribute as metal melted into jars.
e_daric.s3: The foundation deposits of the Apadana at Persepolis held Lydian and Greek coins but no archer coins. Some scholars take this to mean that royal coinage began only after the deposits were laid. Find spots and the Lydian tradition make Sardis the likely mint, but no text names it. Scholars also debate whether the archer is the King himself or a royal hero, and whether the name daric comes from Darius.
e_daric.s4: The Persepolis Fortification tablets record workers' rations mostly in kind: grain, wine, beer and livestock. The Treasury tablets record some payments in shekels of silver measured by weight, not in counted coins. Archer coins are found mostly in western Asia Minor, so coinage probably served the western provinces and dealings with Greeks.
e_datis_expedition.lead: In 490 BCE Darius sent a fleet across the Aegean under Datis the Mede and Artaphernes, son of the satrap of Sardis, to punish Eretria and Athens for their part in the burning of Sardis. It brought the Cyclades under Persian control and destroyed Eretria, but its army was beaten by the Athenians and Plataeans at Marathon.
e_datis_expedition.play: The game shows it as a campaign whose fleet carries cavalry in horse transports, spares Delos and lands at Marathon on Hippias's advice. These details follow Herodotus.
e_datis_expedition.s0: Herodotus says Darius first sent heralds to the Greek cities to demand earth and water, and ordered his tribute-paying coastal cities to build warships and horse transports. Command passed from Mardonius to Datis and the younger Artaphernes, the King's nephew. The army gathered on the Aleian plain in Cilicia and embarked there. Fearing the waters off Athos, the fleet sailed from Samos straight through the islands.
e_datis_expedition.s1: Herodotus says the Naxians fled to the hills, and the Persians burned their town and temples. At Delos the islanders fled to Tenos; Datis anchored off Rhenaea, told them to return in peace and burned three hundred talents of frankincense on the altar. Carystus was besieged until it submitted. Eretria held out for six days before two citizens betrayed it, and its temples were burned in revenge for Sardis.
e_datis_expedition.s2: Herodotus says Hippias, the exiled tyrant of Athens, led the army to Marathon because it was the ground best suited to horsemen and closest to Eretria. After the defeat the fleet rounded Sunium towards Phaleron, found the Athenian army already back, and sailed for Asia. Darius settled the Eretrian captives at Ardericca in Cissia, not far from Susa.
e_datis_expedition.s3: A Persepolis Fortification tablet from Darius's 28th year, about 494 BCE, records rations for the journey of a man named Datiya, who was travelling from Sardis to Persepolis with a sealed authorisation from the King. D. M. Lewis argued that he was the Datis of Herodotus. If so, Datis was already a trusted royal agent in the west during the Ionian Revolt. The identification is probable rather than certain.
e_datis_expedition.s4: Herodotus names revenge on Eretria and Athens and the submission of Greeks who had refused earth and water. Historians still debate whether Darius planned a punitive raid or the conquest of Attica under a restored Hippias. The figure of 600 triremes is probably conventional, and modern estimates of the army are far below later Greek claims. Herodotus never mentions cavalry in the battle, and it is argued whether the horses had been re-embarked.
e_death_of_apis.lead: The Apis was the living sacred bull of Ptah at Memphis, and its death and burial were great events in Egyptian religion. Herodotus says Cambyses wounded the bull in anger and that the Egyptians dated his madness from this crime. Egyptian inscriptions from the Serapeum at Saqqara instead show an Apis buried with full honours in the king's name in 524 BCE. The clash between the two has shaped how historians judge Persian rule in Egypt.
e_death_of_apis.play: The Chronicle sets Herodotus's stabbing story beside the Saqqara epitaph and treats both as one bull's death in 524 BCE. In Herodotus the stabbed bull was a newly found Apis, and which bull he meant is debated.
e_death_of_apis.s0: Egyptians held that one bull at a time, chosen by special markings, was the living image of the god Ptah. When it died it was mummified and buried in the underground galleries of the Serapeum at Saqqara, and a successor was sought. Stelae set up at each burial record the bull's birth, installation and death by regnal years, which makes them a valuable dating tool for the period.
e_death_of_apis.s1: Herodotus says that when Cambyses returned to Memphis from his failed march south, a new Apis had appeared and the city was feasting. Thinking the Egyptians were mocking his defeat, the king had the bull brought and stabbed at its belly but struck its thigh. Herodotus says the Apis wasted away and the priests buried it in secret. He adds that the Egyptians traced Cambyses' madness to this crime, though he thought the king unsound even before.
e_death_of_apis.s2: A stela from the Serapeum records that an Apis died and was buried in the sixth year of Cambyses, in 524 BCE. It shows the king in Egyptian royal dress kneeling before the bull. A large granite sarcophagus in the galleries also bears an inscription naming Cambyses as the one who made it for the god. Both point to a burial carried out with royal honours, not in secret.
e_death_of_apis.s3: A stela of Darius's fourth year records the death of an Apis born in Cambyses' fifth year, so the new bull Herodotus describes seems to have outlived Cambyses. Most historians therefore treat the stabbing as hostile tradition. Some think it came from priests angered by cuts to temple income, which a much later Egyptian text, the Demotic Chronicle, credits to Cambyses. Others argue the dating leaves room for Herodotus, and the question is not fully settled.
e_death_of_apis.s4: Herodotus closes the tale with a moral echo. When Cambyses later leapt onto his horse in Syria, the tip of his sword pierced his thigh at the very spot where he had struck the Apis, and he died of the wound. The neat match of crime and punishment marks this as a story shaped to teach, not a record of events.
e_death_of_cambyses.lead: In 522 BCE Cambyses, son of Cyrus and conqueror of Egypt, died while marching back towards Persia. A man calling himself Bardiya, the King's brother, had already been recognised as king in much of the empire. The death left the throne open, and within months Darius and six Persian nobles killed the new ruler, setting off the revolts of 522-521 BCE.
e_death_of_cambyses.play: The game follows Darius's official version, naming the ruler a man posing as Bardiya. Whether he was an impostor or the real brother is still argued, and the game's brief note does not settle the cause of death.
e_death_of_cambyses.s0: The Behistun inscription says that Cambyses had secretly killed his brother Bardiya before going to Egypt. While the King was away, a magus named Gaumata rose in Persis in March 522 BCE, claimed to be Bardiya and took the kingship in July. Darius then states only that Cambyses died his own death. The phrase gives no place, cause or exact date.
e_death_of_cambyses.s1: Babylonian business texts are dated by the reign of Bardiya from the spring of 522 BCE. This shows that he was accepted as king in Babylonia while Cambyses was probably still alive. Cambyses' death therefore probably fell in the summer of 522 BCE, after the new ruler had already won wide support. The documents do not say how or where Cambyses died.
e_death_of_cambyses.s2: Herodotus says that Cambyses was in Syria, at a place called Ecbatana, when a herald announced the new king. As he leapt on his horse, his sword slipped from its sheath and pierced his thigh. The wound turned bad, and he died after a reign of seven years and five months. Ctesias tells a different story: the King died in Babylon, eleven days after cutting his thigh with a knife while carving wood.
e_death_of_cambyses.s3: Historians do not agree on what happened. Some read Darius's phrase as a natural or accidental death, others as suicide, and some suspect that Cambyses was killed by men who later backed Darius. The question is tied to a larger dispute over whether the man on the throne was really Bardiya. If he was, Darius's whole account would serve to justify his own seizure of power.
e_death_of_cambyses.s4: Herodotus shapes the death as divine punishment. He says the sword struck the same place on the thigh where Cambyses had stabbed the Apis bull in Memphis. He adds that an oracle of Buto had warned the King he would die at Ecbatana, which he had taken to mean the Median city. Egyptian records of an Apis buried with royal honour under Cambyses cast doubt on the story of the stabbed bull.
e_fall_of_babylon.lead: In autumn 539 BCE Cyrus defeated the army of the Babylonian king Nabonidus at Opis on the Tigris. Soon after, his troops entered Babylon without a fight. The conquest gave Cyrus the rich kingdom of Babylonia, with its temples, archives, irrigated fields and western provinces as far as the Mediterranean, and he ruled it as king of Babylon.
e_fall_of_babylon.play: The game marks the fall with a Chronicle entry as Babylonian barley reaches Pasargadae. It pairs the Cylinder with Ezra 1 on the return of exiles, though the Cylinder never names the Judeans.
e_fall_of_babylon.s0: According to the chronicle, in the month Tashritu, about October 539 BCE, Cyrus fought the army of Akkad at Opis, routed it, took plunder and killed people. Sippar fell without battle on the 14th, and on the 16th Ugbaru, governor of Gutium, entered Babylon with Cyrus's army, also without battle. Nabonidus, who had fled, was later captured there. Cyrus himself entered on 3 Arahsamnu, when green twigs were spread before him and peace was proclaimed in the city.
e_fall_of_babylon.s1: The clay cylinder was found at Babylon in 1879 and is now in the British Museum. It was written in Babylonian cuneiform in Cyrus's name. It says that Marduk, angered by Nabonidus's neglect of his cult, chose Cyrus and let him enter Babylon without battle. It claims that Cyrus returned gods to their shrines in cities beyond the Tigris, such as Ashur, Susa and Der, and gathered their people back to their homes.
e_fall_of_babylon.s2: Herodotus says Cyrus beat the Babylonians in battle outside the city, then drew off the Euphrates into a basin so that his men could wade in along the riverbed. He adds that the city was so large that people in the centre went on celebrating a festival, unaware it had fallen. Xenophon's Cyropaedia, more a moral work than a history, tells a similar tale in which the king is killed, although the Chronicle says Nabonidus was taken alive.
e_fall_of_babylon.s3: The Cylinder and the Verse Account of Nabonidus cast Nabonidus as impious and Cyrus as a liberator. Most historians read both as texts composed after the conquest, probably by Babylonian priests, to justify it. The Chronicle's report of fighting and plunder at Opis shows it was not wholly peaceful, and it mentions no siege or river diversion. The Cylinder never names the Judeans; their return rests on Ezra 1, whose decree some scholars think was later reworked.
e_fall_of_babylon.s4: The Book of Daniel, written centuries later, sets the fall on the night of a feast held by Belshazzar. A hand wrote on the palace wall, and the king was killed that night. Belshazzar was real: he was Nabonidus's son and had governed Babylon during his father's long stay at Tayma, but his fate in 539 BCE is unknown. Daniel calls him the son of Nebuchadnezzar and gives the kingdom to a Darius the Mede who is otherwise unknown.
e_fall_of_eretria.lead: In 490 BCE the fleet of Datis and Artaphernes besieged Eretria on Euboea, one of the two Greek cities that had helped the Ionians burn Sardis. After six days of fighting, two leading citizens betrayed the city on the seventh. Herodotus says the Persians burned its sanctuaries and carried its people to Susa, then crossed to Marathon, where the expedition was defeated.
e_fall_of_eretria.play: The game follows Herodotus: six days of defence, betrayal on the seventh, temples burned for Sardis. This is the Greek account only; no known Persian document mentions the siege.
e_fall_of_eretria.s0: Herodotus says Eretria sent five triremes to help the Ionian Revolt in 498 BCE, repaying an old debt to Miletus. Its men marched inland with the Athenians and took part in the burning of Sardis, where a temple of the goddess Cybebe was destroyed. He reports that Darius later ordered Datis and Artaphernes to enslave Athens and Eretria and bring the captives before him.
e_fall_of_eretria.s1: Herodotus tells that Athens sent the 4,000 settlers it held at Chalcis to help. The Eretrians were divided, however, and on the advice of Aeschines son of Nothon the Athenians withdrew to Oropus. The Persians landed near Tamynae, Choereae and Aegilia. The Eretrians chose to hold their walls rather than fight in the open, and on the seventh day Euphorbus and Philagrus betrayed the city to the Persians.
e_fall_of_eretria.s2: According to Herodotus the Persians plundered and burned the sanctuaries in revenge for those burned at Sardis, and enslaved the inhabitants as Darius had ordered. He adds that the captives were brought to Susa and that Darius did them no harm. He settled them at Ardericca in the Cissian land, some 40 stades from a well that yielded bitumen, salt and oil. Herodotus says they still spoke their own language in his day.
e_fall_of_eretria.s3: Plato, writing more than a century later, tells that Datis's soldiers joined hands and swept across Eretrian territory like a net so that no one escaped. The image appears in two of his dialogues and suits his theme of Persian power. Herodotus tells of the same netting method in the Persian capture of Chios, Lesbos and Tenedos after Lade. For this reason some historians see it as a stock tale rather than a record of Eretria.
e_fall_of_eretria.s4: Strabo says the Persians razed old Eretria and that the later city was founded afterwards. Swiss excavations show that the classical city stood on the site of the archaic one, and the destruction of the archaic temple of Apollo Daphnephoros is often dated to 490 BCE. Some scholars think Strabo's old Eretria was an earlier settlement. How complete the deportation was is argued, since Eretria sent ships to Artemisium and Salamis in 480 BCE.
e_fall_of_miletus.lead: In 494 BCE, after the Ionian fleet broke up at Lade, Persian forces besieged Miletus by land and sea and took it. Miletus had led the Ionian Revolt since 499 BCE. Herodotus treats its capture as the revolt's decisive blow: most of its men were killed, its women and children were enslaved, and the survivors were deported deep into Asia.
e_fall_of_miletus.play: The game shows a siege won by mining, as Herodotus tells it. It simplifies: he says most men, not all, were killed, and the revolt did not end at once, since Persia spent 493 BCE retaking the islands and the Hellespont.
e_fall_of_miletus.s0: Herodotus says that after the Ionian fleet scattered at Lade, the Persian commanders closed on Miletus by land and sea. They dug mines under the walls and brought up every kind of siege engine. They took the city in the sixth year after Aristagoras had begun the revolt. Herodotus gives no figure for the besieging army and names no Persian commander for the final assault.
e_fall_of_miletus.s1: Herodotus says the Persians, whom he describes as long-haired, killed most of the Milesian men and made the women and children slaves. The captives were taken to Susa. Darius did them no further harm and settled them at Ampe, on the Persian Gulf near the mouth of the Tigris. The Persians kept the city and its plain for themselves and gave the hill country to Carians from Pedasa.
e_fall_of_miletus.s2: French excavators at Susa found a large bronze weight in the shape of a knucklebone, which is now in the Louvre. Its Greek inscription records a dedication to Apollo, and most scholars think it was carried off from his sanctuary at Didyma. If so, it is a rare physical trace of the plunder Herodotus describes. The inscription itself does not say when the weight was taken or by whom.
e_fall_of_miletus.s3: Herodotus places the plunder and burning of the shrine at Didyma in 494 BCE. Strabo instead says Xerxes burned it, after the Branchidae priests handed over its treasure and went east with him. Excavators find destruction at Miletus, yet Herodotus says Milesians serving the Persians turned against them at Mycale in 479 BCE. The city was probably not wholly emptied.
e_fall_of_miletus.s4: Herodotus says the Athenians grieved deeply at the news. When the poet Phrynichus staged a tragedy called The Capture of Miletus, the audience wept. The Athenians then fined him a thousand drachmas for reminding them of a disaster that touched them closely, and they forbade anyone to perform the play again.
e_fall_of_sardis.lead: Croesus of Lydia crossed the Halys river to attack Cyrus and was driven back to his capital, Sardis, where the Persians beat his cavalry and took the citadel. The fall of Lydia gave Cyrus western Anatolia, its wealth and the road to the Greek cities of the Aegean coast, which his generals conquered in the following years.
e_fall_of_sardis.play: The game follows Herodotus: camels turn the Lydian horse, a climber takes the citadel, and Croesus lives on as adviser. Its firm date of 546 BCE is the traditional one, and Bacchylides gives Croesus a different fate.
e_fall_of_sardis.s0: Herodotus says Croesus consulted Delphi and was told that if he made war on the Persians he would destroy a great empire. He crossed the Halys into Cappadocia and fought Cyrus at Pteria without a clear result. Expecting no campaign before spring, he returned to Sardis and sent his allied troops home for the winter.
e_fall_of_sardis.s1: Herodotus tells that Cyrus followed at speed and met the Lydians on the plain before Sardis. On Harpagus's advice he put his baggage camels in front, and the Lydian horses, unused to their smell, turned away. Croesus was besieged in the citadel, and on the fourteenth day a Mardian soldier named Hyroeades climbed the steep side that the defenders had left unguarded, and the Persians followed him in.
e_fall_of_sardis.s2: The date of 546 BCE rests on later Greek chronology. The Nabonidus Chronicle records that in the ninth year of Nabonidus, about 547 BCE, Cyrus marched against a land and killed its king, but the land's name is damaged. Older readings took it as Lydia; several scholars now doubt that reading, so the chronicle may not mention Sardis at all, and the fall of Lydia cannot be fixed more closely than the mid 540s BCE.
e_fall_of_sardis.s3: Excavators at Sardis have found a burned destruction level of the mid 6th century against the Lydian city wall, with arrowheads, weapons and the remains of men killed in the fighting. It is generally linked to the Persian capture. The remains show the city was stormed with violence, whatever happened to its king.
e_fall_of_sardis.s4: Herodotus says Cyrus set Croesus on a pyre and relented when Croesus called the name of Solon, who had warned him to call no man happy before his end. When the flames would not die, Croesus prayed to Apollo and a sudden rain put them out. Bacchylides, writing about 468 BCE, has Croesus mount the pyre by choice until Apollo carries him away, and an Athenian vase shows him enthroned on it. Both are moral tales, not reports.
e_founding_of_persepolis.lead: From about 518 BCE Darius I had a great stone platform raised at the foot of a mountain on the Marv Dasht plain in Persis, and built palaces on it. Its own name was Parsa, which the Greeks later called Persepolis, and it became the ceremonial centre of the Persian homeland. The administration based there left clay tablets that are the richest surviving record of how the empire worked day to day.
e_founding_of_persepolis.play: The Parsa level is built around the terrace, dated in the game from about 518 BCE, a start historians still debate. The game ties the fortification tablets to the terrace workers, though in fact they cover much of Persis.
e_founding_of_persepolis.s0: Darius placed four inscriptions on the south retaining wall of the terrace, in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. In the Elamite text he says that, by the favour of Auramazda, he built a fortress on this spot where none had stood before, and made it secure and beautiful. Two of the others list the lands he ruled, and an Old Persian prayer asks the god to protect the country from enemy armies, from famine and from the Lie.
e_founding_of_persepolis.s1: Excavations by Ernst Herzfeld from 1931 and Erich Schmidt from 1935 showed how the terrace was made. The builders levelled the rocky foot of the mountain, filled the hollows with rubble and earth, and cut drains into the rock. They faced the platform with huge limestone blocks fitted without mortar and joined by metal clamps. On it stood the Apadana, begun by Darius and completed by Xerxes, whose hall and three porches had seventy-two columns.
e_founding_of_persepolis.s2: In 1933 excavators found thousands of clay tablets in the northern fortification wall, most in Elamite and dated 509 to 493 BCE. They record barley, wine, beer and other goods issued across Persis and into Elam, not only on the terrace. Workers, men and women, drew rations, and mothers received extra after a birth. The later Treasury tablets record silver paid to craftsmen of many peoples working at Parsa.
e_founding_of_persepolis.s3: No text gives the year building started. Many historians place it about 518 BCE, once the revolts were over, and others about 515 BCE. The gold and silver foundation tablets of the Apadana (DPh) carry no date, and the coins buried with them are Lydian and Greek pieces with no darics, which some read as a sign that the deposit came before Darius's own coinage. Historians also argue over whether Cyrus or Cambyses had begun any work at the site.
e_founding_of_persepolis.s4: Greek writers knew little of Parsa before Alexander, and Herodotus never mentions it. Arrian says Alexander burned the palaces in 330 as revenge for Xerxes' burning of Athens, against the advice of Parmenion. Diodorus and Plutarch tell a different story, in which the fire began at a drinking party when the Athenian courtesan Thais urged it. Excavation has confirmed a great fire, with thick layers of ash in the Treasury and the halls.
e_getae.lead: On his march against the Scythians, about 513 BCE, Darius crossed Thrace towards the Ister (the Danube). Herodotus says most Thracian peoples gave in without a fight, but the Getae resisted and were subdued. The episode is known in detail only from Herodotus, who used it to describe the Getae and their belief that they did not die.
e_getae.play: The game shows the episode as a battle and follows Herodotus: the Getae alone stand against the King and are made to march with his army. No Persian source confirms it.
e_getae.s0: Herodotus says Darius crossed the Bosporus on a bridge of boats and led his army north through Thrace, while the Ionian fleet sailed into the Black Sea to bridge the Ister. On the way he camped at the springs of the Tearus and at the river Artescus. Herodotus says that at the Artescus each soldier was ordered to drop a stone, leaving great heaps behind.
e_getae.s1: Herodotus says the Thracians of Salmydessus and those living inland from Apollonia and Mesambria surrendered without fighting. The Getae, whom he calls the bravest and most just of the Thracians, chose to resist and were at once overcome. He adds that, once beaten, they followed the rest of Darius's army north towards the Ister.
e_getae.s2: Herodotus explains that the Getae held that the dead went to a god called Salmoxis, or Zalmoxis. Every fifth year, as he counts it, they chose a messenger by lot and sent him to the god by throwing him onto upright spears. He also says they shot arrows at the sky during thunder and lightning, threatening the god, and recognised no god but their own.
e_getae.s3: Herodotus reports a story told by the Greeks of the Hellespont and the Black Sea. In it, Salmoxis had been a slave of Pythagoras on Samos, grew rich, went home, taught the Thracians that they would live for ever, and hid in an underground room for three years before reappearing. Herodotus says he neither rejects nor fully believes the tale, and he thinks Salmoxis lived long before Pythagoras.
e_getae.s4: No Persian inscription names the Getae. Later royal lists such as DNa include Skudra, usually taken as land in Thrace, but historians disagree on whether Darius set up lasting rule this far north. The campaign's date is uncertain, usually put between about 514 and 512 BCE. Its aims are also argued, with some historians seeing it as a move to secure Thrace and the Black Sea coast rather than to conquer Scythia.
e_hellespont_bridges.lead: To march his army from Asia into Europe, Xerxes had two bridges of ships laid across the Hellespont near Abydos. A storm wrecked the first pair, and a second pair carried the army over in spring 480 BCE. Herodotus describes them in close detail, and for Greek writers they became a symbol of royal pride that defied the sea itself.
e_hellespont_bridges.play: The game follows Herodotus: the broken bridges, the lashing and beheadings, and 674 ships, which he gives as 360 and 314 for two separate bridges. The game shows the lashing as fact; it is Herodotus's story, not a Persian record.
e_hellespont_bridges.s0: Herodotus says the work ran from Abydos on the Asian shore to a rocky headland on the European side between Sestos and Madytus, a crossing of seven stades, a little over a kilometre. Two bridges were built. The Phoenicians made one with cables of white flax, the Egyptians the other with cables of papyrus. Xerxes spent the winter at Sardis while the work went on.
e_hellespont_bridges.s1: When a storm broke both bridges, Herodotus says Xerxes ordered the Hellespont given three hundred lashes and had fetters dropped into it. He adds that he had heard branders were sent as well. The floggers were told to call the water bitter and to say it had wronged a master who had done it no wrong. The overseers of the work were beheaded. The tale fits Herodotus's portrait of a king who overreached, and no Persian source records it.
e_hellespont_bridges.s2: New engineers moored 360 penteconters and triremes for the bridge on the Black Sea side and 314 for the other, held by heavy anchors. Each bridge now had two flax cables and four of papyrus, drawn taut by wooden windlasses ashore. Planks, brushwood and trodden earth made the roadway, with screens so the animals would not see the water. Gaps were left for small boats to pass.
e_hellespont_bridges.s3: No Persian text mentions the bridges, but Aeschylus, writing in 472 BCE, confirms that the strait was bridged. Historians accept the bridging, as Darius had bridged the Bosporus, but argue over the landing places, the anchoring and spacing of the ships, and whether 674 vessels is right. Hammond and Roseman argued that Herodotus's technical account is coherent. Others note that his fetters echo Aeschylus, whose ghost of Darius condemns Xerxes for chaining the sacred Hellespont.
e_hellespont_bridges.s4: Herodotus says that when Xerxes' army came back after Salamis, storms had broken the bridges and the troops crossed by ship. In 479 BCE the Greek fleet sailed to the Hellespont and found them already broken. The Athenians then besieged Sestos, took the bridge cables, and carried them home to dedicate in their sanctuaries.
e_hellespont_crossing.lead: In 480 BCE Xerxes led his army across the Hellespont, the narrow strait between Asia and Europe, on two bridges of boats built from Abydos to the European shore. Herodotus describes ordered rites and a set order of march, then a crossing that went on for seven days and nights. It carried the King's host into Europe for the march on Greece, and Greek writers later made the bridging a symbol of royal pride.
e_hellespont_crossing.play: The game marks the crossing as an event of 480 BCE and repeats Herodotus's seven days and nights under the lash. That figure is his report, not a Persian record, and the size of the army that crossed is still argued.
e_hellespont_crossing.s0: Herodotus says that before dawn incense was burned on the bridges and the roadway strewn with myrtle. At sunrise Xerxes poured a libation from a gold cup into the sea and prayed to the sun that nothing would stop him before he reached the far edge of Europe. He then threw the cup, a gold bowl and a Persian short sword into the water. Herodotus could not decide whether these were gifts to the sun or amends to the sea for its earlier whipping.
e_hellespont_crossing.s1: Herodotus says the foot and horse used the bridge nearer the Black Sea, and the baggage animals and servants the one nearer the Aegean. First came the Ten Thousand Persians wearing garlands, then the mixed host of many peoples. Next day came horsemen and spearmen with their spear-points turned down, the sacred horses and chariot, and then the King with his guards. The fleet crossed at the same time, and he records a report that Xerxes went over last.
e_hellespont_crossing.s2: Herodotus states that Xerxes watched the army cross under whips, and that it took seven days and seven nights without any rest. He uses the same image of men driven by the lash for the digging of the Athos canal and for the fighting at Thermopylae. In his history it helps set the King's subjects against Greeks who fought by choice, though whips may also simply have kept order on a crowded crossing.
e_hellespont_crossing.s3: Herodotus reports 1,700,000 foot soldiers counted at Doriscus and over five million people in all with the followers. Historians reject these figures as greatly exaggerated. Modern estimates vary widely, mostly from several tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand fighting men. Some, such as Maurice, have used the crossing time and the water supply on the route to estimate the force. No Persian document records the crossing or the army's size.
e_hellespont_crossing.s4: In Aeschylus's Persians of 472 BCE, the ghost of Darius condemns his son for chaining the sacred Hellespont, an offence against the gods. Herodotus adds a local man who, seeing Xerxes cross, asked Zeus why he had taken the form of a Persian to destroy Greece. He also tells of a mare that gave birth to a hare, an omen he says was easy to read as a sign of a proud march and a flight home. These are moral tales of pride before a fall, not records.
e_house_of_life.lead: Early in his reign Darius ordered the Egyptian official Udjahorresnet to leave the Persian court and restore the House of Life, probably the one at Sais, a temple institution of sacred writing and medicine that had fallen into decay. The order is known almost entirely from Udjahorresnet's own inscribed statue, which also shows how Persian kings worked with Egyptian temple elites to govern Egypt.
e_house_of_life.play: The game shows this as a decree of 518 BCE sending Udjahorresnet home. The statue gives no year, so 518 BCE is a modern estimate, and the House of Life was a temple scriptorium of sacred learning rather than simply a school.
e_house_of_life.s0: Udjahorresnet had served as a naval commander under the last Saite kings, Amasis and Psamtik III. After Cambyses conquered Egypt in 525 BCE he became chief physician and a court companion, and he composed the King's Egyptian throne name. His career is told in hieroglyphs carved on a statue of him holding a small shrine. It is now in the Vatican Museums, probably brought to Italy in Roman times.
e_house_of_life.s1: The inscription says that Darius, while he was in Elam, ordered Udjahorresnet to go to Egypt and restore the House of Life after it had decayed. Foreigners escorted him from land to land. He says he staffed it with students from respected families, set them under learned men and supplied all their needs. He adds that the King acted because he knew the value of this craft for keeping the sick alive.
e_house_of_life.s2: Egyptian texts from many periods name the House of Life as a body attached to temples where scribes copied, studied and kept sacred books on ritual, medicine and magic. It was less a school in the modern sense than a workshop of written knowledge. The statue does not name the town, but scholars usually place this one at Sais, beside the temple of Neith, whose cult Udjahorresnet had already persuaded Cambyses to protect.
e_house_of_life.s3: Herodotus tells that Amasis sent an Egyptian eye doctor to Cyrus at the King's request. He also says Darius kept Egyptian physicians at court, reckoned the best in medicine, though they failed to treat his twisted ankle until the Greek Democedes cured it. Whatever the truth of the details, his stories fit the statue's claim that Darius valued Egyptian medicine.
e_house_of_life.s4: Historians disagree on how to read Udjahorresnet. Some see a collaborator excusing his service to the conquerors; others a local notable protecting his temple and town as best he could.
