His picture of Cambyses honouring Neith clashes with Herodotus's sacrilegious Cambyses. Scholars also debate the date of the order, usually placed in 519 or 518 BCE, and whether the great turmoil he mentions means the conquest of 525 BCE or the revolts of 522 BCE.
e_ionian_revolt.lead: The Ionian Revolt was the rising of the Greek cities of western Asia Minor against Darius, which began at Miletus in about 499 BCE and was broken with the fall of Miletus in 494 BCE. Athens and Eretria helped burn Sardis, which Herodotus presents as the start of the Persian quarrel with mainland Greece. Almost everything known about the revolt comes from his Histories.
e_ionian_revolt.play: The Sardis level is built around the revolt, with Ionian ports and tribute closed to the King. Herodotus's 400 talents covered a whole tax district, Carians and Lycians included, not Ionia alone.
e_ionian_revolt.s0: In Herodotus's telling the revolt grew out of a failed Persian attack on Naxos in about 499 BCE, urged on Artaphernes by Aristagoras, deputy ruler of Miletus. Fearing for his position, and prompted by a secret message from his kinsman Histiaeus, held at Susa, Aristagoras turned against the King. Herodotus says he gave up his tyranny only in pretence and proclaimed equal rights at Miletus, while the other Ionian cities expelled their tyrants.
e_ionian_revolt.s1: Herodotus says Cleomenes of Sparta refused to help once he learned that Susa lay three months' march from the sea. The Athenians voted twenty ships and the Eretrians five, and Herodotus calls these ships the start of troubles for Greeks and barbarians alike. In 498 BCE the allies took the lower town of Sardis, which burned along with its temple of Cybebe, while Artaphernes held the citadel. They were beaten near Ephesus on the way back, and the Athenians went home.
e_ionian_revolt.s2: After Sardis the revolt spread to Byzantium and the Hellespont, to Caria and to Cyprus, where Onesilus of Salamis led a rising that was crushed within a year. Persian armies retook the Hellespont towns and fought hard battles in Caria. In 494 BCE the Ionian fleet met the royal fleet off Lade, where most of the Samian ships deserted. Miletus was then taken, its men killed or deported, and the shrine at Didyma burned.
e_ionian_revolt.s3: Herodotus explains the revolt mainly through the personal ambitions of Aristagoras and Histiaeus, and he writes of the Ionians with little sympathy. Modern historians look for wider causes. These include resentment of tyrants who ruled with Persian backing, the weight of tribute, and possible strains on trade. They also argue over whether the revolt began in 500 or 499 BCE.
e_ionian_revolt.s4: No royal inscription of Darius mentions the revolt. The Persepolis Fortification archive may give one glimpse of it. A tablet of early 494 BCE records travel rations for a man named Datiya on a journey to the King. David Lewis argued that this Datiya was Datis, later a commander at Marathon, but the identification is not certain.
e_ister_bridge_debate.lead: In about 513 BCE, while Darius campaigned against the Scythians north of the Ister (Danube), Greek contingents from Ionia and the Hellespont guarded the bridge of boats that was his road home. Herodotus tells how their tyrants debated whether to break it and strand the King, and how Histiaeus of Miletus persuaded them to keep it. The story shaped later Greek views of Ionian loyalty and of the men who went on to stir up the Ionian Revolt.
e_ister_bridge_debate.play: The game follows Herodotus: Coes advises keeping the bridge, Miltiades urges breaking it and Histiaeus saves it. The whole episode is known only from Herodotus, and Miltiades' part may be a later Athenian story.
e_ister_bridge_debate.s0: Herodotus says that once the army had crossed the Ister, Darius ordered the Ionians to break the bridge and march with him. Coes, general of the men of Mytilene, advised leaving it standing under its builders' guard as a way back in case the Scythians could not be found or brought to battle, and Darius agreed. He tied sixty knots in a cord and told the Ionians to untie one each day, and to sail home if he had not returned when the knots ran out.
e_ister_bridge_debate.s1: Scythians came to the bridge twice, the second time after the sixty days had passed, urging the Ionians to break it and go. Herodotus reports that Miltiades of Athens, tyrant of the Chersonese, wanted to agree. Histiaeus of Miletus answered that each tyrant ruled his city through Persian power and would fall to popular rule without it. The others sided with him, broke only the stretch nearest the Scythian bank and told the Scythians they would destroy the rest.
e_ister_bridge_debate.s2: Darius reached the river at night and found the northern end gone. Herodotus says an Egyptian with a very loud voice called for Histiaeus, who brought the ships back and restored the crossing. Later, at Sardis, the King rewarded both men: Coes asked to be made tyrant of Mytilene, and Histiaeus received Myrcinus in Thrace. Herodotus adds a Scythian verdict that the Ionians were the most cowardly of free men and the most devoted of slaves.
e_ister_bridge_debate.s3: Historians doubt this part of the story. Miltiades was later tried at Athens for his tyranny in the Chersonese and acquitted, and many think the tale of his proposal grew up to show him as an old enemy of Persia. Others note that he seems to have stayed in the Chersonese, a Persian vassal, until about 493 BCE, although Herodotus's account of those years is confused. The date of the campaign is also uncertain; about 513 BCE is the usual estimate.
e_ister_bridge_debate.s4: No Persian text describes the bridge or the debate. Darius's tomb inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam lists among his subject peoples the Saka beyond the sea, whom many scholars link with this European campaign, though some place them elsewhere. The Persian record shows a claim to lands across the water, but the Greeks' choice at the bridge is known only from Greek tradition.
e_killing_of_gaumata.lead: On 29 September 522 BCE Darius, son of Hystaspes, and six Persian nobles killed the man then ruling the empire as Bardiya, son of Cyrus. Darius said his victim was Gaumata, a magus and an impostor, and the killing made Darius king but set off a year of revolts. Historians still argue over whether the dead king was in fact the real Bardiya.
e_killing_of_gaumata.play: The game presents this as an event of 522 BCE, using Darius's name for the dead king while noting that some historians think he was the real Bardiya. Its date and its count of six helpers match Darius's own inscription.
e_killing_of_gaumata.s0: In the Behistun inscription Darius says that a magus named Gaumata rose up at Paishiyauvada in March 522 BCE. Gaumata claimed to be Bardiya, son of Cyrus and brother of Cambyses, and he took the kingship that July. Darius says no one dared speak against him until he himself came. On the tenth day of the month Bagayadish, about 29 September, Darius and a few men killed Gaumata at the fortress of Sikayauvati in the district of Nisaya, in Media.
e_killing_of_gaumata.s1: Near the end of the inscription Darius names the men who were with him, each with his father's name: Vindafarna, Utana, Gaubaruva, Vidarna, Bagabukhsha and Ardumanish. He asks future kings to protect their families. Herodotus gives almost the same list in Greek forms, such as Intaphernes, Otanes, Gobryas, Hydarnes and Megabyzus. Where Darius names Ardumanish, however, Herodotus has Aspathines.
e_killing_of_gaumata.s2: Herodotus says Cambyses had his brother Smerdis secretly murdered, and a magus of the same name then took the throne with the help of his brother Patizeithes. In this version the seven forced their way into the palace at Susa, not a fortress in Media, and Darius stabbed the magus in a dark room while Gobryas held him. Herodotus adds that the Persians later kept a festival of the killing of the magi, which the Greeks called the Magophonia.
e_killing_of_gaumata.s3: Babylonian contracts were dated by the reign of Barziya through the summer of 522 BCE, which suggests that many subjects accepted him. Darius says he rebuilt the places of worship Gaumata had destroyed and returned the pastures, herds and household workers he had seized, while Herodotus says the king had remitted tribute and military service for three years. Many historians suspect Darius killed the real Bardiya and invented the impostor, but others accept his account.
e_killing_of_gaumata.s4: Herodotus tells how Otanes exposed the impostor. His daughter Phaidyme was one of the king's wives, and she felt his head while he slept and found he had no ears, since Cyrus had once cut them off as a punishment. Herodotus also says the seven chose the new king by whose horse neighed first at sunrise, and that Darius's groom Oebares contrived the result. Both stories read as court tales rather than records.
e_mardonius_expedition.lead: In 492 BCE Darius sent his young general Mardonius across the Hellespont with an army and a fleet, probably to reassert Persian power in the north Aegean after the Ionian Revolt. The army brought the Macedonians and parts of Thrace under Persian rule and the fleet took Thasos, but a storm off Mount Athos destroyed much of the fleet. Herodotus treats the campaign as a failure, and the wreck shaped Persian plans for the invasion of 480 BCE.
e_mardonius_expedition.play: The game gives Herodotus's figures of 300 ships and over 20,000 men, which may be inflated. It says the wreck led to the canal; Herodotus gives that reason but also says Xerxes dug it to show his power (7.22-24).
e_mardonius_expedition.s0: Herodotus says that Darius sent Mardonius, son of Gobryas, young and lately married to the King's daughter Artozostre, down to the coast with a large army and fleet. In Ionia he removed the tyrants and let the cities govern themselves as democracies. Herodotus offers this as proof for Greeks who doubted that Persians had ever debated such a constitution. Historians usually read it as part of the settlement after the revolt.
e_mardonius_expedition.s1: Mardonius crossed the Hellespont and marched west through Thrace while the fleet kept pace along the coast. Herodotus says the stated targets were Eretria and Athens, but the real aim was to subdue as many Greek cities as possible. The fleet took Thasos without a fight, and the army added the Macedonians to the peoples already subject. The Thracian Brygi then attacked the camp at night and wounded Mardonius, though he subdued them before returning to Asia.
e_mardonius_expedition.s2: As the fleet tried to round the Athos peninsula, a strong north wind drove many ships onto the rocks. Herodotus says about 300 ships and more than 20,000 men were lost. Some were killed by sea creatures, some were broken on the rocks, and others died of cold or because they could not swim. His figures are the only ones we have, and historians think they may be exaggerated.
e_mardonius_expedition.s3: Herodotus calls the campaign a disgrace and says Darius later replaced Mardonius with Datis and Artaphernes. Many modern historians see it differently: Thasos, Macedonia and the Thracian coast were brought under Persian control, giving the base used in 480 BCE. They also question whether Athens and Eretria were targets in 492 BCE or whether Herodotus read the later war back into it. Mardonius kept high favour and led armies again under Xerxes.
e_mardonius_expedition.s4: No Persian text describes the campaign or the storm. Darius's tomb inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam lists Skudra among his lands, together with the Yauna takabara, a phrase often rendered as Ionians wearing the petasos hat. Both are usually placed in Thrace and Macedonia, which would fit Persian rule there. However, the inscription cannot be dated closely and the locations are debated.
e_massagetae_war.lead: Cyrus's last campaign, in about 530 BCE, took him against the Massagetae, a horse-riding people of the steppes east of the Caspian. Herodotus says he crossed the Araxes, was defeated by Queen Tomyris and fell in battle, though other ancient writers told the story differently. His death brought his son Cambyses to the throne, and later Greek writers say he was buried in the tomb that still stands at Pasargadae.
e_massagetae_war.play: The Pasargadae Chronicle reports Cambyses named heir and sent home with Croesus, then Cyrus's death and an order to ready his tomb. The tomb was probably built in his lifetime, so that order is a simplification.
e_massagetae_war.s0: Herodotus says that after taking Babylon, Cyrus turned against the Massagetae, who were ruled by the widowed queen Tomyris. He first offered to marry her. She understood that he wanted her kingdom rather than herself and refused, so he began to bridge the river. Herodotus's Araxes is a confused river, and historians have identified it variously with the Oxus, the Jaxartes or another river of Central Asia.
e_massagetae_war.s1: Following advice from Croesus, Cyrus chose to cross and fight in Massagetan land. Before crossing, he named Cambyses his heir and sent him back to Persia with Croesus. A third of the Massagetae, led by Tomyris's son Spargapises, overran a camp left stocked with wine, feasted and were overwhelmed, and Spargapises killed himself in captivity. Herodotus says most of the Persian army died in the battle that followed, and Cyrus fell after reigning 29 years.
e_massagetae_war.s2: Herodotus himself says he chose the most believable of many versions. Ctesias, as summarised by Photius, has Cyrus mortally wounded fighting the Derbices of Central Asia and dying three days later. Xenophon ends his Cyropaedia with Cyrus dying peacefully in old age in Persia, a scene written to teach. Most historians accept that Cyrus died on campaign in the north-east, but not the details.
e_massagetae_war.s3: No Persian inscription describes this war. Babylonian contract tablets were dated by the regnal year of the king. The last ones dated to Cyrus are from August 530 BCE, and those dated to Cambyses follow within weeks, which fixes the year of his death but not its place or manner. Cambyses had briefly been styled king of Babylon beside his father in 538 BCE, which suggests that his succession had been planned.
e_massagetae_war.s4: Herodotus closes the story with Tomyris filling a skin with human blood, finding Cyrus among the dead and plunging his head into it, saying she would give him his fill of blood. He also tells of Cyrus dreaming of a winged Darius, a warning shaped by later events. Both scenes belong to a moral tale about a conqueror who did not know when to stop and are unlikely to be literal history.
e_nile_canal.lead: Darius I had a canal dug, or dug again, from the eastern Nile through the Wadi Tumilat to the Gulf of Suez, linking the Nile, and through it the Mediterranean, to the Red Sea. Herodotus says Pharaoh Necho II had begun it about a century earlier. Darius set up inscribed stelae along its course claiming that ships sailed through it from Egypt to Persia, a statement of the King's reach as much as a record of engineering.
e_nile_canal.play: The game shows the canal as a royal decree of about 515 BCE that finishes Necho's work, following Herodotus. The real date is uncertain and may be later, and the stelae credit Darius alone without naming Necho.
e_nile_canal.s0: Herodotus says the canal left the Nile a little above Bubastis, passed the Arabian town of Patumus and ran to the Red Sea. He gives its length as four days' voyage and says it was wide enough for two triremes to be rowed side by side. He credits Necho with beginning it and Darius with digging it afterwards. He mentions it again when describing the coasts of Asia.
e_nile_canal.s1: Herodotus adds that 120,000 Egyptians died during Necho's digging. He says the work stopped when an oracle warned the king that he was labouring for the barbarian. The figure for the dead cannot be checked. The warning was probably shaped after the event, when a foreign king had in fact completed the canal.
e_nile_canal.s2: Large stelae stood along the canal line at Tell el-Maskhuta, near the Serapeum, at Kabret and at Shaluf. Fragments were found in the nineteenth century, when the modern Suez Canal was dug. One face carried Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian texts, and the other carried an Egyptian text showing Darius as pharaoh. In the cuneiform text Darius says that he, a Persian, took Egypt and ordered the canal dug, and that ships went from Egypt to Persia as he wished.
e_nile_canal.s3: Darius's stelae say the work was completed and that ships passed through it. Strabo and Diodorus, writing centuries later, say instead that Darius stopped short. In their account he was warned that the Red Sea lay higher than Egypt and would flood the land, and later rulers finished the canal. Most historians trust the stelae over these later writers, though the canal probably silted up and needed clearing again and again.
e_nile_canal.s4: No surviving text dates the work. Some historians link it with Darius's presence in Egypt around 518 BCE, while others place the stelae later, near 500 BCE or after. Herodotus tells how Scylax sailed down the Indus and round to Egypt, after which Darius made use of the southern sea. Historians still argue whether the canal carried regular trade or chiefly proclaimed the King's power from Egypt to Persia.
e_return_of_exiles.lead: After Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BCE, he sent cult statues gathered in the city back to their home temples and, by his own account, let the people of those towns go home too. The Hebrew Bible remembers a separate decree allowing the Judeans to return and rebuild their temple in Jerusalem. Together these made Cyrus known as a restorer, though the evidence is more local and more political than later fame suggests.
e_return_of_exiles.play: The game presents this as one decree for all the deported peoples, recorded on the cylinder and in Ezra 1. In fact the cylinder names Mesopotamian and border cities, not Judah, and Ezra is a separate, later text.
e_return_of_exiles.s0: The clay cylinder, found at Babylon in 1879 and now in the British Museum, was written in Babylonian cuneiform soon after Cyrus entered the city. It says he returned to their sanctuaries the gods of cities across the Tigris, among them Ashur, Susa and Der, and gathered their former inhabitants and sent them back to their homes. It also says he restored to their shrines the gods of Sumer and Akkad that Nabonidus had brought into Babylon.
e_return_of_exiles.s1: The Nabonidus Chronicle, a terse Babylonian record of Nabonidus's reign and its end, notes that the gods of Akkad which Nabonidus had brought down to Babylon went back to their cities between the months Kislimu and Addaru, roughly December 539 BCE to March 538 BCE. Nabonidus had gathered the statues into Babylon as the Persians advanced, probably to protect them. Their return undid a recent emergency measure as well as being a gesture of piety.
e_return_of_exiles.s2: The Book of Ezra, written down long after the events, says that in his first year Cyrus proclaimed that the Judeans might go up to Jerusalem and rebuild the house of their god, and gave back the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken. A second version in Aramaic, presented as a memorandum later found at Ecbatana, sets out the size of the temple and royal funding. Isaiah 45, probably composed nearer Cyrus's time, calls him the Lord's anointed.
e_return_of_exiles.s3: Historians debate whether the Ezra decrees are genuine; many think the Hebrew edict was recast by later writers, while the Aramaic memorandum is often judged closer to a real Persian document. The cylinder follows a traditional Mesopotamian genre and attacks Nabonidus to justify Cyrus's rule; it is not a charter of rights. Tablets from Al-Yahudu show many Judeans stayed in Babylonia for generations, so any return was probably gradual.
e_return_of_exiles.s4: Josephus, writing in the late first century CE, tells that Cyrus read the prophecy of Isaiah naming him as the one who would rebuild the temple, and was moved to fulfil it. The story turns a Persian political act into proof of divine foreknowledge. No Persian or Babylonian source mentions anything of the kind.
e_review_at_doriscus.lead: In 480 BCE, after crossing the Hellespont, Xerxes halted on the plain of Doriscus in Thrace and had his army counted and his fleet reviewed. Herodotus uses the halt to list every people in the King's host. His total of 1,700,000 foot soldiers is the best-known number of the war, and almost no modern historian accepts it.
e_review_at_doriscus.play: The Chronicle tells of the count made by filling a pen for ten thousand men again and again, gives Herodotus's 1,700,000 foot, and notes that modern historians put the real army at a tenth of that or less.
e_review_at_doriscus.s0: Herodotus describes Doriscus as a stretch of Thracian coast and a wide plain through which the Hebrus runs to the sea. Darius had built a royal fort there during his Scythian campaign and left a Persian garrison. Xerxes halted there in 480 BCE, and the fleet was beached on the shore nearby. Herodotus adds that Mascames, the governor Xerxes left there, held the fort long after the war and could not be dislodged.
e_review_at_doriscus.s1: Herodotus says that ten thousand men were packed together as tightly as possible and a line was drawn round them. A wall about navel high was then built on the line. The rest of the army was marched into the enclosure in batches until every man had been counted, and the total came to 1,700,000 foot. He gives no figure for each nation, saying that no one recorded it.
e_review_at_doriscus.s2: Herodotus then lists the peoples one by one, with their dress, weapons and commanders. The list runs from Persians in felt caps and scale armour to Medes, Cissians, Bactrians, Saka, Indians, Arabs, Ethiopians and many others. He counts 80,000 horse besides camels and chariots, and 1,207 triremes, the same fleet total Aeschylus gives. Xerxes, he says, drove past the ranks in a chariot while scribes took notes, then sailed past the ships' prows in a Sidonian vessel.
e_review_at_doriscus.s3: No modern historian accepts the figure, chiefly because they judge that 1.7 million men could not have been fed or watered on the march. Herodotus himself raises the total to 2,641,610 fighting men by Thermopylae and doubles it for camp followers. Most modern estimates for the land army fall between about 100,000 and 200,000, and some go lower. The fleet total is argued over less, though many historians reduce it too.
e_review_at_doriscus.s4: Herodotus's catalogue, arranged by peoples, recalls the lists of lands in Darius's inscriptions and the rows of subject peoples carved holding up the King's throne on his tomb. Some historians think he drew on a Persian muster list, or on the army's units of a thousand and ten thousand. O. K. Armayor argued instead that the catalogue owes more to Greek literary tradition. No Persian text mentions the review at Doriscus.
e_revolt_of_arakha.lead: In 521 BCE an Armenian named Arakha took power in Babylon, claiming to be Nebuchadnezzar, son of the last native king Nabonidus. It was Babylon's second rising against Darius within a year. Darius's general Vindafarna, the Greeks' Intaphernes, retook the city and Arakha was impaled, the last rebel defeated in the first year of the reign as Behistun tells it.
e_revolt_of_arakha.play: The game's chronicle records Babylon rising under Arakha as a second Nebuchadnezzar and the King's general retaking it, as Behistun does. It uses the Greek name Intaphernes for the Persian Vindafarna.
e_revolt_of_arakha.s0: Darius's inscription names Arakha as an Armenian, son of Haldita, who rose at a place called Dubala in Babylonia while Darius was in Persia and Media. He told the people he was Nebuchadnezzar, son of Nabonidus, and Babylon went over to him. Darius sent Vindafarna, a Persian he calls his subject, with an army. Vindafarna defeated the Babylonians and captured Arakha and his leading followers, who were impaled at Babylon.
e_revolt_of_arakha.s1: Babylonian contract tablets were dated for a few months in 521 BCE by the reign of a king Nebuchadnezzar, the ruler modern historians call Nebuchadnezzar IV. Scribes then returned to dating by Darius. Behistun gives the day of Arakha's capture in the Persian calendar, usually converted to late November 521 BCE. Arakha is also carved among the bound rebel kings on the Behistun relief.
e_revolt_of_arakha.s2: The Old Persian text calls Arakha an Armenian, and the Babylonian version uses the old name Urartu for his homeland. Historians debate whether he came from a community of Armenian or Urartian deportees settled in Babylonia, or from abroad. Why Babylonians would follow a foreigner posing as Nebuchadnezzar is also argued. It may show how strong the wish for a native king remained after the rising of Nidintu-Bel.
e_revolt_of_arakha.s3: Herodotus counts Intaphernes among the seven Persians who killed the man on the throne in 522 BCE, and Darius's own list of his helpers at Behistun names Vindafarna. Herodotus says Darius later put Intaphernes to death on suspicion of plotting. He does not mention Arakha or the Babylonian campaign at all.
e_revolt_of_arakha.s4: Herodotus tells of a Babylonian revolt under Darius in which the siege dragged on for a year and seven months. It ended only when a noble named Zopyrus cut off his own nose and ears, posed as a deserter and handed over the gates. The tale fits neither of the revolts in Behistun neatly and reads as a story of loyalty. Some scholars link it loosely to the risings of 522-521 BCE, others to later revolts under Xerxes.
e_revolt_of_athamaita.lead: In the second and third year of Darius's reign, Elam rose against him again, led by a man the Old Persian text calls Athamaita. Darius sent the Persian noble Gobryas, who defeated the Elamites and brought Athamaita to the King to be killed. It was the last rising recorded at Behistun, coming a year or more after the great revolts of 522-521 BCE had been put down.
e_revolt_of_athamaita.play: The Susa level opens with this revolt and Gobryas's victory. The game dates the level to 521 BCE, but Behistun places the rising in Darius's second and third regnal years, about 520-519 BCE, and does not itself call it the third.
e_revolt_of_athamaita.s0: The fifth column of the Behistun inscription says that Elam rebelled in the King's second and third year and that the Elamites made a man named Athamaita their chief. Darius sent Gaubaruva, a Persian and his subject, at the head of an army. Gobryas fought the Elamites, defeated them, seized Athamaita and led him to Darius, who had him killed, and the country became Darius's again.
e_revolt_of_athamaita.s1: Column V was carved some time after the first four columns. It survives only in Old Persian, with no Elamite or Babylonian version, and much of it is damaged. The relief above shows Gaumata and the rebel kings of 522-521 BCE, with the Saka leader Skunkha added later, but Athamaita is not among the figures. Calling his rising the third Elamite revolt, after those of Assina and Martiya, is a modern count drawn from the inscription's narrative.
e_revolt_of_athamaita.s2: The text goes on to say that the Elamites were faithless and did not worship Auramazda, while Darius did, and so he dealt with them as he wished. Some historians once read this as a turn to religious intolerance. Others, notably Henkelman, point out that Elamite gods went on receiving offerings from the royal economy in the Persepolis Fortification tablets. On that view the phrase is a charge of political disloyalty framed in religious terms.
e_revolt_of_athamaita.s3: Behistun gives only his name and says the Elamites made him their chief. Some scholars have proposed that he was Atta-hamiti-Inshushinak, a Neo-Elamite ruler known from an inscription, which would make the revolt an attempt to restore a local dynasty. Others think the match of names and dates is too uncertain to build on, and the question remains open.
e_revolt_of_athamaita.s4: Herodotus says that Darius had married a daughter of Gobryas before he became king. He also says that Gobryas married Darius's sister, so that their son Mardonius was the King's nephew. Behistun itself calls Gaubaruva son of Marduniya one of the six Persians who helped Darius kill Gaumata, and says nothing of marriage. The family tie that makes Gobryas Darius's father-in-law comes from Herodotus alone.
e_revolt_of_fravartish.lead: In the winter of 522-521 BCE a Mede named Fravartish claimed to be Khshathrita, a descendant of the old Median king Cyaxares, and the Median troops at the palace went over to him. Many historians count it among the gravest risings of Darius's first year, because it revived the memory of Median kingship and spread east into Parthia and Hyrcania.
e_revolt_of_fravartish.play: The game's entry follows Darius's Behistun account: defeat at Kunduru, capture at Raga and impalement at Ecbatana. It does not mention Hydarnes' earlier battle at Maru or Hystaspes' fighting in Parthia.
e_revolt_of_fravartish.s0: Darius says that a Mede called Fravartish rose in Media and told the people he was Khshathrita, of the family of Cyaxares. The Median troops at the royal residence went over to him, and he became king in Media. In Greek tradition Cyaxares was the king who had made Media a great power, so the claim appealed to Median memories of rule before Cyrus.
e_revolt_of_fravartish.s1: Darius first sent a Persian and Median force under Hydarnes. Hydarnes fought the rebels at Maru in Media and then waited at Kampanda for the King, which suggests the battle settled little. Darius came from Babylon himself and defeated Fravartish at Kunduru, probably in May 521 BCE. Fravartish fled with a few horsemen to Raga, near modern Tehran, where troops sent after him captured him.
e_revolt_of_fravartish.s2: Darius says he cut off the prisoner's nose, ears and tongue and put out one eye, then kept him bound at the palace gate for all to see. Afterwards he impaled him at Ecbatana, the Median capital, and put his chief followers to death in the fortress there. On the Behistun relief Fravartish stands among the bound rebel kings, named in a short label.
e_revolt_of_fravartish.s3: Parthia and Hyrcania declared for Fravartish. Darius's father Hystaspes fought the rebels there and won a final victory at Patigrabana after reinforcements came from Raga. A Sagartian, Chissantakhma, also claimed descent from Cyaxares; he was captured and impaled at Arbela. The Median cause thus drew several regions into the revolt.
e_revolt_of_fravartish.s4: Herodotus names a Median king Phraortes, the Greek form of Fravartish, as father of Cyaxares. He says only that the Medes later revolted against Darius and were beaten. Some historians link the name Khshathrita with a Median leader named in Assyrian texts of the 670s BCE. Nearly all we know comes from Darius's own inscription, so the rebel's real background and the exact order of the campaigns are still debated.
e_revolt_of_nidintu_bel.lead: In autumn 522 BCE, soon after Darius killed the man he called Gaumata, a Babylonian named Nidintu-Bel claimed to be Nebuchadnezzar, son of the last native king Nabonidus, and Babylon accepted him. Darius marched south in person, won two battles in December and took the city. The revolt showed how fragile Persian rule over the richest province still was, and it was the first of two Babylonian risings he had to put down.
e_revolt_of_nidintu_bel.play: The game reports the revolt in a Chronicle message taken from the Behistun inscription: the false Nebuchadnezzar, the battles on the Tigris and at Zazana, and the taking of Babylon. It dates it simply to 522 BCE.
e_revolt_of_nidintu_bel.s0: Darius says that Nidintu-Bel, son of Ainaira, a Babylonian, rose in Babylon and falsely claimed to be Nebuchadnezzar, son of Nabonidus, and that the Babylonians went over to him. Babylonian business tablets of the time bear this out: contracts were dated to the reign of King Nebuchadnezzar, now called Nebuchadnezzar III, for a few months in late 522 BCE.
e_revolt_of_nidintu_bel.s1: Darius went to Babylon himself. He says Nidintu-Bel's army held the Tigris, which could not be forded, and had boats on the river. Darius put some of his troops on inflated skins, mounted others on camels and horses, crossed, and defeated the Babylonians in a battle he dates to 26 Assiyadiya, about 13 December 522 BCE.
e_revolt_of_nidintu_bel.s2: A second battle followed at Zazana, a town on the Euphrates, on 2 Anamaka, about 18 December. Darius says part of the enemy was carried away by the river. Nidintu-Bel fled with a few horsemen to Babylon, and Darius took the city and put him to death there. On the Behistun relief he stands second in the line of bound rebel kings, with a label naming his lie.
e_revolt_of_nidintu_bel.s3: Darius calls the royal claim a lie, and no other source settles it. Historians read the choice of name as a sign that native Babylonian kingship still commanded loyalty. The length of his rule is argued from the tablets, and it is unclear whether Babylon fell in late December 522 BCE or early 521 BCE. Darius says many lands rose against him while he was at Babylon, so his stay may have been longer than the text makes plain.
e_revolt_of_nidintu_bel.s4: Herodotus tells of a Babylonian revolt against Darius that ended only after a siege of about twenty months. The Persian noble Zopyrus cut off his own nose and ears, posed as a deserter and opened the gates, and Darius then had some three thousand leading men impaled. The tale fits neither of Darius's Babylonian revolts well. Some link it to the risings under Xerxes, but most treat it as a story of loyalty rather than history.
e_revolt_of_vahyazdata.lead: Vahyazdata, a Persian of the town of Tarava, claimed to be Bardiya, son of Cyrus, after Darius had killed the man he called Gaumata. He won over the troops of the palace and sent an army east into Arachosia. Darius's commanders defeated both efforts, and the revolt suggests that resistance to Darius ran deep in the Persian homeland itself.
e_revolt_of_vahyazdata.play: The game's Chronicle tells the revolt in the terms of the Behistun inscription, from Vahyazdata's claim at Tarava to his impalement at Uvadaicaya. Calling him a 'second false Bardiya' repeats Darius's own verdict, which no independent source can test.
e_revolt_of_vahyazdata.s0: Darius says that a man named Vahyazdata lived in Tarava, in the district of Yautiya in Persis. He rose up and declared himself Bardiya, son of Cyrus. The people in the palace went over to him. The text describes them as troops who had earlier come from a place or source it calls Yada, a phrase whose meaning is uncertain. He became king in Persis while Darius and most of the Persian army were in Media.
e_revolt_of_vahyazdata.s1: Darius sent the Persian Artavardiya with Persian and Median troops. They defeated Vahyazdata at Rakha in Persis. He fled with a few horsemen to Paishiyauvada, where Gaumata's rising had begun, raised a fresh army and fought again at Mount Parga in summer 521 BCE. He was beaten and captured, and Darius had him and his foremost followers impaled at Uvadaicaya in Persis.
e_revolt_of_vahyazdata.s2: Vahyazdata also sent an army under a commander to Arachosia, in what is now southern Afghanistan, against Vivana, Darius's satrap there. Vivana defeated it at the fortress of Kapishakanish and again in the district of Gandutava. The rebel commander fled with some horsemen to the fortress of Arshada, where Vivana caught and killed him and his leading followers.
e_revolt_of_vahyazdata.s3: Everything known about Vahyazdata comes from Darius, who called both him and Gaumata impostors. Many historians suspect that the man Darius killed in 522 BCE was the real Bardiya, son of Cyrus, and that the story of a magus was invented. Others accept Darius's version, and the question cannot be settled. If the suspicion is right, Vahyazdata may have drawn on real loyalty to Cyrus's line among Persians.
e_revolt_of_vahyazdata.s4: Herodotus tells of a single impostor, a magus he names Smerdis, unmasked and killed by seven Persian conspirators, Darius among them. He says nothing of Vahyazdata. Of the risings that followed, he describes at length only the revolt of Babylon. Darius's inscription, though one-sided in its own way, records a far longer and wider struggle for the throne.
e_revolts_522_521.lead: After Darius and six Persian nobles killed the man ruling as Bardiya in September 522 BCE, provinces from Babylon to Media, Elam, Persis and Margiana rose under their own kings. Darius and his generals crushed them within about a year. He had the story carved at Behistun as proof that Auramazda had given him the throne, and it is still the main source for these events.
e_revolts_522_521.play: The Bagastana level (522-521 BCE) is built around these risings. The game's 'nine captive kings' follows Darius's boast, but by his own text Martiya was killed by the Elamites and Gaumata was slain outright.
e_revolts_522_521.s0: In the summary of the Behistun text, Darius says that in one and the same year after he became king he fought nineteen battles and overthrew nine kings. He names them: Gaumata in Persia, Acina and Martiya in Elam, Nidintu-Bel and Arakha in Babylon, Fravartish in Media, Ciçantakhma in Sagartia, Frada in Margiana and Vahyazdata in Persia. Each of them, he says, lied to the people.
e_revolts_522_521.s1: Darius marched on Babylon himself, beat Nidintu-Bel on the Tigris and at Zazana in December 522 BCE, and took the city. He sent commanders elsewhere: Hydarnes to Media, Dadarshi and Vaumisa to Armenia, troops to his father Hystaspes in Parthia, the satrap of Bactria against Margiana, and Artavardiya against Vahyazdata. Darius defeated Fravartish at Kunduru in 521 BCE, and Intaphernes took Arakha's Babylon late that year.
e_revolts_522_521.s2: Darius made his cruelty a warning. Fravartish had his nose, ears and tongue cut off and an eye put out, was kept chained at the palace gate where all could see him, and was then impaled at Ecbatana. Ciçantakhma met a similar end at Arbela. The text was meant to travel: fragments of a Babylonian version survive from Babylon, and an Aramaic copy on papyrus was found at Elephantine in Egypt.
e_revolts_522_521.s3: Darius calls every rebel a liar against a rightful king, yet he had just seized the throne by killing the man ruling as Bardiya, whom some historians accept as Cyrus's real son. Scholars also debate how his 'one year' fits dates that run from autumn 522 BCE to late 521 BCE, perhaps a year lengthened by an extra month. The Babylonian version's counts of the dead and captured are the King's own figures and are treated with care.
e_revolts_522_521.s4: Herodotus tells that Babylon held out against Darius for more than a year and a half. Then the Persian noble Zopyrus cut off his own nose and ears, went over to the Babylonians as a pretended deserter and opened the gates. The tale is shaped as a story of loyalty to the King, and historians doubt it. It may also belong to a later Babylonian revolt rather than to 522-521 BCE.
e_sack_of_athens.lead: In late summer 480 BCE, a few weeks after Thermopylae, Xerxes' army entered Attica and found Athens nearly empty. A handful of defenders held the Acropolis until the Persians climbed the cliff, killed them and burned the temples. Herodotus links the burning to revenge for Sardis, but the Athenian fleet survived to fight at Salamis. No Persian text mentions the capture.
e_sack_of_athens.play: The game shows a siege of Athens and the burning of the Acropolis and Athena's olive. In Herodotus only the Acropolis held out, since the lower city stood empty, and the refuges were Troezen, Aegina and Salamis.
e_sack_of_athens.s0: Herodotus says that when the Greek fleet came back from Artemisium, the Athenians asked it to put in at Salamis while they moved their families out of Attica. A proclamation told each Athenian to save his children and household as best he could. Most sent them to Troezen in the Peloponnese, and others sent them to Aegina and Salamis. The men then crewed the fleet, to which Herodotus says Athens gave 180 ships at Salamis.
e_sack_of_athens.s1: Herodotus says the Persians found the city empty except for a few temple treasurers and poor men on the Acropolis. These men had built a barricade of doors and planks, taking it for the oracle's wooden wall. From the Areopagus the Persians shot burning arrows into the barricade. The defenders refused terms offered through the Pisistratids. Soldiers then climbed the steep face by the shrine of Aglaurus, killed the defenders, plundered the temple and burned the Acropolis.
e_sack_of_athens.s2: In 1960 a marble slab from Troezen was published as a decree moved by Themistocles, ordering the evacuation of Attica and the manning of 200 ships. It was carved in the 3rd century, about two hundred years after the events. Some historians think it preserves a genuine decree, perhaps passed before Thermopylae. Others see a later patriotic reconstruction. If genuine, it points to a planned evacuation rather than the hurried one Herodotus describes.
e_sack_of_athens.s3: Excavations on the Acropolis in 1885-1890 found statues of korai, inscribed bases and pottery buried in fills, many of them broken and scorched. Archaeologists long linked all this debris with the Persian sacks of 480 and 479 BCE, though some deposits may have been laid down later. Burned column drums from the unfinished Older Parthenon were built into the north wall of the Acropolis, where they can still be seen.
e_sack_of_athens.s4: Herodotus tells two omens. Before the evacuation, the monthly honey-cake for the sacred snake that guarded the Acropolis lay untouched, and the Athenians took this to mean the goddess had left. Plutarch says Themistocles used the sign to urge departure. After the burning, Athenian exiles sent by Xerxes to sacrifice found that Athena's burned olive had put out a shoot about a cubit long. Both stories read as signs of Athenian survival.
e_scythian_campaign.lead: In about 513 BCE Darius led an army out of Asia, across the Bosporus and the Ister, into the steppe north of the Black Sea. The Scythians refused battle and wore his army down, and he returned without a victory. The campaign still left Persia with a foothold in Europe, in Thrace and along the Hellespont.
e_scythian_campaign.play: The Ister level is built around the campaign: the Scythians burn the grass, fill the wells, send a bird, a mouse, a frog and five arrows, and will not fight. The game credits Darius with Thrace; Herodotus gives much of it to Megabazus.
e_scythian_campaign.s0: Herodotus says Darius crossed the Bosporus on a bridge of boats built by Mandrocles of Samos, while the Ionian fleet sailed up the Black Sea to the mouth of the Ister. He counts 700,000 men and 600 ships, figures modern historians judge far too high. On the march through Thrace the Getae resisted and were subdued. At the Ister the Ionians made a bridge of their ships, and the army crossed into Scythian land.
e_scythian_campaign.s1: Herodotus tells that the Scythians, whose kings included Idanthyrsus, chose not to meet the Persians in open battle. They withdrew ahead of the army, filled in wells and springs, stripped the grazing and harried Persian foragers with their horsemen. When Darius told Idanthyrsus to fight or submit, the king replied that the Scythians had no towns or sown fields to lose and would fight only if their fathers' tombs were touched.
e_scythian_campaign.s2: The Scythians then sent Darius a bird, a mouse, a frog and five arrows. In Herodotus's telling Darius read them as an offer of earth and water, but Gobryas warned that unless the Persians could fly like birds, hide in the ground like mice or leap into lakes like frogs, they would never get home. Herodotus wrote the story down some eighty years later. It has the shape of a riddle tale, and no Persian source mentions it.
e_scythian_campaign.s3: Herodotus says the Ionians were left to guard the bridge for sixty days. Miltiades of Athens, then ruler of the Chersonese, urged them to break it and strand the King, but Histiaeus of Miletus argued that the tyrants owed their power to Persia. The Ionians took apart only the northern end to deceive the Scythians and kept the crossing for the retreat. Many historians doubt Miltiades' part, thinking it grew from his later need to excuse his service to Persia.
e_scythian_campaign.s4: Herodotus frames the campaign as revenge for an old Scythian raid on Media, but historians still argue over its aims and its exact date. His account of a march beyond the Tanais is widely doubted. Darius's inscriptions describe no such war, though the list at Naqsh-e Rostam names Saka beyond the sea, perhaps the Scythians of Europe. Megabazus, left in Europe with troops, went on to subdue much of Thrace and the Hellespont region.
e_second_sack_of_athens.lead: In the summer of 479 BCE Mardonius, left in Greece by Xerxes, marched into Attica and took an empty Athens for the second time. When he learned that a Spartan army was on the march, he burned what was still standing and withdrew to Boeotia, where the battle of Plataea was fought soon after.
e_second_sack_of_athens.play: The Chronicle shows this as an event of 479 BCE: Mardonius retakes Athens ten months after Xerxes, burns it when the Spartans march and falls back to Boeotia for his horse. This matches Herodotus 9.3 and 9.13.
e_second_sack_of_athens.s0: Herodotus says Mardonius wintered in Thessaly and marched south in spring. The Thebans urged him to stay in Boeotia and win the Greeks over with bribes. He wanted Athens again, partly so that he could send news of its capture to Xerxes at Sardis by beacon fires across the islands. He found the city empty, ten months after the King had taken it, because the Athenians had again moved to Salamis and their ships.
e_second_sack_of_athens.s1: Herodotus says Mardonius sent a Hellespontine Greek, Murychides, to Salamis to repeat the terms that Alexander of Macedon had already carried to Athens. A councillor named Lycidas proposed putting the offer to the people, and the Athenians stoned him to death. Athenian women then stoned his wife and children. The Athenians sent envoys to Sparta to complain that its army had not come.
e_second_sack_of_athens.s2: Herodotus says the Spartans, after delay over the Hyacinthia festival, sent out Pausanias with a large force, and the Argives warned Mardonius. He burned Athens and pulled down what remained of walls, houses and temples, judging Attica bad ground for cavalry. His horsemen overran the Megarid, and he then withdrew by way of Decelea to a fortified camp on the Asopus.
e_second_sack_of_athens.s3: Thucydides says that when the Athenians returned only short stretches of the city wall stood and most houses were down, except a few where Persian nobles had lodged. Excavators on the Acropolis have found deep fills of broken statues and burnt debris from the Persian destruction. Archaeologists still debate how much of this damage belongs to 480 BCE and how much to Mardonius in 479 BCE.
e_second_sack_of_athens.s4: Later writers say the Greeks swore before Plataea to leave the burnt temples in ruins as a memorial of Persian impiety. A fourth-century inscribed version of the oath lacks this clause. Some historians accept a version of the oath, while others think it was composed or reshaped in the fourth century. The ruined temples of the Acropolis did stand unrebuilt for about thirty years.
e_siege_of_barca.lead: In the late sixth century the Persian satrap of Egypt sent an army west against Barca, a Greek city in Libya, which held out for nine months. Herodotus's account of the siege is one of the earliest Greek descriptions of tunnelling under city walls and of finding the tunnels by sound. The city fell to a trick, and many of its people were deported across the empire to Bactria.
e_siege_of_barca.play: The game shows Persians tunnelling under Barca's walls and a smith finding the tunnels with a ringing bronze shield, as Herodotus tells it, and uses the scene to introduce siege mining. The date of about 513 BCE is approximate.
e_siege_of_barca.s0: Herodotus says that Arcesilaus III, king of Cyrene, was murdered at Barca, and that his mother Pheretime fled to Egypt to ask the satrap Aryandes for help. Aryandes sent an army under Amasis, a Maraphian, and a fleet under Badres of the Pasargadae. Herodotus thought vengeance was only a pretext, and that the real aim was to bring the Libyans under Persian rule.
e_siege_of_barca.s1: The Persians demanded the killers of Arcesilaus, and the Barcaeans replied that the whole city shared the blame. Herodotus says the siege lasted nine months, with assaults and tunnels dug towards the walls. A bronze-smith carried a bronze shield around inside the walls and laid it on the ground, and where digging went on beneath, the shield rang. The Barcaeans dug countermines there, killed the diggers and beat off the assaults.
e_siege_of_barca.s2: Unable to take the city by force, Amasis had a trench dug by night, covered with planks and a layer of earth. Over this spot he swore to keep a treaty for as long as the ground stayed as it was. The Barcaeans agreed to pay tribute and opened their gates. Herodotus says the Persians then broke the planks, treated the oath as void and took the city, and Pheretime had those most to blame impaled around the walls.
e_siege_of_barca.s3: Herodotus says the army marched back past Cyrene, debated seizing it, and lost stragglers to Libyan raiders on the road to Egypt. The enslaved Barcaeans were sent to Darius, who gave them a village in Bactria. They named it Barca, and Herodotus says it was still inhabited in his own time. Moving whole communities in this way was a known Persian practice; the captured Eretrians were later settled near Susa.
e_siege_of_barca.s4: Herodotus places the expedition at the same time as Darius's Scythian campaign, which suggests about 513 BCE, but he names no year and some historians date it a few years earlier or later. Herodotus says the Libyans, Cyrene and Barca had already submitted to Cambyses in 525 BCE, so historians debate whether this was conquest or the punishment of an unruly subject city. Putaya, the Persian name for Libya, appears among the King's lands in Darius's tomb inscription.
e_siege_of_memphis.lead: After their defeat at Pelusium, the Egyptian army and King Psamtik III fell back on Memphis, the old royal city at the head of the Nile delta. Cambyses besieged and took it, probably in 525 BCE, and Psamtik became his prisoner. The fall of Memphis ended the Twenty-sixth Dynasty and made Egypt a Persian province for more than a century.
e_siege_of_memphis.play: The game follows Herodotus 3.13 closely: the herald's ship, the siege, Psamtik's capture and the Libyan gifts. The killing of the herald's crew and the gifts are known only from Greek writers, not from Egyptian or Persian records.
e_siege_of_memphis.s0: Herodotus says the Egyptians fled from Pelusium to Memphis in disorder. Cambyses sent a ship from Mytilene on Lesbos up the Nile, carrying a Persian herald to call on them to surrender. When the ship reached the city, the Egyptians poured out, wrecked it and tore the crew apart, then carried the remains back inside the walls.
e_siege_of_memphis.s1: Herodotus says the Persians then laid siege to Memphis, and after some time the Egyptians surrendered. The Libyans living next to Egypt took fright, submitted without a fight, agreed to pay tribute and sent gifts, and the Greek cities of Cyrene and Barca did the same. He adds that Cambyses welcomed the Libyan gifts but thought the Cyrenaean silver too little and scattered it among his soldiers with his own hand.
e_siege_of_memphis.s2: Herodotus tells a moral tale set ten days after the capture. Cambyses made Psamtik watch his daughter fetch water dressed as a slave and his son led out to execution with two thousand young Egyptians, ten for each man killed on the Mytilenean ship. Psamtik stayed silent, but wept on seeing an old companion reduced to begging. Herodotus also says Psamtik later plotted revolt and died after drinking bull's blood.
e_siege_of_memphis.s3: No Egyptian text from the time describes the siege itself. The inscribed statue of Udjahorresnet, a naval commander under Amasis and Psamtik III, says that Cambyses came to Egypt with foreigners of every land and became ruler of the whole country. Udjahorresnet then became his chief physician and composed his Egyptian royal titles. The statue also speaks of great turmoil in Egypt; historians debate whether this means the conquest or later disorders.
e_siege_of_memphis.s4: The conquest is usually dated to 525 BCE, but some historians argue for 526 BCE, because the Egyptian evidence for the end of Psamtik's reign and the start of Cambyses' can be read either way. Ctesias tells a different story: he calls the Egyptian king Amyrtaeus, says the victory came through the treachery of a court eunuch, and has the captive king sent to Susa with six thousand Egyptians. Historians generally prefer Herodotus on the outline, but not on every detail.
e_siege_of_naxos.lead: About 500 BCE Aristagoras, deputy ruler of Miletus, persuaded the satrap Artaphernes to send a royal fleet to restore exiled Naxian aristocrats. The siege, usually dated to 499 BCE, lasted four months and failed. Herodotus makes it the immediate cause of the Ionian Revolt: Aristagoras, unable to keep his promises, turned against the King.
e_siege_of_naxos.play: The Chronicle reports the failed four-month siege and Aristagoras's fear and debt, following Herodotus 5.30-35. It gives his personal fear as the cause of the revolt, which is Herodotus's view; historians also weigh wider Ionian grievances.
e_siege_of_naxos.s0: Herodotus says that wealthy Naxians, driven out by the common people, came to Miletus for help. Aristagoras, governing the city for Histiaeus, who was held at the King's court, saw a chance for power. He told Artaphernes at Sardis that Naxos was rich, and that taking it would open Paros, Andros, the other Cyclades and even Euboea to the King. He offered to meet the cost of the army himself.
e_siege_of_naxos.s1: Artaphernes promised 200 ships once Darius approved, and gave the command to Megabates, an Achaemenid kinsman of both men. The fleet sailed as if bound for the Hellespont and waited at Caucasa on Chios for a north wind. There Megabates punished Scylax, captain of a ship from Myndus, by binding him through an oar-hole. Aristagoras freed him, and the two commanders quarrelled openly.
e_siege_of_naxos.s2: Warned in time, the Naxians brought their goods inside the walls and laid in food and water. Herodotus says the besiegers sat outside for four months until their money ran out, Aristagoras having spent heavily as well. They built forts on the island for the exiles and sailed back to Asia with nothing gained. Naxos fell to the Persians only in 490 BCE, when Datis burned the town.
e_siege_of_naxos.s3: Herodotus says Megabates himself warned the Naxians out of anger at Aristagoras. Some historians doubt this and suspect a story told afterwards to excuse the failure. No Persian record of the campaign survives. Herodotus also explains the revolt through Aristagoras's fear for his position; modern scholars add wider causes, such as resentment of Persian-backed tyrants and the burden of royal rule on the Ionian cities.
e_siege_of_naxos.s4: Herodotus adds that at this moment a slave arrived from Histiaeus at Susa. Histiaeus had shaved his head, tattooed on it an order to revolt, and sent him once the hair grew back. The tale, with its neat timing and hidden message, reads more like a story told in Ionia afterwards than a firm record of how the revolt began.
e_siege_of_sestos.lead: After the Greek victory at Mycale in 479 BCE, an Athenian force besieged Sestos, the strongest Persian-held town on the European shore of the Hellespont. Its fall through famine broke the King's hold on the crossing Xerxes had used in 480 BCE. It is the last campaign Herodotus narrates in his Histories.
e_siege_of_sestos.play: The game follows Herodotus: Xanthippus's Athenians starve out Sestos, the Persians flee by night, Artayctes dies and the cables go home. It leaves out the Ionian and Hellespontine allies that Thucydides adds.
e_siege_of_sestos.s0: Herodotus says the Greek fleet sailed from Mycale to Abydos to break Xerxes' bridges and found them already broken. Leotychides and the Peloponnesians went home. The Athenians under Xanthippus stayed, crossed to the Chersonese and besieged Sestos, the strongest place in the region. Persians from the nearby towns had gathered there, among them Oeobazus, who had brought the bridges' cables from Cardia.
e_siege_of_sestos.s1: Herodotus says the siege dragged into autumn. The Athenian soldiers asked to go home, but their generals refused until the city fell or Athens recalled them. Inside, the defenders were reduced to boiling and eating the leather straps of their beds, until by night the Persians climbed down the least guarded part of the wall and the townspeople opened the gates. Oeobazus fled into Thrace, where Apsinthian Thracians sacrificed him to their god Pleistorus.
e_siege_of_sestos.s2: Herodotus says Artayctes, Xerxes' governor of Sestos, had robbed the shrine of the hero Protesilaus at Elaeus after tricking the King into granting him the house of a Greek invader. Caught near Aegospotami, he offered a ransom, but the people of Elaeus wanted revenge. Xanthippus had him nailed to planks on the headland where the bridges had landed, and his son stoned before him. The Athenians took the bridges' cables home to dedicate in temples.
e_siege_of_sestos.s3: Herodotus tells that while Artayctes was held prisoner, salted fish leapt and writhed in a guard's pan as if just caught. Artayctes is said to have taken it as a sign that Protesilaus, though dead and dried like the fish, still had the power to punish the wrong done to him. The story turns his death into the revenge of a hero rather than a plain act of war.
e_siege_of_sestos.s4: Thucydides adds that the Athenians were joined by allies from Ionia and the Hellespont who had already revolted from the King. He says they wintered before Sestos and took it once the Persians abandoned it, so the fall may belong to the winter of 479-478 BCE, while Herodotus speaks only of autumn. Historians also note that Herodotus shaped his ending around Persian impiety punished, and no Persian source gives Artayctes' side.
e_storm_off_magnesia.lead: Probably in late summer 480 BCE, as Xerxes' fleet moved south towards Artemisium, an easterly gale caught it at anchor on the exposed coast of Magnesia and blew for three days. Herodotus says at least four hundred warships were lost, along with crews, supply vessels and treasure. The storm reduced the King's fleet just before the fighting at Artemisium and Thermopylae began.
e_storm_off_magnesia.play: The game shows the storm as a 480 BCE event and repeats Herodotus's figure of at least four hundred ships. That number is his alone; historians doubt it, and no Persian record of the losses survives.
e_storm_off_magnesia.s0: Herodotus says the fleet reached the coast of Magnesia between Casthanaea and Cape Sepias. The beach was short, so only the first line of ships could be drawn up on shore, and the rest rode at anchor offshore, by his account eight rows deep. His description implies that the fleet had no sheltered harbour on that stretch of coast.
e_storm_off_magnesia.s1: Herodotus says that at dawn, after calm weather, the sea began to boil and a strong east wind, which the locals called the Hellespontias, struck the anchored ships. Crews who saw it coming hauled their ships ashore, but many were driven onto the rocks called the Ovens of Pelion and the beaches. A local landowner, Ameinocles, later grew rich from gold and silver cups that washed up on his land.
e_storm_off_magnesia.s2: Herodotus reports that the commanders built a palisade from the wreckage and that the magi made offerings and chanted spells to the wind. They also sacrificed to Thetis and the sea nymphs, because the coast was said to be sacred to Thetis. On the fourth day the storm stopped. Herodotus adds, with some doubt, that it may simply have died down of its own accord.
e_storm_off_magnesia.s3: The Athenians said that an oracle had told them to call on their son-in-law for help. They took this to mean Boreas the north wind, who in myth had married the Athenian princess Oreithyia. They prayed to him, afterwards credited him with the storm and built him a shrine beside the Ilissus. Herodotus does not decide whether Boreas was the cause, and the tale reflects Athenian pride more than the weather of 480 BCE.
e_storm_off_magnesia.s4: Herodotus gives the King's fleet 1,207 triremes and says no fewer than four hundred were wrecked here, with a further two hundred lost in a second storm off Euboea. Many historians think the starting figure was inflated and that the storm losses help bring Herodotus's total down to a size that fits the later fighting. Others accept heavy losses but not his exact numbers.
e_susa_charter.lead: Darius's Susa charter (DSf) is a building inscription in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian that records how his palace at Susa was made. It names the lands that sent timber, gold, stone and ivory and the peoples who worked them. It is the fullest picture Darius left of the whole empire labouring on one royal project.
e_susa_charter.play: The game treats the charter as a decree of about 517 BCE and builds the Susa level around the palace. In fact DSf is a building record, not an order, and its date is not known; 517 BCE is an approximation.
e_susa_charter.s0: French excavators at Susa began recovering copies and fragments of the text in the late 1920s, and later digs added more. The copies were written on clay tablets, marble slabs and glazed tiles, in the three royal languages: Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. A closely related version, known as DSz, repeats much of the same content.
e_susa_charter.s1: Darius says the earth was dug out until rock was reached. The pit was then filled with gravel, in some places 40 cubits deep and in others 20, and the palace was raised on it. Babylonians moulded and baked the bricks. The text also states that his father Hystaspes and grandfather Arsames were both living when Auramazda made him king.
e_susa_charter.s2: Cedar came from the mountain called Lebanon: the Assyrians carried it to Babylon, and Carians and Ionians brought it on to Susa. Yaka wood came from Gandara and Carmania, gold from Sardis and Bactria, and lapis lazuli and carnelian from Sogdiana. Turquoise came from Chorasmia, silver and ebony from Egypt, and ivory from Kush, India and Arachosia. The stone columns were cut at a village called Abiradu in Elam.
e_susa_charter.s3: The charter says the stonecutters were Ionians and Sardians. The goldsmiths were Medes and Egyptians, the woodworkers Sardians and Egyptians, and the men who decorated the walls Medes and Egyptians. The Persepolis Fortification tablets record rations for workers from many lands, including Egyptians, Ionians and Sardians, which shows that mixed work groups served on the King's projects in Persis too.
e_susa_charter.s4: The charter carries no date: some historians tie the building to the years just after the Elamite revolts of 522-519 BCE, while others place it later in the reign. Scholars also debate how literal the list is, since it may reflect real supply routes but is arranged, like the lists of lands at Behistun and Naqsh-e Rostam, to show every corner of the empire serving the King. The lapis, for instance, was probably mined in Badakhshan and may have reached Susa by way of Sogdiana.
e_tribute_assessment.lead: Early in his reign, Darius I set fixed yearly payments for the subject peoples, grouped into districts that Herodotus calls satrapies. Herodotus says this replaced the gifts given under Cyrus and Cambyses, and his list of districts and sums is the fullest ancient description of Persian tribute. The revenue helped pay for the court, the armies and the King's building works.
e_tribute_assessment.play: The game presents a decree of about 518 BCE with fixed silver dues, Ionia's 400 talents halting at the revolt. Herodotus gives no date, some peoples paid in gold or in kind, and the halt is inferred, not recorded.
e_tribute_assessment.s0: Herodotus says Darius created twenty provinces, each under a governor, and fixed what each owed, mostly in silver reckoned in Babylonian talents. The Indians paid 360 talents of gold dust, Babylonia 1,000 talents of silver and 500 boys to be made eunuchs, and Cilicia 500 talents with 360 white horses. He gives the grand total as 14,560 Euboic talents. Persis itself paid no tribute, and some peoples sent gifts instead.
e_tribute_assessment.s1: Herodotus puts the Ionians, Aeolians, Carians, Lycians and their neighbours in the first province, owing 400 talents of silver a year. After the Ionian Revolt was crushed, he says, Artaphernes measured the cities' lands in parasangs and assessed tribute on that basis. The new figures stayed close to the old ones. Herodotus does not say outright that payments stopped during the revolt, but rebel cities are unlikely to have paid.
e_tribute_assessment.s2: In the Behistun inscription, Darius lists the lands that obeyed him and says they brought him tribute. His later inscriptions and the delegations carved on the Apadana at Persepolis show subject peoples bringing goods to the King, and the Persepolis tablets record goods in royal stores and silver weighed in karsha and shekels. None of these sources gives Herodotus's twenty districts or his sums.
e_tribute_assessment.s3: Historians disagree whether Herodotus's list rests on a genuine Persian register or is a Greek reconstruction that fits neither the Persian lists of lands nor the satrapies as they worked. Babylonian documents show taxes collected under Cyrus and Cambyses, which tells against his earlier age of gifts. About 518 BCE is only a modern date, and some scholars see the system as built up gradually rather than set by one decree.
e_tribute_assessment.s4: Herodotus reports a Persian saying that Cyrus was a father, Cambyses a master and Darius a shopkeeper. On this telling, Cyrus was kind, Cambyses harsh, and Darius made a profit out of everything. The saying is shaped as a moral comment on three kings and cannot be traced to any Persian source.
e_voyage_of_scylax.lead: Herodotus says Darius sent Scylax of Caryanda, a Carian, with other men he trusted to find where the Indus met the sea. They sailed down the river and then west by sea, probably round Arabia, and reached the Egyptian shore of the Red Sea in the thirtieth month. The voyage linked the far east of the empire to its western seas, and Herodotus places Darius's conquest of the Indians after it.
e_voyage_of_scylax.play: The game shows the voyage as a Chronicle event of about 517 BCE, following Herodotus 4.44. The date is a modern estimate, since Herodotus gives none, and the order of voyage first and conquest second is his version, not certain fact.
e_voyage_of_scylax.s0: Herodotus says Darius wanted to know where the Indus, a river with crocodiles, flowed into the sea. He sent ships with Scylax of Caryanda and others he trusted. They set out from the city of Caspatyrus in the Pactyican land and sailed downstream to the sea. They then turned west across the sea, and in the thirtieth month they reached the place from which an Egyptian king had once sent Phoenicians to sail round Libya.
e_voyage_of_scylax.s1: Herodotus adds that after the voyage Darius subdued the Indians and made use of the southern sea. In his list of tribute districts he calls the Indians the most populous people known to him. He says they paid the largest tribute of all, 360 talents of gold dust. Historians accept that the Indus lands were rich, but treat his exact figures with caution.
e_voyage_of_scylax.s2: The Behistun inscription lists Gandara among Darius's lands but not India. Hindush, the lower Indus country, appears in later royal lists, including the inscription on Darius's tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam. The Persepolis Fortification tablets, written some years after the voyage, record travel rations for parties moving between Persis and Hindush. They show that journeys along this route were organised by the state.
e_voyage_of_scylax.s3: Herodotus says the river ran east, which fits the Kabul river flowing into the Indus better than the Indus itself, so his geography may blur the two. Some historians think the Indus lands were taken before the voyage, which would make it a survey of conquered country rather than a prelude to conquest. Others link it to Darius's plans for a sea route to Egypt through his Nile canal.
e_voyage_of_scylax.s4: Scylax apparently wrote an account of his travels, now lost. Aristotle cites him soberly on Indian kings. Much later, the Byzantine scholar Tzetzes credited him with tales of strange peoples, such as men who shaded themselves with one huge foot or slept wrapped in their ears. These wonder stories cannot be checked. A surviving coastal guide bearing his name was in fact composed much later.
e_xerxes_invasion.lead: In 480 BCE Xerxes led an army and fleet across the Hellespont into Europe to bring the Greek mainland under Persian rule. Persian forces took Athens twice, but defeats at Salamis in 480 BCE and at Plataea and Mycale in 479 BCE ended the attempt. The war shaped Greek memory for centuries, while Persian royal inscriptions say nothing of it.
e_xerxes_invasion.play: The campaign spans the Athos, Thermopylae and Plataea levels and the Mycale epilogue. The Chronicle recalls Xerxes at Abydos letting Black Sea grain ships sail on to Greece, as Herodotus tells it (7.147).
e_xerxes_invasion.s0: Herodotus says Darius was already preparing a new war after Marathon when Egypt revolted and he died. Xerxes, he says, took the war up once Egypt was subdued. Herodotus presents the decision as a council in which Mardonius urged war and Artabanus warned against it, with dreams driving Xerxes on. In his telling the King spoke of avenging the burning of Sardis and the defeat at Marathon, and of extending Persian rule over Europe.
e_xerxes_invasion.s1: Herodotus says the canal through the neck of the Athos peninsula took about three years to dig. It let the fleet avoid the cape where Mardonius's ships had been wrecked in 492 BCE. Food was stored at depots along the Thracian and Macedonian coast, and two bridges of boats were laid across the Hellespont. When a storm broke the first bridges, he says, Xerxes had the water lashed and the overseers of the work beheaded.
e_xerxes_invasion.s2: Herodotus gives 1,700,000 infantry and, with the fleet and camp followers, a total of over five million. He counts 1,207 warships. Aeschylus's thousand ships plus 207 fast ones is usually read as the same total. No modern historian accepts the land figures, which roads, water and supplies could not have sustained. Modern estimates of the army mostly run from under 100,000 to about 300,000, and many think the fleet was smaller too.
e_xerxes_invasion.s3: In August or September 480 BCE the Persians forced the pass at Thermopylae, while the fleets fought indecisively off Artemisium. The army then marched into Attica and burnt the Acropolis of Athens. Probably in late September the Greek fleet defeated the Persian ships in the straits of Salamis. Herodotus says Xerxes then returned to Asia, leaving Mardonius with a picked army to finish the war.
e_xerxes_invasion.s4: In 479 BCE Mardonius reoccupied Athens, then fell in battle near Plataea. On the same day, by Herodotus's account, the Greeks burnt the Persian ships at Mycale. No Persian text records the war. Historians disagree on whether the court saw it as a serious defeat or as a setback on a distant frontier, since the empire's heartland was untouched.
e_xerxes_retreat.lead: After his fleet was defeated at Salamis in September 480 BCE, Xerxes led part of his army back to the Hellespont, crossed to Asia and stayed at Sardis into 479 BCE. He left Mardonius in Greece with a chosen force to finish the war. Greek writers told the journey as a disgraced flight, and no Persian text describes it.
e_xerxes_retreat.play: The Chronicle notes that the King went home in 480 BCE and that Mardonius stayed to winter in Thessaly with picked troops. Herodotus says the army wintered in Thessaly and Macedonia.
e_xerxes_retreat.s0: Herodotus says that Mardonius, fearing he would be blamed for the war, urged Xerxes to go home and leave him 300,000 picked men to conquer Greece. The King asked Artemisia of Halicarnassus for her view, and she told him to accept. If Mardonius won, the King would take the credit; if he failed, little would be lost while Xerxes and his house were safe. Herodotus adds that Xerxes was glad of advice that matched his own fear.
e_xerxes_retreat.s1: Herodotus says the Greek fleet chased the Persians as far as Andros. There Themistocles proposed sailing to the Hellespont to break the bridges, but Eurybiades of Sparta refused, saying a trapped King was more dangerous than a fleeing one. Themistocles then sent Xerxes a secret message taking credit for holding the Greeks back. Plutarch names Aristides as the objector and makes the message a threat meant to hurry Xerxes away; historians doubt it changed his plans.
e_xerxes_retreat.s2: Herodotus says Mardonius chose his troops in Thessaly, among them the Immortals, Persian cavalry, Medes, Saka, Bactrians and Indians, and that Artabazus escorted the King. On the 45-day march to the Hellespont, hunger and dysentery struck, and men ate grass and bark. Storms had already broken the bridges, so the army crossed to Abydos by ship. Aeschylus's Persians, staged in 472 BCE, adds a disaster on the frozen Strymon.
e_xerxes_retreat.s3: Herodotus also heard a story that Xerxes left the army at Eion on the Strymon and sailed home on a Phoenician ship. In a storm the helmsman said the ship must be lightened, so the Persian nobles on deck bowed to the King and leapt into the sea. Herodotus rejects the tale, arguing that Xerxes would have sent the Persians below and thrown Phoenician rowers overboard instead. He adds that the people of Abdera remembered the King passing through by land.
e_xerxes_retreat.s4: Greek sources present the return as panic. Many modern historians, Briant among them, see a reasoned choice: after Salamis the fleet could no longer supply a very large army, and the King's place was at the centre of his empire. A smaller force under Mardonius stayed to hold what had been won, while Herodotus places Xerxes at Sardis until after Mycale in 479 BCE. Most historians think Herodotus's figure of 300,000 for Mardonius's army is far too high.
f_death.lead: Herodotus says the magi leave their dead to birds and dogs before burial, and other Persians coat the body in wax and bury it. Kings had tombs. The towers of silence are much later.
f_death.play: The Burial Ground takes the city's dead, and unburied dead sicken those near them.
f_death.s0: He says it was told to him as a secret and that he isn't sure, except of the magi, who do it openly. Bodies are torn by a bird or dog before the wax and the earth.
f_death.s1: Cyrus lay on a golden couch inside a stone chamber at Pasargadae. Darius and his heirs cut their tombs into the cliff at Naqsh-e Rostam. Neither is exposure, and both were sealed against the earth.
f_death.s2: The towers known from later Zoroastrian practice have no secure Achaemenid example. Rock-cut niches and ossuaries of doubtful date are argued over.
f_egypt.lead: Egyptian documents show Persian kings acting as Pharaoh, paying for temples and burying a sacred bull. Greek stories show Cambyses stabbing it. Both were written by people with reasons.
f_egypt.play: Memphis's main temple is Ptah's. The Persian garrison has its own altar. Its feasts are Sokar's and the new Apis's, and Mourn the Apis is its rite.
f_egypt.s0: Udjahorresnet's statue says Cambyses cleared foreigners camped in Neith's temple, gave back its revenues and festivals, and worshipped there himself. He wrote this to show his own worth to his town, and he is the only witness.
f_egypt.s1: An epitaph from the Serapeum shows Cambyses kneeling before the Apis buried in his sixth year, 524 BCE, with a sarcophagus he gave. Herodotus says he stabbed the Apis in the thigh and went mad. Polyaenus, much later, has Darius offer 100 talents of gold for a new Apis.
f_egypt.s2: In the Kharga oasis, a temple of Amun carries Darius's cartouches and shows him as Pharaoh with Egypt's gods, among the best preserved work of the period. Its dates and how much is Darius's own are argued, but it shows a Persian king paying for an Egyptian god far from any audience.
f_egypt.s3: Egypt's great feast of Opet belonged to Thebes, where Amun went by boat to Luxor in the second month of the flood. The game has no Thebes, so Memphis keeps its own: Sokar going round the walls, on a date the Medinet Habu calendar gives.
f_elam_gods.lead: Elam was old when Persia was young. Its gods went on being fed in Fars and at Susa under Persian kings, on the same receipts as Ahuramazda.
f_elam_gods.play: Elamite quarters at Parsa and Susa want their own shrine, and the sip feast.
f_elam_gods.s0: Inshushinak was the god of Susa for more than a thousand years before Darius built there. Napirisha and Humban were great gods of the Elamite highlands, and Fars itself had been Elamite land before the Persians came.
f_elam_gods.s1: Humban is the god most often supplied in the Fortification tablets, in texts where Ahuramazda appears only rarely. Henkelman traces him as a god of kingship taken over into the Persian court's own practice.
f_elam_gods.s2: Henkelman reconstructs the sip as an old Elamite feast with a procession and a banquet, kept under the Persians, sometimes with Parnakka, head of the Persepolis administration, himself at its head. The tablets give no calendar, so the game's date is its own.
f_fire.lead: The King stands before a burning altar over his tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam. Two stone plinths stand at Pasargadae. Whether the Achaemenids had fire temples as later Iran did is far less sure, so the game does not build one.
f_fire.play: The Altar of the Magi and the Fire Altar are open to the sky. Kindling the fire is a rite you can stage at them. Its form is the game's.
f_fire.s0: Darius's tomb relief shows him on a stepped base before an altar with a flame. Two limestone plinths stand in the sacred precinct at Pasargadae, one with a stair, and their use is inferred. Mark Garrison's study of the seals shows how varied such images were, and asks how sure even the tomb's fire altar is.
f_fire.s1: Herodotus says the Persians build no statues, temples or altars, and think those who do are fools. They climb the mountains to sacrifice. He's too neat: the tablets name altars and offerings, and Darius says he rebuilt sanctuaries. But nothing in his Persia needs a roof over the fire.
f_fire.s2: Later Zoroastrians keep fire in temples, and classical writers describe them, some in Parthian times. Stone buildings such as the Ka'ba-ye Zardosht and the older Nush-i Jan have been called fire temples and denied the name. Encyclopaedia Iranica warns that the words fire altar and fire temple are used loosely. Mary Boyce dated temple fires to the later Achaemenids.
