f_fire.s3: Berossus, quoted by Clement of Alexandria, says Artaxerxes II first set up statues of Anahita at Babylon, Susa and Ecbatana. That's after 405 BCE. It is why Anahita has no shrine in this game, whose last level is 479 BCE.
f_greek_cults.lead: The King's dealings with Greek gods were all over the map: Datis burned incense to Apollo on Delos and spared the island; Darius's generals burned Didyma; Xerxes burned the Acropolis and sent exiles up the next day to sacrifice.
f_greek_cults.play: Ionians and Greeks in the King's service want their own shrine and feast. The Temple of Cybebe at Sardis is the main temple there.
f_greek_cults.s0: The Ionians burned the temple of the local goddess Cybebe with the lower town in 498 BCE. Herodotus says the Persians later gave it as their reason for burning Greek temples. No Lydian calendar survives, so her feast here and its date are the game's own.
f_greek_cults.s1: Datis told the people of Delos to come home, unharmed, and burned 300 talents of frankincense on Apollo's altar. Four years before, after Lade, the temple of Apollo at Didyma was plundered and burned. The same god, treated differently by the same empire, according to who had rebelled.
f_greek_cults.s2: A Greek inscription from Magnesia has Darius scold a governor for taxing Apollo's sacred gardeners. It is often quoted as proof of Persian respect for Greek cults. Briant and others now think it probably a forgery of the Roman period, written by a temple to prove its privileges, so we don't use it.
f_greek_cults.s3: When Artachaees, the giant Persian who oversaw the Athos canal, died at Acanthus, Xerxes gave him a great funeral, and the Acanthians, told by an oracle, sacrificed to him as a hero and called on him by name. Persian and Greek practice could meet in strange ways.
f_jerusalem.lead: The Book of Ezra has Cyrus send the exiles home to rebuild, and Darius find the order in the archive at Ecbatana and confirm it. The temple was finished in Darius's sixth year, 515 BCE. No Persian document mentions it.
f_jerusalem.play: It stands in no level, but it happened while your Susa was rising, and it's the best-known case of the policy behind your shrines.
f_jerusalem.s0: Ezra 1 and 6 give two versions of Cyrus's decree. Most historians accept that the temple was rebuilt under Persian sanction, but read the wording as shaped by those who kept it. It fits the Cylinder's return of gods, and it isn't unique to Judah.
f_jerusalem.s1: Ezra says work stopped, was challenged by the local governor, and went on after Darius's archive search at Ecbatana turned up the order. It was finished on the third of Adar in his sixth year.
f_jerusalem.s2: In 407 BCE the Jewish garrison at Elephantine in Egypt wrote to the governor of Judah after their temple was destroyed. When Cambyses came, they said, he knocked down the temples of Egypt's gods and spared theirs. It is a claim from people with a stake, and it conflicts with the Egyptian record.
f_kings_gods.lead: Darius says he is king by the favour of Ahuramazda, and the inscriptions never say otherwise. They also pray to "the other gods who are", a phrase that leaves a door open that the tablets walk straight through.
f_kings_gods.play: The Persian faith in every level is this: the Sanctuary or Altar of the Magi, the lan and the Sacrifice for the King, and their feasts.
f_kings_gods.s0: The Behistun inscription says it over and over: Darius holds the throne because Ahuramazda gave it to him. His tomb inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam opens with a great god who made this earth, that sky, man, and happiness for man, and who made Darius king.
f_kings_gods.s1: A prayer at Persepolis asks Ahuramazda, with the gods of the royal house, to protect the land from a hostile army, from famine and from the Lie. Nothing in the royal texts of Darius or Xerxes names those other gods. Mithra and Anahita are first named beside him under Artaxerxes II, more than a century after Cyrus.
f_kings_gods.s2: Xerxes says that where the daivas were worshipped he destroyed the place, and commanded that they not be worshipped. He names no place and no people. Scholars have tied it to Babylon, to Egypt, to Greece or to nothing in particular, a king's statement of what kings do. It is the nearest thing to religious war in the royal texts, and we cannot say what it describes.
f_kings_gods.s3: In a fifth column added at Behistun, Darius calls the Elamites faithless and says Ahuramazda was not worshipped by them. Yet his own administration was paying for Elamite gods at the same time, with the same grain. Whatever this is, it isn't a policy of conversion.
f_lan.lead: The commonest offering in the Persepolis tablets is the lan: barley or flour, fruit and wine issued month after month, a clerk's receipt for each. It is the closest thing we have to watching Achaemenid religion happen.
f_lan.play: The lan is the rite you can stage most often. It costs barley, and more if you have wine and fruit.
f_lan.s0: Persepolis Fortification tablets, about 509 to 493 BCE, issue food for religious use. Encyclopaedia Iranica gives the lan as about 30 litres of barley or flour, some fruit and 10 litres of wine each month. The tablet does not describe the ceremony. It records the goods and who took them.
f_lan.s1: One tablet splits 80 units of grain evenly between Ahuramazda and Mishdushi. Others supply Humban, Napirisha, the Babylonian Adad, the Iranian Narishanka, mountains and rivers. Iranica notes that the clerks treat them alike and that Elamite gods appear more often than Iranian ones.
f_lan.s2: Older books describe a Persian religion and separate foreign cults. Wouter Henkelman argued from the tablets that the Persians of Fars and the Elamites had grown together over generations, and that the lan was a shared practice with Elamite roots. How far that goes, and how Zoroastrian the kings were, is still argued.
f_later_feasts.lead: Midwinter bonfires and a midsummer water feast are real parts of the Iranian year, but no one can place them this early. They're in the game because they're beautiful and because the Iranian year deserves to be shown, labelled as what they are.
f_later_feasts.play: The midwinter fires and the water feast cost little, give little, and tell you plainly they come from later tradition.
f_later_feasts.s0: Biruni and Gardizi, about 1000 CE, describe bonfires fifty days before Nowruz. Ferdowsi has Hushang discover fire on that night. Web pages that date it to the Achaemenids give no ancient source, and we found none.
f_later_feasts.s1: Tishtrya the rain star is old: he has an Avestan hymn, and Persians of this age have names like Tiribazus. His midsummer feast with water thrown at friends is known from much later. The story of Arash shooting his arrow to fix Iran's border attaches to it, and yes, that's your advisor's name.
f_later_feasts.s2: Our rule is to mark what's attested from what's later, and the player can read which is which in the tooltip. A game that left these out would teach that they don't matter. A game that called them Achaemenid would teach something false.
f_magi.lead: No Persian sacrifice was lawful without a magus, Herodotus says. The Persepolis tablets show them on the King's payroll. Darius's rival for the throne was one, and the Persians kept a yearly day for killing them.
f_magi.play: Magi walk from the Sanctuary, the Altar of the Magi and the Lodge in their white felt hoods, and lead the Persian rites.
f_magi.s0: Herodotus lists the Magi among the six tribes of the Medes, and says no sacrifice happens without one, who stands by and sings a theogony. They read dreams for Astyages and for Xerxes. They kill anything with their own hands, he says, except a dog or a man, and they make a contest of killing ants and snakes.
f_magi.s1: The Fortification tablets name magi (makush in Elamite) as officiants who draw rations for the lan offering. They also use a plain Elamite word for priest, shatin, far more often. Magi are not a Persian church: they are one kind of paid religious specialist among several, working for several gods.
f_magi.s2: Darius says Gaumata the magus took the throne by claiming to be Cyrus's son, and that he killed him. Herodotus adds that the Persians killed every magus they could find that day, and keep the day as a great feast when no magus may show himself. Modern historians often suspect Darius's story is a cover for killing the real heir.
f_magi.s3: Magi guarded Cyrus's tomb at Pasargadae, father to son, drawing a sheep each day, flour and wine, and a horse each month to sacrifice to him. Alexander's men found the guardians still there, and tortured them over the tomb's robbery.
f_marduk.lead: The Cyrus Cylinder has Marduk himself choose Cyrus. His priests wrote it. It's the best evidence for how an old temple made its peace with a new king, and the worst for what Cyrus believed.
f_marduk.play: Babylonian brickmakers at Susa want a Shrine of Marduk and the Akitu. Marduk's table is the rite that lifts them.
f_marduk.s0: The Cylinder says Marduk searched every land for a just king and took Cyrus by the hand. It says Cyrus returned displaced gods to their shrines. Written for Babylonian eyes in a Babylonian form, it says nothing about Persian religion and is no charter of rights.
f_marduk.s1: The Akitu ran the first twelve days of Nisannu, spring. Marduk's statue went in procession to the Akitu house outside the city. The Nabonidus Chronicle complains year after year that it lapsed while the king was away.
f_marduk.s2: The Chronicle has Cambyses in Babylon at the new year of 538, and older books made that an Akitu. Kuhrt and Sherwin-White read it as an installation, and find no secure Persian-period Akitu with the king present. Their same paper argues that the story of Xerxes destroying Babylon's temples is Greek, and Boiy calls it fiction.
f_mithra.lead: Greek writers knew a Persian feast of Mithra, the Mithrakana. It is the best-attested Iranian feast of the Achaemenid age, though not from a Persian text.
f_mithra.play: Mithra's feast comes in the autumn. Wine and meat make it grand.
f_mithra.s0: Ctesias and Duris, quoted by Athenaeus, say that on Mithra's feast alone the Persian king may get drunk and dance the Persian dance. Ctesias was a doctor at Artaxerxes II's court, so this is about a century after our levels.
f_mithra.s1: Strabo says the satrap of Armenia sent the King 20,000 foals each year for the Mithrakana. That is a large number from a late source, but the name is there.
f_mithra.s2: Iranica's article suggests the name Mehragan came in with the calendar reform of the later fifth century. In Darius's own calendar the autumn month is Bagayadi, "of the worship of the god", and which god is itself argued. The game's date falls in that month.
f_new_year.lead: The Persian year did begin in spring, and so did the Babylonian one. No Achaemenid text names a feast of that day. Calling what you keep here Nowruz would claim more than anyone knows, so the game calls it the spring new year and tells you why.
f_new_year.play: The spring new year comes on the first day of the year. Keep barley in store and the town processes. The tag on it says "disputed", and that's the truth.
f_new_year.s0: The Old Persian month names run from Adukanaisha, around March and April, and the Babylonian year opens with Nisannu. That the year started in spring is firm.
f_new_year.s1: The Apadana's stairs show the peoples of the empire bringing gifts, and many have read them as a New Year audience. Nylander, Calmeyer and Mousavi have denied any evidence for that. Iranica's own article on Nowruz says there's no precise information on its customs before the Sasanians.
f_new_year.s2: The word itself comes later. Boyce and Grenet suggest that Babylon's splendid festival at this season may have helped Iranians shape their own. Modern claims that Cyrus or Darius kept Nowruz, with dates and all, rest on no ancient source.
f_sacrifice.lead: Herodotus gives one close description of a Persian sacrifice, and it is strange on purpose: no altar, no fire, no music, no wine poured out. Some of it the tablets contradict. Some of it they can't test.
f_sacrifice.play: The Sacrifice for the King follows him: crowds, a priest, a victim, no pipes. It reads the omens, and good ones put heart in your soldiers.
f_sacrifice.s0: The man who sacrifices leads the victim to a clean place and calls on the god, wearing a myrtle wreath in his tiara. He may not pray for himself alone, only for the King and all Persians, himself among them. He boils the meat, lays it on the softest grass, and a magus sings. Then he takes the meat home.
f_sacrifice.s1: On the march into Greece, Xerxes sacrifices a thousand oxen to Athena at Ilion while the Magi pour libations to the heroes. At the Strymon the Magi kill white horses for good omens. Off Magnesia they sacrifice to the wind for three days and it stops, or, Herodotus adds, it dropped by itself.
f_sacrifice.s2: Before Plataea, Mardonius used a Greek seer, Hegesistratus of Elis, who had escaped the Spartans by cutting off his own foot. His victims said to wait and defend. Mardonius lost patience, attacked, and died.
history-athos.lead: After Marathon Darius planned a greater war, but Egypt rose and he died in 486 BCE. Xerxes took up the plan. For three years his men dug a canal across the neck of Mount Athos, where a fleet had been wrecked, and bridged the Hellespont.
history-athos.s0: Mardonius's fleet was caught by a storm off Athos. Herodotus says 300 ships and 20,000 men were lost, some to sea creatures. The King did not want to round that cape again.
history-athos.s1: On the same march in 492 BCE the Brygi, a Thracian people, fell on Mardonius's camp by night, killed many of his men and wounded him. He would not leave the land until he had subdued them. Herodotus records no fighting at the canal itself.
history-athos.s1.play: The level's great battle is the Brygi's night attack, set on the canal's ground.
history-athos.s2: The men who dug the canal were also set to bridge the river Strymon, where grain was stored at Eion. The king of the Bisaltae, a Thracian people near the river, would not serve Xerxes and fled to Mount Rhodope. When his six sons marched with the King anyway, he had their eyes put out on their return.
history-athos.s2.play: The Bisaltae's raid on the bridge works is a dramatization.
history-athos.s3: Herodotus says the canal was wide enough for two triremes rowed abreast, and that only the Phoenicians dug its sides sloping, so they did not collapse. Surveys since the 1990s found its line, about two kilometres long, under the fields.
history-athos.s3.play: The canal is the level's great work.
history-athos.s4: The canal's overseer, Artachaees, was the tallest man in the army, says Herodotus, and had the loudest voice. He died at Acanthus, and the Greeks of the town honoured him as a hero.
history-athos.s5: Food for the march was laid up in advance at stores along the Thracian coast, at White Cape, Tyrodiza, Doriscus, Eion and in Macedonia.
history-athos.s5.play: Supply Depots on the King's road fill with barley for the host.
history-athos.s6: A storm broke the first bridges. Herodotus says Xerxes had the Hellespont given three hundred lashes and fetters thrown in, and beheaded the builders. Herodotus tells it to show pride; some historians see a ritual punishment of a river.
history-athos.s7: Two new bridges were laid on 360 and 314 ships, held by cables of flax and papyrus, then decked with planks and earth, with screens so the horses would not see the sea.
history-athos.s8: From a white marble throne at Abydos Xerxes watched his army and fleet fill the shores and the sea, and wept: in a hundred years none of them would be alive. Herodotus gives him a long talk with his uncle Artabanus.
history-athos.s9: On the march through Lydia, Xerxes found a plane tree so beautiful that he adorned it with gold and left one of his Immortals to guard it.
history-athos.s9.play: Here the Plane Tree is Xerxes' own, hung with gold, its guard's spear and shield at its foot.
history-bagastana.lead: In 522 BCE the empire nearly broke apart. Cambyses died, a king calling himself Bardiya held the throne, and after Darius and six nobles killed him, nine rebel kings rose across the empire. Darius told his story himself, in three languages, on a cliff at Bagastana, 'the place of the gods'.
history-bagastana.s0: Darius says Cambyses had secretly killed his brother Bardiya, and that a magus named Gaumata took his name and his throne. Herodotus tells the same tale. Many historians suspect the king really was Bardiya, and that Darius, a distant cousin, seized the throne and needed a story. No other source can settle it.
history-bagastana.s1: Darius names the six men who stood with him: Intaphernes, Otanes, Gobryas, Hydarnes, Megabyzus and Ardumanish. On 29 September 522 BCE they killed the king in the fortress of Sikayauvati in Media. Their families stayed at the top of the empire for generations.
history-bagastana.s2: Elam, Babylon, Media, Persia, Armenia, Sagartia and Margiana all rose. Darius and his generals fought, he says, nineteen battles in one year and took nine kings, each named and dated on the rock.
history-bagastana.s2.play: The revolts map shows each battle on Darius's own dates.
history-bagastana.s3: Fravartish claimed descent from the old Median kings. Darius beat him at Kunduru and caught him at Raga. He was mutilated, chained at the palace gate for all to see, and impaled at Ecbatana. The inscription meant the lesson to be read.
history-bagastana.s3.play: The Medes ride: a quarter of the raids are horsemen of the Nisaean plain.
history-bagastana.s4: High on the rock Darius stands with his foot on the fallen magus, nine bound kings before him and the winged figure of Auramazda above. The text is in Elamite, Babylonian and Old Persian. The ledge below was cut away when the work was done, so no one could climb up to deface it.
history-bagastana.s4.play: The relief is the level's great work.
history-bagastana.s5: Darius says he sent copies of the text to every land. Pieces of a Babylonian copy on stone were found at Babylon, and an Aramaic copy on papyrus, made about a century later, at Elephantine in Egypt.
history-bagastana.s6: Between 1835 and 1847 the British officer Henry Rawlinson copied the inscription from ladders and ropes; a Kurdish boy swung across the rock to take paper casts of the Babylonian text. The Old Persian helped scholars read Babylonian cuneiform, and with it the libraries of ancient Mesopotamia.
history-bagastana.s7: Herodotus says the seven agreed that whoever's horse neighed first at sunrise would be king, and that Darius's groom made sure it was his. It is a good story; Darius's own account gives his descent from Achaemenes as his right.
history-ister.lead: About 513 BCE Darius crossed the Bosporus into Europe on a bridge of boats, marched through Thrace and bridged the Ister, the Danube, to strike at the Scythians. They would not stand and fight. The bridge, held by the Ionian Greeks, became the army's lifeline home.
history-ister.s0: Mandrocles of Samos bridged the Bosporus with boats. Darius rewarded him richly, and he dedicated a painting of the crossing in the temple of Hera on Samos. Darius set up two pillars by the strait, listing his peoples.
history-ister.s0.play: The Ionian boatyard builds the bridge's boats, and the Inscribed Stone stands here as the King's Pillar of the Nations.
history-ister.s1: Herodotus gives 700,000 men and 600 ships. No ancient army of the time could be fed in such numbers; modern historians think of a far smaller force. Even the date is uncertain, between about 519 and 512 BCE.
history-ister.s1.play: The muster shows a modern estimate, and says so.
history-ister.s2: On the march to the Ister, the Getae alone fought and were beaten. Herodotus says they believed in immortality and sent a messenger to their god Zalmoxis every few years.
history-ister.s2.play: Once the King's host is called, a band of Getae comes against the camp: Thracians, not Scythians, who stand and fight on foot.
history-ister.s3: The Scythians drew the Persians east across the steppe, filling wells and burning the grass ahead of them, and would never stand. Their horsemen turned and struck when the Persians were strung out.
history-ister.s3.play: Scythian horse archers feign flight up to three times, and raid faster over the winter ice.
history-ister.s4: Herodotus says the Scythians sent Darius these gifts. Darius read them as surrender of earth and water; Gobryas read: unless you fly like birds, hide like mice or leap into the lakes like frogs, these arrows will kill you. It has the shape of a parable.
history-ister.s5: The Scythians urged the Ionians to break the bridge. Miltiades of the Chersonese said yes; Histiaeus of Miletus said their own rule depended on Darius, and the bridge stood. Miltiades later won Marathon, and the story may have been told to his credit.
history-ister.s5.play: Hold the bridge for the King's return.
history-ister.s6: Coes was made tyrant of Mytilene and Histiaeus was given land in Thrace. Then Darius took Histiaeus to Susa as an honoured adviser, out of reach of Miletus. From there the Ionian Revolt would begin.
history-marathon.lead: In 490 BCE Darius sent Datis and Artaphernes across the Aegean with horse transports to punish Eretria and Athens for Sardis. Eretria fell. At Marathon the Athenians and Plataeans charged and drove the King's army back to its ships.
history-marathon.s0: In 491 BCE the King's heralds asked the Greek cities for earth and water, the sign of submission. Many gave it. Athens threw the heralds into a pit and Sparta down a well.
history-marathon.s1: Datis spared the holy island of Delos and burned three hundred talents of frankincense on Apollo's altar. The Persians honoured the god while they punished his worshippers' cities.
history-marathon.s2: Eretria held for six days until two citizens betrayed it. Its temples were burned in revenge for Sardis and its people carried off to Ardericca near Susa, where Herodotus says they still lived in his day.
history-marathon.s3: Hippias, the old tyrant of Athens, guided the Persians to Marathon. He sneezed and lost a tooth in the sand, and said it was all of Attica that would be his.
history-marathon.s4: Herodotus says Pheidippides ran to Sparta, about 240 km, in two days; the Spartans would not march before the full moon. The run from Marathon to Athens with news of victory first appears in Plutarch and Lucian, five centuries later. The modern race comes from that legend.
history-marathon.s5: The Athenians, Herodotus says, were the first Greeks to charge at the run, for eight stades. The Persian centre broke through, but the Greek wings won and closed on it. Herodotus counts 6,400 Persian dead and 192 Athenian.
history-marathon.s5.play: Marathon's hoplites alone keep their sprint: they came on at the run.
history-marathon.s6: The Greeks chased the Persians to the beach and seized seven ships. Cynegirus, brother of the playwright Aeschylus, had his hand cut off gripping a stern. The rest of the fleet got away.
history-marathon.s6.play: Hold the camp at the ships: the fight at your town.
history-marathon.s7: A shield flashed from the heights, and the fleet sailed round Cape Sunium for Athens. The Athenians marched home in time. Who signalled was argued in Athens; Herodotus defends the Alcmaeonid family that was blamed.
history-marathon.s8: The Athenian dead were buried on the field under a great mound, the Soros, still about nine metres high. When it was dug in 1890 it held ash, bone and pottery of about 490 BCE.
history-memphis.lead: Cyrus took Media, Lydia and Babylon. Egypt, the oldest kingdom of all, was left to his son. In 525 BCE Cambyses crossed the desert, broke Pharaoh's army at Pelusium and took Memphis after a siege. He ruled as Pharaoh, and the Greeks remembered him as a madman. The Egyptian records tell a different story.
history-memphis.s0: Within twenty years Cyrus took Media (550 BCE), Lydia (about 547 BCE) and Babylon (539 BCE). Only Egypt was left of the old great powers, ruled by Amasis, a friend of the Greeks. Cyrus died on campaign in 530 BCE, and his son Cambyses inherited the plan.
history-memphis.s1: Herodotus gives several reasons for the war, among them an Egyptian princess sent in place of Amasis's daughter, and doubts them himself. The firmer story is Phanes of Halicarnassus, a Greek captain of Amasis's mercenaries, who fled to Cambyses and told him how to cross the desert.
history-memphis.s1.play: Phanes' desertion arrives as news in 525 BCE.
history-memphis.s10: Herodotus heard from the oasis people that fifty thousand men sent against the oracle of Ammon vanished in a sandstorm. No trace has ever been proven, though explorers have claimed finds.
history-memphis.s11: Polyaenus, writing about 700 years later, says Cambyses set cats, dogs, sheep and ibises before his army, and the Egyptians would not shoot for fear of hurting sacred animals. Herodotus, who visited Egypt and the battlefield, says nothing of it.
history-memphis.s12: Herodotus walked the field of Pelusium decades later and saw the bones still lying in two heaps. The Persian skulls, he says, broke with a pebble, and the Egyptian ones would hardly crack with a stone, because Egyptians shaved their heads in the sun and Persians wore felt caps. The bones he saw; the reason is his own.
history-memphis.s13: In Memphis, Syloson of Samos gave his red cloak to a young spear-bearer of the guard: Darius, son of Hystaspes. Years later, as King, Darius repaid him with Samos. Cambyses died in Syria in 522 BCE on his way home, of a wound in the thigh; Darius's own inscription says only that he died, in words that may mean 'his own death' or 'by his own hand'.
history-memphis.s13.play: You play Darius, in charge of the army's town: a labelled dramatization.
history-memphis.s2: Three days of waterless desert lay between Gaza and Egypt. Cambyses swore a pact with the king of the Arabs, who loaded camels with skins of water and met the army in the desert. Herodotus also reports, and does not believe, a pipeline of ox-hides from a distant river.
history-memphis.s2.play: The King's men reach your town by the desert road the Arabs watered.
history-memphis.s3: Amasis died before the Persians came. His son Psamtik III, six months a king, met them at the Pelusiac mouth of the Nile with Egyptians and Greek and Carian mercenaries. The mercenaries killed Phanes' sons before the lines in revenge. After a hard fight the Egyptians broke and fled to Memphis.
history-memphis.s3.play: Memphis opens after Pelusium, so it is fought as a memory from the top bar, on its own map of the river mouth, with Psamtik's Greeks and Carians in his line.
history-memphis.s4: Cambyses sent a ship of Mytilene up the Nile with a herald to offer terms. The Egyptians poured out of the walls, wrecked the ship and tore its crew apart. Memphis was besieged and in time surrendered. The Libyans and the Greeks of Cyrene and Barca sent gifts at once.
history-memphis.s4.play: The siege of Memphis is fought at your town, where the sources put it.
history-memphis.s5: Herodotus tells how Cambyses sat Psamtik by the road while his daughter passed dressed as a slave and his son was led to execution. Psamtik did not weep until he saw an old friend begging. Spared, he later plotted revolt and was put to death. Herodotus adds that the Persians usually left a defeated king's son to rule.
history-memphis.s6: Udjahorresnet, an admiral of the last pharaohs, tells on his statue that Cambyses made him chief physician and that he composed the king's throne name, Mesutira, 'offspring of Ra'. At his request Cambyses cleared the foreigners camped in the temple of Neith at Sais, restored its incomes and worshipped there like any pharaoh.
history-memphis.s6.play: You rule as the new Pharaoh's man: honour the gods of Memphis.
history-memphis.s7: Herodotus says Cambyses, mad, stabbed the sacred Apis bull in the thigh and it died. But a stela from the bulls' galleries at Saqqara records an Apis buried with honours in Cambyses' sixth year, 524 BCE, in a granite coffin the king gave, with Cambyses kneeling before the bull in Egyptian dress. The next Apis lived until Darius's fourth year. Most historians think no bull fits Herodotus's story.
history-memphis.s7.play: The Apis vault and the granite barges from Elephantine are the level's great work.
history-memphis.s8: A decree of Cambyses, copied centuries later on the back of the Demotic Chronicle, cut the royal payments to most of Egypt's temples. In 407 BCE the Jews of Elephantine wrote that when Cambyses came he destroyed the temples of Egypt's gods but spared theirs. Angry priests were Herodotus's informants.
history-memphis.s9: Cambyses planned to sail on Carthage, but the Phoenicians would not fight their own colony, and without them the fleet was too weak. He marched south against the Ethiopians, and the march turned back when the food ran out.
history-memphis.s9.play: These ventures reach your town as news in 524 BCE.
history-mycale.lead: On the same day as Plataea, the Greek fleet landed at Mycale, opposite Samos, stormed the Persian stockade and burned the ships. Ionia rose again. The war of 480-479 BCE ended with the Athenians carrying the Hellespont's cables home.
history-mycale.s0: As the Greeks went in to attack, a herald's staff was found on the shore and a rumour ran through the army that the Greeks had won in Boeotia. Herodotus takes it as a sign from the gods: both battles were fought the same day.
history-mycale.s0.play: At Plataea a strip follows Mycale, fought the same afternoon.
history-mycale.s1: The Persians had beached their ships behind a wall of stones and stakes. They disarmed the Samians, whom they did not trust. In the battle the Ionians changed sides, the camp was taken and the ships burned.
history-mycale.s2: The Greeks sailed to break the bridges and found them already down. The Athenians besieged Sestos into the autumn, took it, and carried the cables home to dedicate in their temples.
history-mycale.s3: Artayctes, the King's governor, held Sestos with the Persians of the Chersonese. The Athenians under Xanthippus besieged it into the autumn, until the defenders were boiling the straps of their beds. Artayctes slipped out by night, was caught, and was put to death on the shore.
history-mycale.s3.play: After the epilogue, Sestos is a field of its own: hold the town inside its walls.
history-mycale.s4: Xerxes went on building at Persepolis: the Gate of All Lands, his palace, the Hall of a Hundred Columns begun. His inscriptions never mention the war in Greece. In 465 BCE he was murdered in his palace; the accounts of the plot differ.
history-mycale.s5: To the Greeks it was freedom saved. To the King it was a frontier war lost; the empire kept everything east of the Aegean but the Ionian coast. Within a century Persian gold was paying Greek cities to fight each other, and in 387 the King dictated the peace of Greece.
history-mycale.s6: The empire Cyrus founded and Darius ordered held from the Aegean to the Indus for another century and a half, until Alexander took it between 334 and 330. Its roads, satrapies and ration tablets outlived the wars with Greece.
history-parsa.lead: When Persia itself rose for a second false Bardiya, Darius's generals put it down. Then he began a city of ceremony at the foot of a mountain on the Marvdasht plain. Its stones show how the King wished to be seen; its clay tablets show how the empire really fed its workers.
history-parsa.s0: Vahyazdata of Persis also called himself Bardiya, son of Cyrus, and the Persians at home followed him. Darius's general Artavardiya beat him twice, and he was impaled. His army sent east was broken in Arachosia.
history-parsa.s0.play: Vahyazdata's Persians fight behind the same wicker shields as the King's men.
history-parsa.s1: Part cut from the mountain and part built up, the terrace is about 450 by 300 metres. Its huge blocks fit without mortar, held by metal clamps. Darius's inscription on its south wall asks Auramazda to protect the land from enemies, famine and the Lie.
history-parsa.s1.play: The terrace is the level's great work.
history-parsa.s2: In 1933 excavators found thousands of clay tablets in the fortification wall, dated 509 to 493 BCE and written mostly in Elamite. They record monthly rations of barley, wine, beer and sheep for workers, officials and travellers. Mothers received extra after a birth.
history-parsa.s2.play: Rations, not wages: barley and wine from storage pay most of the wage, and meat in the granaries a little more. A brewery makes the beer, kept with the wine.
history-parsa.s3: The tablets call the workers kurtash. They include Lydians, Ionians, Egyptians, Babylonians and Bactrians, men and women, skilled and unskilled, paid by the state. Greek tales of slave gangs building Persian palaces do not fit the records.
history-parsa.s4: On the stairs of the Apadana, twenty-three delegations bring gifts: horses, cloth, gold and animals. No one is shown in chains or in battle. It is often said to show the New Year festival, but no ancient text says so.
history-parsa.s4.play: When the Apadana is finished, delegations walk your roads to it with their gifts, the peoples the trade panel paints bringing tribute. That they come again each spring is a dramatization.
history-parsa.s5: Darius was buried in 486 BCE in a cross-shaped tomb cut into the cliff at Naqsh-e Rostam. Its inscription lists his lands, and a second text beside it says he is a friend to right and no friend to wrong.
history-parsa.s6: Alexander burned the palaces in 330. Arrian says it was revenge for the burning of Athens; later writers tell of a drunken feast and a woman named Thais throwing the first torch.
history-pasargadae.lead: Pasargadae was Cyrus's own city, laid out on the high plain of Persis among gardens fed by stone water channels. From here a king of a small highland realm built the largest empire the world had yet seen, and here his tomb still stands.
history-pasargadae.s0: Cyrus called himself king of Anshan, son of Cambyses, of the line of Teispes. About 550 BCE the Median king Astyages marched against him, but his own army mutinied and handed him over, and Cyrus took Ecbatana and its treasure. Strabo, five centuries later, says Pasargadae was founded where Cyrus won (an ancient account).
history-pasargadae.s0.play: Hill raiders strike from the east, as the Medes once did.
history-pasargadae.s1: In 539 BCE Babylon opened its gates. A clay cylinder laid in its walls says the god Marduk chose Cyrus, and that he sent gods and peoples home. It is royal propaganda in the old Babylonian style, not the 'first charter of human rights' it is sometimes called, but it shows a conqueror who wished to be welcomed.
history-pasargadae.s2: Excavations in 1961-63 found palaces with columned halls, a gatehouse with a four-winged guardian in relief, and a garden framed by limestone water channels and basins. Our word 'paradise' comes from the Old Persian for such a walled garden.
history-pasargadae.s2.play: Fields watered by canals from the Pulvar feed the city.
history-pasargadae.s3: The tomb is a gabled stone room on six stepped plinths, about eleven metres high. Its blocks are fitted without mortar and held with metal clamps, a technique learned from the stonemasons of Lydia and Ionia. Arrian describes a golden couch and coffin inside.
history-pasargadae.s3.play: The tomb is the level's great work, raised one course at a time.
history-pasargadae.s4: Short inscriptions on the palaces read 'I (am) Cyrus the king, the Achaemenide'. Many scholars think Darius had them cut later, to tie Cyrus to his own family. Herodotus tells that Cyrus dreamed of young Darius with wings over Asia and Europe. The game's meeting of Cyrus and Darius is a dramatized scene.
history-pasargadae.s4.play: The commission from Cyrus to Darius is a labelled dramatization.
history-pasargadae.s5: Babylonian tablets show his reign ended in 530 BCE. Herodotus chose, from many tales, the one where Queen Tomyris of the Massagetae killed him in battle. Ctesias says he died of a wound fighting the Derbices; Xenophon has him die peacefully in bed.
history-pasargadae.s6: Two centuries later, in 324, Alexander of Macedon found the tomb robbed. He had its keepers questioned and ordered Aristobulus to restore the body and seal the door. The tomb survived later centuries as the 'tomb of Solomon's mother'.
history-plataea.lead: At Salamis in September 480 BCE the Greek fleet beat the King's in the narrows. Xerxes went home and left Mardonius with a picked army. In the summer of 479 BCE Mardonius fought the united Greeks under Pausanias of Sparta below Mount Cithaeron, and died there.
history-plataea.s0: Themistocles drew the King's fleet into the narrow strait, where its numbers counted for little. Xerxes watched from a throne on the shore. Aeschylus, said to have fought there, staged 'The Persians' eight years later, the only Greek tragedy on an event of its own time to survive.
history-plataea.s1: Alexander of Macedon brought Athens the King's offer: freedom, its land back and more, and its temples rebuilt. The Athenians said they would never make peace while the sun kept its course.
history-plataea.s2: Mardonius built a square wooden fort about ten stades a side on the Asopus, in the land of Thebes, which sided with Persia. A Theban noble feasted the Persian officers in Thebes before the battle.
history-plataea.s2.play: The fort is the level's great work, and Theban caravans bring its timber.
history-plataea.s3: Masistius led the Persian horse in golden scale armour under a purple tunic. When his horse was shot, the Greeks killed him through the eye, and carried his body along the lines to be seen.
history-plataea.s3.play: Plataea's decree asks for a cavalry stable, and the top bar remembers his fight at Erythrae: he leads the King's horse, and when he falls his riders pull back.
history-plataea.s4: The Persian horsemen fouled the spring of Gargaphia that watered the Greek army, and the Greeks had to move by night.
history-plataea.s4.play: The King's horsemen near a Greek camp at day's end foul its water.
history-plataea.s5: The Greek night move went wrong, and Mardonius attacked the Spartans and Tegeans. The Persians fought bravely, Herodotus says, but without armour against men in armour. Mardonius was killed by a Spartan named Arimnestus, and the fort was stormed.
history-plataea.s5.play: Mardonius rides with the Persians on the field; when he falls, those about him break for the camp.
history-plataea.s6: Artabazus son of Pharnaces commanded some forty thousand men and had argued against giving battle. When it came he held his division back, and when he saw the Persians running he led it off the field, north through Phocis and home over the Hellespont.
history-plataea.s6.play: On the field his division holds back, and marches off when Mardonius falls.
history-plataea.s7: In Mardonius's tent Pausanias had his cooks lay out a Persian feast beside a Spartan meal, and laughed at the folly of a man who lived like that and came to rob Greeks of their poor fare.
history-plataea.s8: The Greeks gave Apollo at Delphi a golden tripod on a bronze column of three twisted serpents, with the names of the cities that fought. Constantine moved it to his new capital. It still stands in Istanbul, and the names can still be read.
history-sardis.lead: In 499 BCE the Greek cities of Ionia rose against their tyrants and the King. With twenty Athenian and five Eretrian ships they marched inland and burned Sardis. Six years later the King's fleet broke them at Lade, and Miletus fell.
history-sardis.s0: Aristagoras of Miletus talked the satrap Artaphernes into a fleet against Naxos. The commander quarrelled with him and warned the Naxians, and after four months the siege failed. Facing ruin, Aristagoras turned against the King.
history-sardis.s1: Herodotus says Histiaeus, kept at Susa, shaved a slave's head, tattooed a message on it, and sent him to Miletus once the hair grew back. It is told as a clever tale.
history-sardis.s2: At Sparta Aristagoras showed King Cleomenes a bronze map of the world. Cleomenes refused when he learned Susa lay three months from the sea. Athens sent twenty ships; Herodotus calls them 'the beginning of evils' for Greeks and barbarians.
history-sardis.s3: Most houses of Sardis were of reeds or had reed roofs. One caught fire, and the whole lower city burned, with the temple of the goddess Cybebe. Artaphernes held the citadel. The Persians later named that temple when they burned Greek temples.
history-sardis.s3.play: Reed roofs: torches catch easily, and fire spreads fast. The town's sanctuary is the Temple of Cybebe, and it burns like the rest.
history-sardis.s4: The Ionians and Athenians could not take the citadel, and marched back to the coast. The Persians of the satrapies west of the Halys came up with them near Ephesus and beat them; Eualcides, general of the Eretrians, fell. The Athenians sailed home and would not help the Ionians again.
history-sardis.s4.play: The Ionian host with its Athenians and Eretrians comes up from Ephesus.
history-sardis.s5: Herodotus says Darius asked who the Athenians were, shot an arrow into the sky, and had a servant say three times at every dinner, 'Master, remember the Athenians.'
history-sardis.s6: The Lydians, says Herodotus, were the first to strike coins of gold and silver. Excavators found Sardis's gold refinery beside the Pactolus. Under the Persians the King's gold daric and silver siglos were struck here.
history-sardis.s6.play: The Royal Mint turns the river's gold into silver for the treasury.
history-sardis.s7: 353 Ionian triremes met the King's fleet off Miletus. Herodotus counts 600 for the King. Most of the Samians sailed away before the fighting; the Chians fought on and were destroyed.
history-sardis.s7.play: Act II brings the fleet at Lade.
history-sardis.s8: Miletus was stormed, its temple at Didyma burned and its people sent to live on the Persian Gulf. In Athens, Phrynichus staged 'The Capture of Miletus'; the audience wept, and he was fined a thousand drachmas for reminding them.
history-sardis.s9: Afterwards Artaphernes measured the Ionians' lands, fixed their tribute and made the cities settle disputes by law, not war. In 492 BCE Mardonius removed the tyrants and let the cities govern themselves as democracies.
history-susa.lead: Susa was the capital of Elam two thousand years before Persia existed. Elam rose against Darius three times. Once it was quiet, he made Susa his chief seat and built a palace of glazed brick, recording on its foundation tablets where every material came from.
history-susa.s0: Açina rose first and was sent to Darius in chains. Martiya rose next, and the Elamites killed him themselves as Darius came near. In his second or third year Athamaita rose, and Gobryas put him down; this last revolt was added to the cliff later.
history-susa.s0.play: Athamaita's Elamites: four in ten of the host are bowmen with the King's own range.
history-susa.s1: Darius's foundation charter lists it all: cedar from Lebanon, gold from Sardis and Bactria, lapis lazuli from Sogdiana, ivory from Ethiopia, Sind and Arachosia. Ionians and Sardians cut the stone, Medes and Egyptians worked the gold, Babylonians baked the bricks.
history-susa.s1.play: Charter caravans bring the cedar, gold, lapis and ivory the charter names.
history-susa.s2: The palace walls shone with moulded, glazed bricks: rows of life-size archers, lions and winged bulls in blue, green, yellow and white. The craft came from Babylon. Pieces of the archers' frieze are in the Louvre.
history-susa.s2.play: The glazed-brick kiln makes the palace's bricks.
history-susa.s3: Herodotus counts 111 stations from Sardis to Susa, about ninety days on foot. Royal riders passed messages from station to station so that 'neither snow nor rain' could stop them. The Persepolis tablets confirm the stations, with travellers' sealed passes and rations.
history-susa.s3.play: Road Stations speed the caravans, and their riders see raiders early.
history-susa.s4: In 1972 French excavators found a headless statue of Darius at Susa's gate. It was carved in Egypt, in Egyptian style, with texts in hieroglyphs and in three cuneiform languages. Its base shows twenty-four subject peoples holding up the King.
history-susa.s4.play: The Statue of Darius stands at Susa as a decoration, the one statue the King's towns raise.
history-susa.s5: Stelae set up along the Wadi Tumilat say Darius ordered a canal dug from the Nile to the sea that goes to Persia, and that ships sailed it. Herodotus says Pharaoh Necho had begun it.
history-susa.s6: Darius sent Scylax of Caryanda down the Indus to the sea and round Arabia to Egypt, a voyage of thirty months. Then he conquered the Indus lands.
history-susa.s7: The Egyptian who had named Cambyses was at Darius's court in Elam. Darius sent him home to restore the House of Life at Sais, where scribes and physicians were trained.
history-thermopylae.lead: In late summer 480 BCE Leonidas of Sparta held the pass at Thermopylae with about seven thousand Greeks while the fleet fought at Artemisium. After three days a local man showed the Persians a mountain path. Leonidas died with his rearguard, and Xerxes marched on Athens.
history-thermopylae.s0: Herodotus counts 1,700,000 foot soldiers, and an epitaph speaks of three million. Supply, water and road space make that impossible; modern estimates run from about 100,000 to 300,000 in all.
history-thermopylae.s0.play: The muster shows the modern estimate, and says it is one.
history-thermopylae.s1: A Persian scout rode up and saw Spartans exercising and combing their long hair before the wall. The exiled Spartan king Demaratus told Xerxes it meant they were ready to die.
history-thermopylae.s2: The pass ran between mountain and sea, with hot springs and an old Phocian wall. The river has since carried so much silt that the shore now lies kilometres away. Herodotus says rivers on the march were drunk dry.
history-thermopylae.s2.play: Thermopylae's decree asks for wells for the host.
history-thermopylae.s3: Before the fighting, a storm off Magnesia blew for three days and wrecked hundreds of the King's ships. Then, on the same three days as the fighting in the pass, the Greek fleet fought at Artemisium, each front guarding the other's flank.
history-thermopylae.s3.play: A strip at the top of the screen follows Artemisium day by day; a trireme rammed hard may break across amidships, as Herodotus describes at Salamis (8.90).
history-thermopylae.s4: The Medes were thrown back, then the Immortals under Hydarnes. Herodotus says the Spartans turned as if to flee, then wheeled on their pursuers.
history-thermopylae.s4.play: The Spartans feign flight once; fallen Immortals are queued again at a barracks.
history-thermopylae.s5: Ephialtes of Trachis led the Immortals at night over the Anopaea path. The Phocians guarding it fell back to a hilltop, and the Persians passed them by.
history-thermopylae.s6: Leonidas sent most of the army away and stayed with his 300 Spartans, 700 Thespians and 400 Thebans. They fought on the little hill in the pass until they were overwhelmed. In 1939 archaeologists found many Persian arrowheads on that hill.
history-thermopylae.s7: Leonidas's famous reply to the demand for his arms comes from Plutarch, six centuries later. Herodotus does record the Spartan who, told the arrows would hide the sun, said they would fight in the shade.
history-thermopylae.s8: The Athenians had left their city for Salamis and the ships. A few held the Acropolis behind wooden barricades until Persians climbed the cliff by a shrine. The temples were burned, as Sardis had been.
l_abdera.lead: Abdera was a Greek city on the coast of Thrace east of the Nestus river. Herodotus says the people of Teos founded it when they fled Harpagus's siege about 545 BCE. It lay on Xerxes' road in 480 BCE, and one of its citizens made the best-known joke of the march.
l_abdera.play: Abdera is named in the Athos level's Chronicle and chatter, through the man of Abdera who thanked the gods that the King ate only once a day.
l_abdera.s0: When Harpagus took the wall of Teos with a mound, Herodotus says, the Teians took to their ships and sailed to Thrace, where they founded Abdera. An earlier settler, Timesius of Clazomenae, had tried and been driven out by the Thracians, and the Teians honoured him as a hero.
l_abdera.s1: The cities on Xerxes' road had to feed his army. Herodotus says Megacreon of Abdera told his people to go to their temples with their wives and thank the gods that Xerxes ate only one meal a day; had he ordered breakfast too, they would have had to flee or be ruined.
l_abdera.s2: On his retreat from Greece, Herodotus says, Xerxes came to Abdera, made guest-friendship with its people and gave them a golden akinakes and a gold-spangled tiara. The Abderites said it was there he first loosened his belt in safety; Herodotus does not believe it.
l_abdera.s3: Abdera struck silver coins with a griffin, the badge of its mother city Teos, from about 540 BCE. The city later became known as the home of the philosophers Democritus and Protagoras.
l_abydos.lead: Abydos was a Greek town on the Asian side of the Hellespont, at one of the narrowest points of the strait. In 480 BCE Xerxes' engineers anchored the Asian end of his two ship bridges here, and the King reviewed his army and fleet from a hill above the town before crossing into Europe.
l_abydos.play: The game marks Abydos as the place where Xerxes bridged the Hellespont. This matches Herodotus, who puts the Asian end of the bridges at Abydos and the European end on a headland near Sestos.
l_abydos.s0: Strabo and Thucydides describe Abydos as a colony of Miletus, and Strabo adds that the Lydian king Gyges allowed the settlement. Under Darius it was ruled by a local tyrant: Herodotus lists Daphnis of Abydos among the Greek rulers who guarded the King's bridge on the Ister. During the Ionian Revolt it joined the rising, and Herodotus says the Persian general Daurises retook it along with other Hellespont towns.
l_abydos.s1: Herodotus says the bridges ran from Abydos to a rocky headland on the European shore between Sestos and Madytus, a crossing he gives as seven stades. A storm broke the first pair. The rebuilt bridges rested on lines of ships, about 360 in one and 314 in the other by his count, tied with cables of flax and papyrus, with a roadway of planks and earth laid on top.
l_abydos.s2: Herodotus tells that the people of Abydos had built a throne of white stone on a hill, from which Xerxes watched his army and a race between his ships. Seeing the strait full of vessels, he is said to have wept at the shortness of human life, and Herodotus gives a long talk on this theme between Xerxes and his uncle Artabanus. The talk is a literary set piece, best read as Herodotus's reflection rather than a record of words spoken.
l_abydos.s3: Herodotus says that after the storm Xerxes had the Hellespont given three hundred lashes and a pair of fetters thrown into it, and had the bridge builders beheaded. Some historians accept a real act behind the story, perhaps a ritual against hostile waters, while others see a Greek tale built to show royal arrogance. No Persian source mentions it.
l_abydos.s4: After Salamis, Herodotus says, the army reached the strait to find the bridges wrecked by storms and crossed by ship to Abydos. In 479 BCE, after Mycale, the Greek fleet sailed to Abydos to cut the bridges and found them already gone. Leotychides and the Peloponnesians then sailed home, while the Athenians under Xanthippus stayed to besiege Sestos on the far shore.
l_acanthus.lead: Acanthus was a Greek city founded from Andros on the coast where the Athos peninsula joins the mainland. Xerxes' canal was dug across the isthmus just beyond it, and in 480 BCE his army passed through on its march west. Herodotus says Xerxes made the Acanthians his guest-friends for their zeal for the work.
l_acanthus.play: The Athos level is built on the coastal plain at Acanthus: its diggers' town, its farms and the mound of Artachaees stand there.
l_acanthus.s0: Herodotus places the canal across the neck of land between Acanthus's sea and the gulf of Torone, about twelve furlongs wide. The diggers came from the King's nations and from the people of Athos itself. The canal's line has been traced by survey near the modern villages of Nea Roda and Tripiti.
l_acanthus.s1: Herodotus says that when Xerxes reached Acanthus he proclaimed guest-friendship with its people, gave them Median dress and praised them, seeing they were eager for the war and hearing of the canal. The gift was an honour; it also bound the city to the King.
l_acanthus.s2: While Xerxes was at Acanthus, Artachaees, one of the canal's overseers and the tallest of the Persians, died. Herodotus says Xerxes mourned him, the army raised a mound over him, and the Acanthians by an oracle's command sacrificed to him as a hero, calling on his name.
l_acanthus.s3: Acanthus struck silver coins showing a lion bringing down a bull from the late sixth century. In 424 BCE it went over to the Spartan Brasidas, as Thucydides reports. The city's coins are the main record of it in the Persian years.
l_acropolis.lead: The Acropolis is the steep limestone hill at the heart of Athens. In 480 BCE it held the old temple of Athena and a half-built marble temple. In late summer 480 BCE Xerxes' army took it after a siege and burned its sanctuaries, which Herodotus presents as revenge for the burning of Sardis. The ruins shaped how Athenians remembered the war and what they later built there.
l_acropolis.play: The game presents the Acropolis as a field stormed in 480 BCE, with the old temple of Athena, the Older Parthenon and the wooden barricade. Herodotus and the excavations support these features. In 480 BCE the Older Parthenon was still unfinished.
l_acropolis.s0: Excavation shows that by 480 BCE the summit held a limestone temple of Athena Polias. Its foundations survive between the later Parthenon and the Erechtheion, and many marble dedications such as korai stood around it. On the south side a new marble temple, now called the Older Parthenon, was under construction, with its columns only partly raised. Most scholars date its start to the years after Marathon.
l_acropolis.s1: Herodotus says the Athenians had abandoned the city. Only a few temple treasurers and poor men stayed behind, and they took the oracle's wooden wall to mean a barricade of doors and timbers on the Acropolis. The Persians camped on the Areopagus opposite and shot arrows wrapped in burning tow into the barricade. The defenders refused terms offered through the exiled Pisistratids and rolled boulders down on the attackers.
l_acropolis.s2: In the end, Herodotus says, some Persians climbed the sheer face near the shrine of Aglaurus, where no guard was posted. Some defenders leapt from the wall and others fled into the temple. The Persians killed them, stripped the sanctuary and set the Acropolis on fire. Xerxes sent a rider to Susa with the news, and the next day he ordered the Athenian exiles with him to go up and sacrifice in their own way.
l_acropolis.s3: Excavations from 1885 to 1890 found broken korai, inscribed bases and burnt fragments buried in fills on the summit, long called the Persian debris, though scholars now debate how much of it belongs to 480 BCE. Column drums of the Older Parthenon, cracked and reddened by fire, were later built into the north wall of the Acropolis. They can still be seen there from the city below.
l_acropolis.s4: Herodotus says the Persians later used the burning of Sardis and its temple of Cybebe in 498 BCE as grounds for burning Greek temples. Later writers said the Greeks swore before Plataea to leave burned temples as memorials, but Theopompus called this oath an Athenian invention. Historians still argue whether the ruins were left by vow or for lack of money, and whether part of the old temple stayed in use after 480 BCE.
l_aegina.lead: Aegina is an island in the Saronic Gulf between Attica and the Peloponnese. It was a great trading state with its own silver coins, the turtles. In 491 BCE it gave earth and water to Darius, which set Athens and Sparta against it, but in 480 BCE its ships were judged the best of the Greek fleet at Salamis.
l_aegina.play: Aegina is named in the Thermopylae level, where the Black Sea grain ships sail past the King toward it, and in Greek tooltips and articles.
l_aegina.s0: Herodotus says the islanders gave Darius's heralds earth and water, and among them the Aeginetans. The Athenians accused them before Sparta of meaning to join the Persians against Athens, and King Cleomenes went to Aegina to seize the men responsible.
l_aegina.s1: At Abydos Xerxes saw ships carrying grain from the Black Sea through the Hellespont to Aegina and the Peloponnese. He let them pass, saying they were carrying grain to where he was going himself.
l_aegina.s2: Aegina sent its thirty best ships to Salamis and kept others at home to guard the island. Herodotus says that in the battle the Aeginetans were the best reported of all the Greeks, with the Athenians next, and the Aeginetan Polycritus was named among the bravest men.
l_aegina.s3: Aegina struck some of the earliest silver coins of mainland Greece, staters stamped with a sea turtle, from about 550 BCE. Its weight standard was used across much of Greece. The coins survive in large numbers.
l_anopaea.lead: The Anopaea was a track over the mountains above Thermopylae that let an army leave the coastal pass and come down behind it. In 480 BCE, after two days of failed attacks, Xerxes sent Hydarnes and his picked troops along it by night. Their descent behind the Greek line ended the defence of the pass and opened central Greece to the Persian army.
l_anopaea.play: The game presents the Anopaea as the path round Thermopylae shown by Ephialtes. This follows Herodotus, who also records other claimed guides and reports that locals already knew the route.
l_anopaea.s0: Herodotus says the path began at the gorge of the Asopus river and shared its name, Anopaea, with the mountain it crossed. It ran along the ridge and came down at Alpenus, the first Locrian town, near a rock called Melampygus. He adds that the Malians had found it long before and led the Thessalians along it to attack the Phocians.
l_anopaea.s1: According to Herodotus, Hydarnes set out at the hour when lamps were lit, crossed the Asopus and climbed through the night. At dawn his men reached the top. A thousand Phocians on guard there heard them tramping through the fallen leaves of the oak woods in the still air. The Phocians withdrew to the summit to make a stand, but Hydarnes ignored them and went on down towards the pass.
l_anopaea.s2: Herodotus names Ephialtes, son of Eurydemus, a Malian who hoped for a reward from Xerxes. He also reports a rival story naming Onetes of Carystus and Corydallus of Anticyra, which he rejects. No Persian text mentions Thermopylae, so the Persian side of the story is unknown. Since the Malians already knew the track, historians think the Persians could have found guides among several local people.
l_anopaea.s3: Modern topographers have walked the hills above Thermopylae and do not agree on the exact line. They differ over how far the route followed the Asopus gorge and which ridge it crossed before coming down near Alpenus. River silt has since pushed the coastline far out, so the ancient narrows are now a broad plain. This makes the ground hard to match with Herodotus.
l_anopaea.s4: Later writers describe the defence at Thermopylae being turned in the same way again. Pausanias says the Gauls who invaded Greece in 279 were led round over the mountain, as the Persians had been. Plutarch tells how Cato climbed the heights in 191 to outflank Antiochus III for Rome. These later cases show that the pass could not be held without guarding the hills above it.
l_anshan.lead: Anshan, now the site of Tall-i Malyan near Shiraz, was an ancient royal city of the Elamite highlands. Its name became the title of the Persian kings before Cyrus: the Cyrus Cylinder calls him king of Anshan, and his father, grandfather and great-grandfather kings of Anshan before him.
l_anshan.play: The game calls Cyrus King of Anshan in the Pasargadae level's intro and briefings, as the Babylonian texts do; Anshan itself is not shown.
l_anshan.s0: In the Cyrus Cylinder, written in Babylonian after 539 BCE, Cyrus calls himself son of Cambyses, great king, king of Anshan, grandson of Cyrus, great king, king of Anshan, descendant of Teispes, great king, king of Anshan. The Nabonidus Chronicle also calls him king of Anshan when it records his victory over Astyages.
l_anshan.s1: For two thousand years Elamite kings styled themselves kings of Anshan and Susa, joining the highland and the lowland halves of their realm. Excavations at Tall-i Malyan found a large walled city and Elamite tablets naming it Anshan. By Cyrus's time the city was much shrunk.
l_anshan.s2: How the Persians came to rule Anshan is not known. Some historians think the title shows that Cyrus's family took over an Elamite kingship and its traditions; others think it was only an old regional name. Darius later traced his line to Achaemenes and never used the title.
l_anshan.s3: Cyrus's revolt against the Median king Astyages began in Persis about 553-550 BCE, and after his victory he built Pasargadae on the plain of the Pulvar, north-east of Anshan's old seat. Herodotus never names Anshan; he speaks only of Persians and their tribes.
l_arachosia.lead: Arachosia was an eastern province of the Achaemenid empire, in the region of modern Kandahar in southern Afghanistan. Darius's inscriptions name it among his lands, and it was the scene of fighting in the revolts of 522-521 BCE. His Susa charter names it as one of the places that supplied ivory.
l_arachosia.play: The game names Arachosia only in the Chronicle and in the Vahyazdata and Susa charter articles, as an eastern province and a source of ivory. It has no mechanic of its own.
l_arachosia.s0: Arachosia (Old Persian Harauvatish) is named in Darius's lists of lands, including the Behistun inscription and the tomb inscription DNa. It lay far to the east of Persis, in the Helmand and Arghandab valleys. Its name is linked to the river Harauvati.
l_arachosia.s1: In the foundation charter of the palace at Susa, Darius says that ivory used in the building was brought from Ethiopia, from Sind and from Arachosia. Arachosia was therefore one source among three. The charter also names the craftsmen who worked the ivory.
l_arachosia.s2: At Behistun Darius says that Vahyazdata, the false Bardiya in Persis, sent an army against Vivana, whom Darius had made satrap in Arachosia. Darius reports battles at Kapishakanish and at Gandutava, and says his side prevailed. The text is Darius's own account and was written to justify his rule.
l_arachosia.s3: Herodotus's tribute list of the satrapies does not name Arachosia as a district. Some of its people may stand under other names in his list of the eastern peoples. Later writers such as Arrian describe the region in Alexander's time, long after the period of the game.
l_arachosia.s4: Herodotus's tribute districts do not match the Persian lists of lands, so historians disagree about how eastern provinces such as Arachosia were grouped. Some think the satrapies were administrative units distinct from the lists of peoples carved on royal monuments. The exact boundaries of Arachosia are not settled.
l_araxes.lead: Herodotus calls the river Cyrus crossed to attack the Massagetae the Araxes. It ran east toward the Caspian, and beyond it lay the lands of the nomads and their queen Tomyris. Which river he meant is not certain: most think the Oxus or the Jaxartes, not the Araxes of Armenia.
l_araxes.play: The Araxes is named in the Pasargadae level's Chronicle and chatter, as the river the King's army crossed on the campaign where Cyrus died.
l_araxes.s0: Herodotus says some called the Araxes larger and some smaller than the Ister, with many islands as large as Lesbos, whose people lived on roots and fruit and grew drunk on the smoke of a burning fruit. He says it rose among the Matieni and ran in forty mouths, all but one into marshes.
l_araxes.s1: Herodotus says Tomyris offered to let Cyrus cross unopposed or to fight on her side of the river. On Croesus's advice Cyrus crossed, left a camp with wine and food, and fell on the Massagetae who feasted there, taking Tomyris's son.
l_araxes.s2: In Herodotus Cyrus was killed beyond the river in a hard battle, and Tomyris put his head in a skin of blood. He admits other tales were told. Ctesias says Cyrus died of a wound fighting the Derbices, and Xenophon has him die peacefully at home. No Persian record tells it.
l_araxes.s3: Herodotus seems to join several rivers into one Araxes. His description of a river flowing east toward the Caspian fits the Oxus (Amu Darya) or the Jaxartes (Syr Darya) better than the Araxes of Armenia, and historians place the Massagetae east of the Caspian.
l_arbela.lead: Arbela, modern Erbil in northern Iraq, was an old Assyrian city on a high mound between the Great and Little Zab rivers. It was a cult centre of Ishtar and a stopping point on roads linking Babylonia, Media and the north-west. Darius named it at Behistun as the place where he executed a rebel leader, which shows its value as a public stage in the King's land of Assyria.
l_arbela.play: The game shows Arbela only as a trade partner, the traders of Arbela. The city did lie on busy roads, but the sources say little about its merchants, so these traders are the game's simplification.
l_arbela.s0: Assyrian texts call the city Arba-ilu, often read as four gods. Its goddess, Ishtar of Arbela, had a major temple there. Prophecies spoken by her devotees for King Esarhaddon in the 670s BCE survive on tablets from Nineveh. The city probably outlived the fall of Assyria, and the Nabonidus Chronicle records that in 547 BCE Cyrus took his army across the Tigris below Arbela.
l_arbela.s1: In the Behistun inscription Darius tells how a Sagartian named Chissantakhma claimed the kingship during the revolts of 522 to 521 BCE. Darius says he cut off the man's nose and ears and impaled him at Arbela. Choosing this city made the punishment visible to the people of the region, much as Darius displayed the Median rebel Fravartish at Ecbatana.
l_arbela.s2: An Aramaic letter of the satrap Arsames, written in the late 5th century and so later than the game's period, lists Arbela among the places where his official Nehtihor could draw rations on his journey to Egypt. It shows the city working as a supply point in the Persian travel system. The Persian-era levels of the citadel mound remain little explored.
l_arbela.s3: Historians generally place Arbela in the Persian land of Athura, the old Assyrian heartland, but its border with Media is not clearly fixed in the sources. Herodotus describes the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa crossing Armenia and Matiene without naming Arbela. Modern scholars disagree over whether the road ran through the city or kept further north and east.
l_arbela.s4: Arrian says that after his defeat by Alexander in 331 Darius III fled through Arbela, where Alexander then seized the royal baggage and treasure. Arrian also complains that the battle was wrongly called after Arbela, since it was fought at Gaugamela, which writers placed some 500 to 600 stades away.
l_argos.lead: Argos was one of the oldest and largest cities of the Peloponnese, set in the plain of the Argolid near a great sanctuary of Hera. Long the chief rival of Sparta, it was crippled by a Spartan victory at Sepeia, probably in the 490s BCE. In 480 BCE it stayed out of the Greek alliance against Xerxes, and Greek writers suspected it of sympathy for Persia.
l_argos.play: The game treats Argos as a trade partner and as neutral in 480 BCE. The neutrality follows Herodotus, but no ancient source describes Argos trading with the Persian empire, so that role is the game's simplification.
l_argos.s0: Argos held the fertile plain of the Argolid in the north-east Peloponnese. Herodotus names an early ruler of Argos, Pheidon, who fixed weights and measures for the Peloponnesians. He also tells of a battle with Sparta over the border district of Thyrea, fought about the time Cyrus was besieging Sardis, which Sparta won. By then Sparta had replaced Argos as the leading power of the peninsula.
l_argos.s1: Herodotus says the Spartan king Cleomenes invaded the Argolid and defeated the Argives at Sepeia near Tiryns, probably about 494 BCE, though some historians date it earlier. Survivors fled into a sacred grove, and Cleomenes had it burned with them inside. Herodotus puts the Argive dead at 6,000. He adds that slaves then ran the city, perhaps meaning its dependent rural population, until the sons of the dead came of age.
l_argos.s2: In 481 BCE the Greeks resisting Xerxes sent envoys to Argos, and Herodotus gives the Argive version of what followed. Delphi had advised the Argives to stay out, and they offered to join only in return for a thirty-year truce with Sparta and half the command. Sparta replied that the Argive king could have one vote beside its own two kings. The Argives refused and ordered the envoys out of their land by sunset.
l_argos.s3: Herodotus reports that Xerxes sent a herald claiming kinship through Perses, son of Perseus, as ancestor of the Persians, and asking only that Argos stay neutral. He adds that Argive envoys later asked Artaxerxes at Susa whether that friendship still held. He says he passes on these tales without vouching for them. No Persian text names Argos, so the charge rests on Greek reports.
l_argos.s4: Herodotus says that in 479 BCE the Argives had promised Mardonius to stop the Spartan army leaving the Peloponnese. When the Spartans marched out, Argos sent its best day-runner to Attica to warn Mardonius that it could not hold them. Mardonius then left Athens for Boeotia, where the war was decided at Plataea. Herodotus is the only source for this message.
l_armenia.lead: Armenia was a mountainous country north of Assyria, called Armina in Darius's inscriptions. It rose against Darius in 522-521 BCE and was won back by commanders he sent, not by the King himself. The Behistun inscription is the main source for these campaigns.
l_armenia.play: The game names Armenia only in the Chronicle and in the event article on the war there, where Dadarshish and Vaumisa fight the rebels. It has no level, building or mechanic of its own.
l_armenia.s0: Armenia appears as Armina in the Behistun inscription, which lists it among the lands that belonged to Darius. The inscriptions treat it as one of the King's countries. They do not give its borders.
l_armenia.s1: In the Behistun account Armenia rebelled in the troubles that followed the death of Cambyses and Darius's seizure of the throne. Darius says he sent out his own men against the rebels while he himself was in Media. The text gives the name of no Armenian rebel leader.
l_armenia.s2: Darius names two commanders, both his servants. Dadarshish, an Armenian, fought three battles against the rebels and Vaumisa, a Persian, fought two more, some in Assyria. The inscription dates each battle by day, month and place, and records that Darius's side won. The victories are told as the King's own, won through his officers.
l_armenia.s3: Herodotus does not describe this revolt. He lists Armenia as a tribute-paying province of Darius, and he says the Armenians were settlers from Phrygia. He also describes the Royal Road crossing Armenia. The royal inscriptions do not confirm the Phrygian origin.
l_armenia.s4: Several battle sites named at Behistun lie in or near Armenia and Assyria, and modern scholars have not agreed on where all of them were. The campaign is known almost only from Darius's own text, which was written to justify his rule. How long the fighting lasted, and how serious the revolt was, rest on that one version.
l_artemisium.lead: Artemisium was the cape at the northern tip of Euboea where the Greek fleet blocked the King's ships in the summer of 480 BCE, while Leonidas held Thermopylae on the mainland opposite. After three days of fighting and heavy losses on both sides, the Greeks sailed south when the pass fell, and later gathered at Salamis. The battle is known almost entirely from Greek writers, above all Herodotus, and no Persian record mentions it.
l_artemisium.play: The game mentions Artemisium only in a chronicle note: the Greek fleet fought the King's for three days while the pass was held. The note agrees with Herodotus.
l_artemisium.s0: Herodotus says the Greeks chose to hold the pass at Thermopylae and the narrow waters off Artemisium together, so that the King's army and fleet could not advance side by side. The cape took its name from a sanctuary of Artemis. The fleet was led by the Spartan Eurybiades, although Athens supplied the largest share. Herodotus counts 271 warships besides penteconters, 127 of them Athenian, with 53 more Athenian ships arriving later.
l_artemisium.s1: Herodotus says a storm off the Magnesian coast wrecked at least 400 of the King's ships, and that a squadron of 200 sent round Euboea to cut off the Greeks was lost in a second storm. On the first evening the Greeks took 30 ships, and on the second they struck Cilician vessels. On the third day the King's fleet attacked in force. Herodotus praises the Egyptians on the Persian side and says half the Athenian ships were damaged.
l_artemisium.s2: Herodotus says the sea fights and the battles at the pass fell on the same days. When a messenger, Abronichus, brought word that Thermopylae was lost, the Greeks sailed south that night. Themistocles had messages cut on rocks at the watering places. They urged the Ionians in the King's fleet to change sides or hold back in battle.
l_artemisium.s3: Herodotus puts the King's fleet at 1,207 triremes before the storms. Most historians think this too high, and some doubt the story of the 200-ship squadron. An inscription found at Troezen in 1959, probably cut in the early third century, claims to be Themistocles' decree sending ships to Artemisium and emptying Athens beforehand. Scholars still argue whether it preserves a genuine order, since it disagrees with Herodotus on when Athens was evacuated.
l_artemisium.s4: Herodotus says the Athenians, prompted by an oracle, prayed to Boreas, the north wind, whom myth made their kinsman by marriage, and credited him with the storm. He also tells of Scyllias of Scione, said to have swum about 80 stades underwater to bring news of the wrecks, though Herodotus thought he came by boat. Plutarch cites a verse of Pindar that calls Artemisium the place where Athens laid the foundation of freedom.
l_athens.lead: Athens was the chief city of Attica, run as a democracy after the reforms of Cleisthenes about 508 BCE, with its sanctuaries on the rock of the Acropolis. Its troops joined the Ionian rebels in burning Sardis in 498 BCE and beat the Persian landing force at Marathon in 490 BCE, and Xerxes and then Mardonius burned it in 480 and 479 BCE. For Greek writers its sack and recovery became the centre of the story of the Persian wars.
l_athens.play: The chronicle presents Athens as the city of the Acropolis that helped burn Sardis, won at Marathon, and was burned by Xerxes in 480 BCE and by Mardonius in 479 BCE. This matches Herodotus.
l_athens.s0: Herodotus says that about 507 BCE Athenian envoys seeking help against Sparta gave earth and water to the satrap Artaphernes at Sardis, and were blamed for it at home (5.73). Later Artaphernes told Athens to take back the exiled tyrant Hippias, and it refused (5.96). Historians debate whether Persia then counted Athens as a subject that had broken faith. If so, the later campaigns were the punishment of rebels rather than new conquest.
l_athens.s1: Herodotus tells that Aristagoras of Miletus won over the Athenians, who sent twenty ships to the Ionian revolt. With the Eretrians they marched on Sardis in 498 BCE, and the lower town and its temple of Cybebe burned (5.97-102). In 490 BCE the force of Datis and the younger Artaphernes landed at Marathon with Hippias as guide, and the Athenians and Plataeans defeated it (6.102-117). Herodotus counts 6,400 Persian and 192 Athenian dead.
l_athens.s2: Herodotus says most Athenians left for Troezen, Aegina and Salamis before Xerxes arrived in 480 BCE (8.41). A few held the Acropolis behind a wooden barricade. Persians then climbed the steep side near the shrine of Aglaurus, killed the defenders and burned the sanctuary (8.51-53). Mardonius reoccupied the empty city in 479 BCE and offered terms, which were refused. On leaving for Boeotia he burned what still stood (9.3-13).
l_athens.s3: Excavations on the Acropolis found deposits of burnt debris, broken statues and marble korai. These were long read as debris the Athenians buried when they cleared the rock after 479 BCE, though some scholars now think the burials took place over a longer period. Drums from the unfinished Older Parthenon were built into the north wall of the citadel, where they can still be seen. Persian royal inscriptions do not name Athens.
l_athens.s4: Herodotus tells that when Darius heard of Sardis he shot an arrow into the sky and prayed to be allowed to punish the Athenians. He then had a servant remind him of them three times whenever dinner was served (5.105). Herodotus also says that on the day after the burning, Athenians sent up by Xerxes to sacrifice found Athena's sacred olive with a new shoot a cubit long (8.55). Both are moral tales of vengeance and survival, not records.
l_athos.lead: Athos is the easternmost of the three peninsulas that reach south from Chalcidice, ending in a steep mountain about 2,000 metres high. A Persian fleet under Mardonius was wrecked off its cape in 492 BCE. Xerxes then had a canal cut through the narrow neck of the peninsula so that his fleet of 480 BCE could avoid the cape altogether.
l_athos.play: Athos is the game's ninth level (483-480 BCE), with Xerxes' Canal and a Supply Depot among its buildings. The game's note calls it the Holy Mountain, a name from the later Christian monasteries that Herodotus never used.
l_athos.s0: Herodotus says that in 492 BCE Mardonius led an army and fleet along the Thracian coast, and that a violent north wind caught the ships as they rounded Athos and drove many onto the rocks. He puts the loss at about 300 ships and more than 20,000 men, figures historians treat as probably too high. With his army also mauled by the Thracian Brygi, Mardonius turned back to Asia.
l_athos.s1: Herodotus says the preparations took about three years, with the digging directed by two Persians, Bubares son of Megabazus and Artachaees son of Artaeus. Men from the forces and the local towns dug in turns under the lash, each people taking a stretch. He adds that only the Phoenicians cut their section wider at the top so its sides did not collapse, and that grain was brought from Asia to a market nearby.
l_athos.s2: Herodotus reports that the canal was wide enough for two triremes to be rowed abreast, and that Xerxes' fleet sailed through it in 480 BCE before heading west along the coast towards Therma. Thucydides, describing the region during the Peloponnesian War, still mentions the King's canal near Acanthus. Neither writer gives a measured width or depth.
