l_athos.s3: The line of the canal survives as a low, silted depression across the isthmus, roughly 2 kilometres long. Geophysical and coring surveys by a British and Greek team in the 1990s and early 2000s found a continuous buried channel with water-laid sediments. This showed that the canal was really dug from sea to sea, which some modern sceptics had doubted.
l_athos.s4: Herodotus judged that Xerxes ordered the canal out of pride and a wish to leave a monument, since ships could have been hauled across the neck on land. Modern historians usually point to the loss of 492 BCE and the danger of the cape. They see the work as a sensible way to protect a large fleet and its supply ships, and note that Herodotus wrote within a Greek tradition that cast Xerxes as arrogant.
l_attica.lead: Attica was the peninsula ruled from Athens, with Marathon on its north-east coast and the plain of Athens inland. Persian forces landed there in 490 BCE, took Athens in 480 BCE, and returned under Mardonius in 479 BCE. Greek writers made these events central to their memory of the wars.
l_attica.play: Attica has no level or mechanic of its own. The game names it in the Chronicle and in the event articles on Marathon, the capture of Athens and Plataea.
l_attica.s0: Herodotus says the Persian fleet under Datis and Artaphernes landed at Marathon on the Attic coast, guided by the exile Hippias, who knew the ground. The Athenians marched out to meet them rather than wait behind their walls. Herodotus gives the Athenian dead as 192 and the Persian dead as 6,400.
l_attica.s1: Herodotus says the Athenians moved most of their people to Salamis, Troezen and Aegina as Xerxes' army advanced. The Persians entered a largely empty city and took the Acropolis, where a small group of defenders held out for a time behind a wooden barricade. Herodotus says the Persians then burned the sanctuaries there.
l_attica.s2: Herodotus tells that after Salamis Mardonius wintered in Thessaly and Boeotia. In 479 BCE, when Athens rejected the offer brought by Alexander of Macedon, he marched into Attica again and found the city once more abandoned. He then withdrew into Boeotia before the Greek army gathered.
l_attica.s3: Excavations on the Acropolis found destruction debris from the Persian sack, including damaged statues and architectural pieces. The Athenians later buried much of this material in fills when they rebuilt. Such finds agree with the Greek accounts that the sanctuaries were burned in 480 BCE.
l_attica.s4: Herodotus presents the 490 BCE expedition as punishment for Athenian and Eretrian help to the Ionian rebels at Sardis. Some modern historians think the Persians also aimed to restore Hippias and to bring the Aegean islands and Euboea under control. The size of the force is also argued: Herodotus gives 600 ships, and historians generally treat the numbers of men in later sources as unreliable.
l_babylon.lead: Babylon was the largest and richest city of Mesopotamia and the capital of the last Babylonian kings. Cyrus took it in 539 BCE, and it became one of the empire's royal cities and a great source of tax. Twice in 522-521 BCE it rose against Darius under men who each claimed to be Nebuchadnezzar, son of its last native king.
l_babylon.play: Babylon is not one of the game's levels. It appears only in the Chronicle, which notes Cyrus's capture of the city in 539 BCE and the two rebels who called themselves Nebuchadnezzar under Darius.
l_babylon.s0: The Nabonidus Chronicle says Cyrus defeated the Babylonian army at Opis on the Tigris in autumn 539 BCE, then took Sippar without a battle. His general Ugbaru entered Babylon two days later, also without fighting, and Cyrus himself arrived a little over two weeks later. The Cyrus Cylinder, written for the new king, claims the god Marduk chose Cyrus to replace Nabonidus and that Cyrus returned displaced gods to their shrines.
l_babylon.s1: Herodotus describes Babylon's huge walls, its bridge across the Euphrates and the temple of Bel. He says Cyrus diverted the river and sent troops along the dry bed, so the city fell while people in its centre were still celebrating a festival. The Babylonian chronicle mentions no siege or river trick, only an entry without a battle, so his version is probably shaped by later storytelling.
l_babylon.s2: Darius says that in 522 BCE Nidintu-Bel seized Babylon calling himself Nebuchadnezzar, son of Nabonidus. Darius defeated him on the Tigris and at Zazana on the Euphrates and put him to death in Babylon. In 521 BCE Arakha, an Armenian, made the same claim. Darius's general Vindafarna (Intaphernes) captured him, and he was impaled at Babylon.
l_babylon.s3: Herodotus tells of a single Babylonian revolt against which Darius laid siege for about twenty months. A noble named Zopyrus cut off his own nose and ears, went over to the Babylonians as a supposed victim of Darius, won their trust and opened the gates. The tale is a moral story of loyalty, and it does not match the two separate revolts in Darius's own record.
l_babylon.s4: Babylonian tablets name two more rebel kings, Bel-shimanni and Shamash-eriba, in Xerxes' second year, about 484 BCE. Many family archives in northern Babylonia end at that time. Herodotus says Xerxes carried off a gold statue from the temple of Bel, and Arrian says Xerxes destroyed the temple. Historians still argue how harsh the reprisals were, and the older view that Xerxes razed the great temple is now widely doubted.
l_bactria.lead: Bactria was the fertile land between the Hindu Kush and the Oxus river (the Amu Darya), with its chief city at Bactra, near modern Balkh. Darius lists it among the lands he held, and it was one of the empire's great satrapies, often governed by a royal prince. Its gold went to the palace at Susa, and its men marched in Xerxes' army.
l_bactria.play: Bactria is named in the Chronicle's inventions and sources, in the Susa level's building charter, and in the 521 BCE revolts. The Bactrian spearman is its soldier, and the nations list carries its flag.
l_bactria.s0: Bactria is among the 23 lands Darius names at the start of the Behistun inscription. In the same text its satrap, a Persian whom Darius calls his servant, marches against Frada, the rebel of neighbouring Margiana, and beats him in 521 BCE. Bactria itself is not recorded as rising against Darius.
l_bactria.s1: Darius's building charter for his palace at Susa says the gold was brought from Sardis and from Bactria, and the lapis lazuli and carnelian from Sogdiana next door. Bactrian gold may have come from the rivers of the Oxus basin or through trade from further north.
l_bactria.s2: Herodotus puts the Bactrians, with their neighbours the Aeglians, in the twelfth tribute district, paying 360 talents of silver a year. In Xerxes' army, he says, they wore headgear much like the Medes and carried bows of their native cane and short spears.
l_bactria.s3: Herodotus tells how Darius settled the captives of Barca in a village in Bactria, which still bore their town's name in his day. Before Lade, he says, the Persians threatened the Ionians that their daughters would be carried off to Bactria. To a Greek it was the far end of the empire.
l_bactria.s4: A group of Aramaic letters and tallies from Bactria, written on leather and wood in the 4th century, show a satrap's office giving orders to local officials about building, supplies and debts. They come from long after this period, but show the same Aramaic chancery that ran the empire's other satrapies.
l_bagastana.lead: Bagastana, modern Bisitun in western Iran, is a limestone cliff above a spring on the main road from Mesopotamia to Ecbatana. There Darius had his victory over Gaumata and the rebel kings carved in a relief with a long inscription in three languages. It is the fullest Persian account of how he took the throne, and in modern times it became the key to reading cuneiform.
l_bagastana.play: Level 3 presents Bagastana as the place where the King's relief is cut into the cliff. The level is set in 522-521 BCE, but the carving probably began only after the victories, about 520 BCE, and was extended over the next few years.
l_bagastana.s0: The name probably comes from a reconstructed Old Persian baga-stana, place of the gods. Diodorus, drawing on Ctesias, calls the mountain Bagistanon and says it was sacred to Zeus, the Greek name for a great sky god. The cliff stood on the busy route between Babylon and the Median capital Ecbatana, so travellers on that road would see the monument, at least from below.
l_bagastana.s1: The relief, about 60 metres above the plain, shows Darius with his foot on the fallen Gaumata, followed by two attendants with bow and spear. Eight captive rebel kings stand before him, roped at the neck, and a winged figure hovers above. A ninth standing captive, Skunkha the Saka, was added after the Saka campaign of about 519 BCE. Carving his figure destroyed part of the first Elamite text, which was cut again nearby.
l_bagastana.s2: The inscription survives in Elamite, Babylonian and Old Persian. It tells how Darius killed Gaumata and, by his own count, defeated nine liar kings, Gaumata among them, in a single year. In §70 he says he sent the text out to the provinces, and pieces of a Babylonian copy on stone were found at Babylon, while an Aramaic version on papyrus survives from Elephantine. Henry Rawlinson copied the cliff text between 1835 and 1847, which helped scholars decipher cuneiform.
l_bagastana.s3: In DB §70 Darius says he made a new form of writing. Many take this to mean Old Persian cuneiform was devised for this monument, as its text was added after the Elamite and Babylonian versions, but others disagree. Darius and Herodotus both call the man he killed a magus who posed as Cyrus's son Bardiya, whom Herodotus names Smerdis. Some historians think he was the real Bardiya, which would make the inscription a defence of a seized throne.
l_bagastana.s4: Diodorus, following Ctesias, says that the Assyrian queen Semiramis camped below the mountain, laid out a park by the spring, and had her own image carved on the cliff with a hundred of her guards. The tale belongs to Greek stories of a half-mythical eastern queen and is not reliable history. It suggests that by about 400 BCE, when Ctesias wrote, Greek writers or their informants no longer linked the relief with Darius.
l_barca.lead: Barca was a Greek city in Cyrenaica, founded from Cyrene, probably in the sixth century. Herodotus tells how a Persian force sent from Egypt by the satrap Aryandes besieged it for nine months and took it by a trick. Many of the survivors were deported to Bactria, a sign of how far the King could move conquered people.
l_barca.play: Barca has no mechanic or level of its own. The game names it only in its event articles, chiefly the siege of Barca, which gives the nine months reported by Herodotus.
l_barca.s0: Herodotus says Barca arose when brothers of the Cyrene royal house quarrelled with their ruling kinsman, left the city and founded a settlement among the Libyans. The story rests on Herodotus alone.
l_barca.s1: Herodotus says Arcesilaus III of Cyrene fled to Barca and was killed there. His mother Pheretime went to Egypt and asked the satrap Aryandes for help. Herodotus presents the avenging of the murder as the reason, and says Aryandes gave her an army and a fleet.
l_barca.s2: Herodotus says the Persians dug mines, but a bronze worker detected them by listening with a bronze shield held against the ground. The Persians then offered terms and swore an oath that would hold while the ground beneath them stayed as it was. The Barcaeans came out, and the Persians broke the oath by letting the hidden covering of a trench give way.
l_barca.s3: Herodotus says Pheretime had the guilty men impaled round the wall and the breasts of their wives cut off. The rest of the Barcaeans were taken to Bactria, where Darius gave them a village. Herodotus adds that it was still called Barca in his own day.
l_barca.s4: Herodotus does not date the expedition closely, and many historians place it about 513 BCE. Historians also differ on how firmly Persia held Cyrenaica afterwards. No Persian inscription or tablet is known to mention the siege, so the account stays Greek.
l_behistun.lead: Behistun is a cliff in the Zagros mountains, near modern Kermanshah, where Darius I had a relief and his account of winning the throne carved after the revolts of 522-521 BCE. Written in Elamite, Babylonian and Old Persian, it is the longest Achaemenid royal inscription and the only one that narrates events at length. In the nineteenth century it became a key to reading cuneiform.
l_behistun.play: The Bagastana level is set in 522-521 BCE, the year of revolts the monument records; the carving itself came afterwards, about 520-518 BCE. The chronicle note's credit to Rawlinson is fair but simplified, as others shared the decipherment.
l_behistun.s0: The monument sits high on the cliff of Mount Bisotun, some 60 metres above a spring and the old road from Babylonia to Ecbatana. The relief shows Darius holding a bow, one foot on the fallen Gaumata, facing nine rebel leaders roped together at the neck, with a winged figure in a disc above. Two attendants stand behind the King, and a short label names each captive.
l_behistun.s1: Darius traces his ancestry back to Achaemenes and tells how he killed Gaumata, a magus who had seized the throne by claiming to be Bardiya. He then lists the rebels he defeated, among them Fravartish in Media, Vahyazdata in Persis and Arakha in Babylon, and names the six men who helped him. He ordered copies sent through the empire. An Aramaic version survives on papyrus from Elephantine, and fragments of a Babylonian version survive from Babylon.
l_behistun.s2: The rock shows the work grew in phases: the relief and an Elamite text, then a Babylonian version, then the Old Persian. The later figure of the Saka captive Skunkha cut into the first Elamite text, which was carved again elsewhere. Scholars debate whether Old Persian script was invented for this monument, as DB §70 may imply. They also debate whether the man Darius killed was an impostor, as Darius and Herodotus say, or the real Bardiya.
l_behistun.s3: Henry Rawlinson, a British officer, began copying the Old Persian text in 1835 and returned in 1844 and 1847, when a local boy helped take paper squeezes of the Babylonian text. He published the Old Persian text in 1846-47, building on Grotefend's earlier work, and his Babylonian copy was central to reading Akkadian. Credit for the decipherment is still argued, since Edward Hincks, Jules Oppert and others made key advances independently.
l_behistun.s4: Diodorus, probably drawing on Ctesias, called the mountain Bagistanon and said it was sacred to Zeus. He credited the carving to the Assyrian queen Semiramis, who was said to have laid out a garden at its foot. The Greek name probably preserves a reconstructed Old Persian Bagastana, place of the gods, but the Semiramis story is a later invention. Medieval Persian poets linked the cliff to Farhad, who cut through mountains for love of Shirin.
l_black_sea.lead: The Black Sea, the Greeks' Pontus or Euxine, lies between Asia Minor, Thrace and the Scythian steppe. Milesian and other Greek colonies ringed its shores, and its grain fed Greece. Darius gazed on it from the Bosporus before his Scythian campaign, and the Ionians sailed up it to bridge the Ister.
l_black_sea.play: The Black Sea is named in the Ister level's intro, where the Ionians sail up it to the river, and in the Thermopylae level's grain ships.
l_black_sea.s0: Herodotus says Darius, on reaching the Bosporus, sailed to the Cyanean rocks, sat in the temple there and gazed on the Pontus, of all seas the most marvellous. He measures it at 11,100 furlongs long and 3,300 at its widest, from a ship's run by day and by night.
l_black_sea.s1: For the Scythian campaign Darius sent the Ionians and the other Greeks of his fleet into the Pontus as far as the Ister, to bridge the river two days' sail up from the sea. Herodotus says they came with six hundred ships.
l_black_sea.s2: At Abydos in 480 BCE Xerxes saw ships carrying grain from the Pontus through the Hellespont to Aegina and the Peloponnese, and let them pass. Herodotus also says some Scythians north of the sea grew grain not to eat but to sell, which the Greek ports shipped out.
l_black_sea.s3: Excavations at Istros, Olbia, Apollonia, Sinope and other cities show Greek settlements on the coasts from the late seventh century, most of them founded from Miletus. Their pottery, coins and inscriptions record the trade between the steppe and the Aegean.
l_boeotia.lead: Boeotia was the region of central Greece north of Mount Cithaeron, with Thebes as its leading city. In Herodotus's account most of its cities sided with Xerxes in 480 BCE, and in 479 BCE Mardonius fell back into it. The battle of Plataea, which ended the Persian invasion of mainland Greece, was fought on Boeotian ground.
l_boeotia.play: The game names Boeotia in Chronicle entries and in event articles for Plataea, as the region where Mardonius fell back and the final battle was fought. It has no mechanic of its own.
l_boeotia.s0: Herodotus treats Boeotia as a region of separate cities, with Thebes the strongest. Plataea, on the slopes of Cithaeron, was the notable exception, being allied to Athens. Herodotus is hostile to the Thebans for going over to the Persians, and modern readers allow that Athenian feeling may have coloured his portrait.
l_boeotia.s1: Herodotus says that when Xerxes' army advanced, most of the Boeotians submitted, while Thespiae and Plataea refused. The Thebans who stood at Thermopylae were held there reluctantly, he says, and surrendered to Xerxes, claiming they had been compelled. He adds that the Persians then burned Thespiae and Plataea.
l_boeotia.s2: Herodotus says that in 479 BCE Mardonius withdrew from Attica after the second capture of Athens, into Boeotia, which suited his cavalry better than the rough ground of Attica. He gives the Thebans' advice and friendship as part of the setting. Herodotus reports that he built a fortified camp beside the Asopus, near Thebes.
l_boeotia.s3: The Greek army crossed Cithaeron and took position on the foothills near Plataea, facing the Persians across the Asopus. Herodotus describes days of skirmishing, in which Persian cavalry harassed the Greek supply routes and fouled the spring of Gargaphia. He says the Greeks shifted their position, and that the Persian camp fell to them in the decisive fighting.
l_boeotia.s4: Modern historians disagree about where on the ground the fighting took place, since Herodotus's topography is hard to match to the landscape. The location of the Island, where the Greeks moved, and the course of the streams are argued. His account of the Greek manoeuvres is also debated.
l_bosporus.lead: The Bosporus is the narrow strait, about 30 kilometres long, that links the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara and divides Asia from Europe, with Chalcedon on the Asian shore and Byzantium on the European. About 513 BCE Darius had it bridged with boats so that his army could cross into Thrace against the Scythians. It was the first time a Persian king led an army into Europe.
l_bosporus.play: The game names the Bosporus in its chronicle, noting Mandrocles' bridge of boats for Darius's Scythian march about 513 BCE, following Herodotus 4.85-88. The year is a modern estimate; Herodotus gives none.
l_bosporus.s0: Herodotus says Darius marched from Susa to Chalcedon, sailed to the temple at the strait's northern mouth to view the Black Sea, and then crossed on a bridge of boats designed by Mandrocles of Samos. By his own guess the bridge lay about midway between Byzantium and that temple. Modern scholars usually put it near the narrowest point, where the strait is well under a kilometre wide. Darius, Herodotus adds, rewarded Mandrocles generously.
l_bosporus.s1: With part of his reward Mandrocles paid for a painting of the crossing, showing Darius enthroned as his army passed over, and dedicated it in the temple of Hera on Samos with verses naming himself. Herodotus adds that Darius set up two pillars of white stone by the strait, one in Assyrian and one in Greek letters, listing the peoples of his army. He gives that army as 700,000 men and 600 ships, figures historians consider greatly exaggerated.
l_bosporus.s2: Herodotus says the general Otanes took Byzantium and Chalcedon after the Scythian campaign. Byzantium joined the Ionian Revolt about 498 BCE. After the Ionian defeat at Lade in 494 BCE, the people of both cities fled to Mesambria on the Black Sea, and about 493 BCE the Phoenician fleet burned their abandoned land. Thucydides says the Spartan Pausanias took Byzantium from the Persians in 478 BCE.
l_bosporus.s3: Herodotus gives no year. Most historians date the crossing to about 513 or 512 BCE, though some have argued for an earlier date in the 510s BCE. Darius's own inscriptions do not describe a European campaign, but the list of lands on his tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam names Skudra, usually taken as Thrace, and Saka living across the sea. Herodotus tells the Scythian war as a failure; many historians think Darius at least secured Thrace and the straits.
l_bosporus.s4: Greek writers explained the name Bosporus as cow's crossing, from the myth of Io, loved by Zeus, turned into a heifer and driven over the sea by a gadfly sent by Hera. In Prometheus Bound Aeschylus gives the name to the Cimmerian Bosporus, at the mouth of the Sea of Azov, while the later mythographer Apollodorus ties it to this Thracian strait. The tale is myth and tells nothing about the Persian use of the strait.
l_cappadocia.lead: Cappadocia was the high plateau of central Anatolia east of the Halys river, called Katpatuka in Darius's inscriptions. Herodotus says the Greeks called its people Syrians. It lay between Lydia and Armenia on the road from Sardis to Susa, and it came into Persian hands when Cyrus beat Croesus in the 540s BCE.
l_cappadocia.play: Cappadocia is named in the Chronicle's sources, in the lists of lands from the Behistun inscription and the Persepolis texts, and among the nations. It is not a level and has no mechanic of its own.
l_cappadocia.s0: Katpatuka appears among the lands Darius names at Behistun, and again in his lists at Persepolis and on his tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam, next to Armenia and Sparda (Sardis). Its delegates are among the tribute bearers carved on the stairs of the Apadana, though which group is theirs is argued.
l_cappadocia.s1: Herodotus says Croesus crossed the Halys into Cappadocia to attack Cyrus, took the city of Pteria and enslaved its people. The two kings fought an indecisive battle there before Croesus went home to Sardis, where Cyrus followed and took the city.
l_cappadocia.s2: Herodotus says the Cappadocians were called Syrians by the Greeks, and that before the Persians they had been subject to the Medes. In Xerxes' army, he says, they were equipped like the Paphlagonians, with plaited helmets, small shields and short spears.
l_cappadocia.s3: Herodotus traces the Royal Road from Sardis across the Halys and through Cappadocia to the border of Cilicia, with its posting stations and inns. The exact line through the plateau is argued; some scholars run it further north, through Pteria, others further south.
l_cappadocia.s4: Strabo, writing about 500 years later, says he saw magi in Cappadocia tending fires that never went out in enclosed sanctuaries. That was the practice of his own day. It should not be read back to the reign of Darius without other evidence.
l_caria.lead: Caria was the rugged south-western corner of Anatolia, south of the Maeander river, with Greek towns such as Halicarnassus on its coast. Its people spoke their own language and served abroad as soldiers. Harpagus brought it under Cyrus about 545 BCE, and in 497 BCE it joined the Ionian revolt and fought the Persians harder than any other rebel land.
l_caria.play: The Sardis Burns level's second act tells how the revolt spread to Caria. Carian mercenaries fight in the game's armies, and the Carians have their flag among the nations.
l_caria.s0: After Sardis fell, Herodotus says, Cyrus left Harpagus to finish the conquest of the western coast. Harpagus took Caria with the help of Ionian levies. The Carians, he says, did little to resist, except the people of Pedasus, who held out on a hill for a time.
l_caria.s1: Herodotus says the Greeks learned three things from the Carians: to put crests on helmets, to paint devices on shields and to fit shields with handles. He reports that the Carians said they had always lived on the mainland, while the Cretans said they had come from the islands.
l_caria.s2: Carians and Ionians, the "bronze men" of an oracle, helped Psammetichus I win Egypt in the 7th century, and he settled them in camps near the Nile. Inscriptions in the Carian script found in Egypt, at Saqqara and elsewhere, confirm Carian soldiers and their families living there.
l_caria.s3: When the Carians joined the revolt, Herodotus says, they met the Persians at the river Marsyas and were beaten, then beaten again at the grove of Zeus of Armies at Labraunda. They then ambushed a Persian army by night on the road to Pedasus and destroyed it with its generals.
l_caria.s4: In 480 BCE the Carian queen Artemisia, ruling Halicarnassus, Cos, Nisyros and Calydna, led five ships in Xerxes' fleet. Herodotus, himself from Halicarnassus, ranks her squadron second only to the ships of Sidon and makes her the wisest of the King's advisers.
l_carthage.lead: Carthage was a Phoenician city on the North African coast. Persian records do not mention it. Herodotus says Cambyses planned to send the fleet against it after the conquest of Egypt, but the Phoenicians refused to sail against their own colony and the plan was dropped.
l_carthage.play: The game names Carthage in Chronicle entries and in event articles such as the abandoned expedition. It has no level, building or mechanic of its own.
l_carthage.s0: Herodotus speaks of the Carthaginians as descendants of Phoenicians, a point on which his story of the refusal depends. Later writers trace the founding to settlers from Tyre, which is probably right but rests on late tradition. No Persian royal inscription names the city, so the Persian view of it is unknown.
l_carthage.s1: Herodotus says that after Egypt fell, Cambyses planned three campaigns: one against Carthage by sea, one against the Ammonians, and one against the Ethiopians. He intended to use the Phoenician fleet for the first and to send part of his land army against the others.
l_carthage.s2: According to Herodotus, the Phoenicians would not sail against Carthage, because they were bound by oaths and did not wish to attack their own children. Cambyses did not force them, since they had joined him willingly and the fleet depended on them. Herodotus adds that the Carthaginians thus escaped Persian rule.
l_carthage.s3: No Persian document confirms the plan, and Herodotus is the only source for it. Historians differ on whether it was a serious design that failed or a later explanation for why Persian power never reached Carthage. Herodotus does record Persian reach in Libya: Cyrene submitted to Cambyses, and Barca was later besieged under Darius.
l_carthage.s4: Diodorus, writing centuries later, says the Carthaginian attack on Sicily was timed with Xerxes' invasion. Herodotus reports the Carthaginian defeat in Sicily but does not describe any agreement with Xerxes. Whether the two were coordinated is uncertain, and the Greek wish to pair victories in east and west may have shaped the tale.
l_chersonese.lead: The Chersonese, the "land-island", is the long peninsula of Thrace that forms the European shore of the Hellespont, today Gallipoli. Athenian lords ruled it in the 6th century, Miltiades last of them, under the Persian King. Xerxes' bridges reached its shore in 480 BCE, and its strongest town, Sestos, fell to the Athenians in 479 BCE.
l_chersonese.play: The Chersonese is the ground of the Sestos field and its briefing, and its ridge shapes the map. The Marathon chatter recalls Miltiades fleeing it, and a house of Sestos stands there.
l_chersonese.s0: Herodotus says the Dolonci, a Thracian people of the peninsula, invited the elder Miltiades from Athens to rule them. He built a wall across the neck of the peninsula, from Cardia to Pactye, to keep out raiders from the north. His nephew, the younger Miltiades, later took over the rule.
l_chersonese.s1: Miltiades served Darius with the other Greek lords in the Scythian campaign of 513 BCE. Herodotus says he urged them to break the Ister bridge and leave the King to the Scythians. Many historians doubt this, since he went on ruling under Persia for years; the tale may have grown when he was tried at Athens.
l_chersonese.s2: When the Phoenician fleet arrived after the fall of Miletus, Miltiades loaded five ships with his goods and fled to Athens. The Phoenicians caught one, with his son Metiochus on board, and took him to Darius, who gave him a house, land and a Persian wife.
l_chersonese.s3: Xerxes' bridges ran from Abydos to the Chersonese shore between Sestos and Madytus, Herodotus says. The army crossed over seven days and nights, then marched up the peninsula and out across its neck into Thrace.
l_chersonese.s4: In 479 BCE the Athenians besieged Sestos, held by the governor Artayctes with the Persians of the peninsula. Herodotus says Artayctes had plundered the shrine of the hero Protesilaus at Elaeus, at the peninsula's tip. When the town fell, the Athenians put him to death near where the bridges had stood.
l_chios.lead: Chios is a large island off the Ionian coast, famous for its wine. It joined the Ionian Revolt, and at Lade in 494 BCE its hundred ships fought on after the Samians and Lesbians fled. The Persians then took the island, and in 479 BCE the Chians joined the Greek alliance after Mycale.
l_chios.play: Chios is named in the Sardis level's Lade texts, where the Chians fight on, and in the chatter about its wine.
l_chios.s0: The Chians brought a hundred ships to Lade, each with forty picked citizens as marines. Herodotus says that when others fled they fought on, breaking through the enemy line again and again, until they had lost most of their ships and the rest escaped home.
l_chios.s1: Histiaeus fell on the Chians who had come home from Lade and killed many. The next year the Persian fleet took Chios, Lesbos and Tenedos and swept the islands, men holding hands across each island to hunt the people out.
l_chios.s2: In 480 BCE Chios was ruled for Persia by the tyrant Strattis. Herodotus says six Chians who had plotted to kill him fled to the Greek fleet and begged it to sail to Ionia; one of them was named Herodotus.
l_chios.s3: After Mycale, the Greeks met at Samos and debated moving the Ionians to Greece. The Athenians refused, and the Samians, Chians, Lesbians and other islanders were taken into the alliance on oath.
l_chios.s4: Chian wine was among the most prized in the Greek world, and its amphorae, often marked with a sphinx, are found from the Black Sea to Egypt. Chian coins of the period show a seated sphinx beside an amphora.
l_cilicia.lead: Cilicia was the coastal plain and mountains of south-eastern Anatolia, facing Cyprus across a narrow sea. Its own kings, each called Syennesis by the Greeks, ruled it under the Persian King. Its harbours and plain were where the King's armies gathered to sail west, against Cyprus in 497 BCE and against Eretria and Athens in 490 BCE.
l_cilicia.play: The Sardis Burns level tells of the army crossing from Cilicia to win back Cyprus, and the Athos and Marathon chatter of the fleets that sailed from it. The Cilicians have their flag among the nations.
l_cilicia.s0: Herodotus names a Syennesis of Cilicia who helped make peace between the Lydians and Medes after the eclipse battle, and another, son of Oromedon, who commanded the Cilician ships in 480 BCE. The name seems to have been a title the Greeks took for a personal name.
l_cilicia.s1: Herodotus says Cilicia paid 360 white horses, one for each day, and 500 talents of silver a year. Of that silver, 140 talents went to the horsemen who guarded the country, and the rest to the King.
l_cilicia.s2: When the Cypriot towns joined the Ionian revolt in 497 BCE, Herodotus says, the Persian general Artybius brought an army by sea to Cilicia and crossed from there to Cyprus. The Phoenician fleet sailed round to Cyprus with it, and within a year the island was the King's again.
l_cilicia.s3: Datis and Artaphernes gathered their army on the Aleian plain in Cilicia, Herodotus says. There the fleet took the soldiers and horses on board, sailed to Samos and then across the Aegean by the islands, to Naxos, Delos, Eretria and Marathon.
l_cilicia.s4: In 480 BCE the Cilicians sent 100 ships to Xerxes' fleet. Herodotus says their crews wore their native helmets and carried shields of rawhide, with woollen tunics, two javelins each and swords like Egyptian ones.
l_cithaeron.lead: Cithaeron is the mountain range that divides Boeotia from Attica and the Megarid, and the Asopus is the small river that runs east across the plain beneath its northern slopes. In 479 BCE the army of Mardonius and the allied Greek army faced each other across this ground for more than ten days, by Herodotus's count, before the battle of Plataea, and the passes, springs and ridges of the area shaped how that battle was fought.
l_cithaeron.play: The game presents this as the ground of Plataea, the setting of its Plataea level. That matches history: the armies of 479 BCE camped and fought on the Asopus plain below Cithaeron, near the town of Plataea.
l_cithaeron.s0: Herodotus says Mardonius left Attica for Boeotia and camped along the Asopus, his line running from Erythrae past Hysiae into Plataean land. There he built a fortified enclosure of timber, about ten stades on each side. The Greeks came over Cithaeron and first took position on its foothills near Erythrae, where the slopes protected them from the Persian cavalry.
l_cithaeron.s1: Herodotus says that after an early clash near Erythrae, in which the Persian cavalry commander Masistius was killed, the Greeks moved down towards Plataea, near the spring of Gargaphia and the shrine of the hero Androcrates. There the seers on both sides, Tisamenus for the Greeks and Hegesistratus for Mardonius, found the omens good only for defence, so neither army crossed the Asopus to attack.
l_cithaeron.s2: The Greek army drew supplies and men over the Cithaeron passes. Herodotus says a Theban, Timagenidas, advised Mardonius to watch the pass called the Oak-heads, and Persian horsemen there captured some 500 pack animals bringing food from the Peloponnese. Later the cavalry drove the Greeks from the Asopus and fouled the Gargaphia spring, which pushed the Greeks into a night withdrawal towards a place called the Island, in front of Plataea.
l_cithaeron.s3: Herodotus gives names and distances but no map, and the ground has changed since antiquity. Modern scholars disagree over where Gargaphia, the Island and the sanctuary of Demeter lay, and so over how far each Greek contingent moved in the night retreat. They also debate whether that retreat was a confused breakdown, as Herodotus tells it, or a planned move. His figure of 300,000 for Mardonius's army is generally thought much too high.
l_cithaeron.s4: In Greek tradition Cithaeron was a wild place sacred to Dionysus, where Pentheus was torn apart and the infant Oedipus was left to die. Plutarch, writing centuries after the battle, tells that an oracle told the Athenians to pray to the gods of Cithaeron and fight on the plain of Demeter, and that the Plataeans gave up their land to Athens to fulfil it. These stories show how the place was remembered, not how the campaign was planned.
l_cyprus.lead: Cyprus was an island of Greek and Phoenician towns, each under its own king, rich in copper and timber. It passed to Persian rule under Cambyses, and in 498 BCE most of its cities joined the Ionian Revolt under Onesilus of Salamis. The Persians crushed the rising within about a year.
l_cyprus.play: Cyprus has no level or mechanic of its own. The game mentions it in the event articles on the revolt of Cyprus and Onesilus's rising, where the siege at Paphos is described.
l_cyprus.s0: Herodotus describes Cyprus as divided among several kings, with Greek cities and a Phoenician settlement at Amathus. He says Amasis of Egypt had earlier conquered the island, and that the Cypriots gave themselves to Cambyses when he marched on Egypt. He lists them among the Darius-era tribute districts, together with the Phoenicians and Syrians.
l_cyprus.s1: Herodotus reports that Cyprus supplied ships to Cambyses for the Egyptian campaign, and that the Cypriots again served in the fleet of Xerxes. He gives their number as 150 ships, a figure that is his own and probably too high. Persian rule seems to have left the local kings in place, but the sources say little about the terms.
l_cyprus.s2: Herodotus says that Onesilus, brother of King Gorgus of Salamis, urged revolt, and that when Gorgus refused he shut him out of the city and took power. All the Cypriot cities joined except Amathus, and Onesilus besieged Amathus.
l_cyprus.s3: Herodotus says a Persian army under Artybius crossed from Cilicia, while a Phoenician fleet also came. The Ionians beat the Phoenicians at sea, but on land Onesilus was killed and the Salaminian chariots and the king of Curium changed sides. The Persians then besieged the remaining cities, and Soli held out for about five months before it fell to mining.
l_cyprus.s4: Excavations at Palaepaphos found a large siege ramp built against the city wall, made partly of stone from nearby sanctuaries and containing many weapons. Most scholars link it to a Persian attack in the revolt of about 498 BCE, but the date and the details of the assault are argued. Herodotus does not describe this siege, so the ramp is the main evidence for it.
l_cyprus.s5: Herodotus says Cyprus was enslaved again after one year of freedom. Cypriot ships later served in Xerxes' fleet. Little is known of Persian rule there after 497 BCE.
l_cyrene.lead: Cyrene was the chief Greek city of eastern Libya, a colony of Thera planted in the late seventh century. It lay on the western edge of the Egyptian world. Herodotus says it gave itself up to Cambyses after the conquest of Egypt, and its later story is bound up with Barca and the Persian governor of Egypt.
l_cyrene.play: The game names Cyrene only in the Chronicle and in event articles, such as the Siege of Memphis entry, which says it sent gifts to Cambyses. It has no mechanic of its own.
l_cyrene.s0: Herodotus tells the founding story in Book 4: settlers from Thera, led by Battus, first occupied an island and then moved to the mainland site of Cyrene. The Battiad dynasty ruled the city for generations. Herodotus links the colony to an oracle from Delphi and gives both a Theran and a Cyrenaean version.
l_cyrene.s1: Herodotus says that after Egypt fell, the Libyans near Egypt and the people of Cyrene and Barca gave themselves up to Cambyses out of fear and sent gifts. He says Cambyses took the Cyrenaean gift, a sum of silver, with little favour, and that the soldiers shared it. No surviving Persian text records the submission.
l_cyrene.s2: Historians doubt how far Cambyses' authority reached over Cyrenaica. The gifts may mark a loose recognition of Persian overlordship rather than direct rule. The later Persian action at Barca suggests the governor of Egypt claimed some authority, but its degree is argued.
l_cyrene.s3: In Herodotus's telling, Arcesilaus III of Cyrene was killed after fleeing to Barca, and his mother Pheretime went to Egypt and asked the satrap Aryandes for an army. Aryandes sent a force that besieged Barca and, after taking it, resettled many of its people in Bactria. Herodotus says the army also reached Euesperides, and he describes Pheretime's death in grim terms.
l_cyrene.s4: Herodotus's list of Darius's districts names the Libyans, Cyrene and Barca together with Egypt in the sixth district. Whether Cyrene paid a regular share is uncertain, and historians treat his list with caution.
l_delos.lead: Delos was a small island in the central Cyclades, held to be the birthplace of Apollo and Artemis. Herodotus says the fleet of Datis and Artaphernes passed it in 490 BCE and did not harm it. The story is told by a Greek writer, and the Persian side has left no account of the visit.
l_delos.play: Delos is named in the Chronicle and in the event article on the expedition of Datis and Artaphernes, as the island of Apollo spared by Datis. It has no mechanic of its own.
l_delos.s0: Excavation on Delos by the French School at Athens has uncovered the sanctuary of Apollo and the remains of earlier cult buildings. The island was a major festival centre for Ionians and islanders. Most of the surviving monuments are probably later than 490 BCE, so the site shows the cult's importance rather than the events of that year.
l_delos.s1: Herodotus says the Delians fled to Tenos when the Persian fleet approached. Datis sent a herald to ask why they had run away and to say that he would not harm the island, since it was the birthplace of the two gods and the King had ordered it spared. Herodotus adds that Datis then burned a great quantity of frankincense on the altar.
l_delos.s2: Herodotus says Delos was shaken by an earthquake soon after, the first and last in his knowledge, and that it was a portent of coming troubles. Thucydides mentions a shock on Delos shortly before the Peloponnesian War, which sits uneasily with Herodotus's claim that there was no later one. The omen is a Greek reading made after the event.
l_delos.s3: Persian respect for Apollo may fit a wider pattern of the King's officials honouring local cults, as with Egyptian and Babylonian temples. It is uncertain how far Datis acted from policy and how far Herodotus shaped the scene. The Persian side leaves no account of the visit.
l_delos.s4: In 478 and 477 BCE the Greek allies formed a league under Athens, and Thucydides says its common fund was kept on Delos and the allies met in the sanctuary. The treasury was later moved to Athens, a step modern scholars usually date to about 454 BCE. Plutarch connects the move with Pericles.
l_delphi.lead: Delphi was the most famous oracle of the Greek world, where a priestess of Apollo, the Pythia, answered the questions of cities and kings. Croesus of Lydia asked it whether to fight Cyrus, and Athens and other Greek cities asked it how to face Xerxes' coming invasion. No Persian text names Delphi, so its dealings with Lydia and Persia are known from Greek writers, above all Herodotus, and from the remains of the sanctuary.
l_delphi.play: The game describes Delphi as the oracle the Greeks and Lydians consulted. That is accurate, though it gives only the Greek side: no Persian document mentions Delphi or any Persian consultation of it.
l_delphi.s0: Delphi lay on the steep slopes of Mount Parnassus above the Gulf of Corinth. French excavations since 1892 have uncovered the terraced precinct of Apollo. It contains the temple, the treasuries built by Greek cities to hold their offerings, and many bases for dedications. The Athenian Treasury, rebuilt from its original marble blocks in the early twentieth century, still stands beside the Sacred Way.
l_delphi.s1: Herodotus says Croesus of Lydia tested several oracles by asking what he was doing on a set day, and Delphi answered correctly. He then sent rich gifts of gold and silver, some of which Herodotus saw there. Told that if he made war on the Persians he would destroy a great empire, Croesus attacked Cyrus in the 540s BCE and lost his own. Herodotus adds that the god later said the answer had been his to misread.
l_delphi.s2: Herodotus says the Pythia first told the Athenians to flee to the ends of the earth, then spoke of a wooden wall that would save them and of divine Salamis. Themistocles argued that the wall meant the fleet. Delphi also discouraged Argos and Crete from joining the defence. Historians debate when these oracles were given, perhaps 481 BCE or earlier. They also debate whether the verses were polished after the victory, and whether Delphi's caution shows it expected the King to win.
l_delphi.s3: Herodotus tells that Xerxes sent troops to plunder Delphi. Sacred weapons moved out of the temple by themselves, thunderbolts fell, rocks crashed down from Parnassus and two local heroes chased the Persians away. The story reads as proof of the god's protection, and many historians doubt that a serious attack was ever made. Elsewhere Herodotus has Mardonius say that an oracle foretold ruin for Persians who plundered Delphi, so they would not go there.
l_delphi.s4: After Plataea in 479 BCE the Greeks set up a gold tripod at Delphi on a bronze column of three twisted snakes. Thucydides says Pausanias of Sparta first had a verse naming himself inscribed, and the Spartans replaced it with a list of the cities that had fought. The column was later taken to Constantinople. Its lower part, with 31 city names on the coils, still stands in Istanbul.
l_didyma.lead: Didyma was the great sanctuary and oracle of Apollo in the territory of Miletus, about 16 km south of the city, kept by a priestly family called the Branchidae. Kings sent it rich gifts. When the Persians took Miletus in 494 BCE, Herodotus says, they plundered and burned it. The huge temple that stands there now was begun long after.
l_didyma.play: The Sardis Burns level's news of Miletus's fall and its chatter tell of the shrine at Didyma burning. It is not a building in the game and has no mechanic of its own.
l_didyma.s0: Herodotus says Croesus sent offerings to the Branchidae equal in weight and kind to his gifts at Delphi. The pharaoh Necho dedicated there the clothes he had worn in his victories. In 499 BCE Hecataeus urged the rebels to pay for a fleet with Croesus's treasures in the shrine, but he was not heeded.
l_didyma.s1: When the Lydian rebel Pactyes fled to Cyme, its people asked the oracle at Didyma whether to hand him to the Persians. Herodotus says the god twice told them to, and that a citizen named Aristodicus drove the birds from the temple, to be rebuked by a voice from the shrine.
l_didyma.s2: Herodotus says that when Miletus fell after Lade, the sanctuary at Didyma, its temple and its oracle were plundered and burned. He links it to a Delphic oracle that foretold Miletus's ruin and that others would tend the shrine of Didyma.
l_didyma.s3: Strabo, writing much later, says Xerxes burned Didyma in 479 BCE and that the Branchidae betrayed its treasures and went east with him. Herodotus puts the burning in 494 BCE, after Miletus fell. Excavation shows destruction of the archaic temple but cannot settle the date or which story is right.
l_didyma.s4: A large bronze knucklebone weight found at Susa carries a Greek dedication to Apollo. Most scholars think it was carried off from Didyma as plunder. If so, it is a rare physical trace of the spoils Herodotus says the Persians took from the shrine.
l_doriscus.lead: Doriscus was a Persian fort and coastal plain in Thrace, near the mouth of the Hebrus river. Darius placed a garrison there during his Scythian campaign. In 480 BCE Xerxes used the plain to review his army and fleet and to count his land forces before the march into Greece. Almost everything known about it comes from Herodotus, whose figures for the army are far too large.
l_doriscus.play: The game marks Doriscus as the place where Xerxes counted his army, which follows Herodotus. The counting method and the vast total are his story, not a Persian record.
l_doriscus.s0: Doriscus was a stretch of shore and a wide plain in Thrace, beside the mouth of the Hebrus river (the modern Evros or Maritsa). Herodotus says a royal fort stood there, and that Darius had kept a Persian garrison in it since his march against the Scythians, about 513 BCE. Xerxes later had food stored at Doriscus, one of several depots along the Thracian coast. The exact site of the fort has not been securely located.
l_doriscus.s1: Herodotus says that in 480 BCE Xerxes halted at Doriscus to number his land army. Officers packed 10,000 men together as tightly as they could, drew a line round them and built a wall about waist high along it. Group after group was then marched into the enclosure until the whole army had passed through. Herodotus gives the result as 170 enclosures, or 1,700,000 foot soldiers.
l_doriscus.s2: No historian today accepts Herodotus's figures. Besides the 1,700,000 infantry he adds 80,000 cavalry and a fleet of 1,207 triremes. Later he reckons more than five million people once camp followers are included. The land could not have fed or watered such numbers. Modern estimates for the fighting army mostly fall between about 100,000 and 300,000, and some are lower still.
l_doriscus.s3: At Doriscus Herodotus lists the army contingent by contingent, with each people's dress, weapons and commanders, from Persians and Medes to Ethiopians and Thracians. Some historians think he drew on a Persian document, or on a list like the royal inscriptions that name the lands of the empire. Others see it as largely his own composition, built from Greek knowledge and meant to show the whole empire on the march.
l_doriscus.s4: Herodotus says Xerxes rode past the ranks in a chariot and then sailed along the line of ships in a Sidonian vessel. He made a Persian named Mascames governor of Doriscus. When the Greeks later drove the other Persian governors out of Thrace and the Hellespont, Herodotus says none could take Doriscus from Mascames. Xerxes sent him gifts every year, and Artaxerxes kept sending them to his descendants.
l_ecbatana.lead: Ecbatana, Hagmatana in Old Persian, was the chief city of the Medes in the Zagros highlands, where modern Hamadan stands. Cyrus took it from Astyages in about 550 BCE, and it remained one of the royal centres of the empire. Darius executed the Median rebel Fravartish there in 521 BCE, so the city stood at the heart of both the Persian rise and the crisis that followed.
l_ecbatana.play: Ecbatana is not one of the game's levels; the chronicle names it as the Median capital where Fravartish was put to death, as the Behistun inscription records. The seven walls come only from Herodotus.
l_ecbatana.s0: Herodotus says the Median king Deioces founded Ecbatana on a hill and ringed it with seven concentric walls. In his account the battlements of each ring were painted a different colour, the two innermost covered in silver and gold, with the king's palace and treasuries at the centre. No excavation has confirmed this plan. Many historians read it as a Greek picture of an eastern capital rather than a survey.
l_ecbatana.s1: The Nabonidus Chronicle, a Babylonian record, says that Astyages marched against Cyrus, king of Anshan, and that his own army rebelled and handed him over. Cyrus then went to Ecbatana, the royal city, and carried silver, gold and other goods back to Anshan. The entry falls in the sixth year of Nabonidus, about 550 BCE, and is the only near-contemporary record of the city's fall.
l_ecbatana.s2: In the Behistun inscription Darius says that Fravartish, who claimed the Median throne as a descendant of Cyaxares, fled after his defeat and was captured at Raga. Darius had his nose, ears and tongue cut off and one eye put out, and kept him bound at the palace gate where all the people saw him. He then impaled him at Ecbatana and hanged his leading followers there within the fortress.
l_ecbatana.s3: Xenophon, in his idealised life of Cyrus, says the king spent two summer months at Ecbatana, three spring months at Susa and seven winter months at Babylon, since the highland city was cool in the heat. The Book of Ezra, written later, places a scroll recording Cyrus's decree on the Jerusalem temple in the fortress at Ecbatana in Media. Both remember the city as a royal seat after the Median kings.
l_ecbatana.s4: Excavations at Tepe Hegmataneh in Hamadan have uncovered a grid of mudbrick buildings that many scholars now date after the Achaemenids, while Median and early Persian levels lie under the modern city. Historians also argue over how large and centralised the Median kingdom was, since its picture as a great empire rests mainly on Herodotus. Gold tablets in the names of Ariaramnes and Arsames said to come from Hamadan are suspected forgeries or later works.
l_egypt.lead: Egypt was the long valley and delta of the Nile, among the oldest and richest kingdoms the Persians ruled. Cambyses conquered it in 525 BCE and took the pharaoh's titles. As the satrapy of Mudraya it paid tribute in silver and grain, sent ships and men, and rose against the King in 522 BCE and again in 486 BCE.
l_egypt.play: The Spear-bearer level is set in Egypt, at Memphis in 525-524 BCE. Its houses, palms, wildlife and weather are Egyptian, and Egypt carries its flag among the nations and on the battle banner.
l_egypt.s0: Herodotus says the part of Egypt the Greeks sailed to was land the Nile had made, "the gift of the river". He describes how the flood each summer covered the fields, so that grain could be sown with little ploughing. The rise and fall of the Nile ruled Egypt's farming year.
l_egypt.s1: Cambyses beat Psamtik III at Pelusium and took Memphis in 525 BCE. The statue of Udjahorresnet, an Egyptian official, records that Cambyses took the titles of a pharaoh and a throne name, and was shown the temple of Neith at Sais. Egyptian records date by his years as king.
l_egypt.s2: Herodotus puts Egypt, with Libya, Cyrene and Barca, in the sixth tribute district, paying 700 talents of silver, plus the income from the fish of Lake Moeris and grain for the 120,000 men of the garrison at the White Wall of Memphis.
l_egypt.s3: Darius set up stelae along a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea, in Old Persian, Elamite, Babylonian and Egyptian. The Old Persian text says he ordered it dug from the Nile to the sea that goes from Persia, and that ships went through it to Persia.
l_egypt.s4: Herodotus says Egypt revolted in the last years of Darius. Xerxes put it down in the second year of his reign, laid a heavier yoke on the country, and made his brother Achaemenes its governor. The revolt delayed the invasion of Greece.
l_eion.lead: Eion was a trading town at the mouth of the Strymon river in Thrace, on the coast route from the Hellespont towards Macedonia and Greece. Xerxes stocked it with food for his invasion of 480 BCE, and a Persian garrison held it after the defeat in Greece until the Athenians under Cimon took it, about 476 BCE.
l_eion.play: The game presents Eion as Xerxes' supply depot on the Strymon, on the road to Greece. This matches Herodotus, who names Eion among the depots stocked before the march.
l_eion.s0: Herodotus says Persian power reached the lower Strymon after Megabazus campaigned in Thrace for Darius, about 512 BCE. Darius granted Histiaeus of Miletus the Edonian town of Myrcinus nearby. Herodotus has Megabazus warn the King that the district had plenty of ship timber, wood for oars and silver mines, and that a clever Greek should not be allowed to build up power there.
l_eion.s1: Herodotus says that while the canal at Athos was being dug, Xerxes ordered the Strymon to be bridged. He also had food for men and animals brought from across Asia to depots on the route. Herodotus names White Cape, Tyrodiza, Doriscus, Eion on the Strymon and places in Macedonia. No document from the Eion depot itself survives.
l_eion.s2: Herodotus says the magi sacrificed white horses to the Strymon, and that at Nine Ways, a crossing upstream of Eion, the Persians buried alive nine boys and nine girls of the local people. He calls burial alive a Persian custom. The Persepolis tablets do record offerings to rivers, but many historians doubt the human sacrifice, which no Persian source supports.
l_eion.s3: Thucydides says the new Athenian-led alliance, under Cimon, besieged Eion while the Persians still held it, captured it and enslaved its people, probably about 476 BCE. Herodotus says its commander Boges refused terms, killed his family, threw his gold and silver into the Strymon and died on a pyre. Herodotus adds that Xerxes praised him and honoured his sons.
l_eion.s4: Herodotus reports a story that Xerxes, retreating in 480 BCE, sailed from Eion in a Phoenician ship. In a storm the helmsman said the ship had to be lightened, and Persian nobles bowed to the King and leapt into the sea. Herodotus himself rejects the tale and says Xerxes went back overland to the Hellespont.
l_elam.lead: Elam was the old kingdom of south-west Iran, the lowland around Susa and the highlands of Anshan to the east. Its language was the main working language of the Persian court's records at Persepolis. Susa became one of Darius's capitals, yet Elam rose against him three times in his first years.
l_elam.play: The Lie level fights Elam's rebels, and the Charter level is set at Susa in Elam. Elamite rebels have their own soldiers and flag, and the Chronicle tells of Elam's revolts.
l_elam.s0: Darius says Elam rose first under Assina, who was taken and put to death, then under Martiya, whom the Elamites seized and killed themselves when Darius came near. A third revolt, under Athamaita, was put down by Gobryas in Darius's second or third year.
l_elam.s1: Thousands of clay tablets from Persepolis, in the Fortification and Treasury archives of about 509-458 BCE, are written in Elamite. They record rations of grain, wine and sheep for workers, travellers and officials. The Behistun inscription was also carved in an Elamite version.
l_elam.s2: Herodotus calls the land around Susa Cissia and its people Cissians. He says they paid 300 talents of silver a year, and that in Xerxes' army they were armed like the Persians but wore turbans. The Royal Road from Sardis ended at Susa.
l_elam.s3: The Cyrus Cylinder calls Cyrus and his forebears kings of Anshan, an old Elamite title and city. Some historians read this as a sign that the early Persian kings ruled a land once part of Elam and took over its traditions; others see a deliberate claim to an ancient crown.
l_elephantine.lead: Elephantine is an island in the Nile at the First Cataract, opposite modern Aswan, where Egypt met Nubia. It was a frontier town, a temple centre and a trading post for goods from the south. Under Persian rule it held a garrison of Judean and Aramaean soldiers whose Aramaic papers give one of the closest views of daily life anywhere in the empire.
l_elephantine.play: The game names Elephantine as a trade partner, the quarrymen of Elephantine. In history the granite quarries lay mostly on the east bank near Syene, and under the Persians the island was better known as a garrison post.
l_elephantine.s0: Excavations show that the island, called Abu by the Egyptians and Yeb in Aramaic, was settled for well over two thousand years before the Persians came. It held temples of Khnum, the ram god of the cataract, and of the goddess Satet. Its position made it the southern gate of Egypt, where river traffic, ivory and other goods from Nubia passed north.
l_elephantine.s1: The red and grey granite of the cataract region was quarried mainly on the east bank around Syene, modern Aswan, not on Elephantine itself. Egyptian rulers drew stone from these quarries for obelisks, statues and shrines from early times, and an unfinished obelisk still lies in one of the pits. Elephantine was the chief town of the southernmost province of Egypt, so the quarries lay within its district.
l_elephantine.s2: Aramaic papyri and ostraca found on the island record a garrison of Judeans and Aramaeans, with a related garrison at nearby Syene. The soldiers were organised in units under commanders with Persian, Babylonian and other names, and were paid in rations and silver from the King's stores. The documents include contracts, letters, accounts and papers about a temple of the god YHW. Most date from after 479 BCE, so they show the garrison under Darius's successors.
l_elephantine.s3: Herodotus says he travelled up the Nile as far as Elephantine himself. He reports that Egyptian kings had kept a garrison there against the Ethiopians and that the Persians still did so in his own day. He also tells that Cambyses fetched from Elephantine some of the Fish-eaters who knew the Ethiopian language and sent them south as spies before his campaign against Ethiopia.
l_elephantine.s4: A petition written by the Judeans of Elephantine in 407 BCE states that their temple stood before Cambyses entered Egypt and that he spared it while destroying the temples of the Egyptian gods. The petitioners had reason to stress Persian favour, and Egyptian evidence from Cambyses' reign, such as the Apis burial and the statue of Udjahorresnet, points to a king who worked with Egyptian cults. Historians also still argue over when and why the Judean soldiers first came.
l_ephesus.lead: Ephesus was one of the Ionian Greek cities under Persian rule and the usual coastal starting point for the road inland to Sardis, the seat of the satrap. In 498 BCE the Ionian rebels marched from its territory to burn Sardis, and on their return the Persians overtook them near the city and defeated them. Herodotus is the main source for the episode.
l_ephesus.play: Ephesus has no level or mechanic of its own. The game mentions it only in the event articles on the battle of Ephesus and the burning of Sardis.
l_ephesus.s0: Herodotus counts Ephesus among the twelve Ionian cities of Asia Minor, and says that the Ionians came under Persian rule after Harpagus's campaigns on the coast in the time of Cyrus. In his account of the Royal Road he gives the stages of the route inland to Sardis. Ephesus was therefore well placed as a way between the sea and the interior.
l_ephesus.s1: Herodotus says the Athenian and Eretrian ships brought the rebels to Coressus in Ephesian territory, and that they took Ephesian guides and marched inland. They took Sardis except the acropolis, which Artaphernes held. A fire started in a house and spread, and the sanctuary of the goddess Cybele was destroyed. Herodotus says the Persians later gave this as a reason for burning Greek temples.
l_ephesus.s2: Herodotus says the Persians stationed west of the Halys gathered and followed the rebels, and overtook them near Ephesus. The Ionians were beaten, and many were killed, among them the Eretrian commander Eualcidas. The survivors scattered to their cities, and the Athenians, Herodotus says, then withdrew and refused further help to the Ionians.
l_ephesus.s3: No Persian inscription or tablet is known that describes the march or the battle, so the details rest on Herodotus. Historians generally accept the burning of Sardis and the defeat in outline, but they question how much weight he gives to Athenian involvement. His story that Darius vowed revenge on Athens after the fire is also debated.
l_ephesus.s4: Herodotus does not describe a punishment of Ephesus in his account of the end of the revolt, but this silence proves little. Scholars debate how far the Ephesians took part in the rising, since Herodotus has Ephesians guiding the rebels yet has them avoid the final fighting. The question cannot be settled from the surviving sources.
l_eretria.lead: Eretria was a seafaring Greek city on the south-west coast of Euboea, facing the mainland across a narrow gulf. It sent five ships to help the Ionian revolt against Persia in 498 BCE. In 490 BCE a Persian fleet under Datis and Artaphernes, son of the satrap of Sardis, besieged it, took it by treachery, burned its temples and carried many of its people off to the King.
l_eretria.play: The game's chronicle presents Eretria as the city that sent five ships to the Ionians and was betrayed after six days of siege in 490 BCE. This follows Herodotus, the only detailed source for these events.
l_eretria.s0: Herodotus says that when Aristagoras of Miletus sought allies, Athens sent twenty ships and Eretria five triremes. The Eretrians came, he explains, to repay Miletus for its help in an old war against their neighbour Chalcis. They joined the march on Sardis in 498 BCE, when the town and a temple of the goddess Cybebe burned. On the way back the Greeks were beaten near Ephesus, and the Eretrian general Eualcides was killed.
l_eretria.s1: Herodotus says the Persian fleet landed at Tamynae, Choereae and Aegilia in Eretrian territory. The Eretrians chose to hold their walls rather than flee to the hills, while 4,000 Athenian settlers sent to help them crossed back to Oropus. After six days of hard fighting, two leading citizens, Euphorbus and Philagrus, betrayed the city to the Persians on the seventh. The Persians plundered it and burned its temples in revenge for those burned at Sardis.
l_eretria.s2: Herodotus says Darius had ordered the Eretrians enslaved and brought to him, but did them no harm when they arrived. He settled them at Ardericca in Cissian land, about 210 stades from Susa and 40 stades from a well yielding bitumen, salt and oil, where in Herodotus's day they still kept their own language. The site has not been identified. Herodotus also records Eretrian ships at Artemisium and Salamis and Eretrian troops at Plataea.
l_eretria.s3: Greek excavators working around 1900 uncovered the temple of Apollo Daphnephoros at Eretria and its late Archaic pediment sculptures, including a group of Theseus carrying off the Amazon Antiope. The Swiss School of Archaeology in Greece, at work in Eretria since 1964, has studied the sanctuary further. Excavators usually link the burned debris and the broken sculptures to the sack of 490 BCE. This dating is an inference from the remains, not a written record.
l_eretria.s4: More than a century later, Plato wrote that Datis's soldiers joined hands and swept across Eretrian land like a net, so that no one escaped. Herodotus tells of this netting only for the islands of Chios, Lesbos and Tenedos after the Ionian revolt, not for Eretria. Plato's version reads as a dramatic image of total conquest and is not supported by the earlier account.
l_euboea.lead: Euboea is the long island that lies along the east coast of mainland Greece, separated from it by a narrow strait. The Persians destroyed its city Eretria in 490 BCE, and off its northern shore the Greek fleet fought Xerxes' ships at Artemisium in 480 BCE. The island therefore figures in both Persian invasions.
l_euboea.play: The game names Euboea only in the event articles on the fall of Eretria and the battle of Artemisium. It has no mechanic of its own.
l_euboea.s0: Herodotus describes Euboea as an island lying close to the mainland, and his narrative of 480 BCE has fleets moving along its coast. Eretria and Chalcis are its best-known cities in his account. The narrow channel between island and mainland is the one later called the Euripus.
l_euboea.s1: Herodotus says the force of Datis and Artaphernes sailed to Euboea after Naxos and the islands, and that Eretria resisted for six days. He reports that on the seventh two prominent Eretrians betrayed the city, that the temples were burned and that the people were enslaved. He gives the cause as Eretria's help to Sardis in 498 BCE, when it sent five ships to the Ionians.
l_euboea.s2: Herodotus says Darius settled the captured Eretrians at Ardericca in Cissia, not far from Susa. He adds that their descendants were still living there in his own day and still spoke Greek. The detail rests on Herodotus alone.
l_euboea.s3: Herodotus places the Greek fleet at Artemisium, on the north coast of Euboea, while Leonidas held Thermopylae. He tells of a Persian squadron sent round the south of the island that was wrecked by a storm, and of fighting on several days that ended without a clear result. The Greeks then withdrew when the pass fell.
l_euboea.s4: The sizes Herodotus gives for the Persian and Greek fleets are hard to check, and historians generally think his totals for the Persian fleet are inflated. The plan to trap the Greeks by sending ships around Euboea is known only from his account. Modern writers also differ on how to judge Artemisium, since the Greek retreat followed the loss of Thermopylae rather than a defeat at sea.
l_euphrates.lead: The Euphrates is the western of the two great rivers of Mesopotamia. It flowed through the middle of Babylon, and its waters fed the canals of the richest farmland in Asia. Herodotus says Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BCE by diverting it, and Darius beat Nidintu-Bel beside it at Zazana in 522 BCE.
l_euphrates.play: The Euphrates is named in the Bagastana level's texts, at the battle of Zazana, and in Babylon's trade partner notes.
l_euphrates.s0: Herodotus says the Euphrates, broad, deep and swift, runs through the middle of Babylon from Armenia to the Erythraean Sea. He says Queen Nitocris made it wind above the city and built a bridge of stone piers in it.
l_euphrates.s1: Herodotus says Cyrus drew off the Euphrates into a lake and sent his men into Babylon along the river bed while the people feasted. The Nabonidus Chronicle says only that Babylon was taken without a battle, and the Cyrus Cylinder that Marduk let Cyrus enter in peace.
l_euphrates.s2: Darius says that after crossing the Tigris he marched on Babylon, and at Zazana on the Euphrates Nidintu-Bel met him again. Darius won, and drove the enemy into the water, where the river carried them away. Then he took Babylon.
l_euphrates.s3: Herodotus says Babylonia was cut by canals, the greatest navigable to the Tigris, and that its grain returned two hundredfold, even three hundredfold. Thousands of tablets from the Persian period record the canals, their fields and the families who leased them.
l_gargaphia.lead: Gargaphia was a spring in the land of Plataea, below the slopes of Cithaeron. In 479 BCE the Greek army camped by it and drew its water there, since the King's archers kept them from the Asopus. Mardonius's horsemen choked and fouled the spring, and the Greeks had to move by night.
l_gargaphia.play: Gargaphia is named in the Plataea level's Chronicle, field briefing and chatter, as the spring the King's horse fouled.
l_gargaphia.s0: After the death of Masistius at Erythrae, Herodotus says the Greeks moved down toward Plataea, which was better watered, and took up their posts by the spring Gargaphia. The Spartans held the right of the line near it.
l_gargaphia.s1: Herodotus says the Persian horsemen and their archers kept the Greeks from the Asopus, so the whole army drew water from Gargaphia. Then the horse rode in, choked and fouled the spring, and harassed the Greeks so that they could not hold their posts.
l_gargaphia.s2: Without water or food, the Greek generals decided to move to the Island, ten furlongs from the Asopus and the spring, where the river divided. The march by night fell into disorder, and the battle of Plataea followed the next day when Mardonius attacked.
l_gargaphia.s3: The spring cannot be placed for certain. Travellers since the nineteenth century have proposed several springs on the slopes north-east of Plataea, and the course of the Asopus and its feeders has shifted. Pausanias, who visited the battlefield, does not settle it.
l_gaza.lead: Gaza, which Herodotus seems to call Cadytis, was a large city of southern Palestine on the coast road to Egypt. Beyond it the road ran through the coastal stations held by the Arabs and across three days of waterless desert to Pelusium. Cambyses' army went this way in 525 BCE.
l_gaza.play: Gaza is named in the Memphis level's muster, field briefing and chatter, as the start of the desert road the King's army crossed.
l_gaza.s0: Herodotus says the only known way into Egypt ran from Phoenicia to the borders of Cadytis, a city of the Syrians of Palestine not much smaller than Sardis. Pharaoh Necho, he says, took Cadytis after beating the Syrians. Most historians take Cadytis to be Gaza.
l_gaza.s1: From Cadytis the trading stations on the coast as far as Ienysus belonged to the king of the Arabs, and from Ienysus to Mount Casius and the Serbonian lake the land was Syrian again. Then came Egypt. Herodotus says the stretch from Ienysus was three days of waterless desert.
l_gaza.s2: Cambyses made a pact with the king of the Arabs, who filled camel-skins with water and set them on his camels and waited in the desert. Herodotus also reports a story of a pipe of hides from a river, which he thinks less likely.
l_gaza.s3: Gaza held out against Alexander for two months in 332 under a Persian commander, Batis, and was taken by storm. Arrian tells the siege. Excavations at Tell el-Ajjul and other sites near the modern city show its long history as a trading town.
l_halicarnassus.lead: Halicarnassus was a port on the Carian coast. Herodotus, who was born there, calls it a Dorian Greek city, and it lay within the Persian empire after the conquest of the Anatolian coast in Cyrus's time. It is known as the home of Phanes and Artemisia, who appear in the wars with Greece, and as the birthplace of Herodotus.
l_halicarnassus.play: The game mentions Halicarnassus only in the Chronicle and in event articles, as the home of Phanes in the Egypt entries and of Artemisia in the Salamis entries. It has no level, building or mechanic of its own.
l_halicarnassus.s0: Herodotus counts Halicarnassus among the Dorian cities of the south-west coast, though it lay in Caria. He says it was shut out of the shared sanctuary at Triopium after a citizen, Agasicles, took home a prize tripod that should have been dedicated there.
l_halicarnassus.s1: Herodotus tells of Harpagus's conquest of the Ionians, Carians and Lycians in Cyrus's reign. The conquest placed the coast under Persian authority. By Xerxes' invasion Halicarnassus is a ruled city that sends ships to the King's fleet under its own ruler, Artemisia.
l_halicarnassus.s2: Herodotus names Artemisia as ruler of Halicarnassus, Cos, Nisyros and Calydna, and says she brought five ships to Xerxes' fleet. He reports that she advised against a sea fight at Salamis and that Xerxes valued her judgement. He is the only full source, so the speeches cannot be checked.
l_halicarnassus.s3: Herodotus says Phanes of Halicarnassus served Amasis of Egypt as a mercenary leader and deserted to Cambyses before the invasion. He reports that Phanes arranged the crossing of the desert with an Arab ruler. Herodotus adds that the Greek and Carian mercenaries left behind killed Phanes' sons.
l_halicarnassus.s4: Later tradition says Herodotus left Halicarnassus after trouble with its tyrant Lygdamis and lived in Samos. This comes from late writers such as the Suda, not from the Histories. Historians accept that he came from the city but argue over how far the later biography can be trusted.
l_halys.lead: The Halys, now the Kızılırmak, is the longest river in Anatolia and curves north to the Black Sea. In the sixth century it was the boundary between the Lydian kingdom and its eastern neighbours. Herodotus makes it the line Croesus crossed to begin the war that ended with the fall of Sardis.
l_halys.play: The game names the Halys only in the event articles on the fall of Sardis and the battle of Ephesus, and it has no mechanic of its own.
l_halys.s0: Herodotus describes the Halys as rising in the south and flowing north past the Syrians and Paphlagonians to the Black Sea. He says it divided the Lydian realm from the Median one, and that the treaty after the battle fought during an eclipse was sealed with a marriage between the two royal houses. The frontier role is his account; no Lydian or Median document survives to confirm it.
l_halys.s1: Herodotus says Croesus marched east over the Halys into Cappadocia, hoping to punish Cyrus and enlarge his kingdom. He fought Cyrus at Pteria without a clear result and withdrew to Sardis for the winter. Cyrus followed him, and Sardis fell. Many historians now identify Pteria with the hilltop city on Kerkenes Dağ; older writers placed it at the Hittite site of Boğazköy.
l_halys.s2: The Nabonidus Chronicle, a Babylonian text, records for Nabonidus's ninth year that Cyrus, king of Parsu, marched against a land whose name, damaged on the tablet, was once read as Lydia; many scholars now read Urartu. The surviving text is damaged at this point and does not name the Halys or any battle site. The Persian side of the war is therefore known mostly through Greek writers. The year is placed around 547 or 546 BCE, and scholars still argue over which.
l_halys.s3: Herodotus tells that Delphi warned Croesus that crossing the Halys would destroy a great empire, and that he took this to mean Cyrus's. The story is shaped as a moral about misreading a god's words. Herodotus also reports a Greek tale that Thales of Miletus diverted the river so that the army could cross, and he says himself that he does not believe it.
l_halys.s4: After the conquest the river lay inside the Persian empire. Herodotus says the road from Sardis to Susa crossed the Halys at a point with gates and a strong guard-post. This shows the river as a controlled crossing in his description of the road, set about 500 BCE. His description is the main evidence for that stretch of the road.
l_hellespont.lead: The Hellespont, now the Dardanelles, is the narrow strait between the Aegean and the Sea of Marmara that divides Asia from Europe. In 480 BCE Xerxes crossed it on two bridges of boats near Abydos to invade Greece. Herodotus made the crossing a central image of royal power and pride, and almost everything known about it comes from Greek writers.
l_hellespont.play: The game's chronicle presents the strait at Abydos, bridged twice on boats for Xerxes in 481-480 BCE after a storm broke the first bridges, with a seven-day crossing. This follows Herodotus, the only detailed source.
l_hellespont.s0: Herodotus says that Phoenician and Egyptian crews first spanned the seven stades from Abydos to the shore between Sestos and Madytus, using cables of white flax and of papyrus. A storm destroyed this work. New engineers then moored 360 ships for one bridge and 314 for the other. They stretched cables across the hulls and laid planks, brushwood and earth on top, with screens at the sides so the animals would not see the water.
l_hellespont.s1: Herodotus says Xerxes had the strait given 300 lashes and a pair of fetters thrown in, and had the overseers of the failed bridges beheaded. He frames this as arrogance, and Aeschylus likewise treats the yoking of the sea as an offence to the gods. Some historians read the story as a Persian rite against a disorderly water; others see Greek moralising. No Persian inscription mentions the bridges at all.
l_hellespont.s2: Herodotus tells how Xerxes sat on a throne of white stone on a hill at Abydos and watched his fleet race and his army fill the shore. At sunrise he poured a libation and threw a gold cup, a bowl and a Persian sword into the water. Fighting men used one bridge and baggage animals the other, and the crossing went on for seven days and nights. Herodotus's total of over five million people is far beyond what modern historians accept.
l_hellespont.s3: Herodotus says that when Xerxes came back after Salamis, storms had already broken the bridges, so the army crossed by ship. In 479 BCE, after Mycale, the Athenians sailed to the strait, besieged Sestos and carried the bridge cables home to dedicate in their sanctuaries. Artayctes, the Persian governor of Sestos, was captured and put to death.
