l_hellespont.s4: Greeks called the strait the sea of Helle. In the myth, Phrixus and his sister Helle fled their stepmother on a ram with a golden fleece, and Helle fell into the water and drowned. Herodotus mentions a tomb of Helle on the Chersonese that Xerxes' army marched past. The love story of Hero and Leander, set on either shore, survives first in Roman-era poetry such as Ovid's and later in the Greek poet Musaeus.
l_hermus.lead: The Hermus, now the Gediz, is the largest river of Lydia. It flows west past Sardis to the sea near Phocaea, and the Pactolus joins it below the city. Its broad plain fed Sardis, and there Cyrus's camels routed Croesus's horse about 547 BCE.
l_hermus.play: The Hermus is the Sardis level's river: its plain is the level's farmland, and its ferrymen and figs appear in the chatter.
l_hermus.s0: Herodotus describes the plain before Sardis as wide and open, crossed by rivers, the Hyllus among them, that flow into the largest, the Hermus. He says the Hermus comes down from the mountain sacred to the Mother of Dindymus and runs into the sea by Phocaea.
l_hermus.s1: On that plain, Herodotus says, Cyrus set men on his baggage camels in front of his army, on Harpagus's advice. The Lydian horses could not bear the smell and sight of the camels and turned, and the Lydians fought on foot and were driven into Sardis.
l_hermus.s2: The Pactolus ran through the market of Sardis, bringing gold dust from Tmolus, and then flowed into the Hermus, which went on to the sea. In 498 BCE the people trapped by the fire gathered in the market and along the Pactolus.
l_hermus.s3: North of the Hermus lies the great Lydian cemetery of Bin Tepe, with the mound Herodotus calls the tomb of Alyattes, father of Croesus, one of the largest tumuli of the ancient world. Its earth and stone base survive, as he describes.
l_indus.lead: The Indus flows from the mountains of the north-west to the Arabian Sea. Its valley became the Persian province of Hindush under Darius. Herodotus says Darius sent Scylax of Caryanda down the river to the sea, then conquered the Indians and used the sea route.
l_indus.play: The Indus is the road of Scylax's voyage in the Susa level: the India trade partner stays closed until Scylax has sailed it, and its ivory comes up for the palace.
l_indus.s0: Herodotus says Darius wished to know where the Indus, a second river with crocodiles after the Nile, met the sea. He sent ships with Scylax of Caryanda, who set out from Caspatyrus in Pactyice, sailed down the river and across the sea westward, and came in the thirtieth month to Egypt.
l_indus.s1: Darius's inscriptions list Hindush among his lands, though the Behistun inscription of about 520 BCE does not. The Persepolis reliefs show its people bringing jars, probably of gold dust, and the Susa charter says ivory came from Hindush, Kush and Arachosia.
l_indus.s2: Herodotus says the Indians paid 360 talents of gold dust a year, the largest tribute of any people. He tells a tale of giant ants that dig up gold-bearing sand, which the Indians steal on fast camels. The ants are a traveller's story; the gold tribute fits the jars on the reliefs.
l_indus.s3: How much of the Indus valley the Persians held is argued. Most historians think Hindush covered the middle and lower Indus, with Gandhara to the north as a separate land. The voyage's route back by sea is also doubted by some, since Scylax's own book is lost.
l_ister.lead: The Ister was the Greek name for the Danube, the great river of Europe. About 513 BCE Darius's Greek subjects bridged its lower course with boats so that the King's army could march north against the Scythians. Herodotus says that when the Scythians urged the Ionians to break the bridge, Histiaeus of Miletus argued for keeping it, and Darius's army escaped across it.
l_ister.play: The Ister is the sixth level, set about 513 BCE. Its Chronicle note follows Herodotus: the Ionians bridged the river where its mouths part, and Histiaeus kept the crossing for Darius.
l_ister.s0: Herodotus calls the Ister the greatest river he knew. He says it flowed across the whole of Europe from the land of the Celts and reached the Black Sea through several mouths. He lists many tributaries and compares it with the Nile. For Greeks the lower river marked the edge of Thrace and the start of Scythian country to the north.
l_ister.s1: Herodotus says a fleet of Ionians, Aeolians and Hellespontine Greeks sailed two days up the river from the sea and bridged it where its mouths divide. Darius marched overland from the Bosporus and crossed. He first meant to break the bridge, but Coes of Mytilene advised him to keep it. Darius then tied sixty knots in a cord and told the Greek tyrants to untie one each day, and to sail home if he had not returned when all were undone.
l_ister.s2: Herodotus tells that Scythians came to the bridge and urged the Ionians to destroy it and leave Darius stranded. Histiaeus of Miletus argued that each tyrant ruled his city only with the King's backing. The Greeks removed a short stretch on the northern bank to satisfy the Scythians. When Darius arrived at night, an Egyptian with a loud voice called for Histiaeus, and the bridge was restored.
l_ister.s3: Herodotus reports that Miltiades, the Athenian tyrant of the Chersonese, spoke for destroying the bridge. Many historians doubt this, since Miltiades went on ruling the Chersonese as a Persian subject until 493 BCE. The story may have been told at Athens to help him when, after his return that year, he was tried for tyranny in the Chersonese.
l_ister.s4: No Persian text describes the campaign, though Darius's tomb inscription lists Saka beyond the sea, usually taken to mean the Scythians of Europe. Herodotus gives 700,000 men and 600 ships, figures historians treat as much exaggerated, and his long chase across the steppe is widely doubted. The date, usually put about 513 BCE, and the aim, revenge as Herodotus says or control of Thrace and the Black Sea, are still debated.
l_istros.lead: Istros, also called Histria, was a Greek city founded by settlers from Miletus on the western Black Sea coast, just south of the Danube delta in modern Romania. It traded with the Scythian and Thracian peoples of the hinterland, and it lay close to the river mouth where Darius's Greek fleet entered the Ister on the Scythian expedition of about 513 BCE.
l_istros.play: The game makes Istros a trade partner in the Ister level. No ancient source records Istros trading with Darius's army; the link is a plausible simplification based on the city's position near the fleet's route.
l_istros.s0: Herodotus, describing the course of the Ister, says the river reaches the sea at Istria, where Milesian colonists lived. Strabo, writing nearly five centuries later, places the small town of Istros some distance south of the Sacred Mouth of the river.
l_istros.s1: The late chronicle tradition of Eusebius dates the founding to about 657 BCE. A geographical poem attributed to Pseudo-Scymnus links it to the time when Scythians pursued the Cimmerians into Asia. The earliest Greek pottery found on the site is usually dated to about 630 BCE or a little earlier. Historians still argue over whether the literary date or the pottery should carry more weight.
l_istros.s2: Romanian archaeologists have dug at Histria since 1914, beginning with Vasile Pârvan. The city stood on a low promontory beside a bay that has since silted into a lagoon, so the ruins now lie away from open sea. Excavators uncovered a sacred area with temples of Zeus Polieus and Aphrodite, houses, and walls rebuilt many times. Greek pottery from native sites inland shows trade with Getic and Scythian neighbours.
l_istros.s3: Herodotus says the Ionian and other Greek contingents sailed into the Ister to bridge it for Darius, but he never names Istros in his account of the campaign. Excavators have found a destruction level in the settlement from around the end of the sixth century. Some scholars connect it with Darius's expedition or with later Scythian raids; others see no link. Whether Istros ever came under Persian control is unknown.
l_istros.s4: Herodotus tells of the Scythian king Scylas, whose mother came from Istria and taught him the Greek language and letters. Scylas, he says, later took up Greek dress and rites in the Greek city of the Borysthenites. The Scythians then rose against him, and his brother Octamasades had him beheaded. The story, whatever its truth, suggests that women of Istros could marry into Scythian ruling families.
l_kuh_e_rahmat.lead: The Mountain of Mercy, Kuh-e Rahmat in Persian, is the ridge that rises behind the terrace of Persepolis on the Marv Dasht plain. Darius set his palace platform against its foot about 518 BCE, and later kings cut their tombs into its face. The name is modern; the ancient name is not known.
l_kuh_e_rahmat.play: The Parsa level is built below the Mountain of Mercy: the Royal Terrace is founded with its back to it, and its quarries must touch its rock.
l_kuh_e_rahmat.s0: The terrace of Persepolis was partly cut from the mountain's lower slope and partly built up with fitted blocks to a platform about 450 by 300 metres. Darius's inscription on its south wall names him its builder. A fortification wall ran up the slope behind it.
l_kuh_e_rahmat.s1: Two rock-cut tombs in the mountain above the terrace, with façades like those at Naqsh-e Rostam, are usually given to Artaxerxes II and Artaxerxes III, of the fourth century. Darius and the next kings were buried at Naqsh-e Rostam a few kilometres to the north.
l_kuh_e_rahmat.s2: Quarries in the mountain and nearby hills supplied the grey limestone of the terrace and its palaces. Unfinished blocks and quarry faces with tool marks survive, and the Fortification tablets record gangs of workers fed from the royal stores.
l_kuh_e_rahmat.s3: Kuh-e Rahmat means 'Mountain of Mercy' and is the name used today. No ancient text gives the mountain a name, and Greek writers who describe Persepolis after Alexander speak only of the royal tombs in the hill behind the palace.
l_kush.lead: Kush was the Nile kingdom south of Egypt, with its heartland in what is now northern Sudan. Persian inscriptions name it Kushiya, and Greek writers called the land Ethiopia. It was never central to Persian policy, but Herodotus says Cambyses marched against it, and Darius's inscriptions list Kusha among the lands that belonged to him.
l_kush.play: The game mentions Kush only in Chronicle entries and event articles, on Cambyses' march south and the Susa charter, where it is the Nile kingdom beyond Egypt and a source of ivory. It has no mechanic of its own.
l_kush.s0: Darius's inscription on his tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam lists Kushiya among the lands that he held. The tomb reliefs there also show peoples carrying the royal platform, with a Kushite among them. These texts show that the Persians counted Kush as part of the empire, or at least as bound to it, by Darius's reign.
l_kush.s1: Darius's foundation charter for the palace at Susa says that ivory used in the building was brought from Ethiopia, Sind and Arachosia. The charter is clear evidence that goods from the far south reached the royal works.
l_kush.s2: Herodotus says that after taking Egypt, Cambyses sent spies, whom he calls Fish-eaters, to the Ethiopian king. The king answered with a bow and a challenge. Herodotus says Cambyses set out without provisions in a fit of rage, and that the army ran short of food before it had covered a fifth of the way, so he turned back. The picture of a reckless king is Herodotus's own.
l_kush.s3: Modern historians doubt that Cambyses reached the heartland of Kush. Some think he advanced only into Lower Nubia, perhaps as far as the second cataract, and that Herodotus's tale of failure may exaggerate the loss. The claim that Cambyses founded a town called Meroe comes from much later writers and has no support from the time.
l_kush.s4: Herodotus says that the Ethiopians bordering Egypt, whom Cambyses had approached, paid no tribute but brought gifts every third year. He lists gold, ebony, ivory tusks and boys, and says the practice continued to his own day. Herodotus places this in his list of Darius's districts, and it suggests a looser tie than that of a province.
l_lade.lead: Lade was a small island in front of the harbours of Miletus. In about 494 BCE the King's fleet, drawn mostly from Phoenicia, Cyprus, Cilicia and Egypt, defeated the combined ships of the rebel Ionian cities there. The defeat left Miletus open to siege and capture, and it effectively ended the Ionian Revolt that Aristagoras had begun.
l_lade.play: The Chronicle names Lade as the place where the King's fleet of 600 beat the Ionians' 353 triremes in 494 BCE after the Samians sailed away. These are Herodotus's figures, and the 600 is probably inflated.
l_lade.s0: In antiquity Lade lay just off Miletus, near the mouth of the gulf into which the Maeander river flowed. Strabo names it as an island close to the city, with smaller islets around it. Silt carried by the Maeander has since filled the gulf, and the former island survives today as a low hill in farmland, several kilometres from the sea.
l_lade.s1: Herodotus says the Persian commanders brought their land army against Miletus and gathered a fleet in which the Phoenicians were the keenest. The Ionians chose to fight at sea and drew up at Lade with 353 triremes. The Chians had the largest contingent with 100, Miletus sent 80 and Samos 60. He gives the King's fleet as 600 ships.
l_lade.s2: Herodotus tells that Dionysius of Phocaea, who brought only three ships, took charge of training and kept the crews rowing and practising manoeuvres in the summer heat. After seven days the men, unused to such labour, refused to go on and sat in the shade on the island. Herodotus presents this as the first sign that the alliance would not hold.
l_lade.s3: According to Herodotus, the Persians sent the exiled tyrants of the Ionian cities to win over their own people. Aeaces, son of Syloson, persuaded most of the Samian captains, and when battle began 49 of the 60 Samian ships left, followed by most of the Lesbians. The Chians fought on and lost heavily. Dionysius took three enemy ships, sailed to Phoenicia to raid merchant ships, and later turned pirate off Sicily.
l_lade.s4: Historians generally treat the 600 Persian ships as a round, probably exaggerated figure. Herodotus admits that the Ionians blamed each other and that he could not say for certain who fought well, so his story leans on Samian excuses and Chian praise. No Persian document records the battle. The usual date of 494 BCE rests on his statement that Miletus fell in the sixth year of the revolt.
l_laurium.lead: Laurium is the hilly district of south-eastern Attica, rich in lead and silver ore. In 483 BCE a new vein was struck there, and Themistocles persuaded the Athenians to spend the silver on ships instead of sharing it out. Those ships fought at Artemisium and Salamis.
l_laurium.play: Laurium is named in the Marathon and Thermopylae levels' Athens trade partner notes and in Themistocles' texts, as the silver that built the fleet.
l_laurium.s0: Herodotus says the Athenians had a great sum in their treasury from the mines at Laurium and meant to share it out at ten drachmas a man. Themistocles persuaded them to build two hundred ships instead, for the war with Aegina, and these were the ships that saved Greece.
l_laurium.s1: The Aristotelian Constitution of the Athenians dates the strike to the archonship of Nicodemus, 483 BCE/2, at Maroneia, with a hundred talents of profit. It says Themistocles had a hundred rich men each build a trireme. The figures differ from Herodotus's, but both make the silver pay for the fleet.
l_laurium.s2: Shafts, galleries, ore-washing tables and cisterns survive across the district, most of them from the fifth and fourth centuries. The work was done mostly by slaves, many thousands of them by the later fifth century. Athens's owls were struck from this silver.
l_laurium.s3: The mining town of Thorikos, on the coast near Laurium, has an early theatre and houses and workshops for processing ore. Its finds show mining from long before the Persian wars, so the strike of 483 BCE was a new rich vein, not the first silver.
l_lebanon.lead: Lebanon was the mountain range behind the Phoenician coast, long known in the ancient Near East for its cedar. Darius's Susa charter names it as the source of the cedar used in his palace at Susa. The Phoenician cities of the coast were Persian subjects who also supplied ships to the King's fleet.
l_lebanon.play: The game mentions Lebanon only in Chronicle entries and event articles, chiefly the Susa charter, where it is the source of the palace cedar. It has no building, unit or mechanic of its own.
l_lebanon.s0: Darius's foundation charter from Susa, DSf, lists the materials and peoples who built his palace. It says the cedar timber was brought from a mountain called Lebanon. Assyrian people carried it as far as Babylon, and Carians and Ionians brought it on from Babylon to Susa.
l_lebanon.s1: DSf is the clearest text naming Lebanon as a source of timber for a Persian building. Cedar is reported in other Persian buildings, but how much came from Lebanon rather than other mountain regions is not settled by the texts. Identifying the source of excavated timber is also difficult.
l_lebanon.s2: Herodotus lists the Phoenicians, with Syria and Cyprus, in the fifth tax district of the empire. He also reports Phoenician ships as the best in Xerxes' fleet. The cedar mountains lay behind these coastal cities.
l_lebanon.s3: Herodotus says the Phoenician contingent in Xerxes' fleet was the most skilled at sailing. The coast that supplied this naval service also lay beside the timber mountains, though the sources do not link the two directly.
l_lesbos.lead: Lesbos is a large island off the Aeolian coast of Asia Minor. Herodotus counts five cities on it, of which Mytilene was the greatest. Its ships sailed for Cambyses in Egypt and for Darius at the Ister, its tyrant Coes advised Darius, and at Lade its seventy ships deserted.
l_lesbos.play: Mytilene's ship carries the King's herald up the Nile in the Memphis level, Coes of Mytilene advises the King at the Ister, and the Lesbians desert at Lade in the Sardis level.
l_lesbos.s0: When the Egyptians shut themselves in Memphis, Herodotus says, Cambyses sent a ship of Mytilene up the river with a Persian herald to call them to terms. They poured out, destroyed the ship and tore its crew to pieces. Cambyses later killed ten Egyptian nobles for each man of Mytilene.
l_lesbos.s1: At the Ister Darius meant to break his bridge and take its guards on with him. Coes son of Erxander, commander of the Mytilenaeans, advised him to leave it standing. On his return Darius made Coes tyrant of Mytilene; in 499 BCE the rebels gave him to the Mytilenaeans, who stoned him.
l_lesbos.s2: In the Ionian line at Lade the Lesbians held seventy ships, next to the Samians at the western end. When the Samians sailed away, Herodotus says, most of the Lesbians followed, and the line broke. The next year the Persian fleet took Lesbos with Chios and Tenedos and swept the islands for their people.
l_lesbos.s3: Herodotus counts the five Lesbian cities among the Aeolians and says the islanders had less to fear from Cyrus than the mainland. Lesbos was the home of the poets Sappho and Alcaeus about 600 BCE, and Herodotus tells how Sappho's brother Charaxus ransomed Rhodopis at Naucratis.
l_magnesia.lead: Magnesia is the hilly coastal region of eastern Thessaly, east of the Pagasaean gulf and including Mount Pelion. Herodotus places the great storm that damaged Xerxes' fleet on its shore in 480 BCE, shortly before the fighting at Artemisium. The coast gave poor shelter to a fleet of that size.
l_magnesia.play: The game names Magnesia only in the Chronicle's entries and in the Encyclopedia's event article on the storm, as the coast where Xerxes' fleet was wrecked. It is not a level and has no mechanic of its own.
l_magnesia.s0: Herodotus says the fleet anchored on the Magnesian shore between the city of Casthanaea and the headland of Sepias. He says the beach was narrow, so the ships were moored in eight rows with their prows to the sea, the rest riding at anchor behind. The poor shelter explains why a storm did so much harm.
l_magnesia.s1: Herodotus says a violent wind from the east, which the locals called the Hellespontian, struck the fleet and blew for three days. He reports that the Magi sacrificed to the winds and to Thetis and the Nereids, and that the wind fell on the fourth day. He adds that it may have dropped of its own accord. He is the main source for the storm.
l_magnesia.s2: Herodotus says not fewer than 400 warships were lost, with many men and much property. Historians doubt his figures for the size of the fleets, so the total is probably too high, though a serious loss is not doubted. Greek lookouts on Euboea, he says, passed on the news of the wreck.
l_magnesia.s3: Herodotus tells of a second storm, off the Hollows of Euboea, which wrecked the Persian squadron sent round the island to cut off the Greeks. He says a god worked to bring the Persian numbers closer to the Greek. The losses therefore lessened the Persian advantage before the battles at Artemisium, in his telling.
l_magnesia.s4: Herodotus reports that the Athenians said they had called on Boreas, the north wind, as their kinsman by marriage, and that he sent the storm. Herodotus says he cannot tell whether this was the reason for the storm. The story belongs to Athenian tradition of divine rescue and is not evidence of how the storm arose.
l_malis.lead: Malis was the small country of the Malians round the head of the Malian Gulf, between the Spercheius river and the pass of Thermopylae. Its towns included Anticyra, Trachis and Anthela. In 480 BCE Xerxes' army crossed it to reach the pass, and a Malian, Ephialtes, showed him the path over the mountain.
l_malis.play: Malis is the land of the Thermopylae level. Its gulf, its shepherds and fishermen, and Ephialtes of Malis appear in the level's notes, chatter and field briefings.
l_malis.s0: Herodotus says Xerxes came into the Malian land along a gulf where the sea ebbs and flows every day, which he thought worth noting. The first city from the north was Anticyra, where the Spercheius flows out, and then came the rivers Dyras, Melas and Asopus. The gulf shore lies kilometres further out today because of the Spercheius's silt.
l_malis.s1: Herodotus names Ephialtes son of Eurydemus, a Malian, as the man who told Xerxes of the path over the mountain, hoping for a great reward. He adds that the Amphictyons later put a price on his head, and that he fled to Thessaly. Others named different men, and Herodotus says he gives his own judgement.
l_malis.s2: The Malians gave earth and water to Xerxes' heralds with the Thessalians and others of the north. At Plataea the next year Malians stood in Mardonius's line among the Greeks of the King's side, facing the Athenians, Plataeans and Megarians.
l_malis.s3: Herodotus says that at Anthela, near the pass, there was a temple of Demeter Amphictyonis, with seats for the Amphictyons, the league of peoples who met there and at Delphi. The meeting place gave the small land of Malis a part in the affairs of all Greece.
l_marathon.lead: Marathon is a bay and coastal plain in north-east Attica, about 40 kilometres from Athens. In 490 BCE a seaborne Persian force under Datis and Artaphernes landed here, guided by the exiled Athenian tyrant Hippias, and was beaten by the Athenians and Plataeans. For Greeks the battle became a founding story of Athenian pride; for the Persian court it was a setback at the far edge of a campaign that had already taken Naxos and Eretria.
l_marathon.play: The Marathon level is set on this bay and plain in 490 BCE. The game's chronicle note follows Herodotus in naming Hippias as the guide and the Athenians and Plataeans as the victors, and it places the Athenian dead under the Soros.
l_marathon.s0: Herodotus says the fleet came on from Eretria, and that Hippias chose Marathon because the plain suited horsemen and lay nearest to Eretria. The Athenians, led by ten generals and the polemarch Callimachus, were joined by the whole Plataean levy, and Miltiades pressed for battle. Herodotus says they charged at a run over eight stades; their thin centre gave way, but both wings won and then turned together on the Persian centre.
l_marathon.s1: Herodotus says the Athenians chased the beaten troops to the shore and took seven ships, and that Callimachus fell in the fighting there. The rest of the fleet sailed round Sunium towards Phaleron, but the Athenians marched home first and the Persians sailed back to Asia. He gives 6,400 dead on the Persian side and 192 Athenians, and says a Spartan force of 2,000 arrived after the battle and went to view the fallen.
l_marathon.s2: The Soros still rises on the plain, about 9 metres high. Valerios Stais excavated it in 1890-91 and found ash, burnt bones and pottery of about the date of the battle, which fits Pausanias's report of an Athenian grave on the plain with the names of the dead on stelae, listed by tribe. A casualty list for the tribe Erechtheis, found in 2000 at the villa of Herodes Atticus at Loukou in the Peloponnese, was probably brought there from Marathon.
l_marathon.s3: No Persian text mentions Marathon, so every detail comes from Greek writers. Herodotus gives the fleet as 600 triremes but no army total; later authors inflate it to hundreds of thousands, and modern estimates are far lower. He also says nothing clear about the Persian cavalry during the battle, and historians still argue whether it was away, re-embarking or simply ineffective, and why the Athenians attacked when they did.
l_marathon.s4: Herodotus says the courier Pheidippides ran to Sparta to ask for help and met the god Pan on the way. The tale of a runner who brought news of victory from Marathon to Athens and died on arrival appears only centuries later, in Plutarch and Lucian, and it inspired the marathon race of 1896. Pausanias reports that the noise of battle was heard on the plain at night and that locals honoured a hero, Echetlaeus, who fought with a plough.
l_margiana.lead: Margiana, Old Persian Margush, was the oasis of the Murghab river in what is now Turkmenistan, around the later city of Merv. In 521 BCE it rose against Darius under a man named Frada, and the satrap of Bactria, Dadarshi, put it down.
l_margiana.play: Margiana is named in the Bagastana and Parsa levels' Chronicle and the King's generals' campaigns, among the lands that rose in 522-521 BCE.
l_margiana.s0: Darius says the land called Margush rebelled and made a Margian named Frada its chief. He sent word to Dadarshi, a Persian, his satrap in Bactria, who marched against the Margians and beat them on 23 Atriyadiya, about December 521 BCE.
l_margiana.s1: The Old Persian text gives no numbers, but the Babylonian version of the Behistun inscription says 55,243 Margians were killed and 6,972 taken. Historians treat such counts with care, but the size suggests a hard war in the oasis.
l_margiana.s2: Darius lists Margiana among the lands that rebelled while he was in Babylon, with Persia, Elam, Media, Assyria, Egypt, Parthia, Sattagydia and the Saka. In the relief Frada stands among the bound kings.
l_margiana.s3: Excavations at Gonur Tepe and other sites show that the Murghab delta had walled towns and irrigated fields from the Bronze Age. In the Achaemenid period the walled town of Erk Kala at Merv was its centre.
l_media.lead: Media was the land of the Medes, around Ecbatana in the hills of the western plateau. Cyrus took over its kingdom from Astyages, usually dated to about 550 BCE, and the Persians afterwards kept Median rank, horses and court practice. Its revolt under Fravartish in 522-521 BCE was one of the risings Darius had to put down at the start of his reign.
l_media.play: The game names Media in the Chronicle and in event articles, including the revolt of Fravartish and the Nisaean horse. It is not a level or place of its own and has no mechanic.
l_media.s0: Herodotus says Deioces gathered the Medes under one king and founded Ecbatana as his capital. This is a Greek account written long after the events, and it is partly a moral tale about kingship. The archaeology of the Median homeland is thin, so the size and organisation of the kingdom are not well known.
l_media.s1: The Nabonidus Chronicle records that Astyages' army revolted against him and delivered him to Cyrus, and that Cyrus took Ecbatana and carried off its silver, gold and goods. This is the contemporary record of the end of Median rule, usually dated to about 550 BCE.
l_media.s2: Herodotus gives a longer story in which Harpagus, wronged by Astyages, helped Cyrus to win. The tale is told from the Greek side and its details cannot be checked against Persian documents.
l_media.s3: Herodotus speaks of Median rule over much of Asia before Cyrus, and some modern historians have imagined a Median empire. Others, such as Briant, doubt that the Medes ruled an organised empire of that kind. Darius's inscriptions list Media among the lands, and Medes served the Persian kings in high posts.
l_media.s4: Darius's Behistun inscription says Fravartish claimed to be Khshathrita of the family of Cyaxares and made himself king in Media. Darius says he sent Hydarnes, a Persian, with an army, and that Fravartish was later captured and taken to Ecbatana, where he was mutilated and impaled. The revolt belongs to the series of risings in 522-521 BCE.
l_media.s5: Herodotus says that large horses called Nisaean drew the sacred chariot in Xerxes' procession, and he names a plain of that name in Media. Where Nisaea lay is still uncertain.
l_memphis.lead: Memphis stood on the west bank of the Nile just south of the Delta, home of the god Ptah and for centuries the chief royal and administrative city of Egypt. Cambyses took it after his victory at Pelusium, probably in 525 BCE. Under Persian rule it held a Persian garrison and was probably the seat of the satrap. Nearby at Saqqara the sacred Apis bulls were buried in underground galleries.
l_memphis.play: The Memphis level is set in 525 BCE, the year of Cambyses' conquest. Its chronicle follows Herodotus on the Apis bulls, a story that the Saqqara stelae complicate.
l_memphis.s0: The Egyptians called the city the White Walls, after its old fortified core, and Greek writers kept the name. Herodotus calls its great temple that of Hephaestus, his name for Ptah. He says Amasis moved Ionian and Carian soldiers to Memphis as his guard, and he mentions a Tyrian quarter there, so the city already had foreign residents before the Persians came.
l_memphis.s1: Herodotus says the Egyptians fled to Memphis after their defeat at Pelusium. Cambyses sent a Persian herald upriver on a ship from Mytilene, and the Egyptians killed him and the crew. The city was then besieged until it surrendered. Herodotus goes on to tell how Cambyses tested the captured king Psamtik III by making him watch his children led past in disgrace.
l_memphis.s2: Herodotus says Egypt supplied grain for the Persians quartered in the White Fortress at Memphis and for their auxiliaries. Thucydides shows that the garrison was still there decades later. When Egypt revolted in about 459 BCE, Persians, Medes and loyal Egyptians held the White Wall, the third part of the city, against the rebels and their Athenian allies.
l_memphis.s3: Herodotus says Cambyses saw the Egyptians celebrating a new Apis and took it as mockery of his failures. He says the king stabbed the bull in the thigh and that it later died of the wound. The Apis stelae excavated at Saqqara tell another story: a bull was buried in Cambyses' sixth year in a sarcophagus dedicated in his name, and the next burial fell under Darius. Most historians treat Herodotus's tale as hostile Egyptian tradition, though how the dates fit is still debated.
l_memphis.s4: Herodotus heard from the priests that the first king, Min, dammed the Nile south of the site and drained the land to build Memphis and the temple of Ptah. The story preserves an Egyptian memory of the city's great age. It was told more than two thousand years after the events it describes.
l_miletus.lead: Miletus was a Greek city on the coast of Caria near the mouth of the Maeander, and Herodotus calls it the ornament of Ionia at its height around 500 BCE. Under Persian rule its tyrants Histiaeus and Aristagoras won the King's trust, until Aristagoras led the Ionians into revolt in 499 BCE. The Persians took the city in 494 BCE, and its fall shocked the Greek world.
l_miletus.play: Miletus is not one of the game's levels. The chronicle calls it the greatest of the Ionian cities and dates its capture by siege and mining to 494 BCE, as Herodotus does.
l_miletus.s0: German teams have excavated Miletus since 1899, uncovering a city on a peninsula with several harbours that are now silted up and lie inland. Archaic houses, shrines and workshops have been found on Kalabaktepe hill and in the sanctuary of Aphrodite on Zeytintepe. Both areas show burning and destruction that excavators date to about 494 BCE. The oracle of Apollo at Didyma, the city's great sanctuary, lay about 16 kilometres to the south.
l_miletus.s1: Herodotus says that when Cyrus took Lydia, Miletus kept the terms it had held under Croesus. Its tyrant Histiaeus helped guard Darius's bridge on the Ister and was rewarded with land in Thrace, but he was later kept at the King's side in Susa. His deputy Aristagoras failed to take Naxos with Persian help in about 500 BCE. To save himself, Aristagoras gave up the tyranny and raised Ionia against the King.
l_miletus.s2: Herodotus says that after the Ionian fleet broke at Lade, the Persians besieged Miletus by land and sea, undermined the walls, brought up engines of every kind and took the city in the sixth year of the revolt. Most of the men were killed and the women and children enslaved. The captives were taken to Susa, and Darius settled them at Ampe near the mouth of the Tigris. The sanctuary at Didyma was plundered and burnt.
l_miletus.s3: Herodotus says Miletus was emptied of Milesians, and adds that Athens fined the poet Phrynichus for staging a play called The Capture of Miletus. Yet Milesians served with the Persian army at Mycale in 479 BCE, where they misled it and then attacked it. The city was rebuilt on a regular grid after 479 BCE. Many historians think Herodotus overstated the loss of people, though the excavated destruction confirms a heavy blow.
l_miletus.s4: Later writers told a different story about Didyma. In their version, its priestly family, the Branchidae, handed the temple treasure to Xerxes and went east with him for fear of punishment. Strabo and Curtius say that Alexander found their descendants beyond the Oxus and destroyed them as heirs of traitors. The tale clashes with Herodotus, who places the burning of Didyma in 494 BCE, and it reads as a moral story of betrayal repaid.
l_mycale.lead: Mycale is the mountainous headland on the Ionian coast facing the island of Samos. In 479 BCE the remnant of the Persian fleet was drawn ashore there under the guard of a land army, and a Greek fleet under Leotychides and Xanthippus stormed the camp and burned the ships. The defeat opened the way for the Ionian cities to break away from the King.
l_mycale.play: Mycale is the game's epilogue for 479 BCE. Its chronicle note follows Herodotus on the storming of the ship camp and the burning of the fleet. The claim that this happened on the same day as Plataea is his, and historians doubt it.
l_mycale.s0: Mycale rises steeply from the sea opposite Samos, across a narrow strait. Herodotus says the Panionion, the sacred place where the twelve Ionian cities met for their common festival of Poseidon Heliconius, lay on its northern side. The headland was a landmark for sailors and a meeting place for the same Ionians who would later fight on both sides there.
l_mycale.s1: Herodotus says that after Salamis the surviving fleet gathered at Samos in spring 479 BCE, about 300 ships including the Ionians. When the Greeks came from Delos, its commanders sent away the Phoenician ships and beached the rest at Mycale, near a precinct of Eleusinian Demeter. They built a rampart of stones and felled trees, guarded by a land army he puts at 60,000 under Tigranes, a figure probably too high.
l_mycale.s2: Herodotus says Leotychides first sailed along the shore calling on the Ionians to remember their freedom. The Persians, distrusting them, disarmed the Samians and sent the Milesians to guard the paths. The Athenians and those beside them on the beach broke the barricade of wicker shields and forced the camp; Tigranes fell. The Samians and other Ionians then turned on the Persians, and the Greeks burned the ships and the rampart.
l_mycale.s3: Herodotus says Plataea and Mycale were fought on the same day, and that word of the victory in Boeotia reached the Greeks before the attack, with a herald's staff found on the beach. Diodorus instead has Leotychides invent the news to hearten his men. Historians accept that both battles fell in late summer 479 BCE but doubt the exact link, which Herodotus treats as a sign from the gods. No Persian document mentions the battle.
l_mycale.s4: Herodotus calls Mycale the second revolt of Ionia from Persia. At Samos the Peloponnesians proposed moving the Ionians to mainland Greece, but the Athenians refused, and Samos, Chios, Lesbos and other islanders joined the Greek alliance. The fleet then sailed to the Hellespont, where Xanthippus and the Athenians besieged Sestos.
l_naqsh_e_rostam.lead: Naqsh-e Rostam is a limestone cliff a short distance north-west of Persepolis where Darius I had his tomb cut high in the rock. Three more tombs of the same design were later carved beside it, probably for his successors. The tomb fronts, with their inscriptions and reliefs, are among the clearest statements of how the Achaemenid kings wished their rule to be seen.
l_naqsh_e_rostam.play: The game mentions the cliff in a chronicle note on the royal tombs near Persepolis. The note gives the three later tombs to later kings. Those tombs carry no inscriptions, and none is known to have been cut before 479 BCE, when the game ends.
l_naqsh_e_rostam.s0: Only one of the four tombs names its owner. Two Old Persian inscriptions, with Elamite and Akkadian versions, are carved on its front. In DNa Darius names Auramazda as the giver of his kingship and lists the lands he held. In DNb he describes his own virtues: just to the weak and the strong, in control of his anger, and skilled as a horseman, archer and spearman.
l_naqsh_e_rostam.s1: Each tomb front is cut in the shape of a cross. The middle band copies a palace porch with four columns and a doorway. The doorway leads to burial chambers, where cists cut into the rock held the bodies. Above, the King stands on a stepped platform before a fire altar, on a dais carried by figures of the subject peoples. On Darius's tomb these bearers are labelled, and DNa invites the viewer to look at them to learn how many lands he held.
l_naqsh_e_rostam.s2: The three uninscribed tombs are usually given to Xerxes, Artaxerxes I and Darius II. This rests on their order and style, not on any text. Scholars also argue over the winged figure above the King, read either as Auramazda or as a symbol of royal fortune. They also disagree about the stone tower facing the cliff, called the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht, which has been explained as a tomb, a store for royal objects or a shrine.
l_naqsh_e_rostam.s3: Ctesias, a Greek physician at the later Persian court, tells that Darius wanted to see his tomb but was talked out of going up himself. His father and mother were hauled up the cliff instead by priests pulling on ropes. Frightened by snakes, the priests let go and both parents fell to their deaths. The story survives only in a later summary, and historians treat it with caution.
l_naqsh_e_rostam.s4: The name means picture of Rostam. Long after the Achaemenids, local people took the carvings at the site for images of Rostam, the hero of Persian epic. These carvings include later Sasanian reliefs of mounted kings. Nothing suggests the Achaemenid kings knew of him, and the name says nothing about who made the tombs.
l_naucratis.lead: Naucratis was a river port in the western Nile Delta where Greek merchants were allowed to live, trade and build their own sanctuaries under Egyptian rule. It was the main gateway for Greek goods into Egypt and for Egyptian grain, linen and other wares bound for the Aegean, and it passed under Persian rule when Cambyses conquered Egypt in 525 BCE.
l_naucratis.play: In the game Naucratis is a trade partner of the Memphis level. Historically it lay well downriver in the western Delta, near Sais, and goods moved between the two towns by boat on the Nile.
l_naucratis.s0: Excavations at Kom Gieif identified the site, which stood on the Canopic branch of the Nile a short distance from the royal city of Sais. Flinders Petrie and later British excavators found Greek sanctuaries, large deposits of East Greek and other imported pottery, and a workshop making faience scarabs and amulets for sale. Recent fieldwork has also traced harbour installations along the old river channel.
l_naucratis.s1: Herodotus says the pharaoh Amasis gave Naucratis to Greeks who came to Egypt as a place to settle and trade. He names nine East Greek cities, among them Chios, Rhodes, Halicarnassus and Mytilene, that jointly ran a shared precinct called the Hellenion, while Aegina, Samos and Miletus kept their own temples. He adds that Naucratis had once been the only port open to Greek traders, so ships arriving at other Nile mouths were sent on to it.
l_naucratis.s2: Herodotus links Naucratis to Amasis, who ruled from about 570 BCE, but Strabo credits Milesian settlers in the time of an earlier Psammetichus. The pottery supports a Greek presence from the late 7th century, before Amasis. Most historians now think Amasis regulated an existing trading community rather than founding it, though how the town was governed and how far it was Egyptian as well as Greek is still argued.
l_naucratis.s3: Naucratis kept trading after Cambyses took Egypt in 525 BCE, and Greek imports continued. An erased Aramaic customs account from Elephantine, dated to about 475 BCE in the reign of Xerxes, lists Ionian and Phoenician ships paying duties on cargoes entering Egypt, including wine, oil and metals. The text does not name its port, and scholars disagree whether it reflects Naucratis or another Delta harbour, but it shows how the King's officials taxed this sea trade.
l_naucratis.s4: Herodotus tells of Rhodopis, a Thracian-born courtesan who became famous at Naucratis in the time of Amasis. Charaxus of Mytilene, brother of the poet Sappho, paid a large sum to free her, and Herodotus says Sappho mocked her brother for it in a poem. Some Greeks claimed Rhodopis built one of the Giza pyramids, a story Herodotus rejects. The tale reflects the town's fame in Greek gossip more than its history.
l_naxos.lead: Naxos was a rich Greek island in the central Aegean. Herodotus links a failed Persian attack on it in 499 BCE to the outbreak of the Ionian Revolt. In 490 BCE the fleet of Datis and Artaphernes came back and burned its town on the way to Eretria and Marathon.
l_naxos.play: The game mentions Naxos only in the event articles on the siege of Naxos and the expedition of Datis and Artaphernes. It has no level or mechanic of its own.
l_naxos.s0: Herodotus says that Naxos was the most prosperous of the islands around 500 BCE. He says it had a large body of hoplites and many ships. He also says that wealthy Naxians, driven out by the people, went to Miletus and asked Aristagoras to help them return.
l_naxos.s1: Herodotus says Aristagoras promised the satrap Artaphernes that Naxos could be taken cheaply and would lead on to other islands. Artaphernes obtained the King's consent and prepared a fleet of 200 ships under Megabates. Herodotus says Megabates quarrelled with Aristagoras and warned the Naxians, who brought in their property and stored supplies. The Persians besieged the island for four months, ran short of money, built a fort for the exiles and withdrew.
l_naxos.s2: Herodotus says Aristagoras feared punishment after the failure and chose to rebel. Modern historians accept that the attack happened but doubt that one private quarrel explains so large a rising. They also look to resentment of tyrants set up by Persia, tribute and trade, and the exact date of the siege is not certain.
l_naxos.s3: Herodotus says that Datis sailed through the Aegean towards Eretria and Athens. At Naxos the inhabitants fled to the hills. The Persians enslaved those they caught and burned the sanctuaries and the town. The fleet then went on to Delos, where Herodotus says Datis spared the sanctuary.
l_naxos.s4: No Persian inscription or tablet known to the compilers describes either attack on Naxos, so the story rests on Herodotus, who wrote from the Greek side a generation or more later. How much damage the island suffered in 490 BCE is therefore uncertain. Herodotus also lists Naxian ships among those that served in 480 BCE, and says they went over to the Greeks.
l_nile_delta.lead: The Delta is the wide, low triangle of land where the Nile divides into branches before reaching the sea. Its towns included Sais, Naucratis and Pelusium. Cambyses entered Egypt at its eastern edge in 525 BCE, and Herodotus, who saw it, calls Egypt the gift of the river.
l_nile_delta.play: The Delta's eastern edge is the Pelusium field and the Memphis level's way in; its mud, mouths and towns appear in the level's texts and chatter.
l_nile_delta.s0: Herodotus says the part of Egypt the Greeks sail to is land the river has brought down, the gift of the river. He gives the coast as sixty schoeni long, from the Plinthine gulf to the Serbonian lake, and describes the land as flat, watery and made of black, crumbling soil.
l_nile_delta.s1: Herodotus reports the Ionian view that only the Delta was Egypt, from the watch-tower of Perseus to the salting-houses of Pelusium. He rejects it: Egypt, he says, is all the land the Egyptians live in, from Elephantine to the sea.
l_nile_delta.s2: Herodotus names the Nile's mouths: the Pelusiac in the east, the Canopic in the west, and between them the Sebennytic, Saitic, Mendesian, Bolbitine and Bucolic, the last two dug by hand. Pelusium guarded the eastern mouth, and Cambyses' army met Psamtik's there.
l_nile_delta.s3: The last native dynasty before the Persians ruled from Sais in the western Delta, and Amasis gave the Greeks Naucratis as their trading town. Excavations at Sais, Naucratis and Tell Defenneh show the Delta's Greek and Carian settlers of the sixth century.
l_opis.lead: Opis was a town on the Tigris in Babylonia, in the region of the later Seleucia. In the month of Tashritu in 539 BCE Cyrus's army fought the Babylonian forces there, according to the Nabonidus Chronicle, and Babylon was entered soon after. The battle opened the last stage of Cyrus's conquest of Babylonia.
l_opis.play: The game has no level or mechanic for Opis. It is named only in the Encyclopedia's event articles, including the fall of Babylon, as the place where Cyrus beat Nabonidus's army.
l_opis.s0: The Nabonidus Chronicle, a Babylonian text on clay, says that Cyrus fought the army of Akkad at Opis on the Tigris in the month of Tashritu. It says the people of Akkad withdrew and that Cyrus's forces killed the inhabitants. The Chronicle is a near-contemporary text, though it favours Cyrus, and it is the main evidence for the battle.
l_opis.s1: The Chronicle says Sippar was taken without fighting a few days later, and that Nabonidus fled. Ugbaru, governor of Gutium, and the army of Cyrus then entered Babylon without a battle. Cyrus himself came into the city about two weeks afterwards. The text describes no fighting at Babylon.
l_opis.s2: The surviving Chronicle text does not say that Nabonidus led the army at Opis, and the game's note that he did goes beyond it. The Chronicle names him again only when he fled from Sippar. Other Babylonian texts show his son Belshazzar active in military affairs, so some historians think he or other commanders held the field.
l_opis.s3: Herodotus tells of Cyrus's move on Babylon and of a battle in the open before the city, after which the Babylonians were shut inside. He also tells of Cyrus dividing the Gyndes river into channels. He does not name Opis, and his story of Babylon being taken by diverting the Euphrates differs from the Chronicle's entry without a battle.
l_opis.s4: Opis stayed a known town. Xenophon places it on the Tigris in the march of the Ten Thousand, and Arrian describes Alexander holding an assembly and facing a mutiny there in 324. These later passages show the place but say nothing about 539 BCE.
l_pactolus.lead: The Pactolus is a small river that runs north from Mount Tmolus through the site of Sardis and into the Hermus. In antiquity it carried flakes of electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver, and the Lydian kings refined this metal beside its banks. Its gold became a byword for the wealth of Croesus, and under Persian rule Sardis remained the main seat of royal power in western Anatolia.
l_pactolus.play: In the Sardis level (498 BCE) the Pactolus is the gold-bearing river beside which the Pactolus Gold Refinery stands. The excavated refinery dates from the Lydian kings, and there is no clear evidence it still worked under the Persians, so the game extends it.
l_pactolus.s0: Herodotus says that Lydia had few marvels worth recording except the gold dust washed down from Tmolus. He describes the Pactolus carrying this gold through the middle of the agora of Sardis before joining the Hermus, which flows on to the sea. Strabo, writing centuries later, says the river had once supplied the wealth of Croesus but that its gold had run out by his own day.
l_pactolus.s1: Excavators at Sardis found a gold refinery on the east bank of the river, in the area called Pactolus North, dated to the 500s BCE before the Persian conquest. Workers removed lead and base metals by cupellation, then heated the gold with salt to draw off the silver, a process called cementation. Crucibles, furnaces and scraps of gold foil survive, along with an altar nearby. It is the earliest well-documented gold-parting workshop known.
l_pactolus.s2: Herodotus tells how Ionian rebels, with Athenian and Eretrian allies, marched on Sardis in 498 BCE. A soldier set fire to a house, and because most houses were built of reeds or roofed with them, the blaze spread through the lower city. The Lydians and Persians trapped by the fire gathered in the agora beside the Pactolus to defend themselves, and the attackers withdrew to the coast. The satrap Artaphernes held the citadel throughout.
l_pactolus.s3: Lydia struck some of the earliest coins in electrum, probably in the late 600s BCE, and probably from river metal. Herodotus says the Lydians were the first to strike coins of gold and silver, and modern scholars call these pure-metal coins Croeseids. Some historians argued that the Persians first struck them after taking Sardis in about 547 BCE. Coins found in the destruction level of that sack led Cahill and Kroll to argue that they began under Croesus, but the debate continues.
l_pactolus.s4: Later Greek and Roman writers explained the river's gold with the story of Midas, the Phrygian king whose touch turned everything to gold. Ovid tells that the god Bacchus sent him to bathe at the source of the Pactolus, and that the curse passed into the water and its sands. The tale was written down more than five centuries after Croesus and is myth, not history.
l_parthia.lead: Parthia, Old Persian Parthava, lay south-east of the Caspian Sea, in what is now north-eastern Iran and southern Turkmenistan. In 522-521 BCE it rose with Hyrcania for Fravartish of Media, and Darius's father Hystaspes, who held it, beat the rebels twice.
l_parthia.play: Parthia is named in the Bagastana and Parsa levels' Chronicle and the King's generals' campaigns, where Hystaspes holds it for his son.
l_parthia.s0: Darius says Parthia and Hyrcania rebelled and declared for Fravartish. His father Hystaspes was in Parthia; he fought the rebels at Vishpauzatish on 22 Viyakhna and won. Darius then sent Persian troops from Raga, and Hystaspes won again at Patigrabana on 1 Garmapada.
l_parthia.s1: Herodotus puts the Parthians in his sixteenth division of the tribute with the Chorasmians, Sogdians and Areians, paying 300 talents. In Xerxes' army the Parthians and Chorasmians served under Artabazus son of Pharnaces, armed like the Bactrians.
l_parthia.s2: Herodotus tells of a plain enclosed by mountains on the borders of the Chorasmians, Hyrcanians, Parthians, Sarangians and Thamanaeans, watered by the river Aces through five gorges. He says the King dammed the gorges and sold the water to the peoples for a price.
l_parthia.s3: This Achaemenid Parthia is not yet the Parthian kingdom of the Arsacids, who rose about 247 BCE and later ruled Iran. Its people appear on the Persepolis reliefs bringing a camel and vessels.
l_pasargadae.lead: Pasargadae was the royal seat that Cyrus the Great built on a high plain of Persis, beside the Pulvar river, after he overthrew the Median king Astyages. It was the first great Achaemenid building site: stone palaces set among gardens rather than a walled city of streets. Cyrus was buried there, and a later Greek writer says new kings still came to it to be made king.
l_pasargadae.play: The first level is set here in 530 BCE, among palaces, a gatehouse and walled gardens fed by stone channels. The game follows Strabo in siting the city on Cyrus's battlefield, which the Babylonian chronicle does not confirm.
l_pasargadae.s0: Excavations, above all David Stronach's in 1961-63, uncovered a gatehouse (Gate R) with a relief of a four-winged guardian figure, a tall-columned audience hall (Palace S) and a residential palace (Palace P). Between them ran cut limestone water channels with small square basins at intervals. A stone platform, the Tall-e Takht, rises on a hill to the north, and one wall of a square stone tower, the Zendan-e Soleyman, still stands nearby.
l_pasargadae.s1: Strabo says Cyrus honoured Pasargadae because he won his final battle against Astyages there and built his palace on the spot. The Nabonidus Chronicle, written in Babylon, says instead that Astyages' own troops rebelled, seized him and handed him over to Cyrus, who then took Ecbatana; it names no battlefield. Herodotus gives Pasargadae as the name of the leading Persian tribe, so the place may simply have been that tribe's home ground.
l_pasargadae.s2: Short texts in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian on the palace doorways name Cyrus as king and an Achaemenid. Many historians think they were added under Darius, who says he introduced a new form of writing, to tie his own line to Cyrus. Others argue some were cut in Cyrus's lifetime. Stronach's neat four-part garden plan has also been questioned by later survey work at the site.
l_pasargadae.s3: The tomb still stands south-west of the palaces: a gabled stone chamber on six stepped courses. Arrian, drawing on Aristobulus, says it held a golden couch and coffin. He adds that it was guarded by magi who received a sheep each day and a horse each month for sacrifice. He reports that Alexander found it robbed on his return from India, about 324, and ordered Aristobulus to restore it.
l_pasargadae.s4: Plutarch, writing around 100 CE, says each new Persian king went to a sanctuary of a warrior goddess at Pasargadae. There he put on the robe Cyrus had worn before he became king, ate a fig cake, chewed terebinth and drank sour milk. Plutarch tells it of Artaxerxes II in 404 BCE, so it describes later practice written down five centuries afterwards. It still shows Pasargadae remained the seat of Cyrus's memory long after Darius built Persepolis.
l_peloponnese.lead: The Peloponnese is the large peninsula of southern Greece, joined to the mainland by the Isthmus of Corinth. Sparta led most of its cities in a league, though Argos held aloof. In 480 BCE the Peloponnesians walled the Isthmus to keep the King out, and in 479 BCE they marched north to Plataea.
l_peloponnese.play: The Peloponnese is named in the Thermopylae and Plataea levels' texts: the grain ships bound for it, the Athenians who fled there, and the Peloponnesians at Mycale and Sestos.
l_peloponnese.s0: When the Peloponnesians heard that Leonidas had fallen, Herodotus says, they gathered at the Isthmus under Cleombrotus, Leonidas's brother, broke up the Scironian road and built a wall across, working night and day with stones, bricks, timber and baskets of sand.
l_peloponnese.s1: Before Salamis the Peloponnesian commanders wanted to fall back and fight by the Isthmus, near their own land. Themistocles argued for the narrows of Salamis and, Herodotus says, sent word to the King to make the Greeks fight there.
l_peloponnese.s2: Herodotus lists the Peloponnesians at the Isthmus: Spartans, Arcadians, Eleans, Corinthians, Sicyonians, Epidaurians, Phliasians, Troezenians and Hermionians. The rest, Argos among them, he says, sat still, and so took the King's side.
l_peloponnese.s3: In 479 BCE the Spartans delayed while the wall was finished, until the Athenians threatened to come to terms with Mardonius. Then five thousand Spartans, each with seven helots, marched out by night, and the other Peloponnesians followed them to Plataea.
l_pelusium.lead: Pelusium stood at the mouth of the easternmost, Pelusiac, branch of the Nile, where the road from Gaza and Sinai reached the Delta. Any army coming from Asia had to pass it. In 525 BCE Cambyses defeated Psamtik III's army nearby, and this one battle opened Egypt to Persian rule, which in its first period lasted until about 404 BCE.
l_pelusium.play: Pelusium is not one of the game's levels. The chronicle names it as Egypt's gate, where Cambyses broke Psamtik III's army in 525 BCE, and recalls Herodotus's story of the skulls on the battlefield.
l_pelusium.s0: The site lies at Tell el-Farama in north-west Sinai, now some distance inland because the coast and the river branch have shifted. The ruins visible there today are mostly Hellenistic, Roman and later, so little of the town of 525 BCE can be seen. Excavated forts elsewhere on the eastern edge of the Delta, such as Tell Defenneh, show that the Saite kings guarded this frontier closely.
l_pelusium.s1: Herodotus says that Phanes of Halicarnassus, one of Amasis's Greek mercenaries, deserted to Cambyses. Phanes advised him to ask the Arab king for safe passage across the waterless desert. According to Herodotus, the Arabs carried water to the army in camel-skins. He also repeats a less likely tale of a leather pipeline from a distant river.
l_pelusium.s2: Herodotus says Amasis had died, and his son Psamtik III waited with his army at the Pelusiac mouth. Before the fighting, the Greek and Carian mercenaries killed the sons of Phanes in sight of their father and drank their blood mixed with wine and water. The battle was hard fought, but the Egyptians broke and fled to Memphis, which Cambyses then besieged and took.
l_pelusium.s3: Herodotus says he saw the bones of the fallen still lying in two heaps. In his account the Persian skulls were so thin that a pebble could pierce them, while the Egyptian ones could hardly be broken with a stone, because Egyptians shaved their heads in the sun from childhood. Historians treat this explanation as local lore. Ctesias tells the war differently: he names the Egyptian king Amyrtaeus and credits the Persian victory to the treachery of a eunuch, Combaphis.
l_pelusium.s4: A tale written down more than six centuries later says that Cambyses won at Pelusium by placing cats and other animals sacred to the Egyptians in front of his troops. In this tale, the Egyptian soldiers would not shoot for fear of harming them. No early source mentions the story, and it is best read as a moral tale about Egyptian piety and Persian cunning.
l_persepolis.lead: Persepolis, called Parsa in Old Persian, was the palace city Darius I founded on a stone terrace below the Kuh-e Rahmat, the Mountain of Mercy, in Persis. Xerxes and later kings added halls and gates for more than a century, and its clay tablets are the richest surviving record of how the King's economy in Persis fed and paid its workers. Alexander burned its palaces in 330.
l_persepolis.play: The Parsa level is set in 521 BCE, a few years before work on the terrace is usually dated to begin, about 518 BCE. Building there in 521 BCE puts the start slightly earlier than the evidence suggests.
l_persepolis.s0: Darius had a platform of about 12 hectares levelled and walled against the mountain, probably beginning around 518 to 515 BCE. Inscriptions on its south wall name him, and one Elamite text (DPf) says a fortress was built here where none had stood before. Foundation tablets of gold and silver (DPh) were found in 1933 in stone boxes under corners of the Apadana. They describe the extent of his kingdom.
l_persepolis.s1: The Apadana was a hall of 36 columns, probably used for royal audiences. Darius began it and it was finished under Xerxes. Xerxes added the Gate of All Nations, whose inscription (XPa) names him, and began the Hall of a Hundred Columns, which was completed under Artaxerxes I. Building on the terrace went on in some form until the end of the dynasty.
l_persepolis.s2: Chicago excavators found thousands of clay tablets, mostly in Elamite with some in Aramaic, in the fortification wall in 1933. They record food issued between 509 and 493 BCE to workers, travellers on the roads and horses, and for offerings to gods. Payments were made in barley, flour, wine and beer. A later group from the Treasury, dated 492 to 458 BCE, records silver paid to craftsmen in place of part of their rations.
l_persepolis.s3: The Apadana stairways show delegations of subject peoples bringing gifts to the King. Some scholars read the terrace as a stage for a yearly festival, perhaps the new year. Others note that no ancient text names such a festival, and that the tablets show a busy administrative and residential centre. Herodotus never mentions Persepolis, and Greek writers seem to have known little of it before Alexander.
l_persepolis.s4: Arrian says Alexander burned the palaces on purpose, against Parmenion's advice, as revenge for the Persian burning of Athenian temples in 480 BCE. Diodorus describes the sack of the city and a drinking party at which the Athenian courtesan Thais urged the king to start the fire. Historians still argue whether the burning was policy or a drunken act. Burnt layers survive in the Treasury and the halls.
l_persis.lead: Persis, in Old Persian Pārsa, was the homeland of the Persians, a land of high valleys and mountains north of the Persian Gulf. From here the family of Cyrus rose to rule an empire. Cyrus built Pasargadae and his tomb here, Darius began Persepolis, and Darius and his successors were buried in rock-cut tombs nearby. Its clay archives make it one of the best documented regions of the early empire.
l_persis.play: The game treats Persis as the homeland province around its Pasargadae and Parsa levels. That is broadly right, though Persis was no ordinary province, and historians still debate how it stood beside the satrapies.
l_persis.s0: Strabo, writing about five centuries after Darius, divided Persis into three belts: a hot, sandy coast on the Gulf, a fertile middle zone of plains and rivers, and a cold, mountainous north. The Achaemenid heartland lay in the high valleys of the Zagros, such as the Marv Dasht plain watered by the Kur and the Pulvar. The modern Iranian province of Fars keeps the old name.
l_persis.s1: On his clay cylinder Cyrus called himself and his forefathers kings of Anshan, an old Elamite royal title. Inscribed bricks found at Tall-i Malyan, in the Kur basin, identify that mound as Anshan. The Persians probably settled among Elamite people in the early first millennium. Their language was Iranian, but much of their writing, administration and art drew on Elam.
l_persis.s2: Thousands of clay tablets, found in 1933 and 1934 in the fortification wall at Persepolis, date from about 509 to 493 BCE and are written mostly in Elamite. They record grain, wine, beer and animals issued to workers, travellers, officials and priests across Persis and into Elam, under the director Parnaka. They also show offerings to Auramazda and to Elamite gods such as Humban.
l_persis.s3: Herodotus says that the Persians alone paid no tribute and lived untaxed. Yet the Fortification tablets show crops gathered into royal stores and labour gangs fed and organised across Persis. Historians debate whether the exemption meant only freedom from the silver tribute of the other lands, and whether Persis had a satrap at all or was run directly from the King's own estates.
l_persis.s4: Herodotus closes his Histories with a story set in Cyrus's day. A Persian named Artembares proposed that they leave their rugged country for a richer one, and Cyrus warned that soft lands breed soft men. The Persians chose to rule from a harsh land rather than sow the plains and serve others. The tale is a moral frame for Greek readers after the Persian defeats, not a record of an actual debate.
l_phaleron.lead: Phaleron was the wide sandy bay south-west of Athens, the city's harbour until Themistocles fortified the Piraeus. After Marathon the Persian fleet rounded Sunium and lay off Phaleron before sailing home. In 480 BCE Xerxes' fleet gathered there before Salamis.
l_phaleron.play: Phaleron is the end of the sea race in the Marathon level's second front, where the fleet sails round Sunium to reach Athens before its army.
l_phaleron.s0: After the battle of Marathon the Persian fleet sailed round Sunium, hoping to reach Athens first. The Athenians marched home as fast as they could and camped at the precinct of Heracles at Cynosarges. Herodotus says the fleet lay off Phaleron, then the Athenians' seaport, for a time and sailed back to Asia.
l_phaleron.s1: In 480 BCE, after Artemisium, the King's fleet came to Phaleron. Herodotus says Xerxes came down to the ships and held a council there, with the king of Sidon in the first seat, and only Artemisia advised against fighting at sea.
l_phaleron.s2: Herodotus calls Phaleron the Athenians' seaport in 490 BCE. Thucydides says Themistocles began fortifying the Piraeus in his archonship, usually dated 493 BCE/2, and the city's harbour moved there after the Persian wars. The open beach at Phaleron was hard to defend.
l_phaleron.s3: Excavations at the Phaleron cemetery since 2012 have found many burials of the seventh and sixth centuries, among them men buried shackled in rows. Their identity is argued, but the cemetery shows a busy shore community long before the Piraeus.
l_plataea.lead: Plataea was a small Boeotian city on the northern slopes of Mount Cithaeron, close to the border with Thebes. A firm ally of Athens, it sent its men to fight at Marathon in 490 BCE. In 479 BCE the plain below it saw the defeat and death of Mardonius, which ended the Persian land invasion of mainland Greece.
l_plataea.play: Plataea is the setting of the game's eleventh level, in 479 BCE. Its chronicle note follows the Greek tradition that Plataea alone sent men to help Athens at Marathon, and that Mardonius was killed near the town.
l_plataea.s0: Plataea stood on the lower slopes of Cithaeron above the Asopus valley, not far from Thebes. Herodotus says the Plataeans, pressed by the Thebans, offered themselves to Athens on the advice of the Spartan king Cleomenes. Thucydides dates the alliance to 519 BCE, though some historians prefer a date about 509 BCE. From then on Plataea was bound to Athens and at odds with Thebes.
l_plataea.s1: Herodotus says that when the Athenians faced the Persians at Marathon in 490 BCE, the Plataeans came to help them with their whole levy. He names no other Greek allies, and the Spartans arrived only after the battle. The Plataeans held the left wing. Herodotus adds that afterwards the Athenian herald included the Plataeans in the prayers at the four-yearly Athenian festivals.
l_plataea.s2: In 480 BCE Xerxes' army burned Plataea after the Thebans named it as hostile. In 479 BCE Mardonius camped along the Asopus and built a wooden stockade in Theban land. Days of skirmishing followed, in which his cavalry commander Masistius was killed and the Greeks lost their water. The Greeks under Pausanias then tried a night withdrawal. Mardonius attacked and fell fighting the Spartans and Tegeans, and the Athenians broke into his fort.
l_plataea.s3: Herodotus gives the Greeks about 110,000 men and Mardonius 300,000 Asian troops plus Greek allies. He claims fewer than 3,000 of these survived, apart from the 40,000 Artabazus led away. Historians treat his Persian figures as heavily exaggerated, and modern estimates vary widely. No Persian source mentions the battle, so its course rests almost entirely on Greek writers, chiefly Herodotus a generation later.
l_plataea.s4: From the spoils the Greeks dedicated at Delphi a gold tripod set on a bronze column of three twisted serpents. The gold is long gone, but the bronze column survives in the Hippodrome of Istanbul, where it was taken in the reign of Constantine. Its coils carry the names of 31 Greek states that fought the Persians, Plataea among them.
l_psyttaleia.lead: Psyttaleia is a small, rocky islet in the narrows between Salamis and the Attic mainland. Before the sea battle of Salamis in 480 BCE, Persians were landed there. Herodotus and Aeschylus both say the party was destroyed by Greek troops, and Herodotus names Aristides as the man who led the attack.
l_psyttaleia.play: Psyttaleia is named only in the Chronicle and in the Salamis event articles, and has no mechanic of its own. The game's note that Aristides killed the Persians there compresses Herodotus, who has him land Athenian hoplites to do it.
l_psyttaleia.s0: Herodotus places Psyttaleia in the strait between Salamis and the mainland, on the line the fleets used. Aeschylus, in his play The Persians, describes it as a small island off Salamis and makes it the scene of a Persian disaster. Both writers knew the waters and the events at first or second hand.
l_psyttaleia.s1: Herodotus says that during the night, as the Persian fleet moved to close the strait, men were put ashore on Psyttaleia. He gives the aim as holding the islet, where wrecks and swimmers were likely to be driven. He does not state their number. Pausanias, writing much later, gives a figure of about 400 BCE.
l_psyttaleia.s2: Herodotus says Aristides son of Lysimachus took a body of Athenian hoplites across to the islet during the sea fight and killed the Persians there. Aeschylus also describes the Persian party on the island being destroyed by the Greeks. Plutarch repeats the story with Aristides in command.
l_psyttaleia.s3: All the evidence is Greek, and no Persian text mentions the islet. The number landed, their rank and the exact part Aristides played cannot be checked against any independent record. Pausanias wrote centuries later, so his figure is better read as tradition than as a count.
l_pulvar.lead: The Pulvar runs through the plain of Pasargadae, cuts south through a narrow gorge, and joins the Kur on the Marvdasht plain below Persepolis. Its water made farming possible on the high Pasargadae plain and probably fed the stone channels of Cyrus's royal garden. Both the first Persian royal seat and the later one at Persepolis lay along its course.
l_pulvar.play: The game shows the Pulvar watering the farms of the Pasargadae plain, which is broadly true. It simplifies the picture: in practice river water reached fields and gardens through dug channels.
l_pulvar.s0: The Pulvar rises in the mountains north of Pasargadae and flows south across the Murghab plain, past the remains of Cyrus's palaces and tomb. It then passes through the Tang-i Bulaghi gorge onto the Marvdasht plain. There it runs past Istakhr and Naqsh-e Rostam and meets the larger Kur south of the Persepolis terrace. Pulvar is a modern name, and the river's Achaemenid name is not securely known.
l_pulvar.s1: Stronach excavated the palace area at Pasargadae and found narrow limestone channels running along the edges of a formal garden, with small square basins set at intervals. The water was probably drawn from the river system of the plain. The channels show that the garden and the setting of the palaces were planned around a controlled water supply.
l_pulvar.s2: Strabo names a river Cyrus that flowed through Persis near Pasargadae, and a river Medus that joined the Araxes near Persepolis. Arrian has Alexander cross the Araxes on his way to Persepolis. The Kur is usually taken as the Araxes, while the Pulvar has been matched both with Strabo's Cyrus and with his Medus. None of these identifications is certain.
l_pulvar.s3: Before the Sivand dam on the Pulvar began flooding the valley in the 2000s, Iranian and foreign teams carried out rescue excavations in the Tang-i Bulaghi gorge. They recorded settlements and other remains of the Achaemenid period along the river. This work suggests that the valley linking Pasargadae and Persepolis was farmed and lived in during the Persian period, not merely passed through.
l_royal_road.lead: The Royal Road was the King's route from Sardis in Lydia to Susa in Elam, described by Herodotus with 111 stations and about ninety days of walking. It was the best-known line in a wider network of guarded roads, rest stations and ration stores that let officials, troops and royal messages cross the empire on the King's authority.
l_royal_road.play: The game's chronicle note for the Sardis to Susa journey follows Herodotus: 111 stations, some ninety days on foot, royal couriers riding in relays, and gates and a fort at the Halys crossing.
l_royal_road.s0: Herodotus says the road ran from Sardis through Lydia, Phrygia, Cappadocia, Cilicia, Armenia, Matiene and Cissia to Susa, with 111 stations where travellers could lodge. He counts 450 parasangs of 30 stadia each, which at 150 stadia a day makes ninety days of walking, and he adds three days from Ephesus to Sardis. Gates and a strong guard-post stood at the crossing of the Halys, with more at the Cilician border and in Armenia.
l_royal_road.s1: Herodotus says men and horses were posted along the way, one for each day's stage, and each rider handed the message to the next whatever the weather. He says the Persians called this service angareion and that nothing mortal travelled faster. He compares it to the Greek torch-race, in which a flame passed from runner to runner.
l_royal_road.s2: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, written mostly in Elamite in about 509-493 BCE, record rations of flour, wine and beer issued to travellers at stations. Parties carried a sealed authorisation from the King or a senior official, and their journeys linked Persepolis and Susa with Sardis, Arachosia, India and Egypt. A later Aramaic letter of the satrap Arshama shows the same system of sealed ration orders still at work in the late fifth century.
l_royal_road.s3: Herodotus's list of regions is hard to fit onto a map, and historians disagree about the line through Anatolia. Some trace a course across central Anatolia, others a more southern one nearer Cilicia. Its route east of the Euphrates, and whether it passed near Arbela, is also argued. Most now see it as a set of maintained routes with stations rather than a single paved highway.
l_royal_road.s4: Xenophon says Cyrus founded the relay system after finding how far a horse could ride in a day, and set stations at that distance with horses and grooms. The Cyropaedia is an idealised portrait of Cyrus written more than a century later, so this credit cannot be checked. The surviving records of the system date from the reign of Darius.
l_sagartia.lead: Sagartia was the land of the Sagartians, Iranian nomads of the plateau east of Media. In 521 BCE a Sagartian named Citrantakhma claimed to be king of Sagartia of the line of Cyaxares and rose against Darius. Herodotus knows the Sagartians as horsemen who fought with the lasso.
l_sagartia.play: Sagartia is named in the Bagastana level's Chronicle and the King's generals' campaigns, among the lands that rose in 522-521 BCE.
l_sagartia.s0: Darius says a Sagartian named Citrantakhma rebelled, saying he was king in Sagartia of the family of Cyaxares. Darius sent against him a Mede, Takhmaspada, who beat him and brought him in. Darius cut off his nose and ears, and impaled him at Arbela.
l_sagartia.s1: Herodotus says the Sagartians were nomads, Persian in race and speech, who brought eight thousand horse to Xerxes' army. They carried no weapons of bronze or iron but daggers, and fought by throwing ropes of plaited leather with nooses, dragging down horse or man.
l_sagartia.s2: Herodotus lists the Sagartians among the tribes of the Persians, with the Daans, Mardians and others who were nomads, as distinct from the farming tribes. For tribute they were put in the fourteenth division with the Sarangians and others, paying six hundred talents.
l_sagartia.s3: Its place is uncertain. Most historians put it on the central plateau east of Media, perhaps toward modern Yazd, and see it as a pastoral land rather than a province with cities. The Sagartians' link to the Median royal line in Citrantakhma's claim is also unexplained.
l_sais.lead: Sais was a city in the western Nile Delta and the home of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty, the last line of native kings before the Persian conquest of 525 BCE. Its temple of Neith and its House of Life made it a centre of Egyptian cult and learning. Under Persian rule it appears in the record of an Egyptian official who served the Persian kings.
l_sais.play: The game names Sais in Chronicle entries and in the articles on the House of Life and Udjahorresnet. It is not a level or a figure, and it has no mechanic of its own.
l_sais.s0: Herodotus says that Amasis, the last strong king before the Persian invasion, came from the Saite district, and he places Amasis's tomb inside the precinct of the temple of Neith at Sais. He also describes that temple as a great one. His picture rests on what he was told in Egypt, and it is a Greek writer's view of the city.
l_sais.s1: The statue of Udjahorresnet, an Egyptian official who served Cambyses and Darius, records his work at the temple of Neith at Sais. It says that Cambyses came to Sais, learned about the temple, and ordered foreign people removed from it. The text presents the king as honouring the goddess and restoring her offerings and festivals.
l_sais.s2: The same statue records that Darius, while in Elam, ordered Udjahorresnet back to Egypt to restore the House of Life at Sais. The House was a temple institution for scribes, probably concerned with sacred writings, medicine and ritual. The inscription says Darius supplied people and means for the work. It is an Egyptian official's own account and naturally praises his service to the king.
l_sais.s3: Historians differ over how far the House of Life was a school or library and how far a temple workshop for texts and rites. Little of the city survives to test the matter. Some scholars see Darius's act as part of a wider policy of winning over Egyptian priesthoods, and link it to later traditions of a codification of Egyptian law.
