l_sais.s4: Sais lies under and around the village of Sa el-Hagar in the Delta. Little of the ancient city stands above ground, and the high water table makes excavation hard. Archaeological work there, including by the Egypt Exploration Society, has examined parts of the site.
l_salamis.lead: Salamis is an island in the Saronic Gulf just west of Athens, divided from the Attic coast by a narrow strait. In September 480 BCE the allied Greek fleet, with Athens supplying the largest share of ships, defeated the King's navy there. The defeat ended Xerxes' hope of a quick conquest; he returned to Asia and left Mardonius to carry on the war on land.
l_salamis.play: Salamis is not one of the game's levels. It appears only as a chronicle note recording the Greek victory of September 480 BCE with Xerxes watching from the shore, which agrees with Herodotus.
l_salamis.s0: Herodotus says that after Thermopylae the allied fleet drew back from Artemisium to Salamis, and the Athenians shipped their families to Troezen, Aegina and Salamis itself. Persian troops then took the abandoned city and burned the Acropolis, where a few defenders had held out behind a wooden barricade. The allied commanders argued over whether to fight at Salamis or fall back to the Isthmus of Corinth.
l_salamis.s1: Herodotus reports that Themistocles, afraid the allies would scatter, sent his slave Sicinnus to tell the Persians that the Greeks meant to slip away. Xerxes' ships spent the night closing the exits of the strait, and troops were landed on the islet of Psyttaleia. Aeschylus, who by later tradition fought in the battle, tells a similar story in his play Persians, staged in 472 BCE.
l_salamis.s2: In the cramped water the larger Persian fleet could not use its numbers, and its ships fouled one another while the Greeks rammed them. Xerxes watched from the foot of Mount Aegaleos, with scribes noting which captains fought well. His brother Ariabignes, an admiral, was killed, Artemisia escaped by ramming a ship of her own side, and Aristides led hoplites who killed the Persians on Psyttaleia.
l_salamis.s3: Herodotus gives the King 1,207 triremes at the start of the campaign and says that losses were replaced. He counts about 380 Greek ships at Salamis. Aeschylus gives the Greeks 310 and Xerxes 1,000, with 207 fast ships either among them or extra. Most historians think the Persian totals exaggerated and cut down by storms and the fighting at Artemisium, so the real odds are still argued. No Persian text mentions the battle; every surviving account is Greek.
l_salamis.s4: Herodotus records stories of the supernatural: a cloud of dust and a ritual cry rising from Eleusis before the battle, and a phantom woman who shamed the Greeks into attacking. Plutarch, writing some six centuries later, repeats a claim by Phanias of Lesbos that Themistocles sacrificed three Persian captives before the fight. Many historians doubt this tale.
l_salamis_cyprus.lead: Salamis was the main Greek city of eastern Cyprus and the seat of Onesilus, who led the Cypriot revolt against Persia during the Ionian Revolt. Herodotus places the decisive land battle of that revolt on the plain by the city. The game calls it the city of Onesilus; Herodotus says he took it from his brother Gorgus, the ruling king.
l_salamis_cyprus.play: Salamis is named in the event articles on the revolt of Cyprus and the Ionian Revolt. It has no mechanic of its own. The game presents it as the city of Onesilus, which simplifies Herodotus's story of his seizing it from Gorgus.
l_salamis_cyprus.s0: Herodotus says the Cypriots gave themselves to Cambyses and so came under Persian rule, and that they were counted in the tribute districts of Darius. He names Gorgus as king of Salamis when the Ionian Revolt began.
l_salamis_cyprus.s1: Herodotus tells how Onesilus, Gorgus's younger brother, urged Gorgus to join the Ionians and rebel. When Gorgus refused, Onesilus shut him out of the city and took power, and Gorgus went over to the Persians. Herodotus says all Cyprus except Amathus joined the revolt.
l_salamis_cyprus.s2: Herodotus says a Persian army crossed from Cilicia while a Phoenician fleet sailed round to Cyprus. The Ionians defeated the Phoenicians at sea, but the Persians prevailed on land by the plain of Salamis. He says Onesilus was killed in the fighting, and that the defection of the Curium contingent and of the Salamis chariots decided the day.
l_salamis_cyprus.s3: Herodotus says the Persians besieged the rebel cities one by one and brought the whole island back under their rule within a year of the revolt's start. His account of Cyprus ends there, and he says nothing more about Salamis.
l_salamis_cyprus.s4: Herodotus is the only continuous source for the revolt of Cyprus, and he writes from a Greek point of view. Modern historians generally accept the outline but debate the details, such as the treachery at Curium and the exact dates. Excavation at Salamis has uncovered rich tombs of the eighth and seventh centuries, but nothing there confirms the battle narrative.
l_samos.lead: Samos was a rich Greek island close to the Asian mainland, and it lay between Persian power and the Aegean. Its tyrant Polycrates built a strong fleet and was killed by the Persian governor Oroetes. Later Samos supplied the engineer of the Bosporus bridge, ships at Lade, and the appeal that brought the Greek fleet to Mycale.
l_samos.play: Samos is named in the Chronicle entries and in the Bosporus, Lade and Mycale articles. The game gives it no level, building or mechanic of its own.
l_samos.s0: Herodotus says Polycrates seized Samos with his brothers, then ruled alone and made an alliance with Amasis of Egypt, which later broke down. He says Polycrates built a large fleet including penteconters, and took islands and mainland towns. Herodotus calls him the first Greek after Minos to aim at mastery of the sea.
l_samos.s1: Herodotus says Oroetes, the Persian governor at Sardis, lured Polycrates to the mainland with promises of money and then killed him. He gives Oroetes' motives as a quarrel with the Persian Mitrobates and his own ambition, though he also reports a second explanation. The story rests on Herodotus, and the date is probably about 522 BCE.
l_samos.s2: Herodotus says Darius, then a guardsman of Cambyses in Egypt, received a cloak from the exile Syloson. When Darius became king he repaid the favour by sending an army under Otanes to take Samos and give it to Syloson. Herodotus says the island was left almost empty of people and was resettled later.
l_samos.s3: Herodotus says the Samian engineer Mandrocles designed the bridge over the Bosporus for Darius's Scythian campaign. He says Mandrocles was richly rewarded and dedicated a painting of the crossing in the Samian Heraion. Herodotus gives the verses that he says accompanied it.
l_samos.s4: Herodotus says that at Lade in 494 BCE most Samian captains sailed away as the battle began, after an agreement with the exiled tyrant Aeaces, and only a few stayed. He says the Samians later honoured those who remained. Modern historians question how far this hostile picture of the Ionian captains can be trusted.
l_samos.s5: Herodotus says Samian envoys came to the Greek fleet at Delos in 479 BCE and urged it to sail east. He says the fleet then crossed to Samos and fought the Persians at Mycale on the mainland, where the Ionians rose against them.
l_saqqara.lead: Saqqara, on the desert edge west of Memphis, was the necropolis of the Memphite kings and nobles. In the area later called the Serapeum, the Apis bulls, living manifestations of the god Ptah, were buried in underground galleries. Stelae from these burials date particular bulls by regnal year and include the Persian kings in the Egyptian reckoning.
l_saqqara.play: The game names Saqqara only in Chronicle entries and in the Encyclopedia's event articles, such as the death of the Apis. It is not a level or a place the player builds, and it has no mechanic of its own.
l_saqqara.s0: Excavations at Saqqara, begun by Auguste Mariette in the early 1850s, uncovered long rock-cut galleries where Apis bulls were laid in great stone sarcophagi. Chapels and stelae stood above and around them. The galleries were extended over centuries, and burials of the Persian period lie among them.
l_saqqara.s1: Dedicatory stelae record the birth, installation and death of particular bulls, with dates by regnal year. Burials of bulls fall in the reigns of Cambyses and of Darius. These are Egyptian documents written under Persian kings, and they give the kings the usual titles of Egyptian pharaohs.
l_saqqara.s2: Herodotus says Cambyses stabbed a newly found Apis in the thigh in a fit of madness, and that the bull died. The Saqqara evidence does not support this: a bull buried in Cambyses' reign received the proper rites, and no stela shows an insult to the cult. Most historians treat Herodotus's story as hostile Egyptian tradition about Cambyses, though the question is still argued, in particular over which bull the dates fit.
l_saqqara.s3: A stela from the reign of Darius records an Apis burial, which shows the cult continuing under Persian rule. This fits other evidence that Darius supported Egyptian temples and law, such as his work on the House of Life at Sais. The Persian kings, in these texts, kept the bull's rites as pharaohs had done.
l_saqqara.s4: The name Serapeum belongs to the Greek-speaking world of later centuries, when the cult of Osiris-Apis was linked with the god Serapis. Strabo describes a Serapeum at Memphis, partly buried in sand. His account is of his own day, not of the Persian period.
l_sardis.lead: Sardis was the capital of the Lydian kings, built beneath Mount Tmolus beside the gold-bearing Pactolus. After Cyrus took it from Croesus, it became the chief Persian seat in the west, home of the satrap and the western end of the Royal Road to Susa. Herodotus treats its burning by the Ionians and their Athenian allies in 498 BCE as the start of Persia's long quarrel with Athens.
l_sardis.play: The Sardis level is set in 498 BCE, the year the Ionians burned the lower town, and presents the city as the satrap's seat and the western end of the Royal Road.
l_sardis.s0: Excavations since 1958 have uncovered a massive Lydian fortification wall and houses of the lower city. By the Pactolus lay a refinery where gold was parted from the river's electrum, probably under Alyattes or Croesus. A destruction layer of the mid-500s BCE, with arrowheads and fallen soldiers, is usually linked to the Persian capture. Darius's Behistun inscription lists Sparda, the Persian name for Sardis and Lydia, among his lands.
l_sardis.s1: Herodotus says Cyrus defeated Croesus on the plain outside the city, placing camels in front so that their smell would panic the Lydian horses. Croesus then withdrew into Sardis and was besieged. On the fourteenth day a Mardian soldier named Hyroeades saw a defender climb down the sheer side of the acropolis, which had been left unguarded, and led others up the same way.
l_sardis.s2: The fall is traditionally dated to 547 or 546 BCE. That date rests largely on the Nabonidus Chronicle, whose entry for Nabonidus's ninth year (547 BCE) records Cyrus marching against a land whose name is damaged and killing its king. Older readings restored the name as Lydia, but many scholars now read Urartu instead. Without that entry, the conquest can only be placed loosely in the 540s BCE.
l_sardis.s3: Herodotus tells how Cyrus placed the captured Croesus on a pyre, then relented after Croesus called out the name of Solon, and how Apollo sent rain to quench the flames. The poet Bacchylides told a different version in which Croesus mounted the pyre himself and was carried away by the god. Both are moral tales about fortune, not reliable history.
l_sardis.s4: Herodotus names Artaphernes, Darius's half-brother, as governor at Sardis and traces the Royal Road from there to Susa. In 498 BCE Ionian, Athenian and Eretrian troops seized the lower town while Artaphernes held the citadel. A fire caught the reed-roofed houses, spread through the city and burned the temple of the goddess Cybebe. Herodotus says the Persians later cited this as reason to burn Greek temples.
l_sestos.lead: Sestos was a Greek town on the European shore of the Hellespont, facing Abydos across the strait. Under Persian rule it guarded the main crossing between Asia and Europe. After the Greek victory at Mycale in 479 BCE, an Athenian fleet besieged and captured it, and the siege is the last event Herodotus narrates in his Histories.
l_sestos.play: The Mycale epilogue includes the fight at Sestos and the House of Sestos, though the real siege was an Athenian blockade lasting months. The sources describe no particular house at Sestos.
l_sestos.s0: Herodotus says that Darius came back from his Scythian campaign by way of Sestos and crossed from there to Asia by ship. In 480 BCE Xerxes' two bridges of boats ran from Abydos to a headland on the European side between Sestos and Madytus. Whoever held Sestos controlled the main crossing of the strait.
l_sestos.s1: Herodotus says the Greek fleet sailed from Mycale to break Xerxes' bridges and found them already gone. Leotychides and the Peloponnesians went home, but the Athenians under Xanthippus stayed and besieged Sestos, the strongest fortress in the area, where the Persians had gathered and stored the bridge cables. The siege dragged on into autumn until the defenders were boiling the leather straps of their beds for food.
l_sestos.s2: The Persian governor was Artayctes, whom Herodotus accuses of looting the shrine of the hero Protesilaus at nearby Elaeus. He and another Persian, Oeobazus, escaped by night. Herodotus says Thracians caught Oeobazus and sacrificed him to their god, while the Athenians captured Artayctes, nailed him to a plank where the bridge had reached land, and stoned his son before his eyes.
l_sestos.s3: Herodotus tells that while a guard was cooking salted fish, the fish leapt and twitched in the pan. Artayctes took this as a sign from Protesilaus that the dead hero could still punish him, and offered a ransom, which was refused. The story is shaped as a moral tale about sacrilege and its reward.
l_sestos.s4: Herodotus places the fall of Sestos in autumn 479 BCE, while Thucydides says the Athenians took it after wintering there, so it may have fallen early in 478 BCE. Historians also debate its meaning: Herodotus closes his story here, but Thucydides treats the siege as the start of the period in which Athens led the Greeks and built its own power in the Aegean.
l_sidon.lead: Sidon, on the coast of Lebanon, was one of the great Phoenician cities with Tyre and Byblos. Under the Persians its kings commanded the best ships of the royal fleet. Herodotus says the Sidonians won the boat race Xerxes held at Abydos, and the king of Sidon took the first seat in his council.
l_sidon.play: Sidon is named in the Memphis and Sardis trade partners' caravans, in the Phoenicians' notes and in sailors' chatter in the fleet levels.
l_sidon.s0: At Abydos Xerxes watched a race between the ships, and the Phoenicians of Sidon won. Before Salamis the commanders sat in the order the King gave them, first the king of Sidon, then the king of Tyre. Herodotus names Tetramnestus son of Anysus as the Sidonian commander.
l_sidon.s1: Herodotus says Xerxes sailed in a Sidonian ship when he reviewed the fleet at Doriscus, and later chose a Sidonian ship to view the Peneus gorge. Sidon's ships also carried Democedes and the Persians sent to spy out Greece under Darius.
l_sidon.s2: Inscribed sarcophagi of Sidonian kings of the Persian period survive, among them Tabnit and his son Eshmunazar II, of the late sixth or fifth century. Eshmunazar's inscription says the Lord of Kings gave him Dor and Joppa, probably a grant from the Persian king for naval service.
l_sidon.s3: Sidon and Tyre were famous for murex purple dye and for fine glass and metalwork. In Homer, Sidonian craftsmen make silver bowls and embroidered robes. The dye-works with their heaps of crushed shells have been found at Sidon.
l_siwa.lead: Ammon was the oasis of Siwa, home of a famous oracle of Amun, whom Greeks equated with Zeus. Herodotus says Cambyses sent an army against it from Thebes and that the army vanished in the sand. What happened to the force is not known, and the story is still argued over.
l_siwa.play: The game names Ammon only in the Chronicle and in event articles such as the marches on Ammon and Ethiopia. It is not a level, a figure or a place with its own mechanic.
l_siwa.s0: Herodotus describes the Ammonians as a people living in the desert west of Egypt, with a temple of Zeus, whom he equates with the Egyptian Amun. Greeks consulted the oracle, and Herodotus knew Greek stories about it. Siwa is a real oasis in the Western Desert, and the ruins of a temple of Amun survive there.
l_siwa.s1: Herodotus says Cambyses, after taking Egypt, planned three ventures: against Carthage, against the Ethiopians and against the Ammonians. He says Cambyses sent fifty thousand men from Thebes, guided by locals, to enslave the Ammonians and burn the oracle. The figure is Herodotus's and is probably inflated.
l_siwa.s2: Herodotus reports that the army reached a place called Oasis, probably the Kharga oasis, and then set off across the sand. According to the Ammonians, a great south wind buried it during the midday meal, and it was never seen again. Herodotus gives this as their account and says nothing more certain about the army's end.
l_siwa.s3: No Persian or Egyptian text mentions the expedition, so it rests on Herodotus alone. Some historians accept a real force lost in the desert, while others doubt that it was meant for Siwa or even that it happened. Claims of modern finds of the lost army are widely doubted.
l_siwa.s4: The oracle became better known in 331, when Alexander the Great visited it, as Arrian reports. That visit lies long after the Persian period and belongs to a different story.
l_sogdiana.lead: Sogdiana lay between the Oxus and the Jaxartes, north of Bactria, and was one of the far eastern lands of the empire. It appears in Darius's royal inscriptions as a subject land and is named in the Susa foundation charter as a source of precious stones. It shows how far the King's rule reached beyond the Persian homeland.
l_sogdiana.play: The game mentions Sogdiana only in Chronicle entries and in the Encyclopedia's event articles, such as the Susa charter, where it supplies lapis lazuli and carnelian. It has no mechanic of its own.
l_sogdiana.s0: Darius's lists of subject lands name Sogdiana (Suguda) among the eastern peoples, near Chorasmia and Bactria. The lists show it was counted as a land of the empire by Darius's reign. They give no borders and no detail of how it was governed.
l_sogdiana.s1: In the foundation charter of the palace at Susa, Darius says lapis lazuli and carnelian were brought from Sogdiana. Turquoise came from Chorasmia. The text presents the palace as built from the whole empire, with each land supplying its own material.
l_sogdiana.s2: Historians do not agree on who first brought Sogdiana under Persian rule. Many think Cyrus campaigned in the east, but Herodotus does not describe the conquest of Sogdiana and no contemporary text records it. Herodotus's tax list puts the Sogdians in one district with the Parthians, Chorasmians and Areians, a grouping the Persian lists do not show.
l_sogdiana.s3: Whether Sogdian troops served in Xerxes' invasion of Greece is uncertain. Herodotus's catalogue of the army is the main source and historians treat its numbers as greatly exaggerated. He lists Sogdians under their commander Azanes son of Artaeus, but no other source confirms them in Greece.
l_sparta.lead: Sparta was the chief city of Laconia in the southern Peloponnese. It was ruled by two kings and lived on the labour of the helots. In the Persian period it led the strongest alliance of Greek states, refused the King's demands, and supplied the commanders of the Greek resistance at Thermopylae and Plataea.
l_sparta.play: The game lists Sparta as a trade partner. This is a simplification: no source shows regular Spartan trade with Persia, and in 480-479 BCE Sparta led the Greek war against the King.
l_sparta.s0: Sparta lay in the valley of the Eurotas river and was made up of a cluster of villages without a city wall. Excavations by the British School at Athens at the sanctuary of Artemis Orthia uncovered thousands of small lead figurines, carved ivories and pieces of Laconian pottery left as offerings. Little monumental building of the period survives on the site today.
l_sparta.s1: Herodotus and Xenophon describe a state with two hereditary kings from the Agiad and Eurypontid houses, five ephors elected each year and a council of elders. The citizen men, the Spartiates, trained for war from boyhood and lived from estates worked by the helots, a subject population of Laconia and Messenia. By about 500 BCE Sparta led most of the Peloponnese through a network of alliances.
l_sparta.s2: Herodotus says Sparta sent a herald to warn Cyrus away from the Greek cities of Asia after the fall of Sardis, and that Cyrus asked who the Spartans were. About 499 BCE King Cleomenes turned down Aristagoras of Miletus once he learned Susa lay three months' march from the sea. Herodotus also says the Spartans threw Darius's heralds into a well, and in 490 BCE their troops reached Marathon only after the battle.
l_sparta.s3: Later writers pictured Sparta as a closed and austere state that used iron bars instead of silver and expelled foreigners. Historians call this picture the Spartan mirage and argue over how far it fits the sixth century, when Laconian pottery and bronzes travelled as far as Samos, Etruria and Cyrene. Herodotus says Sparta was allied with Croesus of Lydia, but no source shows regular trade with the Persian empire.
l_sparta.s4: Spartans credited their way of life to a single lawgiver, Lycurgus. Some versions said he received his laws from the oracle at Delphi. Herodotus already tells this story and Plutarch later wrote a full life of him, but ancient writers could not agree on when he lived. Most historians now treat him as a figure of tradition rather than a known person.
l_sunium.lead: Sunium is the cape at the southern tip of Attica, with a sanctuary of Poseidon on its heights. After the battle of Marathon the Persian fleet sailed round it to reach Athens before the army could march back. In 480 BCE the Greeks dedicated a captured Persian trireme there after Salamis.
l_sunium.play: Sunium is the turning point of the sea race in the Marathon level's second front, and named in its victory card and chatter.
l_sunium.s0: After the fight at the ships, Herodotus says, the Persians took the Eretrian captives aboard and sailed round Sunium, hoping to reach Athens before its army. A shield was shown to them from the heights, and the Athenians marched back in time.
l_sunium.s1: Herodotus says that before Marathon the Aeginetans waylaid the sacred ship the Athenians sent to a four-yearly festival at Sunium and took the leading Athenians aboard prisoner. The raid was part of the war between Athens and Aegina in those years.
l_sunium.s2: After Salamis the Greeks chose three Persian triremes from the spoil to dedicate to the gods: one at the Isthmus, one at Sunium and one to Ajax on Salamis. Herodotus says the one at the Isthmus was still there in his time.
l_sunium.s3: The marble temple of Poseidon whose columns stand on the cape today was built about 440 BCE. Beneath it lie the remains of an earlier temple, begun about 500 BCE, which was unfinished or destroyed when the Persians came in 480 BCE. Archaic kouroi were found in the sanctuary.
l_susa.lead: Susa stood on the plain of lowland Elam and had been one of its chief cities for thousands of years before the Persians came. Darius made it a royal residence, building a palace and a great columned hall with materials and craftsmen drawn from across the empire. Greek writers knew it as the King's city, where the Royal Road from Sardis ended.
l_susa.play: The game presents Susa as Elam's capital, where Darius builds his palace and Apadana at the Royal Road's end. Susa was one of Elam's chief cities beside Anshan, not its only capital, and the works probably began a little after 521 BCE.
l_susa.s0: Excavations show settlement at Susa from about 4000, and for long periods it was a leading city of Elam, sharing that role with Anshan in the highlands. The Assyrian king Ashurbanipal sacked it in about 646 BCE and boasted of the destruction in his own inscriptions. The city was probably reoccupied by the time of Cyrus, though the remains of this period are thin, and no siege is recorded when it passed under Persian rule.
l_susa.s1: In his charter DSf, Darius said his builders dug down to firm ground and filled the pit with gravel before raising the palace. He listed where things came from: cedar from Lebanon, gold from Sardis and Bactria, silver and ebony from Egypt, ivory from Kush and India. Ionians and Sardians cut the stone, Medes and Egyptians worked the gold, and Babylonians made the bricks. Behistun records that Darius put down three revolts in Elam between 522 BCE and about 519 BCE.
l_susa.s2: French excavators from the 1880s onwards uncovered the palace and the Apadana, a square hall of thirty-six stone columns with porches on three sides. Walls were faced with moulded, glazed bricks showing guardsmen with spears and bows, lions and winged creatures; many panels are now in the Louvre. A later inscription says the hall burned under Artaxerxes I and was rebuilt by Artaxerxes II.
l_susa.s3: Herodotus describes the road from Sardis to Susa, with royal stations along its length, and reckons it at about 450 parasangs, some three months on foot. He adds three more days for the stretch from Ephesus on the coast up to Sardis. He also puts in the mouth of Aristagoras the claim that Susa held the King's treasures.
l_susa.s4: Greek writers treated Susa as the chief city of the Persian kings, and Aeschylus set his Persians there. Xenophon says the court moved with the seasons between Babylon, Susa and Ecbatana. Historians agree the King travelled between several residences, including Persepolis, but debate how regular this cycle was and how far Susa outranked the others.
l_thasos.lead: Thasos was a Greek island city off the coast of Thrace. Settlers from Paros founded it in the 7th century, and gold and silver mines on the island and the facing mainland made it rich. It came under Persian control in 492 BCE, pulled down its walls on Darius's order in 491 BCE, and fed Xerxes' army on its march to Greece in 480 BCE.
l_thasos.play: The game lists Thasos as a trade partner. Historically it was an independent Greek city until 492 BCE and then a subject of the King that obeyed his orders, so the trading role is a simplification.
l_thasos.s0: Excavations by the French School at Athens, begun in 1911, have uncovered the ancient city on the north coast of the island. They have found its harbours, agora, sanctuaries of Heracles and Artemis, and a circuit of walls, and ancient mine workings survive on the island. The earliest Greek levels fit a Parian settlement of the 7th century beside an older Thracian presence. The city struck its own silver coins from the late 6th century.
l_thasos.s1: Herodotus says that after the Ionian defeat at Lade, Histiaeus of Miletus besieged Thasos with Ionians and Aeolians. He broke off the siege when he heard that the Phoenician fleet was approaching. In 492 BCE the fleet sent with Mardonius took the island, and Herodotus reports that the Thasians offered no resistance.
l_thasos.s2: Herodotus reports that in 491 BCE neighbours accused the Thasians of planning revolt, and Darius ordered them to pull down their walls and bring their ships to Abdera. They obeyed. They had built the walls and ships after Histiaeus's siege from revenues of 200 talents in an ordinary year and 300 in the best, drawn from the island's mines and the mainland, where Scapte Hyle alone gave 80. Herodotus says he had seen the island's mines himself.
l_thasos.s3: In 480 BCE Xerxes marched through Thrace past the mainland towns held by Thasos, and the Thasians had to feed his army. Herodotus says that Antipater, the leading citizen who organised the meal, reported a cost of 400 talents of silver. He adds the jest of Megacreon of Abdera, who said the cities should thank the gods that Xerxes ate only once a day. The sum is Herodotus's report and may be inflated.
l_thasos.s4: Herodotus believed that Phoenicians reached Thasos before the Greeks. He says Phoenicians searching for Europa founded the temple of Heracles there, and that a Phoenician named Thasos gave the island its name and his people opened the first mines. Archaeologists have found no clear trace of a Phoenician settlement. Many historians read the story as a Greek tale explaining the Heracles cult and the old mine workings, but others think some Phoenician contact is possible.
l_thebes.lead: Thebes was the strongest city of Boeotia, the region north-west of Athens. When Xerxes invaded Greece in 480 BCE it sided with the King, and in 479 BCE its territory became the base of Mardonius's army. The Persian defeat at Plataea, on the Theban border, ended that alliance and left Thebes with a lasting name among other Greeks for medism, the taking of the Persian side.
l_thebes.play: The game shows Thebes as an ally of Mardonius, which is historical for 480-479 BCE. Its role as a trade partner is a game simplification: no ancient source describes Thebes as a commercial partner of Persia.
l_thebes.s0: Herodotus lists the Thebans among the Greeks who gave earth and water to Xerxes' heralds, a sign of submission. Of the Boeotians, he says, only Thespiae and Plataea refused. After Thermopylae, Macedonians sent by Alexander guarded the Boeotian towns that had submitted, showing they were on the King's side. Thespiae and Plataea were burnt.
l_thebes.s1: Herodotus says Leonidas took 400 Thebans under Leontiades to test a city suspected of favouring Persia, and kept them as hostages. On the last day, he says, they surrendered and were branded with the royal mark. Diodorus says these Thebans came from the anti-Persian party. Plutarch, a Boeotian, called Herodotus's story slander, and historians still debate how far it reflects later hostility to Thebes.
l_thebes.s2: Herodotus says the Thebans urged Mardonius to camp in Boeotia and to win over the Greek cities with bribes rather than battle. Mardonius made his camp along the Asopus in Theban territory and built a fortified enclosure there. Herodotus also tells of a banquet given at Thebes by the Theban Attaginus for Mardonius and fifty Persians. There a Persian guest privately foretold that most of the army would soon die.
l_thebes.s3: At Plataea the Boeotians fought hard against the Athenians, and Herodotus says three hundred of the leading Thebans fell. Afterwards Pausanias besieged Thebes and demanded the pro-Persian leaders, chief among them Timagenidas and Attaginus. On the twentieth day the city gave them up. Attaginus escaped and Pausanias spared his sons, but the others were taken to Corinth and executed.
l_thebes.s4: In 427 BCE Theban speakers told the Spartans that in 480 BCE their city had been ruled by a narrow clique of powerful men, not by the citizens as a whole, so the city should not bear the blame. Many historians also point to Thebes' old rivalry with Athens, which had taken Plataea under its protection. How far the choice was a faction's and how far the whole city's is still argued.
l_thermopylae.lead: Thermopylae, the Hot Gates, was a narrow pass between the mountains and the Malian Gulf, on the main land route from Thessaly into central Greece. In 480 BCE a small Greek force under the Spartan king Leonidas blocked Xerxes' army here for three days of fighting, until a mountain path let the Persians get round it. The Greeks lost the battle, but their stand became one of the most retold stories of the war.
l_thermopylae.play: The tenth level is set here in 480 BCE. The chronicle follows Herodotus on the pass, its warm springs and the Phocian wall. Its three days match his three days of fighting, which came after Xerxes had waited four.
l_thermopylae.s0: Herodotus describes a road squeezed between steep slopes and the sea, with warm springs that gave the place its name. Long before 480 BCE the Phocians had built a wall across the pass to keep out Thessalian raids, and by then it lay largely in ruins. The Greeks rebuilt it and made it their line. At the same time the fleet held the strait at Artemisium nearby, so the defence on land and at sea worked together.
l_thermopylae.s1: Herodotus says Xerxes waited four days, then sent Medes and Cissians against the wall, and after them the Immortals under Hydarnes, but the line held. Ephialtes of Malis showed the Persians the Anopaea path, and Hydarnes led troops over it by night past the Phocian guard. Leonidas sent most of the allies away. He stayed with the Spartans and Thespians, and with Thebans whom Herodotus says he kept as hostages. The last fighters died on a low hill.
l_thermopylae.s2: Herodotus puts Xerxes' land army at 1,700,000, a figure historians reject as wildly exaggerated. Modern estimates are far lower, though they vary widely. The Greeks numbered perhaps seven thousand. Herodotus says Leonidas stayed for honour and because of an oracle, while many historians see a rearguard covering the retreat. No Persian text mentions the battle, and for the Persians it was probably one pass forced on the march to Athens.
l_thermopylae.s3: The Spercheius river has since laid down silt, so the shore now lies several kilometres from the old road and the pass has become a wide plain. In 1939 Spyridon Marinatos excavated the hill of Kolonos, which Herodotus names as the scene of the last stand, and found a large number of bronze and iron arrowheads. The warm springs still flow beside the modern highway.
l_thermopylae.s4: The battle soon gathered famous sayings. Herodotus tells how Dieneces, hearing that Persian arrows would hide the sun, replied that the Greeks would then fight in the shade. The reply 'come and take them', said to answer a Persian demand to hand over their arms, appears only in Plutarch, more than five centuries later. Both are best read as Greek moral tales rather than records of the day.
l_thrace.lead: Thrace was the country north of the Aegean and the Hellespont, held by many tribes. Darius's army crossed it on the way to the Ister in about 513 BCE, and Persian garrisons held places on its coast until after 479 BCE. It gave Persia a foothold in Europe for the later campaigns against Greece.
l_thrace.play: The game names Thrace in Chronicle entries and in the event articles on the Scythian campaign, the Getae, Athos and Doriscus. It has no level, building or mechanic of its own.
l_thrace.s0: Herodotus describes the Thracians as the most numerous people after the Indians, divided into many tribes with different names and customs. He says they would be unbeatable if they ever united under one ruler, which he thought unlikely. This is a Greek observer's view of the country.
l_thrace.s1: Herodotus says Darius left Megabazus in Europe after the Scythian expedition, and that he subdued the Thracian coast and the Paeonians, some of whom were moved to Asia. Herodotus also reports a Persian embassy to Macedonia that asked for earth and water. How far inland Persian control reached is not clear from his narrative.
l_thrace.s2: Darius's inscriptions list a land called Skudra among the subject peoples, and DNa is one example. Skudra is usually taken to mean the Persian holdings in Europe, including Thrace, but the exact extent is not fixed by the texts.
l_thrace.s3: Historians disagree about how firmly Persia held Thrace. Some see an organised province with garrisons at places such as Doriscus and Eion. Others see a loose hold on the coast and river valleys, with inland tribes paying little or nothing. Briant treats the control as real but uneven.
l_thrace.s4: Herodotus says Xerxes reviewed his army on the plain of Doriscus in 480 BCE, where a Persian garrison already stood under Mascames. Herodotus says Mascames kept Doriscus afterwards. Thucydides records that Eion on the Strymon, held by a Persian garrison, was taken by the Athenians under Cimon some years later.
l_tigris.lead: The Tigris is the eastern of the two great rivers of Mesopotamia, flowing from Armenia past Nineveh and Opis to the sea. In December 522 BCE Nidintu-Bel's Babylonians held its bank against Darius from boats, and Darius crossed and beat them. The Royal Road crossed it on the way from Sardis to Susa.
l_tigris.play: The Tigris is named in the Bagastana level's Chronicle, chatter and the rebels' field, as the river where Darius beat the first false Nebuchadnezzar.
l_tigris.s0: Darius says Nidintu-Bel's army held the Tigris and had boats there. He put his army on floats of skins, on camels and on horses, crossed, and won on 26 Atriyadiya, in December 522 BCE. A few days later he won again at Zazana by the Euphrates and took Babylon.
l_tigris.s1: Herodotus says the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa crossed four navigable rivers in the land of the Matieni, the first of them the Tigris, which had to be crossed by ferry. He gives the stations and the distances.
l_tigris.s2: The Nabonidus Chronicle says that in 539 BCE Cyrus fought the Babylonian army at Opis on the Tigris and won, and then Sippar and Babylon fell without a battle. The Tigris was the route into the heart of Babylonia from the north.
l_tigris.s3: Herodotus says the Tigris rises in Armenia and flows past the city where Nineveh once stood, and the Gyndes runs into it. The old Assyrian capitals lay along it, and the lands between it and the Zagros were the Persian province of Athura.
l_tmolus.lead: Tmolus, now Bozdağ, is the mountain range that rises south of Sardis in western Lydia. The citadel of Sardis stands on one of its spurs, and the Pactolus runs down from it through the city. Herodotus counts the gold dust it sends down among the few marvels of Lydia.
l_tmolus.play: Tmolus stands behind the Sardis level: the Citadel of Sardis is built with its back to the mountain, and the townsfolk speak of its timber, its vineyards and the road over it.
l_tmolus.s0: Herodotus says Lydia has few marvels to record except the gold dust carried down from Tmolus. He also says the Pactolus, which ran through the market of Sardis, brought the gold down from the mountain. Excavators have found the refinery by the Pactolus where the Lydians parted gold from silver, so the gold of the river is real, though Herodotus says nothing of how much remained in his time.
l_tmolus.s1: The acropolis of Sardis sits on a steep spur of Tmolus above the plain. Herodotus tells how Cyrus's army took it about 547 BCE, when a Mardian soldier climbed the side the Lydians thought too sheer to need a guard. In 498 BCE the same citadel held out for Artaphernes while the lower city burned.
l_tmolus.s2: In 498 BCE the Ionians and their Athenian and Eretrian allies left their ships at Ephesus, marched up the Cayster valley and crossed Tmolus to come down on Sardis. After the city burned they fell back the same way and were beaten near Ephesus. The route shows how close the Aegean coast lay to the satrap's seat.
l_tmolus.s3: Later Greek and Roman writers praise the wine of Tmolus and make the mountain a haunt of Dionysus; Ovid even tells of Tmolus judging a contest between Apollo and Pan. These stories come long after the Persian period and say nothing of the Lydian or Persian Tmolus itself.
l_trachis.lead: Trachis was a small town of the Malians on the plain at the head of the Malian Gulf, under the cliffs Herodotus calls the rocks of Trachis. In 480 BCE Xerxes camped in its land while the Greeks held the pass of Thermopylae just to the east.
l_trachis.play: The Thermopylae level is built on the plain of Trachis: the King's camp town, its farms and the King's Pavilion stand there, and the townsfolk speak of the heat, the dust and the Greeks of Trachis.
l_trachis.s0: Herodotus describes a level space round the Malian Gulf, wide in parts and narrow in others, shut in by high mountains called the rocks of Trachis. Trachis lay five furlongs from the river Melas, where the plain was widest, and the Asopus came out of a gorge in the mountains south of the town.
l_trachis.s1: Herodotus says Xerxes was encamped in the region of Trachis in the land of the Malians, and the Greeks within the pass. He held everything north of Trachis, they everything to the south. The King's horseman rode from this camp to look at the Spartans before the wall.
l_trachis.s2: Herodotus says that before the battle a man of Trachis told the Greeks the Persian archers were so many that their arrows would hide the sun. The Spartan Dieneces answered that then they would fight in the shade. The story is Herodotus's, and he says it was one of several sayings remembered of Dieneces.
l_trachis.s3: In 426 BCE Sparta founded a new colony, Heraclea in Trachis, close to the old town, to hold the road south through the pass. Thucydides reports it. The Persian camp of 480 BCE has not been found on the ground, and the coastline has moved far out since, as the Spercheius has laid down silt.
l_tyre.lead: Tyre was a Phoenician city built on an island off the coast of Lebanon. It founded Carthage and was famous for its purple dye and its temple of Melqart, whom the Greeks called Heracles. Under the Persians its king sat second in Xerxes' council of war, after the king of Sidon.
l_tyre.play: Tyre is named with Sidon in the Phoenicians' notes and in sailors' and merchants' chatter.
l_tyre.s0: Herodotus says he sailed to Tyre to learn about Heracles and saw a richly furnished temple with two pillars, one of pure gold and one of an emerald stone that shone at night. The priests told him it was founded with the city, 2,300 years before.
l_tyre.s1: Before Salamis the commanders sat as Xerxes had assigned them, first the king of Sidon and then the king of Tyre. Herodotus names Matten son of Siromus as the Tyrian commander in the fleet.
l_tyre.s2: When Cambyses planned to send his fleet against Carthage, Herodotus says, the Phoenicians refused to fight their own children, and without them the rest of the fleet was too weak. Carthage was a colony of Tyre, founded by tradition in 814.
l_tyre.s3: Tyre stood on an island until Alexander built a mole to it during his siege of 332, which Arrian describes. The silting of that mole has joined it to the mainland ever since. Tyre's coins of the later fifth century show a dolphin and a murex shell.
n_arabs.lead: The Arabs of Achaemenid times were the camel-herding peoples of the deserts between Mesopotamia, Syria and Egypt. Some held the desert crossing to Egypt, and Arab traders carried incense up from the south. Persian inscriptions count Arabia among the King's lands, while Herodotus says the Arabs were the King's friends rather than his subjects.
n_arabs.play: The game shows the Arabs as trade partners and as camel riders in the King's army. Herodotus calls their yearly frankincense a gift, not trade, and describes Arab camel riders only in Xerxes' army of 480 BCE.
n_arabs.s0: Darius's Behistun inscription names Arabaya among the lands that came to him as king. The name appears again in his later lists of lands, and a labelled throne-bearer on his tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam is called the Arab. On the Apadana stairways at Persepolis, modern scholars identify one delegation leading a dromedary as Arabs, though that relief carries no label.
n_arabs.s1: Herodotus says that when Cambyses planned to invade Egypt in 525 BCE, the Greek deserter Phanes advised him to ask the Arab king for safe passage across the waterless desert. The Arab king swore an oath and had camels carry skins of water to stations along the route. Herodotus describes the Arab way of swearing pledges, with blood smeared on stones, and names their gods as Orotalt and Alilat.
n_arabs.s2: Herodotus says the Arabs were never made subject to Persia and paid no tax. Instead they gave the King a gift of 1,000 talents of frankincense each year. The Persian lists place Arabaya among the King's lands like any other. Historians also argue over which Arabs are meant: the Arabaya of the inscriptions may be the steppe between Mesopotamia and Syria, while Herodotus's allies held the Sinai crossing.
n_arabs.s3: Herodotus says the Arabs in Xerxes' army wore long girded cloaks and carried long bows that curved backwards. Their camels were as fast as horses, and they were placed at the rear so that the camels would not frighten the cavalry horses. They served with the Ethiopians under Arsames, a son of Darius. Herodotus guesses 20,000 Arab camel riders and Libyan charioteers together, part of an army total historians think greatly exaggerated.
n_arabs.s4: Herodotus repeats stories that small winged snakes guarded the frankincense trees of Arabia and were driven off with the smoke of burning storax. He also tells of cassia guarded by bat-like creatures and of cinnamon sticks taken from the nests of great birds. These are travellers' tales about a distant trade, not descriptions of how incense was gathered.
n_arabs.s5: No standard of the Arabs is attested. The game's crescent and star is interpretive: an astral emblem known from Arabian altars and inscriptions. Herodotus describes the Arabs' oath-taking and their gods, but no banner.
n_argives.lead: The Argives were the people of Argos, an old and powerful city in the north-east Peloponnese and Sparta's chief rival there. Weakened by a heavy defeat at Spartan hands in about 494 BCE, they refused to join the Greek alliance against Xerxes in 480 BCE. Greek writers suspected them of friendship with Persia, and Herodotus reports Persian efforts to keep them out of the war.
n_argives.play: The game makes Argos a trade partner. Its neutrality in 480 BCE is historical, but no source records Argos as a Persian trading partner; the trade role is the game's own simplification.
n_argives.s0: Argos long disputed the leadership of the Peloponnese with Sparta. Herodotus tells of a fight between three hundred champions from each side over the border land of Thyrea in the time of Croesus, which ended in Spartan control of the district. In about 494 BCE the Spartan king Cleomenes defeated the Argives at Sepeia and burned many who had fled into a sacred grove. Herodotus puts the Argive dead at six thousand.
n_argives.s1: Allied Greek envoys asked Argos to join against Xerxes. By the Argives' own account, as Herodotus reports it, Delphi had advised them to stay out, but they still set two conditions: a thirty-year truce with Sparta and an equal share of the command. Sparta offered their king only one vote beside its own two kings, and the Argives refused. Argos sent no troops to Thermopylae, Salamis or Plataea.
n_argives.s2: Herodotus gives a rival version in which Xerxes sent a herald claiming that the Persians descended from Perses, son of the Argive hero Perseus, and asking Argos to stay at home. He also mentions Argive envoys at Susa years later asking Artaxerxes whether their friendship with Xerxes still held. Herodotus says he must report what is told without being bound to believe it, and historians still debate how far Argos really dealt with Persia.
n_argives.s3: In 479 BCE, Herodotus says, the Argives had promised Mardonius that they would stop the Spartan army from leaving the Peloponnese. When the Spartans marched out anyway, the Argives sent their fastest runner to Attica to tell him they could not prevent it. Mardonius then withdrew from Athens towards Boeotia, where the battle of Plataea was fought.
n_argives.s4: The bronze Serpent Column was dedicated at Delphi after Plataea and now stands in Istanbul. It lists the Greek communities that fought the Persians. Argos does not appear on it, while its small neighbours Mycenae and Tiryns do. The inscription confirms from the time itself what Herodotus reports about Argive neutrality.
n_argives.s5: Argos's emblem in the game is a wolf, for Apollo Lykeios, the wolf-god of the city's great temple, as on Argive coins of about 490 BCE with a large letter A. Argos stayed out of the war of 480 BCE.
n_assyrians.lead: Arbela, modern Erbil in northern Iraq, was one of the great cities of Assyria and outlived the fall of Nineveh in 612 BCE. Under the Persian kings it lay in the land Darius called Athura, on routes linking Media, Babylonia and the west. Its people, probably Aramaic-speaking heirs of Assyria, served the King as soldiers, labourers and taxpayers.
n_assyrians.play: The game presents Arbela only as a trade partner, 'the traders of Arbela'. Arbela was a real city on the empire's roads, but the sources say almost nothing about its merchants, so this is a simplification.
n_assyrians.s0: Assyrian royal inscriptions and letters show Arbela as a major city and the seat of the goddess Ishtar of Arbela, whose temple Assyrian kings rebuilt and honoured. When Medes and Babylonians destroyed Nineveh and Nimrud in 612 BCE, Arbela was not abandoned. Its citadel mound has been lived on almost without a break, and it still stands at the centre of Erbil today.
n_assyrians.s1: In the Behistun inscription Darius listed Athura, Assyria, among the lands that obeyed him. During the revolts of 522-521 BCE there was a Sagartian rebel, Citrantakhma, who claimed descent from the Median king Cyaxares. Darius says he was captured and mutilated, and then impaled at Arbela. In his Susa charter Darius says the Assyrian people carried cedar from Lebanon as far as Babylon for his palace.
n_assyrians.s2: Herodotus says the Assyrians in Xerxes' army wore bronze helmets and linen corslets and carried wooden clubs studded with iron, and that Greeks called them Syrians. He also says Babylon and the rest of Assyria paid the King a thousand talents of silver and five hundred boys as eunuchs each year. Xenophon, marching north in 401 BCE, passed the deserted ruins of Nimrud and Nineveh, which he knew as Larisa and Mespila.
n_assyrians.s3: Historians still argue whether Athura meant only the old Assyrian heartland on the Tigris or also Syria west of the Euphrates. Greek writers used the name Assyria loosely, often including Babylonia. Many modern maps run the Royal Road through Arbela, but Herodotus does not name the city on that route. A travel pass issued in the late 5th century by Arshama, satrap of Egypt, lists Arbela among the stations for official travellers.
n_assyrians.s4: In 331 Darius III fought Alexander at Gaugamela, a village that Arrian places about 600 stades, roughly 100 kilometres, from Arbela. After the battle Alexander took Arbela and found the Persian king's treasure and baggage there. Arrian explains that the battle came to be named after Arbela because Gaugamela was a small village and Arbela a well-known city. The old Assyrian town's name was thus tied to the fall of the Achaemenid empire.
n_assyrians.s5: The traders of Arbela carry Babylon's emblem in the game, Marduk's snake-dragon, since Arbela lay in the old Assyrian heartland that Babylon and then Persia ruled. Arbela's own goddess was Ishtar; no emblem of the city as a trading partner is known.
n_athenians.lead: The Athenians were the citizens of Athens in Attica, a city that took a new popular constitution under Cleisthenes about 508 BCE. They helped burn Sardis in 498 BCE, defeated a Persian landing at Marathon in 490 BCE, and built the fleet that fought at Salamis in 480 BCE. Most of what is known of Persia's western wars comes from Greek writers, above all Herodotus, who wrote with open sympathy for Athens.
n_athenians.play: The game makes Athens a trade partner, which simplifies a city at war with the King after 498 BCE. It also puts Athenian archers at Marathon, but Herodotus says the Greeks there had neither archers nor cavalry (6.112).
n_athenians.s0: Herodotus says Athenian envoys at Sardis, seeking help against Sparta about 507 BCE, gave the satrap Artaphernes earth and water, the tokens of submission, and were blamed for it at home (5.73). Artaphernes later told Athens to take back its exiled tyrant Hippias (5.96). In 498 BCE Athens sent twenty ships to the Ionian revolt. The force helped burn Sardis, then went home after a defeat near Ephesus.
n_athenians.s1: Herodotus tells that Darius, hearing of the burning of Sardis, asked who the Athenians were, shot an arrow into the sky and prayed for the chance to punish them. He then ordered a servant to remind him three times at every dinner not to forget the Athenians. The story is shaped as a Greek tale about royal anger, and no Persian source mentions it.
n_athenians.s2: Herodotus says the Athenians and the Plataeans beat the army of Datis and the younger Artaphernes at Marathon in 490 BCE, guided by the general Miltiades and the polemarch Callimachus. Later writers put the Plataeans at about a thousand. Herodotus gives 6,400 Persian and 192 Athenian dead. He adds that Themistocles persuaded Athens to spend Laurion silver on two hundred ships for a war with Aegina, and these became the core of the Greek fleet at Salamis.
n_athenians.s3: Herodotus says the Persians took the Acropolis in 480 BCE and occupied Athens again in 479 BCE (8.53, 9.13). Excavations on the Acropolis between 1885 and 1890 found burned statues and building blocks that the Athenians buried when they cleared the hill after the war, and many are now in the Acropolis Museum. At Marathon the burial mound known as the Soros, usually identified as the grave of the Athenian dead, was dug in 1890 and held ash, bones and pottery of about 490 BCE.
n_athenians.s4: Persian inscriptions name the Yauna, the Ionians or Greeks in general, but never Athens, and no Persian text records Marathon or Salamis. Some historians think the King treated these campaigns as frontier affairs at the edge of a vast empire. Others follow Herodotus, whose Xerxes names revenge on Athens as a war aim. Only Aeschylus' Persians of 472 BCE is close in time, and Herodotus wrote about two generations later for Greek readers.
n_athenians.s5: The Athenians and Plataeans carry the owl and olive sprig of Athens's silver coins, the 'owls' struck from the late 6th century. Greek armies fought under the devices on their shields, not under flags, so this is an emblem after Athens's coin.
n_babylonians.lead: The Babylonians lived in the irrigated plain of the lower Tigris and Euphrates, the richest farmland in the empire. Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BCE, and the land became a Persian province whose barley, dates, wool and silver went to the King and his court. It rebelled twice against Darius in 522-521 BCE and again against Xerxes in about 484 BCE.
n_babylonians.play: The game shows the Babylonians as a trade partner supplying barley and woven cloth. Both were real Babylonian staples, but after 539 BCE Babylonia was a Persian province paying tribute, not an outside trading partner.
n_babylonians.s0: The Nabonidus Chronicle records that in 539 BCE Cyrus defeated the Babylonian army at Opis, and that his troops then entered Babylon without a battle. King Nabonidus was captured. The Cyrus Cylinder, written in Babylonian cuneiform for the new ruler, presents Cyrus as the king chosen by the god Marduk to restore proper worship. It is royal propaganda, but it shows Cyrus ruling through Babylonian traditions.
n_babylonians.s1: Darius's Behistun inscription says that in 522 BCE a Babylonian named Nidintu-Bel claimed to be Nebuchadnezzar, son of Nabonidus. Darius beat him on the Tigris and the Euphrates and took Babylon. In 521 BCE Arakha, whom Darius calls an Armenian, made the same claim and was defeated by Darius's general Intaphernes, then impaled at Babylon. Babylonian tablets dated to both rebel kings confirm the revolts.
n_babylonians.s2: Herodotus says Babylon and the rest of Assyria paid the King 1,000 talents of silver a year and 500 boys to serve as eunuchs. He also says Babylonia fed the King and his army for four months of every twelve, so it supplied a third of what all Asia provided. His figures cannot be checked exactly, but they show that Greeks thought Babylonia the empire's wealthiest land.
n_babylonians.s3: Cuneiform archives, such as the Egibi family texts from Babylon and the temple records of Sippar and Uruk, show a busy economy of barley and date farming, flocks of sheep and large-scale wool and textile work. Persian nobles and officials held estates in Babylonia, and taxes and labour service were owed to the Crown. Darius's foundation charter from Susa names Babylonians as the men who moulded and baked the palace bricks.
n_babylonians.s4: Babylonian tablets name two rebel kings, Bel-shimanni and Shamash-eriba, in about 484 BCE. Many family and temple archives in northern Babylonia stop at this time, which some historians link to Persian punishment. Herodotus says Xerxes carried off a gold statue from the temple of Bel, and Arrian says he destroyed the temples, but how much damage was done remains debated.
n_babylonians.s5: Babylon's emblem in the game is the mushhushshu, Marduk's snake-dragon, pale on blue as it strides along the glazed bricks of the Ishtar Gate, built about 575 BCE by Nebuchadnezzar II. Marduk's spade on a pole was his other sign. No national flag existed; this is an emblem after the city's god.
n_bactrians.lead: The Bactrians lived in the fertile plains of the upper Oxus, in what is now northern Afghanistan and the lands just north of it. Their country, Bakhtrish in Old Persian, was one of the most important eastern provinces of the Achaemenid kings. It supplied gold, horsemen and foot soldiers, and Bactrian troops fought in Greece in 480 and 479 BCE.
n_bactrians.play: The game fields the Bactrians as spearmen in the King's army. Herodotus says they carried native cane bows as well as short spears, so the game's spear-only label simplifies their equipment.
n_bactrians.s0: Darius named Bactria among the lands that obeyed him in his Behistun inscription. When Margiana rose in revolt in 521 BCE, the Persian Dadarshi, whom Darius calls his satrap in Bactria, marched against the rebel Frada and defeated him. In his foundation charter for the palace at Susa, Darius says the gold used there was brought from Sardis and from Bactria.
n_bactrians.s1: Herodotus describes the Bactrians of 480 BCE as wearing headgear much like the Medes, with native cane bows and short spears, and says their horsemen were armed like their foot. They and the Saka were led by Hystaspes, a son of Darius and Atossa. He adds that Mardonius kept Bactrians among the picked troops left in Greece, and that at Plataea they faced several smaller Peloponnesian contingents.
n_bactrians.s2: Herodotus lists the Bactrians as the twelfth tribute district, paying 360 talents of silver a year. He says captives from Barca in Libya were resettled in a Bactrian village. He also tells how Masistes, a brother of Xerxes and governor of Bactria, set out for the province to raise a revolt and was killed on the way, which suggests it could serve as a power base for a royal prince.
n_bactrians.s3: Herodotus says only that Cyrus planned a campaign against the Bactrians and the Saka. Ctesias, writing later, says the Bactrians fought Cyrus and then submitted, and that Cyrus gave his younger son Bardiya a large eastern command including Bactria. Historians still argue about how Bactria was won, and about whether it had been an organised kingdom before the Persians or a land of local lords.
n_bactrians.s4: Greek writers drawing on Ctesias told of an ancient Bactrian king who resisted the Assyrian Ninus until Semiramis took his city, a tale with no support in Assyrian records. Much later Iranian tradition, as in the Shahnameh, placed the court of King Goshtasp and the prophet Zarathustra at Balkh. Neither story can be used as evidence for the Bactria that Darius and Xerxes ruled.
n_boeotians.lead: The Boeotians lived in the plain north of Attica, around Thebes. Herodotus says most of their cities gave earth and water to Xerxes, and Boeotians fought for the Persians at Plataea alongside other Greeks of the north and centre. Their choice split the Greeks of central Greece and left Thebes to answer for it after the battle.
n_boeotians.play: The game names the Boeotians in the Chronicle, the decrees and the field briefings for Plataea. They have no mechanic of their own beyond what those texts show.
n_boeotians.s0: Herodotus says that when Xerxes' heralds asked for earth and water, the Boeotians gave it, except the Thespians and the Plataeans. Thebes was the leading city of the region, and the Boeotians lay on the army's line of march.
n_boeotians.s1: Boeotians were on both sides at Thermopylae. Herodotus says the Thespians stayed and died with the Spartans, while about 400 Thebans were held with Leonidas, and that the Thebans themselves said they were kept against their will. He says they surrendered at the end and that Xerxes had them branded as prisoners.
n_boeotians.s2: Herodotus says Mardonius set the Boeotians, Locrians, Malians and Thessalians, with a thousand Phocians, opposite the Athenians, Plataeans and Megarians. Herodotus gives the whole Greek force on the Persian side as 50,000, a figure historians treat as too high.
n_boeotians.s3: Herodotus says the Thebans urged Mardonius to use bribery and to cut the Greek supply lines rather than fight at once. In the battle he says the Boeotians fought hard against the Athenians and lost about 300 of their leading Thebans. After the Persian line broke, he says the Boeotian cavalry covered the retreat.
n_boeotians.s4: Herodotus says the Greeks besieged Thebes for about twenty days and demanded the pro-Persian leaders. They surrendered, and Herodotus says Pausanias had them taken to Corinth and executed. Herodotus also reports the Theban defence that the city had not acted as a whole but under a ruling faction.
n_boeotians.s5: Herodotus sets the choice partly on fear and partly on the pro-Persian faction in Thebes. In Thucydides, the Thebans themselves say their city was ruled by a small group of men in 480 BCE, which fits their excuse but also served their interest. Modern historians weigh geography, rivalry with Athens and the weakness of the Greek defence of central Greece, and no source settles it.
n_carians.lead: The Carians lived in the hills and along the coast of southwest Anatolia, south of Lydia, and spoke their own Anatolian language. They were known across the eastern Mediterranean as hired soldiers and seafarers. Under Persian rule they worked on the King's buildings, rose in the Ionian Revolt and later sent ships to Xerxes' fleet.
n_carians.play: The game includes Carian mercenaries and Carian ships. Both fit the sources, which show Carians hired by the kings of Egypt and, after the Persian conquest, serving as sailors and soldiers in the King's fleet.
n_carians.s0: Caria lay between the Maeander valley and Lycia, with Mylasa inland and Halicarnassus on the coast, where Carians lived alongside Greek settlers. Carian belonged to the Anatolian language family and was written in its own alphabet. Many surviving Carian texts come from Egypt, including grave stelae from Saqqara near Memphis. Bilingual inscriptions helped scholars make real progress in reading the script from the 1980s onwards.
n_carians.s1: Herodotus says that Psamtik I won his throne with the help of Ionian and Carian men in bronze armour who came from the sea, and that he then settled them in camps on the Nile. Later, Amasis moved them to Memphis. In 525 BCE Carian and Greek mercenaries fought for Psamtik III at Pelusium. Herodotus tells how they killed the sons of Phanes, who had gone over to Cambyses, before the battle.
n_carians.s2: Darius's foundation charter from Susa records that Carians and Ionians carried the cedar timber from Babylon to Susa for his palace. Babylonian documents show a community of Carians living at Borsippa in the Persian period, probably settled there by the crown. These records show Carians as working subjects at the heart of the empire, as well as soldiers on its edges.
n_carians.s3: Herodotus says Harpagus conquered Caria for Cyrus with little resistance, except at Pedasa. In the Ionian Revolt the Carians lost two battles, at the Marsyas river and at Labraunda, then ambushed a Persian army near Pedasa and killed its generals. After the fall of Miletus in 494 BCE they were brought back under Persian rule. In 480 BCE, Herodotus says, the Carians sent 70 ships to Xerxes, and Artemisia of Halicarnassus commanded five more.
n_carians.s4: Greek writers told stories about the Carians' distant past. Herodotus reports a Cretan story that the Carians had once been islanders serving King Minos, and adds that the Carians themselves claimed to have always lived on the mainland. He also credits them with inventing helmet crests and shield handles. Thucydides says Minos drove Carian pirates from the islands, and that many old graves opened on Delos were judged Carian from the arms buried in them.
n_chians.lead: The Chians were Ionian Greeks who lived on the island of Chios and came under Persian rule after Harpagus's conquest of Ionia. At Lade in 494 BCE they sent 100 ships, the largest number Herodotus gives for any Ionian city, and they fought on after others left. Persia took their island after that defeat.
n_chians.play: The game names the Chians in the Chronicle, decrees and field briefings, and gives them no mechanic of their own beyond what those texts show. Its note that they went over to the King departs from Herodotus, who has them fight on at Lade and be conquered.
n_chians.s0: Herodotus says the Chians handed over the Lydian rebel Pactyes to the Persians and received the district of Atarneus on the mainland as payment. He tells this after the conquest of Lydia under Cyrus. He adds that the Chians did not use the grain of Atarneus in sacrifices to the gods.
n_chians.s1: Herodotus lists Strattis of Chios among the Greek tyrants who guarded the bridge over the Ister during Darius's Scythian campaign. The Persians relied on local rulers of this kind to hold the Ionian cities. Herodotus says the revolt of 499 BCE began by removing such tyrants.
n_chians.s2: Herodotus says the Chians brought 100 ships to Lade, each carrying forty picked citizens as fighting men. He says the Ionians grew tired of the hard training imposed by Dionysius of Phocaea. Most Samian ships sailed off, and the Lesbians followed them. The Chians kept fighting, repeatedly broke the enemy line, and lost most of their ships.
n_chians.s3: Herodotus blames most of the Samian captains for deserting and says they had made a private arrangement with the Persians. He also names eleven Samian captains who stayed and were honoured at home. Modern historians doubt that this one-sided account can be accepted without question, since it comes from a Greek tradition after the war.
n_chians.s4: Herodotus says Miletus was taken by siege after Lade, with the Persians undermining its walls. He says the Persians then took the islands, and that the Chians who survived Lade were overcome and their island was subdued.
n_chians.s5: After the victory at Mycale in 479 BCE, Herodotus says the Greeks admitted the Samians, Chians, Lesbians and other islanders into their alliance. They took oaths to stay loyal and not to desert it.
n_cilicians.lead: The Cilicians lived on the south-eastern coast of Anatolia, between the Taurus mountains and the sea facing Cyprus. Under the Achaemenid kings they kept rulers of their own, whom the Greeks called Syennesis. Herodotus says they paid tribute in silver and horses and sent warships to the royal fleet at Lade and in Xerxes' war of 480 BCE.
n_cilicians.play: The game shows the Cilicians only as squadrons in the King's fleet, which fits Herodotus for 494 to 480 BCE. Their horse tribute, the cavalry that guarded their land and their native rulers are not part of the game's picture.
n_cilicians.s0: Cilicia had a fertile eastern plain around Tarsus and a rugged western highland along the coast. Assyrian royal texts call the plain Que and the highlands Hilakku. A Babylonian chronicle records that Neriglissar marched in 557 BCE against Appuashu, king of Pirindu in the rough west, and pursued him through mountain country towards the sea. No surviving document says how or when Cilicia came under Persian rule.
n_cilicians.s1: Herodotus says a Syennesis of Cilicia helped arrange peace between the Lydians and the Medes after the battle of the eclipse, and later Cilician rulers bore the same name. In his list of Darius's tribute districts, Cilicia formed the fourth. It paid 360 white horses, one for each day of the year, and 500 talents of silver. Of the silver, he says, 140 talents went to the cavalry that guarded Cilicia.
n_cilicians.s2: Herodotus places Cilician ships beside Phoenician, Cypriot and Egyptian squadrons at Lade in 494 BCE. He says the army of Datis and Artaphernes mustered on the Aleian plain of Cilicia in 490 BCE and boarded the fleet there. For Xerxes in 480 BCE the Cilicians sent 100 ships, whose fighting men wore native helmets and woollen tunics and carried rawhide shields and two javelins. At Artemisium the Greeks destroyed a squadron of Cilician ships.
n_cilicians.s3: Cilicia is not named in Darius's lists of subject lands, and its native rulers stayed in place under Persian oversight. Historians argue whether it was a client kingdom or a province, and whether Syennesis was a name or a title. Herodotus lists Syennesis son of Oromedon among the fleet's chief men, and Aeschylus has a Syennesis die at Salamis. Herodotus says Xerxes later gave Xenagoras of Halicarnassus rule over all Cilicia.
n_cilicians.s4: Herodotus reports that the Cilicians were once called Hypachaeans and took their later name from Cilix, son of the Phoenician Agenor. Cilix belongs to the Greek story of Europa, whose brothers went out to search for her and founded new peoples. The tale shows the Greek habit of explaining foreign peoples through heroes. It does not record their real origins.
n_cissians.lead: The Cissians were the people of the lowland country around Susa, as Greek writers named them. Their land held one of the King's chief residences and lay at the end of the Royal Road, and Cissian troops fought in Xerxes' army in 480 BCE. Persian royal inscriptions never use the name: they speak of Elam and Elamites, and how the Greek and Persian terms map onto each other is still discussed.
n_cissians.play: The game shows Cissian spearmen in the King's army and Cissian levies at Susa. This simplifies Herodotus, who says Cissians were armed like Persians, with bows as well as spears. 'Cissian' is a Greek label for these people.
n_cissians.s0: Herodotus, Aeschylus and later Strabo call the people and country around Susa Cissian, while Darius's inscriptions name the land Elam. Most historians take the Cissians to be the lowland Elamites of Susiana, but some think the Greek term covered only part of that region. The origin of the name is unclear. One suggestion links it to the Kassites of earlier Mesopotamian history, but this remains unproven.
n_cissians.s1: In his list of tribute districts, Herodotus places Susa and the rest of the Cissian land together as the eighth province, paying 300 talents of silver a year. He describes Aristagoras showing the Spartans a map on which Cissia lay beyond the Matieni, with Susa on the Choaspes river. He also says the Royal Road ran through Cissian country on its last stretch to Susa.
n_cissians.s2: Herodotus says the Cissian infantry of 480 BCE were equipped like the Persians, with bows, short spears, daggers and wicker shields. The difference was that they wore a cloth headband or turban in place of the Persian felt cap. Their commander was Anaphes son of Otanes. Herodotus also lists Cissian horsemen among the cavalry, armed in the same way as their foot soldiers.
n_cissians.s3: Herodotus says Xerxes waited four days at Thermopylae for the Greeks to withdraw. When they did not, he sent the Medes and Cissians against them, ordering that the defenders be taken alive. The attack failed with heavy losses, and only then were the Immortals sent in. The story comes from the Greek side alone, and its picture of the fighting may be shaped by that view.
n_cissians.s4: After Eretria was taken in 490 BCE, Herodotus says Darius settled the captive Eretrians at a place of his own called Ardericca, in Cissian land about 210 stades from Susa. He describes a well near it that produced bitumen, salt and oil. He adds that the Eretrians still lived there and kept their old language in his day.
n_corinthians.lead: Corinth was a trading city on the isthmus joining central Greece to the Peloponnese, and it sent men and ships to the Greek alliance against Xerxes. Its hoplites stood at Thermopylae and at Plataea. Its record is also a case of Greeks disagreeing with each other about who had done their share.
n_corinthians.play: The game names the Corinthians in the Chronicle, the decrees and the field briefings, mainly at Plataea, among the cities in Pausanias's army. They have no mechanic of their own beyond what those texts show.
n_corinthians.s0: Herodotus lists Corinth among the cities that sent men to the stand at Thermopylae, giving 400 Corinthian hoplites. He also says Corinth supplied 40 ships at Artemisium and again at Salamis. He names Adeimantus as the Corinthian commander at Salamis and shows him arguing with Themistocles over where to fight.
n_corinthians.s1: Herodotus gives an order of battle for the Greek army under Pausanias in 479 BCE. He puts the Corinthians at 5,000 hoplites, behind the Lacedaemonians at 10,000 and the Athenians at 8,000 in his count. His is the only detailed list, and modern historians accept the general picture of a very large Greek army but doubt that his totals are exact.
n_corinthians.s2: Herodotus says the Corinthians arrived late to the main fighting at Plataea. They took the route over the foothills of Cithaeron and came up only after the Spartans and Tegeans had broken into the Persian camp. This is Herodotus's version, and he does not call it a shameful absence.
n_corinthians.s3: After Plataea the Greeks dedicated a bronze tripod on a column of three intertwined serpents at Delphi. Its inscription lists the cities that fought, and the Corinthians are among them. The bronze coils survive today in Istanbul with the names still legible. Herodotus also mentions the dedication.
n_corinthians.s4: Herodotus reports an Athenian story that Adeimantus and the Corinthians sailed away when the battle began. He adds that the Corinthians denied it and that the rest of Greece spoke in their favour. Plutarch later called the tale malicious. Modern historians generally doubt it and see it as shaped by Athenian rivalry with Corinth.
n_cypriots.lead: Cyprus was divided among small city-kingdoms such as Salamis, Paphos, Kition, Amathus and Soli, with Greek, Phoenician and older native populations. Under Persian rule its kings kept their thrones, paid tribute and sent warships to the King's fleet. In about 497 BCE most of them joined the Ionian Revolt and were defeated within about a year.
n_cypriots.play: The game shows the Cypriots as squadrons in the King's fleet, which matches Herodotus. The island's separate kings, their tribute and their failed revolt of about 497 BCE lie behind that role and are not shown in play.
n_cypriots.s0: Herodotus says the Egyptian king Amasis was the first to conquer Cyprus and make it pay tribute. He then says the Cypriots gave themselves to the Persians of their own accord and joined Cambyses' invasion of Egypt in 525 BCE. Xenophon's Cyropaedia credits Cyrus with ruling Cyprus, but that work is a moral romance, and most historians follow Herodotus in placing the submission shortly before 525 BCE.
n_cypriots.s1: In Herodotus's list of Darius's tax districts, Cyprus belonged to the fifth district with Phoenicia and Palestinian Syria, which together paid 350 talents of silver. The Cypriot kings went on ruling their own cities under Persian overlordship. Herodotus names one of them, Euelthon of Salamis, who gave a fugitive queen of Cyrene a golden spindle and distaff instead of the army she asked for.
n_cypriots.s2: Herodotus tells how Onesilus shut his brother Gorgus, king of Salamis, out of the city and brought every Cypriot kingdom except Amathus into the Ionian Revolt. A Persian army under Artybius landed while the Ionian fleet beat the Phoenicians at sea. On land, Stesenor of Kourion and the Salaminian chariots changed sides, Onesilus was killed, and Soli fell in the fifth month of its siege.
n_cypriots.s3: Excavators at Old Paphos found a great Persian siege ramp against the north-east gate, filled with rubble, broken sculpture and hundreds of arrowheads and spearheads. The defenders dug tunnels beneath it to make it collapse. The remains are dated to the revolt of about 498-497 BCE, a siege that Herodotus does not describe.
n_cypriots.s4: Herodotus says Cyprus sent 150 ships in 480 BCE, behind the Phoenicians with 300 and the Egyptians with 200. He says the kings wore turbans and the others were armed like Greeks, and names Gorgus son of Chersis, the king Onesilus had ousted, among the notable captains. He puts Xerxes' whole fleet at 1,207 ships, a figure most historians think too high, and he has Artemisia call the Cypriots poor allies before Salamis.
n_egyptians.lead: The Egyptians lived along the Nile under pharaohs of the Saite dynasty until Cambyses conquered them in 525 BCE. Egypt then became one of the richest provinces of the empire. Its priests, scribes, craftsmen and sailors served the Persian kings, who ruled there as pharaohs. The country also revolted more than once, first about 486 BCE.
n_egyptians.play: The game shows Egypt as a trade partner, Psamtik III's army defending Memphis in 525 BCE, and Egyptian marines in the King's fleet. Herodotus places the main battle at Pelusium, with Memphis falling afterwards to a siege.
n_egyptians.s0: Cambyses invaded Egypt in 525 BCE. Herodotus tells that Arab allies carried water for his army across the desert, and that the Greek mercenary Phanes, who had deserted Egypt, gave him advice. The Egyptians under Psamtik III, who had reigned only about six months, were beaten at Pelusium and fled to Memphis, which fell after a siege. Psamtik was taken alive and later put to death for plotting.
n_egyptians.s1: The inscribed statue of Udjahorresnet belonged to a naval commander under the last Saite kings. It records that he served Cambyses as chief physician, composed his Egyptian royal name and had foreign troops cleared from the temple of Neith at Sais. He adds that Darius later sent him back to Egypt to restore the House of Life, the temple school of scribes. A Serapeum stela records an Apis bull buried with royal rites in Cambyses' sixth year.
n_egyptians.s2: Darius was presented in Egypt as a pharaoh. Stelae set up along the canal from the Nile to the Red Sea record that he had it dug and sent ships through it towards Persia. His statue found at Susa was carved from Egyptian stone and carries hieroglyphs and a list of subject peoples. His Susa charter names Egyptians among the goldsmiths, woodworkers and wall decorators who built his palace.
n_egyptians.s3: Herodotus says Cambyses went mad, stabbed the Apis bull and mocked Egyptian gods. The Apis stelae fit poorly with this story: a bull was buried in his reign with full honours, and its successor lived on into Darius's reign.
