Many historians think the tale came from priests angered by his cuts to temple revenues, a measure noted in a later Demotic text. Others accept that his rule was harsher than that of Darius.
n_egyptians.s4: Herodotus says Egypt rebelled late in Darius's reign and that Xerxes crushed the revolt, making his brother Achaemenes governor. He counts 200 Egyptian ships in the fleet of 480 BCE, their crews wearing plaited helmets and carrying broad-rimmed shields, naval spears and heavy axes. In his telling they fought best of the King's sailors at Artemisium, taking five Greek ships, and their marines were later landed to fight at Plataea.
n_egyptians.s5: Egypt's emblem in the game is the shield and crossed arrows of Neith, goddess of Sais, home city of Psamtik's Saite dynasty, on a hem of collar blocks. Egyptian armies marched behind standards of gods and nomes; this is an emblem after Neith, not a known field standard.
n_elamites.lead: The Elamites were heirs to a kingdom far older than Persia, centred on Susa and the highlands of Anshan. Elam rose against Darius three times in 522-519 BCE, yet its language became the working tongue of the Persian administration. Persian kingship, dress and scribal practice probably owed much to Elam, though how much is still argued.
n_elamites.play: The game shows the Elamites as trade partners around Susa and as rebels at Susa. Historically Elam was a core province of the empire, not an outside partner. Behistun records three Elamite risings in 522-519 BCE.
n_elamites.s0: Elam called itself Haltamti; the Persians called it Uja. Its kings ruled from Susa in the lowland plain and from Anshan in the highlands that later became Persis. Assyrian annals record that Ashurbanipal sacked Susa in about 646 BCE. Smaller Neo-Elamite kingdoms survived after that, and Susa probably came under Persian rule in Cyrus's reign, though no text records when or how.
n_elamites.s1: Darius's Behistun inscription says that after Gaumata's death Elam revolted under Assina, who was brought to him bound and put to death. Then Martiya, a Persian, claimed to be Imanish, king of Elam, but the Elamites feared Darius's approach, seized him and killed him. In a later fifth column, Darius says that Athamaita led a third rising in his second and third years. Gobryas defeated the Elamites, and Athamaita was brought to Darius and killed.
n_elamites.s2: Most of the thousands of Persepolis Fortification tablets, covering roughly 509 to 494 BCE, are written in Elamite. They record rations, travel and offerings, including offerings to Elamite gods such as Humban beside Iranian ones. The Elamite text of Behistun was probably the first version carved. Elamite stands with Old Persian and Babylonian in the royal inscriptions.
n_elamites.s3: Herodotus does not use the name Elam. He speaks of the Cissians, with Susa as their chief place. He lists Susa and the Cissian land as a tax district paying 300 talents of silver. In Xerxes' army, he says, the Cissians were armed like the Persians but wore a headband or turban rather than a felt cap.
n_elamites.s4: On the Cyrus Cylinder, Cyrus called himself king of Anshan, an old Elamite royal title. Some historians think Persian kingship grew out of a long mixing of Iranian newcomers and Elamites in the highlands. Others stress a clearer break and treat the Elamite borrowings as later choices. The long Persian robe and some court practices are often traced to Elam, but the extent of the debt is still argued.
n_elamites.s5: The game's emblem for Elam is a rearing serpent, a motif of Elamite thrones, seals and temple art for two thousand years, in the turquoise and yellow of the glazed bricks of Susa. No Elamite army standard is known; the serpent stands for the land's own art, not for a banner.
n_eretrians.lead: The Eretrians were the citizens of Eretria, a Greek city on the island of Euboea. Their five ships helped the Ionian rebels burn Sardis in 498 BCE. In 490 BCE a Persian expedition under Datis and Artaphernes took the city and burned its temples. Many of its people were carried to the lowlands around Susa, where Darius settled them on royal land.
n_eretrians.play: The game shows Eretria falling in 490 BCE before Marathon and its people settled at Arderikka in Elam. Herodotus puts Ardericca in Cissia near Susa, the old Elamite lowland, though the site has never been found.
n_eretrians.s0: Eretria stood on the south-west coast of Euboea, facing Boeotia and Attica across a narrow gulf. Thucydides recalls an old war between Eretria and its neighbour Chalcis in which much of Greece took sides. Herodotus says the Eretrians sent five triremes to the Ionian revolt to repay Miletus for help in that war. They sailed with twenty Athenian ships to Ephesus and marched up to Sardis, which was burned in 498 BCE.
n_eretrians.s1: Herodotus tells that the fleet of Datis and Artaphernes crossed the Aegean and landed in Eretrian territory. This Artaphernes was the son of the satrap of Sardis. The Eretrians chose to defend their walls rather than flee to the hills, and for six days both sides lost many men. On the seventh day two leading citizens, Euphorbus and Philagrus, let the Persians in, and the temples were burned in revenge for those of Sardis.
n_eretrians.s2: Excavations at Eretria, begun by Greek archaeologists and continued since 1964 by the Swiss School of Archaeology in Greece, have uncovered the sanctuary of Apollo Daphnephoros. Its late archaic stone temple was built not long before 490 BCE and shows signs of destruction, which excavators connect with the Persian sack. Sculptures from its pediment survive, including a group of Theseus carrying off the Amazon Antiope.
n_eretrians.s3: Herodotus says the captives were left on the islet of Aegilia during the Marathon campaign and later taken to Susa. Darius, once angry with them, did them no harm and settled them on a royal estate at Ardericca in Cissia. It lay 210 stades, about 40 kilometres, from Susa and 40 stades from a well yielding bitumen, salt and oil. They still spoke Greek there in Herodotus's day, and no Persian document names them.
n_eretrians.s4: Philostratus, writing in the third century CE, says that the wandering sage Apollonius of Tyana visited the Eretrians in Cissia centuries after their deportation. In his story Apollonius found their graves inscribed in Greek and tended them. The tale belongs to a work full of marvels and cannot be checked, and Ardericca itself has never been located.
n_ethiopians.lead: Greek writers called the peoples south of Egypt Ethiopians. In Persian royal texts the land is Kush, on the Nile above Egypt. Cambyses marched against it after taking Egypt, and later Persian kings listed Kush among their lands and as a source of ivory.
n_ethiopians.play: The game names the Ethiopians in the Chronicle, the decrees and the field briefings, in the march south and in the ivory texts. They have no mechanic of their own beyond what these texts show.
n_ethiopians.s0: Kush appears among the lands listed in the royal inscriptions of Darius and Xerxes. Darius's Susa foundation charter says the ivory used in the palace came from Kush, India and Arachosia. The texts show that the Persians counted Kush within their world, but they give no account of a conquest.
n_ethiopians.s1: Herodotus says Cambyses, after Egypt, planned three ventures: against Carthage, against the Ammonians and against the long-lived Ethiopians. He says spies went first with gifts, and that the Ethiopian king answered with a bow and a mocking message. Herodotus says Cambyses marched in anger without enough provisions, and that hunger drove the army to eat its pack animals and then to draw lots to eat men before he turned back.
n_ethiopians.s2: Herodotus presents the campaign as the folly of a mad king. Modern historians doubt that picture, since the tradition about Cambyses was hostile to him. How far he got, and how much control Persia held in the south afterwards, is unclear. Later Persian texts list Kush among the lands, but they do not say what that meant in practice.
n_ethiopians.s3: Herodotus says the force sent against the Ammonians set out from Thebes in Egypt and vanished in the desert. He reports the Ammonians' own story that a south wind buried it in sand. The march to Ammon and the march into Kush were separate ventures in his telling.
n_ethiopians.s4: Herodotus says the Ethiopians bordering Egypt gave gifts instead of regular tribute, brought every other year. He lists unrefined gold, ebony logs, five Ethiopian boys and twenty large elephant tusks. His picture of them as tall, handsome and very long-lived reflects Greek ideas of the distant south and should not be read as ethnography.
n_ethiopians.s5: Herodotus lists Ethiopians among the troops Xerxes gathered for Greece, dressed in leopard and lion skins and fighting with long palm-rib bows and stone-tipped arrows. He separates them from the eastern Ethiopians who served beside the Indians. His army list is a literary catalogue, and its details cannot be checked against Persian records.
n_hellenic_league.lead: In 481 BCE the Greek states that meant to resist Xerxes met at the Isthmus of Corinth and swore an alliance under Spartan command. Modern historians call it the Hellenic League; the Greeks called themselves simply the Greeks. It fought at Thermopylae, Artemisium, Salamis, Plataea and Mycale, and most Greek states did not join it.
n_hellenic_league.play: The Greeks of the Hellenic League are the foe at Plataea and on its fields, under their own emblem in the battle banner and beside their name.
n_hellenic_league.s0: Herodotus says the Greeks who took the better side met in 481 BCE, ended their own wars, the bitterest between Athens and Aegina, and sent spies to Sardis and envoys to Argos, Syracuse, Corcyra and Crete. None of those four joined. Sparta led on land and sea, because the allies would not follow an Athenian.
n_hellenic_league.s1: Herodotus says the allies swore that every Greek state that gave itself to the Persian without being forced would pay a tithe of its wealth to the god at Delphi once the war was won. Thebes and most of Boeotia, Thessaly and others had already given earth and water.
n_hellenic_league.s2: After Plataea the allies set up a gold tripod at Delphi on a bronze column of three twisted snakes. The column survives in Istanbul, inscribed with the names of 31 states 'who fought the war'. It is the only list from the time of the states that resisted.
n_hellenic_league.s3: The game marks the League with Apollo's bronze tripod of Delphi, the Greeks' shared sanctuary. The Serpent Column itself is not used, since it was made from the spoils of Plataea, after the battles the League fights in the game. The Greeks fought under their own city devices, not a League flag.
n_hill_raiders.lead: Not everyone in the Persian homeland lived in towns or farmed the valleys. Herodotus counted several Persian tribes as nomads, and later writers describe mountain peoples such as the Uxians who controlled the passes between Susa and Persis. They show that royal power in the heartland rested partly on bargains with herders and hill peoples, not only on force.
n_hill_raiders.play: The game's Hill Raiders attack Pasargadae from camps in the hills. No source records raids on Pasargadae; the raiding is a game simplification of a relationship that Greek writers describe as tolls and gifts.
n_hill_raiders.s0: Herodotus lists the tribes of the Persians. He says the Pasargadae, Maraphii and Maspii were the leading tribes, that the Panthialaei, Derusiaei and Germanii worked the land, and that the Dai, Mardi, Dropici and Sagartii were nomads. In his view, then, the Mardians were not foreigners but Persians who lived by herding.
n_hill_raiders.s1: Herodotus tells how Cyrus took the citadel of Sardis. A Mardian soldier named Hyroeades saw a Lydian climb down a steep and unguarded cliff to fetch a fallen helmet. He climbed up the same way, other Persians followed, and the citadel fell. The story suggests that mountain-bred men served in Cyrus's army.
n_hill_raiders.s2: Arrian says that when Alexander marched from Susa towards Persis in 331, the Uxians of the hills demanded the payment they had always received from the Persian kings for the use of the pass. Alexander attacked them instead and imposed a yearly tribute of horses, pack animals and sheep. Strabo, following Nearchus, names the Mardians, Uxians, Elymaeans and Cossaeans as raiding peoples who took payments from the kings.
n_hill_raiders.s3: The Greek writers present these payments as the King buying off robbers, a sign of weakness. P. Briant argued instead that they were gift exchanges which bound pastoral groups to the King and gave him men, animals and safe roads in return. The Persepolis Fortification tablets show Persis as a closely administered land, which makes a helpless King unlikely, but no surviving Persian text clearly describes the hill tribes.
n_hill_raiders.s4: Nicolaus of Damascus, writing in the time of Augustus and probably drawing on Ctesias, told a story in which Cyrus's father was a Mardian named Atradates who lived by banditry, and his mother a goatherd. This tale of rising from poverty contradicts the Cyrus Cylinder, where Cyrus calls himself son of Cambyses and descendant of kings of Anshan.
n_hill_raiders.s5: The hill raiders carry a great-horned ibex, the beast of the Luristan bronzes and of Achaemenid metalwork. The raiders are a dramatization, and so is their emblem: no source names their tribes or their signs.
n_indians.lead: The Persians called the lands along the Indus river Hindush, and its people the Indians. Darius probably brought the region into the empire some years after 520 BCE, and it became the empire's south-eastern edge. Indians sent gold, ivory and soldiers to the King, and Greek writers knew them as a distant people around whom marvels gathered.
n_indians.play: The game treats the Indians as a trade partner and includes Indian archers in the King's army. The archers match Herodotus, but after Darius's conquest Hindush was a subject land paying tribute, not an outside partner, so this is a simplification.
n_indians.s0: Hindush is the Old Persian form of the river name the Indians called Sindhu. It is missing from the list of lands at Behistun, carved about 520 BCE, but appears among the King's lands in later texts such as Darius's tomb inscription DNa and Xerxes' XPh. In his Susa building charter DSf, Darius says that the ivory worked in the palace came from Kush, Hindush and Arachosia.
n_indians.s1: On the Apadana stairways at Persepolis, a delegation usually identified as Indians walks lightly dressed, carrying jars on a yoke, probably filled with gold dust, and leading a donkey. An Indian also appears among the labelled throne-bearers on Darius's tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam. The Persepolis Fortification tablets record rations for parties travelling on the roads between India and the Persian heartland.
n_indians.s2: Herodotus calls the Indians the most numerous people he knew and says they paid 360 talents of gold dust a year, more than any other province. He says Darius sent Scylax of Caryanda down the Indus and then conquered the Indians. In Xerxes' army of 480 BCE he describes Indians in cotton clothing with cane bows and iron-tipped cane arrows, as well as Indian horsemen and chariots.
n_indians.s3: Historians place Hindush along the Indus, in the lower valley or the Punjab, separate from the provinces of Gandara and Thatagush, but its limits are argued over. Its absence from Behistun suggests conquest by Darius after about 520 BCE, though the exact date is unknown. Many doubt Herodotus's gold figure, which he converts into more silver than any other province paid, and think it inflated or garbled.
n_indians.s4: Herodotus repeats a tale, which he says he had from the Persians, that Indians of the north gathered gold from sand dug up by ants smaller than dogs but larger than foxes, and then fled from them on fast camels. Later Greek writers such as Ctesias added further Indian marvels. Some modern scholars link the story to burrowing marmots in the mountains, but this remains guesswork.
n_indians.s5: India's emblem in the game is a six-armed sun from the earliest punch-marked silver coins of the subcontinent. Those coins are slightly later than the reign of Darius, so the emblem is an anachronism by a few decades, chosen as the earliest sign of the land. Herodotus says the Indians paid the largest tribute, in gold dust.
n_ionians.lead: The Ionians were Greek-speaking cities on the west coast of Asia Minor and the nearby islands, ruled by Persia from the 540s BCE. They paid tribute, cut stone for Darius, and built and crewed ships for the King. Their revolt of 499 to 494 BCE drew Athens and Eretria into a quarrel that led to Marathon and to Xerxes' invasion.
n_ionians.play: The game shows the Ionians as trade partners, levies and shipwrights, as hoplites in the revolt at Sardis and as squadrons at sea. These roles match the sources, though the game treats a dozen separate, often rival cities as one people.
n_ionians.s0: Herodotus names twelve Ionian cities: Miletus, Myus, Priene, Ephesus, Colophon, Lebedos, Teos, Clazomenae, Phocaea and Erythrae on the mainland, and the islands of Samos and Chios. They shared a sanctuary, the Panionion on Mycale. Croesus of Lydia had made them pay tribute, and after Cyrus took Sardis his general Harpagus reduced them city by city, while many Phocaeans and Teians sailed away rather than submit.
n_ionians.s1: In the Behistun inscription, Darius lists Yauna among the lands that came to him. His Susa charter says that Ionians and Sardians cut the stone, and that Carians and Ionians carried cedar from Babylon to Susa. The Persepolis Fortification tablets record rations for workers called Yauna. In Persian and other eastern usage, Yauna came to serve as a general name for Greeks.
n_ionians.s2: Herodotus tells how Aristagoras of Miletus failed in an attack on Naxos and then led the cities to depose their tyrants and rise against Persia. In 498 BCE, Ionians with Athenian and Eretrian help burned the lower town of Sardis, but they did not take the citadel. The rebel fleet was broken off Lade in 494 BCE after most of the Samian ships deserted, and Miletus fell. Herodotus gives 353 Ionian ships against 600 Persian; the second figure is probably inflated.
n_ionians.s3: Herodotus says Artaphernes made the cities settle their disputes by arbitration and measured their land to fix tribute. He adds that Mardonius replaced the tyrants with democracies in 492 BCE. The Ionians sent a hundred ships to Xerxes in 480 BCE, and several Ionian captains fought hard at Salamis. At Mycale in 479 BCE the Samians and Milesians turned on the Persians, and afterwards the island states were taken into the Greek alliance.
n_ionians.s4: Herodotus explains the revolt mainly through the personal ambitions of Aristagoras and Histiaeus, and he is often scornful of Ionian discipline. Modern historians give more weight to resentment of tyrants backed by Persia, to the burden of tribute, and to changes in trade. They also debate how united the rebels were, since Herodotus himself describes cities acting alone and Samians deserting at Lade.
n_ionians.s5: The Ionian Greeks carry the lion of Miletus's coins, the leading city of the revolt, with a Greek meander on the hem. The cities had no shared flag; the lion is one city's coin device standing for them all.
n_islanders.lead: The Cyclades are the ring of islands round Delos in the central Aegean. Naxos, the largest and richest, led them in the late 6th century. Persia's first attack on Greece began there in 499 BCE, and in 490 BCE Datis took the islands on his way to Eretria and Marathon.
n_islanders.play: The islands are a trade partner at Marathon, under their own emblem beside their name.
n_islanders.s0: Herodotus says Naxos then had 8,000 men under arms and was the strongest of the islands. Exiled Naxian nobles asked Aristagoras of Miletus for help, and he persuaded Artaphernes to send 200 ships under Megabates. The four-month siege failed, and Aristagoras, fearing for his position, began the Ionian Revolt.
n_islanders.s1: In 490 BCE the King's fleet sailed straight across the Aegean through the islands. Herodotus says the Naxians fled to the hills and the Persians burned their town and temples, but Datis spared Delos and burned incense to Apollo there. The other islands gave hostages and men.
n_islanders.s2: The game gives the islands the kantharos, a two-handled wine cup, from Naxos's coins: the island of Dionysus struck it on its silver from the 6th century. It stands for all the islands, which had no shared emblem.
n_istros_greeks.lead: Istros, also called Histria, was a Greek city founded by settlers from Miletus on a lagoon south of the Danube delta, in what is now Romania. It lived by trade with the Getae and Scythians of the hinterland. When Darius led his army across the Ister against the Scythians in about 513 BCE, Istros lay close to the route, though no ancient writer says what part, if any, it played.
n_istros_greeks.play: In the game, Istros is a trade partner in the Ister level. No ancient source records the city trading with Darius's army; this is a plausible invention based on its position near the river mouth.
n_istros_greeks.s0: Herodotus places Istria where the Ister flows into the Black Sea and calls it a settlement of the Milesians. Miletus founded many colonies around the Black Sea, and Istros was among the earliest on its western shore. Later Greek chronographers, Eusebius among them, dated its foundation to about 657 BCE.
n_istros_greeks.s1: Romanian excavations since 1914 have uncovered the city on a promontory beside Lake Sinoe. The oldest Greek pottery dates to the later 600s BCE, somewhat after the date the chronographers give. A sacred area held temples, including one of Zeus Polieus and one of Aphrodite, and imported East Greek pottery shows close ties with Ionia.
n_istros_greeks.s2: Herodotus says that on his march to the Ister Darius subdued the Getae, a Thracian people living south of the river. Modern historians place them in the hinterland of Istros. Herodotus also tells of the Scythian king Scyles, whose mother was a woman of Istria. She taught him to speak and write Greek, and Herodotus says his love of Greek ways later cost him his throne and his life.
n_istros_greeks.s3: Herodotus says the Ionian fleet sailed up the Ister two days from the sea and bridged the river there, and that the Ionian tyrants guarded the bridge. He never names Istros in the story. Excavators found a destruction of the archaic settlement in the late 500s BCE. Some link it to the Persian campaign or to a Scythian reprisal, but others doubt any connection.
n_istros_greeks.s4: The Greeks of Istros and the Pontic grain ships carry a dolphin, after the cast bronze dolphins that Olbia and the other Milesian colonies on the Black Sea used as money in the 6th and 5th centuries.
n_lesbians.lead: The Lesbians were the Greek inhabitants of Lesbos, an island off the coast of Asia Minor with cities such as Mytilene and Methymna. Their island lay within the Persian sphere after the conquest of western Asia Minor. They are best known for the naval battle of Lade in 494 BCE, where Herodotus says they followed the Samians and left the line.
n_lesbians.play: The game names the Lesbians in the Chronicle, the decrees or the field briefings about Lade, where most of the Samians sail away and the Lesbians follow. They have no mechanic of their own beyond what these texts show.
n_lesbians.s0: Herodotus counts Lesbos among the Aeolian Greek communities of the eastern Aegean. He says the islanders did not come under the same pressure as the mainland Ionians once Cyrus's commander Harpagus had taken the coast cities. How and when Lesbos itself came under Persian authority he does not set out clearly here.
n_lesbians.s1: Herodotus says Coes of Mytilene, a commander in Darius's Scythian expedition, spoke at the bridge over the Ister and afterwards received the tyranny of his city from the King. This is the Greek writer's report of a Persian practice of backing friendly local rulers in the coastal Greek cities.
n_lesbians.s2: Herodotus says the Lesbians brought seventy ships to the Ionian fleet at Lade in 494 BCE. He gives the Persian fleet as six hundred ships, with Phoenician, Cypriot, Cilician and Egyptian crews, a figure that may be inflated. He also says the Ionians grew tired of the hard training of Dionysius of Phocaea.
n_lesbians.s3: Herodotus says that when the fleets met, most of the Samian ships hoisted sail and left, and the Lesbians, seeing them go, did the same. The Chians fought on, kept breaking the enemy line and lost most of their ships. Miletus was then taken by siege and mining.
n_lesbians.s4: Herodotus blames the Samian captains for a bargain with the Persians, and the flight of the Lesbians follows from theirs in his telling. Modern historians point out that Herodotus is hostile to the Samians in this passage and that panic or fear of defeat could explain the departures. The sources do not allow a firm answer.
n_lesbians.s5: Herodotus says that after Miletus fell, the Persians went on to take the islands off the coast. What this meant for Lesbos in detail is not given in a passage that can be cited with confidence here.
n_libyans.lead: The Greeks used the name Libyans for the native peoples of North Africa west of Egypt. Herodotus describes those between Egypt and Lake Tritonis as herding nomads, with farming peoples further west. After Cambyses took Egypt in 525 BCE, the Libyans nearest Egypt submitted without fighting, and the Persian kings afterwards counted Libya, which they called Putaya, among their lands.
n_libyans.play: The game puts Libyan riders in Psamtik's army at Memphis. No ancient source records this. Herodotus says the Libyans near Egypt submitted to Cambyses without a fight once Memphis had fallen.
n_libyans.s0: Libyans had long lived and served in Egypt, and some earlier pharaohs were of Libyan descent. Some historians think that part of the hereditary warrior class Herodotus describes also had Libyan roots. Yet Herodotus's account of the war of 525 BCE names Egyptians with Greek and Carian mercenaries and mentions no Libyan contingent. Whether any Libyans fought for Psamtik III is unknown, and no source mentions Libyan horsemen.
n_libyans.s1: Herodotus says that after Memphis surrendered in 525 BCE, the Libyans bordering Egypt feared the same fate. They gave themselves up without a fight, agreed to pay tribute and sent gifts, and the Greeks of Cyrene and Barca followed. In his list of Darius's tax districts, he places these Libyans in one province with Egypt, Cyrene and Barca, paying 700 talents of silver a year.
n_libyans.s2: Persian texts call the land Putaya. It is missing from the list of lands in the Behistun inscription but appears in later lists, including Darius's tomb inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam and Xerxes' list of subject lands. On the façade of Darius's tomb, a Libyan figure stands among the peoples shown holding up the King's throne.
n_libyans.s3: Herodotus tells how Aryandes, the Persian governor of Egypt, sent an army and a fleet west around the time of Darius's Scythian campaign. The stated reason was to punish Barca for killing Arcesilaus III of Cyrene, who had taken refuge there. Herodotus thought the real aim was to subdue the many Libyan peoples still outside the King's rule. Barca fell after a nine-month siege, and many of its people were deported to Bactria.
n_libyans.s4: In his catalogue of the army Xerxes led into Greece in 480 BCE, Herodotus describes Libyans dressed in leather and armed with javelins hardened in fire. Their commander was Massages son of Oarizus. He adds that Libyans served among the mounted forces as chariot drivers. His total for the whole army is greatly exaggerated, and he does not place the Libyans in any particular battle.
n_locrians.lead: The Locrians of Opus lived on the mainland coast opposite Euboea, north-west of Boeotia. Herodotus places them with the Greeks at Thermopylae in 480 BCE and with Mardonius's Greek allies at Plataea in 479 BCE. Herodotus does not explain the change, but a Persian army on their land is the likely cause.
n_locrians.play: The game names the Locrians in the Chronicle, the decrees and the field briefings for Thermopylae and Plataea. They have no mechanic of their own beyond what those texts show.
n_locrians.s0: Herodotus speaks of the Locrians of Opus, who lived near the Euboean Gulf. Greek writers also knew a separate group, the Ozolian Locrians, farther west. The Opuntians are the Locrians of the Persian War texts used here.
n_locrians.s1: Herodotus says the Locrians of Opus came to the pass in full force, and that a thousand Phocians came as well. They stood beside the Peloponnesian contingents led by the Spartan king Leonidas. Herodotus also lists Opuntian Locrians among the ships of the Greek fleet at Artemisium.
n_locrians.s2: Herodotus gives no number for the Locrians, saying only that they came in full force. Later writers such as Diodorus give round figures for the Greek force at the pass, and these do not agree with one another. The Locrian numbers are therefore uncertain.
n_locrians.s3: Herodotus lists Locrians among the peoples in Xerxes' land army. At Plataea Mardonius set Boeotians, Locrians, Malians, Thessalians and a thousand Phocians against the Athenians, Plataeans and Megarians. Herodotus does not set out their reasons. Modern historians generally infer that they yielded to a Persian army standing in central Greece.
n_locrians.s4: Herodotus says the Phocians resisted Xerxes for a time and that Phocians at Plataea were mostly with the Persian side, though some are said to have harassed it from the mountains. Locrians, Phocians and their neighbours therefore stood on both sides within a year. The surviving Persian sources say nothing about them.
n_lydians.lead: The Lydians lived in the river valleys of western Anatolia, with their capital at Sardis below a steep citadel. Under the Mermnad kings they ruled much of Anatolia west of the Halys and grew rich on gold from the Pactolus. After Cyrus took Sardis in the 540s BCE, Lydia became the Persian province of Sparda, from which the King's governors watched the Greek cities of the Aegean coast.
n_lydians.play: The game treats Lydia as a trade partner sending gifts from Sardis and raises Lydian levies there. In fact by 498 BCE Lydia was a tribute-paying province; Herodotus says Lydians and Persians defended Sardis together.
n_lydians.s0: Herodotus traces the Mermnad dynasty from Gyges, who seized the throne, through Ardys, Sadyattes and Alyattes to Croesus. These kings attacked the Greek cities of the coast, and he says Croesus was the first to make them pay tribute. He also says an eclipse halted a battle between Alyattes and the Medes, and a peace then fixed the border at the Halys. The great burial mound of Alyattes, which Herodotus describes, still stands at Bin Tepe north of Sardis.
n_lydians.s1: Herodotus says the Lydians were the first people to strike coins of gold and silver and the first to keep retail shops. Excavated electrum coins, among the earliest from a deposit at the Artemision of Ephesus, point to a Lydian or East Greek origin around 600 BCE or a little before. Historians still argue over the pure gold and silver coins called Croeseids. Some think Croesus himself struck them, and others think the Persians did so after the conquest.
n_lydians.s2: Herodotus says Croesus crossed the Halys into Persian territory and then retreated to Sardis. He lost the city after a fourteen-day siege, when a Mardian soldier climbed an unguarded part of the citadel rock. Excavators have found a mid-500s BCE destruction layer with weapons and the remains of men killed in the fighting. The date is uncertain. The Nabonidus Chronicle records a campaign of Cyrus in 547 BCE, but the country's name is damaged and many doubt it reads Lydia.
n_lydians.s3: Herodotus tells that Cyrus set the captive Croesus on a pyre and that Croesus called out the name of Solon. When Cyrus relented and the flames could not be put out, Apollo sent rain. The poet Bacchylides, writing earlier, has Croesus mount the pyre by his own choice, and Apollo carries him away to the Hyperboreans. Both versions are shaped as lessons about the fall of the proud and cannot be taken as reports of what happened.
n_lydians.s4: At Behistun, Darius lists Sparda among the lands that came to him. His Susa foundation charter says gold was brought from Sardis and that Sardians worked stone and wood for the palace. On the Apadana stairways at Persepolis, a Lydian delegation brings vessels, armlets and a chariot. Lydian, an Anatolian language with its own alphabet, survives in inscriptions from Sardis, including a later bilingual in Lydian and Aramaic.
n_lydians.s5: Lydia's emblem in the game follows Croesus's coins: the foreparts of a lion and a bull facing each other, struck in gold and silver about 560-546 BCE. Earlier Lydian electrum showed a roaring lion's head. Herodotus says the Lydians were the first to strike coins.
n_macedonians.lead: The Macedonians lived north of Thessaly around the Thermaic Gulf, ruled by kings who claimed descent from Argos and kept their seat at Aegae. From about 510 BCE their kings gave earth and water to Persia, and Macedonia became the King's foothold in Europe, a source of timber and a road for armies. Its king Alexander I served Xerxes in 480-479 BCE while, as Herodotus tells it, quietly helping the Greeks.
n_macedonians.play: The game treats the Macedonians as a trade partner and brings Alexander I into the story. In history Macedonia was a subject kingdom of the King from about 510 BCE, firmly so after 492 BCE, owing troops and obedience, not an equal trading state.
n_macedonians.s0: Thucydides says the Macedonian kings were Temenids from Argos, who won the coastal lands of Pieria and Bottiaea by driving out the peoples living there. Herodotus tells a story of the same Argive descent. Their old royal seat was Aegae, which most scholars place at modern Vergina. Herodotus notes a silver mine near Lake Prasias that later brought Alexander a talent a day.
n_macedonians.s1: Herodotus says that after Darius's Scythian campaign the general Megabazus sent seven Persians to King Amyntas I to demand earth and water, and Amyntas gave them. Amyntas's daughter Gygaea married the Persian noble Bubares, and their son later held the town of Alabanda in Asia. After the Ionian revolt, Herodotus says, Mardonius's expedition of 492 BCE brought the Macedonians firmly under Persian rule.
n_macedonians.s2: Herodotus also tells that the Persian envoys, drunk at Amyntas's feast, asked for the company of the royal women. The young Alexander sent the women out, dressed beardless youths in their clothes with daggers, and had the Persians killed. When Bubares came looking for the missing men, Alexander ended the search with rich gifts and his sister's hand. Many historians read this as a tale spread later to excuse the kings' service to Persia.
n_macedonians.s3: Herodotus says Alexander advised the Greek force at Tempe in 480 BCE to withdraw before Xerxes' army arrived, and that Macedonians marched in Xerxes' host. In the winter or early spring of 479 BCE Mardonius sent Alexander to Athens to offer an alliance, which the Athenians refused. Before Plataea, Herodotus says, Alexander rode to the Athenian lines at night to warn them of the coming Persian attack.
n_macedonians.s4: Darius's tomb inscription lists among his lands the Yauna takabara, Ionians wearing a hat like a shield; many scholars think these are the Macedonians, others Greeks of Thrace. Herodotus seems to draw on Macedonian court stories that present Alexander as a friend of the Greeks, though his kingdom plainly served Persia. Herodotus also says Alexander was accepted at Olympia as a Greek, a claim some Greeks disputed.
n_macedonians.s5: Macedon's emblem in the game is the goat of Aegae, the old royal seat whose name Greeks linked with goats. Alexander I's coins also show a horseman with two spears. The kings who gave earth and water to Darius had no flag; these are emblems after their coins and their city.
n_malians.lead: The Malians lived round the Spercheios valley and the Malian Gulf in central Greece. Their country held the pass of Thermopylae. Herodotus lists them among the peoples who gave Xerxes earth and water in 480 BCE, and he places them in Mardonius's line at Plataea in 479 BCE.
n_malians.play: The game names the Malians only in Chronicle entries, decrees and field briefings for Plataea, where they appear among the Greeks on the King's side. They have no unit or mechanic of their own beyond what those texts show.
n_malians.s0: Herodotus describes Malis as a coastal plain on the Malian Gulf, narrow in places between the mountains and the sea. He places Thermopylae and the town of Anthela on this ground. An army marching from Thessaly to central Greece had to pass through Malian country.
n_malians.s1: Herodotus lists the Malians among the peoples of northern and central Greece who gave the King's heralds earth and water in 480 BCE. He also names Greeks who did not. The Malians are not reported to have resisted, and the pass lay in their land.
n_malians.s2: Herodotus says a Malian, Ephialtes son of Eurydemus, showed the Persians the path over the mountain, which led to the defenders being outflanked at Thermopylae. He also records that some named other men, Onetas and Corydallus, and he rejects this. The story rests on Greek tradition, and no Persian source mentions it.
n_malians.s3: Herodotus says Mardonius drew up the Greeks on the King's side opposite the Athenians, Plataeans and Megarians. They were Boeotians, Locrians, Malians, Thessalians and a thousand Phocians. Herodotus gives no separate Malian numbers.
n_malians.s4: Herodotus gives no reason for the Malian submission. For other peoples he does give reasons: he says the Phocians were driven to the Persian side by Thessalian hostility. Modern historians generally explain such submissions by a mix of fear, local rivalries and the nearness of the Persian army.
n_margians.lead: The Margians lived in Margiana, an oasis country in the far east of the Persian empire, around the Murghab river. They are known above all from Darius's Behistun inscription, which records their revolt under a leader called Frada and its defeat. Greek writers say almost nothing of them by name.
n_margians.play: The game names the Margians only in the Chronicle, the decrees and the field briefings, and gives them no mechanic of their own. The briefing's mention of Parthia 'under Hystaspes' needs care: in the inscription Hystaspes fought the Parthian rebels for Darius.
n_margians.s0: Darius's inscriptions name Margiana among the countries that belonged to him, which shows that the Murghab oasis was part of the empire in his reign. The Old Persian name of the land was Margu. The Margians are known from such lists and from the Behistun text rather than from any account of their own.
n_margians.s1: The Behistun inscription says that Margiana rebelled against Darius and that a man named Frada became its leader. Darius sent Dadarshish, a Persian in his service and satrap of Bactria, against them. Dadarshish won a battle and Frada was taken. The inscription gives casualty figures, which are a king's claims and should be read as such.
n_margians.s2: Darius presents Margiana's rising as part of a single wave of rebellion in 522-521 BCE, alongside Media, Elam, Babylon, Armenia and Parthia. In Parthia the rebels joined the Median pretender Fravartish, and Darius's father Hystaspes fought them there for the king. In the inscription Hystaspes is thus a loyal commander against the Parthians, not their leader.
n_margians.s3: Herodotus does not name the Margians in his tribute and army catalogues, as far as can be told. Eastern peoples there appear under other names, and the Margians may have been counted with neighbours such as the Bactrians. Strabo describes Margiane as a fertile oasis, but he writes centuries after the Persian period.
n_margians.s4: Historians debate how much of Darius's account of simultaneous rebellions reflects real coordination. Some think the inscription magnifies a series of local risings into one great crisis to justify his seizure of the throne. The Margian rising is known only through his text, so its size and causes cannot be checked against another source.
n_medes.lead: The Medes were an Iranian-speaking people of the central Zagros whose chief city was Ecbatana. Their king helped bring down Assyria in 612 BCE, and Herodotus says Median kings ruled the Persians until Cyrus overthrew Astyages in about 550 BCE. Under the Achaemenids they remained the empire's closest partners, so close that Greeks often called the Persians 'Medes'.
n_medes.play: The game shows Medes as wool- and timber-trading herdsmen, as levies and as Fravartish's rebels at Bagastana. The trade is simplified: Media was famed for horses, and the revolt centred on Ecbatana, not Behistun itself.
n_medes.s0: Assyrian royal inscriptions name the land of Mada from the 9th century onwards. They describe many separate chiefs ruling fortified towns, and Assyrian kings boasted of taking horses from them as tribute. A Babylonian chronicle records that Umakishtar, the king Greeks called Cyaxares, took Assur in 614 BCE and joined Nabopolassar of Babylon in the capture of Nineveh in 612 BCE.
n_medes.s1: Herodotus gives the Medes four kings, Deioces, Phraortes, Cyaxares and Astyages, and says they built Ecbatana and ruled upper Asia. Some historians, following H. Sancisi-Weerdenburg, doubt that a lasting Median state ever existed, since no Median royal inscription or archive has been found. Others accept a powerful but loosely held kingdom centred on Ecbatana, whose customs the Persians later borrowed.
n_medes.s2: The Nabonidus Chronicle records that Ishtumegu (Astyages) marched against Cyrus, but his own army rebelled and handed him over. Cyrus then took Ecbatana and carried its treasure to Anshan. The entry falls in about 550 BCE. A cylinder of Nabonidus from Sippar also mentions Cyrus scattering the Medes and capturing Astyages. Herodotus says the noble Harpagus arranged the betrayal, while Ctesias, known only from later excerpts, described a longer war.
n_medes.s3: Darius's Behistun inscription says that a Mede named Fravartish claimed to be Khshathrita of the family of Cyaxares, and that the people of Media went over to him. Darius's generals fought his supporters, and Darius himself defeated him at Kunduru. Fravartish fled towards Raga, was captured, mutilated and impaled at Ecbatana.
n_medes.s4: Herodotus says the Medes in Xerxes' army were equipped like the Persians, adding that this dress was really Median, and that Medes were sent first against the Spartans at Thermopylae. Medes held high command: Harpagus subdued Ionia for Cyrus and Datis led the expedition of 490 BCE. Greeks called siding with Persia 'medizing'.
n_medes.s5: The Medes had no flag that we know of. The game marks them with the Median felt cap with its side flaps, the dress that tells a Mede from a Persian on the Persepolis reliefs, where Medes and Persians alternate on the Apadana stairs.
n_megarians.lead: The Megarians were the people of Megara, a Greek city between Attica and the Peloponnese. Herodotus says they sent ships to Salamis and a large body of hoplites to Plataea. They are a minor people in the Persian story, but they stood in the Greek line at Plataea and suffered in the fighting before and after the battle.
n_megarians.play: The game names the Megarians only in the Chronicle, the decrees and the field briefings, and gives them no mechanic of their own. Their placing against Mardonius's Greek allies at Plataea follows Herodotus 9.31.
n_megarians.s0: Megara lay between Attica and the Peloponnese, on the land route into the Peloponnese. Herodotus counts the Megarians among the Greeks who stood against Xerxes. He does not list them among those who gave earth and water to the King, but the list of such cities is his own and may be incomplete.
n_megarians.s1: Herodotus says that Megara sent twenty ships to Salamis. This was a modest contribution beside the Athenian and Corinthian fleets. The figure is his, and no Persian source mentions the Megarians.
n_megarians.s2: In his list of the Greek army at Plataea, Herodotus gives the Megarians 3,000 hoplites. He sets them in the long line of city contingents between the Spartan right and the Athenian left. The numbers are his own report and are not confirmed by any document of the time.
n_megarians.s3: Herodotus says Mardonius set the Greeks who had joined him against the Athenians, Plataeans and Megarians. These were the Boeotians, Locrians, Malians, Thessalians and a thousand Phocians. He says the Persians themselves were set against the Lacedaemonians. In this planned order the Megarians faced Greeks, not Persians.
n_megarians.s4: Before the main battle, Herodotus says, the Megarians held the most exposed ground at Erythrae and were hard pressed by Masistius's cavalry. They called for help, and Athenian volunteers came forward, and Masistius was killed in the fighting that followed. After the Persian camp fell, Herodotus says Theban horse cut down some Megarians and Phliasians in the plain.
n_megarians.s5: The Greeks dedicated a bronze serpent column at Delphi from the spoils of Plataea, inscribed with the names of the cities that fought. Its coils survive in Istanbul, where it was later taken, and the Megarians are among the names cut on them. This is the Greek record of their share in the war, not a Persian one.
n_mysians.lead: The Mysians lived in north-west Anatolia, around the Mysian Olympus, and became subjects of the Persian king after the conquest of Lydia. Herodotus names them in Xerxes' army in 480 BCE, serving beside the Lydians under one commander. Almost everything known about them comes from Greek writers.
n_mysians.play: The game names the Mysians only in the Chronicle, the decrees and the field briefings. They have no mechanic of their own beyond what those texts show.
n_mysians.s0: Herodotus places the Mysians in the second tribute district of Darius's empire, together with the Lydians and some smaller Anatolian peoples. He gives the district's yearly payment as 500 talents of silver. The list is Herodotus's own account of the tribute system.
n_mysians.s1: Herodotus says the Mysians and Lydians shared in the sanctuary of Carian Zeus at Mylasa, because they were regarded as kinsmen of the Carians. The claim is a Greek one, and it hints at a common sense of kinship among western Anatolian peoples.
n_mysians.s2: Herodotus describes the Mysians in Xerxes' army with local helmets, small shields and javelins hardened in fire. He calls them Lydian colonists, known as Olympieni from the mountain. The Lydians and Mysians marched under Artaphernes, whom Herodotus calls the son of the Artaphernes who invaded at Marathon with Datis.
n_mysians.s3: Herodotus names Artaphernes as the commander who sailed to Marathon with Datis, and as the satrap of Sardis's family. The commander of the Lydians and Mysians in 480 BCE was a younger man of the same name, the son of that Marathon commander. The two should not be taken as one person.
n_mysians.s4: Herodotus tells how a huge boar ravaged Mysian Olympus, and how Croesus sent his son Atys to hunt it. Atys was killed by the Phrygian exile Adrastus, whom Croesus had purified and set to guard him, in fulfilment of a dream. The tale is a moral story about fate and is not evidence for Mysian history.
n_naucratis_greeks.lead: Naucratis was a trading town on the Canopic branch of the Nile where merchants from many Greek cities lived beside Egyptians. Through it passed Greek silver, wine and oil, and Egyptian grain, linen and natron. When Cambyses conquered Egypt in 525 BCE, the town and its traders came under Persian rule and kept working.
n_naucratis_greeks.play: In the Memphis level the Greeks of Naucratis appear as a trade partner. Naucratis itself lay downstream from Memphis in the western Delta, so the game links them to Memphis by trade, not by place.
n_naucratis_greeks.s0: Flinders Petrie identified the site near modern Kom Gieif in 1884 and dug there, and Ernest Gardner continued the work in 1885-86. They found Greek pottery from about the 620s BCE onwards, sanctuaries of Apollo, Aphrodite and the Dioscuri, and a workshop making faience scarabs. D. G. Hogarth later located the Hellenion and the sanctuary of Hera. Hundreds of pots carry painted or scratched dedications in Greek.
n_naucratis_greeks.s1: Herodotus says the pharaoh Amasis gave Naucratis to the Greeks as a place to live and trade. He lists nine East Greek cities that shared the Hellenion, among them Chios, Rhodes, Phocaea and Halicarnassus, while Aegina, Samos and Miletus kept temples of their own. He adds that Naucratis was once the only port open to Greek ships in Egypt.
n_naucratis_greeks.s2: The pottery shows Greeks at Naucratis well before Amasis began to reign in 570 BCE, probably under Psamtik I. Most historians think Amasis reorganised and limited a settlement that already existed. They still argue about how far the pharaohs controlled its trade and how much was left to the Greek cities.
n_naucratis_greeks.s3: An Aramaic papyrus found at Elephantine, later reused for another text, records customs taken in about 475 BCE on ships entering Egypt. Ionian ships paid dues in gold and silver and a share of their cargoes, such as oil and wine. This shows Greek trade continuing under Persian officials. The surviving text does not name the port, and scholars differ on whether it was Naucratis or another Delta harbour.
n_naucratis_greeks.s4: Herodotus tells of Rhodopis, a Thracian courtesan once owned by Iadmon of Samos, who was freed by Charaxus, brother of the poet Sappho, and lived at Naucratis. Strabo, writing about five centuries after her time, adds that an eagle snatched her sandal and dropped it in the lap of a king at Memphis, who then sought her out and married her. The tale is a romance, not history.
n_naucratis_greeks.s5: The Greeks of Naucratis carry a Greek transport amphora, for the trading port in the Delta that Amasis granted them. The town struck no coins of its own then; the jar stands for the trade that Herodotus describes.
n_parthians.lead: The Parthians were the people of Parthia (Old Persian Parthava), a land south-east of the Caspian Sea. When it came under Persian rule is not recorded, but it was among Darius's subject lands. In 522-521 BCE Parthia joined the rebel Fravartish of Media, and Darius's father Hystaspes fought for the King there.
n_parthians.play: The game names the Parthians in the Chronicle, the decrees and the field briefings only, and they have no mechanic of their own beyond what these texts show. Behistun does list Parthia among the rebel lands.
n_parthians.s0: Darius's inscriptions list Parthia among the lands held by the King. Parthava appears in the lists at Behistun (DB) and Naqsh-e Rostam (DNa), among the eastern countries. The lists give no detail on how it was governed.
n_parthians.s1: Behistun says that Parthia and Hyrcania went over to Fravartish, who claimed to be Khshathrita of the royal house of Media. Darius's father Vishtaspa (Hystaspes) was in Parthia. He fought the rebels at Vishpauzatish and again at Patigrabana, and Parthia returned to Darius.
n_parthians.s2: Behistun gives Hystaspes no title, and does not say why he was in Parthia. Herodotus calls him governor of Persia, which does not fit that account. Historians therefore doubt whether he held a command as satrap or was there for another reason, and the sources do not settle the point.
n_parthians.s3: Herodotus lists Parthians in the army that crossed into Greece in 480 BCE, serving with the Chorasmians, Sogdians, Gandarians and Dadicae under Artabazus, son of Pharnaces. His army figures are not reliable, but the list shows that eastern peoples were thought to have sent levies.
n_parthians.s4: Herodotus puts the Parthians, Chorasmians, Sogdians and Arians in a single tribute district, the sixteenth, paying 300 talents of silver. Historians disagree on how far his list matches Darius's real arrangements, and treat it as a useful guide rather than an exact record.
n_parthians.s5: The Parthian kingdom of the Arsacids arose in the 3rd century BCE, long after Darius, and was a different state from the Persian satrapy. The Achaemenid Parthians should not be confused with it.
n_persians.lead: The Persians were an Iranian-speaking people of Persis, the highland in the south-west of the Iranian plateau that they called Parsa and that is now the province of Fars. Under Cyrus and his successors they rose from a local kingdom centred on Anshan to rule lands from the Aegean to the Indus. Darius and Xerxes called themselves Persians in their inscriptions and placed Persia first among their lands.
n_persians.play: The game presents the Persians as the King's own people of Persis, or Parsa, which agrees with the royal inscriptions. In history they shared that homeland with Elamites and with workers drawn from many subject peoples.
n_persians.s0: Iranian-speaking groups had probably settled in the highlands of Fars by the early first millennium, among an older Elamite population around Anshan. Many historians argue that Persian identity grew from this long mixing, which would explain why Persis kept Elamite as its written language of administration. Cyrus's cylinder calls his forefathers kings of Anshan descended from Teispes and never names Achaemenes, so whether Cyrus and Darius were of one house is also argued.
n_persians.s1: At Behistun Darius traced his line through Hystaspes back to Achaemenes and said this was why his house was called Achaemenid. He placed Persia first in his list of the lands he ruled. On his tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam he called himself a Persian, son of a Persian, an Aryan of Aryan stock, and said that the spear of a Persian man had gone far from home.
n_persians.s2: Herodotus says the Persians were divided into tribes, the noblest being the Pasargadae, whose clan of the Achaemenids gave the kings, while other tribes were farmers or herders. He says boys were taught three things from five to twenty: to ride, to shoot the bow and to tell the truth. He adds that they sacrificed on high places without statues or temples, always with a magus present.
n_persians.s3: Thousands of clay tablets from Persepolis, most of them in Elamite and dated to about 509-493 BCE, record how Persis was run. They list rations of grain, wine and beer for officials, travellers and workers, many of them foreign labourers called kurtash. They also record offerings to Auramazda, to Elamite gods such as Humban and to mountains and rivers, which shows a mixed religious life in the homeland.
n_persians.s4: Herodotus says that Persis alone among the King's lands paid no tribute. The Fortification tablets, however, show produce being collected into royal stores and labour being organised across Persis. Historians debate whether Herodotus meant only the silver tribute assessed on the satrapies, while Persians still owed goods and service, or whether he gave an idealised picture of the King's own people.
n_persians.s5: No cloth flag of the Persians survives or is described. Xenophon says the King's standard was a golden eagle with spread wings on a lance, and the game's emblem follows him, with the stepped merlons of Persepolis on the hem. Greek writers saw the eagle in the 4th century, so it may not show what Darius's army carried a century earlier.
n_phocians.lead: The Phocians lived in central Greece between Boeotia and Thessaly, round Mount Parnassus and Delphi. In 480 BCE a thousand of them guarded the mountain path above Thermopylae and gave way to the Immortals. Their land was then burned by the King's army, and in 479 BCE a thousand served Mardonius unwillingly.
n_phocians.play: The Phocians hold the Anopaea path in the Thermopylae level and its field battle, a Phocian band raids the road to Athens in Act II, and Phocians stand in Mardonius's line at Plataea.
n_phocians.s0: Herodotus says the Phocians long before had built a wall across the pass at Thermopylae against the Thessalians and let the hot springs flood the road. The Greeks of 480 BCE rebuilt it. The Phocians were bitter enemies of the Thessalians, which is why they stood with the Greeks.
n_phocians.s1: A thousand Phocians guarded the Anopaea path. At dawn they heard the Immortals in the fallen oak leaves and armed, but under the Persian arrows they fell back to the peak, ready to die; the Persians passed them by and went down behind the Greeks.
n_phocians.s2: After the pass, Herodotus says, the King's army, guided by the Thessalians, overran Phocis and burned its towns and temples, among them the sanctuary of Apollo at Abae. Many Phocians had fled to the heights of Parnassus or to Amphissa.
n_phocians.s3: In 479 BCE a thousand Phocian hoplites under Harmocydes joined Mardonius, not by their own will. Herodotus says Mardonius had his horse ride at them as if to destroy them, and they closed ranks and stood, and he praised them. Other Phocians on Parnassus raided his army.
n_phoenicians.lead: The Phoenicians lived in the coastal city-states of the Levant, chief among them Sidon, Tyre, Byblos and Arwad. Under Persian rule they kept their own kings and supplied the core of the King's navy, from Cambyses' invasion of Egypt in 525 BCE to Xerxes' war on Greece in 480 BCE. Herodotus counts their ships the best in the Persian fleet.
n_phoenicians.play: The game makes the Phoenicians a trade partner and gives them marines, the King's best ships and the Phoenician Shipyard. Herodotus says each ship carried its own native fighters alongside thirty Persians, Medes or Saka.
n_phoenicians.s0: Herodotus says the Phoenicians gave themselves to the Persians of their own accord, probably soon after Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BCE. Their cities kept their own kings and paid tribute. Herodotus puts them in the fifth tax district with Palestinian Syria and Cyprus, assessed at 350 talents of silver. When Cambyses planned to attack Carthage, they refused to sail against their own colony, and he let it drop because his fleet depended on them.
n_phoenicians.s1: Phoenician ships formed the core of Cambyses' fleet against Egypt in 525 BCE. In 494 BCE they led the fleet that broke the Ionian rebels off Lade, where Herodotus calls them the keenest of the King's crews. At Salamis in 480 BCE they suffered heavily, and when some Phoenician captains blamed the Ionians, Xerxes had them beheaded, Herodotus says. In 479 BCE the Persians sent the Phoenician squadron away before the battle at Mycale.
n_phoenicians.s2: At the Athos canal, Herodotus says, the Phoenicians alone cut their stretch wider at the top so the sides did not collapse. They made the flax cables for one Hellespont bridge, and the Egyptians made the papyrus ones. With the Syrians of Palestine they sent 300 triremes in 480 BCE, and the Sidonians won a ship race held for Xerxes at Abydos. Their crews wore helmets close to the Greek style and linen corslets, and carried rimless shields and javelins.
n_phoenicians.s3: The stone coffin of Eshmunazar II, king of Sidon, carries a Phoenician inscription saying that the Lord of Kings gave Sidon the coastal towns of Dor and Joppa in return for its services. Most scholars take the Lord of Kings to be the Persian King. The date is argued: many now place it in the decades after 479 BCE, while others have proposed an earlier date. Either way it shows a Phoenician king presenting Persian favour as a gift to his city.
n_phoenicians.s4: Herodotus opens his work with a story he credits to learned Persians. In it, Phoenician traders at Argos carried off the king's daughter Io, starting a chain of abductions that ended at Troy and, in their telling, the hostility between Asia and Greece. He adds that the Phoenicians tell it differently, saying Io went with them willingly. It is a tale set in mythical times, not history.
n_phoenicians.s5: The game gives Phoenicia a crescent over a disc, a sign on Phoenician stelae and seals of the 8th to 5th centuries, in Tyrian purple. The galley of Sidon's coins and the coins of Tyre are not used: they begin after about 450 BCE. Herodotus says Phoenician ships carried small figures of gods, the pataikoi, on their prows.
n_plataeans.lead: Plataea was a small Boeotian city on the northern slopes of Mount Cithaeron, at odds with its larger neighbour Thebes and allied to Athens. Its citizens were the only Greeks who stood with the Athenians at Marathon in 490 BCE, and in 479 BCE the decisive land battle against Mardonius was fought on their territory. No Persian document names them, so their story comes almost entirely from Greek writers.
n_plataeans.play: The game presents Plataea as the only city that fought beside Athens at Marathon and as the battlefield of 479 BCE. Both claims agree with Herodotus, who says the Spartans arrived only after the battle of Marathon was over.
n_plataeans.s0: Herodotus says the Plataeans, pressed by Thebes, first offered themselves to the Spartan king Cleomenes. He sent them to Athens instead, hoping to set Athens and Thebes against each other. When the Persians landed at Marathon in 490 BCE, the Plataeans marched out in full force and took the left wing of the Athenian line. Herodotus adds that the Athenians afterwards included Plataea in the prayers at their great festivals.
n_plataeans.s1: Thucydides dates the alliance with Athens to 519 BCE. Some historians prefer about 509 BCE, a time when Cleomenes is better attested in central Greece. Herodotus gives no figure for the Plataeans at Marathon. The much later writers Cornelius Nepos and Justin say they sent 1,000 men, a number modern accounts often repeat but cannot confirm.
n_plataeans.s2: Herodotus says that in 480 BCE Plataeans helped row Athenian ships at Artemisium, then went home to move their families and goods instead of sailing on to Salamis. Xerxes' army, on Theban advice, burned their city. In 479 BCE they sent 600 hoplites to the Greek army that defeated Mardonius on their own land. Thucydides says the Spartan regent Pausanias then swore to respect their independence.
n_plataeans.s3: The bronze Serpent Column, dedicated at Delphi from the spoils of 479 BCE, lists the cities that fought the Persians, and the Plataeans are among them. The column survives today, damaged, in the Hippodrome of Istanbul, where it was taken in the time of Constantine. No Persian text mentions Plataea; the King's inscriptions name lands and peoples, not small Greek cities.
n_plataeans.s4: Plutarch, writing some six centuries later, tells that an oracle promised Aristides and the Athenians victory if they fought on their own soil, in the plain of Demeter and Kore. The Plataeans, he says, solved the problem by removing their boundary stones and giving the battlefield to Athens. The story reads as a tribute to the friendship of the two cities rather than as reliable history.
n_plataeans.s5: Plataea had no coin of its own in 490 BCE, and in the game the Plataeans share the Athenians' owl, since they fought beside them at Marathon. Herodotus says the Athenians prayed for the Plataeans at their festivals ever after.
n_saka.lead: The Saka were horse-riding, mostly pastoral peoples of the steppes and mountains north and east of Bactria. They spoke Iranian languages related to Persian. Darius's inscriptions list several Saka groups among his lands, and Herodotus records Saka fighting for the King at Marathon and judges their horsemen the best on the Persian side at Plataea.
n_saka.play: The game presents the Saka as archers in the King's army, which matches Herodotus's account of Saka bowmen. History also remembers them as horsemen, and Herodotus judged them the best on the Persian side at Plataea.
n_saka.s0: The Behistun inscription names the Saka among the lands that came to Darius in 522 BCE. Later lists, such as the one on his tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam, divide them into three groups: the haoma-drinking Saka, the Saka with pointed caps and the Saka beyond the sea. On the tomb façades and at Persepolis, Saka figures wear tall pointed caps, belted coats and trousers. They are shown holding up the King's throne or bringing gifts.
n_saka.s1: A fifth column was added to the Behistun inscription. In its damaged text Darius says he marched against the Saka, most likely those with pointed caps, defeated them and captured their chief Skunkha, and that he put another man in his place. The campaign probably took place in about 519 BCE. A figure of Skunkha in a tall pointed cap was carved at the end of the line of captive rebels, fitted in after the relief was first finished.
n_saka.s2: Herodotus describes the Saka in Xerxes' army of 480 BCE. They wore tall pointed caps and trousers and carried bows, daggers and axes, and they served with the Bactrians under Hystaspes, a son of Darius. Saka also served as marines on the fleet. Herodotus says the Persians and Saka broke the Athenian centre at Marathon in 490 BCE, and at Plataea in 479 BCE he judges the Saka the best horsemen on the Persian side.
n_saka.s3: Herodotus says the Persians called all Scythians Saka, so the Greek and Persian names do not line up neatly. Historians still argue over where each Saka group lived: the haoma-drinkers are often placed in the Pamir and Ferghana region and the pointed-cap Saka near the Aral Sea or the Tian Shan. The Saka beyond the sea are placed either north of the Black Sea or across the Caspian. How firmly the King controlled these steppe peoples is also debated.
n_saka.s4: Polyaenus, writing in the 2nd century CE, tells of a Saka herdsman who maimed himself and came to Darius as a deserter. He then led the Persian army into a waterless desert, and the King was saved only by rain. The tale echoes Herodotus's story of Zopyrus at Babylon, and no Persian text confirms it. The story of Cyrus dying against Queen Tomyris concerns the Massagetae, a people later writers sometimes counted among the Saka.
n_samians.lead: The Samians were the Ionian Greeks of Samos, an island off the coast of Asia Minor. Samos came under Persian rule under Darius. Herodotus mentions the Samians at two turning points, Lade in 494 BCE and Mycale in 479 BCE, and says a Samian choice mattered at both.
n_samians.play: The game names the Samians in the Chronicle, the decrees and the field briefings, for Lade and Mycale. They have no mechanic of their own beyond what those texts show.
n_samians.s0: Herodotus says the tyrant Polycrates of Samos built a large fleet and was lured to the mainland and killed by the Persian governor Oroetes. Later, he says, Syloson, Polycrates' brother, asked Darius for Samos. Otanes conquered the island and installed Syloson as ruler.
n_samians.s1: Herodotus says 353 Ionian triremes met a Persian fleet of 600 ships off Lade. The Samian commanders had agreed with the Persians to leave the line. When the fighting began, he says, 49 Samian ships sailed away, and 11 stayed and fought. The Lesbians then followed the Samians and the Ionian fleet broke.
n_samians.s2: Herodotus blames the Samian withdrawal for the defeat, though he also says the Ionians were short of discipline. Historians doubt that a single defection decided the battle, and his ship numbers cannot be checked. He says the Samians who stayed were honoured at home, and that Samian sanctuaries were spared by the Persians.
n_samians.s3: Herodotus says Theomestor, a Samian who had served the King at Salamis, was made tyrant of Samos as a reward. Later, he says, Samian exiles came to the Greek fleet at Delos and urged Leotychides to sail east. The Greeks went to Samos, and the Persian fleet withdrew to the mainland.
n_samians.s4: Herodotus says the Persians beached their ships and built a stockade. Mistrusting the Samians, they took away their arms and sent the Milesians to guard the paths. When the Greeks under Leotychides and Xanthippus attacked, he says, the Samians and other Ionians turned on the Persians, and the ships were burned.
n_samians.s5: Herodotus says word of the Greek victory at Plataea ran through the army at Mycale before the fighting and lifted the men's spirits. He gives the two battles as on the same day. Historians doubt that news could have crossed the distance so fast, and read the story as shaped to link the victories.
n_scythians.lead: The Scythians were horse-riding, largely nomadic peoples of the steppes north of the Black Sea, speaking Iranian languages related to Persian. In about 513 BCE Darius led an army across the Bosporus and the Ister into their land. They retreated before him rather than fight, and the campaign became one of Herodotus's great stories of a king outmanoeuvred.
n_scythians.play: The game makes the Scythians a trade partner and the enemy of the Ister level. In fact their trade ran mainly through Greek colonies such as Istros and Olbia, and Herodotus says they avoided pitched battle with Darius.
n_scythians.s0: Excavated burial mounds, or kurgans, across the steppe from the Kuban to the Dnieper hold horses, weapons and gold worked in an animal style from the 7th century onward. Early graves such as Kelermes in the Kuban show contact with the Near East, where Assyrian texts name a northern people called the Ishkuza. The richest royal mounds, such as Chertomlyk and Solokha, are later than Darius and date to the 4th century.
n_scythians.s1: Herodotus says Darius crossed the Bosporus on a bridge of boats built by Mandrocles of Samos, then the Ister on a second bridge guarded by the Ionian tyrants. He gives the army as 700,000 men and 600 ships, figures historians think greatly exaggerated. The Scythians refused battle, stopped up wells and springs and spoiled the grazing. Herodotus says Darius finally slipped away at night, leaving his sick men and donkeys in camp to deceive the enemy.
n_scythians.s2: Herodotus tells that the Scythian king Idanthyrsus answered Darius's challenge by saying his people had no towns or fields to defend, only their fathers' tombs. Later the Scythians sent a bird, a mouse, a frog and five arrows. Darius read them as surrender, but Gobryas said they meant death by arrows unless the Persians could fly, burrow or swim away. The story is shaped as a lesson about royal pride and is best read as a tale.
n_scythians.s3: Modern estimates for the date run from about 519 to 512 BCE, and the route is uncertain. Strabo places the army's crisis of thirst in the desert of the Getae near the Ister, which some take to mean the march went less far than Herodotus says. Herodotus presents a near disaster, but many historians, Briant among them, see a limited war whose real result was Persian control of Thrace and the straits, which Megabazus secured after the King returned to Asia.
n_scythians.s4: In Old Persian inscriptions Saka is the name for several steppe peoples. Darius's tomb inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam lists among the lands of his empire the Saka who are beyond the sea, and a labelled figure of them stands among the throne-bearers carved on the tomb. Many historians identify them with the European Scythians or their neighbours, though how far Darius ruled them, if at all, is debated.
n_scythians.s5: The Scythians carry a curled stag, the beast of Scythian animal-style gold, after the stag plaque from the Kostromskaya burial mound of the 7th-6th century. It is an emblem after their art; Herodotus describes no Scythian banner.
n_spartans.lead: The Spartans were the citizens of Sparta in Laconia, the strongest land power in Greece in the sixth century. A small body of full citizens, the Spartiates, lived off land worked by helots and led a league of Peloponnesian allies. They refused Darius earth and water, and their soldiers fought Xerxes' army at Thermopylae in 480 BCE and led the Greek victory at Plataea in 479 BCE.
n_spartans.play: The game lists Sparta as a trade partner, but no trade between Sparta and the Persian court is recorded, so this is a simplification. Spartan soldiers appear at Thermopylae and Plataea, as they fought there.
n_spartans.s0: The British School at Athens excavated the sanctuary of Artemis Orthia between 1906 and 1910. It recovered thousands of small lead figurines, along with ivories and clay masks. Laconian painted pottery of the sixth century has been found at Samos, at Cyrene and in Etruria. These finds show a city that made and exported fine goods, which complicates the later picture of Sparta as closed and austere.
n_spartans.s1: Herodotus says Croesus of Lydia made an alliance with Sparta. After Sardis fell, the Spartans sent a herald to warn Cyrus away from the Greek cities of Asia. Cyrus is said to have replied that he did not fear men who met in a marketplace to cheat one another. Later, King Cleomenes refused Aristagoras's plea for help in the Ionian revolt, and when Darius's heralds asked for earth and water, the Spartans threw them into a well.
n_spartans.s2: Herodotus says the Spartans agreed to help Athens in 490 BCE but would not march before the full moon. By his account, 2,000 of them reached Attica only after the battle and went to Marathon to view the Persian dead. Plato says instead that a war with the Messenians held them back. Historians still argue over whether the delay came from a religious rule, a helot revolt, or reluctance to fight so far from home.
n_spartans.s3: Herodotus says King Leonidas held the pass at Thermopylae in 480 BCE with 300 Spartiates and several thousand allies, until a mountain path let the Persians surround them. In 479 BCE the regent Pausanias led the Greek army at Plataea. Herodotus counts 5,000 Spartiates there with seven helots each, figures that may be inflated. The Spartans and Tegeans defeated the Persian troops around Mardonius, and Mardonius was killed.
n_spartans.s4: Much of the familiar picture of Sparta comes from writers working centuries later. Plutarch, writing around 100 CE, preserves sayings such as Leonidas daring Xerxes to come and take the Spartans' weapons. He credits the whole Spartan system to a lawgiver, Lycurgus, whose date and very existence are uncertain. Modern scholars call this idealised image the Spartan mirage.
n_spartans.s5: The Spartans carry a Corinthian helmet with a horsehair crest in Spartan red, the colour Xenophon says they wore to war. The lambda on Spartan shields is attested only later and is not used. Sparta struck no coins in this period.
n_tegeans.lead: The Tegeans were the people of Tegea, a city in Arcadia in the central Peloponnese. Long a rival of Sparta, Tegea came under Spartan leadership, and its hoplites stood beside the Spartans in the Greek line at Plataea. Herodotus gives them the first entry into Mardonius's camp and the plunder of his bronze manger.
n_tegeans.play: The game names the Tegeans in the Chronicle, the decrees and the field briefings, as Greeks at Plataea under Pausanias and the first into Mardonius's fort. They have no mechanic of their own beyond what these texts show.
n_tegeans.s0: Tegea lay in Arcadia, north of Sparta. Herodotus says the Spartans fought the Tegeans for a long time without success, until they recovered the bones of Orestes, after which they mastered Tegea in war. Tegea then served as a Spartan ally in the Peloponnesian forces.
n_tegeans.s1: Herodotus lists 500 Tegeans among the Greeks who held Thermopylae in 480 BCE. For Plataea in 479 BCE he gives them 1,500 hoplites, stationed beside the Spartans. Pausanias, regent for Leonidas's young son Pleistarchus, commanded the whole army.
n_tegeans.s2: Herodotus says the Tegeans and Athenians argued before the battle over who should hold the second wing, opposite the Spartans' own place. Each side cited past deeds, and the Spartan side decided for the Athenians on the left, leaving the Tegeans next to the Spartans. The speeches are probably Herodotus's own composition and reflect the later pride of both cities, so the exact words cannot be trusted.
n_tegeans.s3: Herodotus says the Spartans and Tegeans bore the main Persian attack at the shield barrier. When the sacrifices were unfavourable and Pausanias held back, the Tegeans advanced first and the Spartans followed. After the Spartan Arimnestus killed Mardonius, the Persians broke and fled to their timber-walled camp. Herodotus says the Tegeans were first over the wall and plundered Mardonius's tent.
n_tegeans.s4: Herodotus says the Tegeans took a bronze manger from Mardonius's quarters and dedicated it in the temple of Athena Alea at Tegea. He describes it as a piece worth seeing. Whether it survived is unknown, and no excavated trace of it has been identified.
n_tegeans.s5: In the pre-battle argument, Herodotus has the Tegeans recall a single combat in which their king Echemus killed Hyllus, a son of Heracles. This belongs to the Greek heroic past. It served as a claim to honour in the fifth century and is not evidence for events in the Persian wars.
n_thasians.lead: The Thasians were Greek settlers from Paros who held the island of Thasos and a strip of the Thracian coast opposite. Gold from the island and from mainland mines made them rich enough to build warships and walls. After 492 BCE they were subjects of the Persian King, and in 480 BCE they fed Xerxes' army on its march into Greece.
n_thasians.play: The game shows Thasos as a trade partner valued for its gold mines. The mines are historical, but from 492 BCE Thasos was a subject city obeying Persian orders, not an equal partner, and the game simplifies this.
n_thasians.s0: Thucydides calls Thasos a colony of the Parians. The settlement probably dates to the first half of the 7th century. The poet Archilochus of Paros, who took part in it, wrote verses about the colony and its wars with the Thracians. Over time the colonists took control of coastal towns and trading posts on the mainland facing the island.
n_thasians.s1: Herodotus says he saw the Thasian mines himself and that the most remarkable of them were opened by Phoenicians. He reports that the city's income from the island and from mainland mines such as Scapte Hyle was usually 200 talents a year and at most 300. These are his figures. Excavations on Thasos have found traces of ancient mining and a well-built city with rich public buildings.
n_thasians.s2: Herodotus says Histiaeus of Miletus besieged Thasos after the Ionian revolt. He left when he heard that the Phoenician fleet was sailing from Miletus against the rest of Ionia. The Thasians then spent their wealth on warships and stronger walls. In 492 BCE they submitted to Mardonius without a fight. In 491 BCE their neighbours accused them of planning revolt, and Darius ordered them to pull down their walls and send their ships to Abdera. They obeyed.
n_thasians.s3: When Xerxes marched through Thrace in 480 BCE, the Thasians hosted the army on behalf of their mainland towns. Herodotus says the citizen Antipater, son of Orgeus, spent 400 talents of silver on this single meal. After 479 BCE Thasos joined the Athenian alliance. It revolted in 465 BCE over its mainland trading posts and mine, and surrendered after a siege of more than two years.
n_thasians.s4: Greek tradition held that Phoenicians searching for Europa first settled the island under a leader named Thasos, who gave it his name. Herodotus repeats this and links it to a temple of Heracles that he visited on the island.
