Excavations have not confirmed a Phoenician settlement, and many historians treat the story as a founding legend.
n_thasians.s5: Thasos's emblem in the game is a grape cluster, for the island's famous wine. The island's own coins of this period show a satyr carrying off a nymph; the grapes are the game's choice for the trade it is known by.
n_thebans.lead: Thebes was the leading city of Boeotia in central Greece. In 480 BCE it gave earth and water to Xerxes. In 479 BCE it became the chief Greek ally of Mardonius, whose army camped on Theban land and fought beside Theban hoplites and horsemen at Plataea. Its choice made Thebes a byword for medism among the victorious Greeks.
n_thebans.play: The game lists Thebes as a trade partner and fields Theban hoplites for Mardonius at Plataea, as Herodotus records. The trade role simplifies history: in 479 BCE Thebes was an ally that housed and supplied the Persian army.
n_thebans.s0: Thebes lay on the Boeotian plain north of Mount Cithaeron and led a league of Boeotian towns. Herodotus says that Plataea, under pressure from Thebes, put itself under Athenian protection, an alliance Thucydides dates to about 519 BCE. From then on Thebes and Plataea were bitter neighbours. Thebes was often at odds with Athens too, as in the failed Boeotian attack on Attica about 506 BCE.
n_thebans.s1: Herodotus lists the Thebans among the Greeks who gave earth and water to Xerxes' heralds. Yet 400 Thebans under Leontiades stood with Leonidas at Thermopylae. Herodotus says Leonidas kept them as hostages, and that at the end they surrendered to the Persians, who branded them. Plutarch, a Boeotian writing more than five centuries later, called this a slander on his people, and historians still debate where Theban loyalties lay in 480 BCE.
n_thebans.s2: Herodotus says the Thebans urged Mardonius to stay in Boeotia and win over the Greek cities with bribes rather than battle. His fortified camp lay on Theban land by the Asopus. The Theban Timagenidas advised him to watch the passes of Cithaeron and cut off the Greek supply trains. In the battle the Theban hoplites fought the Athenians hard, and Herodotus says 300 of their foremost men fell.
n_thebans.s3: Herodotus says that eleven days after the battle the Greeks besieged Thebes and demanded the leaders of the Persian party, among them Timagenidas and Attaginus. Attaginus escaped, but the others were handed over, and Pausanias had them put to death at Corinth. In 427 BCE Theban speakers in Thucydides blamed the Persian alliance on a narrow ruling clique, not the whole city. Modern scholars weigh this excuse against Herodotus, who presents the Thebans as eager allies of Persia.
n_thebans.s4: Greek tradition held that Thebes was founded by Cadmus, a Phoenician prince searching for his sister Europa. Herodotus says the Phoenicians who came with Cadmus brought letters to Greece, and that he saw old Cadmean writing on tripods in the temple of Ismenian Apollo at Thebes. These are origin stories, not a record of how the city began.
n_thebans.s5: Thebes carries the Boeotian shield, an oval with a cut-out on each side, with a theta on it, as on the city's coins. The shield was the sign of the Boeotian cities. In the game's Greek colours it is drawn in madder red on natural wool.
n_thespians.lead: The Thespians were the people of Thespiae, a small city in Boeotia. Herodotus says they sent seven hundred men to Thermopylae and that these stayed to die with Leonidas and the Spartans. Unlike most Boeotians they did not give earth and water to Xerxes, and Herodotus reports that their city was later burned.
n_thespians.play: The game names the Thespians in the Chronicle, the decrees and the field briefings as part of Leonidas's last stand. They have no mechanic of their own beyond what those texts show. The game's figure of some seven thousand Greeks is higher than Herodotus's own totals.
n_thespians.s0: Herodotus says the Thespians and the Plataeans were the only Boeotians who did not give earth and water to Xerxes. Most of Boeotia, Thebes above all, took the Persian side. Thespiae was a small city, so refusing probably carried real risk.
n_thespians.s1: Herodotus lists the Greek contingents at Thermopylae and gives the Thespians seven hundred men. He names their commander as Demophilus. His own totals for the army are lower than seven thousand. The larger figure of about seven thousand is given by Diodorus, a much later writer.
n_thespians.s2: Herodotus says that when Leonidas dismissed the allies, the Thespians refused to leave him and stayed of their own will. They died with the Spartans on the last day. Herodotus names a Thespian, Dithyrambus son of Harmatidas, as the bravest of them. Leonidas also kept some Thebans, whom Herodotus calls hostages, and they surrendered to the Persians when the end came.
n_thespians.s3: Herodotus gives two reasons for the allies' departure. One is that Leonidas sent them away to save them. The other is that they left in fear and he let them go. Historians still argue over which is right, and over how large the force was. No Persian text mentions the Thespians at all.
n_thespians.s4: Herodotus says the Thespians left for the Peloponnese and that Thespiae was burned as the Persians marched through Boeotia. In 479 BCE he reports that the Thespians fielded about eighteen hundred men at Plataea who had no proper arms.
n_thessalians.lead: The Thessalians held the broad plain of northern Greece, a land of large estates and the best horses in the Greek world, led by noble clans such as the Aleuadae of Larissa. In 480 BCE Thessaly went over to Xerxes. Its submission opened the road south for the Persian army, and Thessalian horsemen later fought for Mardonius at Plataea.
n_thessalians.play: The game lists the Thessalians as a trade partner, which is a game device. Its note that they joined the King in 480 BCE is broadly right, though the Aleuadae had invited Xerxes earlier and most of Thessaly yielded only after Tempe.
n_thessalians.s0: Herodotus calls the Aleuadae of Larissa kings of Thessaly, and he says they sent envoys urging Xerxes to invade Greece. Power in the plain probably lay with a few landowning clans more than with any citizen assembly. Herodotus also tells how Xerxes, camped in Thessaly, raced his own horses against Thessalian mares, having heard they were the best in Greece, and the Greek horses were left far behind.
n_thessalians.s1: Thessaly had ties to the Pisistratid tyrants of Athens. Herodotus says that when Sparta first moved against Hippias, about 511 BCE, the Thessalians sent a thousand horsemen under Cineas, who routed the Spartan landing force near Phaleron. A second Spartan army under Cleomenes then drove the Thessalian riders off. Some years after Hippias was expelled, the Thessalians offered him Iolcus as a refuge, but he declined it.
n_thessalians.s2: In 480 BCE the Thessalians asked the Greek allies to defend the vale of Tempe, and about ten thousand hoplites under the Spartan Euaenetus and the Athenian Themistocles marched north. Herodotus says they soon withdrew, warned by Alexander of Macedon about the size of the Persian host and learning of another route into Thessaly. Left alone, the Thessalians submitted and served the King with energy.
n_thessalians.s3: Herodotus says the Aleuadae acted on their own and that most Thessalians joined Persia only when the Greeks abandoned them. Historians debate whether this reflects real divisions or a later Thessalian excuse. Thessaly's long feud with the Phocians also shaped events: Herodotus says Thessalians guided the Persians into Phocis and had first demanded fifty talents to spare it.
n_thessalians.s4: Herodotus says the Aleuadae kept urging Mardonius on in 479 BCE, and he names Thorax of Larissa and his brothers among Mardonius's companions at Plataea. Thessalians appear in his list of Greeks drawn up on the Persian side. Afterwards the Spartan king Leotychides led an expedition into Thessaly, which Herodotus says failed when he was caught taking a bribe.
n_thessalians.s5: Thessaly's emblem in the game is a horse, from Thessalian coins of about 480-460 BCE. The plain was famous for horses: Herodotus says Xerxes, having heard that Thessalian horses were the best in Greece, raced his own against them there, and the Thessalian horses were left far behind.
n_thracians.lead: The Thracians were many separate peoples living between the north Aegean coast and the lower Ister (Danube), with no single king in this period. Darius brought much of their country under Persian control from about 513 BCE. For a generation Thrace was the King's road into Europe, a land of fighting men, timber and silver mines, and the country Xerxes' army crossed in 480 BCE.
n_thracians.play: The Thracians of the coast appear as a trade partner, and Thracian peltasts and riders appear at Athos. Herodotus records no Thracian horsemen in Xerxes' army; Thracian cavalry is better attested later, in Thucydides.
n_thracians.s0: Herodotus says the Thracians were the most numerous people after the Indians, and would be the strongest of all if they ever united under one ruler, which he thought would never happen. He says they went by many names in different regions, and he sets apart the Getae and Trausi for their customs. He reports that the rest counted tattooing a mark of noble birth, held farming the meanest of trades and thought living by war and plunder the most honourable.
n_thracians.s1: Herodotus says that when Darius crossed the Bosporus to fight the Scythians, an expedition historians date to about 513 BCE, only the Getae among the Thracians resisted, and they were beaten. His general Megabazus, left in Europe, then subdued Perinthus and the coastal Thracians and deported Paeonians from the Strymon valley to Asia. In 492 BCE the Thracian Brygi attacked Mardonius's camp at night and wounded him, though he went on to subdue them.
n_thracians.s2: Darius's tomb inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam lists Skudra among the lands of his empire, and Xerxes' inscription from Persepolis names it again. Skudra is missing from the earlier list at Behistun. Some Persepolis Fortification tablets record Skudrian workers receiving rations in Persis. The Persian texts do not say where Skudra lay or how it was governed.
n_thracians.s3: Most historians identify Skudra with Thrace, or with the King's lands in Europe generally. They disagree on whether it was a full satrapy with its own governor or a looser zone of garrisons, tribute and alliances. Herodotus describes Persian strongholds at Doriscus and Eion but says little about administration. The inland peoples, such as the Satrae, were probably never truly subject.
n_thracians.s4: Herodotus describes the Thracians of Asia, the Bithynians, in Xerxes' army with fox-skin caps, bright cloaks, fawnskin boots, javelins, light shields and small daggers. He says the Thracians along the route, such as the Edoni, were made to follow, coastal peoples by ship and inland ones on foot, except the hill-dwelling Satrae. In 479 BCE, during the siege of Sestos, Apsinthian Thracians caught the Persian Oeobazus and sacrificed him to their god Pleistorus.
n_thracians.s5: The Thracians' emblem in the game is the crescent pelta, the small light shield of the Thracian foot that Herodotus describes in Xerxes' army. The Thracian tribes had no shared flag; the pelta gave Greek peltasts their name.
o_admiral.lead: The warships of the Persian kings were supplied and crewed mostly by subject peoples: Phoenicians, Egyptians, Cypriots, Cilicians, Ionians and Carians. Command over these contingents went to Persian nobles, often close kin of the King, appointed for a campaign. They led the fleets at Lade in 494 BCE, in the crossings of 490 and 480 BCE and at Artemisium and Salamis, until the Greeks burned the ships beached at Mycale in 479 BCE.
o_admiral.play: The game presents the office through Ariabignes, Achaemenes and the commanders of the sea battles. Historically there was no single standing post: Herodotus names four admirals for 480 BCE and different men in other years.
o_admiral.s0: Herodotus names four admirals of Xerxes' fleet in 480 BCE. Two were sons of Darius, Ariabignes and Achaemenes, and the other two were Prexaspes son of Aspathines and Megabazus son of Megabates. Ariabignes led the Ionian and Carian ships and Achaemenes, who also governed Egypt as satrap, led the Egyptian ships, while the other two shared the rest. All four were high Persian nobles bound to the royal house.
o_admiral.s1: The ships came from the King's subjects, and each contingent sailed under its own kings or city lords, such as the rulers of Sidon and Tyre or Artemisia of Halicarnassus. Herodotus says Persians, Medes and Saka served aboard every ship as fighting men. He insists that the native leaders were not true commanders but took their orders from the Persian admirals.
o_admiral.s2: Persian royal inscriptions say little about war at sea. Darius's stelae beside his canal from the Nile to the Red Sea record that ships sailed from Egypt to Persia by it, as he wished. An Aramaic customs account from Egypt dated to 475 BCE lists Ionian and Phoenician ships taxed at a royal port. Such texts show that the empire controlled and counted ships, but the admirals themselves are known almost only from Greek writers.
o_admiral.s3: Herodotus gives Xerxes 1,207 triremes. Aeschylus, writing eight years after Salamis, gives a similar total. Many historians think the figure was inflated, or reflects the full levy on paper, and suggest a smaller fleet fought at Salamis after the losses to storms. Scholars also argue over whether the King kept a standing royal navy, as Wallinga proposed, or called up the subject cities' ships for each war.
o_admiral.s4: Command was given for each campaign, not held for life. Megabates led the fleet against Naxos in 499 BCE, and Datis and Artaphernes led the crossing of 490 BCE. Herodotus says Ariabignes died in the fighting at Salamis. He also says that in 479 BCE the fleet at Samos under Mardontes, Artaÿntes and Ithamitres was beached at Mycale, where the Greeks stormed the Persian camp and burned the ships.
o_archon.lead: The archons were the chief annual magistrates of Athens, a board of nine men who held office for one year. The senior archon gave his name to the year, so Athenians dated events such as Marathon and the Persian capture of their city by archon. The office's changing powers trace Athens's path from tyranny to democracy in the decades when it fought Persia.
o_archon.play: The game presents the archons as Athens's annual magistrates and uses archon-years to date events. Historically, only the senior or eponymous archon of the nine gave his name to the year.
o_archon.s0: The Constitution of the Athenians, written in Aristotle's school in the 320s, describes a board of nine archons serving one year. The eponymous archon named the year and oversaw family and inheritance cases, the king archon ran ancestral rites, the polemarch had once led in war, and six thesmothetai handled lawsuits. Archons who passed their audit joined the council of the Areopagus for life.
o_archon.s1: A fragment of a list of archons, inscribed about 425 BCE and found in the Athenian Agora, names Hippias, Cleisthenes and Miltiades in turn, which scholars date to 526 BCE/5, 525 BCE/4 and 524 BCE/3. A dedication on the altar of Pythian Apollo, set up by Pisistratus son of Hippias during his archonship, also survives, and Thucydides cites its text. The stones show the tyrant family and leading noble houses holding the office.
o_archon.s2: Under Solon's rules only the wealthier property classes could serve, and the third class was admitted only in 457 BCE/6. Thucydides says the Pisistratid tyrants kept the old laws but made sure one of their own always held office. The Constitution of the Athenians says that in 487 BCE/6 archons were chosen by lot from candidates elected by the demes, the first time since the tyranny. Historians think the office then lost weight to the elected generals.
o_archon.s3: Herodotus says the polemarch at Marathon, Callimachus of Aphidna, had been chosen by lot, cast the deciding vote to fight, and led the right wing. The Constitution of the Athenians dates the lot for archons to 487 BCE/6, after the battle. Historians still argue whether Herodotus projected later practice back, and how far command lay with the polemarch rather than with the ten generals.
o_archon.s4: The Athenian year began in midsummer, so each archon-year straddles two modern years. Herodotus, who rarely uses archon dates, places Xerxes' capture of Athens in the archonship of Calliades (480 BCE/79). The Constitution of the Athenians puts Marathon under Phaenippus (490 BCE/89). Persian scribes counted by the King's regnal years instead, and modern chronology lines up the two systems.
o_courier.lead: The Persian kings governed lands from the Aegean to the Indus and depended on messengers who carried sealed orders and reports along guarded roads. Herodotus admired the speed of the mounted relay, which he says the Persians called angareion. The Persepolis tablets show the plainer side of the system: rations, travel documents and officials on the move.
o_courier.play: The game shows the couriers through the Road Station building, the Royal Road and the angaros system. Historically the stations supplied all travellers carrying sealed authorisations, and the Sardis road was one route among many.
o_courier.s0: Herodotus describes how news of Salamis was sent from Greece to Persia in 480 BCE. Men and horses were stationed along the road a day's journey apart, and each rider handed the message to the next, as Greek torch-runners passed on a torch. He says that neither snow, rain, heat nor darkness stopped them, and that the Persians called this relay angareion. The Greek word angaros, for such a courier, probably came from a Near Eastern or Iranian term.
o_courier.s1: Herodotus describes the road from Sardis to Susa as lined with royal stations and good lodgings, with guarded crossings at rivers and passes. He counts 111 stations and reckons the journey at about ninety days for a traveller covering 150 stades a day. His figures describe ordinary travel, not the speed of royal messages.
o_courier.s2: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, written mostly in Elamite between about 509 and 493 BCE, record rations issued to travellers at stations in Persis and Elam. Many travellers carried a sealed document from the King, a satrap or a senior official authorising their journey and supplies. Among them the tablets name express messengers, called pirradaziš in Elamite.
o_courier.s3: Historians debate how fast royal messages really travelled. Modern estimates for a relay from Sardis to Susa run from about one to two weeks, against Herodotus's ninety days of ordinary travel. The exact course of his Royal Road, through Cappadocia or through Cilicia, is also argued over. Scholars further discuss whether the express couriers formed a separate service or were the fastest users of the general station system.
o_courier.s4: Xenophon credits Cyrus with inventing the relay. In his telling, Cyrus found out how far a horse could go in a day and set up posts at that interval, with men to keep fresh horses ready. The Cyropaedia is an idealised portrait of a model ruler, so this story shows how Greeks imagined Persian order rather than recording who founded the system.
o_estate_director.lead: The Persepolis Fortification tablets show a network that fed workers, travellers, officials and gods across Persis and towards Elam. From about 506 to 497 BCE it was run by Parnaka, with Ziššawiš as his deputy. Their sealed letters show how a Persian king turned stored grain, wine and livestock into labour for building and farming.
o_estate_director.play: The game shows Parnaka and Ziššawiš running rations and workers, which is broadly right. The tablets date their work to about 506-497 BCE, well after the Parsa level of 521 BCE, and they acted through scribes and storekeepers.
o_estate_director.s0: Thousands of clay tablets, mostly in Elamite, were found in the fortification wall at Persepolis in the 1930s. They date from 509 to 493 BCE and record the issue of barley, flour, wine, beer, fruit and animals to work groups, travellers, officials and offerings for the gods. Many issues rested on written orders from the head of the system, and most surviving letter-orders were sent by Parnaka or Ziššawiš.
o_estate_director.s1: Parnaka sent letters ordering storehouse officials to release supplies, and he moved between places in the region with his retinue. The tablets record large daily rations for him and his household, a sign of very high rank. His first seal, PFS 9*, was replaced in 500 BCE by PFS 16*, and letters told officials that the old seal was no longer his.
o_estate_director.s2: Ziššawiš issued orders much like Parnaka's, using his own seal, PFS 83*. He seems to have acted when Parnaka was away or busy, which kept supplies moving across a wide region. The pair worked through a large staff of scribes, storekeepers and accountants who drew up memoranda, journals and yearly accounts.
o_estate_director.s3: The same administration that paid masons and farm hands also supplied offerings for many gods: Persian, Elamite and others. Parnaka's office approved these issues alongside ordinary rations. Royal women such as Irdabama and Irtaštuna had their own estates and workers inside the system, so the King's economy reached well beyond the court.
o_estate_director.s4: The tablets give Parnaka no formal title; director of the economy is a modern label. If his father Aršam is the Arsames named by Darius as his grandfather, Parnaka was Darius's uncle, which most historians accept but cannot prove. Some identify him with the Pharnaces whom Herodotus names as father of Artabazus, the general of 480-479 BCE, but the name was common.
o_general.lead: The Persian kings seem to have kept no fixed staff of generals. For each war they named commanders, usually Persian or Median nobles bound to the king by kinship, marriage or long service. Behistun and Herodotus preserve their names, from the men who crushed the revolts of 521 BCE to Datis, Artaphernes and Mardonius, who led the King's armies against the Greeks.
o_general.play: The game names Datis, Artaphernes, Mardonius and Darius's generals of 521 BCE as the King's commanders, which agrees with Behistun and Herodotus. It treats them as one office, though Persian kings appointed commanders campaign by campaign.
o_general.s0: At Behistun Darius repeatedly says he sent an army under a man he calls his bandaka, a loyal subject, and made him its chief. Hydarnes (Vidarna) marched against the Medes, Intaphernes (Vindafarna) against Arakha at Babylon, and Artavardiya against Vahyazdata. Vivana, satrap of Arachosia, defeated the army Vahyazdata sent against him. Dadarshi and Vaumisa fought in Armenia, and Gobryas led the campaign against the Elamite Athamaita.
o_general.s1: A Persepolis Fortification tablet dated to about 494 BCE records rations for a man named Datiya. He was carrying a sealed document of the King on a journey from Sardis towards the court. D. M. Lewis argued that this was probably Datis the Mede, which would show him active in the west on royal business four years before Marathon.
o_general.s2: Herodotus says Darius removed Mardonius from command and gave the expedition of 490 BCE to Datis, a Mede, and Artaphernes, son of the satrap of Sardis and nephew of the King. They took Naxos and Eretria and then landed at Marathon, guided by the exiled Hippias. Herodotus reports 6,400 dead on the Persian side in the defeat that followed.
o_general.s3: Herodotus describes Mardonius, son of Gobryas, as a young man newly married to Darius's daughter Artozostra when he led an army into Thrace and Macedon in 492 BCE; his fleet was wrecked off Athos. Under Xerxes he was one of six generals over the land army. After Salamis he stayed in Greece with picked troops and was killed at Plataea in 479 BCE.
o_general.s4: No Persian text names a standing rank of general; commands seem to have gone to royal kin, satraps and trusted nobles campaign by campaign. Herodotus describes officers over ten thousand, a thousand, a hundred and ten. A Persian title for a commander of a thousand, hazarapatish, is known indirectly from Greek and Aramaic renderings. Historians debate how far his tidy scheme reflects Persian practice.
o_hazarapatish.lead: The hazarapatish, or chiliarch to the Greeks, was the 'commander of the thousand'. The title probably began in the decimal ranks of the Persian army and was later tied to the King's own guard and his audiences. How powerful the post was, and when it became a high court office, is still argued, because most of the evidence comes from Greek writers.
o_hazarapatish.play: The game makes the hazarapatish a battlefield commander unit. The literal meaning is right, but the best-known holders appear in Greek sources as court officers controlling access to the King, not as field generals.
o_hazarapatish.s0: Herodotus describes Xerxes' army of 480 BCE as organised in tens, hundreds, thousands and ten thousands, each with its own officer. In Greek the commander of a thousand was a chiliarch. Modern scholars take this as a rendering of an Old Persian title, reconstructed as hazarapatish, meaning 'master of a thousand'.
o_hazarapatish.s1: Herodotus says that on the march Xerxes was escorted by a thousand picked Persian spearmen and a thousand picked horsemen. He adds that some guard units carried spears ending in golden pomegranates, and that the men nearest the King had golden apples. Many historians think the commander of such an elite thousand became the officer closest to the King's person.
o_hazarapatish.s2: Plutarch tells how Themistocles, arriving at the Persian court around 465 BCE, was received first by the chiliarch Artabanus, who explained that visitors must bow before the King. Cornelius Nepos says the chiliarch Tithraustes told Conon he would have to bow in the same way, so Conon chose to deal with the King by letter. Both writers lived centuries after the events they describe.
o_hazarapatish.s3: Reliefs found in the Treasury at Persepolis show the seated King receiving a dignitary in Median dress, who raises his hand to his mouth in greeting while guards stand behind. The scene shows how a royal audience was staged. Some scholars identify the dignitary as the hazarapatish, but no inscription names him and the identification is debated.
o_hazarapatish.s4: No Old Persian royal inscription names the office, so its powers are reconstructed largely from Greek texts. Diodorus calls Artabanus, who killed Xerxes in 465 BCE, commander of the royal bodyguard. He later says the Persian kings first made the chiliarch's post an honour, and that Alexander gave it to Hephaestion. Some historians see a chief minister; others, including Briant, think Greek writers inflated a guard and protocol post.
o_herald.lead: Heralds were envoys sent to carry a ruler's message and bring back an answer. Greek writers describe Persian kings sending them to cities and peoples to ask for earth and water, a token of submission to the King. Their reception, from willing surrender to murder, shaped the wars between Persia and the Greeks.
o_herald.play: The game shows heralds as the King's envoys asking for earth and water. This follows Herodotus; no Persian inscription or tablet mentions the earth-and-water ritual, so the game's picture rests on Greek accounts.
o_herald.s0: Among the Greeks a herald (keryx) was held to be under divine protection, and harming one was an offence against the gods. Herodotus says that at Sparta the office was hereditary in a family, the Talthybiadae, who traced their line to Talthybius, herald of Agamemnon. Herodotus uses the same word for the men the Persian kings sent out, so the Greek idea of an inviolable envoy colours his stories of Persian heralds.
o_herald.s1: Herodotus treats the gift of earth and water as a sign that a people accepted the King as overlord. Historians still debate its exact sense: some see a plain act of surrender of land and water, others a formal agreement that bound both sides. Herodotus says Athenian envoys at Sardis gave earth and water to Artaphernes about 507 BCE and were blamed for it at home, which suggests the Athenians may not have grasped what it committed them to.
o_herald.s2: Herodotus says Darius sent heralds through Greece, probably in 491 BCE, to ask for earth and water. He reports that many mainland Greeks gave it, as did all the islanders the heralds reached, Aegina among them. In 481 BCE Xerxes sent heralds to every Greek state except Athens and Sparta. Herodotus explains that the Athenians had thrown Darius's heralds into a pit and the Spartans into a well, telling them to fetch earth and water from there.
o_herald.s3: The Persepolis Fortification tablets show how official travellers moved through the empire. Envoys, messengers and their escorts carried sealed authorisations and drew rations of flour, beer or wine at stations along the roads. The tablets record such journeys to and from distant provinces, but they say nothing of earth and water, so the Persian side of the heralds' work is known only in outline.
o_herald.s4: Herodotus tells that after the killing of Darius's heralds the Spartans suffered the anger of Talthybius. Two citizens, Sperthias and Bulis, offered to die at the Persian court in atonement, but Xerxes refused to repeat the crime he blamed on Sparta. Thucydides names Aneristus and Nicolaus among Spartan envoys executed in 430 BCE, men Herodotus calls their sons. The men were probably real, but the divine anger and the King's reply belong to a moral tale.
o_kings_eye.lead: Greek writers describe a Persian official called the King's Eye, a trusted man who watched the provinces and reported to the King. No Persian inscription or tablet yet found names such a post, so the office is known mainly through Greek eyes. It matters because it shows how a vast empire was imagined to keep its governors honest, and how hard it is to separate a real title from a foreign figure of speech.
o_kings_eye.play: The game shows the office as a building, the House of the King's Eye. No such building is known from any site or text; if the post existed, it was a person acting with royal authority, not a fixed house in a city.
o_kings_eye.s0: Herodotus tells how the young Cyrus, raised as a herdsman's son, was chosen king by other boys in a village game. He gave his playmates roles, making some builders and guards and one the King's Eye. The story implies that Herodotus took the Eye to be a known court post. Earlier he also says that the Median king Deioces kept spies and listeners throughout his land.
o_kings_eye.s1: In Aeschylus's Persians, staged in 472 BCE, the chorus asks the defeated Xerxes about a noble it calls his faithful Eye, one of the men lost in the war. In 425 BCE Aristophanes brought a comic Persian official, Pseudartabas, onto the stage in the Acharnians and called him the King's Eye. Athenian audiences clearly knew the phrase, though both poets used it for their own dramatic ends.
o_kings_eye.s2: Xenophon, writing in the 4th century, says the Persian King was thought to have many eyes and many ears. In his account these were not one officer but all the people who were rewarded for bringing the King useful news. He credits Cyrus with creating this habit through generous gifts, which makes it a moral lesson about royal liberality as much as a description of government.
o_kings_eye.s3: The Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian records published so far give no title meaning King's Eye. Some scholars link the Greek phrase to Persian terms for listeners that appear as loanwords in Aramaic texts from Egypt. Others, notably Hirsch and Briant, doubt that a single spy service existed and think Greek writers turned royal watchfulness into a fixed office. The King did send trusted men on missions, but their titles remain unclear.
o_magus.lead: The magi were the ritual specialists of the Achaemenid world, known from Greek writers and from the empire's own records. They made sacrifices, read dreams and drew rations from the royal administration. Darius named one magus, Gaumata, as the usurper he overthrew in 522 BCE, which puts the magi at the centre of the most argued-over episode of the period.
o_magus.play: The game shows the magi through the Lodge of the Magi and through Gaumata the magus in the Bagastana story. No building called a lodge of the magi is known; it is a game simplification, and Gaumata's true identity is still debated.
o_magus.s0: Herodotus counts the Magi among the six tribes of the Medes. He says no Persian could sacrifice without a magus standing by to chant a song of the birth of the gods. He also says they left the dead to be torn by birds or dogs, and that in Xerxes' campaign of 480 BCE magi made offerings and chants to calm a storm off Magnesia. He adds drily that the wind may simply have dropped of its own accord.
o_magus.s1: The Elamite tablets of the Persepolis Fortification archive, from about 509 to 493 BCE, name men called makuš. They received barley, wine and animals for offerings, among them the lan, a regular sacrifice supported by the state. They worked in the same system as priests of Elamite gods, so the King's administration funded several cults side by side. Some magi appear in tasks that are not plainly religious.
o_magus.s2: Darius's inscription at Behistun says that in 522 BCE a magus named Gaumata rose at Paishiyauvada, claimed to be Bardiya, son of Cyrus, and seized the kingship. Darius says he and a few men killed him at the fortress of Sikayauvati in Nisaya, in Media. He also says he restored the cult places that Gaumata had destroyed. The relief above the text shows Gaumata lying beneath Darius's foot.
o_magus.s3: Herodotus tells a fuller story of two Magian brothers who ruled after Cambyses until seven nobles, Darius among them, killed them. He says the Persians later kept a feast called the Magophonia, the killing of the magi. His version broadly agrees with Darius's, but many historians suspect the impostor story was Darius's justification for killing the real Bardiya and taking a throne not his by descent. Others accept the Behistun account as broadly true.
o_magus.s4: Later tradition made the magi the priests of Zoroaster's religion. The Achaemenid inscriptions honour Auramazda but never name Zoroaster, and Herodotus does not mention him. Some scholars hold that the Persian court was already Zoroastrian. Others see the magi of this period as keepers of a wider Iranian ritual, and the tablets show them serving more than one cult.
o_polemarch.lead: The polemarch, or war leader, was one of the nine archons who governed Athens each year. In early Athens he commanded the citizen army. By 490 BCE his place beside the ten elected generals was changing, and Callimachus, polemarch in the year of Marathon, was the last holder of the office known to have led Athenians in battle.
o_polemarch.play: The game presents Callimachus as the Polemarch at Marathon, following Herodotus. Historically the polemarch was a yearly office that shared command with ten elected generals, and Miltiades is usually credited with the battle plan.
o_polemarch.s0: The Aristotelian Constitution of the Athenians says the polemarchy was the second of the great offices to be created, after the king archon, because some holders of the old royal office were weak in war. Later the archon who gave his name to the year was added, and in time six lawgivers joined them to make nine archons. This account was written in the fourth century and rests partly on reconstruction.
o_polemarch.s1: The same work says that in 501/500 BCE Athens began electing ten generals, one from each tribe, but the polemarch remained leader of the whole army. Herodotus says that at Marathon the generals were split five against five on whether to fight, and the polemarch held the deciding eleventh vote by old custom. Miltiades persuaded Callimachus to vote for battle.
o_polemarch.s2: Herodotus says Callimachus was chosen by lot, but the Constitution of the Athenians dates the selection of archons by lot to 487 BCE/6, so he was probably elected. Herodotus also says the generals took turns holding command for a day, yet he credits Miltiades with the plan. Historians still argue whether Callimachus held real command or a largely formal post, with Miltiades directing the fighting.
o_polemarch.s3: Herodotus says the polemarch led the right wing, the place of honour by Athenian custom, with the tribes in order and the Plataeans on the left. Callimachus was killed in the fighting at the Persian ships. Pausanias, writing centuries later, saw him shown in the painting of Marathon in the Painted Stoa at Athens.
o_polemarch.s4: Fragments of a tall Ionic column topped by a winged female figure survive from the Acropolis. They carry an inscription in which Callimachus of Aphidna offers the monument to Athena. The text is broken and its restoration is debated, but it probably called him polemarch and referred to Marathon. If so, it is contemporary evidence that the polemarch was publicly linked with the victory.
o_polemarch.s5: Historians generally think that once archons were chosen by lot, command in war passed fully to the generals. The Constitution of the Athenians describes the later polemarch handling lawsuits involving resident foreigners and freedmen, and offering sacrifices to Artemis the Huntress and to Enyalios. He also arranged the funeral games for Athenians who had died in war.
o_royal_judge.lead: The royal judges were Persians chosen to hear cases and to explain the ancestral laws in the King's name. Herodotus says they held office for life unless found guilty of injustice, and Babylonian documents name judges with a borrowed Persian title meaning 'law-bearer'. They stood for a claim at the heart of Darius's rule: that the King upheld justice and that his law held the lands together.
o_royal_judge.play: The game shows the office through the Judgment Seat building. No Persian building of this kind has been found; the name echoes Herodotus's story of a seat covered in a corrupt judge's skin.
o_royal_judge.s0: Darius's inscriptions present law as the King's gift and duty. At Behistun he says the lands respected his law (Old Persian data) and did as he commanded. At his tomb he states that he did not want the weak wronged by the strong, nor the strong by the weak. Historians usually see judges as the officials who put such royal claims into practice.
o_royal_judge.s1: Babylonian legal texts of the Persian period, including the Murashu archive from Nippur, use a Persian loanword for judges, usually reconstructed as dātabara, 'law-bearer'. These men worked alongside the older Babylonian courts and temple assemblies rather than replacing them. The documents show Persian judicial titles in daily use far from Persia, though they say little about how judges were chosen.
o_royal_judge.s2: Herodotus says the royal judges were chosen Persians who served until death unless found guilty of injustice, and who decided cases and interpreted the ancestral laws. When Cambyses asked whether he might marry his sister, they replied that no law allowed it, but another law let the King do as he wished. Herodotus also says Darius had the judge Sandoces crucified for a bribe, then had him taken down after weighing his past services.
o_royal_judge.s3: Herodotus tells that Cambyses had a royal judge, Sisamnes, put to death for taking a bribe and his skin cut into strips to cover the judgment seat. He then appointed the dead man's son Otanes as judge and told him to remember on what seat he sat. The story is shaped as a warning about corruption and cannot be checked against Persian sources.
o_royal_judge.s4: Historians debate how far a single royal law existed. Diodorus names Darius among the lawgivers of Egypt, and a Demotic papyrus of the Ptolemaic period says he ordered Egypt's laws collected, but many scholars see Persian rule as confirming local laws rather than imposing one code. It is also unclear whether the royal judges formed a fixed college, as Herodotus implies, or were officials named as needed.
o_royal_scribe.lead: Royal scribes wrote, copied, translated and read aloud the documents that held the Persian empire together. At Persepolis they kept accounts of grain, wine, livestock and workers on clay tablets in Elamite, and probably also on leather in Aramaic. Much of what is known about daily life in the King's service comes from the records they left.
o_royal_scribe.play: The game shows the scribes through the Scribal Office building and tablets of the Persepolis archive. That archive covers only 509 to 493 BCE; records of this kind from other years are lost.
o_royal_scribe.s0: In 1933-34 excavators found many thousands of clay tablets and fragments in the fortification wall of Persepolis. They date from 509 to 493 BCE, Darius's 13th to 28th years, and most are written in Elamite. They record rations for workers and officials, travel provisions, animals and stores. Scribes themselves appear among those receiving rations.
o_royal_scribe.s1: Some Elamite tablets mention scribes writing on parchment, which most scholars take to mean Aramaic documents on leather that have perished. Hundreds of Aramaic tablets also survive in the archive. Aramaic served as the common written language across the empire. An Aramaic copy of Darius's Behistun text, made late in the 5th century, was found at Elephantine in Egypt, which shows royal texts being translated and sent to distant provinces.
o_royal_scribe.s2: Herodotus says every Persian governor kept a royal scribe. In his story of Bagaeus and the disobedient governor Oroetes, the scribe read the King's letters aloud to the guards, who then obeyed them. He also says that at Salamis Xerxes had scribes write down the names of captains who fought well, with their fathers and cities.
o_royal_scribe.s3: In the Behistun inscription Darius says he made a new form of writing. Many historians think the Old Persian cuneiform script was devised by his scribes at this time, so the short texts naming Cyrus at Pasargadae would have been added later. Others read the passage more narrowly and argue the script may be older. The question is still debated.
o_satrap.lead: A satrap was the King's governor of a province, usually a Persian noble ruling from a provincial capital such as Sardis, Memphis, Babylon or Bactra. Satraps collected tribute, raised troops, judged disputes and kept order in the King's name. The system let a small Persian ruling class hold together lands that reached from the Aegean to the Indus.
o_satrap.play: In many levels the player governs as a satrap, building up a province for the King. This is a simplification: real satraps were mostly Persian nobles whose main duties were raising tribute and troops and keeping order.
o_satrap.s0: The Old Persian title was xšaçapāvan, usually translated as protector of the kingdom. Darius's Behistun inscription uses it for loyal men who fought the rebels of 522-521 BCE, among them Dadarshi, satrap in Bactria, and Vivana, satrap in Arachosia. Behistun calls both men Persians and subjects of Darius. The Greeks turned the word into satrapēs.
o_satrap.s1: Herodotus says Darius divided the empire into twenty provinces, which the Persians called satrapies, and fixed the tribute each one paid. Most paid in talents of silver, and the Indians paid in gold dust. He lists the peoples in each province with their sums, and says Persis itself paid no tribute. Under Cyrus and Cambyses, he claims, there was no fixed tribute, only gifts.
o_satrap.s2: The royal inscriptions list subject lands, not satrapies, and the lists vary. Behistun names 23 lands and later inscriptions name more. Neither matches Herodotus's twenty, and historians debate whether his list reflects a real tax register or his own arrangement. Babylonian documents show governors already in office before Darius, so his reform probably reorganised an existing system rather than creating a new one.
o_satrap.s3: Babylonian business texts name Gubaru as governor of Babylon and Across-the-River under Cyrus and Cambyses, a huge province reaching the Mediterranean coast. He is not the Gobryas who helped Darius to the throne. The Persepolis Fortification tablets of about 509-493 BCE record travellers drawing rations with sealed travel orders from the King or from satraps, probably including Artaphernes at Sardis. These texts show satraps as working links in the royal road system.
o_satrap.s4: Herodotus tells how Oroetes, satrap at Sardis, defied Darius and was killed by his own guards after a royal envoy read them the King's letters. He also says Darius put Aryandes of Egypt to death on a charge of rebellion, though the real offence was striking pure silver coin to rival the royal gold. Xenophon's idealised Cyropaedia, written over a century later, describes garrison commanders answering to the King and yearly inspections.
o_spartan_kings.lead: Sparta had two kings at once, one from each of two royal houses, who led its armies and held priesthoods for life. Beside them stood five ephors, elected each year, who could summon, judge and restrain the kings. This double system shaped how Sparta met Persia, from refusing help to the Ionian revolt to the campaigns of Thermopylae, Plataea and Mycale.
o_spartan_kings.play: The game presents Leonidas, Cleomenes, Demaratus and Leotychides as Spartan kings, and Pausanias as regent rather than king. This follows Herodotus, who says Pausanias commanded at Plataea for Leonidas's young son.
o_spartan_kings.s0: Herodotus says the Agiad and Eurypontid houses ruled side by side, each claiming descent from Heracles. He lists the kings' privileges: priesthoods, a double share at sacrifices, command in war and an elaborate public mourning at death. He reports that Cleomenes and Demaratus quarrelled on campaign near Eleusis in about 506 BCE, and that a law then barred both kings from going out with the army together.
o_spartan_kings.s1: Five ephors were chosen yearly. Xenophon says they exchanged oaths with the kings each month: the kings swore to rule by the laws, and the city swore to uphold the kingship while they did. The origin of the office is argued over. Herodotus credits the lawgiver Lycurgus, while Plutarch says it was added later, under King Theopompus. In 479 BCE, Herodotus says, it was the ephors who delayed and then sent the army out to Plataea.
o_spartan_kings.s2: Herodotus tells how Cleomenes refused Aristagoras's appeal for help against Persia in about 499 BCE when he learned Susa lay three months inland. Cleomenes later had his fellow king Demaratus deposed on a charge of illegitimacy, backed by a bribed Delphic priestess, and Leotychides took his throne. Demaratus fled to Darius and later advised Xerxes on the march into Greece.
o_spartan_kings.s3: In 480 BCE Leonidas, the Agiad king, held Thermopylae with allies and 300 Spartans, chosen, Herodotus says, from men who had living sons. He died there. Because his son Pleistarchus was a boy, his nephew Pausanias commanded the Greek army at Plataea in 479 BCE as regent. In the same year Leotychides, the Eurypontid king, led the Greek fleet and landed its troops to defeat the Persians at Mycale.
o_spartan_kings.s4: Herodotus reports a Delphic oracle given at the start of the war: either Sparta would be sacked by the Persians or Sparta would mourn a king of Heracles' line. He presents Leonidas as choosing to stay at Thermopylae partly to fulfil it and win glory for Sparta. The verses were probably shaped after the event, and the story works as a moral tale of royal sacrifice.
o_spear_bearer.lead: The spear-bearer stood at the King's side carrying his spear, both as a guard and as a sign of royal trust. An Old Persian label on Darius's tomb gives the title to one of his closest nobles. Herodotus says Darius himself had served Cambyses as a spear-bearer in Egypt before he took the throne.
o_spear_bearer.play: The game notes that Darius was Cambyses' spear-bearer, following Herodotus 3.139. This matches Herodotus, though historians debate how high or humble that post really was.
o_spear_bearer.s0: On the facade of Darius's tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam, a short label (DNc) names a figure as Gobryas, a Patishuvarish, spear-bearer (arshtibara) of Darius the King. A second label (DNd) names Aspathines as bearer of the King's bow-case or battle-axe; the exact wording is uncertain. Gobryas was one of the six nobles who stood with Darius against Gaumata (DB §68), so the title belonged to a man of the first rank.
o_spear_bearer.s1: Herodotus says that during Cambyses' conquest of Egypt, Darius son of Hystaspes followed the King as one of his spear-bearers. He adds that Darius was not yet a man of much standing at the time. This places the future king in Cambyses' personal following in Egypt in about 525 BCE.
o_spear_bearer.s2: The Greek word Herodotus uses, doryphoros, could mean any member of a bodyguard. Some historians link it to the Persian title arshtibara and argue that Darius already held a high court office. Others accept that he was a junior guardsman. Herodotus stresses his obscurity, while Darius's own Behistun text stresses his royal descent, and the two pictures sit uneasily together.
o_spear_bearer.s3: Describing Xerxes' march from Sardis in 480 BCE, Herodotus says a thousand spearmen walked before the King with their spears pointing down. Close behind him came a thousand spearmen of the noblest Persians, with golden apples in place of the butt-spikes of their spears. A body of ten thousand picked foot followed: a thousand with golden pomegranates on their spears and nine thousand with silver ones.
o_spear_bearer.s4: Herodotus tells how Darius, still a spear-bearer in Egypt, admired a red cloak worn by Syloson of Samos. He offered to buy it and was given it freely. Years later, as king, Darius repaid the gift by having Syloson installed as ruler of Samos. The tale is shaped as a lesson about kindness to a man before his rise.
o_strategos.lead: The strategoi were the ten generals of Athens, elected each year by the citizens, at first one from each of the ten tribes created by Cleisthenes. At Marathon in 490 BCE they shared the command with the polemarch Callimachus against the army of Datis and Artaphernes. After 487 BCE, when the archons began to be chosen by lot, the generalship probably became the leading office for men such as Themistocles, Aristides and Xanthippus.
o_strategos.play: The game shows the strategoi as the ten Athenian generals, with Miltiades singled out among them. In 490 BCE command was in fact shared with the polemarch Callimachus, who cast the deciding vote for battle.
o_strategos.s0: Cleisthenes reorganised the Athenian citizens into ten new tribes in about 508 BCE. The Athenaion Politeia, written in Aristotle's school in the 320s, dates the election of generals by tribe, one from each, to about 501 BCE, and says the polemarch still led the whole army. It also records that in its own day generals were elected by show of hands rather than by lot and could hold office again and again.
o_strategos.s1: Herodotus says the Athenians at Marathon were led by ten generals, Miltiades among them. Miltiades had ruled the Thracian Chersonese and had fled when the Phoenician fleet of the Persians came against him. At Athens he was tried for tyranny there, acquitted and then elected general. When the generals split five against five on whether to fight, Miltiades persuaded the polemarch Callimachus to cast the deciding vote for battle.
o_strategos.s2: Herodotus says the presidency of the board passed from general to general day by day. In his account the generals who favoured battle gave their days to Miltiades, who still waited for his own day before attacking. Plutarch credits Aristides with giving up his day first. Historians argue whether the rotation is believable and who held real command. Herodotus's emphasis on Miltiades may reflect the family tradition of his son Cimon.
o_strategos.s3: The Athenaion Politeia reports that from 487 BCE the archons were chosen by lot from a list of candidates. Historians usually conclude that ambitious men then turned to the elected generalship instead. Themistocles led the Athenian ships at Salamis in 480 BCE. In 479 BCE Xanthippus commanded the Athenian ships in the Greek fleet, and Aristides led the Athenian hoplites at Plataea.
o_strategos.s4: Generals could be prosecuted before the citizens. Herodotus tells how Miltiades, soon after Marathon, led seventy ships against Paros and failed to take it. Xanthippus then accused him of deceiving the Athenians. Miltiades, carried into court with a wounded leg, was fined fifty talents and died of the wound, and his son Cimon paid the fine.
o_treasurer.lead: The treasurer, in Persian probably ganzabara, kept the King's treasuries: stores of silver, precious objects and finished goods held at royal centres. At Persepolis the treasurer received written orders, paid workers in weighed silver and managed staff and workshops. The Treasury tablets from his office are among the best evidence for how the Achaemenid court handled wealth.
o_treasurer.play: The game presents the treasurer as the ganzabara of the Persepolis archive and keeper of the King's treasuries. The archive's evidence for treasuries begins only in 509 BCE, so earlier treasurers are not directly documented.
o_treasurer.s0: No Old Persian inscription spells out the title. Scholars reconstruct it as ganzabara, meaning roughly 'treasure-bearer', from its loan forms: kanzabara in Elamite tablets and ganzabar in Aramaic. The same word appears as gizbar in the Hebrew of the book of Ezra. Its spread through so many languages shows how widely Persian administrative terms travelled.
o_treasurer.s1: Excavators working in the Treasury building at Persepolis in the 1930s found several hundred Elamite clay tablets and fragments, dated from 492 to 458 BCE. Most are sealed orders telling the treasurer to pay named groups of workers in silver, often as a substitute for part of their sheep or wine rations. The payments were in weighed silver measured in karsha and shekels, not in coins.
o_treasurer.s2: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, dated from 509 to 493 BCE, mention treasuries, called kapnuški in Elamite, at Persepolis and at other places in Persia. These were not just vaults of bullion. They housed craftsmen and labourers, the so-called treasury workers, and kept finished goods, so the treasurer ran a working establishment as well as a strongroom.
o_treasurer.s3: Herodotus says the King melted his tribute silver and gold and poured it into clay jars, then broke the jars away and cut off metal as he needed it. Diodorus reports that Alexander found about 120,000 talents in the treasury at Persepolis in 330. Neither the method Herodotus describes nor the size of the hoard Diodorus gives can be checked against Persian records.
o_treasurer.s4: Green stone mortars, pestles and plates from the Treasury carry short Aramaic ink notes naming treasurers and sub-treasurers. Their first editor read them as records of a ritual involving the drink haoma. Most later scholars reject this and see the notes as administrative labels for objects handed over to the treasury, so their meaning is still argued.
o_tyrant.lead: After Cyrus took Lydia and his generals subdued the Greek coast, the Persians governed many Greek cities through single local rulers called tyrannoi, a word for a ruler outside the customary constitution, not necessarily a cruel one. These men answered to the King's satraps at Sardis and Dascylium, served in his campaigns and owed their place to Persian backing. That loyalty broke in the Ionian Revolt of 499 BCE.
o_tyrant.play: The game names Histiaeus, Aristagoras and Hippias as Greek rulers under the King. The first two did rule Miletus for Darius, but Hippias had lost Athens in 510 BCE and served Persia as an exile hoping to be restored.
o_tyrant.s0: Herodotus says that during Darius's Scythian campaign, about 513 BCE, the tyrants of the Ionian and Hellespontine cities guarded the bridge over the Ister. When Miltiades urged them to break it and strand the King, Histiaeus of Miletus replied that each of them ruled only because of Darius, and that without him the cities would choose popular government. Herodotus then lists these rulers by name, among them Strattis of Chios and Aeaces of Samos.
o_tyrant.s1: Herodotus says Darius rewarded Histiaeus with land at Myrcinus in Thrace, then kept him at court in Susa after Megabazus warned of his ambitions. His son-in-law Aristagoras governed Miletus in his place. After a failed attack on Naxos with Persian forces, Aristagoras turned against the King in about 499 BCE, gave up his own tyranny and had the tyrants of other cities seized and handed over to their citizens.
o_tyrant.s2: Hippias ruled Athens until 510 BCE, when he was driven out with Spartan help and withdrew to Sigeum in the Troad, a town held by his family. Herodotus says he later went to Artaphernes at Sardis and urged the Persians to restore him. Thucydides adds that he went up to Darius and, as an old man, sailed with the Persians in 490 BCE. Herodotus says he guided them to Marathon.
o_tyrant.s3: Herodotus says that in 492 BCE Mardonius deposed the Ionian tyrants and set up democracies, and he expected Greeks who doubted the Persian debate on democracy to find this surprising. Yet Persian-backed tyrants appear again in his later books: Strattis still ruled Chios in 479 BCE, and the Persians made Theomestor ruler of Samos after Salamis. Historians debate how far the change went, and whether Persia simply backed whatever local regime kept tribute and order.
o_tyrant.s4: Herodotus tells that Histiaeus, held at Susa, shaved a slave's head, tattooed a message urging revolt on his scalp and sent him to Aristagoras once the hair grew back. He also tells that Hippias, landing at Marathon, sneezed out a loose tooth that was lost in the sand and took it as a sign that he would never recover Athens. Both stories have the shape of moral tales.
p_achaemenes.lead: Achaemenes was a son of Darius and Atossa and so a full brother of Xerxes. After an Egyptian revolt was put down early in Xerxes' reign, he governed Egypt and led its squadron in the invasion of Greece in 480 BCE. He was later killed in Egypt fighting the rebel Inaros.
p_achaemenes.play: The game's chronicle presents him as Xerxes' full brother, satrap of Egypt and admiral of its two hundred ships, who warned against splitting the fleet. This matches Herodotus, the main source.
p_achaemenes.s0: Herodotus calls Achaemenes Xerxes' brother on both his father's and his mother's side, which makes him a son of Darius by Atossa, daughter of Cyrus. Egypt rebelled at the end of Darius's reign. Herodotus says Xerxes reconquered it in the second year after his father's death and handed it to Achaemenes to govern.
p_achaemenes.s1: Herodotus counts two hundred Egyptian ships in Xerxes' fleet and names Achaemenes as their commander. He was one of four Persian admirals, alongside his half-brother Ariabignes. Herodotus says the Egyptians fought best on the King's side at Artemisium, taking five Greek ships together with their crews.
p_achaemenes.s2: After Thermopylae the exiled Spartan king Demaratus advised sending part of the fleet to raid Cythera off the Laconian coast. In Herodotus's account Achaemenes argued that the storms had already cost many ships and that the fleet should stay together. He also hinted that Demaratus wished the King ill. Xerxes took his advice on strategy but rebuked him for slandering a guest-friend.
p_achaemenes.s3: Herodotus says Inaros the Libyan killed Achaemenes, and he mentions the skulls of the Persians who fell with him at Papremis. Ctesias calls the commander Achaemenides and makes him a brother of Artaxerxes I. Diodorus names him Achaemenes, the King's uncle. Thucydides and Diodorus describe Athenian help for the rebels, and the date of about 460 or 459 BCE is still argued.
p_achaemenes.s4: Almost everything known about Achaemenes comes from Greek writers, who saw him through the war with Greece. His rule of Egypt lasted roughly two decades but left little trace in surviving documents of the time. Modern accounts of how he governed therefore rest largely on inference from the wider Achaemenid administration of Egypt.
p_adeimantus.lead: Adeimantus, son of Ocytus, commanded the Corinthian ships in the Greek fleet in 480 BCE. Herodotus shows him as a sharp opponent of Themistocles in the debates before Salamis. Herodotus also reports an Athenian story that he fled in the battle, and says the Corinthians and the rest of Greece denied it.
p_adeimantus.play: Adeimantus is named only in the event articles on Artemisium and Salamis and has no mechanic of his own. The game mentions the Athenian charge that he fled; Herodotus says the Corinthians and other Greeks denied it.
p_adeimantus.s0: Herodotus names Adeimantus, son of Ocytus, as the Corinthian commander in the Greek fleet of 480 BCE. Corinth sent a sizeable squadron to the allied fleet under the Spartan Eurybiades, and Herodotus lists it in his catalogue of the fleet. At Artemisium he says Themistocles bribed Adeimantus, among others, to stay and fight, a tale that reflects Athenian sources.
p_adeimantus.s1: In Herodotus's telling, Adeimantus clashed with Themistocles in the council before Salamis. He urged a withdrawal towards the Isthmus of Corinth, and told Themistocles that men who start a race too early are beaten with rods. Themistocles is said to have replied that those left behind are not crowned. The exchange is Herodotus's report, and its exact words cannot be checked.
p_adeimantus.s2: Herodotus says the Athenians told a story that Adeimantus hoisted sail in panic as the battle began and fled with the Corinthian ships. In the story a boat met them with news that the Greeks were winning, and they turned back too late to fight. Herodotus adds that the Corinthians denied this and that the rest of Greece spoke well of them. The sources therefore disagree, and the charge probably owes something to Athenian hostility towards Corinth.
p_adeimantus.s3: Plutarch, writing centuries later, accused Herodotus of unfairness towards Corinth in his treatment of Salamis and of the Corinthians generally. The quarrel over Adeimantus's conduct thus continued long after 480 BCE. No Persian source mentions Adeimantus.
p_alexander_great.lead: Alexander III of Macedon invaded the Persian empire in 334 and within four years had defeated Darius III and taken the royal cities. In 330 the palaces of Persepolis burned while he held them, and in 324 he had the robbed tomb of Cyrus at Pasargadae repaired. His conquest ended the Achaemenid line about a century and a half after Plataea.
p_alexander_great.play: Alexander falls outside the game's eleven levels, which end in 479 BCE with the Mycale epilogue. He appears only in a Chronicle note on the later fate of Persepolis and of Cyrus's tomb.
p_alexander_great.s0: Arrian wrote in the 2nd century CE, drawing on the lost memoirs of Ptolemy and Aristobulus. He tells how Alexander crossed the Hellespont in 334 and won at the Granicus. He then beat Darius III at Issus in 333 and again at Gaugamela in 331, after which Babylon and Susa opened to him. Darius fled east and was killed in 330 by his own satrap Bessus.
p_alexander_great.s1: Arrian says Alexander burned the palace on purpose, as revenge for Xerxes' sack of Athens, against Parmenion's advice, and he judges the act unwise. Diodorus and Plutarch tell instead of a drinking party at which the Athenian courtesan Thais urged the king to set the fire. Historians still argue whether it was policy, a drunken impulse, or both.
p_alexander_great.s2: Excavations at Persepolis in the 1930s found thick burned debris in the Treasury and the great halls. The Treasury had been largely emptied of its valuables before the fire. A Babylonian astronomical diary of 331 notes the defeat of the King's army at Gaugamela and Alexander's approach to Babylon. It is a rare record of the conquest written at the time and not by Greeks.
p_alexander_great.s3: Arrian follows Aristobulus here. He says that on the march back from India, early in 324, Alexander found Cyrus's tomb at Pasargadae plundered, the gold coffin damaged and the body thrown out. He ordered Aristobulus to put the remains back, restore the contents and seal the door. The magi who guarded the tomb were questioned under torture but named no culprit.
p_alexander_great.s4: The Greek Alexander Romance, compiled centuries later, turned him into a wandering hero and made him the son of the Egyptian pharaoh Nectanebo. Persian epic, above all Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, made him a half-brother of Darius. Middle Persian Zoroastrian writings instead remember him as the accursed Alexander who burned sacred texts. All are later portraits, not evidence for the events of 330.
p_alexander_macedon.lead: Alexander I was king of Macedon while it was part of the Persian empire. In 479 BCE Mardonius sent him to Athens to offer the Athenians alliance with the King, and Herodotus says he later rode secretly to the Greek lines to warn them before Plataea. His double role, loyal vassal and self-declared friend of the Greeks, makes him one of the hardest figures of the wars to judge.
p_alexander_macedon.play: The game's chronicle presents Alexander as a subject king who carried Mardonius's offer to Athens and, by Herodotus's account, warned the Greeks before Plataea.
p_alexander_macedon.s0: Herodotus tells how Persian envoys, sent to demand earth and water from Alexander's father Amyntas, insulted the Macedonian women at a feast. Young Alexander had beardless youths dressed as women kill them. When the Persian Bubares came to search for the missing men, Alexander bought his silence with money and his sister Gygaea in marriage. Many historians read the tale as a later Macedonian story of resistance, while the marriage itself shows close ties to Persia.
p_alexander_macedon.s1: Herodotus says Mardonius brought the Macedonians under Persian rule in 492 BCE. In 480 BCE Alexander sent word to the Greeks holding the Vale of Tempe that Xerxes' army was too large and they should withdraw. His men later protected Boeotian towns by showing that they sided with Persia. Herodotus also mentions a gold statue of Alexander set up at Delphi.
p_alexander_macedon.s2: In 479 BCE Mardonius chose Alexander as his envoy because he was related to the Persians by marriage and was an official friend and benefactor of Athens. Alexander offered pardon, land, self-rule and the rebuilding of burnt temples if Athens joined the King. Herodotus gives the Athenians a proud refusal: they would never make terms with the Persians while the sun kept its course.
p_alexander_macedon.s3: According to Herodotus, on the night before the battle Alexander rode alone to the Athenian outposts and asked for their generals. He told them Mardonius meant to attack at dawn, claimed Greek descent as his reason for speaking, and asked to be remembered if the Greeks won. Plutarch tells the same story much later, probably drawing on Herodotus.
p_alexander_macedon.s4: Herodotus stresses Alexander's Greek ancestry and his entry at Olympia, and much later writers gave him the title Philhellene. Many historians, following E. Badian, think Herodotus repeated Macedonian stories that hid how fully Alexander served Persia in 480 and 479 BCE. Darius's tomb inscription lists Ionians wearing shield-like hats among subject peoples. Some scholars take these to be the Macedonians, though the identification is argued over.
p_amasis.lead: Amasis II ruled Egypt for about forty-four years and died in 526 BCE, shortly before Cambyses invaded. His son Psamtik III inherited the war. Most of what is told of him comes from Herodotus, who gathered Egyptian stories about the king, while Egyptian monuments and the statue of Udjahorresnet give the view from Egypt.
p_amasis.play: Amasis is named only in the Encyclopedia's event articles on the conquest of Egypt and the battle of Pelusium. He is not a figure in any level and has no mechanic of his own.
p_amasis.s0: Herodotus says Amasis was sent by King Apries to calm a mutiny of the Egyptian army and was instead proclaimed king by the soldiers. Apries marched against him with Greek and Carian mercenaries and was defeated, and Amasis took the throne. Herodotus gives his reign as forty-four years, which modern historians reckon as 570 to 526 BCE.
p_amasis.s1: Herodotus relates that Amasis was of humble birth and that courtiers despised him. He had a golden footbath melted down and made into a statue of a god, which the people then worshipped. Amasis then told his critics that his own rise followed the same pattern. The tale is a moral about kingship, and no document confirms it.
p_amasis.s2: Herodotus says Amasis favoured Greeks and made Naucratis the one port where Greek merchants were allowed to trade and settle. He also reports an alliance with Croesus of Lydia. Excavation shows Greeks were trading at Naucratis before his reign, so his act is better seen as regulating an existing port.
p_amasis.s3: Herodotus gives conflicting reasons for the invasion. One tale says Amasis sent a daughter of Apries, instead of his own daughter, as a bride for Cambyses, and she revealed the trick. Herodotus says the Persians told the story differently, and he rejects the Egyptian claim that Cambyses was her son, since Cambyses was the son of Cyrus. Modern historians treat these tales as stories and look instead to Persian ambition to take Egypt after Babylon and Lydia.
p_amasis.s4: Herodotus says Amasis died before the Persians arrived and that his son Psamtik III had reigned only six months when Cambyses reached Egypt. He also says Cambyses had Amasis's body taken from its tomb at Sais and abused, then burned. Herodotus adds that burning the dead was against both Persian and Egyptian custom, and many historians doubt the tale.
p_amasis.s5: The admiral Udjahorresnet served under Amasis and Psamtik III. His own statue inscription tells how he came to serve Cambyses and the Persian kings, and it gives an Egyptian account of the change of rule.
p_arakha.lead: Arakha was an Armenian who seized Babylon in 521 BCE by claiming to be Nebuchadnezzar, son of Nabonidus, the last native king. His revolt was the second Babylonian rising against Darius within about a year. Darius's general Intaphernes retook the city late in 521 BCE. Its end helped close the wave of rebellions that followed the death of Cambyses.
p_arakha.play: Arakha appears only in the game's chronicle as a Babylonian rebel of 521 BCE. The note's facts (his Armenian origin, the name Nebuchadnezzar and the capture by Intaphernes) agree with the Behistun inscription.
p_arakha.s0: Darius's Behistun inscription says that Babylon rebelled a second time while he was in Persia and Media. A man named Arakha, an Armenian and son of Haldita, rose from a Babylonian district called Dubala. He told the people he was Nebuchadnezzar, son of Nabonidus, and Babylon accepted him as king. Only months earlier Darius had crushed Nidintu-Bel, who had made the same claim.
p_arakha.s1: Darius sent an army under Vindafarna, the Persian noble whom Greek writers call Intaphernes. He was one of the six helpers named in the inscription. According to Behistun, he defeated the Babylonians and captured Babylon in the month Varkazana, late in 521 BCE. Arakha and his leading followers were seized and impaled at Babylon.
p_arakha.s2: Babylonian business and temple documents were dated by the years of a king Nebuchadnezzar, whom modern scholars number Nebuchadnezzar IV. Scribes in Babylon and nearby cities used his name for a few months in the second half of 521 BCE. These tablets show that his rule was real and recognised in daily life, not only a claim recorded by his enemy.
p_arakha.s3: On the Behistun relief Arakha stands among the roped rebels before Darius, and a short label calls him a liar who claimed to be Nebuchadnezzar. The only narrative of his revolt comes from Darius, who presents every rebel as an impostor. Historians debate the exact chronology of the two Babylonian revolts and what 'Armenian' meant here. His father's name Haldita recalls the Urartian god Haldi.
p_arakha.s4: Herodotus tells of a Babylonian revolt under Darius with a siege of over nineteen months. It ended when the noble Zopyrus mutilated himself, pretended to desert and later opened the gates. Herodotus does not name Arakha, and the tale is shaped as a moral story about loyalty. Some historians link it to the revolts of 522 to 521 BCE, while Ctesias tells of a Babylonian revolt under Xerxes in which a Zopyrus died.
p_ariabignes.lead: Ariabignes was a son of Darius the Great by the daughter of Gobryas, which made him an elder half-brother of Xerxes. In 480 BCE he commanded the Ionian and Carian squadrons of the King's fleet, and he died in the sea battle at Salamis, a royal prince and one of the highest-ranking men to fall there. Almost everything known of him comes from a few lines in Herodotus.
p_ariabignes.play: The game's chronicle describes him as Xerxes' half-brother who led the Ionian and Carian ships and died at Salamis, which agrees with Herodotus. Salamis itself is not one of the game's levels.
p_ariabignes.s0: Herodotus says that Darius, before he became king in 522 BCE, married a daughter of his fellow noble Gobryas and had three sons by her, the eldest being Artobazanes. Herodotus names Ariabignes as a son of Darius and Gobryas's daughter, so he was older than Xerxes, whose mother was Atossa, daughter of Cyrus. Because they were born before the accession, these sons were passed over when Xerxes was chosen as heir.
p_ariabignes.s1: In his survey of Xerxes' forces Herodotus lists four admirals: Ariabignes, Prexaspes son of Aspathines, Megabazus son of Megabates, and Achaemenes, another son of Darius, who led the Egyptian ships. Ariabignes had charge of the Ionian and Carian contingents, subjects of the King from the Aegean coast of Anatolia. Herodotus counts 1,207 triremes in the whole fleet, a figure most historians think too high.
p_ariabignes.s2: Herodotus reports that Ariabignes, son of Darius and brother of Xerxes, was killed in the fighting at Salamis in 480 BCE, together with many other well-known Persians, Medes and allies. He adds that few Greeks died because most could swim, while many on the King's side drowned when their ships were lost. He gives no detail of how Ariabignes himself fell.
p_ariabignes.s3: Plutarch, writing about six centuries later, names the Persian admiral killed at Salamis as Ariamenes, a brother of Xerxes. Most scholars take him to be the same man as Herodotus's Ariabignes, but the name differs and the identification cannot be proved. No Persian document yet published has been securely matched with him, and the fallen commanders named in Aeschylus's Persians cannot be firmly linked to him either.
p_ariabignes.s4: Plutarch tells that Ariamenes fought from a great ship, shooting arrows and javelins as if from a city wall. When his ship met that of two Athenians, Ameinias of Decelea and Socles of Pallene, he tried to board them, and they struck him with their spears and threw him into the sea. Plutarch says Artemisia of Halicarnassus recognised his body among the wreckage and had it carried to Xerxes. The scene is not in Herodotus.
p_aristagoras.lead: Aristagoras governed Miletus for his kinsman Histiaeus. In 499 BCE he turned a failed Persian expedition against Naxos into a revolt of the Ionian cities. He brought Athenian and Eretrian ships into the war, and Herodotus saw this as the beginning of the long conflict between Persia and the Greeks.
p_aristagoras.play: The game names him only in its chronicle notes, as the tyrant of Miletus who led the revolt of 499 BCE and won ships from Athens and Eretria. Strictly, he ruled Miletus as Histiaeus's deputy rather than in his own right.
p_aristagoras.s0: Herodotus says Aristagoras, son of Molpagoras, was the cousin and son-in-law of Histiaeus, the tyrant of Miletus whom Darius kept at his court. Aristagoras ruled the city as his deputy. When exiles from Naxos asked for help, he persuaded Artaphernes, satrap at Sardis, to back an attack, and Darius approved a fleet under Megabates. The siege lasted four months and failed, leaving Aristagoras unable to meet his promises.
p_aristagoras.s1: In 499 BCE, Herodotus says, Aristagoras gave up his tyranny, proclaimed equal rights for the Milesians and had the Persian-backed tyrants of other Ionian cities seized. He then sailed to mainland Greece, where Cleomenes of Sparta refused him but Athens sent twenty ships and Eretria five. In 498 BCE the allies marched inland and burned Sardis. Aristagoras stayed at Miletus and gave the command to his brother Charopinus and to Hermophantus.
p_aristagoras.s2: After Persian armies recovered Cyprus and the cities of the Hellespont and Caria, Aristagoras left Miletus, which Herodotus puts down to a lack of courage. He handed the city to a respected citizen named Pythagoras and sailed to Myrcinus, the Thracian town Darius had once granted to Histiaeus. Thracians killed him while he was besieging a nearby town, probably about 497 or 496 BCE. The revolt went on without him until the Ionian defeat at Lade in 494 BCE.
p_aristagoras.s3: Herodotus tells that Histiaeus, held at Susa, shaved a slave's head, tattooed on it a message urging revolt, and sent him once the hair had grown back. At Sparta, he says, Aristagoras showed Cleomenes a bronze map of the world and offered ever larger bribes, until the king's young daughter Gorgo warned her father that the stranger would corrupt him. Both stories have the shape of moral tales and cannot be checked.
p_aristagoras.s4: Herodotus explains the revolt through the private ambitions and fears of Aristagoras and Histiaeus. Modern historians look wider, and some point to resentment of tyrants imposed by Persia, the burden of tribute and military service, or pressure on Ionian trade. How much weight each cause deserves is still argued. No Persian text mentions Aristagoras, so these events are known only through Greek writers.
p_aristides.lead: Aristides, son of Lysimachus, was an Athenian politician and general, remembered as 'the Just'. Exiled by ostracism in the 480s BCE, he was recalled when Xerxes invaded, fought at Salamis and commanded the Athenians at Plataea in 479 BCE. He then fixed the first tribute of the new Greek alliance against Persia.
p_aristides.play: The game's chronicle note presents Aristides as leader of the eight thousand Athenians on the Greek left at Plataea, facing the Thebans. Herodotus agrees, though he says they faced all the Boeotians, with the Thebans fighting hardest.
p_aristides.s0: Ostracism let Athenian citizens vote to exile a leading man for ten years by scratching his name on a potsherd. Excavators in the Athenian Agora and the Kerameikos have found ostraka naming Aristides son of Lysimachus. These potsherds probably come from the votes of the 480s BCE, when he and Themistocles were rivals.
p_aristides.s1: The Constitution of the Athenians, attributed to Aristotle, dates his ostracism to about 482 BCE. That was the time when Themistocles was persuading Athens to spend its new silver on a fleet.
