It adds that the Athenians recalled all the ostracised men about two years later, as Xerxes' army approached. Herodotus also says that Aristides had been ostracised before he reappeared in 480 BCE.
p_aristides.s2: Herodotus says Aristides crossed from Aegina to Salamis on the night before the battle and told Themistocles that the Persian fleet had surrounded the Greeks. Herodotus calls him the best and most upright man in Athens. During the battle, Aristides landed Athenian hoplites on the islet of Psyttaleia and killed the Persian troops posted there.
p_aristides.s3: In 479 BCE Aristides led the eight thousand Athenians on the left of the Greek line. Herodotus says Pausanias once proposed that the Athenians swap wings with the Spartans to face the Persians, but the move was reversed. In the final battle the Athenians fought the Boeotians, among whom the Thebans fought hardest for Mardonius.
p_aristides.s4: After 478 BCE the Greek allies formed a league against Persia, and the Constitution of the Athenians says Aristides assessed what each member should pay. Thucydides refers to the tribute fixed in his time and gives a first total of 460 talents. Historians debate whether that figure is right for the first year. They also debate how far the assessment followed the Persian tribute that Artaphernes had set for the Ionian cities after their revolt.
p_aristides.s5: Plutarch, writing some six centuries later, tells a story about the vote that exiled him. An illiterate countryman asked a stranger to write 'Aristides' on his sherd, saying he was tired of hearing the man called the Just. The stranger was Aristides himself, and he wrote his own name. Plutarch also says Aristides died so poor that the city paid for his burial.
p_artabazus.lead: Artabazus son of Pharnaces was a senior Persian noble who led troops in Xerxes' invasion of Greece. Herodotus says he argued against giving battle at Plataea in 479 BCE and led his own corps home as the battle was lost. He later governed the satrapy of Dascylium near the Hellespont, where his family held power for generations.
p_artabazus.play: The game's chronicle note follows Herodotus closely. The forty thousand men are Herodotus's figure, which may be inflated. His route ran through Phocis, Thessaly, Macedonia and Thrace to Byzantium before he crossed to Asia.
p_artabazus.s0: Herodotus names him as the son of Pharnaces and says he commanded the Parthians and Chorasmians in Xerxes' army. Many historians identify this Pharnaces with Parnaka, the high official who ran the royal economy around Persepolis in the Fortification tablets and was probably a kinsman of Darius. The link rests mainly on the name, the date and the family's high rank, so it remains a modern inference.
p_artabazus.s1: Herodotus says that after Salamis Artabazus escorted Xerxes to the Hellespont with sixty thousand men and then turned back into Chalcidice. He took Olynthus, killed its people and handed the town to Critobulus of Torone and the Chalcidians. His siege of Potidaea failed after three months when an unusual tide drowned many of his men, which the Potidaeans blamed on Poseidon's anger at a Persian insult to his temple.
p_artabazus.s2: Herodotus reports that in 479 BCE, with the armies facing each other near the Asopus, Artabazus urged Mardonius not to fight. He proposed falling back on Thebes, which was well stocked, and sending gold to the leading men of the Greek cities to break their alliance. Mardonius, trusting his army, overruled him and resolved to attack.
p_artabazus.s3: Herodotus says Artabazus had resented Mardonius's command and, seeing the Persians in flight, led his corps away from the field without fighting. He marched through Phocis and Thessaly, telling the Thessalians that Mardonius was following, and on through Macedonia and Thrace to Byzantium, losing many men to hunger and Thracian attacks. Herodotus gives his force as forty thousand, a number historians treat with caution.
p_artabazus.s4: Thucydides says Xerxes later sent Artabazus to Dascylium as satrap to handle secret dealings with the Spartan regent Pausanias. The appointment suggests the King did not regard his retreat from Plataea as a disgrace. His descendants, often called the Pharnacids, governed this satrapy for much of the following century.
p_artachaees.lead: Artachaees, son of Artaeus, was a Persian noble who shared command of the digging of Xerxes' canal through the Athos isthmus. Herodotus says he died of illness at Acanthus as Xerxes' army marched west in 480 BCE, and that the whole army raised a burial mound over him. Almost everything known about him comes from Herodotus.
p_artachaees.play: The game's chronicle names Artachaees as overseer of the Athos canal, buried at Acanthus under a mound raised by the army. Herodotus adds that he died of illness and that Acanthus later honoured him as a hero.
p_artachaees.s0: Herodotus says two Persians directed the work at Athos: Bubares son of Megabazus and Artachaees son of Artaeus. He describes the ground divided among the contingents of different peoples, with men digging under the lash and passing the earth up in relays. In his telling the preparations at Athos took about three years, before Xerxes' crossing into Europe in 480 BCE.
p_artachaees.s1: A British and Greek survey of the isthmus between 1991 and 2001 traced a buried channel across it, about 2 kilometres long. This confirmed that a canal was really dug where Herodotus placed it. The survey cannot show who directed the work, so Artachaees' role still rests on Herodotus alone.
p_artachaees.s2: Herodotus says that while Xerxes was at Acanthus, Artachaees fell ill and died. He calls him a member of the Achaemenid family, held in high honour by the King. Xerxes grieved for him and gave him a splendid funeral, and the whole army heaped up a mound over his grave.
p_artachaees.s3: Herodotus says Artachaees was the tallest man among the Persians, four fingers short of five royal cubits, and had the loudest voice of anyone. Taken literally, this would make him well over 2 metres tall, and historians treat the figure as exaggerated or as local storytelling. No Persian document known today names him, so the Greek account cannot be checked.
p_artachaees.s4: Herodotus adds that the people of Acanthus, following an oracle, sacrificed to Artachaees as a hero. He says they still did so in his own day, calling on him by name. The story probably reached Herodotus through local Greek tradition, and it shows how a Persian grave could become part of a Greek town's worship.
p_artaphernes.lead: Artaphernes, a son of Hystaspes and brother of Darius, was made satrap of Sardis and governed Persian western Asia Minor through the Ionian Revolt, holding the citadel when rebels burned the lower city in 498 BCE. His son of the same name led the expedition of 490 BCE with Datis. Almost all that is known of both men comes from Herodotus, with only a probable trace in the Persepolis tablets.
p_artaphernes.play: The game names Artaphernes in a chronicle note that follows Herodotus: he holds the citadel of Sardis when the Ionians burn the lower city in 498 BCE, and his son leads the 490 BCE expedition with Datis.
p_artaphernes.s0: Herodotus says Darius appointed Artaphernes, his brother by the same father, governor at Sardis after returning from the Scythian campaign. Athenian envoys came to him in about 507 BCE seeking an alliance and gave earth and water, though Athens later disowned the act. Later, when the exiled Hippias was at Sardis, Artaphernes told the Athenians to take Hippias back if they wished to be safe.
p_artaphernes.s1: Herodotus says Aristagoras of Miletus persuaded Artaphernes to back an attack on Naxos, and Artaphernes won Darius's approval. The siege failed, and Aristagoras then raised Ionia in revolt. In 498 BCE Ionians, Athenians and Eretrians took Sardis but could not take the citadel, which Artaphernes held. A fire spread through the reed-roofed houses and burned the temple of the goddess Cybebe.
p_artaphernes.s2: Herodotus has Artaphernes tell Histiaeus that he had stitched the shoe which Aristagoras put on. After Histiaeus was captured, Artaphernes and a Persian commander named Harpagus impaled him at Sardis and sent his head to Susa, which Herodotus says displeased Darius. In 493 BCE Artaphernes made the Ionian cities settle disputes by arbitration, measured their land in parasangs and fixed a tribute that Herodotus says still stood in his day.
p_artaphernes.s3: In 490 BCE Darius sent Datis the Mede and Artaphernes son of Artaphernes, his nephew, against Eretria and Athens. Herodotus says they took Eretria but were defeated at Marathon. He later lists this younger Artaphernes as commander of the Lydians and Mysians in Xerxes' army in 480 BCE.
p_artaphernes.s4: The Behistun inscription lists Sparda, the Persian name for Lydia and Sardis, among Darius's lands. No royal inscription names Artaphernes, and he is not among the six helpers of 522 BCE. A Persepolis Fortification tablet records travellers from Sardis carrying a sealed document in a name D. M. Lewis identified as his. Otherwise he is known from Greek writers.
p_artavardiya.lead: Artavardiya was a Persian commander whom Darius sent against the rebel Vahyazdata in Persis. He is known from the Behistun inscription, where Darius names him as the man whose army beat the rebels in two battles. Herodotus does not mention him, and no other surviving Greek account of these years names him.
p_artavardiya.play: The game names Artavardiya only in Chronicle entries and in the Encyclopedia's article on the revolt of Vahyazdata. He is not a figure or place in any level and has no mechanic of his own.
p_artavardiya.s0: In the Behistun inscription Darius calls Artavardiya a Persian and his servant, and says he sent him with a Persian army against Vahyazdata. The text gives him no title and says nothing of his family. The inscription is the only contemporary source that names him.
p_artavardiya.s1: Darius records two battles in which Artavardiya's army defeated the forces of Vahyazdata, the first at a place called Rakha and the second at Mount Parga. Vahyazdata was then captured with his chief followers and impaled at Uvadaicaya in Persia. Darius credits Auramazda for the victories and does not describe the fighting.
p_artavardiya.s2: Vahyazdata was a Persian who claimed to be Bardiya, the son of Cyrus, although Darius says Bardiya had been killed earlier. Darius presents him as a liar who deceived the people of Persis. Darius says he sent Artavardiya against him, and the text gives no sign that Darius went himself.
p_artavardiya.s3: Herodotus tells at length of the false Smerdis and of Darius's seizure of the throne, but he does not tell of a second pretender in Persis, and so says nothing of Artavardiya. His version of these years is shaped by stories of the seven conspirators. For this campaign Behistun is therefore the main source.
p_artavardiya.s4: Behistun is Darius's own account, written to justify his rule, and it presents every rebel as a liar who opposed the king. Historians accept that the revolts happened but treat the details of battles and dates with caution. A revolt in Persis itself would have been dangerous for Darius, but that is a modern judgement, and Artavardiya's role beyond what Darius says cannot be checked.
p_artayctes.lead: Artayctes was the Persian governor of Sestos under Xerxes. Herodotus says he plundered the shrine of Protesilaus at Elaeus, then held out in Sestos from the autumn of 479 BCE until hunger forced the garrison to flee. The Athenians under Xanthippus caught and killed him, and Herodotus closes his narrative on that event.
p_artayctes.play: Artayctes has no mechanic of his own. The game mentions him only in its event articles on the siege of Sestos and the battle of Mycale, where Xanthippus has him crucified.
p_artayctes.s0: Herodotus calls Artayctes the son of Cherasmis and a Persian governor of Sestos, and says he helped Xerxes with the bridging of the Hellespont. He describes him as a clever and wicked man. Herodotus is the only source for his career, and no Persian document naming him is known.
p_artayctes.s1: Herodotus says the shrine of Protesilaus at Elaeus, on the Thracian Chersonese, held rich treasure. Artayctes asked Xerxes to give it to him, arguing that its hero had marched against Persian land, and Xerxes agreed. Herodotus adds that Artayctes carried off the treasure, farmed the sacred ground and behaved indecently in the sanctuary.
p_artayctes.s2: After Mycale in 479 BCE the Greek fleet sailed to the Hellespont and found the bridges already broken. The Athenians under Xanthippus besieged Sestos, where Persians and many local people had gathered. Herodotus says food ran short in autumn and Artayctes and Oeobazus slipped away by night. The townspeople told the Greeks, who pursued and caught Artayctes near Aegospotami.
p_artayctes.s3: Herodotus says Artayctes offered a large sum for himself and his son, but Xanthippus refused because the people of Elaeus demanded vengeance for the shrine. Artayctes was nailed to planks and hung up, and his son was stoned before his eyes. Herodotus tells this at the very end of his narrative.
p_artayctes.s4: Herodotus relates that dried fish on a fire leapt and twitched, and that Artayctes took this as a sign from Protesilaus. The tale is shaped as a moral story about divine punishment for sacrilege. It should be read as a story told by Greeks, not as a report of what Artayctes said.
p_artayctes.s5: Herodotus describes nailing to planks, and modern writers often call this crucifixion, though the Greek wording is not exact. Historians also debate how far the story is shaped to close the Histories, with the Athenians punishing a Persian for the same impiety that Xerxes' expedition had shown. Because only Greek sources tell it, the Persian view of Artayctes is unknown.
p_artayntes.lead: Artayntes was a Persian commander of the fleet that wintered at Samos after Salamis. Herodotus says he escaped the Persian defeat at Mycale in 479 BCE. He is known almost entirely from Herodotus, so the Greek account is the main voice on him.
p_artayntes.play: Artayntes is named in the game's articles on the battle of Mycale and on Xerxes' return to Asia. He has no figure, unit or mechanic of his own.
p_artayntes.s0: Herodotus says that after Salamis the fleet wintered at Samos under Mardontes, Artayntes and Ithamitres, with Ithamitres as Artayntes' nephew. Herodotus gives little about Artayntes' career before this.
p_artayntes.s1: In Herodotus's telling the Persians drew their ships up at Mycale behind a barrier of stakes and stones. The Greeks landed and broke the Persian line, and the army commander Tigranes was killed. Herodotus says Artayntes and Ithamitres were among those who got away, while the Greeks burned the ships.
p_artayntes.s2: Herodotus says Masistes, a son of Darius, was angered by the defeat and abused Artayntes as worse than a woman. Masistes drew his sword, and Xenagoras of Halicarnassus is said to have stepped in and saved Artayntes. Herodotus places this on the retreat from the field.
p_artayntes.s3: No Persian inscription or tablet is known to the checker to name Artayntes, so Herodotus is the only voice for his conduct. Historians accept that a Persian force was beaten at Mycale, but they argue over its size and over how far Greek tradition shaped the stories told of Persian commanders. The quarrel with Masistes may owe something to that tradition.
p_artayntes.s4: Herodotus reports that a rumour of victory at Plataea ran through the Greek army before the fight at Mycale and heartened it. He presents the coincidence of the two battles as a sign of divine favour. This is a story shaped to carry a moral, and it is not firm evidence of what happened.
p_artemisia.lead: Artemisia ruled the Greek and Carian city of Halicarnassus under Persian overlordship and led its ships in Xerxes' invasion of Greece in 480 BCE. Almost everything known about her comes from Herodotus, a native of her own city, who made her the shrewdest adviser in the King's war council and the hero of a strange escape at Salamis.
p_artemisia.play: The game's chronicle note presents Artemisia as Herodotus does: leader of five ships in 480 BCE, the best adviser in Xerxes' council, and the captain who rammed a ship of her own side at Salamis. No Persian record confirms these stories.
p_artemisia.s0: Herodotus says Artemisia was the daughter of Lygdamis, Halicarnassian on her father's side and Cretan on her mother's. She took power when her husband died and, though she had a grown son, sailed with Xerxes of her own will. She led five ships from Halicarnassus, Cos, Nisyros and Calydna, which he ranks as the best in the fleet after those of Sidon. Halicarnassus was a Dorian Greek city with a large Carian population, long subject to Persia.
p_artemisia.s1: Before Salamis, Herodotus says, Mardonius polled the commanders at Phalerum on a sea battle. Artemisia alone advised against it: the Greeks were stronger at sea, could not hold out long on Salamis, and would scatter if the army marched on the Peloponnese. Xerxes praised her but followed the majority. After the defeat she urged him to go home and leave Mardonius in Greece, and he sent his sons to Ephesus in her care.
p_artemisia.s2: Herodotus tells that, chased by an Athenian ship during the battle, Artemisia rammed and sank a ship of her own side, from Calynda, with its king Damasithymus aboard. The pursuer took her for a Greek or a deserter and turned away. Xerxes, watching from the shore, thought she had sunk an enemy and said his men had become women and his women men. He adds that the Athenians offered ten thousand drachmas for her capture.
p_artemisia.s3: Herodotus came from Halicarnassus. The Suda, a Byzantine lexicon, says her grandson Lygdamis was the tyrant who drove him into exile, so he may have known her family's own tradition. Some historians read her as a literary type, the wise adviser whose counsel the King ignores, like Croesus or Artabanus. Herodotus himself could not say whether the ramming was deliberate, and no Persian document names her.
p_artemisia.s4: Polyaenus, writing in the 2nd century CE, collected tricks credited to her, such as switching flags to fool pursuers, and Pausanias reports her statue among the Persian figures on the Persian Stoa at Sparta. A romance by Ptolemy Hephaestion, known from Photius, claimed she loved a man of Abydos and leapt to her death from the cliff at Leucas. She is not the same as Artemisia II, wife of Mausolus, who ruled Halicarnassus more than a century later.
p_aryandes.lead: Aryandes was the Persian governor of Egypt, appointed by Cambyses according to Herodotus and still in post under Darius. Herodotus tells of the army he sent against Barca in Libya and of the silver coinage that led Darius to have him killed. The story shows how a satrap's position depended on the King's trust.
p_aryandes.play: Aryandes has no mechanic of his own. The game names him only in the event articles on the siege of Barca and the striking of the daric, where his execution is told.
p_aryandes.s0: Herodotus says Cambyses appointed Aryandes governor of Egypt and that he held the post under Darius. Herodotus gives no account of his earlier career. His rule is known mainly from the episodes Herodotus chose to tell.
p_aryandes.s1: Herodotus says Aryandes sent an army and fleet against Barca to avenge the killing of Arcesilaus III of Cyrene, whose mother Pheretime had sought his help. Amasis, a Maraphian, commanded the land force and Badres, a Pasargad, the fleet. Barca fell after a long siege, and Herodotus says many of its people were settled in Bactria.
p_aryandes.s2: Herodotus tells that the Persians dug tunnels under Barca, and that a smith with a bronze shield detected the digging and the Barcaeans countered it. The Persians then took the city by a sworn truce they never meant to keep. The tale has the shape of a moral story about broken oaths, and it cannot be checked against any Persian record.
p_aryandes.s3: Herodotus says Aryandes struck silver of the purest quality, in rivalry with Darius's gold coinage, which Herodotus calls the purest of all. Darius, he says, then had Aryandes put to death on a charge of rebellion. Herodotus gives the coinage as the reason Darius was angered.
p_aryandes.s4: Modern historians question whether coinage alone could have caused his death and suspect other grounds for the charge. The date of his execution is uncertain, and so is which surviving coins, if any, were his.
p_astyages.lead: Astyages was the last king of the Medes, ruling from Ecbatana until Cyrus, king of Anshan in Persis, overthrew him in about 550 BCE. A Babylonian chronicle records that his own army turned on him and handed him to Cyrus, a fall that made the Persians masters of the Median lands and opened the way to Lydia and Babylon. Herodotus calls Astyages Cyrus's grandfather, but Ctesias denied it.
p_astyages.play: The game mentions Astyages only in its chronicle, as the Median king whose general Harpagus went over to Cyrus. It calls him Cyrus's grandfather on Herodotus's word alone, a tie Ctesias denied.
p_astyages.s0: The Nabonidus Chronicle, under Nabonidus's sixth year (550-549 BCE), names him Ishtumegu. It says he marched against Cyrus, king of Anshan, but his army rebelled, seized him and handed him over. Cyrus then took silver, gold and goods from Ecbatana back to Anshan. Nabonidus's Sippar Cylinder, a building text, also tells of Cyrus scattering the Median host and capturing its king.
p_astyages.s1: Herodotus makes Astyages the son of Cyaxares and says he ruled the Medes for 35 years. He says the Median noble Harpagus, bitter over an old wrong, plotted with Median nobles and urged Cyrus to lead the Persians in revolt. When Astyages sent Harpagus against the Persians, much of the Median army deserted or fled. Herodotus adds that Cyrus kept the old king at his court without harming him until he died.
p_astyages.s2: Herodotus tells that Astyages dreamed the child of his daughter Mandane would reign in his place, so he ordered the newborn Cyrus killed. Harpagus passed the baby to a herdsman, whose wife raised him as her own. When the boy was found out at ten years old, Astyages punished Harpagus by serving him his own son at a feast. The tale follows the old pattern of the hero exposed at birth, and historians do not treat it as history.
p_astyages.s3: Herodotus and Xenophon make Cyrus the son of Astyages' daughter Mandane. Ctesias, a Greek physician at the Persian court around 400 BCE, denied any blood tie and said Cyrus married Astyages' daughter Amytis after the war. He adds that Astyages was later left to die in desert country. The Cyrus Cylinder names only Cyrus's forebears as kings of Anshan, and a Median link may have been claimed later to make him look a rightful heir.
p_astyages.s4: Greek writers describe a great Median empire that the Persians simply took over. Historians still argue over how far Median royal power reached and how organised it was. No Median royal inscriptions or archives have been found, so Assyrian and Babylonian texts and Herodotus are almost all there is. Strabo, writing centuries later, says Cyrus honoured Pasargadae because he defeated Astyages there in the final battle.
p_athamaita.lead: Athamaita led the third rising of Elam against Darius I, in the king's second and third years. Darius's general Gobryas defeated the rebels, captured Athamaita and brought him to the king, who had him killed. He is known only from column V of the Behistun inscription, a late addition that shows how Darius kept recording his victories after the great revolts of 522-521 BCE.
p_athamaita.play: The game's chronicle note matches the inscription: Athamaita led Elam's third revolt, and Gobryas beat and captured him, as column V of Behistun records. The date of about 520-519 BCE is the usual modern estimate.
p_athamaita.s0: Column V of the Behistun inscription says that in Darius's second and third year Elam rose again and made a man called Athamaita its chief. Elam had already rebelled twice. The first rising, under Açina, was quickly put down. In the second, under Martiya, the Elamites killed their own leader as Darius approached. This third rising came after the main wars of succession were over, which suggests Persian control of Elam remained fragile.
p_athamaita.s1: Darius says he sent an army under Gobryas, a Persian and one of the six men who had helped him take the throne. Gobryas fought the Elamites, defeated them and took Athamaita prisoner. He brought him to Darius, who put him to death, and the king says Elam then became his again. The text adds that the Elamites had been faithless and did not worship Auramazda, a charge Darius makes in this column but not in the earlier accounts of revolt, where he blames the Lie.
p_athamaita.s2: Column V was carved after the first four columns and exists only in Old Persian, without the Elamite and Babylonian versions that accompany the main text. It records the Elamite campaign and a campaign against the Saka. The captive Saka leader Skunkha was added to the end of the line of bound rebels on the relief, but no figure of Athamaita appears there.
p_athamaita.s3: No Greek writer mentions Athamaita, so everything rests on Darius's short report. Some scholars connect him with Atta-hamiti-Inshushinak, an Elamite king known from an inscription found at Susa, which would make him a member of a local royal line. Others date that king earlier, in the Neo-Elamite period before Darius, and treat the likeness of the names as coincidence. The question remains open.
p_atossa.lead: Atossa was a daughter of Cyrus the Great who, by Herodotus's account, was married in turn to Cambyses, to the Magus who seized the throne, and to Darius. Her son by Darius was Xerxes. Greek writers made her the most powerful woman at the Persian court, but the Persian record barely names her, if at all, so her real influence is hard to measure.
p_atossa.play: The game's chronicle note follows Herodotus but calls her a wife of Bardiya where Herodotus says the Magus; who that ruler really was is disputed. No Persian text credits her with Xerxes' succession.
p_atossa.s0: Herodotus says Atossa was a daughter of Cyrus, married first to her brother Cambyses and then to the Magus who ruled after him. When Darius took the throne he married her, her sister Artystone, Parmys, a granddaughter of Cyrus, and Phaidyme, daughter of Otanes. Modern historians read these marriages as Darius's way of tying his new line to the house of Cyrus.
p_atossa.s1: Herodotus tells of a dispute between Artobazanes, Darius's eldest son by an earlier wife, and Xerxes, the eldest son born after Darius became king. He says Demaratus of Sparta advised Xerxes on his claim, but adds that Xerxes would have won anyway, because Atossa held all the power. This is his judgement, not a Persian report.
p_atossa.s2: Darius's inscriptions do not name Atossa. Xerxes, in a text from Persepolis, says Darius had other sons but made him the greatest after himself, and does not mention his mother. The Fortification tablets show royal women such as Irtashduna, the Artystone of Herodotus, and Irdabama running estates and workforces, so queens could hold real economic power.
p_atossa.s3: Historians disagree over how far to trust the Greek picture of Atossa as the queen who ruled the palace. Some accept that her descent from Cyrus gave Xerxes a strong claim. Others note that Greek writers liked to show Persian courts run by scheming women, and that the tablets document other wives of Darius far better. A woman called Udusana in one Fortification tablet may be Atossa, but the identification is uncertain.
p_atossa.s4: Herodotus tells how the Greek doctor Democedes cured a growth on her breast and in return had her urge Darius to attack Greece, a tale shaped to explain a war through the bedchamber. Aeschylus's Persians, staged at Athens in 472 BCE, shows Xerxes' mother waiting at Susa for news of Salamis, though the play never names her. The Greek writer Hellanicus, as quoted by the Christian author Tatian, made her the first person to compose letters.
p_bardiya.lead: In 522 BCE a man calling himself Bardiya, the younger son of Cyrus, held the throne for some months. Darius killed him and said he was Gaumata, a magus who had stolen the dead prince's name. That story justified Darius's own kingship, and historians still argue over whether the murdered king was a fraud or Cyrus's real son.
p_bardiya.play: The game's chronicle gives him both names and dates his rule to some months in 522 BCE. It sets Darius's claim that he was an impostor beside the modern view that he may have been the real Bardiya.
p_bardiya.s0: In the Behistun inscription Darius says that Cambyses secretly killed his brother Bardiya before marching on Egypt. In March 522 BCE a magus named Gaumata rose in Persis claiming to be Bardiya, and by July he was king over the lands, after which Cambyses died. In September 522 BCE Darius and six helpers, whom he names, killed Gaumata at the fortress of Sikayauvati in Media, and the relief shows Gaumata lying on his back under Darius's foot.
p_bardiya.s1: Babylonian business tablets are dated by the reign of Bardiya as king, so for some months scribes there treated him as the lawful ruler. Darius himself says that Gaumata had destroyed places of worship and taken pastures, herds, servants and houses from the people, and that he restored them. What these measures were is unclear, but they point to a ruler who had policies of his own.
p_bardiya.s2: Herodotus calls the prince Smerdis and says Cambyses had Prexaspes murder him after a dream. Two magi brothers then seized the throne, one of them also named Smerdis and closely resembling the prince. Herodotus says this false king freed his subjects from tribute and military service for three years and was mourned by all in Asia except the Persians. Seven Persians killed the magi, and the Persians kept the day as a festival called the Magophonia.
p_bardiya.s3: Herodotus tells how Otanes grew suspicious of the king. His daughter Phaidyme, who was one of the king's wives, felt for his ears while he slept and found none. Cyrus had once cut off the magus's ears as a punishment. The tale has the shape of a folk story of the unmasked impostor, and nothing outside Herodotus supports it.
p_bardiya.s4: Many historians suspect that Darius, who came from a side branch of the royal house, killed the true son of Cyrus and invented the impostor. A royal brother murdered in secret, with no one noticing, is hard to believe, and Darius's inscription was written to justify him. Others answer that no evidence disproves his account. Herodotus and Ctesias, who calls the magus Sphendadates, add detail but probably drew on the official version, so the question remains open.
p_bubares.lead: Bubares was a Persian noble of the late sixth and early fifth centuries, known almost entirely from Herodotus. He married into the royal house of Macedon and, with Artachaees, directed the digging of Xerxes' canal through the Athos peninsula. That made him one of the officials who prepared the invasion of Greece in 480 BCE.
p_bubares.play: The Athos level's chronicle names Bubares, son of Megabazus, as overseer of the canal together with Artachaees, following Herodotus 7.22. The game says nothing further about his career.
p_bubares.s0: Herodotus says Bubares was the son of Megabazus, the general Darius left in Thrace after the Scythian campaign of about 513 BCE. Megabazus subdued Perinthus and the Thracians of the coast. He then sent envoys to Amyntas, king of Macedon, to demand earth and water, the tokens of submission to the King.
p_bubares.s1: Herodotus tells how the Persian envoys behaved insolently at a feast and were killed on the orders of the young Alexander, son of Amyntas. When the Persians sent a search party, Bubares commanded it. Alexander silenced him with a large gift of money and his sister Gygaea in marriage, and the inquiry was dropped.
p_bubares.s2: Many historians doubt the murder of the envoys. Alexander later presented himself to the Greeks as their secret friend, and the tale suits that claim. The marriage of Bubares and Gygaea is more widely accepted. It fits a known Persian practice of binding subject rulers to Persian noble families, and Macedon did become a subject kingdom.
p_bubares.s3: Herodotus names Bubares and Artachaees, son of Artaeus, as the Persians in charge of cutting the canal across the Athos isthmus. He says the preparations went on for about three years and that men from many peoples dug under the lash. He adds that the Phoenicians showed the most skill, cutting the trench wider at the top so its sides would not fall in.
p_bubares.s4: No monument or document from the period is securely known to name Bubares, so his career rests on Herodotus. The canal itself is real. Surveys and cores taken across the isthmus in the 1990s traced a filled-in channel along the line Herodotus describes.
p_bubares.s5: Bubares and Gygaea had a son, Amyntas, named after his Macedonian grandfather. Herodotus says the King gave him Alabanda in Phrygia to hold, though the known city of that name lay in Caria. This family tie was one reason, he explains, that Mardonius sent Alexander of Macedon as his envoy to Athens in 479 BCE.
p_callimachus.lead: Callimachus of Aphidna was the polemarch, the war archon of Athens, in the year of Marathon. Herodotus says that when the ten generals split over whether to fight the Persian landing force, his vote decided for battle. He led the Athenian right wing and died in the fighting at the Persian ships.
p_callimachus.play: The game's chronicle follows Herodotus: deciding vote, right wing, death at the ships. It treats his role as settled, though historians still argue over whether he, not Miltiades, held overall command.
p_callimachus.s0: Herodotus says the ten Athenian generals at Marathon were evenly divided, some fearing to engage the larger Persian force under Datis and Artaphernes. Miltiades went to Callimachus, who as polemarch had a vote equal to the generals', and urged him to choose battle for the freedom of Athens. Callimachus voted to fight. Herodotus adds that he had been chosen by lot.
p_callimachus.s1: Herodotus explains that Athenian custom gave the polemarch command of the right wing, so Callimachus stood there in the battle line. After the Athenians broke the Persian wings and then the centre, they pursued the fleeing troops to the shore and tried to seize the ships. Callimachus was killed there, fighting bravely, along with the general Stesilaus, while Cynegirus lost a hand grasping a ship's stern.
p_callimachus.s2: Herodotus makes Miltiades the real leader and has Callimachus only cast a vote. The Aristotelian Constitution of the Athenians says the polemarch then led the whole army, and that archons were chosen by lot only from 487 BCE. Many historians therefore think Callimachus was elected, held formal command, and that Herodotus's story was shaped by later praise of Miltiades and his family.
p_callimachus.s3: Fragments survive of a tall marble column that carried a winged figure, dedicated on the Acropolis with an inscription naming Callimachus of Aphidna as polemarch. The text is broken and its restoration is argued over, but it probably recorded a vow fulfilled after Marathon and was set up after his death. The monument was smashed, probably when the Persians sacked the Acropolis in 480 BCE.
p_callimachus.s4: Callimachus was shown beside Miltiades in the Marathon painting of the Painted Stoa, made a few decades after the battle; Pausanias saw and described it centuries later. The orator Polemon of Laodicea and other writers of the Roman period went much further, telling that his body was pierced by so many spears that it stayed upright after death. That image belongs to later rhetoric, not to Herodotus.
p_cambyses.lead: Cambyses, son of Cyrus the Great, was king of Persia from 530 to 522 BCE. He added Egypt to the empire in 525 BCE and ruled it as pharaoh, bringing one of the oldest kingdoms of the Near East under Persian rule. Greek tradition remembered him as a mad tyrant, while Egyptian inscriptions and Darius's own record tell different stories.
p_cambyses.play: The Memphis level is set in 525 BCE, the year of his conquest. The chronicle note's return home to face a usurper follows Herodotus; Darius's inscription says only that he died after the magus seized power.
p_cambyses.s0: The Cyrus Cylinder names Cambyses as Cyrus's son and asks the god Marduk to bless him alongside his father. The Nabonidus Chronicle records that after the capture of Babylon in 539 BCE, Cambyses son of Cyrus took part in a rite at the temple of Nabu during the New Year festival. Babylonian tablets briefly date by him as king of Babylon while Cyrus still reigned, and he succeeded his father in 530 BCE.
p_cambyses.s1: Herodotus says Cambyses marched on Egypt with help from Phanes of Halicarnassus, a mercenary officer who had deserted the pharaoh Amasis, and from an Arab king who supplied water across the desert to Egypt. Amasis died before the invasion, and his son Psamtik III met the Persians near Pelusium and was defeated. Memphis was besieged until it surrendered; Herodotus adds that Psamtik was later put to death for plotting revolt.
p_cambyses.s2: The statue of Udjahorresnet, a naval commander and physician of Sais, records that Cambyses took a pharaoh's throne name, Mesutira, and at Udjahorresnet's request cleared foreign troops from the temple of Neith and restored its rites. A stela from the Serapeum at Saqqara shows an Apis bull buried in his sixth year in a sarcophagus given by the king. These sources present him as a pharaoh who honoured the gods.
p_cambyses.s3: Herodotus calls Cambyses mad, saying he stabbed the Apis bull, mocked Egyptian gods and killed his brother and his sister-wife. The royal burial of an Apis in his reign sits badly with the stabbing story, though scholars argue over which bull and which year. Many historians think the hostile picture came from Egyptian priests angered by his cuts to temple revenues, noted in a later Demotic text, and from Persian accounts that served Darius.
p_cambyses.s4: Herodotus says news of a usurper reached Cambyses in Syria; leaping onto his horse, he wounded his thigh on his own sword and died at a town called Ecbatana. Like Herodotus, Darius's Behistun inscription says Cambyses had secretly killed his brother Bardiya and that a magus, Gaumata, then seized the throne, but it says only that Cambyses died his own death. Scholars debate what that phrase means, and whether the usurper was in fact Bardiya.
p_cleomenes.lead: Cleomenes I was the Agiad king of Sparta from about 520 BCE to about 490 BCE. He drove the tyrant Hippias out of Athens, crushed Argos at Sepeia and turned away Aristagoras of Miletus when the Ionians sought help against Persia, then forced out his fellow king Demaratus, who fled to Darius. Nearly everything known of him comes from Herodotus, whose portrait of him is largely hostile.
p_cleomenes.play: The game names Cleomenes only in its chronicle, as the Spartan king who refused Aristagoras once he learned how far inland Susa lay, following Herodotus 5.49-51.
p_cleomenes.s0: Herodotus says Cleomenes was the son of Anaxandridas by a second wife, whom the ephors made the king take because his first marriage was childless. The first wife later bore Dorieus, Leonidas and Cleombrotus. Cleomenes succeeded as the elder son, probably about 520 BCE. Herodotus adds that the passed-over Dorieus left Sparta to found colonies abroad.
p_cleomenes.s1: In about 499 BCE Aristagoras came to Sparta with a bronze map of the world and urged an attack on the King. Herodotus says Cleomenes asked how far Susa lay from the coast. When told it was a three months' journey, he ordered the Milesian out of Sparta by sunset. Aristagoras then offered bribes of rising size, and Cleomenes' young daughter Gorgo warned her father that the stranger would corrupt him, so he left the room.
p_cleomenes.s2: In 510 BCE Cleomenes led the Spartan force that expelled Hippias and his family from Athens. A few years later he returned to back Isagoras against Cleisthenes, but the Athenians besieged him on the Acropolis and he left under a truce. His larger invasion of Attica about 506 BCE broke up at Eleusis when the Corinthians and his fellow king Demaratus withdrew.
p_cleomenes.s3: When Darius's heralds asked the Greeks for earth and water about 491 BCE, Aegina submitted, and Cleomenes went to arrest the men responsible, but Demaratus worked against him. Herodotus says Cleomenes then joined with Leotychides and, through a bribed go-between, had the Delphic oracle declare Demaratus illegitimate. The deposed king fled to Darius, received lands and cities in Asia, and later accompanied Xerxes in 480 BCE.
p_cleomenes.s4: Herodotus reports that when the Delphi plot came out Cleomenes fled, was recalled, went mad and cut himself to death with a knife while in the stocks, probably about 490 BCE. Most Greeks blamed the bribed oracle, the Athenians his ravaging of the sacred precinct at Eleusis, and the Argives his killing of suppliants and burning of their grove after Sepeia. The Spartans blamed unmixed wine, a habit learned from Scythian envoys; some modern historians suspect murder.
p_coes.lead: Coes, son of Erxander, was a Greek from Mytilene on Lesbos who followed Darius on the Scythian campaign. Herodotus says he advised Darius to keep the bridge over the Ister standing, and that Darius rewarded him with the rule of his home city. Only Herodotus tells the story.
p_coes.play: The game names Coes only in the event articles on the debate at the Ister bridge and Darius's Scythian campaign. He has no figure, building or mechanic of his own.
p_coes.s0: Herodotus names Coes, son of Erxander, as a commander of the Mytileneans who went with Darius to the Ister. He appears among the Greek leaders who served the King there, alongside Histiaeus of Miletus. Herodotus is the only ancient writer to name him.
p_coes.s1: Herodotus says Coes gave Darius advice as the King considered the bridge: it should stay in place, guarded by the Ionians who had built it, in case the campaign went badly. Darius approved. Later, when the Scythians urged the Ionians to break the bridge, Herodotus reports a separate debate in which Miltiades the Athenian favoured breaking it and Histiaeus argued against.
p_coes.s2: Herodotus says Darius offered Coes a reward of his choice, and Coes asked for the tyranny of Mytilene. Herodotus reports that when the Ionian Revolt began, the people of Mytilene seized Coes and stoned him to death.
p_coes.s3: No Persian text mentions Coes or the debate, so the account rests on Herodotus alone. Historians argue over how much of the Ister bridge episode and the speeches goes back to real events and how much was shaped by later tellings and by the Ionian Revolt. The course of the Scythian campaign itself remains uncertain.
p_croesus.lead: Croesus was the last king of Lydia, whose wealth from the gold of the Pactolus became proverbial among the Greeks. He ruled the Greek cities of western Asia Minor until Cyrus defeated him and took Sardis, probably in the 540s BCE. The fall of Lydia gave Persia its first foothold on the Aegean and brought the Ionian Greeks under the King.
p_croesus.play: The game's chronicle note presents Croesus as Herodotus does, as Cyrus's counsellor sent home with Cambyses. That survival is Herodotus's story; no Persian or Babylonian text names him.
p_croesus.s0: Herodotus says Croesus, son of Alyattes, was the first foreign ruler to make the Greeks of Asia pay tribute, attacking Ephesus first and then the other Ionian and Aeolian cities. He made alliances with Sparta, with Amasis of Egypt and with Babylon. After Cyrus overthrew Astyages, Croesus crossed the Halys and fought an indecisive battle at Pteria. When he went home, Cyrus followed and took Sardis on the fourteenth day of the siege.
p_croesus.s1: Fragments of marble column bases from the archaic temple of Artemis at Ephesus carry a short, partly restored inscription naming King Croesus as dedicator. They are now in the British Museum. They support Herodotus, who says Croesus gave most of that temple's columns. His rich gifts to Delphi are known mainly from Herodotus, who says some were damaged when the temple there burned.
p_croesus.s2: The usual date of 547 or 546 BCE rests on Greek chronology and on the Nabonidus Chronicle, which says Cyrus marched against a king in Nabonidus's ninth year. The name of that country is broken, and many scholars now doubt that it reads Lydia. Excavations at Sardis found a violent destruction of the mid-sixth century with many arrowheads, which fits a Persian siege. Historians also disagree over whether Croesus really survived the city's fall.
p_croesus.s3: Herodotus tells that Cyrus placed Croesus on a pyre. Croesus called on Solon, who had warned him that no man should be called happy before his end, and Apollo sent rain to put out the fire. The dates make a meeting with Solon very unlikely. In the poet Bacchylides, writing in 468 BCE, Croesus climbs the pyre by choice and Apollo carries him to the Hyperboreans.
p_croesus.s4: In Herodotus, Croesus advised Cyrus to turn the rebellious Lydians from arms to trade and music rather than enslave them. He also urged Cyrus to cross the Araxes against the Massagetae, a campaign that ended in Cyrus's death. Cyrus sent him back to Persia in Cambyses' keeping. Herodotus later places him in Egypt rebuking Cambyses, who tried to shoot him. Nothing is recorded of his death.
p_cyaxares.lead: Cyaxares was remembered by the Greeks as the king who made Media a great power. Herodotus credits him with reorganising the Median army, fighting the Lydians and taking Nineveh. Darius's Behistun inscription shows that the rebel Fravartish later claimed descent from him.
p_cyaxares.play: The game names Cyaxares only in Chronicle entries and event articles, such as the revolt of Fravartish. He has no figure, place or mechanic of his own. The note that he gave Median boys to Scythian exiles to train follows Herodotus's tale, which is told as a moral story.
p_cyaxares.s0: Herodotus says Cyaxares was the son of Phraortes and the father of Astyages. He reports that Cyaxares was the first to divide the Median troops into separate spear, archer and horse units, where they had earlier been mixed together. Herodotus treats this reform as the basis of Median strength.
p_cyaxares.s1: Herodotus says Scythians invaded Media while Cyaxares was besieging Nineveh, defeated the Medes, and ruled Asia for twenty-eight years. He says Cyaxares then killed many of them at a banquet and recovered his power. Historians treat the length and the details of this episode with caution.
p_cyaxares.s2: Herodotus tells that Cyaxares took in Scythian exiles and gave them Median boys to learn the Scythian language and archery. When they came back from hunting with no game, he says, they served him the flesh of a boy and fled to Lydia. This reads as a tale shaped by a moral, and not as a firm record.
p_cyaxares.s3: Herodotus says Cyaxares fought Alyattes of Lydia for six years, and that a solar eclipse, which he says Thales had foretold, stopped a battle. He says Syennesis of Cilicia and Labynetus of Babylon arranged the peace, sealed by a marriage between Alyattes' daughter and Astyages. The eclipse is usually dated to 585 BCE, but modern historians dispute the identification and the date.
p_cyaxares.s4: Herodotus says Cyaxares captured Nineveh. The Babylonian Chronicle of the fall of Nineveh, a document from the time, shows that the city fell in 612 BCE to the Babylonians and the Medes together. It names the Median king as Umakishtar, the Babylonian form of Cyaxares, fighting beside Nabopolassar of Babylon, not alone as in Herodotus. How large the Median role was cannot be settled from the sources.
p_cyaxares.s5: In the Behistun inscription Darius says that Fravartish, a Median rebel, called himself Khshathrita and claimed descent from Cyaxares, whom the text names Uvakhshtra. The claim shows that the name still carried weight among the Medes about sixty years after his death, though Darius presents it only as a lie.
p_cyrus.lead: Cyrus II, king of Anshan in Persis, overthrew the Median king in about 550 BCE, then conquered Lydia and the Greek cities of western Asia Minor, and in 539 BCE took Babylon. These conquests made the Persians rulers of the largest empire the Near East had yet seen. He founded Pasargadae, died in 530 BCE, and his stone tomb still stands there.
p_cyrus.play: The Pasargadae level is set in 530 BCE, the year Cyrus died. The game's scene of Cyrus commissioning Darius is dramatized; Herodotus (1.209) says only that Cyrus dreamed the young Darius would come to rule Asia and Europe.
p_cyrus.s0: On the clay cylinder written for him at Babylon, Cyrus calls himself son of Cambyses, grandson of Cyrus and descendant of Teispes, all kings of Anshan. Anshan was the old Elamite name for a city and region in the highlands of Persis. The Nabonidus Chronicle records that the army of the Median king Astyages rebelled and handed him over to Cyrus. Cyrus then took Ecbatana and carried its silver and gold to Anshan, in about 550 BCE.
p_cyrus.s1: Herodotus tells how Croesus of Lydia crossed the Halys river to attack Cyrus and fought an indecisive battle at Pteria. Cyrus then followed him home, besieged Sardis and took it. Cyrus's generals, first Mazares and then the Mede Harpagus, went on to subdue the Greek cities of Ionia and Caria. The date is uncertain: a Babylonian chronicle entry for 547 BCE was once read as naming Lydia, but the name in it is damaged.
p_cyrus.s2: The Nabonidus Chronicle records a battle at Opis in 539 BCE and the taking of Sippar without battle. Two days later Cyrus's army entered Babylon under Ugbaru, and Cyrus himself followed about two weeks after. The Cyrus Cylinder, written by Babylonian scribes, says Marduk chose him to replace a neglectful king and that he returned gods and displaced people to their homes. It is royal propaganda in an old Mesopotamian style, not a charter of rights.
p_cyrus.s3: Babylonian documents show that his reign ended in 530 BCE, but no record says how. Herodotus says he fell fighting the Massagetae beyond the Araxes, and that their queen Tomyris steeped his severed head in blood. Herodotus admits that other versions existed. Ctesias has him die of a wound taken fighting the Derbices, and Xenophon makes him die peacefully at home among his sons.
p_cyrus.s4: Herodotus tells that Astyages, warned by dreams, ordered his infant grandson Cyrus killed. The herdsman told to expose the child raised him instead, and at about ten the boy was recognised by his royal manner at play. Herodotus says he chose this version from several that Persians told. It follows an old pattern of tales about an abandoned future king, and Ctesias denied that Cyrus was related to Astyages at all.
p_dadarshish.lead: Dadarshish was a general whom Darius sent against the Armenian rebels in the revolts that followed the killing of Gaumata. He is known from the Behistun inscription, where Darius names him as his servant and lists three battles he won. A man of the same name appears later in the text as satrap of Bactria, and historians argue over whether this is one person.
p_dadarshish.play: The game names him only in the event articles, chiefly the war in Armenia, and gives him no mechanic of its own. Its description of him as the five-battle general departs from Behistun, which credits him with three battles and Vaumisa with two.
p_dadarshish.s0: The Behistun inscription says that Armenia rebelled and that Darius sent Dadarshish, whom it calls an Armenian and his servant, against the rebels. The text presents his army as acting on the King's authority. It tells nothing of his earlier life.
p_dadarshish.s1: Darius lists three battles fought by Dadarshish against the rebels, at Zuzahya, at Tigra and at Uyama, each with a date by the Old Persian calendar. In each Darius credits the victory to the help of Auramazda. The report is the King's own, written after the events.
p_dadarshish.s2: Darius also sent a Persian servant, Vaumisa, against the same rebels. The inscription gives Vaumisa two battles, so the war had two field commanders, and the five battles belong to the two men together.
p_dadarshish.s3: Later the inscription names a Dadarshish, called a Persian and the King's servant, as satrap in Bactria who sent an army against rebels in Margiana. Some historians identify him with the general of the Armenian war, while others think two men shared the name. The differing labels, Armenian in one place and Persian in the other, feed the doubt.
p_dadarshish.s4: Dadarshish is known only from the royal inscription, which was composed to praise Darius. No Greek writer is known to name him. His own view of events is therefore lost.
p_darius.lead: Darius I ruled the Persian empire from 522 to 486 BCE. A Persian noble outside Cyrus's direct line, he seized the throne after Cambyses died, put down a year of revolts, and gave the empire much of the tribute system, building programme and royal ideology it kept for nearly two centuries. Herodotus says he had earlier served Cambyses in Egypt as a spear-bearer.
p_darius.play: The game's chronicle credits Darius with organising the empire into satrapies. Satraps already governed under Cyrus and Cambyses; Darius reorganised their tribute rather than creating the system.
p_darius.s0: In the Behistun inscription Darius says that a magus named Gaumata seized the kingship by claiming to be Cyrus's son Bardiya, whom Cambyses had secretly killed, and that Cambyses then died. With six Persian nobles, whom he names, Darius killed Gaumata at a fortress in Media in autumn 522 BCE. He then claims to have fought nineteen battles and captured nine rebel kings within a single year, in lands from Persis and Elam to Babylonia, Media and the east.
p_darius.s1: Many historians doubt the Behistun story. Darius's father Hystaspes was still alive, and Darius's right to rule rested on a shared ancestor, Achaemenes, whom some scholars think he promoted to tie his family to Cyrus's. The man he killed may have been the real Bardiya, with the impostor tale serving to justify a coup. Herodotus tells a similar story, probably drawn from Persian informants who repeated Darius's version.
p_darius.s2: Darius began the stone terrace at Persepolis about 518 BCE and built a palace at Susa. Its foundation charter lists materials and craftsmen drawn from across the empire. The Elamite Fortification tablets from Persepolis, dated 509 to 493 BCE, record rations for workers, travellers on the royal roads and offerings to many gods. He was buried in a rock-cut tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam, inscribed with a statement of his kingship.
p_darius.s3: Herodotus says Darius divided the empire into twenty provinces, each paying a fixed tribute, and that the Persians called him a shopkeeper for it. Historians accept that he set tribute on a more regular footing. But satraps already governed under Cyrus and Cambyses, and Darius's own lists of subject lands, 23 at Behistun, do not match Herodotus's twenty provinces.
p_darius.s4: Herodotus tells that about 513 BCE Darius crossed the Bosporus on a bridge of boats built by Mandrocles of Samos and led an army over the Ister against the Scythians, who retreated before him. Later he faced the Ionian revolt of 499-494 BCE and sent Datis and the younger Artaphernes against Eretria and Athens, a force defeated at Marathon in 490 BCE. He died in 486 BCE while preparing a new invasion, as Egypt rose in revolt.
p_datis.lead: Datis was a Mede who commanded the seaborne expedition Darius sent against Eretria and Athens in 490 BCE, sharing the command with Artaphernes the younger. He took Naxos and Eretria and treated Delos with respect, but his army was defeated at Marathon. He was one of several Medes who held high command under the Persian kings, and Greek writers remembered him as the face of the first invasion.
p_datis.play: The Chronicle names Datis as the Median commander of 490 BCE who spared Delos, took Eretria and lost at Marathon, which follows Herodotus. It leaves out that he shared the command with Artaphernes the younger.
p_datis.s0: One Persepolis Fortification tablet, dated to about 494 BCE, records travel rations for a man called Datiya who carried a sealed document of the King and was going to the King. David Lewis argued that this was Datis and linked his journey to the years of the Ionian revolt. If the identification is right, it is the only trace of him in Persian records, and it shows a trusted officer travelling on the royal ration system some years before Marathon.
p_datis.s1: Herodotus says Darius gave the command to Datis, a Mede, and to his own nephew Artaphernes son of Artaphernes, in place of Mardonius. The fleet sailed from Cilicia through the islands and burned Naxos. At Delos Datis reassured the islanders and burned a large offering of frankincense on Apollo's altar. Eretria held out for six days until two citizens betrayed it; its temples were burned and its people taken captive.
p_datis.s2: Guided by the exiled Athenian tyrant Hippias, the army landed at Marathon, where Athenians and Plataeans defeated it; Herodotus gives 6,400 Persian dead against 192 Athenians. Sailing home, Datis found a gilded statue of Apollo on a Phoenician ship and left it at Delos to be returned to Delium. He brought the Eretrian captives to Darius, who settled them at Ardericca in Cissia, and Herodotus later names two sons of Datis among Xerxes' cavalry commanders.
p_datis.s3: Ctesias, in the summary made by Photius, says Datis was killed at Marathon and that the Athenians refused to give up his body. Herodotus has him alive after the battle, sailing home by Mykonos and Delos and delivering the Eretrians to Darius. Most historians prefer Herodotus here, since Ctesias is often unreliable on this period, but the question cannot be fully settled.
p_datis.s4: The Lindian Chronicle, an inscription set up on Rhodes in 99, tells how Datis besieged Lindos until its water ran out. Athena appeared in a dream and promised rain. When the rain fell, Datis made peace and dedicated his own robe, torque and other ornaments to the goddess. The story was written down four centuries later to glorify the temple, and Herodotus does not mention it.
p_demaratus.lead: Demaratus was one of Sparta's two kings until about 491 BCE, when his fellow king Cleomenes had him deposed. He fled to Darius, received lands in western Anatolia and, according to Herodotus, marched with Xerxes in 480 BCE as an adviser on Greek and especially Spartan ways. Almost everything known of him comes from Herodotus, and no Persian document names him.
p_demaratus.play: The game shows Demaratus only in its chronicle note, as the exile who told Xerxes that Spartans fear their law more than his subjects fear him. This follows Herodotus 7.104, a speech probably of Herodotus's own making.
p_demaratus.s0: Herodotus says Demaratus, son of Ariston, belonged to the Eurypontid royal house, the junior line of Sparta's double kingship. During the invasion of Attica in about 506 BCE he broke with the Agiad king Cleomenes and went home, and the army broke up. Herodotus links this quarrel to a Spartan rule that both kings should not lead the same campaign. The rivalry flared again when Demaratus obstructed Cleomenes' action against Aegina in about 491 BCE.
p_demaratus.s1: Herodotus tells how Cleomenes backed Leotychides, who claimed that Demaratus was not truly Ariston's son. The question was put to Delphi, and Cleomenes used a Delphian named Cobon to persuade the priestess to give the answer he wanted. Demaratus was removed and Leotychides became king. When the fraud later came out, Herodotus says, Cobon was exiled and the priestess lost her office.
p_demaratus.s2: Leotychides insulted Demaratus at the Gymnopaediae festival. Demaratus then left Sparta, evaded pursuit by way of Elis and Zacynthus, and reached Darius, who Herodotus says gave him land and cities. Xenophon reports that his descendants Eurysthenes and Procles still ruled Teuthrania and Halisarna in Mysia in 399, but says the land was a reward for joining the expedition against Greece. Historians see such grants as a regular Persian way of rewarding useful exiles.
p_demaratus.s3: Herodotus places Demaratus beside Xerxes at several points. At Doriscus he warned that the Spartans would fight whatever the odds. Before Thermopylae he explained that Spartans combing their hair were preparing to die. After the pass fell he urged sending ships to Cythera to distract Sparta, a plan Herodotus says Achaemenes talked Xerxes out of.
p_demaratus.s4: Historians treat the Doriscus dialogue as largely Herodotus's own composition, setting free Greeks ruled by law against subjects ruled by one man. Herodotus also credits Demaratus with advising Xerxes on the succession, while adding that Xerxes would have become king anyway through Atossa's power. His tale of a warning sent to Sparta under the wax of a writing tablet is doubted, by Herodotus as to motive and by some scholars as a later addition.
p_demaratus.s5: Herodotus gives a folk tale behind the doubt over his birth. His mother, an ugly infant, was made beautiful by a woman who appeared at Helen's shrine, and Ariston later won her from his friend Agetus by a trick. She is said to have told Demaratus that his father was either Ariston or the hero Astrabacus, who came to her in Ariston's likeness. The tale has the shape of a story, not a record.
p_dieneces.lead: Dieneces was a Spartan citizen soldier who fought with Leonidas at Thermopylae in 480 BCE and probably died in the last stand. Herodotus reports that he was said to be the bravest of all the Spartans and Thespians there, and preserves a dry remark about Persian arrows that made him remembered. Nothing else is known of his life, and his fame rests on that single passage.
p_dieneces.play: The game mentions Dieneces in a chronicle note that follows Herodotus 7.226. It leaves out that Herodotus gives the story as hearsay and names a man of Trachis as the one who warned about the arrows.
p_dieneces.s0: Herodotus says that of all the Lacedaemonians and Thespians who held the pass, the one said to have been best was Dieneces, a Spartiate, meaning a full Spartan citizen. He gives no father, age or rank for him, and does not describe how he died. Like almost all of the Spartans at Thermopylae, he probably fell on the last day, when the Greeks were surrounded after the Persians came round by the mountain path.
p_dieneces.s1: Herodotus passes on a story told about Dieneces. Before the fighting began, a man of Trachis warned that the Persian archers were so many that their arrows would hide the sun. Dieneces, unmoved, answered that this was good news, since the Greeks would then fight in the shade. Herodotus adds that he was said to have left other sayings of this kind as memorials, though he records none of them.
p_dieneces.s2: Herodotus names two more Spartans as outstanding, the brothers Alpheus and Maron, sons of Orsiphantus. Among the Thespians he names a man called Dithyrambus, son of Harmatides. The list shows that Greek tradition after the battle ranked individual courage, and that the Thespians who stayed to the end were also remembered.
p_dieneces.s3: The shade remark belongs to a type of short, dry answer that Greeks thought typically Spartan, and it travelled. Plutarch's collection of Spartan sayings gives a version of it to Leonidas. Cicero tells it in Latin of an unnamed Spartan answering a boasting Persian. These later retellings show the line becoming a free-floating moral example of contempt for death rather than a remembered fact about one man.
p_dieneces.s4: No Persian source mentions Thermopylae, Dieneces or the Spartan stand, and the royal inscriptions of Xerxes are silent on the Greek campaign. Greek writers describe Persian infantry shooting in volleys from behind wicker shields, so the image of massed arrows fits their picture of Persian fighting. But Herodotus puts Xerxes' host at over five million with its followers, a figure historians judge greatly exaggerated, so the scale of the archery belongs to the story.
p_dionysius_phocaea.lead: Dionysius was a general from Phocaea, an Ionian Greek city, during the revolt of the Ionians against Darius. Herodotus says he briefly trained the rebel fleet at Lade in 494 BCE. After the Ionian defeat he took up raiding at sea. His story is our main picture of how the revolt's last fleet prepared, quarrelled and broke apart.
p_dionysius_phocaea.play: The game's chronicle names him as the Ionians' admiral at Lade and follows Herodotus closely. Herodotus, though, describes him drilling the fleet by consent rather than holding a formal supreme command.
p_dionysius_phocaea.s0: In 494 BCE the rebel Ionians gathered their ships at the island of Lade, off Miletus, while a Persian army besieged the city by land. Herodotus counts 353 Ionian ships, of which Phocaea, led by Dionysius, sent only three. Against them he sets 600 ships on the King's side, drawn from the Phoenicians, Cypriots, Cilicians and Egyptians. Historians treat both totals with caution.
p_dionysius_phocaea.s1: Herodotus says Dionysius told the assembled Ionians that their affairs stood on a knife's edge between freedom and slavery, and he offered to train them if they would accept hardship. Each day he led the ships out in column, practised rowing through an enemy line, and kept the marines under arms. After seven days the crews, unused to such labour, complained of heat and exhaustion. They pitched tents on the island and refused to go on.
p_dionysius_phocaea.s2: The Samian leaders had already been approached through Aeaces, son of Syloson and their former tyrant. Herodotus says that when the fleets met, most Samian ships sailed away, leaving only eleven, and the Lesbians followed them. The Chians fought hard and lost heavily. The Ionian fleet was broken, and Miletus was taken soon afterwards.
p_dionysius_phocaea.s3: Herodotus says Dionysius, seeing the cause lost, captured three enemy ships and did not go home, since he expected Phocaea to be enslaved with the rest of Ionia. He sailed to Phoenicia, sank merchant ships and took much money. He then went to Sicily and raided Carthaginians and Etruscans but never Greeks. Phocaean emigrants who had abandoned their city to Harpagus had fought these same peoples at sea off Corsica about fifty years earlier.
p_dionysius_phocaea.s4: No Persian document mentions Lade or Dionysius, so everything rests on Herodotus and his Greek informants. Those informants had reasons to blame Ionian softness and to excuse the Samian desertion. Historians debate whether Dionysius held overall command or only led the training. They also debate what the diekplous he drilled actually involved in 494 BCE, and some read the seven days of drill as a moral tale.
p_ephialtes.lead: Ephialtes son of Eurydemus was a Greek from Malis, the district around Thermopylae. Herodotus says he came to Xerxes hoping for a large reward and told him of a path over the mountain that led behind the Greek position. Persian troops under Hydarnes used it, and Leonidas's force in the pass was surrounded. His name later became a Greek byword for betrayal.
p_ephialtes.play: The game's chronicle follows Herodotus's main version: the Malian who showed Xerxes' men the path for a reward, later with a price on his head. It leaves out the rival names Herodotus reports and rejects.
p_ephialtes.s0: Herodotus says that while Xerxes was unsure how to break the Greek line, Ephialtes came to him expecting a great reward and told him of the path over the mountain. Xerxes was pleased and sent Hydarnes with the troops he commanded. Herodotus adds that the Malians had found the path long before and had used it to lead the Thessalians against the Phocians.
p_ephialtes.s1: According to Herodotus the Persians set out at the hour when lamps were lit, crossed the Asopus and climbed all night along the ridge called Anopaea. At dawn they came on a thousand Phocian hoplites guarding the path. Hydarnes feared they were Spartans and asked Ephialtes who they were. Told they were Phocians, he drove them up the peak, then ignored them and marched down behind the pass.
p_ephialtes.s2: Herodotus says Ephialtes later fled to Thessaly for fear of the Spartans. The delegates of the Amphictyonic council, meeting at Pylae, as Thermopylae was also called, set a price on his head. Later he went to Anticyra and was killed there by Athenades of Trachis, who Herodotus says acted for another reason that he promised to explain but never did; the Spartans honoured Athenades all the same.
p_ephialtes.s3: Herodotus knew a rival story naming Onetes of Carystus and Corydallus of Anticyra as the guides, and rejected it because the bounty was set on Ephialtes. Diodorus speaks only of a man of Trachis. Local people knew the path well, and Herodotus says the Greeks themselves learned of it from the Trachinians; many historians think the Persians could have found guides without any single traitor. No Persian source mentions him.
p_ephialtes.s4: In later Greek tradition Ephialtes became the type of the man who sells out his own side. By chance his name is also the Greek word for nightmare, an older meaning taken from a night demon and unconnected with him. Modern retellings, such as the film 300, turn him into a deformed Spartan outcast, which has no basis in the ancient sources.
p_eurybiades.lead: Eurybiades, son of Eurycleides, was the Spartan who held supreme command of the Greek fleet that fought Xerxes' navy in 480 BCE. Sparta sent only a few ships, but the allies refused to serve under an Athenian, so the command went to him. Herodotus shows him as a cautious leader pushed by Themistocles, and historians still argue over how far that picture is fair.
p_eurybiades.play: The game's chronicle names Eurybiades as the Spartan who commanded the Greek fleet at Artemisium and Salamis because the allies would follow no Athenian. This matches Herodotus.
p_eurybiades.s0: Herodotus says the allies would not follow an Athenian and threatened to break up the fleet, so the Athenians gave way. In his figures Sparta supplied only ten ships at Artemisium against 127 Athenian ones, and sixteen at Salamis against 180. He adds that Eurybiades was not of royal blood, so he was not one of Sparta's two kings. His post rested on Sparta's standing as leader of the alliance, not on its naval strength.
p_eurybiades.s1: Herodotus tells how the Euboeans, afraid of being abandoned, paid Themistocles thirty talents to keep the fleet at Artemisium. Themistocles passed five to Eurybiades and three to Adeimantus of Corinth and kept the rest himself. The fleet stayed, fought for three days, and withdrew south only after news came that the pass at Thermopylae had fallen. Some historians think the bribe story came from a tradition hostile to Themistocles.
p_eurybiades.s2: When news came that the Persians had taken the Acropolis of Athens, the allied commanders voted to fall back to the Isthmus of Corinth. Herodotus says Themistocles persuaded Eurybiades to call the council again. There he argued that fighting in the narrow strait favoured the Greeks, and he threatened that the Athenians would sail off to Siris in Italy. Eurybiades then decided to stay and fight at Salamis.
p_eurybiades.s3: Plutarch, writing nearly six centuries later, says Eurybiades raised his staff to strike Themistocles during the argument. Themistocles is supposed to have answered that he could strike if he would also listen. Herodotus does not tell this story. It reads as a moral tale about patience and good counsel, and it is probably not a record of what happened.
p_eurybiades.s4: Herodotus says that after Salamis Eurybiades argued against sailing to break Xerxes' bridges, because a trapped king would fight harder in Greece. The Spartans later gave him an olive crown for valour and Themistocles one for wisdom. Herodotus probably drew heavily on Athenian informants, and some historians think they made Eurybiades look weaker than he was. Persian sources are silent: no royal inscription or tablet mentions him or the defeat at Salamis.
p_fravartish.lead: Fravartish (Greek Phraortes) was a Mede who rose against Darius in late 522 BCE, claiming to be Khshathrita, a descendant of the old Median king Cyaxares. His revolt was one of the most dangerous of the risings that followed Darius's seizure of the throne, drawing support as far as Parthia and Hyrcania. Darius defeated him at Kunduru in 521 BCE and had him executed at Ecbatana.
p_fravartish.play: The game's chronicle note presents Fravartish as a Median rebel of 522-521 BCE, beaten at Kunduru and put to death at Ecbatana. It follows Behistun but shortens it, leaving out his flight to Raga and his mutilation.
p_fravartish.s0: The Behistun inscription says that while Darius was in Babylon, a Mede named Fravartish rose in Media. He told the people he was Khshathrita, of the family of Uvakhshtra (Cyaxares). The Median army at the palace went over to him, and he became king in Media. Darius lists Media among the lands that rebelled while he was in Babylon.
p_fravartish.s1: Darius first sent a Persian, Vidarna (Greek Hydarnes), against the Median army. Vidarna fought the rebels at Marush in Media, then waited in the district of Kampanda until the King arrived. Parthia and Hyrcania declared for Fravartish, and Darius's father Vishtaspa had to fight the rebels there. In spring 521 BCE Darius marched from Babylon and defeated Fravartish at Kunduru in Media.
p_fravartish.s2: Fravartish fled with a few horsemen to Raga, where Darius's troops caught him and brought him back. Darius says he cut off his nose, ears and tongue, put out one eye and kept him bound at the palace gate for all the people to see. He then impaled him at Ecbatana and executed his leading followers in the fortress there. On the Behistun relief, Fravartish stands among the bound rebel kings with a label naming him.
p_fravartish.s3: Herodotus does not name this rebel. He says only that the Medes, who had submitted to Cyrus, later regretted it and revolted against Darius, but were beaten in battle and subdued again. His Phraortes is a different man, a Median king of an earlier century whom he makes the father of Cyaxares.
p_fravartish.s4: Historians debate what Fravartish's claim meant. The name Khshathrita resembles Kashtaritu, a city lord who led a coalition including Medes in Assyrian texts of the 670s BCE, and some think Herodotus's early Phraortes blurs memories of such men. Scholars also argue over how far a unified Median kingdom existed before Cyrus. Behistun is Darius's own case against his rivals and calls each of them a liar, so Fravartish's descent cannot be checked.
p_gobryas.lead: Gobryas (Old Persian Gaubaruva) was one of the six Persian nobles who helped Darius seize the throne in 522 BCE. Darius named him in his inscriptions, sent him to crush a revolt in Elam, and had him carved on the façade of his tomb as his spear-bearer. Herodotus says two marriages made him the King's close kinsman, and his son Mardonius later commanded the Persian war in Greece.
p_gobryas.play: The game's chronicle note presents Gobryas as one of the six, the King's double in-law, and the general who ended Elam's third revolt. The first and last points come from Behistun; the marriages come from Herodotus.
p_gobryas.s0: In the Behistun inscription Darius tells how he killed the man he calls Gaumata the magus in 522 BCE, and later lists the six men who stood with him. Among them is Gaubaruva, son of Marduniya, a Persian. Darius asks future kings to protect the families of these helpers, which marks them as a privileged circle at the new court. Herodotus's list of the conspirators differs slightly, but both include Gobryas.
p_gobryas.s1: An added fifth column at Behistun, covering Darius's second and third years as king (about 520-519 BCE), records that Elam rebelled again under a leader named Athamaita. Darius sent Gobryas with an army. He defeated the Elamites, captured Athamaita and brought him to the King, who put him to death. Athamaita does not appear on the relief: of the later captives, only the Saka chief Skunkha was added to the line of bound rebels.
p_gobryas.s2: On the façade of Darius's rock tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam, a short label names a figure as Gobryas, a Persian of the Patishuvarish clan, spear-bearer of Darius the King. The title placed him among the King's most trusted attendants. Elamite tablets from the Persepolis Fortification archive probably refer to him under the form Kambarma, receiving rations on official journeys.
p_gobryas.s3: Herodotus says Otanes first brought Gobryas into the conspiracy against the false Smerdis. In the fight in the palace, Gobryas grappled with one of the magi in a dark room and told Darius to strike even at the risk of hitting him. Herodotus adds that Darius had married a daughter of Gobryas before he became king, and that Gobryas married Darius's sister, the mother of Mardonius.
p_gobryas.s4: During Darius's campaign north of the Ister, Herodotus tells that the Scythians sent a bird, a mouse, a frog and five arrows. Darius read them as a sign of surrender, but Gobryas explained them as a warning: unless the Persians could fly, hide underground or leap into marshes, they would die by Scythian arrows. The tale has the shape of a Greek riddle story and cannot be checked.
p_harpagus.lead: Harpagus was a Median nobleman who, Herodotus says, helped Cyrus overthrow the Median king Astyages and then served the new Persian king as a general. In the 540s BCE he brought the Greek cities of Ionia, and then Caria and Lycia, under Persian rule. Almost everything known about him comes from Herodotus, who tells his story as a tale of betrayal and revenge.
p_harpagus.play: The game's chronicle note presents Harpagus as Herodotus does: the Mede who betrayed Astyages and took the Ionian cities with earth mounds. Only Herodotus names him; no Persian or Babylonian record does.
p_harpagus.s0: Herodotus says Astyages, warned by dreams, ordered Harpagus, a trusted man of his own household, to kill the newborn Cyrus. Harpagus passed the baby to a herdsman, who raised him instead. When the boy was found alive years later, Astyages punished Harpagus by serving him the flesh of his own son at a banquet. The story has the shape of a folk tale and cannot be checked against any Persian or Babylonian record.
p_harpagus.s1: According to Herodotus, Harpagus nursed his grudge and urged Cyrus to rebel, sending him a letter sewn inside a hare. When Astyages gave Harpagus command of the Median army, many of the soldiers deserted or went over to Cyrus. After Astyages was captured, Harpagus is said to have mocked him. The old king replied that Harpagus had made the Medes slaves of the Persians.
p_harpagus.s2: The Nabonidus Chronicle, a Babylonian record, says that in the sixth year of Nabonidus, about 550 BCE, Astyages marched against Cyrus. His army then rebelled against him, seized him and handed him over to Cyrus. Cyrus took Ecbatana and carried its spoil to Anshan. The chronicle agrees with Herodotus that the Median army deserted its king, but it names no Harpagus.
p_harpagus.s3: After the fall of Sardis, the Mede Mazares died, and Harpagus succeeded him in command on the coast.
