Herodotus says he took the Ionian cities one by one by piling earth mounds against their walls. The Phocaeans and Teians abandoned their cities by sea, though more than half the Phocaeans soon sailed home. He then subdued Caria and Lycia, where the Xanthians burned their families on their citadel and died fighting.
p_harpagus.s4: The Inscribed Pillar at Xanthus, set up about 400 BCE, honours a Lycian dynast called the son of Arppaxu, given as Harpagus in its Greek verse. Many historians think the ruling house of Xanthus descended from the conqueror and that the name recurred in the family. Others doubt any link. Herodotus calls the Harpagus who captured Histiaeus around 494 BCE a Persian, and he was probably a different man.
p_hippias.lead: Hippias, son of Pisistratus, was the last of his family to rule Athens as tyrant, from about 527 BCE until the Spartans drove him out in 510 BCE. In exile he turned to the Persians, and in 490 BCE he guided the fleet of Datis and Artaphernes to Marathon, hoping to be restored. His career shows how Persia used exiled Greek rulers as allies and guides in the west.
p_hippias.play: The game's chronicle names Hippias as the exiled tyrant who guided Datis's fleet to Marathon, which follows Herodotus. Its dates of 527-510 BCE are approximate, since his father probably died in 528 BCE/7.
p_hippias.s0: Herodotus says that when Pisistratus seized Athens for the third time, probably in about 546 BCE, he landed at Marathon with his sons beside him. After Pisistratus died, probably in 528 BCE/7, power passed to his sons. Thucydides insists that Hippias, the eldest, held the rule, not his younger brother Hipparchus as many Athenians believed. He adds that the family kept the city's laws in form while placing their own men in office.
p_hippias.s1: In 514 BCE Harmodius and Aristogeiton killed Hipparchus at the Panathenaic festival, and later Athenians honoured the pair as the liberators of the city. Thucydides disagreed with that view. He says the motive was a private love quarrel, that Hippias himself escaped unharmed, and that his rule grew harsher afterwards. Herodotus also says the tyranny lasted four more years and pressed harder on the Athenians.
p_hippias.s2: Herodotus says the exiled Alcmaeonids bribed the Delphic priestess to urge Sparta to free Athens, and in 510 BCE King Cleomenes besieged Hippias on the Acropolis. When his children were captured, Hippias agreed to leave for Sigeum near the Hellespont. Sparta's allies later refused to restore him, so he went to Sardis and urged the satrap Artaphernes against Athens. When Athens refused to take him back, Herodotus says, it became an open enemy of Persia.
p_hippias.s3: Herodotus says Hippias led the Persians to Marathon because its plain suited cavalry and lay close to Eretria. He also placed the Eretrian captives on the islet of Aegilia. Thucydides says Hippias went by way of Lampsacus to Darius, and years later came to Marathon as an old man with the Medes. No Persian document names him, so his whole story comes from Greek writers.
p_hippias.s4: Herodotus tells that Hippias dreamed of lying with his mother and read it as a sign that he would regain Athens and die old in his homeland. On landing he sneezed and coughed so hard that a loose tooth fell into the sand and was lost, and he declared that the land would never be theirs. The story is shaped as an omen of failure. Herodotus does not say how Hippias died, while much later writers such as Justin claimed he fell at Marathon.
p_histiaeus.lead: Histiaeus was tyrant of Miletus, the leading Greek city of Ionia, in the reign of Darius. Herodotus makes him the man who saved the King's bridge over the Ister about 513 BCE, and later one of the instigators of the Ionian revolt of 499 BCE. Rewarded, kept close at Susa, distrusted and finally executed, he shows how Persia ruled Greek cities through loyal local tyrants, and how fragile that loyalty could be.
p_histiaeus.play: The game's chronicle presents him as keeper of the Ister bridge and repeats Herodotus's tattoo story. It dates his death to 494 BCE, but Herodotus places his capture after the fall of Miletus, so it may have come in 493 BCE.
p_histiaeus.s0: Herodotus says that when Darius crossed the Ister against the Scythians, about 513 BCE, the Ionian tyrants were left to guard the bridge of boats. When the Scythians urged them to break it, Miltiades of the Chersonese spoke in favour, but Histiaeus argued that each tyrant held his city only through Darius's power. The Ionians took apart only the northern end as a show and kept the crossing open for the retreating King.
p_histiaeus.s1: Herodotus's version makes Histiaeus the King's loyal man and Miltiades a would-be liberator. Many historians suspect Miltiades' part was told later in Athens, perhaps when he was tried there, to clear him of having served Persia. He stayed in the Chersonese for years afterwards. No Persian text names Histiaeus, so his career is known almost wholly from Herodotus, who treats him with both admiration and suspicion.
p_histiaeus.s2: As a reward Darius granted him Myrcinus on the Strymon in Thrace, a site near timber and silver. Herodotus says the general Megabazus warned that a clever Greek fortifying such a place was a danger. Darius therefore called Histiaeus to Sardis and then took him to Susa as counsellor and companion at the royal table. His cousin and son-in-law Aristagoras governed Miletus in his place.
p_histiaeus.s3: Herodotus tells that Histiaeus, eager to leave Susa, shaved a trusted slave's head and marked a message on his scalp. He waited for the hair to grow back, then sent the slave to Aristagoras with orders to shave it again, and the message urged revolt. Herodotus admits Aristagoras had his own motives after his failed attack on Naxos, and the tale has the shape of a trickster story that cannot be checked.
p_histiaeus.s4: Once the revolt began, Histiaeus persuaded Darius to send him west to calm Ionia. At Sardis the satrap Artaphernes told him that he had stitched the shoe and Aristagoras had put it on. He fled to Chios, was shut out of Miletus, and raided shipping from Byzantium. After Miletus fell, the Persian commander Harpagus captured him near Atarneus, and he was impaled at Sardis. Darius, displeased, had his head buried with honour.
p_hydarnes.lead: Hydarnes was the Persian general who commanded the Ten Thousand, the royal infantry the Greeks called the Immortals, during Xerxes' invasion of Greece in 480 BCE. Herodotus says he led them by night over the mountain path at Thermopylae and came down behind the Greek defenders, which decided the battle. He was probably the son of the Hydarnes who helped Darius take the throne.
p_hydarnes.play: The game's chronicle presents Hydarnes as the commander who led the Immortals over the mountain path to turn the pass, which follows Herodotus closely. The story of the night march rests on Greek accounts alone.
p_hydarnes.s0: Darius's inscription at Behistun names Vidarna son of Bagabigna, a Persian, among the six men who stood with him when he killed Gaumata in 522 BCE. Darius also sent Vidarna against the Median rebels, and Vidarna fought them at Maru. Herodotus calls the commander of 480 BCE Hydarnes son of Hydarnes, so the general at Thermopylae was probably the son of this companion of Darius.
p_hydarnes.s1: Herodotus says the Ten Thousand were picked Persian foot soldiers under Hydarnes. They were kept at full strength, so that a man who died or fell sick was replaced at once, and for this the Greeks called them the Immortals. He says they wore the richest gear in the army. After Salamis, when Mardonius chose troops to stay in Greece, Herodotus reports that Hydarnes refused to leave the King and went back with Xerxes.
p_hydarnes.s2: Herodotus says the Immortals first attacked the pass and failed, as the Medes had before them. Xerxes then sent Hydarnes and his men out at lamp-lighting time with Ephialtes of Malis as guide. At dawn they met a thousand Phocians guarding the path. Hydarnes feared they were Spartans, but once told otherwise his men shot at them, the Phocians drew back to the summit, and the Persians went on down behind Leonidas.
p_hydarnes.s3: Historians still argue over the line of the Anopaea path and how long the march took, and many doubt that all ten thousand men went, though Herodotus implies it. The Greek name Immortals may come from a misunderstood Persian word, perhaps one meaning companions, but this is only a guess. Herodotus also mentions a Hydarnes as general of the coastal peoples of Asia, and it is unclear whether he meant this man or his father.
p_hydarnes.s4: Herodotus tells how two Spartans, Sperthias and Bulis, travelling to the King to atone for Sparta's killing of Darius's heralds, were entertained by a Persian named Hydarnes. He urged them to serve the King and so win rule in Greece. They answered that he knew what it was to be a slave but had never tasted freedom. The story is shaped to praise Spartan liberty and cannot be checked.
p_hystaspes.lead: Hystaspes, in Old Persian Vishtaspa, was the father of Darius I and a Persian noble whose life spanned the reigns of Cyrus, Cambyses and Darius. Darius named him first in his genealogy. In 521 BCE Hystaspes led the fight against rebels in Parthia during the wars that secured his son's throne. Herodotus says his other son Artaphernes later governed Sardis.
p_hystaspes.play: The game's chronicle note says he governed Parthia under Darius. Behistun only places him in Parthia leading troops in 521 BCE and gives him no title, and Herodotus calls him governor in Persis in 522 BCE.
p_hystaspes.s0: At the start of the Behistun inscription Darius calls himself son of Vishtaspa, son of Arshama (Arsames), son of Ariyaramna, son of Chishpish, son of Hakhamanish (Achaemenes). Hystaspes is never called king. In a foundation charter from Susa, Darius states that his father and his grandfather Arsames were both still alive when Auramazda made him king.
p_hystaspes.s1: Behistun records that Parthia and Hyrcania joined the Median rebel Fravartish in 521 BCE. Hystaspes was in Parthia, and the people there turned against him. He fought the rebels at Vishpauzatish. Darius then sent him a Persian army from Raga, and he defeated them again at Patigrabana, ending the revolt in that region.
p_hystaspes.s2: Herodotus says Hystaspes, son of Arsames, marched with Cyrus against the Massagetae. Cyrus dreamed that the young Darius had wings that shaded Asia and Europe, and took it as a sign of a plot. He sent Hystaspes home to Persia to hold his son until the King returned. Herodotus adds that the dream really foretold Cyrus's own death. It reads as a prophecy shaped after Darius came to power.
p_hystaspes.s3: Herodotus says that in 522 BCE Hystaspes was governor of the Persians, meaning Persis, when Darius came to Susa to join the conspirators. Behistun shows him in Parthia a year later but gives no title. Many historians think he governed Parthia and Hyrcania, while others see him only as a commander there. Some also question how closely Darius's branch was related to Cyrus's, and think the shared ancestor Achaemenes was stressed to strengthen the new king's claim.
p_hystaspes.s4: Ctesias, writing about a century later, says Darius's parents wanted to see the rock tomb being cut for the King. The priests hauling them up the cliff were frightened by snakes and let go of the ropes, and both died. No Persian source confirms the story, and Ctesias is often unreliable.
p_idanthyrsus.lead: Idanthyrsus is the name Herodotus gives to the Scythian king who faced Darius's army north of the Ister. In Herodotus's story he refused a set battle, drew the Persians across the steppe, and answered Darius's demand that he fight or submit. The name is known from Herodotus; no surviving Persian or Scythian text is known to name him.
p_idanthyrsus.play: The game names Idanthyrsus only in the event articles on Darius's Scythian campaign and the debate at the Ister bridge. He has no figure, level or mechanic of his own.
p_idanthyrsus.s0: Herodotus calls Idanthyrsus a king of the Scythians and names him as the leader who faced Darius. He says two other Scythian kings, Scopasis and Taxacis, joined him, so the defence was shared between three rulers and their peoples.
p_idanthyrsus.s1: Herodotus says the Scythians had no towns or fields to defend, so they withdrew before the Persians, blocked wells and drove off their herds. They drew the Persians after them and harassed foragers with horsemen. Darius, on this telling, could not force a decisive fight.
p_idanthyrsus.s2: Herodotus reports that Darius sent a rider to Idanthyrsus asking why he kept running and why he would not either fight or submit. Idanthyrsus replied that he was doing nothing unusual, that the Scythians had no cities or crops to lose, and that Darius would learn who he was when he tried to disturb the Scythian ancestral graves. He added that Darius was not his master.
p_idanthyrsus.s3: Herodotus says the Scythians sent Darius a bird, a mouse, a frog and five arrows. Darius took it as a surrender of land and water, while Gobryas read it as a warning that the Persians would be shot unless they escaped like birds, mice or frogs. The scene has the shape of a moral tale and cannot be tested against any other source.
p_idanthyrsus.s4: Herodotus presents the campaign as a failure, and Darius's retreat as a narrow escape. Many modern historians doubt that the aim was ever to destroy the Scythians, and note that the Persians kept their hold on Thrace afterwards. How far Herodotus's named Scythian leaders reflect real individuals cannot be confirmed.
p_leonidas.lead: Leonidas was a king of Sparta from the Agiad house. He commanded the Greek force that held the pass of Thermopylae against Xerxes in 480 BCE, and he died there after the Persians found a way round. Almost everything known of him comes from Herodotus, and later Greek writers made his death the model of Spartan courage.
p_leonidas.play: The chronicle names Leonidas as the Spartan king at Thermopylae. Its note leaves out the Thebans, who Herodotus says also stayed, though they later surrendered to the Persians.
p_leonidas.s0: Herodotus says Leonidas was a son of King Anaxandridas by his first wife, while his half-brother Cleomenes, son of a second wife, was born earlier and became king first. Leonidas was not expected to rule, but his elder full brother Dorieus died in Sicily. When Cleomenes died, about 490 BCE, Leonidas took the throne, and he was married to Gorgo, the daughter of Cleomenes.
p_leonidas.s1: In summer 480 BCE Leonidas led a force that Herodotus lists contingent by contingent: three hundred Spartans, chosen from men who had living sons, with other Peloponnesians, Thespians, Thebans, Phocians and Locrians. Modern totals come to roughly six or seven thousand. Herodotus says the main Spartan army stayed at home for the Carneia festival. For two days the Greeks threw back attacks in the narrow pass, including attacks by the Immortals.
p_leonidas.s2: Ephialtes of Malis guided Hydarnes and his troops over the Anopaea path by night, and the Phocians guarding it fell back. Herodotus gives two versions of what followed: Leonidas sent most of the allies away, or they left of their own accord. He says Leonidas fell fighting, the Greeks fought over his body, and the last of them died on a low hill. He adds that Xerxes had the dead king's head cut off and set on a stake.
p_leonidas.s3: Herodotus says an oracle had warned that either Sparta or a Spartan king must fall, and that Leonidas wanted glory for Sparta. He also claims the Thebans were held as hostages, a charge Plutarch later called malice against Thebes. Modern historians debate whether Leonidas was covering the allies' retreat or obeying Spartan custom. No Persian source mentions the battle, and Herodotus's figures for Xerxes' army and losses are thought far too high.
p_leonidas.s4: Later writers added sayings and scenes. Plutarch, writing some six centuries on, has Leonidas tell the Persians to come and take the Greek arms themselves, and Diodorus describes a night raid on Xerxes' tent. The travel writer Pausanias says the king's bones were brought home to Sparta forty years after the battle. None of these stories can be checked against earlier sources.
p_leotychides.lead: Leotychides (Leotychidas II) was a Eurypontid king of Sparta who came to the throne about 491 BCE after helping Cleomenes depose Demaratus. In 479 BCE he commanded the Greek fleet that crossed the Aegean, landed at Mycale and destroyed the Persian ships beached there. That defeat opened the way for the Ionian cities to break from the King.
p_leotychides.play: The chronicle names him as the Spartan king who led the Greek fleet in 479 BCE, called on the Ionians to change sides and won at Mycale. Its reign dates, about 491-469 BCE, follow one modern reckoning; the end date is uncertain.
p_leotychides.s0: Herodotus says Cleomenes, the other Spartan king, wanted to be rid of Demaratus. He made a bargain with Leotychides, a kinsman of Demaratus who resented him for taking the bride he had been promised. Leotychides swore that Demaratus was not the true son of King Ariston. The question went to Delphi, where a go-between had won over the priestess. Demaratus was deposed, Leotychides took his place, and Demaratus later fled to Darius.
p_leotychides.s1: Herodotus says that early in spring 479 BCE a Greek fleet of 110 ships gathered at Aegina under Leotychides, and he traces the king's descent back to Heracles. At Delos, envoys from Samos urged him to sail east, promising that the Ionians would revolt. He found the Persian ships beached at Mycale behind a wall. He then sailed close along the shore and had a herald call on the Ionians to remember their freedom.
p_leotychides.s2: Herodotus says the Persians distrusted the Samians, so they disarmed them and sent the Milesians away to guard the mountain paths. The Athenians and the allies beside them attacked along the beach and broke through a wall of shields before the Spartans arrived by a harder route. The Persian general Tigranes was killed. The Ionians turned on the Persians, and the Greeks burned the ships and the camp.
p_leotychides.s3: Herodotus says Mycale was fought on the same day as Plataea. A rumour of that victory reached the Greek camp and a herald's staff was found on the beach, which he took as signs from the gods. Diodorus says instead that Leotychides spread the report himself to hearten his men. Many historians doubt the exact coincidence and his figure of 60,000 men under Tigranes. No Persian text records the battle.
p_leotychides.s4: Herodotus says Leotychides later led an army into Thessaly and could have conquered it. Instead he took bribes and was caught in camp sitting on a sleeve full of silver. He was tried, fled to Tegea, and his house in Sparta was pulled down. The dates are argued: the campaign is usually placed about 478-476 BCE, and Diodorus puts his death in 476 BCE/5, while others prefer about 469 BCE.
p_lycidas.lead: Lycidas was a member of the Athenian council in 479 BCE. Herodotus says he was killed by his fellow citizens after he advised that Mardonius's offer be put to the people. The story shows how firmly the Athenians, in Herodotus's telling, refused terms from the Persians.
p_lycidas.play: Lycidas has no mechanic of his own. He is named in the event articles on Mardonius's capture of Athens and on Alexander of Macedon's embassy to Athens.
p_lycidas.s0: Herodotus says that Alexander of Macedon brought Mardonius's offer to the Athenians in 479 BCE: the King would rebuild their temples, leave them free and in possession of their land if they became his allies. The Athenians refused. When Mardonius then marched on Attica, he sent an envoy named Murychides to the Athenians, who had again left their city and were on Salamis.
p_lycidas.s1: Herodotus says Lycidas, a councillor, gave it as his opinion that the council should accept the envoy's words and bring them before the assembly. The councillors and the Athenians gathered outside were enraged and stoned him to death. Murychides was sent back unharmed.
p_lycidas.s2: Herodotus adds that the Athenian women, hearing of the uproar, went to the house of Lycidas on their own initiative and stoned his wife and children. He gives this as part of the same event and does not describe any trial or decree.
p_lycidas.s3: Later Athenian orators tell a similar story but name the man Cyrsilus and set it at the time of Xerxes' invasion, as in Demosthenes and Lycurgus. Herodotus is the earliest source and gives Lycidas. Historians cannot say whether the name and setting changed in retelling or whether the orators drew on another version. Demosthenes also says Cyrsilus was bribed, a charge Herodotus does not make.
p_lycidas.s4: Herodotus uses the incident to show Athenian resolve while the Spartans delayed sending an army. It is told from the Greek side only, and no Persian document mentions Lycidas or the terms. Whether the story is exact in detail cannot be checked.
p_mandrocles.lead: Mandrocles was a Samian engineer who built the bridge of boats on which Darius led his army from Asia into Europe for the Scythian campaign, probably about 513 BCE. Almost all that is known of him comes from Herodotus. His bridge is the earliest crossing of the Bosporus recorded in Greek sources, and it shows how the Persian kings drew on the skills of their Greek subjects.
p_mandrocles.play: The chronicle presents Mandrocles as the Samian who bridged the Bosporus with boats for Darius and dedicated a painting of the crossing on Samos, following Herodotus.
p_mandrocles.s0: Herodotus says Darius came from Susa to Chalcedon and crossed into Europe on a bridge of boats made by Mandrocles, by his guess midway between Byzantium and the temple at the mouth of the strait. Darius set up two pillars of white stone there, inscribed in Assyrian and Greek letters with the peoples of his army. The Byzantines later used them for an altar of Artemis, leaving one stone by their temple of Dionysus.
p_mandrocles.s1: Herodotus says Darius was so pleased with the bridge that he gave Mandrocles ten of every kind of gift. Mandrocles spent part of the reward on a painting of the whole crossing, with Darius seated on a throne watching his army pass, and dedicated it in the temple of Hera on Samos. Its verse inscription, which Herodotus quotes, claims a crown for Mandrocles and glory for Samos for carrying out the King's wish. The painting is lost.
p_mandrocles.s2: Herodotus says the Samians made the three greatest works in the Greek world: a water tunnel cut through a mountain by Eupalinus of Megara, a great harbour mole, and the largest temple he knew, begun by Rhoecus. Samos had been under Persian rule since Otanes installed Syloson as tyrant early in Darius's reign. At the Ister Herodotus lists Syloson's son Aeaces among the Greek tyrants, so Mandrocles served Darius as a subject.
p_mandrocles.s3: Herodotus gives no year for the Scythian campaign. Historians usually place it about 513 BCE, but some argue for a date several years earlier, and the campaign's aims are also debated. Herodotus says Darius led 700,000 men and 600 ships. Modern historians regard these figures as greatly exaggerated, though a large army clearly crossed.
p_mardonius.lead: Mardonius was a Persian noble of the highest rank, son of Darius's fellow conspirator Gobryas and husband of one of Darius's daughters. He led the campaign of 492 BCE into Thrace and Macedonia, urged Xerxes to invade Greece, and commanded the army left behind after Salamis. The defeat of his army at Plataea in 479 BCE, where he was killed, ended the King's attempt to conquer mainland Greece.
p_mardonius.play: The game's chronicle note sums Mardonius up in one line: Gobryas's son and Darius's son-in-law, who lost his fleet off Athos in 492 BCE, urged Xerxes to war, stayed in Greece after Salamis and fell at Plataea.
p_mardonius.s0: Darius's inscription at Behistun names Gaubaruva, son of Marduniya, among the six Persians who stood with him against Gaumata in 522 BCE. Gaubaruva is the Gobryas of the Greeks, and Marduniya is the Old Persian form of Mardonius. The general therefore probably bore his grandfather's name, and he came from one of the families that helped put Darius on the throne.
p_mardonius.s1: Herodotus says Mardonius, young and newly married to Darius's daughter Artozostra, came to Ionia, removed the Greek tyrants and allowed democracies. His fleet took Thasos without a fight, and his army added the Macedonians to the King's subjects, though Macedon had given earth and water years before. A storm off Mount Athos wrecked the fleet, by Herodotus's count 300 ships and over 20,000 men, and the Thracian Brygi wounded him in a night attack.
p_mardonius.s2: Herodotus makes Mardonius the chief courtier urging Xerxes to punish Athens, against the caution of Artabanus. After Salamis he offered to stay with picked troops while the King went home. He wintered in Thessaly, sent Alexander of Macedon to offer Athens an alliance, and in 479 BCE reoccupied Athens and burned it before withdrawing to Boeotia.
p_mardonius.s3: Herodotus says Mardonius fought on a white horse among a thousand picked Persians, and that the Persians broke once a Spartan named Arimnestus killed him. His body vanished the next day, and Herodotus heard several rival claims about who had buried it. He also reports that Pausanias refused advice to mutilate the corpse in revenge for Leonidas.
p_mardonius.s4: Herodotus portrays Mardonius as ambitious and eager to govern Greece. Modern historians answer that the campaign of 492 BCE secured Thrace and Macedonia despite the storm, and that the invasion was royal policy rather than one courtier's scheme. Herodotus gives him 300,000 men at Plataea, a figure historians regard as greatly exaggerated.
p_mardontes.lead: Mardontes, son of Bagaeus, was a Persian officer who served in Xerxes' invasion force and, according to Herodotus, died at Mycale in 479 BCE. He is known only from Herodotus. His name is close to that of Mardonius, but the two were different men.
p_mardontes.play: Mardontes has no mechanic of his own. The game names him only in its event articles on the war of 480-479 BCE, including the battle of Mycale, and not in any level's scenes or on the map.
p_mardontes.s0: Herodotus lists Mardontes, son of Bagaeus, among the commanders in Xerxes' army when it was reviewed on the march. He says Mardontes led the peoples from the islands of the Red Sea, whom he describes among the contingents of the empire.
p_mardontes.s1: Herodotus says the Persians were beaten at Mycale in 479 BCE after the Greeks landed and attacked the camp below the mountain. He names Mardontes among the Persian commanders who died there, together with Tigranes. He says that Artayntes and Ithamitres were among those who survived or escaped.
p_mardontes.s2: Herodotus tells of Mardonius as a separate man. He was Darius's son-in-law and the general in command in Greece, and he was killed at Plataea in 479 BCE. Mardontes died the same summer on the other field, at Mycale. The similar names are easy to confuse.
p_mardontes.s3: Only Herodotus mentions Mardontes, and no Persian text names him. His exact rank and the command he held at Mycale are not clear from the narrative. His name and role cannot be checked against any independent source.
p_masistius.lead: Masistius led the Persian horse in the first fighting before the battle of Plataea in 479 BCE. Herodotus says the Persians and the King valued him more than any man after Mardonius. His death in a cavalry attack near Erythrae gave the Greeks their first success of the campaign. It raised their confidence, and soon after they moved down from the slopes of Cithaeron to better-watered ground near Plataea.
p_masistius.play: The game's chronicle names Masistius as commander of the horse before Plataea, mounted on a Nisaean horse with a golden bit and killed at Erythrae. This follows Herodotus; no Persian document is known to record him.
p_masistius.s0: Herodotus says Mardonius sent his whole cavalry against the Greeks camped on the lower slopes of Mount Cithaeron, with Masistius in command. He rode a Nisaean horse with a golden bit and rich trappings. The horsemen attacked in squadrons and taunted the Greeks as women. The Megarians held the most exposed ground and sent word that they could not hold without help.
p_masistius.s1: In Herodotus's telling, three hundred picked Athenians under Olympiodorus, with archers, went to help the Megarians. An arrow struck Masistius's horse in the flank, and it reared and threw him. He wore a corselet of golden scales under a purple tunic, so blows had no effect until a man stabbed him in the eye. The Persian horse fought over the body but drew back when more Greek infantry came up.
p_masistius.s2: Herodotus says Mardonius and the army mourned Masistius by shaving their own heads and the manes of their horses and draught animals, and that their wailing carried across Boeotia. The Greeks laid his body on a cart and drove it along their lines, because men left their posts to see his size and beauty. Soon after, the Greeks moved to new positions near Plataea.
p_masistius.s3: Pausanias, writing in the second century CE, says the corselet of Masistius was kept in the temple of Athena Polias on the Acropolis, with a sword said to be that of Mardonius. Pausanias himself doubted the sword, since Mardonius fell fighting Spartans. He reports these as objects shown in his own day, long after the battle, so their history after 479 BCE is unknown.
p_masistius.s4: No Persian document is known that can be tied to Masistius; the whole story comes from Greek writers. Herodotus names a Masistius son of Siromitres as leader of the Alarodians and Saspeires in Xerxes' army, and it is uncertain whether this is the same man. Plutarch tells much the same story with small differences. Some historians think the Athenian sources behind it enlarge the Athenian part in the fight.
p_mazares.lead: Mazares was a Median commander in the service of Cyrus. Herodotus says Cyrus sent him against Pactyes, the Lydian who rebelled at Sardis after Cyrus left, and that he began to subdue the Greek cities nearby before he died. Harpagus then took over his command.
p_mazares.play: The game names Mazares only in the event articles on the fall of Sardis and on Harpagus's conquest of Ionia. He has no mechanic of his own.
p_mazares.s0: Herodotus says Cyrus left Pactyes, a Lydian, in charge of the treasure of Croesus at Sardis and went east. Pactyes then hired troops with the gold, brought down men from the coast and besieged the Persian governor Tabalus in the citadel. Cyrus sent Mazares with a force to deal with him.
p_mazares.s1: Herodotus reports that Pactyes fled to Cyme when Mazares approached. The Cymaeans consulted the oracle at Branchidae and were told to give him up, but sent him on to Mytilene and then Chios. The Chians surrendered him in return for the land of Atarneus.
p_mazares.s2: Herodotus says Mazares attacked the Greeks who had helped Pactyes, enslaved the people of Priene and overran the plain of the Maeander, including Magnesia. He fell ill and died soon after.
p_mazares.s3: Herodotus says Cyrus then sent Harpagus, also a Mede, to take command. Harpagus took the Ionian cities by building siege mounds against their walls, beginning with Phocaea.
p_mazares.s4: Herodotus tells that Croesus advised Cyrus to forbid the Lydians arms and make them live as shopkeepers and musicians. This is a Greek moral story about luxury and softness, and it is not confirmed by any document of the time.
p_mazares.s5: Almost everything about Mazares comes from Herodotus. No Persian inscription or tablet names him, so his rank and the date of his death are uncertain. The revolt is placed soon after the fall of Sardis, about the mid-540s BCE, but the order of events is reconstructed from Herodotus.
p_megabates.lead: Megabates was a Persian of the Achaemenid house who commanded the allied fleet in the attack on Naxos. Herodotus says he quarrelled with Aristagoras of Miletus, and that the failure of the expedition pushed Aristagoras towards revolt. Only Herodotus tells the story in any detail.
p_megabates.play: Megabates has no mechanic of his own. He is named only in the event articles on the siege of Naxos and the Ionian Revolt, where he appears as the Persian fleet commander.
p_megabates.s0: Herodotus says Aristagoras, who governed Miletus for the Persians, persuaded the satrap Artaphernes to attack Naxos. Darius approved, and Megabates was appointed to command the fleet of 200 ships. Herodotus calls him a Persian of the Achaemenid family, related to Darius.
p_megabates.s1: Herodotus says Megabates inspected the ships and found a vessel from Myndus with no sentry posted. He had its captain, Scylax of Myndus, bound in an oar-port with his head outside the ship. Aristagoras protested and freed the man himself, and Megabates, angry at the insult, is said to have sent word to the Naxians of the coming attack.
p_megabates.s2: Warned in advance, the Naxians brought their goods inside the walls and prepared for a siege. Herodotus says the Persians besieged the city for four months, spent their money and Aristagoras's own, and withdrew after building forts for Naxian exiles. Aristagoras was left unable to pay what he had promised and feared the King's anger.
p_megabates.s3: The tale of a personal feud makes Megabates the cause of a failure, but modern historians doubt that one quarrel explains so large an event. The story may reflect a tradition that shifted blame onto a Persian, and a four-month siege defeated by supplies and a determined defence is plausible without any treachery.
p_megabates.s4: Herodotus does not follow Megabates after Naxos. He says Aristagoras, fearing the consequences, was then urged to revolt by a message from Histiaeus, and so began the Ionian Revolt.
p_megabazus.lead: Megabazus was the Persian commander whom Herodotus says Darius left in Europe when he returned to Asia from the Ister. Herodotus credits him with subduing Perinthus and much of Thrace and with sending envoys to Macedonia to ask for earth and water. His work helped to extend Persian reach along the northern Aegean coast.
p_megabazus.play: Megabazus is named in the event articles on Darius's Scythian campaign and the debate at the Ister bridge. The game gives him no unit, building or mechanic of his own, and the history in this entry follows Herodotus.
p_megabazus.s0: Herodotus says that Darius crossed back to Asia, reached Sestos, and left Megabazus in charge of the forces in Europe. He adds that Darius held Megabazus in high regard. Herodotus is the only detailed source for the appointment.
p_megabazus.s1: According to Herodotus, Megabazus subdued the Perinthians, who had resisted, and then marched through Thrace, bringing its peoples and cities under Persian rule. Herodotus also says that Paeonians were uprooted and sent to Asia on his orders. Which groups submitted by force and which by agreement is not clear from the narrative.
p_megabazus.s2: Herodotus says Megabazus sent envoys to Amyntas of Macedonia asking for earth and water, the signs of submission, and that Amyntas gave them. Macedonia then stood in some form of submission to the King.
p_megabazus.s3: Herodotus goes on to tell how Persian envoys were killed at a banquet by young Macedonians led by Alexander, and how the matter was hushed up. The story reads as a Macedonian tale that flatters Alexander, and historians doubt its details.
p_megabazus.s4: Herodotus reports that Megabazus warned Darius about Histiaeus of Miletus, who was building a fortified town at Myrcinus on the Strymon. Darius then summoned Histiaeus to Susa. Herodotus presents Megabazus as a far-sighted adviser, but the account is told from the Greek side.
p_megabazus.s5: The Scythian campaign is usually dated about 513 BCE, though the date is argued, and the conquests that followed are dated loosely after it. Historians debate how firm Persian control was and whether the Thracian coast became an organised province. Later Persian royal inscriptions name Skudra, usually read as Thrace, among the subject lands. Megabazus does not appear in these texts, so his role rests on Herodotus.
p_melanthius.lead: Melanthius was the Athenian who, according to Herodotus, commanded twenty ships sent to help the Ionian Greeks against the King in about 498 BCE. The ships joined the march on Sardis, which ended with the city burning. Herodotus calls the ships the beginning of evils for Greeks and non-Greeks alike.
p_melanthius.play: The game names Melanthius only in the Chronicle and in the Ionian Revolt article, as commander of the Athenian ships. He has no figure, unit or mechanic of his own.
p_melanthius.s0: Herodotus says that Aristagoras of Miletus, after failing to win Sparta, came to Athens and persuaded the assembly to send help. The Athenians voted for twenty ships and put Melanthius in command. Herodotus describes him as a respected citizen.
p_melanthius.s1: Herodotus judges the twenty ships to have been the beginning of evils for Greeks and non-Greeks. Eretria sent five more ships, which Herodotus ties to earlier help given to Eretria by Miletus. Herodotus also reports that Athens had earlier sent earth and water to Artaphernes under pressure, so the aid was a sharp change of course.
p_melanthius.s2: Herodotus says the ships landed near Ephesus and the allies marched inland with Ionian guides and took Sardis, apart from the citadel. A fire started there and spread through the lower city. He names the Eretrian Eualcidas among the dead after the Persian counterattack, and he does not mention Melanthius again. The Athenians went home after the defeat near Ephesus and refused further aid, despite Aristagoras's appeals.
p_melanthius.s3: Herodotus is the main surviving source for the commander's name, which appears once in his account. No Persian document known to us mentions him or the Athenian contingent. The name and the ship count therefore rest on Herodotus's report alone, and historians differ over how much weight Athenian aid carried beside the Ionian and Eretrian forces.
p_miltiades.lead: Miltiades son of Cimon was an Athenian aristocrat who ruled the Thracian Chersonese as a tyrant under Persian overlordship, then fled to Athens when the Ionian Revolt collapsed. In 490 BCE, as one of the ten Athenian generals, he pressed for battle at Marathon, and Herodotus credits him with the victory over the army of Datis and Artaphernes.
p_miltiades.play: The game's chronicle note presents him as the general who led the charge at Marathon. It also states the Ister bridge story as plain fact, though many historians doubt that tale.
p_miltiades.s0: Herodotus says the Pisistratid rulers of Athens sent Miltiades to the Chersonese, the peninsula on the European side of the Hellespont, where his family already held power. He governed there as a tyrant, kept five hundred hired men and married Hegesipyle, daughter of the Thracian king Olorus. When Darius advanced into Europe about 513 BCE, Miltiades became a Persian subject and sailed with the other Greek tyrants on the Scythian campaign.
p_miltiades.s1: Herodotus reports that while the Ionians guarded Darius's bridge of boats on the Ister, Miltiades urged them to destroy it and leave the King stranded among the Scythians. Histiaeus of Miletus argued that the tyrants owed their power to Persia, and the bridge was kept. Many historians suspect the tale was spread later, perhaps when Miltiades stood trial in Athens for his tyranny, to show him as an enemy of Persia.
p_miltiades.s2: In 493 BCE, as the Phoenician fleet reconquered the rebel coasts, Miltiades escaped to Athens. His son Metiochus was captured, and Darius gave him a Persian wife and an estate. Elected general, Miltiades persuaded the polemarch Callimachus to cast the deciding vote for battle. Herodotus says the Athenians charged at a run and that about 6,400 of the King's men died against 192 Athenians. The Athenian toll is widely accepted, the Persian one less so.
p_miltiades.s3: After Marathon Miltiades asked the Athenians for ships without saying where he would lead them, and sailed against the island of Paros. The siege failed and he injured his leg. Back in Athens he was prosecuted by Xanthippus and fined fifty talents. He died soon after when the wound turned gangrenous, and his son Cimon paid the fine.
p_miltiades.s4: A bronze Corinthian helmet excavated at the sanctuary of Zeus at Olympia carries an inscription saying that Miltiades dedicated it to Zeus. It is usually identified with this Miltiades and may come from one of his campaigns. It is one of the few objects from his own lifetime that names him, and it is now in the Olympia museum.
p_nabonidus.lead: Nabonidus ruled Babylon for about seventeen years and was its last native king before Cyrus took the city in 539 BCE. Texts written under Cyrus portray him as an impious ruler, and that portrayal shapes much of what is known of him. Two rebels against Darius claimed to be his son, which shows that his name still carried weight.
p_nabonidus.play: Nabonidus has no level or mechanic of his own. The game names him only in the event articles on the fall of Babylon, the return of the exiles, and the revolts of Nidintu-Bel and Arakha.
p_nabonidus.s0: Nabonidus came to the throne in 556 BCE after a coup in the unstable years that followed the reign of Nebuchadnezzar II. He was not of Nebuchadnezzar's line. Inscriptions from his reign, including the stele of his mother Adda-guppi found at Harran, show his devotion to the moon god Sin.
p_nabonidus.s1: The Nabonidus Chronicle records that the king spent years in the Arabian oasis of Tayma, and that the New Year festival went uncelebrated in Babylon in those years. The Chronicle does not give his reasons. Historians have suggested control of the caravan trade, his devotion to Sin, and a quarrel with the Babylonian priesthood, and hostile texts offer other explanations.
p_nabonidus.s2: The Nabonidus Chronicle says that Cyrus's army defeated the Babylonian army at Opis in 539 BCE and took Sippar. Ugbaru, governor of Gutium, then entered Babylon without a battle in mid-October, and Nabonidus was captured. Cyrus himself entered the city about two weeks later.
p_nabonidus.s3: The Cyrus Cylinder blames Nabonidus for neglecting the cults of Babylon and for impious acts. It says that Marduk chose Cyrus to restore order. This is the victor's version, written in Babylonian temple style, and it is propaganda; the Chronicle is less hostile to the king.
p_nabonidus.s4: Herodotus calls the Babylonian king Labynetus, says Cyrus defeated him in battle, and describes the capture of the city by diverting the Euphrates. Berossus, as reported by Josephus, says that Nabonidus surrendered and was settled by Cyrus in Carmania. The two accounts do not agree on the details, and neither matches the Chronicle closely.
p_nabonidus.s5: Darius's Behistun inscription says that Nidintu-Bel, in 522 BCE, took the name Nebuchadnezzar and claimed to be the son of Nabonidus. Arakha, an Armenian, made the same claim in 521 BCE. Darius says both were defeated and killed at Babylon.
p_nabonidus.s6: The Book of Daniel makes Belshazzar the last king of Babylon and tells of a feast cut short by writing on a wall. Cuneiform texts show that Belshazzar was the son of Nabonidus and that he probably acted for his father while the king was away. He was not king himself, and the feast story is a moral tale written long after.
p_nebuchadnezzar.lead: Nebuchadnezzar II was the greatest king of the Neo-Babylonian empire, the builder of much of the Babylon the Persians took. In 522-521 BCE two men raised Babylon against Darius under his name: Nidintu-Bel, who claimed to be Nebuchadnezzar son of Nabonidus, and the Armenian Arakha.
p_nebuchadnezzar.play: The game names Nebuchadnezzar through the two rebels in the Bagastana level's Chronicle, chatter and Encyclopedia.
p_nebuchadnezzar.s0: Nebuchadnezzar's building inscriptions describe the walls, the Ishtar Gate with its glazed-brick dragons and bulls, the palaces and the great ziggurat of Babylon. Bricks stamped with his name are found across the city. The Babylon Herodotus describes is largely his.
p_nebuchadnezzar.s1: The Babylonian Chronicle records that he took Jerusalem in 597 BCE, and the Hebrew Bible says he destroyed it in 587-586 BCE and carried its people to Babylon. Cyrus later let the exiles return, as the book of Ezra tells.
p_nebuchadnezzar.s2: Darius says a Babylonian named Nidintu-Bel lied to the people, saying he was Nebuchadnezzar son of Nabonidus, and Babylon went over to him. Darius beat him on the Tigris and at Zazana and took Babylon. Tablets dated to a Nebuchadnezzar of 522 BCE confirm the reign.
p_nebuchadnezzar.s3: In 521 BCE, Darius says, an Armenian named Arakha rose at Babylon, also calling himself Nebuchadnezzar son of Nabonidus. Darius's general Intaphernes took the city, and Arakha and his chief men were impaled. Taking the old king's name shows how strong his memory still was.
p_necho.lead: Necho II was a king of the Twenty-sixth (Saite) Dynasty and the son of Psamtik I. He campaigned in the Levant and, according to Herodotus, began a canal from the Nile towards the Red Sea. Darius later completed a canal on this line, and the canal's stelae are from Darius's reign.
p_necho.play: The game names Necho II in the Chronicle and in the Nile canal event article, as the pharaoh who began the canal. He has no figure, building or mechanic of his own.
p_necho.s0: Herodotus says Necho was the son of Psamtik and ruled Egypt after him. He tells of Necho's wars and works, and Herodotus wrote long after the reign, so his account rests on later Egyptian and Greek tradition.
p_necho.s1: Herodotus says Necho began digging a canal from the Nile eastwards towards the Red Sea and that a very large number of Egyptians died in the work. He adds that an oracle warned Necho he was labouring for a foreigner, and that the king stopped. Herodotus later says Darius finished it.
p_necho.s2: Fragmentary stelae of Darius found along the line of the canal in Egypt record the work as his. They do not name Necho, so the earlier digging rests on Herodotus. The game's Nile canal article treats the canal's completion as Darius's.
p_necho.s3: Herodotus says Necho built triremes on both the Mediterranean and Red Sea coasts. He also says Necho sent Phoenicians to sail round Africa, and they returned in the third year. Modern historians argue over whether the voyage happened, since a detail such as the sun being on their right cannot be checked.
p_necho.s4: Herodotus says Necho defeated the Syrians at Magdolos and took the city of Cadytis, which some identify with Gaza. The Hebrew Bible says he killed King Josiah of Judah at Megiddo. Necho was later beaten by the Babylonians at Carchemish, as the Babylonian Chronicle records.
p_nidintu_bel.lead: Nidintu-Bel was a Babylonian who seized the throne of Babylon in the autumn of 522 BCE and ruled as Nebuchadnezzar, the third king of that name. Darius defeated him in two battles and killed him at Babylon, probably within about two months. The episode is known chiefly from Darius's own Behistun inscription and from Babylonian dated tablets.
p_nidintu_bel.play: The game names him only in the event articles on the revolt of Nidintu-Bel and the revolts of 522-521 BCE. He has no unit, building or mechanic of his own.
p_nidintu_bel.s0: Darius says a Babylonian named Nidintu-Bel, son of Aniri, lied to the people of Babylon and claimed to be Nebuchadnezzar, son of Nabonidus. According to the inscription, all Babylon went over to him. The text is the King's own account, and it presents every rebel as a liar.
p_nidintu_bel.s1: Darius says Nidintu-Bel held the bank of the Tigris with ships. Darius's army crossed the river and defeated him there. A second battle followed at a place called Zazana on the Euphrates, after which Nidintu-Bel fled to Babylon with a few horsemen. Darius then took Babylon and killed him there.
p_nidintu_bel.s2: Business tablets from Babylon and some other Babylonian cities were dated to the reign of Nebuchadnezzar for a few weeks in late 522 BCE. They show that scribes and local people treated the rebel as a real king. Darius's text is the only source for the claim that he was Nabonidus's son.
p_nidintu_bel.s3: Darius calls him an impostor, but modern historians doubt that this tells the whole story. The revolt came when Persian rule was shaken by the death of Cambyses and the rise of Darius, and the throne name recalled the great Babylonian king. Whether Nidintu-Bel had any real link to Nabonidus's family cannot be settled from the surviving evidence.
p_nidintu_bel.s4: Herodotus does not mention Nidintu-Bel. He tells of a long siege of Babylon under Darius, ended by the stratagem of Zopyrus. Most historians connect that story with the later revolt of Arakha in 521 BCE, which Darius also records, and not with the revolt of Nidintu-Bel.
p_oeobazus.lead: Oeobazus was a Persian at Sestos on the Hellespont when the Greeks besieged it in the autumn and winter after Plataea. Herodotus is the main source for him, and he records him in connection with the cables of Xerxes' bridges and with a sacrifice among the Thracians. He was not the governor of the town; that was Artayctes.
p_oeobazus.play: Oeobazus appears only in the event articles on the siege of Sestos and the Hellespont bridges, and has no mechanic of his own. Herodotus makes Artayctes the governor of Sestos, not Oeobazus.
p_oeobazus.s0: Herodotus says that Sestos was the strongest place on the Hellespont and that Persians and their allies gathered in it when the Greek fleet came after Mycale. Among them was Oeobazus, who had brought the cables of the bridges there from Cardia. The cables were the heavy ropes that had held Xerxes' bridges in place.
p_oeobazus.s1: The man in charge of Sestos was Artayctes, a Persian governor of the region, according to Herodotus. Oeobazus is named as one of those shut in the town, not as its commander. Any presentation of him as leader of the defence goes beyond what Herodotus says.
p_oeobazus.s2: When hunger worsened in the siege, Herodotus says that the Persians, Artayctes and Oeobazus among them, slipped out by night over the rear wall. Oeobazus reached Thrace, where the Apsinthians seized him and sacrificed him to their god Pleistorus in their own manner.
p_oeobazus.s3: After the town fell, Herodotus says the Athenians took the cables home to dedicate them. Artayctes was caught and put to death. The cables thus became part of the Greek story of the war's end, while Oeobazus passes out of it.
p_oeobazus.s4: Herodotus also names an Oeobazus who asked Darius to leave one of his three sons at home during the Scythian campaign, and whom Darius answered by having all three sons killed. Herodotus does not say that this is the same man, and the name could belong to several people. Nothing in the surviving Persian record settles the question.
p_onesilus.lead: Onesilus was the younger brother of Gorgus, king of Salamis on Cyprus, and the man who took the island's cities into the Ionian Revolt. Herodotus is the main source for him. The revolt lasted about a year before Persian forces beat the Cypriots on land and the Ionian fleet sailed home.
p_onesilus.play: The game names Onesilus only in the event articles, chiefly the revolt of Cyprus. He has no figure, level or mechanic of his own.
p_onesilus.s0: Herodotus says Onesilus was the son of Chersis and the brother of Gorgus, king of Salamis on Cyprus. He had often urged Gorgus to revolt, and when Gorgus refused he shut him out of the city and took power. Gorgus fled to the Medes, as Herodotus calls the Persians.
p_onesilus.s1: Herodotus reports that Onesilus persuaded the Cypriot cities except Amathus to revolt, and that he besieged Amathus. A Persian force then crossed to the island, and the Ionian fleet arrived to help. The Cypriot leaders chose to meet the Persians on land and leave the sea to the Ionians.
p_onesilus.s2: Herodotus says the Ionians won the sea battle. On land Onesilus faced the Persian commander Artybius, whose horse was trained to rear against hoplites, and Onesilus's Carian shield-bearer cut the horse down. Herodotus adds that the Curians went over to the Persians, the Salaminian chariots followed, and Onesilus was killed along with Aristocyprus, king of Soli.
p_onesilus.s3: Herodotus says the Amathusians cut off Onesilus's head, took it to Amathus and hung it above their gate. It filled with bees, and an oracle told them to bury it and honour him yearly as a hero. He reports the rest as the end of the revolt: the Persians retook the Cypriot cities one by one, and Cyprus was enslaved again after a year of freedom.
p_onesilus.s4: No Persian or Cypriot text of the time is known to name Onesilus, so the story rests on Herodotus. Historians accept the revolt on Cyprus as real, but details such as the horse duel and the bees probably owe something to storytelling. The date, about 497 BCE, is inferred from the sequence of the Ionian Revolt.
p_pactyes.lead: Pactyes was a Lydian to whom Cyrus entrusted Croesus's treasure after the fall of Sardis. After Cyrus had left for the east, he used it to raise a revolt on the Lydian coast. The rising collapsed, and Greek cities handed him on. Herodotus is the only continuous source.
p_pactyes.play: The game names Pactyes only in the event articles on the fall of Sardis and Harpagus's conquest of Ionia. He has no mechanic of his own.
p_pactyes.s0: Herodotus says that Cyrus, after taking Sardis, went towards Ecbatana and took Croesus with him. He left a Persian, Tabalus, in command at Sardis. Pactyes, a Lydian, was told to bring Croesus's gold and other treasure. Pactyes was therefore a treasure bearer, and Tabalus held the command.
p_pactyes.s1: Herodotus says that once Cyrus was on his way, Pactyes persuaded the Lydians to rise against Tabalus and against Cyrus. He went down to the coast, used the treasure to hire mercenaries and brought the coastal people over to his side. He then besieged Tabalus in the citadel of Sardis.
p_pactyes.s2: Herodotus says that Cyrus sent the Median commander Mazares with an army. On hearing of its approach, Pactyes fled to Cyme and his mercenaries scattered. Mazares then demanded Pactyes from the Cymaeans. In Herodotus's telling, Harpagus enters the story only after Mazares died of illness, and continued the conquest of the Ionian cities.
p_pactyes.s3: Herodotus says that the Cymaeans consulted the oracle at Branchidae, which told them to give Pactyes up. They sent him to Mytilene, which was ready to sell him, and then to Chios. The Chians took him from the temple of Athena and handed him over, and Herodotus says they received the land of Atarneus in Mysia in return. Herodotus does not say what became of Pactyes.
p_pactyes.s4: Herodotus reports that Cyrus wanted to enslave the Lydians, and that Croesus talked him out of it. In this story Croesus advised forbidding the Lydians weapons and making them wear soft clothes and teach their sons to play instruments and to trade. It reads as a moral tale about softness and empire, and should not be taken as a record of Persian policy.
p_pactyes.s5: Herodotus is the only source for these events, and no Persian text mentions Pactyes. Historians generally treat the revolt as a sign that Lydia was unsettled in the first years of Persian rule. The exact dates and the details of the treasure are uncertain.
p_pausanias.lead: Pausanias, son of Cleombrotus, was regent of Sparta for his young cousin Pleistarchus, the son of Leonidas. In 479 BCE he commanded the allied Greek army that defeated Mardonius at Plataea and ended the Persian land invasion of Greece. Within a decade he was accused of plotting with Xerxes and was starved to death at a Spartan sanctuary.
p_pausanias.play: The game's chronicle calls him regent for Leonidas's young son and commander of the largest Greek army at Plataea. This matches Herodotus, though the army's size rests on his figures.
p_pausanias.s0: Herodotus says Pausanias was the son of Cleombrotus and so a nephew of Leonidas, who had died at Thermopylae. Because Leonidas's son Pleistarchus was still a child, Pausanias acted as his guardian and took command. Herodotus reports that Sparta, pressed by the Athenians, sent out 5,000 Spartiates by night, each with seven helot attendants.
p_pausanias.s1: Herodotus counts 38,700 hoplites and about 110,000 men in all on the Greek side. Many historians accept the hoplite total as roughly possible but doubt the large numbers of light troops and helots. After days of manoeuvre near the Asopus, a disordered night withdrawal left the Spartans and Tegeans exposed. Mardonius attacked, was killed, and his army broke.
p_pausanias.s2: From the spoils of Plataea the Greeks dedicated a gold tripod at Delphi on a bronze column of three twisted serpents. The coils bear the names of the Greek states that fought the Persians, with no individual commander named. The bronze column still stands, damaged, in the old Hippodrome of Istanbul.
p_pausanias.s3: Thucydides says Pausanias had a boastful verse naming himself carved on the Delphi tripod, and that at Byzantium he wore Persian dress and wrote to Xerxes offering to bring Greece under him. Recalled, he fled to the temple of Athena of the Bronze House, was walled in, and was carried out only as he was dying of hunger. Historians still argue whether the letters were genuine or the charges grew from Spartan and Athenian politics.
p_pausanias.s4: Herodotus tells that after the battle Pausanias had Mardonius's cooks prepare a Persian feast beside a plain Spartan meal, and laughed that men so rich had come to rob men so poor. In the same spirit he is said to have refused advice to mutilate Mardonius's body. Both tales read as moral lessons shaped by the storyteller.
p_phanes.lead: Phanes was a Greek from Halicarnassus who commanded mercenaries for the Egyptian king Amasis and then went over to the Persian king Cambyses. Herodotus says he gave Cambyses inside knowledge of Egypt and advised him how to get an army across the waterless desert to the Nile. His story is known only from Herodotus, who makes him a key figure in the Persian conquest of Egypt in 525 BCE.
p_phanes.play: The game's chronicle names Phanes as the Greek captain who deserted to Cambyses, showed him the desert route and lost his sons before Pelusium. It does not name the pharaoh he left; Herodotus says it was Amasis, not Psamtik III.
p_phanes.s0: Herodotus describes Phanes as one of the foreign mercenaries of Amasis, sound in judgement and brave in war. He says Phanes had some grievance against the king, though he does not say what it was, and slipped away by ship to join Cambyses. Egypt relied heavily on Greek and Carian soldiers in this period, so a senior mercenary officer probably knew a great deal about its defences.
p_phanes.s1: Herodotus says Amasis sent a trusted eunuch in a warship after Phanes, who was caught in Lycia but escaped after making his guards drunk. Reaching Cambyses, he explained the state of Egypt and urged him to ask the king of the Arabs for safe passage. Herodotus says the Arabs then supplied water for the march, and he gives two versions of how: camels carrying skins, or a long pipe of hides from a river.
p_phanes.s2: By the time the Persians arrived, Amasis had died and his son Psamtik III ruled. Herodotus says the Greek and Carian mercenaries, furious that Phanes had led a foreign army against Egypt, brought his sons out between the armies, cut their throats over a bowl, mixed wine and water with the blood and drank it before going into battle. The Egyptians were then defeated after a hard fight near the Pelusiac mouth of the Nile.
p_phanes.s3: No Persian or Egyptian document names Phanes; the statue inscription of Udjahorresnet records Cambyses' arrival in Egypt but says nothing of him. The pursuit, the drunken guards and the blood oath read like storytelling, and historians debate how far Herodotus shaped them. Some scholars link him to a Phanes named on a dedication found at Naucratis, but the name was common and the identification is uncertain.
p_pheidippides.lead: Pheidippides was a trained runner whom the Athenian generals sent to Sparta in 490 BCE to ask for help against the Persian force that had landed at Marathon. Herodotus says he reached Sparta the day after he left Athens, a distance of about 240 km by modern reckoning. He is remembered today for a run he never made, the one from Marathon to Athens.
p_pheidippides.play: The game presents him in a chronicle note: the runner sent to Sparta before Marathon, arriving the day after he left Athens. The note rightly keeps him apart from the later Marathon-to-Athens story.
p_pheidippides.s0: Herodotus says that while the generals were still in the city, they sent Pheidippides, an Athenian and a trained day-runner, to Sparta. He reached Sparta on the day after he left Athens and asked the Spartans not to let one of the oldest Greek cities fall into slavery to foreigners. He pointed out that Eretria had already been enslaved.
p_pheidippides.s1: Herodotus says the Spartans wished to help but would not march before the full moon, because of religious law. They arrived with 2,000 men after the battle was over. Some historians accept the religious reason, often linking it to the Carneia festival. Others suspect an excuse or a real crisis at home, since Plato mentions a war with the Messenians delaying Sparta at the time.
p_pheidippides.s2: Herodotus reports Pheidippides' own claim that on Mount Parthenion, above Tegea, the god Pan called him by name. Pan asked why Athens paid him no honour, though he had helped them before and would again. Herodotus says that after the victory the Athenians founded a shrine of Pan below the Acropolis, with yearly sacrifices and a torch race.
p_pheidippides.s3: The manuscripts of Herodotus disagree on his name. Some give Pheidippides and others Philippides, and many scholars prefer the second, the form used by later writers. Some doubted that anyone could run so far so fast, but modern runners have shown it can be done. The Spartathlon, a race from Athens to Sparta first held in 1983, grew out of a test of his reported time.
p_pheidippides.s4: Herodotus says nothing of a runner carrying news of victory from Marathon to Athens, and that tale appears much later. Plutarch says Heraclides Ponticus named the messenger Thersippus, but most writers named Eucles, who died after giving the news. Lucian, in the 2nd century CE, gave the deed to Philippides. Robert Browning's poem of 1879 fixed this version, and the marathon race of the 1896 Olympics took it as its model.
p_pheretime.lead: Pheretime was the mother of Arcesilaus III, king of Cyrene in Libya. Herodotus tells her story in book 4: after her son was killed at Barca, she appealed to Aryandes, the Persian governor of Egypt, and a Persian force took Barca. Her end, as Herodotus tells it, is a moral tale about the anger of the gods.
p_pheretime.play: Pheretime is named in the Encyclopedia's event article on the siege of Barca and in related articles on the Persians in Egypt. She has no figure, building or mechanic of her own in the game.
p_pheretime.s0: Herodotus says Pheretime was the mother of Arcesilaus III, a king of the Battiad dynasty of Cyrene. When her son fell out with his people, she went to Salamis in Cyprus while he went to Samos and then to Barca. After he was killed at Barca, Herodotus says she went to Egypt to seek vengeance.
p_pheretime.s1: Herodotus says Pheretime went to Aryandes, the Persian governor of Egypt, and asked him to avenge her son. She argued that Arcesilaus had died because he had placed Cyrene under Persian rule. Aryandes gave her an army and a fleet, though Herodotus says he had his own reasons for the campaign.
p_pheretime.s2: According to Herodotus, the Persians besieged Barca for nine months, digging mines that the Barcaeans detected with a bronze shield. The Persians then took the city by a trick, swearing terms that they did not intend to keep. Pheretime had the leading men impaled and, he says, had the breasts of their wives cut off and fixed along the wall. He adds that the Persians settled the surviving Barcaeans in Bactria.
p_pheretime.s3: Herodotus says Pheretime returned to Egypt and died of worms swarming over her body. He draws the lesson that excessive vengeance brings the anger of the gods. This is a moral tale, and the manner of her death is known only from Herodotus.
p_pheretime.s4: Herodotus's account is the only detailed one, and Cyrenaean and Barcaean tradition may have shaped it. Historians debate the date, usually placed around 515 BCE, and how far Aryandes acted for the King rather than on his own account. The surrounding drama is hard to test.
p_polycrates.lead: Polycrates made himself tyrant of Samos and built the strongest Greek fleet of his day. Herodotus says he sent forty triremes to Cambyses for the Egyptian campaign, though what became of them is disputed. Herodotus also says Oroetes, the Persian governor at Sardis, lured him to the mainland and killed him.
p_polycrates.play: The game names Polycrates only in the Chronicle and in event articles, as the sender of forty triremes for Egypt. He has no figure, building or mechanic of his own.
p_polycrates.s0: Herodotus says Polycrates seized Samos with his brothers and then ruled alone, allied himself with Amasis of Egypt, and raised a large fleet and many archers. Thucydides likewise notes that Polycrates had great naval strength and conquered islands, and says he dedicated Rhenaea to Apollo at Delos. Both writers show a Greek island state powerful enough to matter to Persia.
p_polycrates.s1: The tunnel of Eupalinus, which Herodotus attributes to a man of Megara, can still be walked, and the Heraion of Samos has been excavated. Herodotus also credits the Samians with a harbour mole and the largest temple he knew. These remains show the wealth of the island in the sixth century, though they do not tell how much belonged to Polycrates' own reign.
p_polycrates.s2: Herodotus says Cambyses asked Polycrates for ships, and that Polycrates picked citizens he suspected of disloyalty, manned forty triremes with them and asked Cambyses to see that they never came home. Herodotus gives two versions. In one they turned back at Carpathus, in the other they reached Egypt and escaped. He says he does not accept the Samian claim that they reached Egypt and returned. Whether Samian ships served in Egypt is therefore uncertain.
p_polycrates.s3: Herodotus tells how Amasis advised Polycrates to throw away his dearest possession because he was too fortunate. Polycrates threw a ring into the sea, and it came back in the belly of a fish. Amasis then ended the alliance. The story is a moral tale about excess of good fortune, and it should not be read as a record of why the alliance ended.
p_polycrates.s4: Herodotus says Oroetes, the Persian governor at Sardis, lured Polycrates to the mainland with promises of money, then killed him and had the body crucified. The date is about 522 BCE, in the troubled time around the death of Cambyses. Herodotus says Samos later passed to Polycrates' brother Syloson, after a Persian force under Otanes took the island for Darius.
p_prexaspes.lead: Herodotus uses the name Prexaspes for two men. One was a trusted servant of Cambyses who was drawn into the story of Bardiya's death. The other, son of Aspathines, was one of the four admirals of Xerxes' fleet in 480 BCE. Whether they were related is not known.
p_prexaspes.play: The game names Prexaspes in Chronicle entries and event articles, including the Admirals entry, where he is one of four admirals of Xerxes' fleet. He has no figure or mechanic of his own.
p_prexaspes.s0: Herodotus describes a Prexaspes who was among the most trusted men of Cambyses and carried his messages. The source is Greek and was written long after the events.
p_prexaspes.s1: Herodotus tells that Cambyses, in a fit of madness, shot the son of Prexaspes to show that his hand was steady. The tale is built as a lesson about a king's cruelty and a servant's endurance, and no Persian record confirms it.
p_prexaspes.s2: Herodotus says Cambyses sent Prexaspes to kill his brother Bardiya, called Smerdis by the Greeks, and gives a second version of how the death was carried out. Darius's Behistun inscription says only that Cambyses killed Bardiya in secret, and names no agent. Historians therefore cannot say whether Prexaspes did it, and some doubt the Gaumata story as Darius presented it.
p_prexaspes.s3: In Herodotus the conspirators made Prexaspes announce to the Persians that the new king was truly Cyrus's son. He instead confessed to killing Bardiya and threw himself from a tower. The scene reads as a moral tale about a servant's conscience.
p_prexaspes.s4: Herodotus names Prexaspes, son of Aspathines, among the four Persian admirals of Xerxes' fleet in 480 BCE. The others he lists are Ariabignes, Achaemenes and Megabazus. An Aspathines is named as the bearer of Darius's bow and battle-axe in the inscription DNd at Naqsh-e Rostam, so the admiral may have come from a family close to the throne, though the link is not certain. Herodotus's fleet figures are widely held to be exaggerated.
p_psamtik.lead: Psamtik III, called Psammenitus by Herodotus, was the son of Amasis and the last king of Egypt's 26th dynasty. He had ruled for only a few months when Cambyses invaded, defeated his army at Pelusium and took Memphis. His fall brought Egypt into the Persian empire, which held it until about 404 BCE and again from 343 to 332.
p_psamtik.play: The chronicle presents him as the Pharaoh beaten at Pelusium in the Memphis level (525 BCE), following Herodotus. His execution for plotting revolt is Herodotus's version; other ancient writers told his end differently.
p_psamtik.s0: Herodotus says Psammenitus came to the throne when his father Amasis died, just as the Persians were preparing to invade. He reports that rain fell at Egyptian Thebes during the new reign, which the Egyptians took as a strange sign. By Herodotus's reckoning Psamtik ruled for six months before he was captured.
p_psamtik.s1: Herodotus tells that Psamtik met Cambyses at the Pelusiac mouth of the Nile and was routed. His Greek and Carian mercenaries had killed the sons of Phanes, a Greek who had gone over to the Persians. The Egyptians fled to Memphis, killed the crew of a ship sent to demand surrender, and were then besieged until the city gave in.
p_psamtik.s2: Few objects survive from so short a reign. The naophorous statue of Udjahorresnet, now in the Vatican, records that he commanded the royal fleet under Amasis and Psamtik before serving Cambyses. It describes Cambyses coming to Egypt with men of every foreign land and later mentions a great turmoil in the country. It says nothing of Psamtik's defeat or his fate.
p_psamtik.s3: Herodotus says Cambyses made the captive king watch his daughter carry water as a slave and his son led to execution; Psamtik wept only for an old friend reduced to begging. Cambyses relented and kept him at court, but Psamtik was caught stirring revolt and died after drinking bull's blood. The scene is shaped as a moral tale, and death by bull's blood is a Greek story told of others too.
p_psamtik.s4: Ctesias names the defeated king Amyrtaeus and says Cambyses sent him to Susa with six thousand Egyptians, with no execution. A much later writer, Polyaenus, claims the Persians shielded themselves with sacred animals at Pelusium, a story most historians reject. Most date the conquest to 525 BCE, though some scholars argue for 526 BCE from the Egyptian evidence.
p_pythius.lead: Pythius, son of Atys, was a Lydian whom Herodotus calls the richest man of his time after the King. He entertained Xerxes' army at Celaenae on its march towards Sardis and offered his wealth for the war. The stories about him are shaped as moral tales on wealth and royal power, and no document from the time mentions him.
p_pythius.play: The game names Pythius in the Chronicle and in event articles, and the Sardis mint entry calls him a Lydian who offered Xerxes vast wealth. He has no mechanic of his own.
p_pythius.s0: Herodotus says that Pythius, son of Atys, received Xerxes and his whole army at Celaenae in Phrygia on the march to Sardis, probably in autumn 481 BCE. He says Pythius feasted them and offered money for the war. Herodotus names him as the richest man known after the King.
p_pythius.s1: Herodotus reports that Pythius offered his silver and gold, saying he had enough to live on without them. Xerxes is said to have praised him and made him a guest-friend. Herodotus adds that Pythius's coin stood at a little under four million darics, and that the King supplied the missing sum himself. The figures are Herodotus's own and are not confirmed elsewhere.
p_pythius.s2: Herodotus has the Persians at Xerxes' side remember Pythius as the man who gave Darius a golden plane tree and a golden vine. The tale presents Pythius as a long-standing servant of the Persian court. It proves nothing about the size of his actual fortune.
p_pythius.s3: Herodotus tells that Pythius later asked Xerxes to excuse his eldest son from service. Xerxes is said to have been enraged, had the son cut in two, and marched the army between the halves. The story works as a lesson on pride and the danger of testing a king. It is told in a moral shape, and no Persian source supports it.
p_pythius.s4: Historians generally accept that a rich Lydian notable may have hosted the army, since Sardis was the satrapal seat. They are more cautious about the huge sums and the killing of the son. Herodotus's Xerxes serves partly as a figure of arrogance, and the Persian view of such events is not preserved.
p_scylax.lead: Scylax was a Carian from the small coastal town of Caryanda in south-west Asia Minor. Herodotus says Darius sent him to sail down the Indus to the sea and then west to Egypt, and that the King conquered the Indians after the voyage. He is one of the first named explorers in Greek writing, and his voyage, if it happened as told, linked the empire's eastern and western edges by sea.
p_scylax.play: The game mentions Scylax only in a chronicle note that follows Herodotus 4.44. It calls him a Greek explorer, but he was a Carian from Caryanda who probably wrote in Greek; the voyage's date and route are uncertain.
p_scylax.s0: Herodotus says Darius wanted to learn where the Indus met the sea, so he sent ships manned by men he trusted, among them Scylax. They set out from Caspatyrus in the Pactyic country, followed the river down to the sea, then sailed west and reached the head of the Red Sea in the thirtieth month. Herodotus adds that Darius then subdued the Indians and made use of this sea.
p_scylax.s1: The list of lands at Behistun, made about 520 BCE, names Gandara but not Hindush, the Indus country. Hindush appears in later lists of Darius, such as the one on his tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam. Persepolis Fortification tablets record travel rations for parties moving between Persia and Hindush. None of these texts mentions Scylax or a voyage.
p_scylax.s2: Historians argue over the date, usually placed between about 519 and 510 BCE, and over whether the conquest of Hindush came before or after it. Herodotus has the ships sail east down the Indus, though the river flows south-west, which suggests muddled geography. Some doubt the full voyage round Arabia; others note that Darius's canal from the Nile to the Red Sea fits an interest in this sea route.
p_scylax.s3: Later Greek authors treated Scylax as a writer on India. Aristotle cites him for the claim that Indian kings stood far above their subjects. A surviving description of Mediterranean coasts carries his name, but scholars date it to the 4th century, long after him, so it is now called Pseudo-Scylax. How much of his own report later writers truly read is unknown.
p_scylax.s4: Herodotus also tells of a different Scylax, a ship captain from Myndus in Caria, whom the Persian commander Megabates punished during the failed attack on Naxos about 499 BCE. The two are separate men, though both show Carians serving the King at sea.
p_skunkha.lead: Skunkha was a chief of the pointed-hat Saka whom Darius says he captured after crossing a sea. He is the last figure carved on the Behistun relief, added to it after the first design. Only Darius's own inscription names him, and it leaves his lands and the date uncertain.
p_skunkha.play: Skunkha is named only in the Encyclopedia's event articles, chiefly the campaign against Skunkha, and has no mechanic of his own.
p_skunkha.s0: In DB §74 Darius says he marched against the Saka who wear pointed caps and crossed a sea with his army. He says he defeated them heavily. Skunkha, named as their chief, was seized and brought to him. Darius then says he set another man over them as he wished.
p_skunkha.s1: Skunkha stands at the end of the line of bound rebels before Darius, in a tall pointed cap. He was not part of the original design. The relief was extended to fit him, and the added inscription in column V was cut later. The monument was therefore updated after the first carving.
p_skunkha.s2: The other bound figures at Behistun are men who rose against Darius in 522 and 521 BCE, told in the first four columns. Skunkha belongs to the added fifth column, which describes a later campaign. There Darius calls these Saka faithless and says they did not worship Auramazda, but he tells their war apart from the revolts of his first year.
p_skunkha.s3: Darius's royal inscriptions name several groups of Saka, and the pointed-hat group is one of them. Historians disagree on where they lived and which sea Darius crossed. Proposed answers include the Aral and Caspian regions, and the date is also open, though the campaign probably came a year or more after the first carving.
p_skunkha.s4: Herodotus never names Skunkha. He lists the Saka and Caspians together in one tribute district, and he describes the Amyrgian Saka among the troops of Xerxes. Skunkha therefore comes only from the Persian side, with no Greek story about him.
p_syloson.lead: Syloson was a brother of Polycrates, the tyrant of Samos. Herodotus says he gave a red cloak to the young Darius in Egypt, and that Darius later made him ruler of Samos with a Persian force. The story is the Greek account of how a favour was repaid at the Persian court.
p_syloson.play: The game names Syloson in the Chronicle's entries and the Encyclopedia's event articles, not in a level of his own, and he has no mechanic. The Memphis market entry mentions him giving his red cloak to the young Darius.
p_syloson.s0: Herodotus says Syloson had been driven out of Samos by his brother Polycrates and was in Egypt with Cambyses' army. He was walking in the market of Memphis in a red cloak when Darius, then a spear-bearer in Cambyses' guard and of no rank, admired it and wished to buy it. Syloson gave it to him as a gift.
p_syloson.s1: Herodotus says that after Darius became king, Syloson came to Susa and presented himself as the man who had given him the cloak. Darius thanked him and offered gold and silver. Syloson asked instead for Samos, to be taken without bloodshed or enslavement.
p_syloson.s2: In Herodotus's telling, Otanes led a Persian force to Samos and took the island after fighting in which many Samians died.
