Syloson received the island, which Herodotus describes as largely emptied of people. The date of the conquest is not certain; it is usually placed about 520 to 517 BCE.
p_syloson.s3: Only Herodotus gives the cloak episode, and it has the shape of a moral tale about gratitude. Historians accept that Samos came under Persian control and had a Persian-backed ruler in this period. Few treat the details of the cloak, the market scene or Darius's rank at the time as established.
p_syloson.s4: Strabo and other later writers preserve a Greek saying about Syloson and wide open spaces, which they explained by the emptying of Samos. The explanation was recorded long after his time and is better treated as popular tradition than as evidence of what Syloson did.
p_themistocles.lead: Themistocles was an Athenian politician and general who persuaded his city to build the fleet that fought Xerxes in 480 BCE. Herodotus credits him with holding the Greek ships together at Artemisium and bringing on the battle of Salamis, where the Persian navy was defeated. He ended his life in Asia, an exile living on revenues granted by the Persian king.
p_themistocles.play: The game's chronicle follows Herodotus: the Laurium ships, the gifts at Artemisium and the plan of Salamis. The figure of two hundred ships is Herodotus's; another ancient source gives a hundred.
p_themistocles.s0: Herodotus says that when a rich new vein of silver came in at the Laurium mines, Themistocles talked the Athenians out of sharing the money among the citizens. Instead they built two hundred ships for their war with Aegina. Herodotus also says he read the Delphic oracle of the wooden wall as meaning ships. The Aristotelian Constitution of the Athenians gives a hundred ships, so the figure is uncertain.
p_themistocles.s1: Herodotus tells that the Euboeans, afraid of being left undefended, paid Themistocles thirty talents to keep the Greek fleet at Artemisium. He passed five talents to the Spartan commander Eurybiades and three to Adeimantus of Corinth, and kept the rest himself. The fleet stayed and fought the Persian ships over three days, then withdrew south when news came that Thermopylae had fallen.
p_themistocles.s2: Herodotus says Themistocles sent his slave Sicinnus to Xerxes with word that the Greeks meant to slip away, so the Persian ships moved by night to close the straits. Aeschylus, who probably fought in the war, describes a similar message from a Greek in his Persians of 472 BCE. Historians still argue whether this trick caused the battle or whether the Persian commanders had already decided to attack.
p_themistocles.s3: Ostracised from Athens and later condemned for siding with Persia, Themistocles fled to Asia. Thucydides says he wrote to the new king Artaxerxes, spent a year learning the Persian language and customs, and was given Magnesia on the Maeander for his bread, Lampsacus for his wine and Myus for his other food. Some later writers named Xerxes instead, as Plutarch notes. He died at Magnesia, of illness according to Thucydides.
p_themistocles.s4: Thucydides already reports a rumour that Themistocles poisoned himself because he could not deliver what he had promised the King. The tale that he drank bull's blood appears in Aristophanes' Knights of 424 BCE. Plutarch, writing more than five centuries after his death, shapes it into a moral story: asked to lead an army against Greece, he chose death over fighting his own people. No Persian document is known to name him.
p_tigranes.lead: Tigranes was a Persian of the royal Achaemenid clan who led the Median contingent in Xerxes' invasion of Greece. He later commanded the land army that Xerxes had left to guard Ionia, and he was killed when the Greeks stormed the Persian camp at Mycale in 479 BCE. Almost everything known about him comes from Herodotus.
p_tigranes.play: The game's chronicle presents Tigranes as an Achaemenid who led the Medes and fell commanding at Mycale. This follows Herodotus, the main source for him.
p_tigranes.s0: Herodotus lists Tigranes, an Achaemenid, as commander of the Medes in the muster of Xerxes' army. He says the Medes were equipped like the Persians, with felt caps, sleeved tunics, scale armour, wicker shields, short spears and large bows. Placing a Persian noble at the head of the Median troops fitted the way Persian kings gave senior commands to men of their own clan.
p_tigranes.s1: Herodotus says Xerxes had left a land army under Tigranes at Mycale, on the coast facing Samos, to keep watch over Ionia. When the Greek fleet approached in 479 BCE, the Persian ships sailed to Mycale. There they were drawn up on the shore and enclosed with a rampart of stones and timber. Herodotus gives the army as 60,000 men.
p_tigranes.s2: The Greek fleet under Leotychides of Sparta and Xanthippus of Athens landed and attacked the camp. Herodotus says the Athenians and the troops beside them broke into the rampart, and that the Persians fought on in small groups after others fled. Of four Persian commanders, Artayntes and Ithamitres escaped, while Mardontes and Tigranes, general of the land army, died fighting. The Greeks then burned the ships and the rampart.
p_tigranes.s3: Herodotus remarks that Tigranes surpassed the Persians in beauty and stature. He praises other Persians in similar terms: Masistius, whose body the Greeks paraded after he was killed at Plataea, and Xerxes himself. The detail may be genuine, but it also suits Herodotus's habit of marking notable figures on the enemy side.
p_tigranes.s4: No Persian document is known to name this Tigranes, so his career rests on Greek testimony. Historians generally treat Herodotus's figure of 60,000 men at Mycale as too high. Herodotus also says Mycale was fought on the same day as Plataea, a coincidence many scholars doubt. It is usually assumed, though Herodotus does not say so outright, that the commander of the Medes and the general at Mycale were the same man.
p_tomyris.lead: Tomyris was queen of the Massagetae, a nomadic people who lived east of the Caspian Sea. Herodotus says Cyrus the Great invaded her land in 530 BCE and was defeated and killed there, and that she then took a cruel revenge on his body. No Persian source mentions her, and other Greek writers describe Cyrus dying in different ways. Later versions of her story, such as Justin's, follow Herodotus.
p_tomyris.play: The game's Chronicle names Tomyris as the queen who, Herodotus says, killed Cyrus in 530 BCE, and it notes that other accounts differ. This is a fair summary of the sources.
p_tomyris.s0: Herodotus says Tomyris ruled the Massagetae after her husband died. They were a horse-riding people living beyond a river he calls the Araxes. Cyrus first asked to marry her, but she saw that he wanted her kingdom and refused. When he began bridging the river, she offered to fight on either bank, either withdrawing three days' march to let him cross or crossing over herself.
p_tomyris.s1: Herodotus says Cyrus took the advice of Croesus: cross the river, leave a camp of weak troops with wine and food, and fall back. A third of the Massagetae, led by the queen's son Spargapises, took the camp, feasted and were overrun while drunk. Spargapises later killed himself in captivity. In the battle that followed, which Herodotus calls the fiercest ever fought between non-Greeks, most of the Persian army died and Cyrus was killed.
p_tomyris.s2: Herodotus ends the story with Tomyris searching among the dead for Cyrus's body. She put his head into a skin filled with human blood and told him she was giving him his fill of the blood he had craved. The scene answers her earlier warning to him and reads as a moral tale about a conqueror's greed. Herodotus says he had heard many versions of Cyrus's death and chose this one as the most believable.
p_tomyris.s3: Ctesias, a Greek doctor at the Persian court around 400 BCE, said Cyrus was wounded fighting the Derbices and died three days later. Xenophon has him die peacefully in Persia after advising his sons. Justin's much later Latin summary of Trogus keeps the Tomyris story with new details. Historians mostly accept that Cyrus probably died on campaign in Central Asia, but who his enemy was and which river the Araxes was remain open questions.
p_tomyris.s4: Babylonian documents, which were dated by the king's regnal year, show that Cyrus's reign ended in 530 BCE and that Cambyses was recognised as king by late summer. No text from the time names Tomyris or the Massagetae war, so the details of where Cyrus died and who killed him rest on Greek writers. The stone tomb at Pasargadae generally identified as his still stands, although it was found empty in modern times.
p_udjahorresnet.lead: Udjahorresnet was an Egyptian official from Sais who commanded ships for the last native kings and then served Cambyses and Darius. His inscribed statue is the fullest Egyptian account of the Persian conquest. It shows how a foreign king could be fitted into Egyptian kingship, and how local elites kept their temples and careers under the new rulers.
p_udjahorresnet.play: The game's chronicle note credits him with composing the Egyptian royal names of both Cambyses and Darius. His statue claims this only for Cambyses; for Darius it records the restoration of the House of Life at Sais.
p_udjahorresnet.s0: His statue says he commanded the royal warships under Amasis and Psamtik III, the last kings of the Saite dynasty. He also held priestly titles at Sais, the dynasty's home city and the seat of the goddess Neith. When Cambyses conquered Egypt in 525 BCE, he moved into Persian service and kept his standing.
p_udjahorresnet.s1: Cambyses made him chief physician and a companion of the king. Udjahorresnet says he composed Cambyses' Egyptian throne name, Mesutira, meaning offspring of Ra. He persuaded the king to expel foreigners who had settled in the temple of Neith, to restore its revenues and festivals, and to come to Sais and worship the goddess in person.
p_udjahorresnet.s2: The text says he was with Darius in Elam when the king ordered him back to Egypt. His task was to restore the House of Life, the temple institution where scribes copied texts and physicians trained. He says he staffed it and supplied it with everything it needed, because Darius knew the value of the healing art.
p_udjahorresnet.s3: Herodotus portrays Cambyses as a mad king who killed the Apis bull and insulted Egyptian gods. The statue shows him honouring Neith, and an Apis stela records a bull buried with royal honours in his reign. Historians still argue whether Udjahorresnet was a self-serving collaborator or a patriot who protected his town. They also disagree whether the great turmoil he describes was the conquest of 525 BCE or the unrest of 522 BCE.
p_udjahorresnet.s4: His standing statue holds a small shrine and is covered with his autobiography. It was probably carried to Italy in Roman times and is now in the Vatican Museums. Czech archaeologists working at Abusir, near Memphis, excavated a large shaft tomb identified as his and published it in 1999.
p_ugbaru.lead: Ugbaru appears in the Nabonidus Chronicle as governor of Gutium, whose troops entered Babylon without a battle in October 539 BCE. The Chronicle then seems to record his death a few weeks later. His identity is debated, because Greek writers never name him and Xenophon's Gobryas may be the same man.
p_ugbaru.play: The game names Ugbaru only in event articles, such as the fall of Babylon, and gives him no mechanic of his own. It describes him as the governor of Gutium who entered Babylon for Cyrus.
p_ugbaru.s0: The Nabonidus Chronicle says that Ugbaru, governor of Gutium, and the army of Cyrus entered Babylon without fighting on the sixteenth of Tashritu. Nabonidus was captured after he returned to the city. Cyrus himself entered on the third of Arahsamnu, and the text says that he proclaimed peace for the city.
p_ugbaru.s1: The Chronicle's entry for the eleventh of Arahsamnu says that a governor died, and most scholars read the subject as Ugbaru. The tablet is damaged here, so the reading rests on interpretation. The text does not say how he died.
p_ugbaru.s2: Gutium was the old name for the hill country east of the Tigris. Historians disagree over whether Ugbaru was a Babylonian official who changed sides or a commander appointed by Cyrus. The Chronicle does not settle the question.
p_ugbaru.s3: Many scholars identify Ugbaru with the Gobryas of Xenophon's Cyropaedia, since Gobryas is the Greek form of the Persian name Gaubaruva. Xenophon makes him an Assyrian noble who turned against his king and helped Cyrus. Others hold that the two are separate men, and Xenophon's book is a work of moral instruction, not plain history.
p_ugbaru.s4: Herodotus describes the capture of Babylon by diverting the Euphrates and sending troops along the riverbed, and he never names Ugbaru. Xenophon tells a similar story of a diversion and a night attack. The Chronicle mentions neither, and says the city was entered without battle.
p_vahyazdata.lead: Vahyazdata was a Persian who claimed to be Bardiya, the son of Cyrus, soon after Darius seized the throne. He was the second man to make that claim, and he won over troops in Persis, the Persians' own homeland. Darius's generals crushed him, and his rising shows that Darius faced resistance even among his own people.
p_vahyazdata.play: The game's chronicle note matches the Behistun inscription: second false Bardiya, a rising in Persis, defeats at Rakha and Mount Parga, and impalement. His followers appear in the game as the rebels of Vahyazdata.
p_vahyazdata.s0: Darius's inscription at Behistun says Vahyazdata lived in a town called Tarava, in the district of Yautiya in Persia. He told the people that he was Bardiya, son of Cyrus. Persian troops of the palace went over to him, and he became king in Persia. Darius counted this as the second rebellion in Persia, after that of the magus Gaumata.
p_vahyazdata.s1: Darius sent Persian and Median troops under the Persian Artavardiya, while he went on to Media himself. Artavardiya beat Vahyazdata at Rakha in Persia. Vahyazdata fled to Paishiyauvada, raised a new army and was beaten again at Mount Parga in the summer of 521 BCE. He was captured with his chief followers, and Darius says he impaled them at Uvadaicaya in Persia.
p_vahyazdata.s2: Vahyazdata also sent an army east against Vivana, Darius's satrap in Arachosia. Vivana defeated it at the fortress of Kapishakanish and again in the district of Gandutava. The rebel commander fled to the fortress of Arshada, where he and his leading men were taken and killed. On the Behistun relief Vahyazdata stands among the bound rebels, labelled as the liar who claimed to be Bardiya.
p_vahyazdata.s3: Herodotus tells at length how a magus impersonated Smerdis, his name for Bardiya, and was killed by seven Persian nobles. He knows only that one pretender and says nothing of Vahyazdata or the fighting in Persis. For this rising the Persian record is the only real source.
p_vahyazdata.s4: Darius says the real Bardiya had been secretly killed by Cambyses, but some historians suspect the man Darius overthrew was the true Bardiya. Either way, a second Bardiya who rallied troops in Persis suggests that many Persians doubted Darius's account or rejected his claim to rule. Historians differ over how deep this opposition went.
p_vaumisa.lead: Vaumisa was a Persian whom Darius sent against the Armenian rebels in the revolts that followed the killing of Gaumata. He is known from the Behistun inscription, where Darius calls him his servant. Herodotus does not mention him.
p_vaumisa.play: Vaumisa is named in the Encyclopedia's event articles, including the war in Armenia, and has no mechanic of his own.
p_vaumisa.s0: Darius's Behistun inscription names Vaumisa as a Persian and as his servant. Darius says he sent him to Armenia with orders to defeat the rebels who would not acknowledge him. The text gives no rank or family, and Vaumisa is not otherwise attested.
p_vaumisa.s1: According to the inscription, Vaumisa met the rebels in battle more than once, and the first fight took place at a place called Izala in Assyria. Darius credits the victories to the help of Auramazda. Vaumisa then waited in Armenia until the King reached Media.
p_vaumisa.s2: Darius also sent an Armenian servant, Dadarshish, against the same rebels, and Behistun reports his battles in separate paragraphs. The two campaigns belong to the same war. Dadarshish has his own entry.
p_vaumisa.s3: Historians cannot locate every place Darius names, and Izala in particular is uncertain. How the two commanders' campaigns fitted together in time is reconstructed from a single royal text. That text was written to praise Darius, and the fighting is known only in this form.
p_vaumisa.s4: Herodotus tells of the conspiracy and Darius's accession, but in his account of that period he does not mention Vaumisa or the Armenian war in any detail. The name survives only in the Persian inscription.
p_vindafarna.lead: Vindafarna, called Intaphrenes by Herodotus, was a Persian nobleman who stood with Darius when Gaumata was killed in 522 BCE. Darius's Behistun inscription names him as a conspirator and as the general who defeated the second Babylonian rebel, Arakha. Herodotus gives him a different ending, a story of arrest in the palace.
p_vindafarna.play: Vindafarna is named in the Encyclopedia's articles on the revolt of Arakha and the killing of Gaumata. He has no mechanic of his own. The game credits him with retaking Babylon and capturing Arakha, which follows Behistun for the second revolt.
p_vindafarna.s0: The Behistun inscription lists the men who helped Darius kill Gaumata and names Vindafarna, son of Vayaspara, a Persian, among them. Darius sets out the list as part of his own account of how he took the kingship. He also charges later kings to protect the families of these men.
p_vindafarna.s1: Herodotus calls him Intaphrenes and counts him among the seven Persians who plotted against the false Smerdis and killed him. He also says the seven were given the right to enter the king's presence without being announced, except when the king was with a woman.
p_vindafarna.s2: Darius says that Arakha, a man of Armenian descent, rebelled in Babylon a second time, claiming to be Nebuchadnezzar. Vindafarna, a Persian, is named as the commander who defeated him there and had him taken. Darius himself led the army against the first Babylonian rebel, Nidintu-Bel, so Babylon was not retaken by a single general.
p_vindafarna.s3: Herodotus says Intaphrenes was refused entry to the palace and mutilated the royal messengers who stopped him. Darius arrested him and his family and condemned them. The king spared one man whom Intaphrenes' wife chose, and she chose her brother. The story reads as a moral tale about a king's justice, and no Persian source confirms it.
p_vivana.lead: Vivana was a Persian governor of Arachosia, in what is now southern Afghanistan, in the first years of Darius's reign. He is known from the Behistun inscription, which names him as Darius's servant and satrap there and tells of his fighting against a rebel force. The episode shows that the revolts of 522-521 BCE reached the far east of the empire.
p_vivana.play: The game names Vivana in the Chronicle's Behistun entries and in the Encyclopedia's event articles, not in a level of his own, and he has no mechanic. The game says he beat Vahyazdata's army in Arachosia, which follows Darius's own account.
p_vivana.s0: The Behistun inscription calls Vivana a Persian and Darius's servant, and says Darius made him satrap in Arachosia. It gives no family or later career for him. Everything firm about him comes from a few lines in Darius's own account of the revolts.
p_vivana.s1: Vahyazdata, a Persian, claimed to be Bardiya, the king's brother, and raised Persis in revolt. Darius says he sent an army under the Persian Artavardiya against him. After Vahyazdata's defeat in Persis, Darius says, he sent a force to Arachosia against Vivana. Darius presents the whole affair as the work of a liar.
p_vivana.s2: According to the inscription, Vivana's troops fought the rebel force in two battles, at a fortress called Kapishakanish and in a district called Gandutava, and Darius says his side won. The text gives the dates of the actions by month and does not state the numbers engaged.
p_vivana.s3: Darius's text reports only Persian victories and was written to justify his rule, so the true scale of the fighting cannot be checked. Historians generally read the Arachosian campaign as showing that the revolt, or Darius's enemies, reached the eastern provinces, but the inscription is the only source for it. Herodotus does not mention Vivana or this fighting.
p_xanthippus.lead: Xanthippus son of Ariphron was an Athenian aristocrat who prosecuted Miltiades, was ostracised in 484 BCE, was recalled in 480 BCE and in 479 BCE commanded the Athenian fleet. After the Greek victory at Mycale he stayed on to besiege Sestos, the Persian stronghold on the Hellespont, and sent the cables of Xerxes' bridges home to Athens. He was the father of Pericles.
p_xanthippus.play: The chronicle names Xanthippus as the Athenian general of 479 BCE and father of Pericles, who led the Athenians at Mycale, besieged Sestos and brought home the bridge cables. This follows Herodotus.
p_xanthippus.s0: Herodotus says Xanthippus married Agariste, a niece of the reformer Cleisthenes, and that their son was Pericles. In 489 BCE, after Miltiades failed in his attack on Paros, Xanthippus prosecuted him before the Athenian people and asked for the death penalty. Miltiades, the victor of Marathon, was spared death but fined fifty talents, and died of his wound soon after.
p_xanthippus.s1: Potsherds inscribed with the name of Xanthippus son of Ariphron have been excavated in Athens. They were votes cast in an ostracism, the procedure by which the Athenians could exile a leading citizen for ten years. One carries a short elegiac couplet accusing him of doing more wrong than any other leader. The sherds themselves carry no date.
p_xanthippus.s2: The Aristotelian Constitution of the Athenians dates his ostracism to 484 BCE and says the exiles were recalled in 480 BCE as Xerxes advanced. In spring 479 BCE, Herodotus says, Xanthippus commanded the Athenian ships in the Greek fleet gathered at Aegina under the Spartan king Leotychides. At Mycale that summer the Greeks stormed the Persian camp and burned the beached ships, the Athenians fighting along the shore.
p_xanthippus.s3: Finding Xerxes' bridges already broken, Leotychides and the Peloponnesians sailed home. Xanthippus and the Athenians stayed to besiege Sestos, which held out into the autumn or winter. When it fell, the Persian governor Artayctes, accused by local Greeks of plundering the shrine of Protesilaus, was put to death near where the bridge had ended. The cables went to Athens for the temples. No Persian record of these events survives.
p_xanthippus.s4: Plutarch, writing nearly six centuries later, tells a story about the abandonment of Athens in 480 BCE. The dog of Xanthippus would not be left behind and swam beside his ship to Salamis, then collapsed and died. It was buried on a headland afterwards called the Dog's Grave.
p_xerxes.lead: Xerxes (Old Persian Xshayarsha), son of Darius and Atossa, ruled the empire from 486 BCE until he was killed in a palace plot in 465 BCE. He put down revolts in Egypt and Babylonia, completed and extended the palaces at Persepolis, and in 480 BCE led the invasion of Greece that took Athens but failed at Salamis. Greek writers made him a model of royal pride, while his own inscriptions present a pious king continuing his father's work.
p_xerxes.play: The game's chronicle note sums up his reign from Herodotus books 7-9: Egypt's revolt, the Athos canal, the Hellespont bridges, the taking of Athens in 480 BCE and his return home after Salamis. It leaves out the Babylonian revolts.
p_xerxes.s0: In an inscription from Persepolis (XPf), Xerxes states that Darius had other sons but, by the will of Auramazda, made him the greatest after himself. The same text traces his line through Darius and Hystaspes to Arsames. Darius died late in 486 BCE, and Babylonian documents soon begin to be dated by Xerxes' reign.
p_xerxes.s1: Herodotus (7.7) says Xerxes crushed the Egyptian revolt begun under Darius and made his brother Achaemenes governor. Babylonian tablets name two rebel kings, Bel-shimanni and Shamash-eriba, probably in 484 BCE, after which several family archives end. Herodotus (1.183) says Xerxes took a gold statue from Bel's sanctuary, and Arrian later claimed he destroyed the temples. Historians doubt a general destruction and still argue over his reprisals.
p_xerxes.s2: At Persepolis Xerxes completed the Apadana begun by his father, built the Gate of All Lands named in its inscription (XPa), and added his own palace. In the XPh inscription he says that in one land the daiva had been worshipped. He says that by the favour of Auramazda he destroyed their sanctuary, forbade their worship and worshipped Auramazda there. The land is not named, and scholars do not agree which event, if any, it describes.
p_xerxes.s3: Herodotus tells how Xerxes had a canal cut behind Athos and bridges of boats laid over the Hellespont, then marched through Thrace in 480 BCE. After Thermopylae his army took Athens and burned the Acropolis. When his fleet was beaten at Salamis he returned to Asia, leaving Mardonius in Greece. Herodotus (7.186) puts the host above five million, a figure historians regard as greatly exaggerated.
p_xerxes.s4: Herodotus (7.35) says that when a storm broke the first bridges, Xerxes had the strait given three hundred lashes and the overseers beheaded. Aeschylus' Persians, staged at Athens in 472 BCE, shows a king humbled by the gods for his pride. Such scenes served Greek moral lessons about arrogance and are not confirmed by any Persian source.
p_zopyrus.lead: Herodotus credits Zopyrus, a Persian nobleman, with delivering Babylon to Darius by mutilating himself and pretending to desert. The story is told only by Greek writers. Darius's Behistun inscription describes the Babylonian revolts without naming him.
p_zopyrus.play: Zopyrus is named only in the event articles on the revolts of Nidintu-Bel and Arakha and has no mechanic of his own.
p_zopyrus.s0: Herodotus says Babylon revolted against Darius and held out for twenty months behind its walls. He names Zopyrus as the son of Megabyzus, one of the conspirators against the false Bardiya. In his telling Zopyrus cut off his own nose and ears, had his hair shorn and went to the Babylonians as a victim of Darius's cruelty.
p_zopyrus.s1: Herodotus says the Babylonians trusted Zopyrus and gave him troops. He let a small force and then a larger one win easy victories, and at a later attack the gates were opened to the Persians. Darius, Herodotus says, gave him Babylon's revenue for life and declared that he would rather have Zopyrus unharmed than many Babylons.
p_zopyrus.s2: Darius's own text records two Babylonian revolts. The first, under Nidintu-Bel, who took the name Nebuchadnezzar, ended when Darius defeated his forces on the Tigris and the Euphrates. The second, under Arakha, was put down by Vindafarna, a Persian, and Arakha was impaled in Babylon. The inscription does not name Zopyrus and has no siege of twenty months.
p_zopyrus.s3: Historians commonly treat Herodotus's single long siege as a compressed or confused version of the two revolts known from Behistun, which Babylonian business documents also reflect. Whether a Zopyrus took part in the recovery of Babylon is uncertain, and many regard the mutilation as a literary tale. The inscription gives no support to it.
p_zopyrus.s4: The self-mutilated deserter belongs to a familiar type of story in which a loyal man wins an enemy's trust through visible suffering. Later Greek writers, including Polyaenus in his collection of stratagems, retold such tricks. The tale also presents Persian nobles as models of loyalty to the king.
r_grain_dole.lead: The Persian King's administration fed the people who worked for it. Clay tablets from Persepolis record monthly rations of barley, with wine, beer and flour, issued to workers, officials and travellers in Persis and the neighbouring lands toward Elam. These rations were a form of pay for royal service, not a free handout to every household. They show how the crown turned the harvest of its estates into labour.
r_grain_dole.play: A standing order on the Ledger's Taxes page has every lived-in house draw barley monthly, and the King's favour rises when it is met. The tablets record rations to workers and officials in royal service, not to every household.
r_grain_dole.s0: The Persepolis Fortification tablets are thousands of mostly Elamite clay documents found in 1933-34. They cover roughly the years 509 to 493 BCE, in the reign of Darius. Many record barley drawn from royal stores and handed out month by month, with the responsible officials, the recipients and the amounts, measured in units of about a litre. A common monthly ration for a grown man was around thirty of these units.
r_grain_dole.s1: Much of the grain went to workers the tablets call kurtaš, organised in groups by trade and origin, among them Persians, Lydians, Egyptians and Ionians. Men, women and children appear, with amounts graded by age, sex and skill. Some women received extra rations after giving birth, more for a boy than a girl. Travellers on the roads drew daily rations at way stations by showing a sealed authorisation.
r_grain_dole.s2: Grain was the base, but the same system issued wine, beer, flour, fruit and livestock, often to officials, for special occasions or as offerings to the gods. For much of the archive's span the network answered to Parnaka, a senior noble and probably an uncle of Darius, who ran the King's economy in Persis. The Persepolis Treasury tablets, a later archive, show some workers receiving part of their pay in silver in place of goods.
r_grain_dole.s3: Herodotus tries to work out how much grain Xerxes' army consumed in 480 BCE, assuming a daily ration of one choinix of wheat per man, roughly a litre. His total rests on his own army figures, which historians regard as greatly exaggerated. The passage still shows that Greeks thought of the Persian host as a body fed by the King from organised stores.
r_grain_dole.s4: Historians still argue over the status of the kurtaš. Some see them as dependants or deportees tied to royal estates. Others stress that many were skilled, mobile and paid at different rates, closer to hired labour. It is also unclear whether rations were their whole living or a supplement, and how far the system known from Persis ran in other provinces.
r_labour_levy.lead: The Persian kings raised palaces, roads and canals with the labour of thousands of workers drawn from across the empire. Some served as a duty owed for land, some were deportees or dependants, and some were skilled men paid for their work. The clay tablets of Persepolis show these workers being counted, grouped and fed from royal stores, which makes them one of the best-documented workforces of the ancient world.
r_labour_levy.play: A standing order on the Ledger's Taxes page: royal works rise faster, but settlers come less readily. The game's note calls kurtaš levied; the word covered workers of mixed and still debated status, not only conscripts.
r_labour_levy.s0: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, mostly Elamite records from about 509 to 493 BCE, list rations of grain, wine and beer issued to groups of workers called kurtaš. The groups included men, women, boys and girls, and often named their origin: Egyptians, Ionians, Lycians, Bactrians, Babylonians, Skudrians (probably Thracians) and many more. Women who had just given birth received extra rations, and mothers of boys received more than mothers of girls.
r_labour_levy.s1: Darius's foundation charter from Susa names the peoples who supplied materials and labour for his palace: Ionians and Sardians cut stone, Babylonians moulded bricks, and Medes and Egyptians worked gold and decorated walls. The Persepolis Treasury tablets, which begin in 492 BCE, record workers on the royal buildings receiving part of their pay in silver alongside their rations.
r_labour_levy.s2: Babylonian documents show another form of royal labour. Holders of bow land, horse land and chariot land owed the King military or work service in return for their plots, and the Murashu archive of Nippur shows that by the late fifth century this duty was often paid off in silver. Babylonian temple archives under Darius also mention men and supplies sent to royal building work in Elam.
r_labour_levy.s3: Historians still argue over what kurtaš were. Some see them largely as deportees and dependants bound to royal estates. Others see a mixed body that included conscripted labourers serving for a term and skilled specialists who moved between projects. The word itself simply means workers or household personnel, so the tablets alone do not settle how free any given group was.
r_labour_levy.s4: Herodotus describes the cutting of Xerxes' canal through the Athos peninsula about 483 to 480 BCE. He says men from the many nations of the army dug in relays, driven by whips, and passed the earth from hand to hand up to the top. The Phoenicians, he says, worked more skilfully by cutting the trench wider at the top. Historians note that his picture of forced labour also suits his wider theme of royal pride.
r_road_works.lead: Road works stands for the King's upkeep of the roads and way stations that tied his empire together. Under Darius, routes linking Persepolis and Susa with Sardis, Egypt and India carried officials, couriers, troops and supplies, fed from royal stores at stations along the way. Greek writers admired the system, and the Persepolis tablets show how it was run from day to day.
r_road_works.play: A standing order on the Ledger's Taxes page: it costs silver each month and caravans carry more per visit. This simplifies history, since the King's stations issued rations to authorised official travellers, not to merchant caravans.
r_road_works.s0: Herodotus describes the road from Sardis to Susa as running through settled and safe country, with royal stations and good lodgings along its whole length. He counts 111 stations over 450 parasangs and reckons the journey at 90 days for a traveller covering 150 stades a day. He adds three more days from Ephesus to Sardis. His totals are his own reckoning and probably rest on informants rather than measurement.
r_road_works.s1: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, written between about 509 and 493 BCE, record grain, flour, beer and wine issued to travellers on roads linking Persepolis and Susa with Sardis, Arachosia, India and other provinces. Parties carried a sealed authorisation from the King, a satrap or another high official, and were often led by a guide. The tablets show the stations as depots stocked by the royal economy rather than as private inns.
r_road_works.s2: Herodotus tells how news of the defeat at Salamis was carried to Persia by relays of riders, with a fresh man and horse posted for each day's stage. He compares the handover of the message to a Greek torch race and gives the Persian name of the system as angareion. He says nothing mortal travelled faster, and that neither weather nor darkness stopped the riders.
r_road_works.s3: Historians debate how much the Persians built and how much they inherited from Assyrian, Elamite and Lydian routes. Most roads were probably unpaved tracks, improved at passes, fords and river crossings and marked by stations. The line of Herodotus's road across Anatolia, whether north by the Halys or south through the Cilician Gates, is still argued, and few stations have been securely identified on the ground.
r_road_works.s4: Xenophon credits Cyrus the Great with founding the relay posts after measuring how far a horse could travel in a day without being worn out. He wrote more than a century after Cyrus, in a work shaped as a portrait of the ideal ruler, so the story is better read as praise than as a record of who began the system.
r_tax_relief.lead: Achaemenid kings took tribute from their provinces and could also release lands and men from it. Herodotus says Darius was the first to fix each province's dues. He records that Persis paid no tribute, and that the King could grant a favoured man land free of tax. Remitting tax was a political act, used to win loyalty, reward service or mark a people's standing.
r_tax_relief.play: A standing order on the Ledger's Taxes page lowers the city's dues and raises the King's favour each month. This reverses history, where remission was the King's own grant and an official who cut tribute would hardly have won his favour for it.
r_tax_relief.s0: Herodotus says Darius divided the empire into twenty provinces, which the Persians called satrapies, and fixed the tribute each had to pay. Most paid in silver, and India paid in gold dust. Herodotus says that under Cyrus and Cambyses there had been no set tribute, only gifts. Because Darius put a price on everything, the Persians called him a trader, Cambyses a master and Cyrus a father.
r_tax_relief.s1: Herodotus names Persis as the one land that paid no tribute. Some peoples on the edges of the empire, among them the Ethiopians beyond Egypt, the Colchians and the Arabs, brought gifts instead, and he says some of them set the amount themselves. He says the Arabs sent a thousand talents of frankincense each year. Modern historians read these gifts as a sign of a special standing with the King.
r_tax_relief.s2: The Persepolis Fortification tablets are mostly Elamite records from about 509 to 493 BCE. They show royal officials collecting grain, wine and livestock across Persis and neighbouring Elam, and some deliveries are recorded as a levy. Historians therefore debate what Herodotus meant by tax-free. Many think the Persians were spared the silver tribute of conquered provinces but still owed dues in kind and labour to the royal economy.
r_tax_relief.s3: Herodotus says that the man who ruled as Smerdis in 522 BCE granted every people of the empire three years' freedom from military service and tribute. He adds that after this ruler's death everyone in Asia except the Persians missed him. Darius's Behistun inscription calls him Gaumata, a magus and usurper, and says Darius restored the pastures, herds, workers and houses he had seized. Historians still argue over who this ruler was and what his measures were.
r_tax_relief.s4: Herodotus says that after the Ionian revolt, Artaphernes, the satrap at Sardis, had the lands of the Ionian cities measured in parasangs and set their tribute by those measurements. He adds that the new assessment was about the same as the old one and was still in force in his own day. On this account a satrap could reassess tribute, but he did not simply reduce it.
r_temple_offering.lead: The King's administration paid for sacrifices. Clay tablets from Persepolis record barley, flour, wine, beer and animals issued from royal stores to priests who offered them to Persian, Elamite and other gods, above all for a regular rite called the lan. They show the crown supporting many cults across Persis and Elam, a picture that sits uneasily beside Herodotus's description of Persian worship.
r_temple_offering.play: A standing order on the Ledger's Taxes page sends barley from the granaries to the gods each month, and full payment raises the King's favour. The tablets show wider issues and many gods, and Herodotus's no-temples claim is contested.
r_temple_offering.s0: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, Elamite administrative texts from about 509 to 493 BCE, record regular issues of commodities for a rite called the lan. Grain made up most of the payments, though flour, wine and beer also appear, often as fixed monthly amounts through the year. Henkelman argues the lan was a state offering paid for by the royal economy. Most texts name no god for it, though a few link it with Auramazda.
r_temple_offering.s1: The same archive funds offerings to Elamite gods such as Humban, to the Mesopotamian storm god Adad, to Auramazda, and to mountains and rivers. The officiants were often Elamite priests called shatin or Iranian magi, and they drew their supplies from local storehouses. The administration seems to have funded the worship of the region's mixed population, not one exclusive royal cult.
r_temple_offering.s2: Herodotus says the Persians set up no statues, temples or altars, and that they sacrificed to the sky god on mountain tops and also to the sun, moon, earth, fire, water and winds. He adds that no sacrifice was lawful without a magus present to chant, and that the worshipper prayed for the King and all Persians. He was describing a foreign custom from outside, in Greek terms.
r_temple_offering.s3: The game's note follows Herodotus, but the Persian record complicates it. At Behistun, Darius says he restored the ayadana, places of worship, that Gaumata had destroyed. In XPh, Xerxes says he destroyed a sanctuary of the daivas and worshipped Auramazda in its place. Historians still argue over what these sanctuaries were and whether any excavated building was a temple, so the claim that the Persians built no temples cannot be stated as settled fact.
r_trade_charter.lead: No Achaemenid order called a trade charter is known. The Persian kings drew goods from every land through tribute, requisition and tolls, and merchants moved along roads, rivers and sea lanes that royal power kept open and taxed. The surviving evidence shows a state that profited from commerce more than it granted trading privileges.
r_trade_charter.play: A standing order on the Ledger's Taxes page costs silver each month; in return the city pays less for goods and is paid more. This is a game simplification. DSf records materials and workers sent to Susa, not trade privileges.
r_trade_charter.s0: Darius's foundation charter for his palace at Susa names the materials brought for it and the peoples who brought or worked them. They include cedar from Lebanon, gold from Sardis and Bactria, lapis lazuli and carnelian from Sogdiana, and ivory from Kush, India and Arachosia. Ionians and Sardians cut the stone and Babylonians made the bricks. The text celebrates the King's reach over his subjects and records royal demand, not free trade.
r_trade_charter.s1: An Aramaic customs account from Egypt survives at Elephantine, erased and reused for the story of Ahiqar. Dated to 475 BCE, Xerxes' eleventh year, it records Ionian and Phoenician ships entering Egypt, probably at a harbour near one of the Nile mouths. Officials took part of each cargo or set sums in gold and silver, and recorded further payments for the King's house. It is the clearest evidence that the crown taxed sea trade systematically.
r_trade_charter.s2: Stelae set up by Darius between the Nile and the Red Sea say that he ordered a canal dug and that ships then went through it from Egypt to Persia. Herodotus says the pharaoh Necho had begun it and Darius finished it, though Strabo and Diodorus later claimed Darius left it unfinished. The work linked Egypt by sea with the Persian Gulf. It served royal traffic and tribute at least as much as private merchants.
r_trade_charter.s3: Herodotus says the Persians called Cyrus a father, Cambyses a master and Darius a trader. He explains that Darius earned the name by fixing the tribute owed by each province and making a profit out of everything. The nickname may be a Greek joke as much as a Persian one. It shows how outsiders saw Darius's careful ordering of revenue.
r_trade_charter.s4: Babylonian archives such as that of the Egibi family show merchants dealing in silver, goods and tax collection under Cyrus, Cambyses and Darius. Some historians argue that the crown encouraged exchange because tolls and silver revenue served it. Others stress that tribute and payments in kind, as seen in the Persepolis tablets, dominated the royal economy. No document granting trading rights to a city or merchant is known.
r_water_rights.lead: Water decided where crops could grow in the dry lands the Persian kings ruled. The Greek historian Polybius, writing centuries later, says the kings let anyone who brought water to unwatered land enjoy its use for five generations. Later Achaemenid documents from Babylonia and Egypt show water being leased, shared and paid for. Together they suggest that control of water was an important way royal government touched ordinary farmers.
r_water_rights.play: A standing royal order on the Ledger's Taxes page raises harvests and lowers dues. The game's citation of Polybius 10.28 is accurate, but the order simplifies a grant of land use into a tax cut; the kings also charged for water.
r_water_rights.s0: Polybius, writing in the 2nd century, describes the underground channels of the dry country Antiochus III crossed on his march toward Hyrcania about 209. He says that when the Persians ruled Asia, those who brought spring water to land not irrigated before were granted its use for five generations. He adds that people therefore spared no labour or expense in digging long channels underground.
r_water_rights.s1: Herodotus tells of a plain ringed by hills and watered by the river Aces, where the King blocked the gorges with gates so that the river formed a lake. The peoples below had to go to the King in Persia and plead for water, and he had the gates opened only for a large payment beyond the tribute. Many historians doubt the details, but the story shows a Greek view of water as a source of royal income.
r_water_rights.s2: The Murashu archive from Nippur, dating from about 440 to 415 BCE, long after the game's period, records a family firm that managed land held by royal grantees. Its tablets show fees paid for water drawn from canals run by royal officials, and irrigation organised through these managers. Water here was a resource leased and paid for, not free to whoever could reach it.
r_water_rights.s3: At Ayn Manawir in the Kharga oasis, demotic ostraca of the 5th and early 4th centuries record the sale and rental of shares in underground water channels; some were written after Egypt broke from Persian rule in 404 BCE. Rights were counted in days of flow and passed between villagers by written contract. These texts are among the clearest evidence for how water rights worked in this period.
r_water_rights.s4: Polybius's channels are usually identified with qanats, tunnels that carry groundwater to the surface. Some historians credit the Persians with spreading them, while others argue they are older in places or became widespread only later. Since Polybius wrote long after the Achaemenids, how far his grant reflects general royal policy is also debated.
u_arabian_camel_rider.lead: Arab peoples of the desert edge between Egypt, Syria and Mesopotamia helped the Persian kings and, in 480 BCE, served Xerxes as camel-mounted archers. Herodotus describes them in Xerxes' army. He also tells a separate story of camels, ridden by Cyrus's own men, frightening the Lydian horses at Sardis. Together these explain why camels had a place in Persian warfare.
u_arabian_camel_rider.play: In the game horses will not face him and he shoots riders down, but spearmen in the open drive him off. The idea comes from Herodotus's Sardis story. Herodotus also has Xerxes keep the camels at the rear, and no source shows them fighting in Greece.
u_arabian_camel_rider.s0: Darius's inscription at Behistun names Arabia among the lands that came to him, and later royal lists such as the one at his tomb repeat the name. On the stairways of the Apadana at Persepolis, one delegation of gift-bearers leads a dromedary, and it is usually identified as Arab. The Persian record therefore counts Arabs as one of the peoples of the empire.
u_arabian_camel_rider.s1: Arab camel warriors were known long before Cyrus. Assyrian palace reliefs from Nineveh show Ashurbanipal's wars against Arab tribes in the 600s BCE. In them, each camel carries two men, one guiding the animal and one shooting a bow. Assyrian records also name Arab queens and chiefs who paid tribute in camels and spices.
u_arabian_camel_rider.s2: Herodotus says the Arabians in Xerxes' army wore long belted cloaks and carried long bows that curved backward. Arsames, a son of Darius, commanded them. He adds that they rode camels no slower than horses, and that they were posted at the rear so the horses would not take fright. He puts the Arabian camel riders and Libyan charioteers together at 20,000, within an army total that historians regard as greatly exaggerated.
u_arabian_camel_rider.s3: Herodotus tells how Harpagus advised Cyrus to mount men on the baggage camels and send them against Croesus's cavalry outside Sardis. The Lydian horses could not bear the sight and smell of camels and turned away. Xenophon's romance of Cyrus uses a similar camel tactic but places it in an earlier battle. Historians accept that horses unused to camels can shy, but doubt that the trick alone decided the battle.
u_arabian_camel_rider.s4: Herodotus says the Arabians were never reduced to subjects. He reports that an Arab king pledged safe passage to Cambyses' army on its march to Egypt in 525 BCE and set out water in camel skins across the desert. He also says the Arabians sent the King a yearly gift of frankincense instead of tribute. Modern historians think this applied to some Arab groups, while others lived inside the satrapies.
u_archer.lead: The bow was the main weapon of Persian infantry, and Greek writers describe Persian armies opening battle with heavy volleys of arrows. Herodotus pictured Persian foot soldiers with large bows, cane arrows and wicker shields, and Persian kings presented themselves as archers in art and inscriptions. The bow served the empire well against many enemies, but in close combat with Greek hoplites it proved too little.
u_archer.play: The game shows archers as a separate unit that shoots raiders from behind spearmen and dies quickly in melee. This is a simplification: many Persian foot soldiers carried both spear and bow, and the split into two units is the game's.
u_archer.s0: Herodotus describes the Persian contingent of Xerxes' army as wearing soft felt caps, sleeved tunics, trousers and iron scale armour. They carried wicker shields, short spears, large bows with arrows of cane, and a dagger hanging at the right thigh. He adds that this dress was Median in origin and that the Medes in the army were equipped the same way.
u_archer.s1: In the inscription on his tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam, Darius counts among his abilities that he was a good bowman both on foot and on horseback. The glazed-brick friezes from Susa show rows of guardsmen holding a spear, with a bow and quiver on the shoulder. From late in Darius's reign, royal gold and silver coins showed a crowned figure with a bow.
u_archer.s2: Herodotus says Persian boys were taught three things from the age of five to twenty: to ride, to shoot the bow and to tell the truth. Strabo gives a similar, later picture of Persian education. Both are summaries by Greek outsiders, but they agree that archery was central to how Persians trained their young men.
u_archer.s3: Herodotus describes Persians at Plataea setting up their wicker shields as a barrier and shooting from behind it. Many modern historians reconstruct a formation with shield-bearers in front and archers in the ranks behind, sometimes calling it the sparabara. Others warn that this term and the neat division of roles are modern reconstructions, and that most Persian infantry may have carried both spear and bow.
u_archer.s4: Herodotus says the Athenians at Marathon advanced at a run, and that the Persians thought them mad to attack without horsemen or archers. Modern historians often read the run as a way to cross the arrow zone quickly. At Plataea he judged the Persians equal in courage but lacking armour and skill against hoplites. At Thermopylae the Persians shot many arrows at the Phocians guarding the mountain path.
u_archer.s5: Herodotus tells how a man from Trachis warned that Persian arrows would blot out the sun, and the Spartan Dieneces replied that they would then fight in the shade. The story is a Greek tale of courage, and its exact words cannot be checked, but it shows the reputation Persian archery held among the Greeks.
u_bactrian_spearman.lead: Bactria, the rich land between the Hindu Kush and the Oxus river, was one of the King's great eastern provinces, and its men marched in Xerxes' army against Greece in 480 BCE. Herodotus describes them with cane bows and short spears. Bactrians stayed in Greece with Mardonius after Salamis and fought at Plataea in 479 BCE.
u_bactrian_spearman.play: The game makes the Bactrian a quick, shieldless light fighter who hunts archers and loses to hoplites. Herodotus gives the cane bow and short spear but says nothing of shields, and the battlefield role is the game's own simplification.
u_bactrian_spearman.s0: In his list of Xerxes' forces, Herodotus says the Bactrians wore headgear much like the Median kind. He says they carried cane bows of their own country and short spears. The Bactrians and the Saka served together under one commander, Hystaspes, a son of Darius and Atossa. Herodotus does not mention shields or body armour for them.
u_bactrian_spearman.s1: Darius's Behistun inscription names Bactria among the lands that obeyed him. During the revolts of 522-521 BCE, Dadarshi, the Persian satrap of Bactria, marched against rebels in neighbouring Margiana and defeated them. In his Susa building charter, Darius says that gold used in the palace came from Sardis and Bactria.
u_bactrian_spearman.s2: Herodotus says that in Xerxes' army the Bactrians also sent horsemen, equipped in the same way as their foot soldiers. After Salamis, he says, Mardonius chose picked Bactrians to stay in Greece for the next year's campaign, along with Persians, Medes, Saka and Indians. At Plataea he places them next to the Medes, facing troops from several smaller Peloponnesian cities.
u_bactrian_spearman.s3: Historians argue over whether Herodotus's list of nations reflects real units he had information about or an idealised roll of the empire's peoples. Some scholars compare it to the rows of subject peoples shown on Persian reliefs. His total figures for Xerxes' army are generally thought to be greatly exaggerated. How many Bactrians actually reached Greece is unknown.
u_carian_mercenary.lead: Carians came from the hill country of south-western Asia Minor. Greek tradition remembered them as early makers of shield gear and as soldiers for hire. Egyptian kings kept Carian and Ionian troops for well over a century, and those troops faced the Persians at Pelusium in 525 BCE. Yet Carians also rowed, carried timber and laboured for the Persian King, so they stood on both sides of the empire's wars.
u_carian_mercenary.play: The Carian Mercenary is armoured hired foot of the King's enemies, with a label that changes by level. It holds against spearmen and riders, and archers wear it down. This simplifies history: Carians also served the King.
u_carian_mercenary.s0: Herodotus tells how an oracle promised the exiled Egyptian prince Psammetichus revenge when bronze men came out of the sea. Ionian and Carian raiders in bronze armour then landed in Egypt, and Psammetichus hired them and won the throne with their help. The story is shaped as a fulfilled prophecy and should not be read as a plain report.
u_carian_mercenary.s1: Herodotus says Psammetichus gave his Ionian and Carian troops land on either side of the Pelusiac branch of the Nile, at a place called the Camps. A later king, Amasis, moved them to Memphis to serve as his guard against his own Egyptians. Their descendants formed a lasting community there, which later Greek writers called the Caromemphites.
u_carian_mercenary.s2: Carian soldiers left graffiti on the colossal statues at Abu Simbel, probably during Psamtik II's campaign into Nubia in the early 6th century. Funerary stelae from Saqqara near Memphis, some with Egyptian scenes and Carian texts, show mercenary families settled and buried in Egypt. These texts from Egypt, together with a bilingual found at Kaunos in Caria, helped scholars decipher the Carian script in recent decades.
u_carian_mercenary.s3: Herodotus says that at Pelusium in 525 BCE the Greek and Carian mercenaries of Psamtik III killed the sons of Phanes, who had deserted to Cambyses, before the armies met. In the Ionian Revolt the Carians fought for themselves, not for pay. They lost to Persian forces on the Marsyas river and at Labraunda, then ambushed a Persian army on the road to Pedasus and killed its commanders, Daurises among them.
u_carian_mercenary.s4: Darius's foundation charter at Susa names Carians and Ionians as the men who carried cedar timber from Babylon to Susa for his palace. Babylonian documents show a community of Carians at Borsippa, probably settled there under the Babylonian kings, and still recorded under the early Persian kings. Carians were subjects of the King as well as his enemies.
u_cissian_spearman.lead: The Cissians were, to Greek writers, the people of the land around Susa, which the Persian inscriptions call Elam. Herodotus says they marched with Xerxes in 480 BCE armed like Persians apart from their headgear. He also says they were among the first troops sent against the Greeks at Thermopylae. Their home lay at the heart of the empire, close to one of the King's chief residences.
u_cissian_spearman.play: The game shows Cissians as cheaper, quicker-to-raise spearmen, lighter than Persians. Herodotus says they were armed like Persians, bows included, apart from the mitra, so this is a game simplification.
u_cissian_spearman.s0: The name Cissian is Greek. Herodotus calls the land round Susa Cissia and counts it as one tax district, and Aeschylus speaks of Cissian women mourning Xerxes' defeat. The Persian inscriptions never use the name and speak only of Elam. Most historians take Cissians to mean the people of the Susa plain, broadly Elamites, but whether the term covered all Elamites or only the lowland is still argued.
u_cissian_spearman.s1: In his list of Xerxes' army, Herodotus says the Cissians were equipped like the Persians but wore the mitra, a cloth head-wrap, instead of the Persian felt cap. Persian foot, he says, wore scale armour and carried wicker shields, short spears, large bows with reed arrows, and daggers. Their commander was Anaphes son of Otanes. The Cissian infantryman was therefore probably an archer as much as a spearman.
u_cissian_spearman.s2: Herodotus says that in 480 BCE Xerxes, angered that the Greeks held the pass, first sent the Medes and Cissians with orders to take them alive. They fought all day and lost heavily without breaking the Greek line, after which the King sent in Hydarnes and the Immortals. Herodotus uses the episode to show that the King had many men but few true soldiers, a Greek judgement shaped by the outcome.
u_cissian_spearman.s3: At Behistun, Darius lists Elam among his lands and records that it rose against him three times, under Assina, Martiya and later Athamaita. An Elamite appears among the labelled throne-bearers on Darius's tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam. The Persepolis Fortification tablets were written mostly in Elamite, which shows how far Elamite scribal practice shaped Persian administration.
u_cissian_spearman.s4: Glazed-brick panels from Darius's palace at Susa show rows of robed guards holding spears, with bows and quivers on their shoulders. They are often linked to the King's guard, but they carry no labels. Whether they show Persians, Elamites of Susa or an idealised royal guard is debated, so they cannot be taken as a portrait of Cissian soldiers.
u_drummer.lead: The War Drummer stands for the men who kept an attacking force moving together and gave it its signals. Ancient armies of this period did use sound in battle, but the sources speak of pipes, trumpets and shouting far more than drums. No source of the period describes a drummer leading an assault on a wall.
u_drummer.play: The War Drummer, whose label changes by level, beats the enemy assault on from before the gate; archers on the wall can reach him. He is a game invention: period sources speak of pipes and trumpets in war, not drums.
u_drummer.s0: Herodotus says that when Alyattes of Lydia raided the land of Miletus each year, his army marched to the sound of pan-pipes, harps and pipes. Thucydides, writing of a later battle at Mantinea in 418 BCE, describes the Spartans advancing slowly to many pipe-players. He explains that this was not for religion but to keep the line in step, so that it did not break apart as it closed with the enemy.
u_drummer.s1: Greek armies and fleets gave commands with the salpinx, a straight bronze trumpet. Aeschylus, who fought against the Persians, makes his messenger in the Persians tell how a trumpet set the Greek ships alight with spirit at Salamis. Xenophon's Anabasis also mentions trumpet calls used to signal the advance and to break camp.
u_drummer.s2: Xenophon, who was at Cunaxa in 401 BCE, says that the Greeks expected the King's army to come on shouting, but it advanced as quietly as it could, in a slow and even line. The battle is later than this game's period, yet it is one of the few eyewitness descriptions of how a Persian royal army sounded as it moved. It gives no hint of war drums.
u_drummer.s3: Drums were well known in Mesopotamia, where large drums were played in temple ritual. Assyrian palace reliefs, carved a century and more before this game's period, show musicians with frame drums, pipes and harps, mostly in ceremonies and victory processions. The same reliefs show sieges in detail, with rams, archers, slingers and ladders, but they do not show drummers urging troops against a wall.
u_drummer.s4: Plutarch says the Parthians at Carrhae in 53 used hollow drums hung with bronze to unnerve the Romans before they attacked. Some writers assume older Iranian armies did the same, but no Achaemenid-period source confirms it. The Greek drum, the tympanon, belonged mainly to the cults of Dionysus and the Mother of the Gods, not to war.
u_earth_carrier.lead: A siege mound was a ramp of earth, stone and timber piled against a city wall until attackers could reach the rampart. It needed many carriers working under fire. In the Near East it was an old Assyrian method, and the Persians used it to take the Greek cities of Ionia and Cyprus.
u_earth_carrier.play: Enemy earth carriers pile a mound behind wicker screens until it becomes a road over the wall, and archers on the wall can kill them. Historically the mound was chiefly a tool of the King's own armies, so the game reverses the roles.
u_earth_carrier.s0: When Sennacherib of Assyria besieged Lachish in Judah in 701 BCE, his army built a great ramp of stones against the city's south-west corner. Excavators have traced it on the ground, along with a counter-ramp raised by the defenders inside. Reliefs from Sennacherib's palace at Nineveh show rams and soldiers moving up such ramps to the walls.
u_earth_carrier.s1: Herodotus says that after Cyrus conquered Lydia, his general Harpagus took the Greek cities of the coast by shutting their people inside the walls and then building mounds against them. He describes Phocaea under this threat, where the citizens took to their ships and left rather than wait for the city to fall.
u_earth_carrier.s2: At Old Paphos in Cyprus, excavators found a Persian siege mound built against the city wall, probably during the Cypriot part of the Ionian Revolt in about 498 to 497 BCE. Its fill held earth, stones, timber and many broken statues and votive pieces, probably taken from a sanctuary outside the walls. The defenders dug tunnels under the mound and tried to burn it, and hundreds of arrowheads and spearheads lay in the debris.
u_earth_carrier.s3: Thucydides gives the fullest ancient description, for the Peloponnesian siege of Plataea under the Spartan king Archidamus in 429 BCE. The attackers held the sides of their mound with a lattice of timber and filled it with wood, stones and earth. The Plataeans raised their wall higher and dug out earth from beneath the mound. Herodotus says the Persians took Soli in Cyprus by the related method of undermining its wall.
u_earth_carrier.s4: The sources rarely say who did the carrying. It may have been soldiers, labour raised from the surrounding countryside, or prisoners, and historians differ on how far Persian armies relied on each. Whoever they were, they worked within bowshot of the wall, and losses among them were probably heavy.
u_egyptian_marine.lead: Egypt sent ships and fighting men to the fleet Xerxes led against Greece in 480 BCE. Herodotus describes their arms closely and singles them out as the best fighters on the King's side at Artemisium. After Salamis some of them were put ashore and fought on land at Plataea in 479 BCE.
u_egyptian_marine.play: The game shows a heavy shield unit with corslet, broad-rimmed shield, boarding spear and great axe, as Herodotus describes. He also mentions plaited helmets and long knives. The edge against shield men is a game rule, not history.
u_egyptian_marine.s0: In his catalogue of Xerxes' fleet, Herodotus says Egypt supplied 200 ships. Its men wore plaited helmets and carried hollow shields with broad rims, spears made for sea fighting and large axes. He adds that most of them wore corslets and carried long knives. The squadron served under Achaemenes, Xerxes' brother, whom Xerxes had made governor of Egypt.
u_egyptian_marine.s1: Herodotus says the Egyptians fought best of Xerxes' forces at Artemisium, capturing five Greek ships together with their crews. In a speech he gives to Artemisia before Salamis, the Egyptians are named with the Cypriots, Cilicians and Pamphylians as worthless allies. After the defeat, Mardonius blames the Phoenicians, Egyptians, Cypriots and Cilicians. These speeches are probably largely Herodotus's own composition.
u_egyptian_marine.s2: Herodotus says Mardonius took the Egyptian fighters off the ships at Phaleron and kept them with his land army for 479 BCE, since they had not marched with Xerxes' army to Athens. At Plataea he lists them among Mardonius's troops and identifies them with Egypt's hereditary warrior classes, the Hermotybies and Calasirians. Elsewhere he describes these classes as men barred from any trade except war.
u_egyptian_marine.s3: Herodotus says every ship in the fleet carried Persians, Medes and Saka as fighting men, and elsewhere counts thirty of them per ship in addition to each people's own fighters. Historians debate how many armed men each ship really carried and how duties were shared between the native fighters and the Iranian ones. Some scholars think the Iranians were placed aboard partly to watch the loyalty of the subject crews.
u_egyptian_soldier.lead: Egyptian soldiers defended the kingdom of the 26th (Saite) dynasty when Cambyses invaded in 525 BCE. Native warriors, whom Greek writers called machimoi, fought beside Greek and Carian mercenaries. After their defeat at Pelusium and the fall of Memphis, Egypt became a Persian satrapy, and Egyptians went on to serve in the King's garrisons and fleets.
u_egyptian_soldier.play: In Memphis they appear as archers, bowmen, spearmen and levies behind tall hide shields, with a captain and 'Psamtik's Champion'. No such champion of Psamtik is known from the sources.
u_egyptian_soldier.s0: Herodotus says Egypt's fighting men formed a hereditary class in two divisions, the Hermotybies and the Calasirians. Each man held a plot of land free of tax and was barred from other trades. His totals of 160,000 and 250,000 men are generally thought far too high. Historians still debate how closed this class was, and many see its core in Libyan soldiers settled in the Delta centuries earlier.
u_egyptian_soldier.s1: Herodotus tells that Psamtik III, whose reign he says lasted only six months, met Cambyses at the Pelusiac mouth of the Nile. His Greek and Carian mercenaries killed the sons of Phanes, the mercenary captain who had gone over to the Persians. After a hard battle the Egyptians fled to Memphis, killed a Persian herald and the crew of his ship, and were besieged until they surrendered. Herodotus gives no figures for either army.
u_egyptian_soldier.s2: The statue of Udjahorresnet records that he commanded the royal warships under Amasis and Psamtik III, then served Cambyses and Darius. It mentions a great turmoil in the land, perhaps the conquest, but describes no fighting. Aramaic papyri from Elephantine, mostly of the 5th century, show the southern frontier garrison still manned under Persian rule, partly by Judean and Aramaean soldiers.
u_egyptian_soldier.s3: Herodotus says Egypt revolted at the end of Darius's reign and was retaken by Xerxes. He reports that Egypt then sent 200 ships against Greece, their men armed with plaited helmets, broad-rimmed shields, boarding spears, large axes and long knives. He judges them the best of the King's contingents at Artemisium, and says Egyptian marines were landed to fight on foot at Plataea.
u_egyptian_soldier.s4: Polyaenus, writing some seven centuries later, says Cambyses placed dogs, sheep, cats and ibises in front of his army, so that the Egyptians would not shoot for fear of harming creatures sacred to them. No earlier writer tells this story, and it reads as a stratagem anecdote rather than history.
u_elamite_rebel.lead: Elam, the old kingdom of the Susa plain and the hills beyond it, rose against Darius three times in his first years as king. The Behistun inscription names the leaders as Açina, Martiya and Athamaita, and each rising ended with its leader seized and killed. The revolts mattered because Susa, which Darius soon rebuilt as a royal seat, lay at the heart of Elam.
u_elamite_rebel.play: At Susa the game fields Elamite archers, horse archers, spearmen, captains and Athamaita's Champion. These troop types are the game's own; Behistun names no units and says only that Gobryas's army beat the rebels.
u_elamite_rebel.s0: Behistun says that after Darius killed Gaumata, an Elamite named Açina, son of Upadarma, made himself king in Elam. Darius sent word there, and Açina was brought to him bound and put to death. Soon afterwards Martiya, son of Cincikhri, who lived at Kuganaka in Persis, claimed to be Imanish, king of Elam. The inscription says the Elamites feared Darius, who was nearby, so they seized Martiya and killed him themselves.
u_elamite_rebel.s1: A fifth column, added later to the Old Persian text only, records a third rising in Darius's second and third regnal years. The Elamites made Athamaita their chief. Darius sent an army under the Persian Gobryas, who defeated the Elamites, captured Athamaita and brought him to the King, who had him killed. The text then says the province became Darius's again.
u_elamite_rebel.s2: Column V says the Elamites were faithless and did not worship Auramazda. Some scholars read this as a religious reason for the war. Others see a formula about loyalty, because Elamite gods received offerings alongside Auramazda in the Persepolis Fortification tablets. It is also unclear who the rebels were. Possibilities include people of the Susa plain, hill peoples, or local lords hoping to revive the old Elamite kingship.
u_elamite_rebel.s3: The game's picture of Elamites as archers has old roots. Assyrian palace reliefs from Nineveh show Elamite bowmen at Ashurbanipal's battle of Til-Tuba, more than a century before Darius. Behistun itself says nothing about how the rebels of Darius's time fought or what weapons they carried.
u_elamite_rebel.s4: Herodotus places Susa and the Cissians in the eighth tax district, paying 300 talents of silver a year. Cissians was his name for the people of the Susa plain. In his list of Xerxes' army he describes Cissian foot soldiers equipped like Persians but wearing turbans. He says nothing about the Elamite revolts against Darius.
u_field_physician.lead: Armies of this age carried physicians for the wounded, though few sources name them. The Persian court prized foreign doctors, above all Egyptians and then Greeks. Xenophon, marching home with the Ten Thousand, says how the Greeks chose eight men as doctors because of the many wounded.
u_field_physician.play: In the game the barracks trains him. He walks to the worst wounded man he can see and tends those around him, so your men last longer in a fight. He picks no fights, earns no rank, and does not count toward the garrison decree.
u_field_physician.s0: Retreating through Mesopotamia with their wounded, the Greek Ten Thousand halted for three days and appointed eight men as doctors, because there were so many hurt. Xenophon does not say how much these men knew. What mattered was that someone was named to do the work.
u_field_physician.s1: Herodotus says Cyrus asked Egypt's king for the best eye doctor there, and that Darius kept Egyptian physicians at court. When they failed with his twisted ankle, the Greek Democedes, a slave among the prisoners, cured him and was made rich.
u_field_physician.s2: Ctesias, a Greek physician at the court of Artaxerxes II, was in the field at Cunaxa in 401 BCE and said he treated the King's wound himself. Xenophon cites him for this, so at least one royal doctor rode with the army.
u_field_physician.s3: No source describes Persian army doctors at work among the ranks, or gives them a uniform. The robe, the satchel and a physician walking the line are this game's picture of them, not a record.
u_greek_archer.lead: Greek city armies of this period were built around the hoplite, the heavily armoured spearman, and most cities had few trained archers. Light troops existed, often poorer citizens, slaves or helots, but Greek writers rarely describe them. Their small role helps explain why Persian archers and horsemen seemed so dangerous to the Greeks, though by 479 BCE Athens had bowmen of its own.
u_greek_archer.play: The game gives the raids Athenian archers, which its own note says is invented (Herodotus 6.112). Its Locrian and Boeotian bowmen serve the King: true of Plataea, but at Thermopylae the Locrians fought against him.
u_greek_archer.s0: Herodotus says that when the Athenians ran at the Persian line at Marathon in 490 BCE, the Persians thought them mad, because they were few and had neither horsemen nor archers. They fought as a phalanx of hoplites, with the Plataeans beside them. Herodotus does not mention archers among the Athenians who sailed to help the Ionians burn Sardis in 498 BCE either.
u_greek_archer.s1: By 479 BCE Athens had a body of archers. Herodotus tells how, when the Persian cavalry under Masistius pressed the Megarians, 300 picked Athenians under Olympiodorus went to help them, with the archers alongside. Masistius's horse was struck by an arrow and threw him, and he was killed. Plutarch later says each Athenian ship at Salamis carried four archers among its fighting men.
u_greek_archer.s2: Herodotus says each Spartan citizen at Plataea was attended by seven armed helots, and he counts 69,500 light troops in the Greek army, more than the hoplites. Historians doubt these round figures, which look calculated rather than counted. Many, including van Wees, still think unarmoured men with javelins, slings or stones were present in large numbers even though the sources mostly ignore them.
u_greek_archer.s3: Athenian vase paintings of about 530-490 BCE often show archers in Scythian caps and patterned trousers beside hoplites. Some scholars take them as real Scythian mercenaries hired by the tyrants of Athens. Others see them as an artistic type for any archer, or for heroes of myth. The paintings do not settle whether Athens kept foreign bowmen before the Persian Wars.
u_greek_archer.s4: In 480 BCE the Opuntian Locrians sent their whole force to hold Thermopylae against Xerxes. The Thessalians had already gone over to him. After the pass fell, Herodotus says the Locrians, Malians and most Boeotians joined the Persians too. He lists them among the Greeks who fought for Mardonius at Plataea, with the Thebans most committed, but he does not say which of these men were archers.
u_greek_general.lead: The Greek cities that fought Persia had no single supreme commander. Athens elected ten generals, the strategoi, beside an older magistrate, the polemarch. The Ionian cities in revolt drove out their tyrants and chose generals of their own, with Aristagoras of Miletus at their head. Their councils and quarrels shaped the campaigns from 499 to 490 BCE.
u_greek_general.play: In the Sardis and Marathon levels the Greek side fields commanders named Athenian General, Athenian Strategos, Ionian Captain and Callimachus the Polemarch, each standing for a real office or man of the time.
u_greek_general.s0: Herodotus says Athens sent ten generals to Marathon, Miltiades among them, and that they were divided over whether to fight. The Constitution of the Athenians dates the election of one general from each of the ten tribes to 501 BCE/0, a few years after the reforms of Cleisthenes. A general served for one year and could be re-elected. He probably led his own tribe's contingent and debated strategy with the other nine.
u_greek_general.s1: Herodotus says Aristagoras gave up his tyranny at Miletus and had the Ionian cities appoint generals. For the march on Sardis in 498 BCE he named his brother Charopinus and Hermophantus as commanders. Melanthius led the twenty Athenian ships, and Eualcides led the Eretrians until he fell near Ephesus. Before Lade in 494 BCE, Dionysius of Phocaea drilled the fleet for seven days until the crews refused to go on.
u_greek_general.s2: Herodotus says the ten generals at Marathon were divided and the cautious view was close to winning, but the polemarch also had a vote. Miltiades persuaded Callimachus of Aphidna to vote for battle. The generals held command in turn, one day each, and those who favoured battle gave their days to Miltiades, who still waited for his own day. By custom the polemarch held the right wing, and Callimachus died in the fighting.
u_greek_general.s3: Herodotus says Callimachus was chosen polemarch by lot. The Constitution of the Athenians, however, dates the use of the lot for archons to 487 BCE/6, three years later, which suggests he was elected. Historians still argue whether the polemarch in 490 BCE was the real commander or only a senior colleague of the generals. Herodotus's picture of Miltiades as the guiding mind may also reflect stories later told by Miltiades' family and supporters.
u_greek_general.s4: A bronze Corinthian helmet found at Olympia is inscribed as a dedication by Miltiades to Zeus. It is usually linked to the victor of Marathon. On the Acropolis, fragments of a marble column carry an epigram naming Callimachus of Aphidna as polemarch. Its restored text is often read as a vow completed after his death at Marathon. The helmet is in the Olympia museum and the column in the Acropolis Museum.
u_greek_hoplite.lead: Hoplites were the heavy infantry of the Greek cities: men wealthy enough to buy a bronze helmet, body armour, greaves, a thrusting spear and a large round shield. They fought in close ranks. In the wars of 499 to 479 BCE they marched on Sardis and faced the King's armies at Marathon, Thermopylae and Plataea. Greeks also served the King, as the Ionians did before and after their revolt and the Thebans did in 479 BCE.
