u_greek_hoplite.play: The game fields Athenian, Ionian, Greek and Theban hoplites: tough foot that outlast the King's spearmen and hold against horse but turn few arrows. At Marathon the Athenians come on at the run, as Herodotus tells it.
u_greek_hoplite.s0: Excavated arms, many dedicated at Olympia, show the kit. It comprised a bronze helmet, often of the closed Corinthian type, greaves, and a bronze or linen corslet. It also included an iron-tipped spear about two to two and a half metres long and a wooden shield faced with bronze, close to a metre across. One Olympia helmet bears the name of Miltiades, perhaps the general of Marathon. Another, of eastern type, carries an Athenian dedication saying it was taken from the Medes.
u_greek_hoplite.s1: Hoplites were citizens who paid for their own equipment, not hired professionals. Spartan citizens, who trained for war full time, came closest to an exception. At Athens most hoplites came from the middle and upper property classes. Herodotus lists 38,700 hoplites in the Greek army at Plataea in 479 BCE. Many historians accept that figure as roughly plausible, unlike his far larger totals for the Persian side.
u_greek_hoplite.s2: Herodotus explains Greek victories largely by equipment and skill. At Thermopylae he says the Persians used shorter spears than the Greeks. At Plataea he says the Persians were not inferior in courage or strength, but they fought without armour and with less skill, rushing out in small groups against a formed line. He also records that Persian arrows wounded and killed many Spartans while they waited for favourable sacrifices.
u_greek_hoplite.s3: Herodotus says the Athenians at Marathon charged at a run over no less than eight stades, about 1.5 kilometres, the first Greeks he knew of to do so. Historians disagree over whether this was possible. Many think armoured men could not run so far and still fight in order, and that they ran only the last stretch, within range of the Persian bows. P. Krentz argues that hoplite kit was lighter in 490 BCE and the full run was feasible.
u_greek_hoplite.s4: Hoplites did not fight only against Persia. Ionian and other eastern Greek cities were the King's subjects and supplied men and ships. After their revolt failed at Lade in 494 BCE, they served him again in 480 BCE. In 479 BCE the Thebans and other Boeotians fought for Mardonius at Plataea. Herodotus says they fought hard against the Athenians and lost about three hundred of their best men before giving way.
u_greek_mercenary_hoplite.lead: Greek hoplites who fought for pay served foreign rulers long before the Persians reached the Aegean. The kings of Egypt's Saite dynasty relied heavily on Ionian and Carian soldiers, and such men faced Cambyses at Pelusium in 525 BCE. Their armour and close formation made them strong opponents, and their presence shows how far Greek warfare had spread across the eastern Mediterranean.
u_greek_mercenary_hoplite.play: The game fields them as armoured shield troops of the King's enemies, named differently by level, holding against spearmen and riders but worn down by archers. In fact Persian horse and archers harried hoplites hard at Plataea.
u_greek_mercenary_hoplite.s0: Herodotus says Psamtik I won his throne with Ionian and Carian raiders in bronze armour, then gave them land on the Pelusiac branch of the Nile called the Camps. He adds that Amasis later moved them to Memphis as his guard. Herodotus also credits Apries with 30,000 Carian and Ionian mercenaries, a figure that may well be inflated.
u_greek_mercenary_hoplite.s1: Around 591 BCE, Greek soldiers on Psamtik II's campaign into Nubia scratched their names on the legs of the colossal statues of Ramesses II at Abu Simbel. The graffiti name men from Ionian and Dorian cities and mention separate commanders for the Egyptians and for the foreign-speaking troops. They survive today as some of the earliest dated Greek inscriptions.
u_greek_mercenary_hoplite.s2: Excavated helmets, greaves and shields, many dedicated at sanctuaries such as Olympia, show the hoplite's kit: a bronze helmet, bronze greaves, and a large round shield held by an arm-band and a hand-grip. Bronze breastplates survive, and vase paintings also show corselets of layered linen. He fought with a thrusting spear and carried a short sword. The gear was heavy and costly and worked best in a tight line on level ground.
u_greek_mercenary_hoplite.s3: Herodotus tells of Phanes of Halicarnassus, one of Amasis's Greek mercenaries, who deserted to Cambyses and advised him to cross the desert with the help of the Arab king. In 525 BCE the Persians met Psamtik III's army, Greeks and Carians among it, at Pelusium and defeated it. Herodotus says he later saw the bones of the fallen still lying on the field.
u_greek_mercenary_hoplite.s4: Herodotus also reports that before the battle the mercenaries in Egyptian pay brought out Phanes' sons, killed them in sight of their father, and drank their blood mixed with wine. No other source confirms the story. It reads as a tale of betrayal and revenge and is best treated as such.
u_greek_rider.lead: Greek horsemen were riders from the wealthy families of the Greek states. The strongest of them came from the open plains of Thessaly and Boeotia. In the wars with Persia, the best Greek cavalry fought on the King's side, while the allied army that won at Plataea in 479 BCE relied almost entirely on infantry.
u_greek_rider.play: The game fields a Greek Rider at Plataea. Herodotus gives Pausanias's allied army no cavalry; the Greek horsemen on that field were Thebans and other Boeotians, with Thessalians, serving Mardonius.
u_greek_rider.s0: Keeping a horse in mainland Greece was costly, because good pasture was scarce outside a few plains. Athenian vase paintings and grave monuments of the later sixth century show young men of rich families on horseback. They often appear in parades, hunts or as mounted attendants of hoplites rather than charging in battle.
u_greek_rider.s1: Herodotus says that in about 511 BCE the Thessalians sent a thousand horsemen under their king Cineas to help the Athenian tyrant Hippias. On the cleared plain of Phalerum they routed a Spartan force and killed its commander Anchimolius. When Xerxes came in 480 BCE the Thessalians went over to him. Herodotus says the King raced his own horses against Thessalian ones, said to be the best in Greece, and the Persian horses won.
u_greek_rider.s2: Herodotus lists Pausanias's army at Plataea as hoplites and light-armed men and names no cavalry. His total of 110,000 is probably too high. When Masistius led the Persian horse against the Greek line, 300 picked Athenians with archers held firm until his horse was shot and he was killed. Later the Persian riders choked the Gargaphia spring, and the Greeks had no horsemen to stop them.
u_greek_rider.s3: Boeotians and Thessalians marched with Mardonius, and the Thebans had advised him to make his stand in Boeotia. Herodotus says that when the Persian line broke, the Boeotian cavalry covered the flight. Theban horsemen caught the Megarians and Phliasians advancing in disorder, killed 600 of them and drove the rest towards Cithaeron.
u_greek_rider.s4: The Athenian Constitution names the hippeis, the horsemen, as a property class under Solon. Historians disagree over whether Athens had an organised cavalry corps before the Persian Wars. Some link a small early force to the naukraries; others follow Andocides, who says Athens first set up 300 horsemen after the Persian Wars. By 431 BCE Thucydides counts 1,200 Athenian riders, including mounted archers.
u_hill_archer.lead: The Hill Archer is the game's name for the bowmen of the mountain peoples who lived beside the Persian heartland and along the routes between the royal cities. No ancient writer describes a unit by this name. Later Greek writers describe highland groups such as the Uxians and Cossaeans who held their own passes, and Strabo credits the Cossaeans with many archers.
u_hill_archer.play: The game shows him as an enemy archer whose label changes by level. He picks off walkers and archers while spearmen shrug off his arrows, which is a game simplification rather than a recorded troop type.
u_hill_archer.s0: Herodotus lists the Mardians among the Persian tribes he calls nomads rather than farmers, alongside the Dai, Dropici and Sagartians. Arrian describes the Uxians, highlanders on the route from Susa into Persis, who held the passes against Alexander in about 331, long after the game's period. These writers saw such groups from outside and say little about how they organised themselves or fought.
u_hill_archer.s1: In his tomb inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam, Darius names skill with the bow, on foot and on horseback, among his own virtues. This shows that archery belonged to the royal picture of the ideal Persian man. Excavations at Persepolis recovered large numbers of bronze and iron arrowheads, many of the three-bladed type common across the region. Such arrowheads cannot be tied to one people, so they show the weapon in use rather than the hill archers themselves.
u_hill_archer.s2: Arrian says the Uxians demanded the payments they had received from Persian kings for passage through their country. Strabo says the kings gave gifts to the Cossaeans and that the Cossaeans could field many archers. This evidence is late, and it may not describe the period before 479 BCE. Older readings saw the payments as royal weakness, but Briant argues they were a negotiated exchange that bound the highlanders to the king.
u_hill_archer.s3: Herodotus describes Persian infantry at Plataea setting up a wall of wicker shields and shooting from behind it. He says many Spartans were killed or wounded before that wall was pushed over. His account shows that both archery and shields mattered in battle in this period. It does not support the idea that spearmen could simply ignore arrows.
u_horseman.lead: Persian horsemen were the mounted arm of the King's army, raised from the Persian nobility and from men who held land in return for service. They fought mostly with bow and javelin, riding close to shoot and pulling back before infantry could reach them. At Plataea in 479 BCE they pressed the Greek army hard for days.
u_horseman.play: The game shows Persian horsemen as fast riders who run down archers and raiders and lose to spearmen. This simplifies history: many Persian riders were mounted archers and javelin men who harassed foot soldiers from a distance.
u_horseman.s0: On his tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam, Darius had it written that he was a good horseman, and a good bowman and spearman both on foot and mounted. Riding and shooting were the skills by which a Persian noble showed his worth. The Persepolis Fortification tablets record grain issued as fodder for horses, including those of travellers on the royal roads.
u_horseman.s1: Babylonian business archives, above all the Murashu texts, record plots called horse-land alongside bow-land and chariot-land. Groups of holders received such land and owed military service from it, or paid silver instead. These texts date from the later 5th century, after 479 BCE, but they show how the empire supported its soldiers, horsemen among them.
u_horseman.s2: Herodotus says Persian boys were taught three things from five to twenty: to ride, to shoot the bow and to speak the truth. In his list of Xerxes' army he says the Persian cavalry carried the same arms as the foot, bow, short spear and dagger, though some wore helmets of beaten bronze or iron.
u_horseman.s3: Herodotus says the horsemen under Masistius attacked the Greeks in relays until Masistius was killed. Afterwards the cavalry kept up its attacks, shooting arrows and javelins from horseback so that the Greeks could not close with them. They also fouled the Gargaphia spring that the Greek army drank from.
u_horseman.s4: Herodotus says Hippias guided the Persians to Marathon because the ground suited horsemen, yet cavalry plays no part in his account of the battle. Some historians think the horses had been re-embarked or sent elsewhere, and the Suda, a Byzantine dictionary, links the phrase "the cavalry are away" to Marathon. Others think few horses were landed at all. No source settles the question.
u_horseman.s5: Xenophon wrote his Education of Cyrus in the 4th century as a moral tale about kingship, not as a history. In it Cyrus persuades the Persians, who had fought on foot, to become horsemen, and makes it shameful for a Persian of rank to be seen going on foot. The story fits Greek ideas of Persia better than the record of Cyrus's reign.
u_immortal.lead: The Immortals were a body of ten thousand chosen Persian foot soldiers. Herodotus describes them in Xerxes' army of 480 BCE, commanded by Hydarnes. They are the best-known unit of the King's army, but nearly everything about them, including their name, comes from Greek writers rather than from Persian documents.
u_immortal.play: When an Immortal falls, the barracks queues and pays for his replacement, following Herodotus's account of the name. Making them a heavy shield unit simplifies him: he arms them with spear, bow and wicker shield.
u_immortal.s0: Herodotus says the Immortals were picked Persians led by Hydarnes son of Hydarnes. He explains the name by their number, which never changed: when a man died or fell sick, another was chosen in his place, so the unit always stood at ten thousand. He adds that they outshone the rest of the army in their gold ornaments, and that wagons carried their women and servants while camels and pack animals brought their own food.
u_immortal.s1: Herodotus gives the Immortals the same gear as the other Persian foot. They wore soft felt caps, sleeved tunics and scale armour like fish scales, and carried wicker shields, short spears, large bows with reed arrows and daggers. In Xerxes' procession a thousand spearmen near the King had golden apples on their spear butts. Behind them came ten thousand foot: a thousand with golden pomegranates and nine thousand with silver.
u_immortal.s2: Herodotus says Xerxes sent the Immortals against the pass at Thermopylae after the Medes and Cissians failed, and that they did no better, because their spears were shorter than those of the Greeks. Guided by Ephialtes, Hydarnes then led them over the mountain path at night and came behind the defenders. After Salamis, Herodotus says, Mardonius kept the Immortals in Greece, though Hydarnes chose to stay with the King.
u_immortal.s3: Glazed-brick panels from Darius's palace at Susa show long rows of guards in robes, holding spears with round butts and carrying bows and quivers. Reliefs at Persepolis show similar spearmen. These images are often linked to the Immortals or to the King's spear-bearers, but no Persian text labels them, so the identification is a modern reading.
u_immortal.s4: No Persian source uses the name Immortals. Some historians suggest the Greeks confused an Old Persian word meaning followers or companions with a similar word meaning deathless; others reject this. Scholars also disagree on how the ten thousand related to the thousand royal spear-bearers, and on whether the unit was a fixed guard or a figure Herodotus used for the King's best troops.
u_indian_archer.lead: Indian archers came from Hindush, the Indus valley province that Darius probably added to the empire some years after 520 BCE. Herodotus describes them marching with Xerxes in cotton clothes, carrying cane bows and iron-tipped cane arrows, and says Mardonius kept them for the final campaign in Greece in 479 BCE. They show how far the King could draw soldiers, from the Indus to Boeotia.
u_indian_archer.play: The game takes the cotton, cane bow and iron-tipped cane arrows from Herodotus. Its long reach, slow rate of fire and frailty are game choices: no ancient source measures the range or speed of Indian archery.
u_indian_archer.s0: Hindush does not appear in the list of lands in the Behistun inscription, so it was probably conquered after about 519 BCE. It is named in later lists of Darius, including his tomb inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam, where an Indian figure helps carry the King's throne. Darius's Susa charter says ivory was brought from India among other lands, and the Persepolis Fortification tablets record travellers going to and from Hindush on rations.
u_indian_archer.s1: Herodotus lists the Indians among Xerxes' infantry in 480 BCE, dressed in garments made of tree-wool, meaning cotton, with cane bows and cane arrows tipped with iron. He names their commander as Pharnazathres son of Artabates. He adds that Indian horsemen came armed the same way, with riding horses and chariots drawn by horses and wild asses. His total for the whole army, over 1.7 million foot, is regarded by historians as greatly exaggerated.
u_indian_archer.s2: After Salamis, Herodotus says, Mardonius chose the troops he wanted to stay with him in Greece, and the Indians were among them, foot and horse, alongside Persians, Medes, Saka and Bactrians. At Plataea in 479 BCE he places them in the battle line facing part of the Greek army. He records no particular deeds of theirs in the fighting.
u_indian_archer.s3: Arrian, drawing on writers who went east with Alexander, describes Indian foot archers with a bow as tall as the man, braced on the ground, and very long arrows. Historians debate whether this fourth-century picture fits the Indus troops of Xerxes' day, and whether Herodotus's cane means reed or bamboo. Neither source gives any range, so claims that Indian bows outshot Persian ones rest on inference.
u_indian_archer.s4: To explain the 360 talents of gold dust he says the Indians paid each year, Herodotus tells a tale of desert ants smaller than dogs but larger than foxes, which threw up gold-bearing sand as they dug. Indians, he says, raced in on fast camels to steal the sand before the ants could catch them. The story belongs to traveller's lore, though the gold tribute itself may reflect real river gold from the north-west.
u_ladder.lead: The scaling ladder was the simplest way to get soldiers over a wall: a long timber frame carried forward, set against the defences and climbed under covering fire. It was cheap and quick to make, but dangerous for the men on it. Near Eastern and Greek armies used ladders alongside ramps, rams and mines, and the Persians, heirs to Assyrian siege practice, probably did too.
u_ladder.play: In the game two men carry a ladder for the King's enemies; once set, raiders climb it, while defenders topple it and archers shoot the bearers. In history Persian armies were far more often the besiegers than the besieged.
u_ladder.s0: Assyrian palace reliefs from Nimrud and Nineveh show soldiers climbing ladders against city walls while archers behind them shoot at the parapet. On the reliefs Sennacherib set up at Nineveh after his siege of Lachish in 701 BCE, rams are pushed up a ramp and defenders throw down stones and torches. The Persians later ruled the lands where these methods had been developed.
u_ladder.s1: Herodotus describes Persian captures of cities mostly through mounds, mines and surprise. He says Harpagus took the Ionian cities by heaping earth against their walls, and that the citadel of Sardis fell when a soldier climbed an unguarded cliff. Miletus, he says, was taken in 494 BCE by undermining the walls and using every kind of siege engine.
u_ladder.s2: At Old Paphos on Cyprus, excavators found a Persian siege ramp built against the city wall, probably during the Cypriot revolt of about 498 BCE. Arrowheads, sling bullets and stone balls lay in and around the fill, and the defenders had dug tunnels beneath it to make it collapse. The site shows how Persian armies combined several methods to reach the top of a wall.
u_ladder.s3: A ladder had to be the right length, or the attack failed. Thucydides says the besieged Plataeans, in the winter of 428-427 BCE, counted the courses of bricks in the enemy siege wall to judge how long to make their ladders. Polybius, writing much later, stressed that commanders had to calculate the height of a wall and cited attacks that failed because the ladders were the wrong length.
u_ladder.s4: Greek writers tend to explain Persian captures of cities through treachery or tricks, which may understate Persian skill. Many modern historians think the Persians inherited Assyrian and Babylonian siege practice and used it well. The sources rarely say whether ladders were used in particular sieges, so their exact role remains uncertain.
u_levy_archer.lead: The Persian kings raised much of their army by levy from the peoples of the empire, and many of the men who answered were archers. In Babylonia, documents show land granted on condition that the holder served as a bowman or supplied one. Massed archery was central to Persian infantry fighting, so the levied bowman, mustered through the satraps, was probably among the most common soldiers in the King's wars.
u_levy_archer.play: The game shows the Levy Archer as a townsman with a hunting bow who shoots from behind the levy spearmen. This is a simplification: the surviving documents point more to landholders owing service than to townsmen.
u_levy_archer.s0: Babylonian documents of the Achaemenid period record bow-land, plots granted on condition that the holder provided an archer for the King. The fullest evidence comes from the Murashu archive of Nippur, written in the later fifth century, after the period of the game. By then the duty was often paid in silver or met by equipping a substitute, and bow-land was split among many shareholders.
u_levy_archer.s1: The glazed-brick friezes from Darius's palace at Susa show rows of guardsmen holding a spear, with a bow over the shoulder and a quiver on the back. Reliefs at Persepolis show bow-cases among the arms of some Persian and Median guards. In this art the bow and spear are often carried by the same man, which fits uneasily with a strict division into spearmen and archers.
u_levy_archer.s2: Herodotus says Persian boys were taught three things: to ride, to shoot the bow and to tell the truth. In his description of Xerxes' army he gives the Persian foot wicker shields, short spears, large bows, cane arrows and daggers. He also lists many subject contingents armed with bows, among them Bactrians, Saka, Indians and Arabs.
u_levy_archer.s3: Herodotus describes the Persians at Plataea fighting from behind a fence of wicker shields while shooting volleys of arrows. Modern historians have reconstructed units with shield-bearers in the front rank and archers behind, but how far the ranks were separated, and how often this formation was used, is still argued. The evidence is thin and comes mostly from Greek writers describing Persian defeats.
u_levy_archer.s4: Herodotus gives Xerxes' land army as 1,700,000 foot in 480 BCE, a figure historians reject as greatly exaggerated; modern estimates are a small fraction of it and vary widely. Herodotus also says officers drove men forward with whips at Thermopylae, and Greek writers often set trained Persians against poorly armed subject levies. How far this reflects real differences, rather than Greek bias, is argued.
u_levy_spearman.lead: Beyond his guards and standing garrisons, the Persian King raised much of his infantry by levy from Persians, Medes and subject peoples. In Babylonia at least, many such men owed service because they held land on that condition. Levied men filled the great armies of Darius and Xerxes, and Greek writers judged them by how they fared against heavily armoured hoplites.
u_levy_spearman.play: In the game, a townsman with spear and wicker shield who holds a line in numbers but breaks against trained men. Historically, much of the levy came from land held for service, and Persian foot often carried bows as well.
u_levy_spearman.s0: In Old Persian the word kara meant both the people and the army, a sign that fighting men were drawn from the population at large. In the Behistun inscription Darius tells how he sent his generals with the Persian and Median army that stood by him against the rebels of 522-521 BCE. The inscription records battles and dates but says little about how these men were armed.
u_levy_spearman.s1: Babylonian documents show land grants that carried military duty: bow-land, horse-land and chariot-land, whose holders owed a soldier or a payment in silver. The fullest evidence, the Murashu archive from Nippur, dates to the second half of the 400s BCE, after the game's period. Scattered earlier texts suggest bow-land already existed under the first kings, and the system helps explain how the King could call up large numbers of men.
u_levy_spearman.s2: Herodotus says the Persian infantry of Xerxes wore soft felt caps, sleeved tunics and scale armour. He adds that they carried wicker shields, short spears, large bows with cane arrows, and daggers at the right thigh. He then lists dozens of subject contingents, each in its own native gear. His total of 1,700,000 foot soldiers is regarded by historians as greatly exaggerated.
u_levy_spearman.s3: Herodotus tells that at Plataea in 479 BCE the Persians set their wicker shields together as a barrier and shot arrows from behind it. When the Spartans broke through, the Persians fought hand to hand, grabbing at enemy spears. Herodotus says they were not inferior in courage or strength, but lacked armour and skill for close combat and rushed out in small groups.
u_levy_spearman.s4: Modern writers often call the front-rank shield men sparabara, from a reconstructed Persian word for shield, but the term is not attested as a unit name in the sources. Historians disagree on whether shield-bearers formed a separate rank screening archers or whether every man carried both bow and spear. How much training levied men received, and how far Greek authors understated it, is also debated.
u_libyan_rider.lead: The Libyans were the peoples of the desert and coast west of the Nile valley. When Cambyses took Memphis in 525 BCE, Herodotus says the nearby Libyans submitted without a fight and sent gifts. Darius later listed Libya, Putaya in Old Persian, among his lands, and Libyan charioteers marched in Xerxes' army in 480 BCE.
u_libyan_rider.play: The Memphis level (525-524 BCE) includes a Libyan Rider unit. The sources describe Libyans in Persian service as charioteers rather than riders, and Herodotus records no Libyan fighting against Cambyses, so the unit simplifies the history.
u_libyan_rider.s0: Herodotus says that after Memphis fell in 525 BCE, the Libyans living next to Egypt took fright and surrendered without fighting. They agreed to pay tribute and sent gifts, and the Greek cities of Cyrene and Barca did the same. Cambyses accepted the Libyan gifts kindly but, Herodotus says, scorned the small Cyrenaean offering and scattered it among his troops.
u_libyan_rider.s1: Darius's tomb inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam names Putaya, generally taken to be Libya, among the lands he ruled. On the tomb front, labelled figures of the subject peoples hold up the raised platform on which the King stands, and a Libyan is among them. Xerxes repeated Putaya in his own list of lands.
u_libyan_rider.s2: Herodotus describes the Libyans of 480 BCE as dressed in leather and armed with fire-hardened javelins, under a commander named Massages. In his list of mounted troops he says the Libyans all drove chariots. He counts Arab camel riders and Libyan charioteers together at 20,000, a figure historians treat as unreliable like his other army totals.
u_libyan_rider.s3: Greek writers stress Libyan skill with horses, and Herodotus says the Greeks learned to yoke four horses from the Libyans. Yet his evidence is mostly for chariots, not riders on horseback. The famous Numidian cavalry belongs to a much later age, and historians caution against reading it back into the sixth century.
u_libyan_rider.s4: Herodotus places the Libyans, Cyrene and Barca in the same tribute district as Egypt, and tells how the governor Aryandes sent an army against Barca. Historians debate how firmly Persia held the Libyan tribes and Cyrenaica, and whether tribute there was regular or only occasional gifts.
u_median_horse_archer.lead: The Medes of the western Iranian plateau were the Persians' nearest kin and their first great conquest under Cyrus. Their horsemen, raised to ride and shoot, served in the King's cavalry. Greek writers describe the King's riders harrying infantry with arrows, and the Persian record shows Medes fighting and commanding for the King alongside the Persians themselves.
u_median_horse_archer.play: The game shows a rider who shoots from the saddle, outpaces infantry and loses to other horsemen. Herodotus says Median horse carried their infantry kit, spear and shield as well as bow, so the pure skirmisher is a simplification.
u_median_horse_archer.s0: Herodotus describes the Median foot in Xerxes' army of 480 BCE as dressed like the Persians, in felt caps, sleeved tunics, scale armour and trousers, with wicker shields, short spears, large bows and cane arrows. He adds that this dress was really Median and that the Persians had adopted it. He says the Median cavalry was equipped like the infantry, so a Median rider carried spear, shield and dagger as well as a bow.
u_median_horse_archer.s1: Herodotus says Persian boys were taught to ride, to shoot the bow and to speak the truth. At Plataea in 479 BCE he describes the King's cavalry under the Persian Masistius attacking Greek infantry squadron by squadron, until Masistius fell after his horse was hit by an arrow. Later, he says, the horsemen harassed the Greeks with javelins and arrows, as mounted archers hard to close with. He does not single out Medes in these passages.
u_median_horse_archer.s2: Darius's Behistun inscription records a Median revolt under Fravartish in 522-521 BCE, crushed by Darius and his generals, and Fravartish was impaled at Ecbatana. It also names a Mede, Takhmaspada, as commander of a Persian and Median army sent to Sagartia. On the Apadana stair reliefs at Persepolis, men in rounded caps and riding dress, usually taken as Medes, alternate with Persians in long robes.
u_median_horse_archer.s3: Historians debate how far Achaemenid horsemen were horse archers in the later steppe manner. Herodotus mentions javelins beside bows, and Xenophon, writing later, gives Persian riders javelins, so many think they used both. Herodotus also tells a story of Scythians teaching Median boys archery under Cyaxares, which some read as a sign of steppe influence. Whether Medes formed separate horse-archer units is unknown.
u_median_rebel.lead: Late in 522 BCE, soon after Darius seized the throne, a Mede named Fravartish claimed descent from the old Median king Cyaxares and raised Media in revolt. His followers fought Darius's generals and then the King himself before they were crushed in 521 BCE. Historians count the Median rising among the most dangerous of the revolts Darius recorded at Behistun, because Media was one of the core lands of the empire.
u_median_rebel.play: In Bagastana and Parsa, Median rebels appear as spearmen, archers, captains, a champion of Fravartish and Nisaean horse archers who join raids. The champion and captains are game inventions; Behistun names no such men.
u_median_rebel.s0: Darius says that a Mede named Fravartish rose in Media and told the people he was Khshathrita, of the family of Cyaxares. The Median people at home, probably meaning the troops at the palace, went over to him, and he became king in Media. Parthia and Hyrcania soon declared for him too, and Darius's father Hystaspes had to fight there.
u_median_rebel.s1: Darius sent Hydarnes (Vidarna) with an army of Persians and Medes loyal to him, so Medes fought on both sides. Hydarnes fought the rebels at Marush in Media and then waited in the district of Kampanda for the King. Darius marched from Babylon and defeated Fravartish at Kunduru in 521 BCE. The Babylonian version of the text adds casualty figures for these battles.
u_median_rebel.s2: Fravartish fled with a few horsemen towards Raga but was taken. Darius says he cut off his nose, ears and tongue, put out one eye, and kept him chained at the palace gate for all to see, then impaled him at Ecbatana and hanged his leading men in the fortress there. A Sagartian named Chissantakhma, who made the same claim to Cyaxares' line, was impaled at Arbela. Fravartish stands among the bound rebels on the Behistun relief.
u_median_rebel.s3: Herodotus says the Medes were armed like the Persians, with felt caps, tunics, wicker shields, short spears, bows and daggers, and that the Persians had in fact taken this dress from the Medes. He also mentions the large horses bred on the Nisaean plain in Media. His descriptions come from Xerxes' army about forty years later, not from the revolt itself.
u_median_rebel.s4: Herodotus notes only briefly that the Medes later revolted against Darius and were beaten. Historians still debate whether Fravartish was truly of the old royal house or simply used the name, how much of the Median nobility backed him, and how the battle dates in Darius's text fit his claim of nineteen battles in a single year. All detailed knowledge comes from the victor's own account.
u_penteconter.lead: The penteconter was a long, narrow oared ship rowed by about fifty men, roughly twenty-five a side. Before the trireme spread in the late sixth century, it was the main warship and long-distance vessel of Greek and Phoenician seafarers. It still served in Persian fleets and ship-bridges in the age of Darius and Xerxes.
u_penteconter.play: The game shows penteconters at the Ister bridge and along the coasts. Herodotus does not name the ship types used for Darius's Ister bridge, so penteconters there are a reasonable reconstruction, not a recorded fact.
u_penteconter.s0: Greek vase paintings of the eighth to sixth centuries show long open ships with a single bank of oarsmen and a pointed ram at the bow. Assyrian palace reliefs of about 700 BCE from Nineveh show Phoenician oared warships, some with rowers on two levels, which allowed a shorter hull for the same crew. Modern reconstructions suggest a single-level penteconter was probably roughly 30 metres long or more.
u_penteconter.s1: Herodotus says the Phocaeans of Ionia were the first Greeks to make long voyages. He says they sailed to the Adriatic, Iberia and Tartessus in penteconters rather than round-hulled merchantmen. He also says Polycrates, tyrant of Samos, built his sea power on a hundred penteconters, though the ships he sent to help Cambyses against Egypt in 525 BCE were triremes.
u_penteconter.s2: Herodotus says the Ionian fleet sailed into the Black Sea and bridged the Ister for Darius's Scythian campaign about 513 BCE, but he does not say what kind of ships formed the bridge. For Xerxes' bridges over the Hellespont in 480 BCE, he states that penteconters and triremes were lashed together. He also lists penteconters among the many smaller craft that followed Xerxes' fleet.
u_penteconter.s3: Thucydides says Greek navies before the Persian Wars were made up mostly of penteconters and long boats. He dates the first large trireme fleets, in Sicily and at Corcyra, to shortly before Darius died. Historians debate how fast the change came and who drove it. H. T. Wallinga argued that big trireme navies were largely a Persian creation from Cambyses onwards, paid for by the King, while others give more weight to Greek and Phoenician states.
u_penteconter.s4: In the Homeric Catalogue of Ships, Philoctetes leads seven ships, each rowed by fifty men. Later Greek tradition gave the Argo a crew of about fifty heroes. These poems were shaped long after any real expedition and show only that Greeks imagined their heroes sailing in fifty-oared ships.
u_persian_ram.lead: A covered ram was a heavy beam, often metal-tipped, swung or pushed against a wall or gate from inside a wheeled shed that shielded its crew from arrows and stones. The Assyrians used it widely, and the Persians who followed them besieged many cities. No Achaemenid source clearly shows a ram, however, so how often Persian armies used one is an open question.
u_persian_ram.play: In the game the ram quickly breaks a raider camp's fence and huts but cannot fight, so spearmen must guard it. Real rams were used against city walls and gates, not hill camps, and Persian sieges in the sources lean on mounds and mines.
u_persian_ram.s0: Neo-Assyrian palace reliefs from Nimrud and Nineveh show wheeled rams under wicker or hide covers, worked against city walls while archers gave covering shot. Such scenes appear from the 9th century, under Ashurnasirpal II, onwards. Sennacherib's Lachish reliefs show the siege of 701 BCE, with rams pushed up a built ramp against the town wall.
u_persian_ram.s1: Herodotus says Harpagus took the Ionian cities about 545 BCE by heaping mounds against their walls. He tells of Persian mines at Barca in Libya, of Soli on Cyprus falling in the fifth month to undermining, and of Miletus taken in 494 BCE by mines and every kind of engine. He does not describe what these engines were, and he nowhere names a ram in Persian hands.
u_persian_ram.s2: Excavations at Old Paphos on Cyprus uncovered a siege ramp that the Persian besiegers built against the city wall during the Cypriot revolt of about 498-497 BCE. The defenders dug tunnels under the ramp to undermine it. Hundreds of arrowheads and spearheads and many stone balls were found there, along with broken sculpture from a nearby sanctuary used as fill. Such ramps were raised to bring troops, and perhaps engines, up to the wall.
u_persian_ram.s3: No Achaemenid relief, inscription or tablet clearly shows a battering ram, and Herodotus leaves the engines at Miletus unnamed. Some historians assume the Persians kept the Assyrian ram, citing ramps like the one at Paphos. Others note that the sieges we know of were won mainly by mounds, mines, blockade or betrayal, as at Eretria in 490 BCE. Ephorus, cited by Plutarch, called the engines at Samos in 440 BCE a novelty, so rams were probably rare in the Aegean.
u_persian_rebel.lead: In 521 BCE, while Darius was fighting rebels in Media and Babylonia, a Persian named Vahyazdata claimed to be Bardiya, son of Cyrus, and was accepted as king in Persis. Part of the Persian army went over to him. The revolt mattered because it broke out in the Persians' own homeland, among the people Darius most needed to hold.
u_persian_rebel.play: In the Parsa level, Vahyazdata's rebels carry the King's wicker shield and resist arrows and horse, joined by horse archers and a champion. The champion is invented; the real battles were at Rakha and Mount Parga, not Parsa.
u_persian_rebel.s0: Darius's Behistun inscription says that Vahyazdata lived in a town called Tarava in the district of Yautiya in Persis. He declared himself Bardiya, son of Cyrus. The inscription adds that Persian troops who had been stationed at the palace turned away from Darius and joined him, so that he became king in Persis.
u_persian_rebel.s1: Darius sent Persian and Median troops under a Persian named Artavardiya, while he led the rest into Media. Artavardiya beat the rebels at Rakha in Persis. Vahyazdata escaped with a few horsemen to Paishiyauvada, raised a new force and fought again at Mount Parga, where he was defeated and taken. Darius had him and his leading followers impaled at Uvadaicaya in Persis.
u_persian_rebel.s2: Vahyazdata also sent an army east against Vivana, Darius's satrap in Arachosia. The inscription records that Vivana defeated it near the fortress of Kapishakanish and again in the district of Gandutava. The commander of the rebel army fled and was caught and killed with his followers at the fortress of Arshada. Vahyazdata's figure appears among the bound rebels on the Behistun relief, named in a caption.
u_persian_rebel.s3: No source describes the rebels' equipment. Since many of them had been royal Persian troops, historians assume they fought like other Persians. Herodotus describes Persian infantry with felt caps, scale armour, wicker shields, short spears, large bows and daggers. That description comes from his account of Xerxes' army of 480 BCE, so applying it to these men in 521 BCE is reasonable guesswork, not record.
u_persian_rebel.s4: Darius's account calls every rebel a liar, and Vahyazdata is the second man he names as a false Bardiya. Herodotus does not mention him at all. Some historians suspect that the real Bardiya had been killed by Darius and his allies, and that support for Vahyazdata reflects Persian loyalty to Cyrus's line. Others accept Darius's version. Only the winner's account survives.
u_phoenician_marine.lead: The Phoenician cities of the Levant coast, above all Sidon and Tyre, supplied the largest and best squadrons of the Persian fleet from Cambyses' reign onward. Herodotus describes the Phoenician fighting men of 480 BCE as armed with Greek-style helmets, linen corslets, rimless shields and javelins, and Persian kings relied on these ships at Lade, Salamis and many smaller campaigns.
u_phoenician_marine.play: The game's arms follow Herodotus 7.89 closely. Using these men as a land unit of the army is a simplification: they fought mainly from ships, and Herodotus says Persians, Medes and Saka also served aboard as marines.
u_phoenician_marine.s0: In his list of Xerxes' fleet, Herodotus says the Phoenicians, with the Syrians of Palestine, brought 300 ships, a figure that, like his fleet total, may be inflated. Their men wore helmets made much like Greek ones and corslets of linen, and carried shields without rims and javelins. Light linen armour probably suited men who had to move on a crowded deck and might end up in the water.
u_phoenician_marine.s1: Herodotus says that on every ship of the fleet, besides the native crew and fighters, there served marines who were Persians, Medes and Saka. When he totals the army he counts thirty such men on each ship. A Phoenician galley therefore went into action with a mixed company, Phoenician javelin men alongside Iranian archers and spearmen.
u_phoenician_marine.s2: Herodotus names the kings who led the Phoenician contingents in 480 BCE, among them Tetramnestus of Sidon, Matten of Tyre and Merbalus of Arados. The Sidonians won the ship race Xerxes held at Abydos, and he chose a Sidonian ship for himself. Earlier, Herodotus says, the Phoenicians refused Cambyses' order to sail against Carthage, their own colony, and he did not force them.
u_phoenician_marine.s3: Herodotus tells that after Salamis some Phoenicians blamed the Ionians for the loss. Xerxes had just seen a Samothracian ship on his side ram an Athenian one, and he had the accusers beheaded. Before Mycale the Phoenician squadrons were sent away. No Phoenician account of these wars survives, so the story rests on the Greek side alone. Historians debate whether the Phoenician fleet was badly beaten or mainly withdrawn.
u_raider.lead: The Persian kings ruled settled plains and valleys, but the mountains between them held herding peoples who lived partly by raiding and by charging for passage. Greek writers describe such groups, the Uxians, Mardians and Cossaeans above all, as robbers, mostly in accounts of Alexander's campaigns. They mattered because the King's roads crossed their country, and his officials dealt with them by force, payment or bargain.
u_raider.play: The game uses the Hill Raider as a fast light enemy, renamed by level, that runs down archers and civilians and loses to spearmen. This simplifies history: the hill peoples were often bargained with rather than simply fought.
u_raider.s0: Herodotus lists the peoples of Persis and sorts them into leading, farming and nomad tribes. He names the Pasargadae, Maraphians and Maspians as the chief tribes, and the Daans, Mardians, Dropicans and Sagartians as nomads. He gives no detail of raiding here, but his list shows that Persis itself was not one uniform people.
u_raider.s1: Arrian says that the lowland Uxians obeyed the Persian satrap, but the mountain Uxians did not. When Alexander marched from Susa toward Persis about 331, the mountain Uxians held the pass and demanded the payment they said the Persian kings had always given them. Alexander attacked them by a side route and imposed a tribute of livestock. Strabo adds that the Cossaeans received gifts from the kings travelling between Ecbatana and Babylon.
u_raider.s2: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, written in Elamite between about 509 and 493 BCE, record travellers on the roads of Persis. They drew rations at stations on sealed authorisations, often in parties under a named leader. The tablets show a closely administered heartland. They do not name hill raiders, so it remains open how far outlying mountain groups stood inside or outside this system.
u_raider.s3: Greek writers of the Roman period read the kings' payments to mountain peoples as a sign that the empire could not control its own hills. Pierre Briant argued instead that the gifts were part of a lasting relationship of exchange and recognition, in which herders supplied animals and fighting men and the King kept the passes open. Historians still differ on how far these groups were enemies and how far they were partners of the crown.
u_raider_chief.lead: The mountains between Susa and Persis, and towards Media, were home to herding peoples such as the Uxians and Cossaeans, whom Greek writers portray as never fully subject to the Persian kings. Arrian and Strabo report that the kings gave them payments or gifts for safe passage. No surviving source names a chief of these peoples between 530 and 479 BCE, so the game's war chief is a reconstruction built on later reports.
u_raider_chief.play: A light enemy unit, named differently in each level, whose raiders within 10 cells strike 15% harder; kill him and his division falls back. No source shows hill chiefs leading divisions of a great host; that framing is the game's.
u_raider_chief.s0: Herodotus lists the tribes of the Persians and says some were settled farmers while others, among them the Mardians, were nomads. Later writers on Alexander's campaigns name further mountain peoples on the edges of Persis, Elam and Media, such as the Uxians and the Cossaeans. They describe these peoples as herders who held the passes between the lowlands and the Persian heartland.
u_raider_chief.s1: Arrian says the mountain Uxians would let Alexander through their pass between Susa and Persis only if he paid what they had received from the Persian kings. Strabo, drawing on Nearchus, names four robber peoples of these mountains and says the Cossaeans received gifts from the kings. Alexander refused to pay and attacked the Uxians in the winter of 331-330, and later campaigned against the Cossaeans in winter.
u_raider_chief.s2: Greek and Roman writers present these payments as a sign of royal weakness. Pierre Briant argued instead that they formed a negotiated relationship, in which the King exchanged gifts with mountain leaders to keep the routes open and bind them to him. The reports concern the time of Alexander and survive through much later authors, so how these peoples dealt with Cyrus or Darius is unknown.
u_raider_chief.s3: Ancient armies often broke when their commander died. Herodotus says the Persian resistance at Plataea collapsed once Mardonius was killed, and Xenophon describes how the death of Cyrus the Younger at Cunaxa ended his cause. The game's rule that a division falls back when its chief dies follows this general pattern, not any report about hill peoples.
u_raider_great_chief.lead: The Great Chief of the Hills stands for the men who led the mountain peoples of Persis and the Zagros, such as the Mardians, Uxians and Cossaeans, when they gathered in strength. No source from the period names such a leader. Later Greek writers knew these peoples as raiders who held the mountain passes, and their dealings with the Persian kings suggest that the empire's heartland still contained communities with a degree of independence.
u_raider_great_chief.play: The game shows him as a war leader whose reserve makes raiders within 10 cells strike 20% harder, and whose fall breaks the host at half strength. This is a game invention: no ancient source describes a single great chief of the hills.
u_raider_great_chief.s0: Herodotus lists the tribes that made up the Persian people. Three, led by the Pasargadae, stood above the rest; some others farmed; and others, among them the Mardians and Sagartians, he calls nomads. The list suggests that pastoral groups in the uplands of Persis were counted as Persians, yet lived differently from the court and the farming villages of the valleys.
u_raider_great_chief.s1: Strabo, drawing on Nearchus, Alexander's admiral, names four predatory peoples of the mountains: the Mardians, Uxians, Elymaeans and Cossaeans. He says the Cossaeans received gifts from the Persian kings when the court travelled between Ecbatana and Babylon. Arrian tells how the mountain Uxians demanded from Alexander in 331 the payment they claimed the Persian kings had always given them for passage.
u_raider_great_chief.s2: The Greek accounts speak of these peoples as groups and rarely name their leaders, and nothing survives from 530-479 BCE about how they chose men to lead them in war. Most historians think leadership was local, by clan or valley, but how far any one chief could unite them is unknown. A single great war leader commanding a united host is therefore a reconstruction, not a fact attested in the sources.
u_raider_great_chief.s3: Greek writers present the payments to the Uxians and Cossaeans as a sign that the kings could not master the mountains. Pierre Briant argues instead that the gifts were part of a negotiated relationship, in which the King's generosity bound the hill peoples to him and secured the roads. Historians still debate how far these peoples stood outside royal control and how far they were woven into it.
u_raider_great_chief.s4: Arrian and Diodorus say that Alexander broke the old arrangements by force. Arrian tells how he attacked the Uxians in 331 and imposed a tribute of livestock, and both describe his winter campaign of 324-323 against the Cossaeans. These are the fullest accounts of the hill peoples, but they were written centuries later from the histories of Alexander's side.
u_raider_horse_archer.lead: Horse archers shot from the saddle, rode in close, loosed their arrows and pulled back before foot soldiers could reach them. The Persians fought this way themselves, and the King met it among nomads and the Scythians beyond the Ister. The game's Hill Horse Archer is a composite of such enemies, not one people recorded in the sources.
u_raider_horse_archer.play: His label changes by level; he circles the town's flanks, shoots and wheels away, and horsemen run him down while spearmen's shields stop his arrows. History was harsher: at Plataea mounted archers badly harassed Greek foot.
u_raider_horse_archer.s0: Herodotus says Persian boys were taught three things from the age of five to twenty: to ride, to shoot with the bow and to speak the truth. In the Greek picture, then, riding and archery were part of a Persian upbringing. Herodotus also calls the Persian cavalry at Plataea mounted archers, so the King's own horsemen fought in the style the game gives to his enemies.
u_raider_horse_archer.s1: The Persepolis Fortification tablets were written mostly in Elamite between about 509 and 493 BCE. They record grain issued as fodder to horses and other animals, including animals moving along the roads. They show how closely the administration counted feed. They say nothing about hill raiders, but they help explain why mounted men cost far more to keep than men on foot.
u_raider_horse_archer.s2: Herodotus describes the Scythians as a people without towns or walls who lived from wagons and fought as mounted archers. He says that when Darius crossed the Ister in about 513 BCE, they refused battle, fell back, fouled wells and springs, and attacked Persian foragers with their cavalry. In his telling the Scythian horse regularly routed the Persian cavalry, and Darius at last withdrew across the river.
u_raider_horse_archer.s3: Herodotus tells how Masistius led the Persian cavalry near Plataea in 479 BCE, attacking in squadrons that rode up in turn and pressed the Megarians hard. Athenian picked men and archers came up. Masistius's horse was shot and he was killed, and after a fight over his body the cavalry drew off. Later the horse, which Herodotus calls mounted archers, shot at the Greeks and choked the Gargaphia spring.
u_raider_horse_archer.s4: Herodotus counts the Mardians and Sagartians among the nomad Persian tribes, and says the Sagartians rode for Xerxes with lassos and daggers, not bows. Arrian says the Uxians of the Zagros took payment from the King for passage. Greek writers read this as royal weakness, while Briant argues it was a negotiated exchange of gifts. No source shows these hill peoples as horse archers, so the game's unit borrows that style.
u_ram.lead: A covered ram was a heavy beam, usually tipped with metal, driven against a wall or gate by a crew sheltering in a roofed wooden shed that guarded them from missiles and fire. The device was already centuries old by the time of Cyrus, as Assyrian palace reliefs show. In this period Persian armies took cities mostly with earth mounds, mines and blockade, and Herodotus says little about rams in their sieges.
u_ram.play: The game gives the King's enemies a slow, hide-covered ram that arrows barely harm and spearmen and horsemen break. This simplifies: wet hides guarded mainly against fire, and Persia's foes in these years seldom used rams.
u_ram.s0: Assyrian palace reliefs show wheeled rams with high covered sheds attacking walls, most fully in Sennacherib's reliefs of the siege of Lachish in 701 BCE. In one scene a crewman pours water from a long ladle over the front of the machine while defenders throw torches down on it. The scene suggests that fire, more than arrows, was the danger the crews guarded against.
u_ram.s1: Herodotus says that Harpagus took the Ionian cities in the 540s BCE by raising earth mounds against their walls. At Barca in Libya the Persians dug mines, which a bronzesmith found by listening at a bronze shield, and in the end they took the town by a trick. Herodotus also says Soli on Cyprus fell when its wall was undermined, and that Miletus fell in 494 BCE to mining and every kind of engine.
u_ram.s2: Excavators at Old Paphos on Cyprus found a Persian siege ramp built against the north-east gate during the Cypriot revolt of about 498-497 BCE. It was filled partly with broken statues and building stone. The defenders dug tunnels beneath it and lit fires to bring it down, and hundreds of stone balls, arrowheads and spearheads lay on the site. Herodotus does not describe this siege; it is known only from excavation.
u_ram.s3: Thucydides describes Peloponnesian rams brought against Plataea in 429 BCE, fifty years after this game ends. The defenders caught the ram heads with nooses and snapped them off by dropping heavy beams hung on chains. Herodotus says that in 479 BCE the Spartans could not break into the Persian stockade at Plataea until the Athenians arrived, and that the Athenians took Sestos by blockade once its defenders were starving.
u_ram.s4: Later writers told stories about who invented the ram. The Roman architect Vitruvius, writing more than four centuries after this period, says the Carthaginians first used one at the siege of Gades. He adds that a Carthaginian named Cetras later set it on wheels under a hide-covered roof. These are late tales about origins, and the Assyrian reliefs show covered rams in use long before.
u_royal_archer.lead: The bow was the main weapon of the Persian foot soldier and a sign of royal power. Herodotus says Persian boys were trained to shoot from childhood, and the King himself appeared on reliefs and coins as an archer. Archery played a large part in Persian battles, and Greek writers remembered the arrow storms long afterwards.
u_royal_archer.play: The game fields the King's Archer as a separate trained archer. Most Persian infantry seem to have carried a spear as well as a bow, so splitting spearmen and archers into different units is a simplification.
u_royal_archer.s0: On the Behistun relief Darius holds a bow and rests his foot on the fallen Gaumata, while the other rebel leaders stand bound before him. In his tomb inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam he claims to be a good bowman both on foot and on horseback. The gold and silver coins struck from about 515-500 BCE onwards show a crowned archer, usually taken to be the King.
u_royal_archer.s1: Glazed-brick panels from Darius's palace at Susa show rows of soldiers in long robes. Each carries a spear, with a bow over the shoulder and a quiver on the back. Many of these panels are now in the Louvre. Guards on the Persepolis reliefs carry the same pairing of spear and bow, which suggests that a royal soldier was trained in both.
u_royal_archer.s2: Babylonian documents record plots called bow land, held in return for military service to the crown. Such holdings already appear under Darius. They are best known from the Murashu archive of Nippur, which dates from about 455 to 403 BCE. By then the service was largely paid in silver. The system shows how the empire raised bowmen from settled subjects as well as from Persians.
u_royal_archer.s3: Herodotus says Persian boys were taught from five to twenty years old to ride, to shoot the bow and to speak the truth. He describes Persian infantry in Xerxes' army with felt caps, sleeved tunics, scale armour, wicker shields, short spears, long bows with cane arrows, and daggers. At Plataea, he says, the Persians shot from behind a wall of wicker shields but lacked the heavy armour of the Greeks.
u_royal_archer.s4: Historians still argue over whether the Susa archers show the royal guard, often linked with the Immortals, or Persian and Elamite soldiers in general. The robes are of court style rather than field dress. The battle arrangement of archers and shield-bearing spearmen is reconstructed mostly from short Greek remarks, so modern pictures of the formation vary.
u_royal_commander.lead: The hazarapatish was the Persian 'chief of a thousand', called chiliarch by the Greeks. The title named officers of thousand-strong units in the King's army and, at court, the commander of the royal guard who controlled access to the King. The evidence is thin and mostly Greek, so how powerful the court office was is still debated.
u_royal_commander.play: The game shows the hazarapatish as a shield unit whose presence makes men within 10 cells strike 15% harder and take blows better; that bonus is a game abstraction. Historically the title also named the King's chief guard and court officer.
u_royal_commander.s0: Herodotus says that the army Xerxes led in 480 BCE was organised in units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand. The commanders who mustered each contingent appointed the commanders of thousands and of ten thousands. The commanders of ten thousand then appointed the captains of hundreds and of tens. In this scheme the commander of a thousand stood between the captains of hundreds and the commanders of ten thousand, and a large army had many of them.
u_royal_commander.s1: Describing Xerxes' march from Sardis, Herodotus places a thousand picked Persian spearmen directly behind the King, followed by a thousand horsemen and then ten thousand foot. A thousand of these ten thousand had golden pomegranates on their spear butts, and the rest had silver ones. Herodotus names no chiliarch here. The link between this guard and the court office is a modern inference.
u_royal_commander.s2: Plutarch, writing more than five centuries later, tells how the exiled Themistocles, around 465 BCE, first went to the chiliarch Artabanus, who explained that anyone seeking an audience had to bow before the King. In this story the chiliarch manages who reaches the King and how they behave. The episode falls after the period of the game and comes through a late writer, so it shows the later office rather than its origins.
u_royal_commander.s3: The Old Persian word hazarapatish is reconstructed from renderings in other languages and does not appear in the royal inscriptions. Some historians saw the chiliarch as a chief minister second only to the King. Others, Briant among them, read the Greek evidence as showing a guard commander and master of audiences. Diodorus says the rank was first honoured by the Persian kings and was later held under Alexander, when Hephaestion had it.
u_royal_horse_archer.lead: The King's Horse Archer stands for the mounted bowmen of the Achaemenid army. Persian nobles prided themselves on riding and shooting, and Greek writers describe Persian cavalry pouring arrows and javelins onto infantry that could not reach them. No surviving source names a separate royal corps of horse archers.
u_royal_horse_archer.play: The game shows a royal cavalryman who shoots from the saddle and outrides foot soldiers, which fits Herodotus on Plataea. The counter is simplified: there, Masistius fell to Athenian archers and hoplites, not to horsemen.
u_royal_horse_archer.s0: In the inscription on his tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam, Darius lists his skills as a warrior. He claims to be a good horseman, and a good bowman both on foot and on horseback, as well as a good spearman. Riding and archery were therefore part of how the King himself wished to be seen.
u_royal_horse_archer.s1: Herodotus says that Persian boys were taught only three things between the ages of five and twenty: to ride, to shoot with the bow, and to tell the truth. The claim is simplified, but it agrees with the royal inscriptions in placing horse and bow at the centre of elite Persian training.
u_royal_horse_archer.s2: Herodotus describes Xerxes leaving Sardis in 480 BCE. A thousand picked Persian horsemen rode ahead of him and another thousand behind his spearmen, and after ten thousand Persian foot came ten thousand Persian cavalry. He says Persian cavalry were armed much like the infantry, some with metal helmets. His figures for the whole army are greatly exaggerated, and he does not say these royal horsemen were archers.
u_royal_horse_archer.s3: Herodotus tells how Mardonius sent his cavalry under Masistius against the Greeks in 479 BCE. Charging in squadrons, they pressed the Megarians hard until Masistius's horse was struck by an arrow and threw him, and Athenian troops killed him. Later, he says, these horsemen, whom he calls mounted archers hard to come to grips with, harassed the Greeks with javelins and arrows and choked the Gargaphia spring.
u_royal_horse_archer.s4: Historians debate how far Persian cavalry were true horse archers. Herodotus calls the horsemen at Plataea mounted archers yet shows them throwing javelins too, and Xenophon, writing later, recommends two javelins for a horseman. Many scholars think Persian riders carried mixed weapons, while steppe peoples such as the Saka specialised in mounted archery. Whether the King kept a distinct guard of horse archers is unknown.
u_royal_horseman.lead: The King's horsemen were picked Persian riders who escorted the King in procession and on campaign. Herodotus places two bodies of a thousand chosen Persian horsemen around Xerxes in 480 BCE. Riding was a mark of rank among the Persians, and in Herodotus's account of Plataea the cavalry was the Persian arm the Greeks found hardest to face.
u_royal_horseman.play: The game shows the King's Horseman as a trained cavalry unit of the King's army. The picked royal horsemen were Persians of standing chosen to ride close to the King, so the game's simple trained unit is a simplification.
u_royal_horseman.s0: Herodotus describes Xerxes leaving Sardis in 480 BCE with a thousand horsemen chosen from all the Persians riding ahead of him. Another thousand chosen horsemen rode behind his chariot and spearmen, and ten thousand more Persian horse followed the ten thousand foot. He says the Persian cavalry were armed like the Persian infantry, though some wore head-pieces of hammered bronze and iron.
u_royal_horseman.s1: In his tomb inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam, Darius claims to be a good horseman, and a good bowman and spearman both on foot and on horseback. The King presented skill in the saddle as a royal virtue. The Persepolis Fortification tablets, from about 509-493 BCE, show the practical side: officials issued grain as fodder for horses kept by the administration.
u_royal_horseman.s2: Herodotus tells how Mardonius sent his cavalry against the Greeks below Cithaeron in 479 BCE, led by Masistius on a Nisaean horse with a golden bridle, wearing a golden scale corslet under a purple tunic. His horse was struck by an arrow and threw him, and the Athenians killed him. Later the horsemen raided Greek supply trains in the Cithaeron passes and fouled the Gargaphia spring, forcing the Greeks to move camp.
u_royal_horseman.s3: Historians debate how the King's cavalry was organised and how large it was. Herodotus's totals for Xerxes' army are generally thought greatly exaggerated, and it is unclear whether his ten thousand Persian horse formed a standing corps. Why cavalry plays no part in his account of Marathon in 490 BCE is also argued. The Suda, a tenth-century Byzantine lexicon, says the horsemen were away, while some modern scholars think they were re-embarking or out of reach.
u_royal_horseman.s4: Xenophon's Education of Cyrus says the Persians had no horsemen of their own until Cyrus persuaded his peers to learn to ride and formed them into a cavalry force. The book is an idealised portrait written about a century and a half after Cyrus. Its tale of one wise king inventing Persian cavalry is better read as a moral lesson than as history.
u_royal_physician.lead: The King kept doctors at his court, and some rode with him to war. Ctesias, a Greek physician of Artaxerxes II, was on the field at Cunaxa in 401 BCE and said he treated the King's own wound. In the game such men march with the King's soldiers on the great fields.
u_royal_physician.play: In the game the King's men bring a physician to every forty of them, up to two hundred, standing back with the bowmen. Each walks to the wounded and tends them. They go home with the King's army and not to your town.
u_royal_physician.s0: When Cyrus the Younger charged his brother at Cunaxa and wounded him through the breastplate, Ctesias says he himself healed the wound. Xenophon, who fought on the other side, cites him for the story.
u_royal_physician.s1: Herodotus describes Egyptian doctors at the Persian court in Darius' day, and the Greek Democedes after them. The sources speak of such men treating the King and his household far more often than his soldiers.
u_royal_physician.s2: How many doctors marched with a Persian army is unknown. One for every forty men is a rule of this game, chosen so the wounded can last longer in its battles, and no ancient author gives a figure.
u_royal_spearman.lead: The King's spearmen were Persian foot soldiers who marched closest to the ruler and stood guard at his palaces. Persian reliefs and glazed bricks show them in rows, holding spears with round counterweights, while Herodotus describes Persian infantry fighting from behind walls of wicker shields. Together these sources give a picture of the core infantry on which Achaemenid kings relied.
u_royal_spearman.play: The game shows the King's Spearman as a trained shield unit with a wicker shield. This merges two things the sources keep apart: the palace guards of the reliefs, often with bows, and Herodotus's shield-wall infantry.
u_royal_spearman.s0: The staircases of the Apadana at Persepolis show long files of guards in Persian and Median dress, holding upright spears with a ball at the butt end. Some carry a bow and quiver as well, and some hold large shields. At Susa, glazed-brick panels from Darius's palace show similar spearmen in richly patterned robes, each with a spear and a bow on his shoulder.
u_royal_spearman.s1: Bearing the King's spear was an honour of high rank. At Naqsh-e Rostam, a label beside a figure on the tomb of Darius names Gobryas, a Patischorian, as the King's spear-bearer. This shows that the spear stood for close service to the ruler, not only for a soldier's weapon.
u_royal_spearman.s2: Herodotus describes the order of Xerxes' army as it left Sardis in 480 BCE. Near the King's chariot marched a thousand spearmen chosen from the best and noblest Persians, their spears ending at the butt in golden apples. Behind them came picked horsemen and then ten thousand foot, whose spears ended in pomegranates instead of butt-spikes, gold for the outer thousand and silver for the rest. He says nothing about how they were trained or paid.
u_royal_spearman.s3: Herodotus says Persian infantry wore soft felt caps, sleeved tunics and scale armour, and carried wicker shields, short spears, large bows and daggers. At Plataea in 479 BCE, he reports, the Persians set their shields together as a barrier and shot from behind it. When the Spartans broke through, the Persians fought bravely but had no heavy armour and lacked skill in close combat.
u_royal_spearman.s4: Historians still argue how these groups related. Some identify the relief guards with the ten thousand Immortals of Herodotus, while others see a separate royal guard or simply an ideal image of the Persian army. The word sparabara, often used today for shield-bearing infantry, is a modern term built on the Old Persian word for shield and is not attested as a unit name in surviving texts.
u_saka_archer.lead: The Saka were Iranian-speaking peoples of the Central Asian steppe and mountains. They were probably first brought under Persian rule by Cyrus, and Darius campaigned against one group of them. Persian inscriptions name them among the King's lands, and Herodotus ranks Saka troops among the best of the royal army at Marathon and Plataea.
u_saka_archer.play: The game fields the Saka Archer behind the spearmen, shooting faster and taking more punishment than a Persian archer at slightly shorter range. No ancient source supports these comparisons, and many Saka fought on horseback.
u_saka_archer.s0: Darius lists the Saka among the lands that obeyed him at the start of his reign. His tomb inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam names separate groups: the hauma-drinking Saka, the pointed-cap Saka and the Saka beyond the sea. The fifth column of the Behistun inscription records a campaign against the pointed-cap Saka, probably about 519 BCE, and the capture of their chief Skunkha, whose figure in a tall cap was added to the relief.
u_saka_archer.s1: Herodotus describes the Saka in Xerxes' army of 480 BCE as wearing tall, stiff pointed caps and trousers. He says they carried their own native bows, daggers and the battle-axe called the sagaris. He adds that the Persians called all Scythians Saka, and that the Saka marched with the Bactrians under Hystaspes, a son of Darius and Atossa.
u_saka_archer.s2: Herodotus says the Persians and Saka held the centre at Marathon in 490 BCE and broke the Athenian line there before the Greek wings closed in. He reports Saka fighting men serving as marines on the King's ships, and says Mardonius chose Saka among the troops he kept in Greece. At Plataea in 479 BCE he judges the Saka the best horsemen on the King's side.
u_saka_archer.s3: Herodotus lists the Saka among Xerxes' infantry, yet later writes of Saka horsemen, and steppe peoples are usually thought of as mounted archers. Historians debate how many Saka fought on foot and whether those in Persian service came from home or from settlements elsewhere in the empire. The homelands of each named Saka group, from the Syr Darya to the Pamirs or beyond, are also argued over.
u_saka_archer.s4: The reliefs of the Apadana at Persepolis show a delegation of pointed-cap Saka bringing gifts to the King. On the royal tombs at Naqsh-e Rostam, figures of the subject peoples hold up the King's throne. On Darius's tomb short labels name each bearer, including the three Saka groups, shown in their distinctive dress.
u_sapper.lead: Sappers were the diggers of ancient siege warfare. They tunnelled beneath walls or prised out their foundations so that the stonework above would collapse. In the period of the game, the clearest evidence for mining comes from Persian armies attacking walled cities in Libya, Cyprus and Ionia, and from the countermines that defenders dug to stop them.
u_sapper.play: In the game, sappers serve the King's enemies, digging under the player's walls and towers, and fall easily to any soldier. History mostly reverses this: the best-attested mining of the period was done by Persian armies, at Barca, Soli and Miletus.
u_sapper.s0: Undermining walls was an old technique in the Near East. Assyrian palace reliefs of the 9th to 7th centuries show soldiers attacking the foot of city walls with picks and levers under the cover of large shields. They also show rams and siege ramps, such as those carved for Sennacherib's siege of Lachish in 701 BCE. Persian armies probably inherited much of this Mesopotamian siege practice.
u_sapper.s1: Herodotus says that a Persian army sent by Aryandes, the satrap of Egypt, besieged Barca in Libya for nine months and dug tunnels towards its walls. A Barcaean bronze-smith found the tunnels by carrying a bronze shield around inside the walls, listening for where it rang over hollow ground. The defenders countermined there and killed the Persian diggers. According to Herodotus, the city finally fell to a trick, not to the mines.
u_sapper.s2: Herodotus reports that during the Ionian Revolt the Persians took Soli on Cyprus in the fifth month of the siege by undermining its wall. In 494 BCE, after the naval victory at Lade, they captured Miletus by mining its walls and using every kind of siege engine. In both cases digging was part of a long and costly siege, not a quick assault.
u_sapper.s3: Excavations at Palaepaphos (Kouklia) on Cyprus uncovered a Persian siege mound built against the city's north-east gate, probably during the revolt of about 498-497 BCE. The defenders dug tunnels beneath the mound and lit fires in them to make it collapse. Arrowheads, spearheads and stone balls were found in the fill. These works are among the clearest physical remains of mining and countermining from this period.
u_sapper.s4: No source of the period says whether Persian armies kept specialist miners or set levies and subject troops to dig under skilled direction. Herodotus describes the mines at Barca, Soli and Miletus but never names or describes the diggers. How far Persian siegecraft rested on dedicated experts rather than on mass labour therefore remains an open question, and modern views differ.
u_scout.lead: A scout was a rider sent ahead of an army or out from a garrison to look and report. Persian boys were trained from childhood to ride and shoot, so a Persian army never lacked men who could cover ground fast. Herodotus' story of the horseman who rode up to the Spartans at Thermopylae shows the work: see, count and come back.
u_scout.play: In the game a scout rides out by himself to the nearest land no one has seen, lifting the fog, and turns back when raiders come near. He fights only if you send him at a foe, and he does not count toward the garrison decree.
u_scout.s0: Herodotus says Persian boys were taught three things from the age of five to twenty: to ride, to shoot the bow and to speak the truth. A people who rode so well had no lack of riders who could be sent far and fast with a message or a report.
u_scout.s1: Before attacking at Thermopylae, Xerxes sent a horseman to see what the Greeks were doing. The rider counted the men he could see outside the wall, watched Spartans exercising and combing their hair, and brought the report back. Xerxes could not understand it, and asked the exiled Spartan king Demaratus what it meant.
u_scout.s2: Herodotus describes the King's mounted messengers, a fresh man and horse posted for each day's stage, so that word passed from rider to rider without stopping. Nothing mortal travelled faster, he says. Scouts and messengers were not the same men, but the relays show how fast a report could reach a commander.
u_scout.s3: No Persian source describes how the army organised its scouting, and the Greek writers mention scouts only in passing. Whether scouts were a standing body, picked riders from the cavalry, or local guides hired for a campaign is not known. The game's trained scout is a simplification.
u_scythian.lead: The Scythians were Iranian-speaking nomads living on the steppe north of the Black Sea, famous as mounted archers. When Darius crossed the Ister into their land in about 513 BCE, they withdrew rather than give battle, wore down his army, and forced him back to his bridge. Their success became a lasting Greek lesson about the limits of royal power.
u_scythian.play: In The Ister, Scythians appear as archers, horse archers, spearmen, a chief and a champion. The game has Persian horsemen run down Scythian riders; Herodotus (4.128) says Scythian horse routed Persian cavalry.
u_scythian.s0: Burial mounds (kurgans) north of the Black Sea and in the Kuban, such as Kelermes and the Melgunov mound of the 7th century, hold the gear of mounted warriors. Finds include composite bows carried in a combined bow and quiver case, three-bladed bronze arrowheads, short swords, battle-axes, spears and scale armour. Horses were often buried with their masters, along with gold work in animal style.
u_scythian.s1: Herodotus says the Scythians had no cities or walls, lived in wagons and fought as mounted archers, so no invader could catch them. He also describes warriors taking enemy heads and scalps as trophies and making drinking cups from skulls. His long Scythian survey mixes travellers' reports with Greek assumptions and should be read with care.
u_scythian.s2: Herodotus says the Scythians, under three kings of whom Idanthyrsus was the chief, refused open battle, retreated ahead of the Persians and filled in wells and springs. Their horsemen kept routing the Persian cavalry, which fled back to the infantry. The braying of the Persians' donkeys and mules unsettled the Scythian horses. Darius at last slipped away by night, leaving his sick men behind, and reached the bridge the Ionians had kept.
u_scythian.s3: Herodotus gives Darius 700,000 men and a march as far as the Oarus river, and both are widely doubted as exaggerated. Ctesias, known through a later summary, gives an even larger army and a short campaign ending in hasty retreat. Historians still argue whether the campaign was a failed conquest or a limited show of force. Darius's own lists of peoples include Saka beyond the sea, which may mean he claimed some result in Europe.
u_scythian.s4: Herodotus tells that the Scythians sent Darius a bird, a mouse, a frog and five arrows. Darius read it as surrender, but Gobryas explained it as a threat: unless the Persians could fly, hide underground or leap into marshes, the arrows would kill them. The story is shaped as a moral tale about royal pride and should not be taken as a record.
u_siege_tower.lead: A siege tower was a wheeled timber frame pushed up to a city wall so that archers could shoot down on the defenders and soldiers could reach the battlements. Assyria used tower-like engines long before the Persians.
