For the Achaemenid wars of 530-479 BCE, however, the sources describe Persian armies taking cities mainly with earth mounds, mines and unnamed engines, and say nothing clear about towers.
u_siege_tower.play: The game fields the tower as an enemy engine with archers and a gangway, which fire or a sally can destroy. No rebel or Greek force of 530-479 BCE is known to have used one, so this unit is a simplification.
u_siege_tower.s0: Assyrian palace reliefs from the 9th century onwards show wheeled engines with a ram in front and archers in a turret above. The reliefs of Sennacherib at Nineveh show the siege of Lachish in 701 BCE. In them such engines are pushed up earth ramps against the walls while the defenders throw torches down on them. These scenes are the best pictures of tower-like engines from the world the Persians inherited.
u_siege_tower.s1: Herodotus says Harpagus took the Ionian cities about 545 BCE by penning the defenders in and heaping mounds against their walls. At Barca in Libya the Persians dug mines. At Miletus in 494 BCE they undermined the walls and brought up engines of every kind. He describes no mobile tower in any of these sieges.
u_siege_tower.s2: At Old Paphos on Cyprus, excavators found the ramp the Persians built against the city wall when they put down the Cypriot revolt, probably about 497 BCE. It was packed with rubble, broken sculpture and hundreds of arrowheads and other missiles. The defenders dug tunnels under the ramp and tried to burn its timbers to bring it down. Herodotus tells of the Persian sieges of the Cypriot cities but does not describe Paphos.
u_siege_tower.s3: It is uncertain whether the Persians kept Assyrian-style tower engines. Herodotus's word for the engines at Miletus is vague, and no Achaemenid image or text shows a mobile tower. Tall wheeled towers are clearly described only later in Greek sources, for the Carthaginians at Selinus in 409 BCE and for Dionysius at Motya in 397. For this reason many historians think towers became common only around 400 BCE.
u_siege_tower.s4: Xenophon wrote more than a century and a half after Cyrus. He has Cyrus build great wheeled towers, drawn by teams of oxen, to carry fighting men into a field battle. The Cyropaedia is a moral romance about the ideal ruler. This scene probably reflects the military thinking of Xenophon's own day rather than any evidence from the 540s BCE.
u_spartan.lead: Spartan soldiers were the hoplites of Sparta, the strongest land power in Greece, whose full citizens, the Spartiates, lived off the labour of helots and trained for war from boyhood. They formed the core of the Greek forces that held the pass at Thermopylae in 480 BCE and broke Mardonius's army at Plataea in 479 BCE. Nearly everything known of them comes from Greek writers, since no Persian document names them.
u_spartan.play: Spartans appear in the Thermopylae and Plataea levels as the Spartan Champion and Spartan Officer. These are game labels: Spartan armies had officers but no rank of champion, and the battle of Plataea itself was fought in 479 BCE.
u_spartan.s0: Herodotus and Xenophon describe the Spartiates as a small body of full citizens whose land was worked by helots, a subject population of Laconia and Messenia. Boys passed through a state upbringing, and men ate together in common messes. Alongside them fought the perioikoi, free men of the surrounding towns, while helots often served as attendants or light troops.
u_spartan.s1: Herodotus says Leonidas brought 300 Spartiates, all chosen from men who had living sons, together with several thousand other Greeks. They held the narrows for two days and drew the Persians on with feigned retreats. When Ephialtes guided Hydarnes over the Anopaea path, Leonidas sent most of the allies away. He died there with the Spartans and the Thespians, while most of the Thebans kept back with him surrendered.
u_spartan.s2: Herodotus says Sparta sent 5,000 Spartiates, each with seven helots, and 5,000 hoplites of the perioikoi. Many historians accept his hoplite figures more readily than his helot total. Under Pausanias the Spartans held the right wing, facing the Persian troops themselves. Herodotus says a Spartan named Arimnestus killed Mardonius, after which the Persian line broke and the survivors fled to their fortified camp.
u_spartan.s3: Collections of sayings made by Plutarch, nearly six centuries later, have Leonidas reply to a demand to give up his arms by telling the Persians to come and take them. Another has a Spartan mother tell her son to come home with his shield or upon it. These are moral tales from a later age, and they are not evidence for what was said in 480 BCE.
u_spartan.s4: Modern historians speak of a Spartan mirage: an image of austere, unbeatable warriors shaped by admirers in Athens and by later writers. Some, such as Stephen Hodkinson, argue that Spartan wealth, family life and training were less exceptional than the sources claim, while others defend a truly distinctive military system. Because the Persian record is silent, the Persian side of these battles survives only through Greek writers, Herodotus above all.
u_spearman.lead: The Persian foot soldier carried a spear, a wicker shield and often a bow, and he formed the core of the armies that won the empire for Cyrus, Cambyses and Darius. Persian art shows him as a guardsman of the King, while Greek writers describe how he fought and how he fared against heavy Greek infantry at Thermopylae and Plataea.
u_spearman.play: The game makes the Persian Spearman a shield unit that holds raiders and horsemen, stops most arrows and is too slow to chase. Historically many Persian foot soldiers also carried bows, so spear and bow often belonged to the same man.
u_spearman.s0: Herodotus, listing Xerxes' army, says the Persians wore soft felt caps, sleeved tunics, scale armour and trousers. They carried wicker shields, short spears, large bows with reed arrows, and daggers hung at the right thigh. Elsewhere he has Aristagoras tell the Spartans that Persians fought with bows and short spears in trousers and turbans, as an argument that they would be easy to beat.
u_spearman.s1: Glazed-brick panels from Darius's palace at Susa show rows of guards holding long spears with a round weight at the butt, with bows and quivers on their shoulders. Spear-bearers also line the stairways of the Persepolis reliefs. In his tomb inscription Darius boasts that the Persian man's spear had reached distant lands, and he counts skill with the spear and the bow among a ruler's virtues.
u_spearman.s2: Herodotus says that at Plataea and again at Mycale the Persians set up their wicker shields as a fence and shot from behind it. Modern historians often call such troops sparabara, shield-bearers, and reconstruct a file with a shield-and-spear man in front and archers behind. How fixed this formation was, and whether the term was used in the period, is still argued, since it rests on Greek descriptions and later analogy.
u_spearman.s3: Herodotus says that at Thermopylae the Persians fought in a narrow pass with spears shorter than those of the Greeks and could not use their numbers. At Plataea, he writes, they were not inferior in courage or strength, but lacked armour and the Greeks' skill, and some seized Greek spears with their bare hands. These judgements come from a Greek writer explaining Greek victories.
u_spearman.s4: Herodotus describes the army as organised in units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand under Persian commanders. Historians accept a decimal structure but debate how many native Persians served as regular soldiers and how many were levied for single campaigns. His figure of 1,700,000 for Xerxes' land army is generally held to be a great exaggeration.
u_subject_levies.lead: The Persian kings fought with soldiers drawn from many subject peoples, each serving in its own dress and with its own weapons under Persian command. Medes, Cissians, Lydians, Ionian Greeks and dozens of others marched beside the Persians, which let the King put large armies into the field and showed the reach of his rule.
u_subject_levies.play: The game splits each people into a levy who holds the line and a bowman who shoots from behind, though Herodotus's Persian-armed infantry carried spear and bow together. Its notes on Median, Cissian and Lydian arms follow his catalogue.
u_subject_levies.s0: On Darius's tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam, figures from the subject lands hold up the royal throne, and the inscription invites the reader to look at them to learn how many lands the King held. At Behistun, Darius says he fought the rebels of 522-521 BCE with the Persian and Median army that stood by him. Murashu texts of the later 400s BCE show Babylonian bow land, whose holders owed a soldier or paid silver instead.
u_subject_levies.s1: Herodotus lists the peoples Xerxes led to Greece in 480 BCE. He says the Medes were armed like the Persians, adding that this dress was Median rather than Persian in origin, and that the Cissians were equipped the same way but wore turbans instead of felt caps. The Lydians, he says, had arms most like the Greeks, and the Ionians served in the fleet in Greek equipment.
u_subject_levies.s2: Herodotus says Xerxes' infantry was counted at Doriscus by packing ten thousand men into an enclosure and filling it again and again. Each people had its own native leaders, but Persian commanders of ten thousand appointed the officers over thousands, hundreds and tens. Earlier, he says, Darius set up pillars at the Bosporus naming the peoples who marched against the Scythians, and left the Ionians to guard his bridge over the Ister.
u_subject_levies.s3: At Thermopylae, Herodotus says, Xerxes first sent in the Medes and Cissians, who suffered heavy losses before the Immortals replaced them. He also describes officers driving men forward with whips, a picture that fits the Greek contrast between free citizens and the King's subjects. At the Ister, he says, the Ionian tyrants broke only the Scythian end of the bridge as a pretence, after Histiaeus argued against destroying it.
u_subject_levies.s4: Herodotus gives Xerxes 1,700,000 foot soldiers, a figure historians reject as greatly exaggerated; modern estimates run from under a hundred thousand to a few hundred thousand. Some scholars think his catalogue draws on a Persian list of subject peoples rather than the army in the field. How willing the levies were is also argued, since Greek writers stressed coercion while royal inscriptions present the peoples as loyal supporters.
u_thracian.lead: The Thracians were the many peoples living between the Aegean, the Black Sea and the Ister, divided into tribes under their own chiefs and kings. Persia drew coastal Thrace into the empire under Darius, and in 480 BCE Thracian contingents marched with Xerxes, lightly armed with javelins, small shields and daggers.
u_thracian.play: At Athos the game fields Thracian archers, riders, peltasts and chiefs; the peltast is an unarmoured javelin-man with a crescent shield. Herodotus mentions no Thracian bows, and by 480 BCE most coastal Thracians were the King's subjects.
u_thracian.s0: Herodotus calls the Thracians the most numerous people on earth after the Indians. He says they would be the strongest of all if they could unite under one ruler or one purpose, but that they never did. He names many tribes, among them the Getae, the Edoni, the Bistones, the Satrae and the Brygi, each with its own customs and leaders.
u_thracian.s1: Herodotus says Darius subdued the Getae on his march to the Ister about 513 BCE, and that his general Megabazus then brought the peoples of the Thracian coast under the King. The Persian hold probably weakened during the Ionian revolt. In 492 BCE Mardonius reasserted it, though the Brygi attacked his camp by night and wounded him; Herodotus says he did not withdraw until he had subdued them.
u_thracian.s2: Darius's inscriptions, including his tomb inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam, list a land called Skudra among the King's peoples, and the Persepolis Fortification tablets record workers labelled Skudrians. Many historians equate Skudra with Thrace or part of it. Others argue the name covered a wider or shifting area in Europe, and that the tablet label need not mean the workers had come from Thrace at all.
u_thracian.s3: Herodotus describes the Thracians in Xerxes' army wearing fox-skin caps, tunics under many-coloured cloaks and fawn-skin boots, and carrying javelins, light shields and small daggers. He mentions no body armour. He adds that these were Thracians who had crossed into Asia, where they were called Bithynians. Greek vase painters often showed Thracians with a crescent shield, the pelte, which gave its name to the light troops later called peltasts.
u_thracian.s4: Herodotus lists the Thracian peoples whose land Xerxes crossed and says they were made to march with his army. The Satrae of the mountains, he says, had never been anyone's subjects and kept an oracle of Dionysus. He adds that in his own day the Thracians still honoured the road Xerxes had taken and would not plough or sow it.
u_trireme.lead: The trireme was a fast oared warship with three banks of rowers and a bronze ram at the bow. By the late sixth century it had become the main warship of the eastern Mediterranean. Phoenician, Egyptian, Cypriot and Cilician squadrons crushed the Ionian rebels at Lade in 494 BCE. With Ionian and Carian ships added, the King's fleet fought the Greeks at Artemisium and Salamis in 480 BCE.
u_trireme.play: The game fields trireme squadrons at Lade, Artemisium, Salamis and Mycale, each with its own pace, marines and skill. At Mycale the real Persian fleet was beached and the fight was on land, so the game departs from history.
u_trireme.s0: Thucydides says the Corinthians were the first Greeks to build triremes, and that the Corinthian Ameinocles built four ships for Samos about three centuries before 404 BCE (Thucydides 1.13). Herodotus says the pharaoh Necho II had triremes built in Egypt about 600 BCE (Herodotus 2.159). Some later writers credited the Phoenicians. Historians still argue whether the type began in Greece or the Levant, and how early large fleets of it existed.
u_trireme.s1: No trireme wreck has been found, so the design is rebuilt from Athenian ship-sheds, a few reliefs and fourth-century naval inventories. Most scholars accept a hull of about 35 metres carrying some 170 oarsmen in three tiers. The Greek navy's reconstruction Olympias, launched in 1987, showed that such a ship could be rowed fast. Details of the oar system are still debated, and Phoenician ships may have been built differently.
u_trireme.s2: Herodotus gives Xerxes 1,207 triremes in 480 BCE. Among them were 300 Phoenician, 200 Egyptian, 150 Cypriot, 100 Cilician, 100 Ionian and 70 Carian ships, all carrying Persian, Median and Saka marines, and he rates the Sidonian ships the best sailers (Herodotus 7.89-96). Aeschylus gives the same total, but many historians think it too high. Herodotus says the navy of Cambyses already depended on the Phoenicians (Herodotus 3.19).
u_trireme.s3: A trireme fought by ramming, or by laying its marines alongside to board. Herodotus names the diekplous at Lade in 494 BCE and Artemisium in 480 BCE (Herodotus 6.12, 8.9). It was probably a breakthrough of the enemy line to ram from the side. He has Themistocles argue that the narrows at Salamis would favour the Greeks' fewer, heavier ships (Herodotus 8.60). At Mycale in 479 BCE the Persians beached their ships and fought on land (Herodotus 9.96-106).
u_trireme.s4: Herodotus was himself from Halicarnassus. He says that at Salamis its queen Artemisia was chased by an Athenian ship and escaped by ramming and sinking a friendly ship from Calynda. Xerxes was watching from the shore, thought she had sunk an enemy, and is said to have remarked that his men had become women and his women men (Herodotus 8.87-88). The story is shaped as a tale of luck and wit and cannot be checked.
w_aurochs.lead: The aurochs (Bos primigenius) was a huge wild ox, the ancestor of domestic cattle, and it lived across Europe, western Asia and North Africa. Herodotus says wild oxen lived in the country Xerxes' army crossed in northern Greece in 480 BCE. The last known aurochs died in Poland in 1627 CE.
w_aurochs.play: The game draws aurochs as wildlife on the Ister and Athos levels, on land the town has not taken. They are scenery only, and no rule reads them.
w_aurochs.s0: Modern zoologists describe the aurochs as a wild ox much larger than most domestic cattle, with long, forward-curving horns. All domestic cattle are thought to descend from it. Julius Caesar, writing in the Gallic War, describes the animal in the forests of Germany, long after the Persian age.
w_aurochs.s1: Herodotus says lions attacked the camels carrying Xerxes' supplies as the army marched through the country of northern Greece in 480 BCE. He adds that lions and wild oxen lived in that land, and that the horns of the oxen were taken to Greece. He is the only source for this march in these terms.
w_aurochs.s2: Assyrian kings boasted of hunting wild bulls, and the bull appears in Achaemenid art, as in the bull-headed column capitals of Persepolis. Whether these images show the aurochs specifically is not settled, and they should not be read as proof of how Persian kings hunted.
w_aurochs.s3: Hunting and the loss of forest and grazing land reduced the aurochs across Europe over many centuries. Historians date the last animal, a cow, to 1627 in the Jaktorów forest in Poland. That date comes from later Polish records and modern study, not from Persian-age evidence.
w_bat.lead: Bats almost certainly lived in all the regions the game covers, roosting in caves, tombs and old buildings. Ancient writers mention them rarely, and the Persian sources give them no clear place. What can be said rests on a Greek natural historian and on later fables.
w_bat.play: Bats are drawn as scenery among the birds overhead on eleven levels, from Pasargadae to Plataea, and no rule reads them. The game shows them as birds in the sky; they are mammals.
w_bat.s0: Aristotle, writing in the fourth century, treated the bat as a winged animal with a membrane rather than feathers. He placed it apart from the true birds. The game's habit of drawing bats among the birds is a visual shortcut and not an ancient classification.
w_bat.s1: Insect-eating bats live today in the Persian highlands, the Nile valley and the Greek coasts, and they roost in caves, cliff crevices, wells and old buildings. The same habits probably held in the period, but no source of the time describes the species, so this is inference from modern natural history. Which species were present is not documented in the sources used here.
w_bat.s2: The royal inscriptions and administrative tablets name many animals, such as horses, sheep and camels, but bats are not known to figure in them. Absence from the surviving texts and images does not show that bats were unnoticed, and a complete survey of the evidence is not attempted here. Bats probably shared the buildings of Pasargadae, Susa and Memphis.
w_bat.s3: Fables collected under the name of Aesop use the bat as a figure of someone who belongs to no side. The collection was put together long after the Persian wars, and the stories are moral tales. They say nothing about events in 490 or 480 BCE.
w_boar.lead: The wild boar lived in many of the landscapes that Persian armies and officials crossed, from river thickets to oak woods and hill country. The surviving writers say little about it as an animal. Herodotus uses it in a tale of fate, and Xenophon places hunting in the parks of the Persian elite.
w_boar.play: The boar is drawn as scenery on the Athos, Bagastana, Ister, Marathon, Plataea, Sardis, Susa and Thermopylae levels. No rule reads it. Its placing in Elam, Media and Thrace is the designers' interpretation of habitat, not a statement of any source.
w_boar.s0: No ancient source lists the boar's range for the years of the game. Wet thickets along lowland rivers, oak woods and hill country suited the animal, so its presence in Elam, Media and Thrace is inferred from habitat. The game's placing of boar there is a reconstruction, not something a source states.
w_boar.s1: Herodotus tells how a huge boar ravaged the fields of Mysia, and how the Mysians asked Croesus for help. Croesus sent his son Atys on the hunt, and the Phrygian exile Adrastus killed him by accident with a spear thrown at the boar. Herodotus presents the tale as fate working through a fatal accident.
w_boar.s2: Xenophon, writing in the fourth century BCE, describes Persian nobles hunting in enclosed parks stocked with game, and the Cyropaedia has Cyrus hunt in such a park as a young man. His picture is later than the game's years and idealised, so it shows how a Greek imagined Persian elite life. Boar is among the game he names in hunting scenes.
w_boar.s3: Hunting was a recognised image of kingship in the Persian world, and scholars discuss how far royal art presented the king as a hunter, mostly of lions. Evidence naming the boar as royal quarry in these years is thin, so the boar's place in that image is uncertain.
w_boar.s4: Herodotus says that when Xerxes marched, lions attacked the supply camels in the country between the Nestos and the Achelous, and wild oxen lived there too. He does not mention boar in that passage. The game's deer and boar of Thrace come from habitat, not from Herodotus.
w_crane.lead: Cranes cross the lands of the Persian empire twice a year, flying between northern breeding grounds and winter quarters in the south. Greek writers noticed them as signs of the seasons and as birds that wintered in Egypt. Direct evidence of how Persians regarded cranes is thin, so most of what is said below comes from Greek sources.
w_crane.play: The game draws cranes as birds overhead on the Athos, Bagastana, Ister, Marathon, Memphis, Parsa, Pasargadae, Plataea, Sardis, Susa and Thermopylae levels. They are scenery only, and no rule reads them.
w_crane.s0: Hesiod, in Works and Days, treats the cry of cranes passing overhead as a signal for ploughing and for the coming of winter rains. He wrote well before the Persian wars, but the poem shows that Greek farmers knew the crane as a calendar bird. Aristotle later described the migration of cranes in his work on animals.
w_crane.s1: Herodotus says that cranes leave the cold lands of Scythia to spend the winter in Egypt and the upper Nile country. This is reported knowledge, not something he set out to test, though the broad pattern of migration to the south is correct.
w_crane.s2: No Achaemenid inscription or tablet known to the compilers of this entry treats the crane as a sacred or royal bird. Persian attitudes to the bird are therefore unknown, and what is said about cranes in this period comes from Greek writers.
w_crane.s3: Homer compares the Trojan army to cranes crying as they flee winter and fly toward the Ocean, bringing death to the Pygmies. The picture belongs to poetry and myth, not to natural history, and it has no bearing on the Persian period.
w_crocodile.lead: The Nile crocodile lived in the Egyptian river and was feared in some places and honoured in others. Herodotus gives the fullest Greek description of it, probably from his own visit to Egypt after the Persian conquest of 525 BCE. It shows how Egyptian life looked to outsiders in the world that Cambyses and Darius ruled.
w_crocodile.play: The game draws a crocodile lying on the river bank in the Memphis level only. It is scenery: no rule reads it.
w_crocodile.s0: Herodotus describes the crocodile in his Egyptian book. He says it spends the day on land and the night in the water, lays its eggs on the bank, and has no tongue. The egg-laying on land is right. The claim that it has no tongue is wrong, since the tongue is fixed to the floor of the mouth and hard to see.
w_crocodile.s1: Herodotus says that some Egyptians held the crocodile sacred and others treated it as an enemy. Around Thebes and Lake Moeris, he says, a tame one was kept and decked with ornaments, and it was embalmed at death. At Elephantine, he says, people ate crocodiles and did not count them as sacred.
w_crocodile.s2: Herodotus says that a small bird enters the crocodile's open mouth and picks leeches from it, and that the crocodile does it no harm. Whether any such partnership occurs is still uncertain, and the story rests on Herodotus's report alone. It is best read as what he was told in Egypt.
w_crocodile.s3: Herodotus tells how Cambyses stabbed the Apis calf and mocked the Egyptians' gods. Historians doubt this portrait of him, and Egyptian sources of the time suggest that Persian rule left animal cults in place. The story concerns the Apis bull, not the crocodile, and it shows how Greeks and Egyptians shaped the memory of the conquest.
w_crocodile.s4: Herodotus describes the hippopotamus in the next chapter. He gives it cloven hooves, a horse's mane and tail, and tusks. The hooves and mane are wrong, though the tusks are real. He treats both animals as marks of Egypt, which shows what Greek visitors found strange there.
w_crow.lead: The hooded crow is a grey-bodied, black-headed crow that lives in open country, farmland and settlements across much of Europe and western Asia. It is likely to have been a familiar bird beside the farms, roads and towns of the Persian empire. No Persian text known to this encyclopedia describes it, and Greek writers mention crows mainly as signs of weather and in tales.
w_crow.play: The game draws the hooded crow as wildlife flying overhead on all eleven levels, from Pasargadae to Plataea. It is scenery only, and no rule reads it.
w_crow.s0: No text from the Persian world describes the hooded crow, so its presence is inferred from the bird's modern range and habits, not from evidence of the time. Modern ornithologists describe it as a bird of open country, farmland and settlements that feeds on grain, carrion and refuse. It is therefore probable, though not documented, that crows of this kind lived near the places the game depicts.
w_crow.s1: Greek authors knew the crow well. Hesiod, writing long before the Persian wars, treats the crane's cry and the crow's cry as signs for the farmer's year. Aristotle, writing in the fourth century, discusses crows among the birds in his natural history. These passages show how Greeks saw the bird and say little about Persian attitudes.
w_crow.s2: Crows appear in the animal tales credited to Aesop, a name attached to fables collected long after the Persian wars. These stories are moral tales about cunning and vanity. They say nothing about how crows behaved in 490 or 480 BCE and should not be read as observation.
w_deer.lead: Deer were part of the woodland game of the lands the Persians ruled, from the Balkan woods to Anatolia. The surviving notices are Greek and mostly describe hunting in general terms. Deer are rarely singled out, so what can be said of them rests largely on habitat and on later Greek pictures of Persian hunting.
w_deer.play: Deer are drawn as scenery on the Athos, Ister, Marathon, Plataea, Sardis and Thermopylae levels, on land the town has not taken. No rule reads them. Their placement is a design choice, not a sourced record.
w_deer.s0: Xenophon, writing in the 4th century, has the young Cyrus hunt deer, gazelles, wild sheep and wild asses. The scene belongs to an idealised account of a prince's education and is not a report of Cyrus's own life. It shows how a Greek writer of a later age pictured Persian hunting and its link to training for war.
w_deer.s1: Xenophon describes a park at Celaenae in which Cyrus the Younger kept and hunted wild animals. The word paradise is of Iranian origin and came into Greek through such descriptions. Xenophon writes about 400 BCE, so this shows later Achaemenid practice, and the contents of parks in 559 to 479 BCE are not recorded.
w_deer.s2: Herodotus says that lions attacked the baggage camels of Xerxes' army in the region between the Nestos and the Achelous, and that wild oxen lived there too. He does not mention deer in this passage. Deer in Thrace are therefore an inference from the woodland setting and not a statement of this source.
w_deer.s3: Herodotus says that wild white horses grazed by the lake at the source of the Hypanis. This is the nearest game notice for the steppe country on the Ister level, and it concerns horses, not deer. No ancient text consulted here records deer on the Ister, at Sardis or at Marathon, so their presence in those places rests on habitat alone.
w_dove.lead: The rock dove (Columba livia) is the wild ancestor of the domestic pigeon and nested on cliffs and buildings across the lands the empire held, from Persis to Egypt and the Aegean. No surviving text of the Achaemenid period describes the bird or Persian dealings with it. What the period's sources say about doves comes from Greek writers, and concerns Greek and Egyptian cult.
w_dove.play: The game draws doves as birds overhead on all eleven levels, from Pasargadae to Plataea. They are scenery only, and no rule reads them.
w_dove.s0: The wild rock dove nests on cliffs and in rock crevices, and it has long lived beside farms and walled towns. It is a natural inhabitant of the regions the empire held. No document of the period describes the wild birds, so their presence rests on the modern natural history of the species, not on any text of the time.
w_dove.s1: Scholars agree that pigeons were kept in western Asia and Egypt in earlier ages, but the date and extent of organised dovecotes in Iran are debated. The surviving documents of the sixth and fifth centuries do not show clearly whether Achaemenid estates ran dovecotes. Claims for them in this period should be treated with caution.
w_dove.s2: The Persepolis Fortification tablets record rations and supplies in Persis under Darius, and they show that the administration tracked livestock and foodstuffs closely. No tablet is cited here for doves, and the tablets cannot be used to claim that doves were a regular ration.
w_dove.s3: Herodotus gives the priestesses of Dodona's story that two black doves flew from Thebes in Egypt, one to Libya and one to Dodona (2.55), beside the Theban priests' story of two priestesses carried off by Phoenicians (2.54). He explains the doves as foreign women whose speech sounded like birds' (2.57).
w_duck.lead: Wild ducks lived on the rivers, lakes and marshes of the lands the Persian kings ruled. Ancient writers of the period say almost nothing about them, and no Achaemenid text is known to record a duck hunt. What can be said rests on the natural setting and on a few indirect clues.
w_duck.play: The game draws wild ducks as scenery on the land the town has not taken, on ten levels from Pasargadae to Plataea, with duck calls heard on the water near them. No rule reads them.
w_duck.s0: No ancient source of the period lists the water birds of any region of the empire. Which species were present, and in what numbers, is therefore inferred from modern ornithology and from the geography of wetlands. Rivers, lake margins and marshes in Egypt, Mesopotamia, Anatolia and Greece all offered habitat, but this is an inference and not a record.
w_duck.s1: Herodotus says the Egyptians ate some birds raw after salting them, naming quails and ducks together with small birds. He wrote some decades after the Persian conquest and reports what he learned in Egypt. His words show that ducks were eaten there in his day. They do not describe Persian practice.
w_duck.s2: Egyptian tomb paintings and reliefs, mostly from centuries before the Persians, show fowling in the marshes with throw-sticks and nets. They show that waterfowl were long a source of food and sport in Egypt, the country Cambyses conquered. They are Egyptian evidence, not Persian.
w_duck.s3: Xenophon describes a walled park with wild animals at Celaenae, kept by Cyrus the Younger, and uses the Greek word paradeisos for it. The animals he mentions are mammals, and no source says that ducks were hunted in such parks. Any picture of royal duck-shooting would be a guess.
w_egret.lead: Egrets are white herons that feed in shallow water, and in Egypt they lived along the Nile, its canals and its flooded fields. No surviving source from the Persian period names the egret, so what can be said rests on Egyptian bird art and on the natural setting of the Nile valley.
w_egret.play: The game draws egrets as birds overhead on the Memphis level only. They are scenery: no rule reads them, and they have no effect on play.
w_egret.s0: Several white heron species, including the little egret and the cattle egret, live in the Nile valley, and the ancient Egyptians probably knew them all. Which species an artist meant in a given picture is often uncertain, because herons and egrets were drawn in similar ways. Modern naturalists and Egyptologists do not always agree on the identifications.
w_egret.s1: Egyptian tomb paintings and reliefs from many centuries show marsh birds in papyrus thickets, hunted or simply observed, and herons are among them. These pictures show that the Nile marshes were rich in wildfowl long before the Persians came. They give a picture of the setting, though none dates the egret to 525 BCE.
w_egret.s2: Herodotus describes the Egyptians as holding certain animals sacred and mentions the ibis among their birds. He does not, as far as can be confirmed, single out the egret. No claim that the Persians took notice of the egret in particular has support in his text.
w_egret.s3: Herodotus says the Nile flooded the land each year and that the Egyptians lived by the river's rise and fall. Marshes and canals of the Delta and the Memphis region would then have drawn waterbirds, which is an inference and not something he reports. No source describes a particular flock of egrets.
w_fox.lead: The red fox lived across much of the lands the Persian armies crossed, from Lydia and Thrace to Greece. It left little trace in Persian royal texts. Greek writers mention it in fable and, most usefully, in the fox-skin caps worn by Thracian soldiers.
w_fox.play: The game draws foxes as scenery on the Athos, Bagastana, Ister, Marathon, Plataea, Sardis and Thermopylae levels. No rule reads them.
w_fox.s0: No source from the period describes the fox's range. The red fox is widespread across Europe and western Asia today and lives in woodland, scrub, farmland and steppe. Modern zoologists assume a similar spread in the 5th century, but this is inference from the living animal, not from an ancient count.
w_fox.s1: Herodotus describes the Thracians of Asia in Xerxes' army as wearing fox-skin caps. Xenophon, writing some decades later, says Thracians wore fox-skin caps that covered the ears against the cold. Both show that fox pelts were an ordinary material for clothing in Thrace.
w_fox.s2: Xenophon's treatise on hunting, written in the 4th century, shows Greek hunting practice a little after the Persian wars, with the hare as its main quarry. It does not show that the Persian court hunted foxes, and the royal hunting parks of the period are usually linked with larger game.
w_fox.s3: The fox became the cunning character of Greek fable. The poet Archilochus, in the 7th century, already used fox and eagle tales. Herodotus names Aesop as a fable writer who had been a slave on Samos. The fables gathered under Aesop's name were written down much later, so they show Greek storytelling and not the animal's real habits.
w_gazelle.lead: Gazelles were ordinary game animals in the lands the Persians ruled: the goitered gazelle on the steppes of the plateau and the dorcas gazelle at the desert edge of Egypt. Persian texts say little about them, and most of what is known comes from Greek writers on Persian hunting and from Egyptian art. They belong to the landscape the King's officials worked in.
w_gazelle.play: Gazelles appear as wildlife on the Pasargadae, Parsa, Bagastana, Susa and Memphis levels. They are scenery only and no rule reads them. The Median and Elamite placements are the designers' interpretation, not documented.
w_gazelle.s0: The goitered gazelle is the usual gazelle of the steppe and semi-desert of Iran, and the game places it in Persis, Media and Elam on that basis. No Achaemenid text known to the author names where particular herds lived. The distribution is therefore inferred from the animal's later range and its habitat, not from ancient reports.
w_gazelle.s1: Xenophon, writing in the 4th century, has the young Cyrus hunt deer, gazelles, wild sheep and wild asses in the Cyropaedia. The work is an idealised, partly philosophical portrait, so it is not a record of what Cyrus actually hunted. It does show that Greeks of Xenophon's time thought of gazelles as ordinary Persian game.
w_gazelle.s2: Xenophon says that Cyrus the Younger, satrap in Anatolia, kept a paradeisos at Celaenae, an enclosed park full of wild animals which he hunted from horseback. He does not name gazelles there, so their presence in Persian parks is a reasonable guess, not a reported fact.
w_gazelle.s3: Gazelles of the desert edge appear in Egyptian art and offering scenes long before the Persians, and the dorcas gazelle is the species usually identified in the Nile valley and nearby desert. Evidence for hunting them in the Persian period is thin. The game's use of the animal at Memphis rests on Egyptian tradition and habitat more than on texts from 525 BCE.
w_goose.lead: The Egyptian goose (Alopochen aegyptiaca) is a long-legged, goose-like bird of the Nile valley and Africa south of the Sahara. Egyptian artists painted and carved marsh birds for thousands of years before the Persian conquest. The bird gives a small touch of Nile scenery to Memphis, though the sources say little about this species.
w_goose.play: The game draws the Egyptian goose as a raft of birds afloat on the Nile at Memphis. It is scenery only and no rule reads it.
w_goose.s0: Waterfowl appear throughout the marsh scenes painted and carved in Egyptian tombs, where the tomb owner is shown hunting birds and fishing among papyrus. These scenes are centuries older than the Persian conquest of 525 BCE. They show that Nile marshes were rich in birds, and the wetlands near Memphis probably were too when Cambyses arrived.
w_goose.s1: The painting of geese from a tomb chapel at Meidum, from the Old Kingdom, is sometimes taken to show Egyptian geese. Modern students of the painting identify its birds as bean, white-fronted and red-breasted geese. The Egyptian goose is a separate bird, more closely related to shelducks than to true geese. Identifications of painted birds rest on modern judgement of the pigment and outline, so individual cases are argued.
w_goose.s2: Egyptian tomb scenes and offering scenes show birds as food, as offerings to the dead and as game taken with nets and throw-sticks. Fowling in the marsh appears as a pursuit of the elite as well as a source of food. The scenes do not by themselves show which species were taken in the Persian period.
w_goose.s3: Herodotus describes Egypt's customs and animals at some length, including sacred animals. He mentions a bird he calls the fox-goose as sacred to the Nile god. The fox-goose is usually identified with the Egyptian goose, but claims about the bird in Persian-period Memphis rest mainly on its natural range.
w_gull.lead: Gulls are drawn along the coasts where the Persian fleet and army fought in Greece. No ancient source ties them to these campaigns, so their place in the game comes from the setting, not from a reported fact. The sea shaped the whole war, and the birds mark that setting.
w_gull.play: The game draws gulls as birds overhead on the Athos, Marathon and Thermopylae levels. They are scenery only, and no rule reads them. Their presence is an atmospheric choice, not drawn from a source.
w_gull.s0: Herodotus describes the landing at Marathon, the digging of the Athos canal and the fighting at Thermopylae at length. In the passages cited here he speaks of ships, winds and beaches, but gulls do not appear in them. Any gull on these shores is therefore supplied by the modern reader, not by the ancient writer.
w_gull.s1: Herodotus says that a storm wrecked much of Mardonius's fleet off Athos in 492 BCE. He later says that Xerxes had a canal cut across the peninsula, and gives pride and a wish to show his power as the reason. The narrative shows how much the war depended on the sea, but it does not mention birds.
w_gull.s2: Aristotle, writing in the fourth century, discusses sea and shore birds in his works on animals. His texts show that Greeks knew such birds well, but they do not place any gull at a particular battle.
w_gull.s3: Gulls live along the Aegean today, and nothing in the sources suggests that the coasts of Attica, Athos or the Malian Gulf lacked seabirds in antiquity. This is an inference from the present, not a documented fact for any single species. The game uses gulls as colour only.
w_hare.lead: The hare was a common animal of open ground from Greece to Egypt. Greek writers treated it as the usual quarry of the hunt, and Herodotus mentions it in two passages, one on its breeding and one on an omen. Evidence for Persian hare hunting is thin, and most of what is known comes from Greek authors.
w_hare.play: The game draws hares as scenery on open ground on eleven levels, from Pasargadae to Plataea, but not in the Mycale epilogue. No rule reads them, and they do not affect play.
w_hare.s0: Xenophon, writing in the early 4th century, gave much of his treatise on hunting to the hare. He describes hounds that follow scent and the use of nets, and he treats the hare as the usual quarry of the Greek hunter. His evidence concerns Greece after the Persian wars, not the Persian court.
w_hare.s1: Xenophon describes Persian hunting in the Cyropaedia, chiefly of larger game, and he knew of enclosed parks, called paradises, kept for the King and his nobles. His picture of Cyrus's court is idealised, and he does not single out hares for the royal hunt.
w_hare.s2: Herodotus says that the hare is hunted by every creature and by man, and that it alone conceives while already pregnant. He offers this as a sign of divine providence in keeping prey animals fertile. Modern biology shows that hares do breed often and can conceive while pregnant, though not in the exact way he describes.
w_hare.s3: Herodotus tells that as Xerxes' army set out, a mare gave birth to a hare. He says Xerxes took no notice of the portent, although it was understood as a sign of the army's later flight. The story is Herodotus's, and no Persian source mentions it.
w_hare.s4: The Cape hare lives in Egypt and in dry country across the region, and the game uses it on the Memphis level. Hares appear in Egyptian art, and a hare sign was used in hieroglyphic writing, notably for the name of the Hare nome that held Hermopolis. These Egyptian sources do not show how far Persian officials there joined in hunting hares.
w_heron.lead: The grey heron is a wading bird of marsh edges and slow rivers, and it was at home in the Nile delta and valley and in the river plains of western Anatolia. Egyptian artists drew herons and other waders for thousands of years. For the Persian period itself the evidence is thin, and the Greek writers say little about the bird.
w_heron.play: The game draws a grey heron as scenery on the marsh edges at Memphis and Sardis. No rule reads it.
w_heron.s0: Egyptian tomb paintings and reliefs, many of them from the Old and New Kingdoms, show herons and other waders among papyrus thickets, in scenes where the tomb owner hunts birds or fishes. These images are far older than the Persian conquest of 525 BCE. They show the bird as part of the marsh in Egyptian eyes, but they do not date its presence at Memphis under Persian rule.
w_heron.s1: Herodotus describes the Nile in flood turning the land into a sea with only the towns standing out like islands. He also says that Egyptians ate some birds and fish raw after salting them. He does not name the heron in these passages, so a heron at Memphis is an inference from the habitat.
w_heron.s2: Herodotus places the Gygaean lake close to Sardis, near the great tomb of Alyattes. Wetland of this kind would suit herons, though no ancient writer names them there. The bird at Sardis rests on the landscape, not on a recorded sighting.
w_heron.s3: The Egyptian bennu bird, linked with the sun and rebirth, is usually drawn as a heron-like bird, and many Egyptologists identify it with a heron, though the identification is an interpretation. No Persian royal inscription or administrative text known to this entry names the heron. Whether Persian courtiers hunted or kept waders in royal parks is not documented.
w_hippo.lead: The hippopotamus lived in the Nile when Cambyses and Darius ruled Egypt, and Herodotus gave it a short description in his Egyptian book. It was a familiar animal in Egyptian art and religion, and a large and dangerous one. In the Memphis level it appears as river scenery.
w_hippo.play: The game draws the hippopotamus in the river at Memphis, as wildlife on land the town has not taken. It is scenery only and no rule reads it. Crocodiles keep to the bank and hippos to the water.
w_hippo.s0: Herodotus describes the hippopotamus in his Egyptian book. He says it was sacred in the district of Papremis but not elsewhere in Egypt. He gives it cloven hooves, a horse's mane and tail, and large tusks, and he calls it the river horse, as its Greek name means. Some of these details are wrong, since its feet are not cloven in the way he says and it has no true mane, so his account is better read as report than as close observation.
w_hippo.s1: Egyptian art showed the hippopotamus for thousands of years, in marsh hunting scenes and in faience figures placed in tombs. It was both feared and revered, and the goddess Taweret, shown with a hippopotamus body, protected women in childbirth. These images come from Egyptian monuments and objects of many periods, not from the Persian period alone, but they show the animal's lasting place in the culture the Persians ruled.
w_hippo.s2: Hippopotamuses lived in the Egyptian Nile in antiquity and later disappeared from Lower Egypt. Historians and zoologists do not agree on when, since hunting, drainage and farming all played a part, and texts and images do not always show living animals. Herodotus's description may mean that the animal was still known in his day, but he does not say how common it was.
w_hippo.s3: Cambyses conquered Egypt in 525 BCE, and Egypt became a Persian satrapy. The statue of Udjahorresnet and the Apis stelae show that Egyptian priests, officials and cults continued under Persian rule. No Persian source discusses the hippopotamus itself.
w_ibis.lead: The sacred ibis was a white wading bird with a black head and neck, common in Egypt and linked to the god Thoth. Egyptians kept and buried it as a sacred animal, and Herodotus recorded that killing one was punished. The Persians ruled Egypt from 525 BCE, in a land where animal cults were old and widespread.
w_ibis.play: The game draws ibises as birds overhead on the Memphis level only. They are scenery: no rule reads them.
w_ibis.s0: Herodotus describes two kinds of ibis in Egypt. One is black all over and fights winged snakes. The other has a white body with black head, neck, wing tips and tail, and bare legs. He ties the snake-fighting bird to a story about winged serpents coming from Arabia.
w_ibis.s1: In Egyptian religion the ibis was a form of Thoth, god of writing and reckoning, who was also shown as a baboon or as a man with an ibis head. Temple and cult evidence shows that ibises were kept as sacred animals and offered to the god.
w_ibis.s2: Excavations at the necropolis of Saqqara, near Memphis, have found vast numbers of mummified ibises buried in galleries. Most of the great deposits belong to the later first millennium, so in their bulk they are later than the Persian period. They show a practice that grew over centuries and was not fixed in 525 BCE.
w_ibis.s3: Herodotus says that in Egypt anyone who killed an ibis or a hawk, even by accident, was put to death. This is the report of a Greek visitor, and it may overstate the law. It does fit the reverence for sacred animals that he records elsewhere.
w_ibis.s4: Herodotus says Cambyses mocked Egyptian customs and stabbed the Apis bull. Egyptian sources from the time, including the Apis stelae and the statue of Udjahorresnet, show Persian rulers supporting some temples and cults. Historians still argue over how far Herodotus's hostile picture of Cambyses can be trusted.
w_jackal.lead: The golden jackal (Canis aureus) lives across the Near East and north-east Africa, and it probably did so in the Achaemenid period. It is a small scavenger and hunter on the edges of settlements and fields. In Egypt, canine gods such as Anubis and Wepwawet gave the animal a religious meaning that Persian officials there found already in place.
w_jackal.play: The game draws the jackal as scenery on the Pasargadae, Memphis, Parsa and Susa levels, on land the town has not taken. No rule reads it, and the Anubis link belongs to Egypt only.
w_jackal.s0: Jackals are adaptable animals that live on plains, scrub and the margins of farmland, and they eat carrion, small prey and fruit. Their presence in Persis, Elam and Egypt in the sixth and fifth centuries is an inference from the modern range, since no source from the period describes it. The game's placement is therefore plausible rather than documented.
w_jackal.s1: Egyptian religion linked jackal and dog forms with the dead and with the roads of the necropolis. Anubis was a god of embalming and the cemetery, and Wepwawet, the opener of the ways, was also shown as a canine. Both appear in Egyptian tomb art and temple reliefs, which were made throughout the pharaonic period.
w_jackal.s2: The statue of Udjahorresnet records an Egyptian official who served Cambyses and Darius. It says he cleansed the temple of Neith at Sais, and that Darius ordered the House of Life there restored. Persian kings therefore worked through existing Egyptian temples and officials.
w_jackal.s3: Herodotus describes Egyptian respect for sacred animals at length and says that killing some of them was punished. His account is a Greek visitor's view and should be read as such. He gives no clear passage on the jackal in Persia.
w_jackal.s4: Herodotus says the magi killed ants, snakes and other creatures with their own hands and thought it a merit. Historians debate how far this reflects Achaemenid religious practice. The sources do not allow a firm statement about how Persians treated jackals.
w_jackdaw.lead: The jackdaw (Corvus monedula) is a small crow with a grey nape that nests in cliffs, ruins and old buildings. It lives across western Asia and Europe, and it probably lived beside the towns, forts and terraces of the Persian empire. No Persian text is known to describe it, so what can be said rests on the bird's habits as observed today and on later Greek natural history.
w_jackdaw.play: The game draws jackdaws as birds overhead on ten levels: Pasargadae, Bagastana, Parsa, Susa, the Ister, Sardis, Marathon, Athos, Thermopylae and Plataea. They are scenery only, and no rule reads them.
w_jackdaw.s0: The jackdaw is about 33 centimetres long, black with a grey nape and pale eyes. It lives in flocks and pairs are thought to hold together over years. It nests in holes in cliffs, rocky gorges, tree hollows and the crevices of buildings. Its range today covers Europe, North Africa and western Asia, including the Iranian plateau. This is modern observation, not evidence from the period.
w_jackdaw.s1: Jackdaws favour tall stone and brick structures with ledges and gaps, so terraces, towers and ruins would probably have suited them. No excavation report for the sites in this game is known to the author to record jackdaw remains from the period. Their presence at these places is therefore an inference from habits, not a finding.
w_jackdaw.s2: The Persepolis Fortification tablets record poultry and other supplies issued on the royal estates in Persis. Nothing in them is known to the author to name the jackdaw, so Persian documents give no direct evidence about it.
w_jackdaw.s3: Greek natural history treated the jackdaw as a bird of the crow kind. Aristotle, writing in the fourth century, described birds of this sort in his natural history. Such works show how the bird was seen in the Greek world, not in Persia, and they were written after the events of this game.
w_jackdaw.s4: Crows and their relatives appear in later Greek fable and omen lore as talkative birds and as signs of weather or fortune. These stories were written down well after 479 BCE and say nothing certain about how Persians or Greeks of the war years regarded jackdaws.
w_kite.lead: The kite is a medium-sized raptor that lives largely by scavenging, and in the Near East and the Mediterranean it was a common sight over towns, camps and markets. The sources of the Achaemenid age say little about it directly. Most of what is known about the bird comes from Greek and Egyptian material and from the habits of the species today.
w_kite.play: The game draws kites as birds overhead on the Pasargadae, Memphis, Bagastana, Parsa, Susa, Ister, Sardis, Marathon, Athos, Thermopylae and Plataea levels. They are scenery only, and no rule reads them.
w_kite.s0: Greek writers knew the kite as a bird of prey that lived near people. Aristotle, in his works on animals, discusses kites among the birds of prey. The black kite still gathers around towns, markets and refuse across the Near East, Egypt and Greece, which suggests that the ancient bird behaved in the same way.
w_kite.s1: Egyptian art and funerary texts show Isis and Nephthys in the form of kites mourning Osiris. Memphis, where the game also draws the bird, was a place where such imagery was old and familiar. The link comes from Egyptian religious material of many periods, not from anything specific to the Persian period.
w_kite.s2: Greek writers treated the flight of birds as a sign from the gods, and birds of prey were among those watched. Herodotus reports omens in several places in his narrative. No passage is confidently tied to the kite in the Persian wars, so none is claimed here.
w_kite.s3: The royal inscriptions and the administrative tablets from Persepolis, as far as is known, give the kite no notice. Birds appear in Persian art and in the royal hunt and table, but the evidence does not allow the kite to be told apart from other raptors. Whether the Persians gave the bird any special meaning is unknown.
w_kite.s4: The black kite is a widespread species whose range covers the Near East, Egypt and the Aegean today. Its habit of living near people makes it a plausible bird over a city, camp or building site. No ancient source says that kites flew over any named battle or building.
w_leopard.lead: The leopard was a native hunter of the mountains of western Asia, including the Zagros, where the game places Media. Ancient texts of the Persian period say little about the animal itself, so the picture rests mostly on the natural range of the species and on what Greek writers record about wild beasts and royal parks.
w_leopard.play: The game draws one leopard on the hills of Media in the Bagastana level. It is scenery only and no rule reads it. Nothing in the sources ties a leopard to the events at Behistun.
w_leopard.s0: Greek writers knew the leopard as the pardalis. Herodotus names it in passing among wild animals, but he gives no description of a Persian leopard. Xenophon records that Persian parks held wild animals for the hunt, though the passage does not single out leopards.
w_leopard.s1: The leopard of Iran, the subspecies Panthera pardus tulliana, survives in small numbers in the Zagros, the Alborz and the Caucasus. It lives in rocky uplands and takes wild goat, urial and deer. That the same hills held leopards in the Achaemenid period is a reasonable inference from the present range, not a documented fact; no study is cited here for the ancient bones.
w_leopard.s2: Persian kings kept enclosed parks called paradeisoi, and Greek writers describe them as stocked with game. Whether leopards were hunted or held in such parks is not firmly attested for this period. Claims about pelts or live animals as tribute rest on later or indirect evidence.
w_leopard.s3: The game gives the animal a pale coat with small dark discs, in a low-poly faceted style. This matches the living animal. It is the game's own stylisation and does not copy any ancient image.
w_lion.lead: Lions lived in the Near East in the Achaemenid age, and Herodotus places some in northern Greece. Seals and palace art show the king hunting or overcoming lions, an image of royal power. Herodotus says lions attacked Xerxes' baggage camels on the march between the Nestos and the Achelous.
w_lion.play: The game draws lions as scenery on the Athos, Parsa, Pasargadae and Susa levels: on hills in Persis and Thrace, and at the marsh edge in Elam. No rule reads them. Those placings are the designers' choice, not a documented range.
w_lion.s0: Herodotus says that on the march between the Nestos and the Achelous lions came down at night and killed the camels that carried the army's food. He adds that they touched no men and no other baggage animals, and that he found this strange. He says lions were found only in that stretch of Europe, together with wild oxen.
w_lion.s1: Seals and sealings from Persepolis, including impressions on the Fortification tablets, show a royal figure hunting or fighting lions. Modern scholars read the scene as the king acting as protector against wild beasts. The images come from the time itself, but they show an ideal and not a record of any one hunt.
w_lion.s2: Lions appear in the glazed-brick decoration of the palace at Susa, and at Persepolis a lion is shown attacking a bull on the Apadana. Such images use the animal as a symbol of power, not as a sign of real lions near the building.
w_lion.s3: Lions survived in south-western Iran into recent times, so they probably lived in Persis and Elam in the sixth century. The sources give few direct reports, and the numbers and range cannot be fixed. Historians also debate how far royal lion hunting was real sport and how far it was staged.
w_lion.s4: Xenophon describes a paradise, a park full of game, kept by Cyrus the Younger, and later Greek writers describe royal hunting parks. Whether lions were kept in such parks under Darius and Xerxes is not clear from the evidence. Many modern scholars see the royal lion hunt image as owing something to Assyrian kings, who also had lion hunts recorded.
w_mist.lead: Morning mist is common on river plains and coasts in the cooler months, and it suits the places where the game's campaigns are set. The ancient writers who describe those campaigns say little or nothing about it. The mist in the game is atmosphere, not a documented event.
w_mist.play: The game lays morning mist over the river plains and coasts of its levels, from before dawn until it burns off, likeliest in autumn and spring and in winter at Memphis. It is scenery only and has no effect on play.
w_mist.s0: Herodotus pays attention to weather when it changes events. He describes the north wind that wrecked Mardonius's fleet off Athos and the storm that struck the Persian ships off Magnesia. In his accounts of Marathon, Thermopylae and Plataea he does not mention mist, and I know of no other ancient narrative that does.
w_mist.s1: Herodotus says Hydarnes' troops climbed the Anopaea path by night and reached the summit at dawn. He mentions the rustling of oak leaves that alerted the Phocian guards, and he says nothing of poor visibility. This suggests that he noted conditions underfoot and in the trees when they mattered to his story, though silence is not proof.
w_mist.s2: Mist and fog form on river valleys and coasts in the cooler months today, including in the Nile valley in winter. Ancient climate can only be reconstructed cautiously, and no text gives the weather on a particular morning of these campaigns. The game's pattern of autumn and spring mist, and winter mist at Memphis, is therefore a plausible setting rather than a reported fact.
w_onager.lead: The onager is a wild ass, slimmer and faster than a donkey, that lived on the steppes of Persis, Elam and lands to the west. Ancient writers prized it as fast and hard to catch. The Assyrians hunted it as royal quarry, and Xenophon shows Cyrus hunting it.
w_onager.play: The game draws onagers as wildlife scenery on the Pasargadae, Parsa and Susa levels, and no rule reads them. The model is a donkey graded toward an onager. The Susa placement is the designers' interpretation, not a documented fact.
w_onager.s0: The onager is a wild ass of the species Equus hemionus. It is lighter in build than a domestic donkey, with a sandy coat and a pale belly. It was a familiar part of the steppe fauna of western Asia, and several races of it are known.
w_onager.s1: Reliefs from the palace of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, made in the 7th century, show wild asses chased and caught during royal hunts. They are the best contemporary picture of how rulers of the region treated the animal before the Persians. The Persian kings probably inherited a court tradition in which hunting wild game showed royal skill.
w_onager.s2: Xenophon, who marched with Cyrus the Younger in 401 BCE, describes wild asses on the plain by the Euphrates in Arabia. He says that horsemen could not easily run them down, because they ran far ahead and then waited. His account shows how the animal was seen, not where it lived on the plateau of Persis.
w_onager.s3: In the Cyropaedia Xenophon has the young Cyrus hunt deer, gazelles, wild sheep and wild asses. The work is an idealised portrait written in the 4th century, and the hunts are part of its picture of a perfect prince. It shows what a Greek reader expected of Persian royal sport, not what Cyrus actually did.
w_onager.s4: Herodotus lists the Indian contingent in Xerxes' army and says that some of its chariots were drawn by horses and others by wild asses. His report suggests that the animal could be broken to harness in some regions. It does not show that Persians did the same.
w_onager.s5: Several races of wild ass lived in western Asia, and modern zoologists treat the Syrian type as extinct. Whether the animals described by Greek writers were the same race as those on the plateau around Pasargadae and Parsa cannot be settled from the texts.
w_onager.s6: In Persian tradition, written down centuries after the Achaemenids, the Sasanian king Bahram V is named Gur, a word for the wild ass, and is a famed hunter of the animal. This is a later story and has no bearing on the Achaemenid period. It shows how long the wild ass stayed linked with kingship in Iranian memory.
w_ostrich.lead: The Arabian ostrich lived on dry open ground in south-west Asia and survived into the twentieth century. For the Persian period it is known mainly from Xenophon's report of it on the Euphrates plain. Whether it lived near Susa is not documented.
w_ostrich.play: The game draws ostriches as scenery on the Susa level only; no rule reads them. Susa is the designers' inference, since Xenophon places them on the Euphrates plain, not in Elam.
w_ostrich.s0: Xenophon, who marched with Cyrus the Younger in 401 BCE, describes a treeless plain by the Euphrates where wild asses, ostriches, bustards and gazelles lived. He says the horsemen chased the ostriches and none was caught, because the birds outran the horses.
w_ostrich.s1: Xenophon's plain lay far to the north-west of Susa. His passage therefore does not place ostriches in Elam. It shows only that the bird lived on the Near Eastern steppe under Achaemenid rule, and the extent of its range further east is a matter of inference.
w_ostrich.s2: No source used here puts ostriches on the Susiana plain. The lowlands of south-west Iran may lie at or beyond the edge of the bird's range. Showing them at Susa is a reasonable guess, not an attested fact.
w_ostrich.s3: Pliny, writing in the first century CE, treated the ostrich as a creature of Africa and Ethiopia. This is long after the Persian empire and says little about Elam in the sixth and fifth centuries.
w_owl.lead: The little owl is a small, round-headed bird that hunts at dusk over fields, rocky ground and ruins around the Mediterranean and across the Near East. Its best-documented ancient role is Greek: it was the emblem on Athenian silver coins and was linked with Athena. No Persian source known to this entry gives it a meaning, so any Persian view of the bird is unknown.
w_owl.play: The game shows the owl as scenery among birds overhead on eleven levels, from Pasargadae to Plataea, and in the battle sounds. No rule reads it. Its placing in the Susa lowlands is a design choice, not a documented habit.
w_owl.s0: Athenian silver tetradrachms carried the head of Athena on one side and an owl on the other, with the first letters of the city's name. Scholars date the start of the owl coinage to the late sixth century, but argue over the exact decade. The type was in wide use by the time of Marathon. The coins survive in large numbers, including in hoards found far from Greece.
w_owl.s1: Aristophanes, writing in the late fifth century, joked about owls being carried to Athens, meaning the coins, and treated the bird as Athena's companion. His remarks describe Athenian habit after the war, not Persian belief. No passage in Herodotus on the Persian wars is known to the checker that makes the owl an omen for either side.
w_owl.s2: No royal inscription, relief or Persepolis tablet known to this entry gives the little owl a religious or political meaning for the Achaemenids. Historians therefore cannot say how Persians in the field regarded the bird, and any claim about it is inference from Greek material.
w_owl.s3: Plutarch, writing centuries after the war, says an owl was seen flying along the Greek fleet before Salamis and was taken as a sign of victory. The story fits the Athenian emblem and has the shape of a patriotic tale. Herodotus's account of the battle is the earlier source, and the owl is not part of it as far as is known.
w_partridge.lead: Partridges lived on the dry, rocky slopes of the Iranian plateau and of Attica, and people there probably hunted and ate them. Written evidence for them in the Achaemenid world is thin, so the entry rests mostly on the natural history of the birds and on a few Greek remarks.
w_partridge.play: The game draws partridges as scenery on the Pasargadae, Bagastana, Parsa and Marathon levels. No rule reads them. One model stands in for the chukar, the see-see partridge and the Attic rock partridge.
w_partridge.s0: Modern zoology places the chukar and the see-see partridge on the rocky hills of the Iranian plateau, and the rock partridge on the hills of Greece, including Attica. The chukar and rock partridge are close relatives. Ancient writers do not name species in this way, so matching their birds to modern ones is an inference. Aristotle describes the partridge as a bird of stony ground.
w_partridge.s1: Greek natural historians such as Aristotle describe the partridge as a ground-nesting bird that is easy to hunt, and note the fighting spirit of the male. Herodotus gives no useful detail on partridges in Persian lands. These remarks are Greek, written about Greek birds, and do not show how Persians treated the bird.
w_partridge.s2: Persian kings and nobles kept enclosed parks, and the Greek word paradeisos comes from an Iranian word. Xenophon describes such a park at Celaenae stocked with game. Whether partridges were taken in such hunts or eaten at court is not shown by the sources used here, so any such picture is a guess from the habits of the bird.
w_partridge.s3: Later writers told moral tales in which the partridge stands for lust or cunning, and some said it stole the eggs of other birds. These stories belong to natural-history lore, written centuries after the Persian wars, and say nothing of Persian life. They are kept apart here for that reason.
w_sandstorm.lead: Fronts of wind-borne sand and dust are a regular hazard of Egypt's spring and of the dry plains of Khuzestan. The best-known ancient tale of one is Herodotus's report that a Persian army sent by Cambyses against the oracle of Ammon was buried in the desert. Historians doubt the story as told, but it shaped how Greek readers pictured Persian power meeting the desert.
w_sandstorm.play: The game shows a sandstorm front crossing the map at Memphis in the khamsin months and at Susa in its summer dust, dimming the day. It is scenery only and changes no rule.
w_sandstorm.s0: Herodotus says Cambyses sent a force from Thebes in Egypt against the oracle of Ammon. He reports what the Ammonians told him: the army had gone about halfway across the desert when, as the men took their midday meal, a violent south wind buried them in sand. Herodotus says the army never reached the oasis and never came back.
w_sandstorm.s1: Modern historians doubt the tale as told. The distances involved, the lack of any contemporary record of such a force, and the Greek habit of shaping disasters into moral stories all weigh against it. Some historians suggest the force was probably lost to thirst, ambush or local resistance, with the sand offered afterwards as the explanation. Claims of discovering the remains in the western desert have not won general acceptance.
w_sandstorm.s2: Herodotus also tells of the Psylli, a people of Libya. He says their water cisterns were dried up by the south wind, so they marched out to fight it, and the wind buried them in sand. He gives this as what the Libyans say, and it reads as a tale of human pride against the desert.
w_sandstorm.s3: Spring winds off the desert in Egypt and summer dust in Khuzestan are well known from modern climate records. For the Persian period the surviving sources say almost nothing about dust storms at either city. Placing storms there in the game therefore rests on modern climate, not on anything a Persian official or a Greek writer recorded.
w_stork.lead: The white stork breeds across Europe and western Asia and winters in Africa, so its passage through the Levant and the Nile valley was probably a regular sight in the Persian empire. Surviving Persian documents say almost nothing about it. Most of what can be said about storks in this period rests on the bird's known habits, not on texts of the time.
w_stork.play: The game draws storks as scenery on the wild land of eleven levels, wading in shallows and wet fields; no rule reads them. Their placement at Memphis reflects the winter habitat of European storks.
w_stork.s0: The white stork feeds on frogs, fish, insects and small animals in shallow water and damp meadows. European populations migrate to Africa for the winter, mostly by the eastern route through the Levant and down the Nile. No source of the period describes this, so the picture comes from the bird's modern behaviour, which is assumed, not proved, to have been much the same then.
w_stork.s1: The Nile floodplain gave wading birds wet fields and marsh. Egyptian marsh scenes show many birds, but the identification of particular species in painted and carved scenes is often uncertain, so they cannot be taken as firm evidence for storks. Egypt came under Persian rule after Cambyses' conquest in 525 BCE.
w_stork.s2: Herodotus describes Egyptian animals, including the ibis and the hippopotamus, but gives no clear passage on the stork. Aristotle later discussed the stork and its migration, but he wrote after the Persian period. A claim that Persians or Greeks of 500 BCE held particular beliefs about storks cannot be supported from the sources used here.
w_stork.s3: A tradition that storks care for their aged parents appears in later Greek and Roman writing, and it belongs to moral fable. It says nothing about Persian attitudes and should not be read back into the sixth or fifth century.
w_swallow.lead: The swallow was a familiar summer bird in the lands the Persians ruled, from Greece and Anatolia to Egypt and Mesopotamia. No Persian source about it is known to the encyclopedia. What can be said of it rests on Greek writers, who treated its return as a sign of spring, and on the bird's known habits.
w_swallow.play: The game draws swallows as birds overhead on the Pasargadae, Memphis, Bagastana, Parsa, Susa, Ister, Sardis, Marathon, Athos, Thermopylae and Plataea levels. They are scenery only and no rule reads them.
w_swallow.s0: Swallows breed across Europe, western Asia and North Africa and winter further south, so they passed through every region in the game. This is inferred from the bird's modern range and habits. No inscription or excavated find from the period is known to name the bird.
w_swallow.s1: Greek writers treated the swallow's arrival as a marker of the season. Hesiod, in Works and Days, uses its return as a sign in the farming year, and Aristophanes uses the same idea in Birds. This is a Greek habit and tells nothing of Persian practice.
w_swallow.s2: Aristotle describes the swallow building its nest of mud and straw. Such nests suit the eaves and beams of mud-brick and timber buildings, which stood in Persian and Greek towns alike. No source from the period describes swallows nesting in Persian halls or houses.
w_swallow.s3: Later Greek tradition told of Procne and her sister Philomela, who were turned into a swallow and a nightingale after a crime within a family, and the tale was set in Thrace. The versions differ on which sister became which bird. It belongs to Greek storytelling and has no bearing on the Persian empire or the events of 559-479 BCE.
w_urial.lead: The urial is a wild sheep of the dry hills of Iran and Central Asia. The rams are red-brown with pale legs and large, curved horns. Sources of the period say little about it directly, so what can be said rests on records of managed flocks, Greek accounts of Persian hunting and the Persian habit of keeping hunting parks.
w_urial.play: The game draws the urial as scenery on the Pasargadae, Bagastana and Parsa levels, among the animals on land the town has not taken. No rule reads it.
w_urial.s0: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, which date from about 509 to 493 BCE, record rations and livestock, including sheep and goats, issued in Persis. The tablets deal with managed flocks and do not describe wild animals. They show how much the economy of Persis depended on sheep, but they give no information about the urial.
w_urial.s1: Xenophon, writing in the fourth century, describes the young Cyrus hunting in Media with his relatives. The work is partly an ideal of kingship, so these scenes are not a record of what Cyrus did. They do show that Greeks saw hunting as part of a Persian gentleman's upbringing.
w_urial.s2: Xenophon has the young Cyrus hunt wild sheep among deer, gazelles and wild asses (Cyropaedia 1.4.7). He does not say which wild sheep; the urial is one candidate in Persis and Media, the mouflon of the Zagros another, so the identification is a modern guess.
w_urial.s3: Xenophon says that Cyrus the Younger kept a park at Celaenae full of wild animals, which he hunted on horseback for exercise. This was in 401 BCE, after the period of the game, but it shows a practice that Greek writers linked to Persian nobles and satraps, whose enclosed parks they called paradeisoi. Wild sheep may have been taken in the open hills around such places, but the sources do not say so.
w_vulture.lead: The griffon vulture (Gyps fulvus) is a large soaring scavenger that nests on cliffs and feeds on carcasses. It lives today in mountain country from Greece and Turkey to Iran, and it probably did so in the Achaemenid period. Ancient writers do not name it in connection with Persian burial, so the link to the dead rests on Herodotus's mention of birds.
w_vulture.play: The game draws griffon vultures as birds overhead on the Athos, Bagastana, Ister, Parsa, Pasargadae, Plataea and Thermopylae levels. They are scenery only and no rule reads them.
w_vulture.s0: Herodotus says the Persians kept their burial customs quiet, but that he knew for certain that the magi exposed bodies to be torn by dogs or birds. He adds that the Persians generally coated a body in wax before burying it. He does not name the birds as vultures.
w_vulture.s1: Historians disagree about how widely exposure was practised in the Achaemenid period and by whom. The rock-cut and built royal tombs at Naqsh-e Rostam and Pasargadae show that kings were entombed, not exposed. The later Zoroastrian tower of silence is not attested for this period and should not be read back into the empire of Cyrus or Darius.
w_vulture.s2: No surviving source from the time describes vultures over Behistun, Pasargadae or the Greek battlefields. Their place in the game is an atmospheric choice, reasonable for mountain and open country where carrion lay, but it is not drawn from an ancient report.
w_wild_goat.lead: The wild goat of the Iranian highlands, the bezoar goat (Capra aegagrus), lived on the cliffs and screes of Persis and Media. It is the wild ancestor of the domestic goat. The surviving sources say little about it directly, and it matters here mainly as part of the highland landscape the Persians knew.
w_wild_goat.play: Wild goats appear as scenery on the Pasargadae, Parsa and Bagastana levels, keeping to rock, steep ground and screes. No rule reads them. Their place in the game's hunting scenery is an inference from the landscape, not from a Persian text.
w_wild_goat.s0: The bezoar goat is native to the mountains of western and southern Iran, the Zagros and its neighbours, and to parts of Anatolia and the Caucasus. It lives on rocky slopes and cliffs and is a sure-footed climber. Excavated animal bones show that goats were first domesticated in the Zagros region thousands of years before the Achaemenids, so the wild form was ancient local stock.
w_wild_goat.s1: Xenophon, writing in the fourth century BCE, describes the young Cyrus hunting in a Median game park and lists the quarry as deer, gazelles, wild sheep and wild asses. Wild goats are not named in that list. Xenophon wrote an idealised life of Cyrus, so the scene shows what a Greek reader thought a Persian prince did, not a record of Cyrus himself.
w_wild_goat.s2: Xenophon describes a paradeisos of Cyrus the Younger at Celaenae, an enclosed park full of wild animals where he hunted. The word is of Iranian origin. Which species lived in any given park is mostly unrecorded, so the wild goat can be placed there only as a likely hill animal, not by a named text.
w_wild_goat.s3: The Persepolis Fortification tablets record rations and livestock, and goats and sheep appear among the animals issued or tallied. These texts concern domestic flocks, so they do not show wild goats being hunted. They give no evidence for the wild species either way.
w_wild_goat.s4: No Persian inscription is known to this entry that names the wild goat as a hunted animal or gives it a ritual role. Horned animals in Achaemenid art are sometimes read as wild goats or ibex and linked to royal hunting or fertility, but this is interpretation, and the sources do not settle it. The wild goat is best treated as part of the highland landscape.
w_wild_horse.lead: Herodotus says that wild white horses grazed beside the lake from which the river Hypanis rises, in the land of the Scythians. The Scythians were a mounted people, and Darius's march against them about 513 BCE took a Persian army into this grassland, where it found no battle to win.
w_wild_horse.play: Wild horses appear as scenery on the Ister level, on the Scythian side of the river. No rule reads them. Herodotus calls them white, but the game tints a chestnut coat lighter, which is a simplification.
w_wild_horse.s0: Herodotus, describing the river Hypanis in Scythia, says that wild white horses grazed beside the lake from which it rises. The Hypanis lay well to the north-east of the Ister, and his report probably came from Greek informants of the Black Sea coast, though he does not name them here. He did not claim to have seen the horses himself.
w_wild_horse.s1: Herodotus does not say whether the horses were truly wild or simply unowned stock. Modern research has shown that even the Przewalski's horse, once called the last wild horse, descends from feral animals of early domesticated stock. The colour he gives cannot be checked against surviving remains.
w_wild_horse.s2: Herodotus portrays the Scythians as nomads who lived with their herds and wagons and had no fixed towns to defend. He also describes horses sacrificed and buried around the dead king. Excavated steppe burial mounds (kurgans) do contain horse burials, though they do not confirm each detail he gives.
w_wild_horse.s3: Herodotus says the Scythians withdrew before the Persians and drove off their herds, so that the army had little to attack or feed on. How far Darius went into the steppe is argued, and Herodotus gives the only detailed account.
w_wild_horse.s4: The Persepolis Fortification tablets record rations and fodder issued to horses and other animals travelling on royal business in Persis. They show how closely the Persian state counted its horses.
w_wild_horse.s5: Herodotus mentions Nisaean horses in Xerxes' army and places the Nisaean plain in Media. The steppe herds were a different stock, kept by peoples outside Persian rule.
w_wolf.lead: The wolf lived in many of the lands of the Persian wars, from Media to Thrace and Boeotia. Surviving sources of the period say little about it, and what the Greek writers tell is mostly hearsay, hunting practice or tales. Little is known from the time about how people dealt with it.
w_wolf.play: Wolves are drawn as scenery on the Bagastana, Ister, Athos, Thermopylae and Plataea levels, on land the town has not taken. No rule reads them.
w_wolf.s0: No source of the time counts wolves or maps their range. Their presence in Media, Thrace, Malis and Boeotia is an inference from the animal's wide habitat, not a documented fact for 480 BCE. The game's choice of levels is a reasonable guess rather than a record.
w_wolf.s1: Xenophon, writing in the fourth century, wrote a treatise on hunting with hounds. It deals mainly with hare, deer and boar, and the wolf is not its main quarry. It is a later Greek work, not evidence from the Persian wars.
w_wolf.s2: Herodotus reports that the Neuri, a people north of the Scythians, were said to turn into wolves for a few days each year and then return to human form. He says the Scythians and the Greeks settled in Scythia told him this, and that he did not believe it, though they swore to it. It is a travellers' tale about a distant people, not evidence about wolves.
w_wolf.s3: The Persian royal reliefs and inscriptions that survive are dominated by lions, bulls and composite beasts, and no wolf plays a notable part in them. Whether Persians hunted wolves in the royal parks, or gave them any religious meaning, is not shown by sources of this period. Claims tying the wolf to Persian belief usually rest on much later texts and should be treated with caution.
